body:
Sunlight falls through a long sequence of rock arches towards a distant gold disc.
Engineering without filters.
Software, research and consulting for businesses finding their next way of working. Radio became Spotify. The need stayed; the possibilities changed.
Enter the work
The rock corridor opens towards a gold disc cut with a crescent.
Follow the question. Into the system.
A useful system brings the model, the people and the work around it into the same picture.
The work continues
A gold disc with a crescent cutout hangs in a shaft of light at the end of the passage.
Work continues. Questions follow.
An experiment exposes an assumption. A working system raises a new question.
Explore the practice
Products
Together the products form one system a person runs, with people deciding: the records hold the world, something is observed, a person decides what to do about it, a direction can be tried before anyone commits to it, the act goes out, and its outcome returns as a record that shapes what is learned next.
Thoughts
Follow the mechanisms behind useful intelligence, from an application to the infrastructure and economy around it, in collections and in single arguments on the Blog.

body:
An idea becomes clearer when someone has to use it.
RawThoughts brings together software, consulting and writing around a practical question: what would make this idea useful in the world? That can mean composing intelligence around a person’s work, making a business process reliable or finding a better way to describe the problem itself. We use the work to test what a team needs to remember when a decision or responsibility passes to someone else.
The name began with Harsh Joshi’s blogging and exploration and became his working identity in March 2020. Since 2023, it has also been the consulting and enterprise face of RawThoughts Enterprises Private Limited (RTEPL). “Without filters” means a question can be examined before it fits a product category or a polished thesis; it still needs judgement.
Radio became Spotify is the lens: a human need persists while the way of meeting it changes the business, its measures and our habits. We work with business owners making their own transition, following what AI can change from the customer’s request through the organisation’s response.
An argument
Follow a difficult question through the mechanism, the example and the consequence. The writing connects AI applications to useful compute, organisational decisions and the economy around them, and single arguments stand on their own in the Blog.
Follow the inquiries
A build
Build intelligence around a person’s world, connect commercial relationships with delivery, publish connected knowledge or rehearse the effects of a decision. The products give these ambitions concrete forms.
Explore the products
A collaboration
Bring one valuable workflow into focus, find what prevents the result and make the agreed change. Consulting connects product judgment and hands-on engineering to an outcome the team can recognise.
Consider an engagement
The work changes the question. The question changes what gets built.
A model’s answer becomes useful through the decisions and actions it makes possible. Understanding the customer’s day, the team’s responsibilities and the systems already in use can change the right intervention. Sometimes that calls for new software; sometimes it reveals a simpler change to what is already there.
Building and inquiry keep informing one another. An operational difficulty can expose a research question; a better explanation can make a smaller, more useful product possible.
More capable systems change the work and the questions worth asking.
RawThoughts itself is the applied work: the systems we build and the consulting we do. It carries beliefs about what AI changes in how organisations work and in the economy around them, and tests them against real problems. Two inquiries grow from those beliefs, each with its own publication, methods and questions. Post-AGI Economics follows cheaper machine agency into the economy: what becomes scarce, who owns it and how the gains reach households. Causality asks what intelligence needs to represent and how its organisation can learn. Practical work gives them new problems to examine, and their ideas can change the next system we build.
RawThoughts is RTEPL’s consulting and publishing brand. Harsh Joshi is its Principal Consultant and the author of this work.

body:
A portable model needs a runtime
An application sends a request through a familiar API and receives text. Swapping the server appears easy until the same request loses a required output constraint, handles its images differently or takes too long to finish. The envelope travelled. The useful behaviour did not necessarily travel with it.
Portability interests me because it can make a system less dependent on one implementation without forcing the application to forget what it needs. The difficulty is choosing a stable boundary that carries meaning, not just a common spelling for incompatible operations. Model files, loading formats, request protocols and workload behaviour provide different kinds of portability. A successful conversion at one layer opens the next question rather than answering all of them.
The application asks for a capability
Consider an illustrative document assistant. It needs to read a permitted document, extract named fields into a specified structure, and return the relevant passages for review. A second application needs a vector representation for comparison. Both might use related model architectures, but the requested capabilities differ. Returning plausible prose cannot substitute for a valid extraction, and generating a paragraph cannot substitute for a vector with the dimensions and interpretation its consumer expects.
vLLM's supported-model documentation distinguishes generative and pooling tasks and describes architecture-specific feature support. That is a useful model for a service boundary: identify the task and required features before selecting the execution path. The application can remain independent of many implementation details while still declaring the input types, output meaning and constraints on which its own work depends.
A capability declaration also needs failure meaning. If structured output is unavailable, silently returning unstructured text gives the next component a different job. It may now need to interpret and repair what it expected to validate. An explicit unsupported capability is more useful than success on an easier task, because the caller can select another path without confusing adaptation with fulfilment.
For the document assistant, the stable requirement could be “return these five fields, evidence passages and an explicit missing-value representation.” The deployment can then vary behind that requirement:
Application requirement	Deployment choice	Compatibility question	
Read text and supplied page images	Checkpoint and input preprocessing	Are both input types actually supported?	
Return five structured fields	Constraint mechanism and output validation	Does failure remain distinguishable from a valid empty field?	
Cite the admitted source passages	Passage identifiers carried through the adapter	Can each result be traced to the same source text?	
Finish within the task's time and memory budget	Precision, runtime, device and scheduling	Does the selected request mix fit, not just one example?	
The adapter owns translation between these two vocabularies. A backend-specific setting belongs to the deployment unless the application genuinely depends on its meaning. That leaves room to replace the runtime without silently dropping a field or turning missing evidence into prose.
State has to fit the chosen path
Attention-based generation carries keys and values from preceding tokens. Recurrent and hybrid models can carry a different mixture of state. That difference matters to allocation, scheduling, concurrency and recovery, even when the user sees the same request interface. It belongs close to the runtime where that state is managed. A service carrying many requests needs the actual memory shape, not merely the size of the model weights.
Suppose two hypothetical backends accept the same maximum input length. Under one, each additional token substantially increases retained per-request attention state; under the other, a recurrent component has a different growth pattern. The application need not manage those internals directly. But the platform cannot assume that a scheduling policy derived for one has the same capacity consequences on the other. Portability at the task boundary allows a different implementation precisely because its resource management can remain different.
Compiled artifacts introduce another boundary. NVIDIA's TensorRT support matrix documents platform, version and hardware-compatibility conditions for serialized engines. A file being portable in storage does not make its executable representation portable to an arbitrary target. The selected artifact, runtime and hardware form a configuration whose compatibility has to be established together.
An adapter translates meaning
A narrow adapter can translate request fields, preserve identifiers and map failure results. It may also need to describe the differences it cannot translate. An embedding model's output dimension, a tokenizer's treatment of the input, a constraint mechanism or a model-specific preprocessing path can be material to the consumer. Concealing all variation behind one generic success response makes the interface simple by making the application uninformed.
The opposite extreme is exposing every runtime option as a common requirement. That ties callers to the first engine's vocabulary and turns each replacement into an application migration. A useful separation keeps the application's requirements stable while a deployment profile supplies the checkpoint, preprocessing, precision, runtime and hardware decisions needed to fulfil them. Extensions can expose particular capabilities explicitly instead of pretending that every backend implements the same maximal feature set.
Replacement changes an experiment
Imagine two hypothetical extraction configurations. A handles one hundred prepared cases and returns ninety-five valid outputs. B returns ninety-seven, but takes twice as long and misses a rare field that A consistently finds. Choosing B cannot be justified by the headline total alone if that field determines the downstream decision. Equally, retaining A solely because it is incumbent misses a possible improvement. The test needs the errors and resource costs that matter to the actual task.
The comparison binds model revision, runtime, precision, preprocessing, workload and evaluator. It can then examine a replacement against the same required capability. A transport conformance test establishes that requests and responses cross the interface; task evaluation establishes whether the result remains useful. A narrow judgement service makes this concrete by selecting a configuration for the questions it will face rather than for a general prestige ranking.
Backend neutrality is therefore a constructive constraint. It gives the application a stable way to say what it needs and the implementation room to improve how that work happens. The boundary is successful when a replacement can be evaluated and adopted without either rewriting the whole application or quietly changing the job it performs.

body:
AI 101
What is artificial intelligence? Why is everyone so excited about it? And if it is this magical, why does getting it to do one ordinary job still involve so much work?
Let's start with the machinery. I wrote this introduction in June 2024, when every software product seemed to be acquiring a copilot. Follow a request through an application and the terms begin to make sense: what does the model do, what surrounds it, and where can we reach the work to improve it? Those questions also led us to build YOJN.
What are we calling intelligence?
AI is a broad field concerned with making machines perform tasks associated with intelligence: recognising patterns, reasoning, planning, communicating and acting. It includes more than one way of doing that.
Suppose a process has a hundred rules. You can write routines that say, “If this condition holds, do that.” An expert system can represent knowledge through such rules and reason with them. But as the exceptions accumulate, maintaining all the combinations becomes a serious job. Can the system learn something from examples instead of requiring us to specify every distinction ourselves?
That is the attraction of machine learning. It is not a technology that suddenly replaced rules in the 1990s: learning systems and rule-based systems have long, overlapping histories. Arthur Samuel was already publishing work on learning to play checkers in 1959. They also coexist inside ordinary applications. A learned model may recognise the request; a written rule may decide whether the account is permitted to act on it.
A decision tree gives us one way of learning a set of distinctions from data. A small tree can be easy to follow. Other models represent the problem differently, and the trade-offs depend on the task. Neural networks are a particularly flexible family. Their terminology borrows from brains, but they are mathematical systems, not miniature biological brains running inside a computer.
Start with a curve in a spreadsheet
You have some data in a spreadsheet and fit a line through it. Given another input, the line supplies an estimated output. You have a model.
For a tiny invented example, take the observations (0,1), (1,3) and (2,5). The rule y = 2x + 1 fits all three. Put in x = 3 and it predicts 7. Easy enough.
But another curve can fit those same observations and predict something else at three. The data did not uniquely determine everything the model will do beyond it. The choice of model and the assumptions behind fitting it matter.
Two curves pass through the same three observations but predict different values beyond the observed range.
Both curves fit the three invented observations exactly. The straight line is 2x+1; the alternative adds 0.2x(x-1)(x-2), which is zero at each observed input. At x=3, their predictions are 7 and 8.2.
A neural network is also a function with adjustable parameters, usually called weights. Training changes those parameters to improve an objective on examples. Layers let the network build complex transformations, often over far more dimensions than we can draw on a sheet of paper. For classification, the result can define boundaries between categories. For other tasks it might predict a number or the probabilities of possible next tokens.
This is what I mean by a function approximator. It gives us a useful starting point without pretending the entire subject is a spreadsheet trendline. The important question is how well the learned function behaves on the cases we actually need, including ones it has not seen before.
From recognising things to generating them
An email filter learns patterns associated with spam. A recommendation system uses patterns in interactions to suggest something a person might want. These are different tasks, with different data and objectives, but both make use of regularities in examples.
A colour photograph can be represented as a grid with red, green and blue values at each pixel. To the model, the input begins as numbers. A learned representation can make patterns in those numbers useful for identifying a nose, an ice-cream cone or a face. It does not begin with our everyday vocabulary already attached to every pixel.
Generative models learn patterns that let them produce new outputs: text, images, audio and other forms. Classification and generation are related, but a good classifier does not automatically become a good generator. They may need different architectures, objectives and training procedures.
The excitement after 2022 came partly from how accessible generation became. People could ask for a draft, a picture or a piece of code and receive something they could immediately inspect and use. A capability previously encountered through specialist software became an entrance to many kinds of work.
That is real economic possibility. It also raises the next question: does the generated thing actually satisfy the task? Producing a plausible answer is not evidence that all the decisions required for the job were made correctly. The distinction is where much of the engineering begins.
What are LLMs and GPTs?
A language model assigns probabilities to sequences of tokens. A token may represent a word, part of a word, punctuation or another unit chosen by the tokenizer. It is a close relative of “word” for a first explanation, but the difference matters when you count context or cost.
An autoregressive language model generates by repeatedly selecting a next token from the distribution it computes for the preceding context. The choice becomes part of the context for the next step. A large language model applies this sort of language modelling at scale; different model families organise the computation differently.
GPT expands to Generative Pre-trained Transformer. The Transformer architecture was introduced in 2017. Its attention mechanism lets representations draw on other positions in a sequence. GPT uses a decoder-style Transformer to predict continuations, rather than being the encoder side of the original encoder–decoder design.
Pre-training develops broad capability from a large body of data. Later training can adapt how a model responds to instructions or particular tasks. The architecture, pre-training and later adaptation all contribute; the letters in the name are not a recipe that makes any chat system reliable.
And diffusion models?
Diffusion takes another route to generation. During training, noise is added to examples, and a model learns how to reverse that corruption. Generation can then begin with noise and use learned denoising steps to produce a sample, often conditioned on something such as a text prompt.
That is different from the generator-versus-discriminator contest used in a generative adversarial network, or GAN. It is also different from choosing one next token at a time. These are ways of organising a generative problem, rather than three names for the same mechanism.
The broad attraction is familiar: learn enough structure from the data to make something new. Whether the new thing has the right fingers, the intended words or continuity with the previous video frame is a further question. A method for generating an image does not supply a guarantee about every detail in it.
What are agents?
An AI application can call a model once and return the answer. It can also place the model inside a larger operation: inspect a request, choose a tool, examine what came back and decide what to do next. “Agent” is commonly used for systems in that latter territory, although people use the word at different levels of ambition.
An agent is not another kind of neural network by definition. It is an arrangement of model calls, state, tools and control over what happens next. Some workflows prescribe the steps in advance. Others let a model choose among allowed actions. More freedom changes what the application has to check; it does not automatically make it more useful.
Think of an operating system coordinating processes, memory and access to resources. An agent framework coordinates activities, their context and their access to tools. We still have to check what those activities produce and what happens when one fails.
Where retrieval and memory fit
RAG stands for retrieval-augmented generation. The application retrieves information and provides it to the model as part of the material it can use when generating an answer. The information might be a product manual, a policy or a record that was never included in the model's training.
In the OS analogy, retrieval is a little like bringing information in through input/output, while the model's context is a kind of working space. Neither is a perfect equivalence. A context window is not a general-purpose memory store, and placing a document in it does not update the model's weights.
Imagine asking which payment terms apply to a purchase. The application first needs the relevant agreement and version. It may retrieve passages, ask a model to interpret them, then check or present the answer. The retrieval can select the wrong agreement. The interpretation can be wrong even when the right passage arrives. Each step has a job, and each can fail in a different way.
An orchestrator keeps those steps together. It might invoke several agents or just ordinary software functions. It may summarise information to fit the context, which creates another choice about what gets left out. The result can feel like one instantaneous act of intelligence to the person using it. Underneath, there is work being coordinated, sometimes with substantial delays and dependencies.
What is prompt engineering?
It is the work of giving a model instructions, context and examples that help it produce the intended behaviour.
“Give me the answer as a Markdown table with these three columns” is more specific than “make it readable”. A relevant example can clarify what belongs in a column. A request to identify missing information can be better than quietly encouraging the model to fill every gap.
The effect depends on the model and the task. “Markdown” is not a magic word that activates a known table-making compartment. If a particular format matters, the application can validate it and handle a failure. A prompt is part of that arrangement, not a substitute for the checks.
In 2024 I wondered whether prompt engineering as a separate profession might disappear as quickly as it had appeared. Predictions here are wobbly. The more durable problem is communicating the task clearly enough and checking whether the system did it.
What are vector embeddings?
Think of a graph with two coordinates, date and revenue. A point gives you two numbers. A vector is a list of numbers; it can have two entries or many more.
An embedding maps an object, such as a token, passage or image, to such a vector. Learning can arrange that space so that some relationships in the data become useful relationships between vectors. Then an application can compare representations to retrieve related passages or recognise similar images.
The dimensions do not necessarily have convenient labels such as “nose”, “colour” and “trustworthiness”. Nor does every embedding have the same number of dimensions. The representation and the distance measure are part of a particular model and task.
My nose and your nose might land near one another in a space useful for recognising noses. If horse poop lands nearby too, I would quite reasonably question whether we had learned the distinction we needed. There is no universal distance of 0.00001 at which a model decides those things are equivalent. The point is that closeness in a learned representation is not the same as a human judgement that two things should be treated alike.
The model operates on the representation it has. Our job includes testing whether that representation preserves what the use requires.
The demonstration worked. What is MLOps for?
There is a considerable distance between the engineer's laptop in the boardroom and customers using the system every day.
MLOps concerns the practices and infrastructure for developing, deploying, monitoring and maintaining machine-learning systems. The work includes data and model versions, evaluations, serving, reliability and the changes needed when the world or the data changes. It draws on software operations while adding the particular problems of learned models.
“AIOps” is often used for applying AI to IT operations, so I would not use the two terms interchangeably. For this discussion, we are concerned with operating the AI application itself.
Cost, latency, security and recovery all become part of the product. The model may answer correctly when everything is available and still leave the customer stuck when a source is missing. The product around the model has to decide what happens then.
Can we see it, explain it and control it?
Observability asks what we can learn about the running system from its outputs and measurements. Which request used which model and source? Where did the delay occur? What did the tool return, and what did the operation cost?
Explainability asks a different question: what account helps us understand the behaviour or decision? A trace records steps. It may not tell a domain expert why the wrong agreement was selected or why a proposed answer is justified. A model's own explanation is another output to assess, not privileged access to the actual cause of its answer.
Controllability concerns what we can deliberately influence: permitted actions, available information, selected versions, checks and interventions. Alignment addresses whether behaviour follows the goals and constraints it is intended to serve. These are related fields, each much larger than this paragraph. Seeing the work helps us investigate it; an explanation helps us judge it; a control gives that judgement somewhere to go.
There is a useful technical distinction here. A neural network can compute a repeatable output under fixed inputs and execution conditions. Sampling can introduce variability, and changing context or tools can change the result. But even a perfectly repeatable answer can be wrong. Reliability is not solved merely by making the system say the same thing twice.
Fine-tuning: science, or art?
Pure art, obviously. Just kidding.
Suppose a pre-trained model has useful general capability but struggles with the task's specialised language or expected responses. Fine-tuning continues training from that model using examples and objectives chosen for the adaptation.
It need not change only the top few layers. Full fine-tuning can update all trainable weights; parameter-efficient methods update a smaller set or add a limited adaptation. LoRA, for example, keeps the original weights fixed while learning low-rank updates. Changing a prompt is not the same operation as changing weights.
The practical judgement is in preparing representative examples, choosing what to optimise and deciding what counts as improvement. You try something, inspect the results, double down or change direction. A subject expert may notice that the answer uses the wrong definition even when a general quality score looks healthy.
That feedback has to become something useful: a corrected example, a clearer source, a changed evaluation or a candidate training run. It does not mean every correction should immediately retrain the model or replace the version serving customers. Test the candidate against the failures that motivated it and the behaviour worth preserving. The art is in the judgement; the comparison still needs evidence.
The piece of the model I actually need
This is the question that most interested me: decomposability.
Ordinary software gives us functions and modules with interfaces. We can reuse one routine without bringing the whole application along. A model exposes components too, but a useful learned capability does not necessarily line up with one neatly removable component. Knowing how to call the model is different from knowing which internal part to extract for a particular skill.
Imagine dissecting a brain, finding “what he ate for breakfast”, and transferring that bit to someone else. Now they remember a samosa. Or we adjust it and give them a pineapple. A ridiculous picture, but it catches what is missing from the simple idea that we can take a model's useful knowledge apart as easily as a software library.
Pruning, adapters, specialised experts and other forms of modular design offer ways to work with parts of models. They do not amount to a universal method for isolating any semantic capability and transferring it while everything else remains unchanged. That stronger question is what I was getting at with the “0 or 1” complaint: so often, the usable interface gives you the whole model's behaviour when you want one intelligible part.
The distinction matters for explanation, reuse and quality assurance. If we cannot confidently locate the behaviour we want to change, we also have more work to do when checking what else a change affected.
Why isn't it doing every job already?
Compute and skilled work can be expensive. Even after paying for them, we still need quality assurance.
The maddening experience is a system that appears to understand the task beautifully and then fails in a way no one anticipated. Think of a hyperactive five-year-old: good luck figuring out why that particular power socket was so interesting.
You really don't want your AI front desk telling a customer to go fuck themselves! An exaggeration, of course, but an incorrect promise made in perfectly polite language can cause plenty of trouble too. A leveraged-buyout model with a subtly wrong assumption creates a different risk again. The presence of a chat box cannot decide what evidence is enough for either use.
This is why I kept returning to explanation and control. We need to know what can go wrong, which checks catch it and where a person can intervene. A good demonstration can reveal a possibility. Daily use requires an arrangement that can carry the consequences. There are useful applications before every research problem is solved; there are also tasks for which the remaining errors matter too much to ignore.
Why all the excitement about open models?
When model weights and tools are available, more people can experiment, adapt and build. Hugging Face helped make that activity easier to find and share. The analogy to GitHub is useful: a place where work becomes accessible to others, rather than an isolated result behind one interface.
But “open” needs care. Available weights, source code, training information and permitted uses are different dimensions. Mistral's original 7B release used Apache 2.0; other model releases use their own terms. A downloadable file does not automatically make every model an open-source project in the same sense.
My economic reading in 2024 was that this was more than generosity. Compute, talent and data require capital and distribution. A company that reaches more users can gain more opportunities to improve its product and finance the next round. Open releases can be a way for other participants to weaken dependence on a dominant provider and build a different position in that market.
The rebel alliance, if I may get dramatic for a moment. Why should the incumbent get to own everything? Releasing a useful model can serve a business strategy and help a wider community at the same time.
The stakes are larger than winning a benchmark. The question is who supplies the systems through which people will work and consume, and how easily others can build an alternative.
What does the enterprise have to run?
One route is to use a hosted model API. The provider operates the model; the application concentrates on the experience and the work around it. Another is to run a model whose weights are available, or develop one. That gives the team different control and different operating obligations. Applications can also combine these routes.
In either case, someone still maintains the configuration, sources, access, checks and feedback. An orchestration framework can help organise that work. Merely placing a model inside an “agent” does not give it a learning process or prove that its actions are safe.
This brings the subject expert back into the picture. They may recognise the mistake immediately, while the engineering team has to work out which source, step or model behaviour produced it. The useful system lets those contributions meet. Better tokens and feedback matter because they carry relevant information; data quality does not make architecture, access control or careful evaluation disappear.
Our attempt with YOJN
At DAO Studio we built YojnAI around that problem: compose an application, inspect its intermediate work and let feedback inform a deliberate improvement. Agents combined models and tools; checked playbooks arranged their work; an application supplied the organisation's connections and context.
The design associated traces and feedback with particular agents and versions. It paired model snapshots and improvement work with ways for a domain expert to inspect a step, explain what was wrong and compare a candidate change. That was our practical approach to making the application more decomposable. It did not extract a self-contained skill from arbitrary neural weights or solve the stronger research question above.
Callbacks and retained intermediate state mattered because the person needed to reach the work while it was happening, rather than receive only a final answer. If one part needed correction, the useful information from another part should remain available. The public composition account develops that mechanism, and the review walkthrough follows a disputed result into an improvement decision.
The aim was to explain enough of the operation to the person who knew the subject. They should not have to learn the mathematics of the model before pointing out that it had used the wrong payment term. Evaluation and version choice were intended to make that correction more useful than a complaint collected in a log.
For the finance team funding the application, the related question was what the improvement bought. Consider the illustration of roughly $1.70 an hour of compute for a smaller adapted model rather than paying for a much larger one.
Note
The conditions behind the cost. That historical figure is not a current hosting quote or a like-for-like cost benchmark. Request length, throughput, hardware, quality and operating work determine the actual comparison. Self-hosting also leaves real infrastructure and service costs; the absence of a per-token API bill does not make use free.
The intended shift was to spend more effectively on the people and evidence that improved the task, with a clearer view of what the compute was doing. Where the application and its data actually run remains a separate part of that choice.
The 8086 era of AI
My expectation in June 2024 was that many constraints we were carefully engineering around would become much less important as the technology improved. The computer analogy was the 8086 era: limitations that once shaped an entire application can later become small enough to forget.
Retrieval, for example, helps an application select useful information within context and cost constraints. Larger context alone would not settle source quality or access, but it could change some of the trade-offs that made a particular retrieval arrangement attractive.
Imagine a thousandfold efficiency improvement allowing a model a hundred times larger to use a tenth of the resources. Under a simple proportional model, the arithmetic is 100 / 1{,}000 = 0.1. That calculation describes the possibility I had in mind; it is not a measured gain, a timetable or a guarantee that latency follows the same ratio.
I expected some AI services eventually to feel free to the user, as search and social media often do, with other business models paying for them. Useful capability would become easier to obtain, while distinctive data about the problem could become more valuable. New policies and energy demands would follow the changing use.
Then come the stranger possibilities: specialised AI personas, systems finding and commissioning one another, something like Fiverr or Amazon with AI on the requesting side. Their practical demands are substantial. A medical adviser, a plumber's assistant and a robot doing physical work need very different evidence and capabilities; robotics does not reduce to manufacturing merely because conversation has improved.
My larger expectation was that progress on decomposability would eventually let us trade and combine useful intelligence more directly. That remains a research and product ambition, distinct from calling a few APIs in sequence. It is the question underneath the vocabulary: can the useful thing the system has learned become something another person can understand, improve and build with?
IBM's account of its early game-playing research describes Samuel's checkers work. Machine learning was already an established research term decades before the 1990s; rule-based and learned approaches are not consecutive, mutually exclusive eras.
Vaswani and colleagues, Attention Is All You Need, 2017; Radford and colleagues, Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training, 2018. The latter explicitly uses a multi-layer Transformer decoder for its language model.
Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues, Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics, 2015; Ho, Jain and Abbeel, Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models, 2020. These describe diffusion and learned reverse processes, rather than the adversarial training contest of GANs.
Lewis and colleagues, Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks, 2020, combines a trained generator with retrieved passages. Retrieval adds usable context; it does not itself establish that the passage or generated answer is correct.
Mikolov and colleagues, Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space, 2013, is a foundational example of learned word vectors. Different embedding models and tasks use different representations; a coordinate has no universal human meaning.
Google Cloud's MLOps: Continuous delivery and automation pipelines in machine learning describes the development, evaluation, deployment and operational work around models.
Hu and colleagues, LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models, 2021. Its smaller trainable updates are one adaptation method; fine-tuning as a category is not restricted to a model's final layers.
Mistral's September 2023 release announcement identifies the original Mistral 7B licence as Apache 2.0. The statement concerns that release, not every model subsequently published by the company.

node.title: What can it understand, and what can it change?
node.description: A staffing paradox separates causal judgement from an AI application's power to change the operation.

body:
What can it understand, and what can it change?
A service team adds workers to reduce late orders. Its dashboard then shows more lateness on shifts with extra staff. Did the intervention make things worse, or did the team send help precisely where work was already hardest?
An AI application might confidently recommend a staffing change from that dashboard and also have the API access to apply it. Its ability to find a pattern, its ability to reason about an intervention and its reach into the rota are three different properties. I find that separation more useful than a single label such as "agentic" or "causal": it tells us which question to test, and what a mistaken answer can actually change.
Beyond the Mirage develops the wider proposal: describe intelligence by its depth of causal reasoning and, separately, by how much it can act on the world. Here I want to follow those two questions through one operational decision. What would the team need to know before changing the rota?
Three questions hiding in one dashboard
Consider a service team trying to reduce late orders. These questions sound related, but ask for different answers. "Which orders are likely to be late?" asks for a prediction under the observed conditions. "Would adding another worker reduce lateness?" asks about the effect of a change. "Would this particular late order have arrived on time if another worker had been assigned?" asks about a counterfactual for one event. The output format might be identical: a probability, a short explanation and a recommendation. That does not make the evidential requirements identical. A useful forecast may exploit a pattern that would disappear when the operation changes. An average effect need not resolve what would have happened to a particular order.
The causal-inference literature formalises distinctions between observational, interventional and counterfactual questions. It also explains why identifying an effect from observations depends on the available information and assumptions about the causal structure. Observational data can sometimes support an identified effect; the assumptions must do real work rather than remain implicit.
The staffing team needs to choose which of these questions its decision depends on, then test whether the application can answer it under the stated assumptions.
When the helpful worker looks harmful
Suppose the team recorded these orders. The numbers are constructed to show how the workload mix changes the comparison.
Workload	Extra worker: late / total	Ordinary staffing: late / total	
Quiet	1 / 20 = 5%	8 / 80 = 10%	
Busy	32 / 80 = 40%	12 / 20 = 60%	
Combined	33 / 100 = 33%	20 / 100 = 20%	
Pooling the rows makes extra staffing look associated with more lateness. Looking within each workload group reverses that association. Extra workers were assigned much more often during busy periods, when lateness was higher in either staffing condition.
Giving both staffing conditions the same quiet/busy mixture makes the arithmetic visible. With equal weights on the two workload groups, the extra-worker rate is (0.05+0.40)/2=0.225; the ordinary-staffing rate is (0.10+0.60)/2=0.35. These standardised associations are 22.5% and 35%, rather than the pooled 33% and 20%. Adjustment has changed which population is being compared. Whether it identifies the causal effect still depends on why workers were assigned and what the workload measure leaves out.
The table alone does not prove that an extra worker helps. Other differences could affect both assignment and lateness, including complexity that the quiet/busy label misses. It does show why an answer based on the pooled percentage can address the wrong question.
An evaluator should ask what staffing decision was being estimated, how assignment happened, whether workload is measured appropriately and which remaining influences the analysis assumes away. If a suitable experiment is available, its assignment and measurement design matter. If observational identification is proposed, the causal assumptions and adjustment must be justified. Better prose cannot fill that gap.
Nor should the evaluator turn this into an impossible demand that every recommendation predict an individual's alternative history. A decision may appropriately use an estimated population effect. The point is to choose the question the decision requires, not always demand the strongest-sounding one.
A solver can reason without acting
Imagine a read-only application given an explicit causal model of a small queueing system. A solver computes the consequences of changing one parameter under that model. It has no permission or interface to alter production staffing. Its answer can be checked against the supplied model, even though the model's fit to the actual workplace remains a separate question.
Now imagine a bot that can add a worker to the rota through an API. It may execute a straightforward rule correctly while having no demonstrated ability to estimate the change's effect on lateness. The operation succeeded; the causal question remains unanswered.
These countercases are enough to reject a shortcut: counting tool calls does not measure causal competence, and withholding write access does not imply an inability to analyse interventions. Tools can extend a system's information or computation, but their contribution must appear in the evaluated system rather than be attributed automatically to the language model alone.
A combined application may use a language model to translate the request, a retrieved source to supply assumptions and a solver to calculate an answer. Its performance is a property of that composition under those conditions. An ablation that removes the solver answers a different question from one that tests the full workflow. Both can be useful if their objects are named.
An evaluation should survive a change of story
For the service-team application, I would first evaluate prediction on held-out conditions that resemble its intended use. I would then assess intervention estimates in settings where the target effect has an independently justified reference, and include changes that break convenient correlations. I would separately test the bot's operations, including partial failures and the consequences of repeating an action.
The test report would state the task, data, assumptions, system composition and metric. It would show where performance failed instead of converting the average into a universal capability claim. A model that solves a supplied causal exercise has demonstrated something useful. It has not thereby demonstrated that it can discover a correct causal model from an arbitrary organisation's records.
Metric choice also shapes the picture. Schaeffer, Miranda and Koyejo demonstrated how particular discontinuous metrics can make smooth changes in model outputs appear as abrupt capability emergence. That result is a reason to inspect the measurement, not a proof that every surprising behaviour is predictable or that genuine transitions are impossible.
Where possible, I would keep the underlying errors and partial successes alongside the headline score. For a staffing estimate, getting the direction right while being badly wrong about magnitude is different from getting both wrong. For an action, choosing correctly but applying the change twice is different from choosing badly and executing precisely. One total score can hide the distinction that matters for deployment.
More reach changes the consequences
Operational reach deserves its own description: which systems the application can affect, how long it can continue without review, how actions compose and whether a mistake can be reversed. That is not a second intelligence score. It describes the consequence of being wrong.
A weak predictor with broad write access can cause substantial harm. A stronger analytical system kept read-only may produce a bad recommendation without directly changing the world. Neither case settles overall safety, but they demand different controls and different evidence. Improving the answer and limiting the consequence are complementary jobs, not substitutes.
The same method applies to generated code. Writing plausible code, satisfying an independently reviewed contract and being allowed to execute the result are distinct achievements. For the person running the service, a capability label needs to lead back to this practical account: what the system has demonstrated, what it is allowed to change and which test would justify the next step.
Bareinboim, Correa, Ibeling and Icard's account of the causal hierarchy.
Schaeffer, Miranda and Koyejo's original paper.

node.description: A program can satisfy order and length while discarding the input; the missing sorting contract reveals what checking must preserve.

body:
The sorting program that passed the wrong test
For [3, -1, 3], a sorting program returns [0, 0, 0]. Its output is in ascending order. Its length matches the input. Both tests pass, yet the program has discarded every value it was asked to sort.
We can construct that failure without a language model: the checker was never asked whether the program kept the input values. Model-written code makes the gap especially interesting because it can produce an implementation, tests and an explanation together. All three could agree that those zeros are a success. What did we actually ask them to check?
A perfectly checked wrong answer
The missing property is preservation of the values being sorted. No dishonest checker is necessary: a correct proof of order and length would still accept the zeros. The requirement has to connect the output to this input, rather than merely describe the shape of an acceptable-looking list.
Adding set equality is not enough either. The outputs [-1, 3, 3] and [-1, -1, 3] have the same set of values and the same length, but different multiplicities. The contract needs to preserve the count of each value, as well as establish order. Whether the input may be modified also needs an answer: returning a new list and sorting the caller's list in place are different promises.
The gap fits in a few lines of Python. This example checks the output of a function intended to return a new list of integers; it does not execute an unknown generated program.
from collections import Counter

def looks_sorted(before, after):
    return len(before) == len(after) and all(
        left <= right for left, right in zip(after, after[1:])
    )

def preserves_sorting_contract(before, after):
    return looks_sorted(before, after) and Counter(before) == Counter(after)

values = [3, -1, 3]
assert looks_sorted(values, [0, 0, 0])
assert not preserves_sorting_contract(values, [0, 0, 0])
assert not preserves_sorting_contract(values, [-1, -1, 3])
assert preserves_sorting_contract(values, [-1, 3, 3])

The first assertion succeeds for the wrong reason: nothing in that check connects the returned values to the supplied values. Counter supplies the missing multiplicities. The second contract also accepts an empty input and handles repeated values, but it remains an executable check of a candidate output.
Note
What this check leaves open. It does not check that the caller's list stayed unchanged or that a fresh list was allocated; those promises need observations of the call itself. Nor is it a termination argument or a proof about every execution of the function that produced it.
The constructed example exposes a requirement problem before it becomes a tool choice. Dafny's official guide develops the same distinction through preconditions and postconditions: a nonnegative result alone does not sufficiently specify an absolute-value function. Verification establishes the written conditions, so those conditions have to capture the computation the caller actually needs.
Five greens with different meanings
A generated artifact can pass several checks without those checks answering the same question.
Check	What its success can establish	What remains outside that result	
Schema validation	The artifact has the required representational shape	Whether that representation describes the intended computation	
Compilation	The selected compiler accepts and translates the program	Whether the resulting behaviour meets the need	
Tests	The checked cases produced their expected observations	The unchecked cases and the adequacy of those expectations	
Formal verification	The declared properties hold within the selected semantics and proof assumptions	Whether those properties capture the actual requirement	
Operational qualification	The selected system met its criteria in the observed setting	Other configurations, environments and future conditions	
These are not five grades on one confidence scale. They are different obligations. A compiler error cannot be dismissed because tests looked plausible; a proof cannot compensate for a requirement that permits the wrong result.
Even the word "verification" needs its object. LLVM's verifier checks that an LLVM module is well formed, including structural conditions beyond what its parser accepts. That is valuable compiler infrastructure. It is not a proof that a user wanted this computation or that every memory access is safe.
Independence is a control boundary
The generator can help propose a specification. It can suggest an invariant, find an edge case or explain a failed proof. None of those contributions requires giving it the power to accept its own changes to the acceptance conditions.
For the sorting example, fixing a failure by replacing "preserve every value's multiplicity" with "preserve the length" would change the problem. So would adding a precondition that the input contains only zeros, or weakening the allowed input to already sorted lists without the caller's agreement. A successful result after either change says nothing about the original request.
Keeping the reviewed contract and the range of inputs it must handle outside the candidate's writable area preserves the question through repair. A repair attempt changes the candidate; a proposed contract change returns to requirement review and starts a different evaluation if accepted. Generated annotations can supply useful invariants, but unchecked assumptions or exemptions would remove the very property an independent judge is supposed to assess.
The independent judge need not be a single magical oracle. It can combine a type checker, executable reference behaviour, property tests, a solver and human review. What matters is which claim each component decides, which assumptions it relies on and who can alter its inputs. Another model is useful for criticism, but agreement between generators does not become a proof simply because the critics have different names.
This question already has a research setting. Clover, for example, checks consistency among generated code, documentation and formal annotations using verification tools and models. That can filter candidates within the study's conditions. The question here is whether a separately reviewed requirement survives the whole process: consistency among three generated descriptions cannot, by itself, show that they express what the caller needed.
The arithmetic has a world
Mathematical integers and fixed-width machine integers obey different arithmetic rules. A specification that ignores overflow may be adequate for comparisons but inadequate for an implementation that subtracts two values to compare them. The translation into machine code must preserve the behaviour the proof establishes.
Likewise, proving a return-value property does not automatically establish termination, a memory bound, an acceptable runtime or harmless behaviour in surrounding code. A precondition may rule out inputs that a real caller still supplies. An external library or unchecked escape hatch may sit outside the verified fragment. Those boundaries are part of the result, not footnotes to remove after the badge turns green.
A small, explicitly supported fragment makes this approach testable. Its semantics can be stated, its failures inspected and its checks compared with ordinary development without executing unknown generated artifacts in an uncontrolled environment. Extending that fragment then becomes a concrete question about which new constructs the contract and checking system can faithfully handle.
A rejected candidate is information
For this approach to be useful, the report must distinguish a counterexample from a tool failure, a resource limit from a proved property and an unsupported construct from an accepted one. "Could not establish" is not "established false", but neither is it permission to report success.
A finite repair budget also matters. Repeatedly regenerating until a weak checker passes can hide how often the system failed and how much review it consumed. The failures needed to understand that process belong in the evaluation, alongside the cost of obtaining a correctly checked result. A pipeline that saves typing but multiplies specification review may still be useful; the comparison with ordinary implementation needs to show where its benefit actually lies.
The ambition is to let candidate generation explore freely inside a question that survives its attempts. A rejected program can lead to a better implementation, a missing invariant or a proposed correction to the requirement. Those are different kinds of progress. Keeping them distinct lets cheap generation contribute without making the meaning of success equally cheap.
LLVM's language reference.

body:
Choosing an API means reading its contract
A developer looking for an API usually has a task in mind, not a provider name. An application needs to establish where a parcel can go, reconcile a payment or receive an event when some work finishes. Could a discovery assistant find the relevant services and show which parts of their contracts matter to that task? It would save us reading unrelated documentation, and might catch a constraint before we built around the wrong service.
A plausible match is the beginning of the comparison
Suppose an application needs to check whether a delivery address can be served. A general address-search API, an address-validation API and a logistics provider's serviceability API can all look relevant. They may answer different questions. Finding a place, deciding that an address is well formed and deciding that a particular delivery service will accept it are not equivalent capabilities.
The comparison becomes useful when it explains what each candidate actually establishes. An address that exists may still fall outside a courier's delivery area; a courier may accept that area while requiring a different pickup arrangement. Familiar words such as "availability" and "completion" conceal these distinctions. Ranking by similarity alone can put the most fluently described service first while leaving the application's real question unanswered.
For this imagined integration, the comparison might look like this:
Candidate capability	Inputs it needs	Answer it can supply	What the application still needs	
Place search	Address text	A candidate place and coordinates	Whether the chosen courier carries this parcel there	
Address validation	Structured address	Address components accepted under its rules	Courier coverage, pickup and parcel constraints	
Courier serviceability	Origin, destination and parcel details, under the relevant account	Available services under that courier's contract	Quote validity, booking permission and final acceptance	
The third candidate is closest to the question. Even then, an account-specific exception could matter more than its advertised geographic coverage. That is the passage to retrieve next. The table has narrowed the reading instead of pretending to finish it.
A capability description can preserve those dependencies without pretending every provider has one schema. In this hypothetical case it would carry “serviceability for this account”, the required origin, destination and parcel details, the source passage defining the answer, and the conditions still needed before booking. A returned available: true is ambiguous without that account and parcel context. It might mean a service exists for the supplied inputs, not that capacity has been reserved, a price has been fixed or the shipment has been accepted.
The schema is only part of the contract
The developer needs the shapes of requests and responses. They also need authentication, permissions, quotas, errors, applicable commercial terms and the conditions under which data may be sent or retained. Some of those conditions can change while the response schema stays the same. A compatibility check that compares only endpoint shapes can therefore miss a material change in the integration. Conversely, a documentation edit may clarify prose without changing behaviour. Treating every changed byte as a breaking change is as unhelpful as treating identical schemas as identical contracts.
The comparison needs evidence tied to its source: which provider document, which version or observation, and which part of the application it affects. An announcement feed says that something changed. A useful explanation says what that change would mean for the use in front of us.
Suppose the imagined provider keeps the same response shape but changes its parcel-weight limit from 20 to 15 kilograms. A cached comparison can still parse correctly and recommend the wrong service for an 18-kilogram parcel. A useful version comparison flags the affected capability and input condition, retains the earlier source for interpreting older decisions, and makes the old answer unavailable as evidence for the new limit. A changed limit matters to this application; an unrelated wording correction need not trigger the same response.
A common comparison, with native behaviour intact
A common comparison can describe the outcome, required inputs, limits and evidence across different services. It should not imply that request-response interfaces, queries and event subscriptions have the same operational behaviour. The integration still needs its native contract. An event may arrive later or more than once. A request may return a response without completing the business operation. A documented capability may require a plan or permission the application does not have. A tidy capability table can help select the next read; it cannot replace that read.
A local cache needs an honest horizon
Keeping selected documentation locally can reduce repeated retrieval and support offline work. It also creates a horizon: the cache cannot know about a change it has not received. The answer needs to make that boundary visible rather than calling itself current because it is available. A saved copy can identify the exact words used in an earlier decision; it cannot establish that the provider still follows them. Matching a file’s hash establishes that the bytes match, not that two differently described services mean the same thing.
Caution
A cache can disclose more than it should. Public access is not automatically permission to redistribute a documentation corpus. Internal specifications stay with the audience and use they were written for. Search analytics can reveal the work a team is considering even when no secret is present in the indexed text.
A selected, versioned subset can still be valuable. The developer can inspect the original passage beside the comparison, reuse it offline within its permitted audience and see when a material premise needs checking again. The cache earns its place by making that evidence easier to work with, rather than by presenting an unobserved provider as current.
Recommendation should stop before the effect
Producing an example request or a testing collection can cross from explanation towards execution. The assistant must still know whether the caller may disclose the inputs, use the credential and perform the effect. Discovery establishes none of those permissions. That connects this small integration problem to larger questions in Scope and Counsel: giving an agent useful understanding of its setting, then applying semantic judgment where the available alternatives still need interpretation. Relevant evidence can support a recommendation without widening the task or giving the recommender control of the action. Neither product is the API-discovery assistant imagined here; each has its own job.
A better integration decision
The useful test is whether a source-grounded comparison reduces wrong integrations, missed constraints or unnecessary investigation for a defined set of tasks. It needs a competent manual baseline and examples where abstaining is the right answer. A large catalogue or a fluent generated explanation cannot settle that test.
That gives the assistant a concrete ambition. For a serviceability task it might eliminate an address-search API, explain why a courier API needs an account-specific agreement and leave two suitable contracts for a developer to examine. The value lies in the wrong turn avoided and the constraint understood: the developer can now decide how to answer the application's question, rather than merely which endpoint resembles its words.

node.description: Remote generation changes the learning loop: policy lag, execution checks and admission costs determine which work becomes useful training data.

body:
Distribute the rollouts, keep the learning loop coherent
Imagine a training system with a learner in one cluster and generation workers in several locations. The learner improves a model. The workers use copies of that model to attempt tasks and return the resulting sequences. A remote worker can be busy, produce a genuine result and still contribute nothing to the next update: by the time its work arrives, the learner may no longer admit data from that version.
That is a different problem from finding a faster link between GPUs. Geography changes when information becomes available, while learning changes which information remains useful. The opportunity is to separate work that can proceed independently from work that needs tight coordination. The cost is keeping those pieces part of the same experiment.
Independent generation around a connected learner
A rollout records a policy attempting a task: generated tokens, or actions and observations in an environment, together with the information needed to evaluate and learn from that attempt. It is data produced for learning, not a guarantee that the answer is right or a transparent account of how the model thinks.
Distributing rollout generation need not mean distributing every gradient update across the same wide-area network. The learner can retain its tightly connected training cluster while remote workers generate sequences independently. The expensive coordination boundary then moves: model versions travel out; training data comes back. This complements rather than replaces the questions about parallelism inside a cluster.
There is a concrete public example. The May 2025 INTELLECT-2 report separates trusted central policy updates from geographically distributed inference workers, with weight broadcasts and checks on returned data. Its described deployment retains central orchestration and discovery. The distribution of workers therefore does not imply that every coordinating function is decentralized. INTELLECT-2 technical report, sections 2 and 3.
This arrangement makes geography less restrictive for one part of the experiment. Generating independent attempts can move towards available compute while the learner retains the tightly coordinated update. Its usefulness depends on which exchanges must block progress and which can overlap with other work.
Two versions can both be genuine
Consider an illustrative sequence. A worker receives policy version 10 and begins a long task. While it works, the learner advances to version 12. The worker returns a sequence genuinely generated by version 10. An execution check confirms that fact. The result is authentic, but authenticity has not answered whether it belongs in a version-12 update.
Event	Worker	Learner	Question carried forward	
Dispatch	Starts with version 10	Publishes version 10	Which task, environment and reward definition apply?	
Overlapping work	Continues its attempt	Advances through versions 11 and 12	How much policy mismatch does this recipe tolerate?	
Return	Supplies the version-10 trajectory	Receives it under version 12	Is execution genuine, and is this trajectory admissible?	
Update decision	Waits for its recorded disposition	Uses or rejects the returned data	Did checking and lag consume the economic advantage?	
The record makes a rejection intelligible. “Late” otherwise compresses a coordination problem, a learning constraint and possibly a payment dispute into one word.
Policy lag is more than a stale file. Different policies assign different probabilities to actions. Using data produced by one policy to update another changes the learning problem. IMPALA made this distinction explicit in 2018: actors send experience to learners, and the learner can advance while an actor is still collecting it. The paper's V-trace correction addresses that actor-critic mismatch. Another learning recipe still needs its own justified treatment of policy lag. IMPALA paper, sections 3 and 4.
The returned record needs to identify the policy, task, environment and reward definition that produced it, along with behaviour probabilities where the learning algorithm requires them. Those facts give the learner something a timestamp cannot: the relationship between the attempt it received and the update it is about to make.
An admission rule can then say what lag is supported and what happens outside it. That rule needs evidence from the selected learning recipe. A number of tolerated versions demonstrated for one model, task distribution and update rate is not a universal time allowance. Two updates can represent a small or a large change; one long rollout can span very different amounts of learning in different runs.
The INTELLECT-2 report describes delayed rollout generation and the rejection or disposal of outdated-checkpoint data. That is evidence of a managed trade-off, not unlimited tolerance for delay. INTELLECT-2 technical report, sections 2.2 and 3.2.
Three questions about one returned answer
Suppose the task is to multiply 14 by 17. The worker returns 243, while the expected answer is 238. The first check concerns execution: did the worker run the prescribed model configuration on the prescribed input? A genuine computation can produce that wrong answer.
Second, does the answer meet the task's criterion? Here an arithmetic checker can reject it. In a coding task, tests check their specified cases. In an open-ended task, the reward may be a much less direct proxy. Reward design has its own adequacy problem, just as the judge of generated code needs the right contract.
Third, is the returned record suitable for this update? A correct answer generated by a disallowed version may fail admission. Conversely, an incorrect answer may be useful learning data. Reinforcement learning can learn from unsuccessful attempts; filtering every failure away is not synonymous with improving the training set.
The learning loop needs all three distinctions. It can admit a genuine failure because that failure contains useful information, reject a correct answer because it arrived under an unsupported policy, or reject fabricated work before task evaluation begins.
TOPLOC addresses the execution question through compact representations of intermediate activations, checking consistency with the authorized model configuration. Its paper evaluates detection of changes to models, prompts and precision. That is narrower than proving an answer true, and the reported empirical coverage is not a universal guarantee against every possible adversary. TOPLOC, ICML 2025.
A worker can optimize the wrong thing
Once contributors receive compensation, the returned data is also an economic object. A payment rule changes what it is rational to submit.
Paying only for correct answers can favor easy tasks if workers choose the tasks themselves. Paying only for long sequences can encourage useless length. Paying for every delivered file can encourage duplicates. These are possible failure modes of hypothetical rules, not claims that a particular network suffers them. They show why the incentive must be evaluated alongside task assignment, execution checking and admission.
A penalty is only as useful as the evidence that triggers it. The operator must distinguish cheating from a corrupted transfer, an unsupported configuration or work that became stale while in flight. Otherwise, a mechanism intended to improve trust can punish honest work for a coordination failure. Sampling checks also require a threat model: what is sampled, when contributors can learn the selection, and which attacks that selection can expose.
Task selection also determines where generation can run. A worker that sees a prompt has received its contents, regardless of whether its output is later checked. Public mathematical problems can have a wider permitted execution boundary than a private customer workflow or proprietary weights. Correct execution is useful evidence about the work, but supplies no confidentiality for material already disclosed to the worker.
The economics of admitted trajectories
Asynchrony can let a worker generate while a learner trains or a new checkpoint travels. It can hide a wait from the critical path. It does not eliminate the bytes transferred, the resources used for checking or the consequences of arriving too late.
Suppose remote workers complete long independent tasks, model updates are comparatively infrequent, and the admitted lag is well tested. There may be substantial time to overlap communication with useful generation. Now change the conditions: tasks are short, checkpoints change frequently, and the learner needs tightly current data. Workers may spend much of their time downloading versions or returning sequences that cannot enter the update. The same network can be attractive for the first workload and poor for the second.
The comparison spans the complete loop: generation, weight distribution, result transport, checking, retry and duplicate handling, plus any learner idle time. A low worker-hour price can be consumed by frequent checkpoint downloads or by cheap sequences that reach the learner too late. Conversely, a long independent task may give the system enough time to overlap those exchanges and put otherwise unsuitable compute to useful work.
The first useful intermediate measure is the cost of obtaining data that the learning recipe actually admits and uses. "Useful" must include legitimate negative examples where appropriate, not just positively rewarded answers. The eventual measure is the cost and time of reaching the same independently evaluated learning target. More admitted trajectories are not automatically more learning, particularly if their diversity or reward information differs.
That puts the network in the workload's economics without requiring every communication path to be local. The opportunity lies in a deliberate asymmetry: varied resources produce independent experience, while a coherent learner decides how that experience enters the experiment. The return is measured in progress towards the learning target, after the cost of keeping both sides connected.
