node.title: Machine learning is flat!
node.description: An argument about the vocabulary between machine-learning researchers, the people affected by their systems and those asked to govern them.

body:
Machine learning is flat!
Okay, first things first: the title is not a new theory of geometry.
When I first wrote this in February 2020, I began by asking people to watch Johnny Harris's Why People Think the World Is Flat. This has nothing and everything to do with that video. My question is about machine learning, explainability and the people trying to regulate a black box. More particularly, it is about the conversation we need to have before we can do any of those things well.
And by conversation, I don't mean throwing mathematics and algorithms at one another. I mean talking about the problem and what would count as a solution. We have a problem. Accepting that is a useful place to start.
What do you mean by that?
Communication needs some interpretation of a shared vocabulary. Either the machine-learning person learns how to explain the work through the other person's world, or the other person learns enough of the mathematics to enter theirs. Usually, both have some work to do.
An abstraction helps us cross that distance. It leaves things out so we can discuss the part that matters. Trouble starts when we forget what was left out. One person says “the model learned”; another hears “it understands”. One says “accurate”; another hears “I can rely on it in my situation”. We can agree on every word in the sentence and disagree about what it means.
Then our biases helpfully fill the gaps. We build another explanation on the first, borrow another analogy, and carry a small misunderstanding into a much larger claim. Somewhere along the way, a useful simplification becomes an absurdity. The mathematics inside the model may be unchanged throughout. The communication has failed around it.
That is the catch-22: machine learning is already a forest of abstractions. We describe the data through numbers, the learning through an objective and the result through a measure. To explain what happened, we have to carry those abstractions into the vocabulary of someone who needs to make a decision. Merely repeating the technical vocabulary more slowly does not finish the journey.
Showing the machinery helps
Training a model combines mathematical methods with a great deal of experimental judgement: choosing data, testing assumptions and adjusting a system when the first attempt fails. Calling that judgement an art expresses the experience of doing it. It does not put the result beyond scientific investigation.
Visual explanations can give us a way in. What pattern activates a feature? Which part of an image contributed to a classification? What changes when a layer is removed? Work such as Zeiler and Fergus's visualisation of convolutional networks made some of those questions concrete. Other methods, such as LIME, approximate a model's behaviour around a particular prediction to provide a more interpretable local account.
Andrej Karpathy's explanations and the TensorFlow Playground were accessible entrances to this world. A reader could follow a sequence through a network, or change a small network and watch its learned boundary move. That matters to communication: an abstraction becomes something we can examine together, rather than another word one side is expected to accept.
None of these turns every learned system into a fully explained one. A local approximation is local. A picture of a feature is not a complete account of why a decision is appropriate for this person. But these are ways of replacing “trust the maths” with something another person can inspect and question.
There is also a distinction between a system performing well on a task and our having a satisfactory explanation of it. We can measure a useful result without yet understanding every internal mechanism. We can also understand an algorithm and still deploy it in the wrong situation. “It cannot explain itself, therefore it cannot work” misses the first point. “It works on our test, therefore you should accept it” misses the second.
There are people on the other side
I have witnessed the fear of being automated in the energy and agriculture sectors. It is easy to stand beside a good demonstration and dismiss that fear as a misunderstanding. It is harder to ask what the person actually expects to lose, and whether our explanation addresses it.
At the time, I did not expect humans to be completely automated. I expected people to be augmented by their silicon counterparts, with more room to investigate, create and understand. That expectation was not an answer to every person's concern about their livelihood. Fear and belief are powerful forces; a technical conversation that ignores them will not remain technical for long.
This is where we need to separate questions that have been bundled together. What can the system do? What evidence supports that claim? Who benefits from using it? Who bears the cost of a mistake? What future do we want? An explanation of a neural network can contribute to that discussion. It cannot settle all of it.
Two different clocks
Even the people building these systems struggle to keep up. There is another paper, another result, another approach that makes last month's limitation look smaller. Objects in the mirror are closer than they appear.
Regulation moves through a different process. It has to consider people who did not choose the experiment, consequences outside the benchmark and rules that can be applied consistently. Due diligence takes time. A fast research cycle and a slower institutional response are a difficult combination, especially when the public conversation mixes measured results, speculative futures and conspiracy theories into one alarming story.
I don't have a complete solution to that. Pretending the research has stopped until the vocabulary catches up will not help. Neither will treating every objection as evidence that the speaker has failed to understand the science.
Both sides need to recognise the communication problem. The people developing the systems have to make their evidence and its limits intelligible. The people questioning them need to distinguish what the evidence says from what they fear or hope it might eventually mean. Philosophical possibilities deserve discussion; the decision about a particular use needs a sufficiently concrete account of that use.
That is why I began with the flat-Earth conversation. Scientific evidence does not become irrelevant because it is difficult to communicate. Difficulty communicating it is a reason to work harder at the explanation, without losing sight of what the scientific community has actually established.
Matthew Zeiler and Rob Fergus, Visualizing and Understanding Convolutional Networks, 2013. The paper investigates intermediate features and the contribution of layers to a classifier. It is one example from the interpretability work that predates this essay, rather than a claim that visualisation began with one researcher.
Marco Tulio Ribeiro, Sameer Singh and Carlos Guestrin, “Why Should I Trust You?”: Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier, 2016. Its explanations approximate behaviour near a selected prediction; they do not supply a universal account of the model or a decision's social legitimacy.
Andrej Karpathy, The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks, 2015; Daniel Smilkov and Shan Carter's TensorFlow Playground, which credits Karpathy's ConvNetJS demonstration and Chris Olah's writing among its predecessors. These are examples of visual teaching, not the first or only work on interpretability.

body:
Radio became Spotify
My grandfather listened to songs on a transistor. My father listens on a phone. The music still plays. The person listening still wants something familiar, something surprising, something that keeps him company. But between those two devices, an entire arrangement of people, businesses and habits has changed.
TV didn't go away. It just became YouTube. Radio became Spotify. Cable became on-demand services such as Netflix. The newspaper became LinkedIn; the magazine became Instagram. The need survived; the way of meeting it opened possibilities that the old arrangement could barely accommodate. That is the lens I use when thinking about AI and a business going through its own transition.
It is easy to tell this story as a parade of faster chips and smaller screens. I grew up with Doordarshan and a roof antenna that needed adjusting. Now each family member can choose a programme, carry it in a pocket, reply to its creator and become a creator themselves. The interesting change is what became possible between the person watching and the person making it. A horizontal flip became a vertical scroll. We changed how we reached the world, and that changed how the world reached us.
When the measure changes
A broadcast programme brings an audience to a time slot. An on-demand service lets someone choose a programme and a time. A creator can publish for a particular audience and hear back from it. Each arrangement gives the people running it different decisions to make, and different things they can observe.
Marketing moved from space in print and a cost per word to keyword bids and advertising built around particular audiences. In that change, the business question moved from TRP toward CAC: from the audience a programme reached to the cost of acquiring a customer. How many people watched? Who responded? What did it cost to bring in someone who pays? When distribution changes, a business can follow more of that path and organise itself around the parts it can now see. Engagement, reach and acquisition cost become operating questions, changing both what the business measures and what it tries to improve.
This is how an interface change grows into a business change. A personal screen makes personal choice possible. That choice produces a different kind of feedback. Feedback changes recommendations and advertising; those change what gets made, who can make a living making it, and what the audience expects next. A new attention economy grows around an old human appetite.
The tempting mistake is to keep the old operating arrangement and add the new interface. Put the same scheduled programme on a smaller screen. Put the same form behind a chatbot. You have changed where the customer presses the button. Have you changed what the customer can do?
The front desk needs the business behind it
In Evolution of AI and its future in B2B, I imagined an AI front desk: a customer could say what they needed instead of learning the company's software. The front desk would draw on what the organisation knew, and the organisation would learn from what happened at the front desk. Distribution, retention, control, efficiency and contracts would all have to develop around that relationship.
Consider a customer whose export has failed. “I have passed this to the team” is an easy answer to generate. Getting the customer a usable export requires more. Someone needs to know what failed, who can investigate, what may be changed and which result will satisfy the customer. If the investigation discovers an old product decision, the reason for that decision matters too. A fluent answer cannot supply a reason the organisation has already forgotten.
Now imagine that the customer can describe the problem, the system can find the relevant history, and the people doing the work can agree the next step in that same conversation. The customer need has stayed the same. The arrangement around it has changed: less re-entry, fewer handovers that lose their purpose, and a shorter path between a question and someone able to act on it.
That is the question behind Weave's design for relationships and work. A conversation can carry a commitment while still being a conversation. The system has to preserve who agreed, what they agreed to and what happened afterwards. Moving a card is a small part of that job. Making the commitment intelligible to the next person is the part that lasts.
For a business considering AI, this changes where the work begins. Start with one costly process and the people who understand it. Follow a real request through to its accepted result. Where does someone have to reconstruct context? Where does the same decision get made again? Where can nobody explain an exception? Those are places where better intelligence might matter, provided the process can make use of it.
What happens to what we remember?
There is another side to the transistor and the phone. A better tool also changes what we practise doing for ourselves. I no longer need to remember every phone number or every turn on a route. The convenience is real. So is the dependency when the information is needed and the tool cannot supply it.
An organisation can do the same thing with its memory. The code still runs, but nobody knows why that feature exists. The document is there, but its conclusion has become detached from the question it answered. A summary travels faster than the conversation that qualified it. Then we ask an AI to work from the summaries and wonder why its confident answer misses the point.
Faster answers can make this worse. The easier it becomes to obtain the next output, the less time we may spend understanding the previous one. Faster, cheaper, better becomes an expectation; that expectation encourages the next tool, which makes the pace feel ordinary again. By the time we look up, the habits and institutions around the work may have changed more than the latest product announcement suggests.
I want to use these tools. I am building them because they can let me pursue more of the questions I care about. The difficulty is carrying the learning forward while the machinery changes. What was tried? Why did it fail? What should the next attempt keep? If every new tool makes us reconstruct that account, we are buying speed by repeatedly losing the explanation.
A publication is a small example
The same problem appears in the writing you are reading. One idea may belong in a standalone essay, help explain a product and become a step in a longer reading journey. Copy the paragraph into three places and each copy can gradually acquire a different meaning. Keep only a private note and the reader never gets the explanation at all.
Gazette gives an article one source while allowing several reading paths to lead to it. The writer still has to do the intellectual work: decide who the explanation is for, keep its assumptions visible, and write a different treatment when a different reader needs one. The publishing system can preserve the relationship between those pieces. It cannot decide that two superficially similar arguments mean the same thing.
Say a second agent takes over a code review. It needs to know which project it is working on, what it may use and how the review is meant to work. Pale’s local tools let you inspect those choices and prepare the repository’s instructions. What I want from the broader design is for that context and responsibility to carry when work moves between applications.
Follow the change through
The radio-to-Spotify lens asks three connected questions. What need persists? What does the new arrangement make possible? And what does using it change about us and the business around it?
Those questions reach beyond a single workflow. If an organisation needs fewer people to produce the same result, where do the savings go? What do its customers now have the money and time to buy? Post-AGI Economics follows that question into income, ownership and demand. A technical improvement has an economic life after the demo.
For the person running a business today, the useful starting point is close at hand. Look at a customer request that ought to be simple and follow what actually happens. Then ask what you would build if the customer could state the need directly, the right history could be found and the people responsible could act without reconstructing the whole story. Keep following it until the result reaches the customer and the organisation learns from it.
My grandfather wanted to hear a song. My father still does. The need gives us continuity. Everything we build around it is where the next possibility begins.

body:
Serving tokens is a service problem
Twenty requests reach a model at once. Another twenty arrive evenly over the same period. The machine can finish the same amount of work in both cases, yet the people waiting experience very different services.
That difference is where inference becomes interesting to me as an operating problem. Learned parameters and fast token generation are necessary ingredients, but the service also has an arrival pattern, a queue, live memory and people expecting a result. A steady base load can justify one capacity arrangement while unpredictable peaks justify another. Long documents, short conversational turns and overnight processing need different schedules even when they use the same model. The economics follows that larger object: what the held-ready capacity can deliver to the work arriving.
The same throughput can feel very different
Imagine a deliberately simple service with one worker. Every request takes exactly 100 milliseconds, and there is no batching or overhead. The arrivals begin at time zero. Only their spacing changes.
Arrival pattern for twenty requests	First result	Last result	Mean arrival-to-completion time	Work completed over two seconds	
All arrive at time zero	0.1 s	2.0 s	1.05 s	20 requests	
One arrives every 0.1 s	0.1 s	2.0 s	0.10 s	20 requests	
For the burst, completion times are 0.1, 0.2, …, 2.0 seconds, whose average is 1.05 seconds. In the spaced case each request arrives just as the worker becomes free. Throughput is ten requests per second in both cases; the 10.5-fold difference in mean response time lives in the queue.
A real inference engine is more complicated, but this example isolates an important point. The arrival process and the queue belong in the performance claim. A throughput figure cannot recover them after they have been discarded.
Rejecting some requests can protect the latency of the rest. That can be a deliberate overload response, but it changes how much attempted demand the service fulfils. A chart of successful requests alone hides the trade.
An answer has more than one clock
Time to first token is the wait before output begins. Time between generated tokens affects the pace of a streamed answer. Total completion time tells a downstream process when the whole result is available. For a conversation, a prompt beginning can make the service more usable. For a process waiting on a complete structured result, the first token may do little to unblock the work. Neither use is wrong. They place value on different points in the same generation process.
Long prompts and long outputs also create different loads. A service processing short questions is not carrying the same work as one reading substantial documents, retaining long contexts and producing extended answers. An average token rate blurs that distinction if it combines input processing and generated output. This is why a benchmark includes a request distribution and an arrival pattern, not just a model name and a device.
Live memory changes the number of users a machine can carry
Autoregressive attention models retain earlier keys and values for each active request. The cache grows as sequences grow, and a serving system has to manage many such sequences together. The PagedAttention paper identifies wasted space from fragmentation and duplicated cache state as limits on batching. Its block-based memory management makes allocation and sharing more flexible, allowing useful serving capacity to change without increasing the model's parameter count or adding another accelerator. How much that helps depends on shared prefixes, sequence lengths and concurrency; the paper's measured speedups describe its evaluated workloads and baselines.
A longer-context feature therefore has a service cost as well as a model meaning. Fitting one request establishes that the state can fit. Carrying many such requests while retaining a latency target is a different operating condition.
Batching trades work efficiency against waiting
Sharing computation across requests can improve hardware use. Waiting for a group can add delay. A long request can occupy resources after shorter requests would otherwise be ready to leave. Continuous batching changes the schedule by bringing new work into the active batch as other requests finish, instead of making every request wait for one fixed group. But scheduling cannot make demand, memory and quality disappear. A policy that is useful under one mix can behave differently when context lengths or arrival bursts change.
The resource model can change too. An attention cache, recurrent state and a hybrid architecture need not have the same memory shape. A serving interface can hide those differences from the application only where it genuinely supports the required behaviour through its selected runtime. The stable boundary is the task the application can rely on, while the implementation remains free to manage its particular kind of state.
The accepted result is the economic denominator
Suppose an illustrative service spends 10 currency units carrying one hundred attempted requests. Ninety meet both the quality and latency condition; ten do not. Cost per attempted request is 0.10. Cost per accepted request is about 0.111, before any correction work outside the service.
If a new configuration doubles raw throughput but increases unacceptable results, its economic benefit depends on that trade. A shorter context, lower precision or smaller model can be an excellent choice for one task and a poor choice for another.
The calculation also includes the idle capacity held for bursts, startup, data movement, retries and the application surrounding the model where those costs apply. Owning a steady base load and renting peaks can produce one cost pattern; renting everything can produce another. Neither arrangement eliminates demand uncertainty.
Procurement has to price the completed work those resources can deliver, including the cost of keeping capacity ready between requests. The distinction from training remains important: a training experiment has a result to reach; a service has people continuing to arrive. Its useful capacity is the work it can give those people under the conditions they depend on.

node.title: The autocorrect paradox
node.description: A decade from image recognition to conversational AI, and why the last distance to useful work keeps demanding better data, adaptation, operations and tools.

body:
The autocorrect paradox
Time has a weird sense of humour. Its cruelty makes prediction harder. And, as usual, what follows wanders through AI, causality and economics.
Let's begin by admitting that FOMO in this field is real. Its scale is distorted, like almost everything else around AI. I wrote this at the end of 2023, the year that made AI cool again. The expectations below belong to that moment: a decade of work behind me, and a particularly loud year ahead.
I started working with machine learning in 2012, as an Electronics and Communication Engineering undergraduate. Digital signal processing, and more particularly digital image processing and computer vision, were my way into it. We were beginning to see flashes of what the field might become. ImageNet and AlexNet made that possibility much harder to ignore.
And if you don't know what OpenAI is, good morning! It's the end of 2023 now. The world's a bit different today, but the little things are the same as ever. :)
Then came the race. Architectures, models, datasets and infrastructure changed in front of us. My own work passed through agriculture, energy efficiency, education, emergency response, wellness and finance. I built products, teams and solutions. Some survived, some changed, and some didn't. My entrepreneurial journey developed alongside the technology, to the point that I couldn't keep up with this shit any more. But I still tried.
And thank God, it was finally cool again.
From AlexNet to GPT-4, the architectures had come a long way. But there was a recurring part of the work. I'll get to it. Wait.
A playground with a much larger entrance
I remember the reinforcement-learning experiments around OpenAI Gym: environments in which we could watch an agent learn by trying things and receiving a reward. TensorFlow and game-development tools gave more people ways to experiment. The playground kept growing.
The Transformer came from a different line of work, sequence modelling, with the 2017 Attention Is All You Need paper. OpenAI built its GPT work on that family of architectures and put extraordinary amounts of capital, talent and data into developing it. The history is more interesting than one invention producing the next in a straight line. The product consequence was simpler: the playground became accessible to people who could type a request.
You could even argue that English had become 2023's most popular programming language. You no longer needed to begin by installing a research environment.
Calling the result a fancy autocomplete can sound dismissive. I don't mean it that way. Predicting a continuation at this scale produced a remarkable range of behaviour. The engineering achievement was enormous. Pre-training supplied broad capabilities; subsequent instruction training and human feedback helped turn those capabilities towards what people were trying to ask. They are different stages, and the chat experience depended on more than simply choosing an architecture.
Almost there. Again.
Here is the recurring part: making the system fit the task.
Across a decade of projects, the relevant data, the training choices and the adaptation kept mattering. “Fine-tuning” names one particular form of that work, further training an existing model. It is not a catch-all for everything done to a model, and it is not the sole reason a system succeeds. But the distance between a generally impressive model and one that behaves usefully in a particular setting kept bringing me back to it.
The model gets almost accurate enough. Almost consistent enough. Almost ready for the person who isn't prepared to spend their day fixing its output. Another improvement moves the boundary, and a new application immediately asks something harder of it.
That is my autocorrect paradox. Always almost intelligent, never quite finished with the last awkward part. A system can be useful before it is perfect. The problem is what it costs to close the remaining gap, and whether the operation around it can live with the errors left over.
By the end of 2023, that limbo was wearing a very fancy dress: trillion-dollar markets and billion-dollar valuations. Underneath were diminishing returns: more infrastructure and operational effort to close the next gap in accuracy. As a society, we are rather good at turning a problem into a newer, fancier problem. Sometimes we even call that solving it.
Looking into 2024, I expected further gains in accuracy, but also systems learning to work with an error-prone AI rather than waiting for perfect accuracy and consistency. The practice round was over; the field was warming up for the big leagues. That adjustment would put pressure on five connected parts of the industry.
Show me the money!
You cannot burn an indefinite amount of capital running a fancy autocomplete. Somewhere, somebody has to explain why the result is worth the bill.
I expected that pressure to favour efficient models and more deliberate adaptation. A smaller general capability, made good at the task that actually earns its place, could be a better investment than paying for the largest model on every request. The comparison has to include the work that succeeds, the retries and the people correcting the failures. A low price per token is a small part of that calculation.
The “autocompletion tax” was my name for the feeling that every extra interaction brought another charge whose relationship to useful work was difficult to see. The answer was not necessarily to avoid an API. It was to make the economics intelligible enough to choose. Capital spent understanding the task and preparing good adaptation data could buy something a larger inference bill would not.
Talk to me like I'm five years old!
As the stakes rose, I expected people to become less willing to pretend they understood what a system was doing or how long it would take.
That creates pressure for observation, explanation and control. Show the work. Explain the failure in terms the person running the operation can recognise. Give them a way to change the relevant part. A reassuring paragraph generated by the same model is not enough to establish why its answer occurred.
This was an engineering opportunity as well as a research problem. A system whose work could be understood would be easier to improve and easier to trust with a consequential task. The question was what kind of explanation would let the responsible person act, rather than merely admire a diagram.
Get your basics right!
Fixing a broken process with AI gives you a broken AI-driven process.
Take a thought experiment: can you write an objective definition of morality that your five closest friends will all accept? Even that small group may discover assumptions it has never had to articulate. Now imagine asking a model to resolve the organisation's undefined exceptions while everyone confidently calls them “the policy”.
Some failures belong to the model. Others reveal a gap in how we have specified the work. If the people responsible cannot say what should happen in a case, the model has not been given a clear decision merely because the request arrived in a polished prompt.
That does not mean every process can be reduced to exhaustive rules, or that a clearer document eliminates hallucination. It means the business has to own its choices. Skip a few of the PowerPoints. Get to the one-pagers that say what we do, why we do it and where a person needs to decide. A win for the process and operations nerds, finally.
Separation of church and state
I expected organisations to become clearer about three different jobs: research, fine-tuning and deployment.
Research explores what a model or method can do. Adaptation brings a selected capability towards a particular task. Deployment keeps the resulting application available and usable. These activities inform one another, but they need different experiments, different measures and often different people.
The tooling around deployment was already drawing attention. I expected more investment in adaptation: collecting useful feedback, preparing datasets, comparing candidate versions and deciding whether the new one actually improved the intended work. Versioning and A/B tests would give the improvement an observable shape. A thumbs-up counter by itself would not.
My 80:20 intuition was that a large share of practical success would come from doing this less spectacular work well. A company did not have to make an architectural breakthrough before learning to use what existed.
I also expected more specialised models and better ways of combining them: a cocktail of intelligence, if you will. The combination needs an application that knows which contribution is appropriate and how to deal with disagreement. Pouring several models into the same glass does not do that for us.
And, of course, FOMO
Anyone who was anyone would try putting AI in X. Some of the combinations would resemble ideas from beer conversations years earlier, finally made feasible by a new capability. Most would still need a useful measure of whether anybody benefited.
My particular bet was on products with a tangible device or experience, with local models playing a large role in consumer adoption. I expected that to make profiling, latency measurement and optimisation more valuable. The software would have to fit the thing people carried or used, not just perform on an engineer's demonstration machine.
A local model would still face the same pressure as the other four: useful work has to survive contact with cost, delay, context and ordinary human expectations.
Better tools under the hood
These pressures pointed towards engineering and productisation that could sustain the field. They also returned me to a deeper question: can we articulate the relationships a model has learned well enough to know what an intervention will change? A useful statistical association and a causal account are not interchangeable. Better tools should help us examine that difference rather than conceal it beneath a more fluent answer.
Data quality, feedback and deliberate adaptation were where I expected much of the practical work to land. From a model answer to a useful product follows the related product decision: what complete job are we promising the person who uses it?
The autocorrect paradox is not a reason to stop. It is a reason to notice what keeps returning. The demonstration gets better, the expectations move, and the work around the model still needs doing. Time has a weird sense of humour.
Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton, ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks, 2012. Its classification result is a milestone in this account, not the beginning of machine learning.
Greg Brockman and colleagues, OpenAI Gym, 2016, describes a common interface to reinforcement-learning benchmark environments. It is distinct from the later Transformer architecture.
Ashish Vaswani and colleagues, Attention Is All You Need, 2017; Alec Radford and colleagues, Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training, 2018. The latter combines generative pre-training and task-specific fine-tuning.
Long Ouyang and colleagues, Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback, 2022, describes supervised demonstrations and reinforcement learning from ranked outputs. Its results support the importance of adaptation; they do not establish that fine-tuning accounts for a fixed percentage of every AI product's success.

node.title: The Blue Pill: if you can’t win AI, survive
node.description: A December 2023 argument for agencies and SaaS businesses: as production gets cheaper, survival depends on focused distribution, trust and outcomes.

body:
The Blue Pill: if you can’t win AI, survive
… and you'll eventually win if you are winning.
Every industry has some form of a power law. In December 2023, I expected AI to skew the rewards disproportionately, making it harder to get a foothold even as it made production easier. The predictions that follow belong to that moment. So how does a business owner keep going within the game as its rules become less comfortable?
Take content creation.
A channel with a million subscribers gets the brand deals. A channel with nine gets none. Yes, that's a deliberately sharp contrast; a small specialist audience can be valuable too. But nobody starts with a million subscribers, and an established distribution gives the next piece of work an advantage that the nine-subscriber channel has to fight to obtain.
For the sake of the calculus, imagine each subscriber has an attention pool. Every view they give your channel spends an attention token from it. There is no cryptocurrency involved here. It's a way of thinking about finite attention and the competing claims on it.
As more content is created, there are more opportunities to ask for those tokens. But the share of any one person's attention that you can capture gets squeezed. Producing more is easier; persuading the same person to spend more of their day with you is a different matter.
Now add AI to that unequal starting position. More published work gives a creator more observations about what people respond to. More distribution gives each new experiment a quicker response. Those observations can inform the next piece of work, and AI can help produce and vary it. Production, feedback and distribution reinforce one another.
The creator with nine subscribers can use the same kind of tool. They do not thereby inherit the million-subscriber channel's history, access or speed of feedback. The larger channel can also offer a brand partner a stronger route to an outcome. Getting a deal can make the next deal easier to get. Getting none leaves you without that particular advantage.
AI did not invent this concentration of rewards. My concern was that it would accelerate it.
What happens to the service business?
Now run that argument through an agency or a software business.
The marginal cost of creating another design, piece of content, collateral or portion of software was, in my expectation, going to move towards something close to zero. Not literally zero. There would still be work, infrastructure and consequences. But enough of the production could become cheap that the commercial expectation would change.
For a particular task, when would AI become inexpensive enough that the old way was no longer a feasible competing offer? I saw the direction as a “when”, not an “if”. The ordering of tasks along that path mattered more than pretending that all of them would change on the same day.
That would push the number of experiments expected per launch up, and the time allowed to reach market down. A customer who can obtain ten plausible variants cheaply will ask why you only tried one. If production is no longer the scarce part, billing for the effort of producing an artefact becomes harder to defend.
The deal starts moving towards the outcome.
What happened after the launch? Did the work produce the result the customer came for? As instrumentation improves, it becomes harder to bullshit your way past that question. The operations involved still matter, but the customer's willingness to pay need not track how many hours you spent performing them.
I expected that pressure to pull down familiar SaaS subscription prices and agency retainers, whether because the costs actually fell or because customers came to believe that they had. Those are different causes with a similar negotiating consequence. The customer expects more for the old price.
More of the contract would therefore concern the result. You would be paid for the trust someone had in your ability to reach it, and for being on call to pacify them when it was “not there yet”. That last bit is less glamorous than a generated demo. It is also much of the relationship.
B2B would begin to absorb more of the tendencies familiar from B2C: the struggle for attention, the expectation of a quicker response and the power of a recognisable voice. So how the hell does one survive in that market?
Win the distribution that sells outcomes
Like it or not, I thought the most consequential move was to win distribution that could sell the outcome.
There was a time when you had websites, and now, you have content distribution.
No one is out there discovering you via your website. SEO nerds will have you believing anything. It can sound like a desperate cry for help.
Waiting for a website to do the work of a relationship is the problem. “We have a site” does not explain who will encounter the business, why they will care or what will earn their trust. Nor does a visit establish that someone paid attention. The argument is not improved by treating discovery, arrival and persuasion as the same event.
Ads give you a more visible mechanism to buy that arrival. They can also make an agency's growth model easier to sell: spend this, measure that, iterate. My argument in 2023 was that ads were becoming more expensive and harder to crack. A black box controlled by a platform remains a black box controlled by a platform. You pay to take part in somebody else's system, under conditions you do not fully control.
Consider an agency proudly presenting a 7% conversion rate from that black box. Are you kidding me? I don't blame them. It's friggin hard. The figure was a rhetorical example, not an industry benchmark or a universal target. Its denominator and the value of the conversion would matter enormously in a real engagement.
Organic growth is harder again, and harder to price as a service. You cannot just promise to buy a predictable amount of someone else's distribution. You have to make work that people choose to encounter, recognise and return to.
No matter how you arrange the commercials, sales is about monetising trust. Branding is about building it. If attention is already divided among a thousand competing demands, a website sitting at the end of a link has very little of it to work with. You have to distribute more, learn what people value and keep earning those tokens until every encounter no longer begins from nothing.
The business has to confront that work. A technically discoverable page and a business people trust answer different parts of the same problem. The point survives whichever search or recommendation surface brings the person to you: what have you done to make the arrival mean something?
More experiments, faster contact with reality
The production-cost argument comes back here. A lower cost per experiment means more experiments per launch. The market's expectation of cheap production puts pressure on your price. An outcome promise puts pressure on the time it takes you to learn what works.
Eventually one of those experiments may help you land “that deal”. Then the deal count grows, and the feedback you can use grows with it.
I expected more of the routine work to become automated and some forms of human error to fall, bringing a capable team to its outcome faster. The expertise still had to be there. If you had it, the tools could help you deliver. If you didn't, your delusion would meet reality faster than you could type “outcome”.
And all of that was going to happen after you had won enough distribution to get the opportunity.
That is why a reusable mechanism can matter to a service business. Work done for one engagement may teach the team something it can apply again, without making a client's records or particular design everybody else's property. DAO Studio's account of turning service work into reusable capability develops that operational question: what can accumulate between engagements, and what must remain with the partner? Reuse can improve the ability to deliver. Distribution still has to earn the next conversation.
The bitter pill: you cannot win all distribution
You cannot be everywhere. You cannot win everyone's attention. The survival argument therefore ends in focused, hyper-specific niches.
The calculus changes when a small group cares deeply about a particular problem. Nine subscribers drawn at random and nine people who share a costly, urgent problem are not the same starting position. The niche does not remove the need for trust. It gives that work a more definite subject and a more plausible audience.
That also leads to an uncomfortable valuation prediction. If a business's realistically reachable market was much smaller than its story suggested, I expected the willingness to accept outrageous price-to-earnings ratios to disappear. A claimed total addressable market would have to meet the resources actually available to win it. These were conditional expectations about how the business landscape might change, not a measured market result or a valuation rule supplied by AI.
With limited resources, survival would become a matter of dominating a useful niche's distribution. Keep improving at the margin until the industry's concentration of rewards begins working in your favour. If you are still surviving as an agency and keep winning deals, those deals can make further deals easier. The same reinforcing pattern can work for a product subscription. It can also work against you when the opportunities keep shrinking.
That is the blue pill. Keep playing, get specific about the outcome, earn the trust and survive long enough for the work to compound.
There is another option: The Red Pill. It asks why the framework for exchanging value has to remain organised around jobs and the same competitive game at all. This essay asks how a business survives inside it. The next asks what else we might choose to build.

node.title: The clock starts before the model
node.description: A streaming speech interface must meet its latency, memory and language obligations in the same operating conditions.

body:
The clock starts before the model
A speech model can process audio faster than real time and still make a person wait too long. The processing rate says whether the system can keep up. It does not say when enough audio arrives, when the recogniser commits its answer or when the interface responds.
Imagine an on-device voice interface that must follow a short command through background noise and language switching. Its promise is a person speaking naturally and receiving a usable response without depending on the cloud. That promise connects the listening window, the model and the action that follows the transcript. The examples below ask what a complete measurement would have to include.
Where the clock begins
Suppose a hypothetical recogniser collects 320 milliseconds of audio before processing a chunk. Its computation takes 150 milliseconds. Those numbers describe different intervals. Measuring only the second makes the recogniser look faster than the experience that includes waiting for the first. Continuous processing can overlap collection and computation after the pipeline starts. That does not erase the initial wait or a final decision to hold an unstable transcript until more speech arrives. A timer starting at the beginning of a command will also include the command's duration; a timer starting at the end asks a different question.
These stipulated timings expose different interface questions. Time to first partial text tells us when a person begins to see recognition; time from the end of speech to a committed response tells us when they can expect the command to proceed. The design may need both. A single “latency” figure becomes useful only when the events it measures are clear.
Interval in the illustrative first chunk	Starts	Ends	Duration	
Audio collection	First sample	Complete chunk available	320 ms	
Chunk computation	Complete chunk available	Chunk result available	150 ms	
First-chunk path without overlap	First sample	Chunk result available	470 ms	
Note
This is a timing sketch, not a benchmark or the final command-response time. In a pipeline, later collection and computation may overlap. Endpoint detection, lookahead and committing the transcript add their own intervals. They need positions on the same clock rather than disappearing into an average processing rate.
A model file is only part of memory
Now suppose a quantised model's weights fit on the device. The runtime still needs activations, audio buffers, decoder state, caches and workspace. Other services need memory too. The useful quantity is peak demand under the intended operation, not the size of the downloaded file.
Compression can also move the cost instead of removing it. If the accelerator cannot execute an operator, computation may fall back to the CPU. Transfers and conversions can consume time even when the nominal arithmetic count falls. The deployed graph and its actual placement matter more than a precision label in a proposal. For example, ONNX Runtime’s execution providers select the nodes or subgraphs a backend can execute. The model’s presence in one file does not mean every operation runs on one processor.
That is especially consequential in a streaming encoder. A convolution may map neatly to the accelerator while normalisation or another unsupported operation returns to the CPU. Repeating that crossing through several layers can spend the latency saved by compressing the weights. A useful profile separates accelerator work, CPU fallback and transfer time for the same chunk. It can then test whether changing an operator, reducing depth or choosing a different streaming architecture helps the complete path.
A cold start, a long utterance and several active streams stress different parts of that budget. The intended use determines which conditions matter: a brief-command interface needs a representative command test, while a system carrying continuous streams has another memory and scheduling problem. A useful measurement follows the operation being promised.
The language task has to stay the same
A command can cross languages inside a sentence. A recogniser tested separately on clean English and Hindi has not thereby been tested on that switch, particularly when names and place names carry the meaning of the request.
Consider “Rajesh ko call karo.” A transcript might preserve most ordinary words while getting the person's name wrong. Average word error is useful, but the contact error matters differently to the intended task. That does not justify abandoning the transcript metric. It means pairing it with the consequences the interface is supposed to handle.
Evaluation also needs consistent transcription and tokenisation rules. Apparent differences can reflect spelling or segmentation conventions rather than recognition alone. Comparing different systems on different audio cannot establish a winner for the same on-device task.
The strongest test names its audio set, streaming policy and target device. It examines noise, switching and regional variation together, with enough detail to see which cases became worse after compression. A mean can improve while a particular group or command becomes harder to recognise.
One configuration has to carry the whole task
Imagine one configuration meets the memory limit but loses important names, a second improves recognition but misses the response window, and a third runs quickly only on clean audio. Each result teaches something. None establishes a configuration that meets all the obligations together. An architecture proposal therefore needs a joint operating test. The report should identify the exact model, precision, compiler, device, stream and data conditions, then show latency, memory and recognition quality for that same configuration. Sustained behaviour matters when heat or accumulated state can change performance after the first successful command.
Even that result would not establish safe action. A transcript is a candidate interpretation of speech. Choosing a contact, placing a call and handling ambiguity belong to the surrounding interface, with their own confirmation and failure behaviour.
Published architectures give us concrete choices to examine. Conformer combines convolution and attention to model local and wider relationships in audio. Squeezeformer revisits that design, reducing sequence-processing work and simplifying parts of the network. Those papers establish particular architecture and benchmark comparisons. Selecting either for this hypothetical interface would still require a streaming policy and a complete measurement on the intended device.
The choice becomes clearer when the same command is carried through each design. Does a simpler encoder reduce CPU fallback enough to compensate for a recognition loss? Does keeping attention at higher precision preserve a switched-language name while exhausting the memory margin? Does a model that recognises the whole utterance well need too much future audio to answer at the intended moment? Each choice changes another part of the budget. Borrowing a small footprint from one model, an accuracy score from another and a speed figure from another chip would conceal that conflict rather than resolve it.
The first useful comparison would therefore be a small joint experiment: the same noisy, code-switched commands, an explicit chunk and endpoint policy, each candidate's complete runtime, and its own target device. It would report the command's name and intent errors alongside peak memory and response intervals. That comparison could reject an architecture before expensive training, or show exactly which part deserves further work.
An experiment that can change the design
Comparing architectures under those same conditions lets the experiment change the design. A smaller model may leave room for a more useful decoder; another streaming policy may shorten the wait without changing the model. The winning configuration is the one that carries the command through the whole interface, rather than winning one isolated metric.
What makes the problem worth exploring is that the interface can improve at several points. Earlier useful partial recognition can shorten perceived waiting; a suitable streaming policy can limit accumulated state; a confirmation step can recover from a misheard name before the wrong call begins. The model contributes to all of this, but the person's experience begins before it runs and continues after it returns.

body:
The cluster is only the beginning
Sixteen accelerators have been allocated. The status is green. The training team is still waiting: its image cannot reach the dataset, one worker has a different library version, and the checkpoint destination has not been configured. The hardware exists, but the experiment has nowhere coherent to happen.
This imagined scene exposes a product boundary that a capacity catalogue can miss. A developer buys a path through work, not merely possession of devices. The useful path begins before allocation and continues after computation, through preparation, access, observation, retained results and release. Building a GPU service means deciding which parts of that path the platform makes dependable and which choices remain with its user.
Different journeys need different products
An inference service is expected to keep receiving requests. Fine-tuning has a bounded dataset, a base model and an artifact to produce. Distributed training coordinates workers whose collective state matters. Each can use accelerators, but their useful beginnings and endings differ. For inference, an endpoint becoming reachable is only the start of carrying its actual request mix. For training, a healthy group has to agree on the run and eventually preserve a checkpoint that can be resumed or evaluated.
A common allocation interface can support all three without making their readiness identical. Kubernetes illustrates the distinction at a narrower layer: its GPU scheduling documentation describes device plugins, resource declarations and node selection. Those mechanisms make devices available to a workload. They do not supply the application's dataset, determine its experiment or establish that its result met the user's need. The platform's opportunity is to connect these layers into a recognisable journey rather than present every lower-level success as completion.
Consider a hypothetical fine-tuning request. The user supplies an approved dataset reference, a base-model revision, a training configuration and a destination for the resulting adapter. The service resolves the environment and storage, acquires suitable capacity, records the run configuration, exposes progress and retains the artifact. A worker becoming available is one useful milestone. An artifact reaching its destination is another. The evaluation of that artifact answers a further question. Keeping those milestones visible lets the user recover the position of the work when it stops.
The journey exposes a different recovery question at each point:
Position in this fine-tuning job	Evidence useful to the user	If work stops here	
Environment prepared	Image, dependencies, base-model revision	Repair the environment before consuming the booked run	
Data reachable	Approved dataset and successful access within its limits	Resolve the access failure without changing the dataset silently	
Workers joined	Intended group and shared run configuration	Identify the missing or inconsistent worker	
Run advancing	Progress and retained checkpoints	Resume from declared state or make the restart explicit	
Adapter retained	Artifact destination and producing configuration	Recover the result independently of the rented machines	
Resources released	Removed allocations and deliberately retained storage	Investigate resources still accruing cost without destroying the artifact	
This is why a useful status view follows the job, not just the devices. “Data access blocked” and “training failed” lead the user to different next actions even when both leave the accelerators idle.
Responsibility has a shape above the hardware
Suppose the provider supplies a functioning machine, the platform selects its operating environment, and the tenant supplies application code. A failed job may begin in any of those places. An interface that reports only “provider error” gives each party an incentive to send the problem elsewhere. A better account connects the failure to the layer that can investigate it: device health, environment construction, dataset access, scheduler admission or the application's own exception.
The exact division depends on the service. Bare metal and a managed container do not hand over the same responsibilities. Neither label settles who patches the operating system, controls network access, gathers usage, removes a volume or preserves a result. Those decisions influence the API, support process and price. They also determine what the platform must observe itself rather than assume from the provider's reply.
Cleanup is a revealing example. Deleting a training allocation can be successful while leaving a paid volume behind. Removing every resource together can destroy a checkpoint that another run needs. The meaningful operation is therefore attached to the lifecycle of the work: release this allocation, retain this artifact and remove these temporary resources. The platform needs resource identities and dependencies precise enough to carry that decision through the provider's actual controls.
Readiness belongs to a particular workload
A provider screen becomes more useful when it begins with the journey's hard dependencies. Can the desired allocation be obtained and released at the required granularity? Can the environment reach the data? Can the needed communication pattern run? What happens to retained state when a machine is replaced? A score may compare eligible offers afterwards, but a high average cannot repair a missing prerequisite.
Imagine two offers. One supplies a single node quickly and can remove workers independently; the other takes longer but supplies the tightly connected group a training run needs. There is no contradiction in choosing the first for an elastic service and the second for a scheduled experiment. A product that pools them into one undifferentiated inventory asks its users to rediscover the workload boundary themselves. A more useful catalogue describes the capabilities through which each offer becomes usable.
The same boundary gives the start clock a practical meaning. Allocated, reachable and workload-ready are different times. A benchmark that begins only after successful setup can explain execution while hiding most of the user's wait. For procurement, that wait remains part of the completed job's economics.
The result should survive the rented machine
A compute service becomes more valuable when the user can leave it with the useful work intact. That means more than an export button. An artifact needs enough configuration and provenance to be understood elsewhere, storage needs a deliberate retention policy, and the next environment needs an actual way to consume the result. A checkpoint that restores only on the original shape gives a different freedom from one that supports the intended replacement.
This is where a platform can reduce a developer's burden without pretending to remove the underlying complexity. It can remember the environment, make failure attributable, expose the interval that remains and preserve the result separately from the allocation. The rented cluster then becomes one stage in the experiment rather than the container of its entire history. The product is the dependable passage through those stages.

node.description: Installed capacity keeps consuming resources; a smaller bill can conceal a larger cost per useful result.

body:
The cost of an idle fleet
A quiet compute fleet can have a smaller electricity bill and a worse cost per completed job. The apparent contradiction disappears once we separate what the operator spends from what the capacity produces. Expense can fall more slowly than useful work.
The customer's cost per accepted result includes the resources bought to obtain it. The operator faces another question: what does the installed system cost across the periods in which it works, waits and remains available? A paid reservation, an active device and useful output are different quantities on this side of the marketplace too.
Idle is a state, not zero power
An awake server can consume energy without advancing its intended workload. ENERGY STAR's guidance on unused servers identifies this waste and describes why removing unnecessary equipment can also reduce cooling and power-infrastructure demand. That does not supply a universal idle percentage for modern GPU systems. The actual equipment and its operating states need measurement.
An unallocated machine, an allocated machine waiting for data, a busy machine repeating failed work and a powered-down machine can all appear as "not producing" on an output report. Their electrical behaviour and obligations differ. A spare machine kept ready for recovery is not necessarily abandoned capacity. A server with little CPU activity may still provide a service whose availability matters.
The accounting boundary also has to include the supporting system. Host processors, memory, storage, networking, fans and power conversion are not free because the accelerator is waiting. Neither does the entire facility's cooling load disappear when one job stops.
A smaller bill can buy fewer results
Consider a deliberately invented 100-hour operating period. An IT group draws 12 kW while working and 4 kW while awake but idle. Assume facility overhead is a constant 2 kW, electricity costs 0.2 arbitrary currency units per kWh, and continuing cash expenses excluding electricity are 600 units for the period. Assume the same workload produces two accepted jobs per working hour, with no failed attempts.
These assumptions are a toy model, not a GPU specification, tariff or facility measurement. They hold the workload and acceptance condition constant so that the denominator can be seen clearly.
Measure over the same 100 hours	Working for 25 hours	Working for 75 hours	
IT energy	600 kWh	1,000 kWh	
Facility overhead energy	200 kWh	200 kWh	
Total facility energy	800 kWh	1,200 kWh	
Electricity expense	160 units	240 units	
Continuing cash expense including electricity	760 units	840 units	
Accepted jobs	50	150	
Cash expense per accepted job	15.20 units	5.60 units	
The first IT-energy figure is 12 × 25 plus 4 × 75. The second is 12 × 75 plus 4 × 25. Each then adds 2 × 100 for facility overhead.
For w working hours in this fixed hundred-hour period, the same assumptions give:

\begin{aligned}
E_{\text{facility}}(w)&=12w+4(100-w)+2(100)=600+8w\quad\text{kWh},\\
K_{\text{cash}}(w)&=600+0.2E_{\text{facility}}(w)=720+1.6w,\\
J(w)&=2w,\\
\frac{K_{\text{cash}}(w)}{J(w)}&=\frac{360}{w}+0.8,\qquad w>0.
\end{aligned}

The last expression reveals the shape of the cost: a fixed period expense spread across more work, plus a per-job term. At zero working hours there are expenses and no jobs over which to divide them. A chart should leave that point undefined, not quietly display a zero cost.
The quieter period spends 80 units less, yet produces one-third as many accepted jobs. Its cost per job is consequently much higher. This does not mean more activity is always desirable. It means that a lower aggregate expense cannot by itself demonstrate a more economical service.
Cash expense and capital consumption answer different questions
The toy model's 600 units represent expenses that continue during the period, such as a declared combination of staffing, maintenance and committed space or connectivity. Actual costs may change in steps rather than remain fixed indefinitely. The assumption is about this interval, not every possible scale of operation.
It deliberately excludes equipment acquisition. Paying for a machine and allocating its cost across its useful life are not the same event. For a longer-run cost comparison, suppose we separately assign 400 units of equipment cost to this period. The combined cost becomes 1,160 or 1,240 units, giving approximately 23.20 or 8.27 units per accepted job.
That added allocation is not another electricity invoice or proof of a cash payment during these hundred hours. It is an explicit assumption about spreading equipment cost. A real lifecycle comparison also needs its horizon, replacement and residual-value assumptions, with financing treated consistently. Mixing purchase payments, depreciation and repayments without a stated boundary can count the same equipment more than once.
Conversely, equipment already paid for is not free to own indefinitely. Continuing support, replacement and the capacity reserved for it remain questions even when the immediate cash needed to run one more job is small. Marginal dispatch and long-run capacity planning require different calculations.
PUE measures a boundary, not useful work
The Green Grid defines power usage effectiveness as total data-centre energy divided by ICT-equipment energy:

\mathrm{PUE}=\frac{E_{\text{facility}}}{E_{\text{IT}}}.

In the toy example, that ratio is 800/600, about 1.33, in the quieter period and 1,200/1,000, or 1.20, in the busier one.
The busier case has the lower ratio and consumes more total electricity. The arithmetic follows from the assumed constant overhead. It is not evidence that real overhead is constant: cooling and electrical-system behaviour must be measured over the relevant loads and conditions.
More importantly, neither ratio contains accepted jobs. Two systems can have the same PUE and deliver different work. Within one system, failed work can increase IT energy and alter the ratio without improving the service. PUE helps locate infrastructure overhead; it cannot certify application efficiency or commercial viability.
Occupancy is useful only alongside the workload
A supplier may earn revenue for an allocation even when the customer is still preparing data. That allocation can be commercially meaningful without creating accepted output yet. Conversely, a faster model can finish the customer's work in fewer allocated hours, improving the customer's economics while leaving the operator more capacity to sell or manage.
The operator therefore needs to distinguish occupied time, activity, accepted work and the terms under which capacity is paid for. An energy bill does not establish revenue, and dividing cost by accepted jobs does not establish profit. Different services may have different acceptable output units; summing unlike tokens, experiments and simulations into one flattering fleet total does not make them comparable.
For the toy model, if the busier period accepts only 135 rather than 150 jobs, its unchanged 840-unit cash expense becomes about 6.22 per accepted job. The machine hours have not changed. The outcome has. Model efficiency and acceptance remain separate observations that help explain the difference.
Energy management has to preserve the promised work
Consolidating work or powering down unnecessary equipment can reduce waste. But an idle interval may be the headroom required for an imminent booking, a recovery path or a burst of requests. Removing it without understanding the promise can trade a visible energy saving for a service failure.
Moving a workload can consume the saving before useful work resumes. Its data must arrive, the destination must support the same environment, and a checkpoint must restore the right state. If the job's data must remain in a particular location, a cheaper remote machine cannot supply the booked service at all. If restarting takes longer than the recovery window, shutting down the idle spare removes capacity the customer was paying to have ready. The occupancy report alone contains none of those obligations.
The useful test is whether the change reduces resources for the same accepted service, including startup, checkpointing, restoration and the deadline. An alternative that saves energy but cannot restore progress in time has changed the product. That may be an acceptable renegotiation; it is not the original promise fulfilled more efficiently.
The aim is neither to keep every device busy nor to minimise electricity at any cost. It is to match installed capacity, operating states and available demand to useful work, while keeping the commitments that make the work worth doing. The fleet's quiet periods belong in that account, not outside it.

body:
The label is a decision
“The delivery arrived, but I still cannot use it.” One annotator marks the message as resolved because the package arrived. Another marks it unresolved because the customer cannot do the work. Both have read the same sentence. Their disagreement begins in the task's definition, before either person makes a careless click.
This invented example is why I find annotation interesting as a product problem. A label compresses a judgement into a form another system can use. Its value depends on the distinctions that survive the compression: what counts as an item, what the category means, which context the annotator sees and how ambiguity is resolved. Recruiting more annotators can increase throughput while multiplying an unclear decision.
The task determines the object being labelled
If the intended model detects delivery complaints, the sentence may belong to that category. If it decides whether a support matter can close, arrival alone is inadequate. If it extracts events, it might record the arrival and the inability to use the item separately. A single “positive” or “negative” label would obscure all three tasks in different ways. The question is therefore not how detailed an ontology can become, but which distinctions the downstream job actually needs.
An annotation project also differs from its dataset. The same source items can support different tasks, using different guidelines, access and output definitions. A dataset may contain whole conversations while a task labels individual turns. Deciding where a unit begins and ends affects what the annotator can infer and what the model is later evaluated against. A short utterance separated from its preceding question can acquire a different meaning.
The label system needs to carry those choices. In a hypothetical support dataset, “arrival reported,” “usable result confirmed” and “matter closed” can be separate observations. If the product only needs one of them, unnecessary fields add work. If it needs all three, forcing them into one status teaches the model a convenient ambiguity. The ontology is part of the product's theory of the work.
Guidelines turn a category into a repeatable judgement
A category name rarely carries enough meaning by itself. A guideline can supply its definition, positive and negative examples, boundary cases and an honest way to mark missing context. In the delivery example, the rule could explicitly say that arrival is insufficient for usable completion. A pilot then reveals whether annotators can apply that distinction consistently or whether the rule still leaves difficult cases unresolved.
An illustrative guideline for usable result confirmed could require an explicit statement that the customer can perform the intended task. It would produce these different decisions:
Source statement	Annotation	Reason under this guideline	
“It arrived, but I still cannot use it.”	No	The customer explicitly reports unusability	
“It arrived.”	Unknown	Arrival is reported; usability is not	
“It arrived and I can complete the job now.”	Yes	The intended use is explicitly confirmed	
The middle row is the important one. An annotator inferring “yes” from delivery and another choosing “unknown” have exposed a missing rule if the guideline never addressed absent evidence. Once the rule is explicit, the same disagreement has a different diagnostic meaning. A missing statement should not be forced into a negative outcome either: unknown and unusable are different training targets.
Disagreement is useful here. One participant may have missed an explicit rule; another may have found a case the rule never considered. Those failures need different responses. Training can help the first. Revising the task or its guideline may be necessary for the second. Treating every disagreement as worker error prevents the product from learning where its own meaning is incomplete.
Changing a guideline also changes the interpretation of the output. Suppose earlier batches treated any delivery report as closing the matter and later batches require usability. Combining them without their rule versions gives the learner two definitions under one label. The model may appear inconsistent while accurately following the inconsistent training material. Versioning links an annotation to the meaning under which it was made, and identifies which earlier items need review rather than silently reinterpreting them.
Agreement measures consistency
Imagine one hundred hypothetical items, all marked resolved by three annotators. Agreement is complete. If thirty items actually describe unusable deliveries and the task requires usability, unanimous labelling has preserved the same error. Consistency answers a different question from the adequacy of the task's interpretation.
Artstein and Poesio's survey distinguishes agreement, reliability and validity and examines the assumptions of agreement coefficients. The important practical consequence is to ask what a score measures before turning it into acceptance. Category prevalence, annotation units and the treatment of missing or uncertain answers affect the comparison. A threshold borrowed from an unrelated task cannot decide whether these labels are useful for this product.
An independent review can inspect the interpretation, including difficult cases and repeated errors. Majority convergence can resolve some variation, but three people trained on the same inadequate rule do not supply three independent grounds for its correctness. Expertise also belongs to the task: recognising a technical failure, a linguistic ambiguity and a domain-specific consequence may require different kinds of review.
Completion has a quality path
Submission means someone supplied an annotation. Review, correction and acceptance have different work to do afterwards. A fast queue with high rework may deliver less useful data than a slower first pass. Counting only accepted items can hide the effort spent getting them there. Conversely, a difficult disagreement that improves the guidelines may create value beyond the particular item that triggered it.
Assistance can change that path. A model may pre-label items so people correct rather than begin from nothing. The experiment then concerns the combined process: time saved, errors retained, cases ignored and the effect of showing the suggestion before an independent judgement. If every reviewer sees the same suggestion, apparent agreement can reflect a shared starting point. Comparing an assisted route with a suitable independent baseline gives the claimed efficiency an actual object to measure.
In learning whether context helped, a system faces the same choice of what to reward. Offered information, use, agreement and eventual task outcome are related observations, but rewarding one in place of another can train the wrong behaviour. Useful quality begins by keeping the outcome the annotation is meant to support in view.
The dataset carries the circumstances of its making
A released or transferred dataset needs more than rows and labels. Its sampling, sources, task definitions, rule changes and review process affect what another person can learn from it. Datasheets for Datasets proposes documenting motivation, composition, collection and intended uses to make those decisions intelligible to consumers. Such an account helps a team recognise when the material fits its task and when another population or context needs new work.
The delivery example could become a useful training resource if its categories preserve the distinction between an item arriving and a customer succeeding. It could become a misleading one if the same words conceal changing definitions. Annotation makes human judgement available to another system; its quality lies in how faithfully that judgement carries the task's meaning into the next use.
