body:
Frame a useful judgment
Someone tells you they received the same notice twice. You can investigate how it was prepared, check delivery or ask for another record. Which would help you find the cause? When an agent reaches a choice like this and Pale's rules allow several options, something has to say which one to look at first. That is the Judgment Host's job, the first of Counsel’s two. No host runs yet; this example follows one recommendation through the design: the question, the evidence behind possible answers and what you can do with the advice.
Turn an open problem into a question the model can answer
Suppose the preparation record shows one notice and the delivery record shows two events. You have a reason to look at delivery, but you do not yet know what caused the duplicate. Pale gives the model those records and the choices it may compare, with a deadline and resource limits for the answer.
A useful question connects that evidence to the choice:
Which part of this duplicate notice should we investigate next? One notice was prepared, and its delivery record contains two events. Compare investigating preparation, investigating delivery and asking for a missing observation. Recommend a next step and explain what supports it. Do not resend the notice or assign work.
“Why did this happen?” asks for a cause the records do not yet explain. Asking where to investigate gives the model a choice it can support. The distinction also makes the next human action clear.
Important
Supply only records you may share with the host. Say when they were recorded and flag gaps or conflicts that could change the answer. Leave out unavailable choices. The model cannot make an option available or fetch missing records itself.
See what the advice rests on
One prepared notice and two delivery events point toward investigating delivery. They do not yet prove a delivery fault. Each event could represent an attempted delivery, for example, rather than a received copy.
Different evidence should lead to different advice. These illustrative answers show what changes:
Available evidence	Useful answer	Your next step	
One prepared notice and two delivery events	Recommend investigating delivery	Find out what each event did	
Two received copies, with no preparation or delivery history	Ask whether one notice was delivered twice or two were prepared	Obtain the record that distinguishes those cases	
Conflicting preparation records with no way to tell which applies	Explain why the evidence cannot support a choice	Resolve the conflict before relying on a recommendation	
A recommendation proposes one option. A ranking orders the choices you supplied. A clarifying question asks for information that could tell them apart, and can be sent only to a destination Pale has allowed. An abstention means the model cannot support a choice, even if it has no useful question to ask.
Decide what to do next
The task’s rules determine whether Pale may act on the advice or must ask a person. You can follow it, reject it or ask for a decision. Here, following it means starting a delivery investigation through the normal process. Counsel does not assign the work or resend the notice.
Keep what the model advised, what you decided and what the investigation found. If you corrected the advice, record the correction. Pale keeps each call and its result as a record in its genealogy, the history of context, which is what Reckon learns from to tell whether the advice helped. A useful later discovery tells you what the investigation found, while the earlier records tell you whether the model's answer was reasonable. Advice at the decision boundary explores the distinction.
If no answer arrives
A model saying “these records cannot support a choice” has answered the question. A timeout, cancellation, unavailable host or malformed response leaves you without a usable judgment. Those failures need different remedies: restoring the host may let it answer, but repeating the same question cannot supply missing evidence.
If the question requires a judgment, Pale must escalate or stop when the host cannot answer. An optional judgment uses its configured fallback; unrelated work can continue.
Find the records before comparing the choices
Counsel’s separate Memory host helps Scope find relevant records: compare passages by meaning, suggest links, summarise and reorder results. That is a different job from deciding where to investigate. Find knowledge with model assistance follows a maintenance search through that service and its own permissions.
Understand which model supplied the advice
The answer identifies its model, runtime and machine. Those details help explain an answer’s quality and the time it took. Understand a model and its improvement explains how to compare replacements and why learning happens outside live operation.

body:
Find knowledge with model assistance
You need the maintenance procedure for a machine, but searching for “maintenance” misses a manual filed under “servicing the equipment.” Counsel’s Memory host helps Scope find that connection, with Pale or, where Scope works over Weave, without it. No host runs yet; this example follows one search through the design.
Find the procedure that applies
A passage about servicing gets you closer, but it may describe another machine or an older procedure. You need the current instruction for this equipment. The four kinds of model assistance help at different points in that search.
Aid	How it helps	What to check	
Embedding	Represent the meaning of your question and passages as numbers, so similar meanings can be compared	Does the passage actually apply to this machine?	
Candidate link	Suggest a connection between a machine record and a service instruction	Is the connection supported by its sources and permitted for this request?	
Summary	Give you a shorter account of a passage	Can you still tell when the procedure applies and what its warnings require?	
Reranking	Put the most relevant of the eligible results first	Is the highest result current, rather than simply a close match?	
An embedding could bring the differently worded passage into the search results. A suggested link could connect it to the machine record, and reranking could put it ahead of less relevant instructions. You would still check the machine and revision before relying on it. A summary helps you see what a long procedure covers; it cannot safely replace the procedure when you act.
Caution
Open the procedure before acting. A summary can omit a required shutdown warning or hide a conflict the original makes clear.
Check whether the instruction may go to a model
You may be allowed to read the maintenance instruction without being allowed to send it to a model or share a summary with someone else. In the integrated design, Pale checks permission to send it. The memory host checks whether it may process that material, and Scope checks whether it may store and use the returned aid. Permission at one step cannot stand in for the next.
A result identifies its source revision, producing model and purpose. The host works from the material supplied for the request, without browsing source systems or obtaining more records on its own.
When a summary becomes out of date
If the service interval changes, an old summary must not keep presenting the previous interval as current. Scope checks freshness and permission each time a summary or embedding is used, including results restored from a backup. Depending on those rules, the old result may need to be refreshed, invalidated or removed.
The same applies when access is revoked: a cached summary or embedding cannot preserve permission to use its source. Removing that aid does not delete the owner's original instruction.
The model profile also stays attached to each result. Changing models would not silently relabel old embeddings or summaries as the new model's work. The memory service could be replaced independently of Counsel's judgment service.
Find the instruction without model assistance
Scope’s strict mode is designed to work without this host, since it needs no model. It can still retrieve items their owner has pinned: a maintenance owner might require the shutdown procedure to accompany a machine's service instructions. That pin says to include an item; it is different from fixing a particular source version. Access and freshness checks still come first, so a pin cannot restore a revoked or obsolete instruction. Understand the retrieval modes explains the available retrieval methods and what full mode could add through this host.
If the host becomes unavailable, a request allowing strict fallback could continue without model assistance and report that limitation. It would exclude cached model-made aids as well as new calls. A request requiring full mode would stop instead of quietly returning a different kind of search.
Scope working with Weave alone also offers model assistance without running a Pale daemon. It uses Pale’s Counsel port as a library to reach the configured memory host. Scope checks the retrieval request, the host separately checks permission to process the instruction, and Scope checks the returned aid before storing or using it.
Once you have the applicable instruction, you may still have a choice to make. Frame a useful judgment follows that next question through Counsel’s separate judgment service.

body:
Understand a model and its improvement
Suppose a model recommends investigating delivery every time someone reports a duplicate notice. Sometimes it is right. Sometimes the records give it no reason to choose delivery over preparation. A replacement is useful if it can tell those cases apart within the time and memory available. This is how Counsel compares models. No Counsel host runs yet, so this page follows the comparison as the design sets it out.
Compare answers to the same questions
The duplicate-notice example supplies several cases: one prepared notice and two delivery events, two received copies with no history, and conflicting preparation records. A useful model could recommend an investigation in the first case, ask for the missing record in the second and explain why it cannot choose in the third. A model that always abstains avoids some wrong answers but offers little help.
Important
Set the cases and passing criteria before comparing models. Check answer quality, when the model knows to abstain, response time, memory use and what happens when requests arrive together. A larger model has to improve the actual task enough to justify its cost.
Keep the setup with each result. A model may answer differently if its prompt template changes, and it may take longer on another machine. Counsel calls this account a model profile: the saved model weights, tokenizer and prompt template, numerical precision, runtime, backend and machine. Without those details, a later comparison could attribute a change to the model when something else changed.
The first setup would use a fixed model or a test stand-in with predefined answers. The stand-in could show whether requests, cancellation and recovery work. A fixed model would let you compare the quality of answers and return to a known setup when testing a replacement.
The Memory host would need its own comparison. A model that recommends the right investigation might still miss a useful passage or omit a warning from a summary.
Improve judgment through experience
Suppose the model recommends delivery, a reviewer notices that two notices were prepared, and the team fixes preparation instead. The problem is solved, but training on the successful outcome alone would reward the wrong recommendation. Learning needs to keep what the model knew and advised separate from the correction, the decision and the eventual result.
One proposed research path starts with supervised learning from independently assessed judgments. Learning from measured outcomes would be a further step. Both would happen outside live operation, using evidence separately permitted for training. The cases would come from Pale's genealogy, the history it keeps of each question, and from the evaluations Reckon records against them. Held-out cases would check whether a candidate improves useful answers without losing earlier capabilities or exposing private information. What a judgment can learn from develops the research question.
A model and the procedure around it can change together. Compare each separately as well as the combination, or an improvement in the procedure could be mistaken for a better model. Improving the system between runs explains that distinction.
Could a learning unit become the judge?
The first local judge gives the work a starting point while research explores a different kind of model. MUON studies a small reasoning unit that could learn within a defined task and resource budget. That makes it a candidate for Counsel’s narrow judgment questions. Everyday decisions could supply useful comparison cases, where their owners permit research use.
HENA asks how many such units might communicate, use limited memory and develop useful hierarchy. A system built from those units might eventually take over some of Pale’s explicit coordination; how it would do so and where it would fit remain research questions. A HENA-backed model could also be tested as a model provider behind a coding harness, a separate use from Counsel’s local judge. A future unit would have to improve on the initial model on the same cases before replacing it; the ability to learn is not itself evidence that it gives better advice.
Any successor would need to improve the work while preserving the capabilities people rely on. It would take questions and return answers through the same interface, so replacing the model would not require Pale to change how it asks for advice. Pale would check that the new setup is approved for its questions before switching. Keep the previous setup available to compare results and switch back if needed.

arguments.label: A question through its pieces, order and crossings

questions.question: Who is Gazette for?
questions.answer_html: Authors, researchers, engineers and publishing teams working with connected material: a single site, several publications, or a publication alongside product documentation. Agents can help author and operate it without becoming the source of its meaning or visual style.

questions.question: What can a publication contain?
questions.answer_html: Articles, collections, ordered journeys, product help and landing pages. Add equations, diagrams, saved notebook results and notes where they help explain the work. A theme can supply interactive figures. Developer guides and generated API or library reference can be built for Mintlify.

questions.question: What does the theme decide?
questions.answer_html: The theme keeps meaning and appearance separate: it controls layout, type, colour and interactions. Gazette tells it what the page contains, where it belongs and where its links go. A theme can preview a linked publication's look or make a figure interactive while the article still reads without JavaScript or motion.

body:
Gazette
Write an article once and let readers reach it on its own, in a collection or in a product guide. A collection develops a question, a journey gives the argument its order, and a crossing lets readers follow it into another publication. Gazette checks those relationships and carries them through the site and its machine-readable outputs.
The writing, research and documentation stay with the projects that own them. Gazette compiles the sources you choose into one publication or several connected ones, each with its own address and design. Create your first publication to start writing locally, edit an article and preview the result.
One structure, followed by readers and machines
Give a reader a way into the work. Group articles around a question, put a series in reading order, or link from one publication to another. The theme shapes each page. Search, feeds and machine-readable files use the same titles, descriptions, addresses and declared relationships.
Among the products, Gazette publishes a body of thought: it is the act that goes out once its publisher has approved the work. It publishes for a person directly today and takes its sources from their owners; Pale calling it and Weave supplying an organisation's facts are the two connections in front.
From a question to a connected publication
Take a question a reader brings, such as how a product's design led to its guide. The pieces that develop it, the order that carries it and the crossing into another inquiry are the reader's way through. Gazette gives the editor, command line and connected agents the same account of that structure; write in VS Code or work with an agent to see it from the author's side.
Each publication's theme gives it a world, a visual language: this site uses Carrier, for applied systems and consulting, and MONAD's research uses Lattice, for research and exact notation. Follow the link to see how one thought can cross between distinct publications. Choose a reading form explains the shared foundation and the worlds built on it.
Start from the question
Name what the writing is trying to answer. A collection holds the pieces that develop it, and a subcollection takes up a branch. An article that stands alone can stay on its own, with links from the discussions it helps.
Develop it in pieces
Keep each argument with its notes, mathematics and supporting resources, written once. A piece has one home, and other discussions can lead readers into it without copying it. Then choose which sources to publish, where the pages live and which theme gives them their look.
Set the order that carries it
When a later piece builds on an earlier one, make them a journey so the reader always has the next step and the way back. Shared keywords alone do not make an order.
Cross into another inquiry
A link can leave for another publication. Gazette knows it is a crossing, so the reader stays on the essay while the theme borrows the destination's look. When you are ready to see the result, preview it as you save with your first publication, follow your links in the preview to check that the article and its search entry agree, and export a copy of the build from the command line or through your agent for review.
What a publication needs to preserve
Arguments and supporting detail
A derivation can stay beside the article without interrupting everyone who only needs the main argument.
Branches, order and crossings
A reader should be able to tell a branch of the question from a step in the argument and a link into another inquiry, and correcting an article's title should update the page, search results and related reading together.
Guides and technical reference
A guide and API reference need to agree about the system, even when they need different reading forms.
Questions about Gazette
Who is Gazette for?
Authors, researchers, engineers and publishing teams working with connected material: a single site, several publications, or a publication alongside product documentation. Agents can help author and operate it without becoming the source of its meaning or visual style.
What can a publication contain?
Articles, collections, ordered journeys, product help and landing pages. Add equations, diagrams, saved notebook results and notes where they help explain the work. A theme can supply interactive figures. Developer guides and generated API or library reference can be built for Mintlify.
What does the theme decide?
The theme keeps meaning and appearance separate: it controls layout, type, colour and interactions. Gazette tells it what the page contains, where it belongs and where its links go. A theme can preview a linked publication's look or make a figure interactive while the article still reads without JavaScript or motion.
How can one article serve several reading paths?
Readers arrive with different questions, so Gazette lets several discussions lead into one article while it keeps a single home. Navigation, related reading and search use those declared connections. A collection develops a shared question; a journey adds an order within one. Linking to an independent article gives readers another way into the work without copying it.
How is Gazette different from Astro or Hugo?
Gazette carries the structure of a body of thought, which a static-site generator leaves to the author. Astro's content collections supply loaders, schemas and queries for structured content. Hugo organizes pages through sections and page bundles. Gazette makes the relationships between publications part of its publishing model: an article's home, an ordered journey and a link into another site have declared meanings that it checks and carries into navigation and machine-readable outputs. The workspace chooses the sources and publications; themes give them their appearance. From one site to many follows one small writing project as it grows into connected publications.
Where should I start?
Start on your own machine. Gazette builds a publication from the sources you choose and rebuilds its local preview as you save. Create your first publication takes you from an article to a browser preview. When it is ready, export the build for your publishing destination.

body:
Choose a reading form
Give the first Field Notes article a narrower reading column and serif text. The starter theme has two page templates. You will use its reading template for one article and keep the default on the rest.
Select a prepared reading form
In gazette.toml, find the existing [composition] table. Keep its theme and add page_templates below it:
[composition]
theme = { package = 'theme:field-notes' }
page_templates = { 'content:keep-the-context' = 'field-notes/reading.html' }

Edit the existing [composition] table and keep any other entries in page_templates. content:keep-the-context is the article's ID. field-notes/reading.html is the template the theme supplies. Leave the article and its address as they are.
Compare the two pages
Stop the preview with Ctrl+D and restart from the Field Notes directory. Gazette reads the template settings when the session starts. If your request includes the workbook, keep --listen site:workbook=127.0.0.1:0 too.
cat "$GAZETTE_REQUEST" - | "$GAZETTE" preview-sites \
  --local --allow-listeners --local-urls --watch \
  --listen site:field-notes=127.0.0.1:0

Keep the request you last used, including the math request if you enabled it. In the new preview, open /keep-the-context/ or its current journey address. Check the narrower column and serif text. The font depends on your computer. The article and its link to the next note still work at the same addresses.
Open Review a note from its collection or journey, then return to the collection at / to compare. To restore the default for the first note, remove just its entry from page_templates and restart the preview.
Choose the publication's Theme separately
The theme supplies the reading form; the workspace selects it for the article. From one site to many explains how the writing, workspace, compiler and theme share the work.
Use theme to choose a package already declared in theme_packages, with its sources available. Field Notes includes only theme:field-notes. Its styles set light and dark appearance, and there are no named palettes to choose from. For another theme, use the palette and template names that package documents.
For a fuller publication, Base supplies shared navigation, reading, search and controls. Each publication's world, the visual language its theme adds, brings its own type, material and light:
World	Reading character	
Carrier	Applied systems and consulting	
Lattice	Research and exact notation	
Folio	Institutional inquiry	
Chassis	A studio and its products	
Chronicle	A personal publication	
Nocturne	Atmosphere and narrative	
These themes have their own repositories and setup requirements; they are separate from the Field Notes starter.
page_templates overrides a template named in the article. When neither names one, Gazette uses the theme's default. For sites that share settings, see template precedence and defaults.
Let a crossing reveal its destination
In How Pale fits together, the link to MONAD connects a system's working description with the research question of changing that description. RawThoughts' Carrier world owns the article's type and layout. The link borrows the small destination mark supplied by Causality's Lattice world. That mark gives the reader a glimpse of where the thought leads while leaving the sentence in the publication they are reading.
Gazette resolves the destination and gives those facts to the theme. Base's shared link treatment uses the destination world's configured signature; the author does not select a colour or draw a mark for each link. Field Notes' starter teaches the same cross-site reference, but does not supply this visual treatment.
Know when you need Theme development
If Gazette reports a missing reading.html, check which templates your package includes or update an older starter. To create a template or component, see the theme contract and Tera guide. A search box also needs a theme that supplies it, even after you generate search data.

body:
Connect publications
Give readers a way from a Field Notes article to a separate workbook and back. Both sites will run on your machine. If you moved the first note into a journey, use its current address in the example below.
Add the workbook source and publication
Stop the preview. In your publication directory, create workbook/index.md:
+++
[content]
id = 'content:field-notes-workbook'
site = 'site:workbook'
title = 'The Field Notes workbook'
description = 'Bring an observation into the next question you want to explore.'
lifecycle = 'draft'
language = 'en'
route = { path = '/' }
attributions = [{ principal = 'owner:field-notes', role = 'author' }]
structure = { kind = 'page', family = { kind = 'article' } }
+++

# The Field Notes workbook

Begin with an observation whose context you can still explain. [[site:field-notes.example/keep-the-context/|Keep the observation with its context]] supplies the starting note; this workbook gives it another reason to be read.

Append these tables to gazette.toml, replacing the source root with the actual absolute path to your new workbook folder:
[[sites]]
id = 'site:workbook'
publisher = 'owner:field-notes'
deployable = false

[sites.composition]
page_templates = { 'content:field-notes-workbook' = 'field-notes/reading.html' }

[[brands.publications]]
site = 'site:workbook'
public_base_url = 'https://workbook.example/'
authored = [{ source = 'source:workbook', target = 'workbook' }]

[[sources]]
id = 'source:workbook'
location = { kind = 'filesystem', root = '/absolute/path/to/gazette-notes/workbook' }

The workbook uses the existing publisher and the theme's reading template. Each publication can use its own theme without changing the other site's articles.
In content/keep-the-context/index.md, add the return reference where it helps your reader:
Continue in [[site:workbook.example/|the Field Notes workbook]].

This link gives readers another path to the work. Both pages keep their own addresses and memberships.
Preview both sides of the crossing
Open the request named by GAZETTE_REQUEST. Replace sites with the two entries below. Keep the workspace and other settings, including math_generation if you enabled it:
"sites": [
  {"site": "site:field-notes", "model_output": "model.json"},
  {"site": "site:workbook", "model_output": "model.json"}
]

Save the complete JSON request on one line. Preview reads the first line as its request.
Start with an explicit listener for each publication:
cat "$GAZETTE_REQUEST" - | "$GAZETTE" preview-sites \
  --local --allow-listeners --local-urls --watch \
  --listen site:field-notes=127.0.0.1:0 \
  --listen site:workbook=127.0.0.1:0

Use the two URLs Gazette reports. Open the first note, follow the workbook link and then follow Keep the observation with its context back. The workbook should use the reading template. The port numbers belong to this preview. Leave them out of the articles. A link to a configured site outside the request keeps that site's public address.
Keep the public destinations in the sources
Important
The .example hosts are placeholders. The preview resolves them to the two local sites. A regular build uses the public addresses in gazette.toml. Set and verify your own addresses before delivery.
Field Notes shows the change of address and a different reading template. A theme can style cross-site links using the destination information Gazette supplies. To link to a separate Mintlify site, see Publish developer documentation.
From one site to many connects this starter to the publications you are reading, with writing, configuration and each site’s design kept distinct.

Authorship, citation and reuse
Add a byline, citation and content licence to the first Field Notes article, content/keep-the-context/index.md. Use its current title and address if you changed them in an earlier guide.
These fields answer different questions:
You want to	Use	
Credit the writer	An author attribution	
Identify the copyright holder	A rights-holder attribution	
Give readers a citation for this article	citation	
Cite another work in your argument	A link or footnote in the article	
State the article's reuse terms	license with the content licence's URL	
Credit the writer
The starter already credits owner:field-notes as the article's author. In gazette.toml, find that principal and add your display name:
[[principals]]
id = 'owner:field-notes'
kind = 'person'
name = 'Your name'

Replace Your name with the byline name. Edit the existing owner:field-notes entry and keep its key. The key points to the same person even if you change the name later.
In the article's existing [content] table, keep its attribution:
attributions = [{ principal = 'owner:field-notes', role = 'author' }]

For several writers, declare each in the workspace and list their attributions in byline order. To credit a different copyright holder, declare them and give them the rights-holder role. If the writer also holds copyright, use their key for both roles. Enter the article's own credits. Gazette cannot fill in a missing author from the publisher or collection.
Restart the preview. Your name should appear under the heading. A named rights holder appears below the article. These credits also reach structured data.
Supply a citation for the article
Write the citation readers should use. At the end of the article's frontmatter, before the closing +++, add:
[content.citation]
text = 'Keep the observation with its context. Field Notes. https://field-notes.example/keep-the-context/'

For your own publication, use the article's current title, public address and any real author or date details. Gazette displays the citation as you wrote it. If the title or address changes, update the citation too. Save and refresh after the rebuild, then open Cite this article to see it.
To offer a BibTeX download, save this as content/keep-the-context/reference.bib, adjusting the title and public address to the article you are publishing:
@misc{field_notes_context,
  title = {Keep the observation with its context},
  url = {https://field-notes.example/keep-the-context/}
}

Add bibtex = 'reference.bib' inside [content.citation]. After the rebuild, use Cite this article → Download BibTeX to check the file. This download works without static_assets. For a named format or a PDF, see citation downloads. To cite work you used, put the reference in the body or in a footnote.
Record the content licence
Once the owner has chosen the article's reuse terms, record the licence's actual URL in the article's [content] table, above any [content.citation] table:
license = 'https://your-site.example/licenses/writing/'

Important
Use the URL of the terms that apply to the article. Leave license out if none were declared. The article has its own licence, independent of the collection, theme or Gazette's software.
Save and refresh. Content licence appears beneath the citation and Notes. Follow it to check the terms. Gazette also adds that URL to structured data. Confirm that you can publish any work you reuse, and put its required credit beside it. For example, use Image: [creator's name], [work title], used under [licence](the-actual-licence-url). The article's licence leaves the image's own terms in place.
See the licence field rules or Review and export a publication.

body:
Figures, notes and notebooks
A reader may need to see where you stood, understand a measurement’s limit or check the calculation behind your note. Add the material that answers that question: a figure, a short qualification, a longer explanation or saved working. Use the first note from Field Notes, content/keep-the-context/index.md, and keep its supporting files beside it.
The figure and note examples can be used separately. The worked calculation follows a publishing question: how much do three image files add up to? It first saves the answer in a notebook, then lets readers compare combinations in the browser. Field Notes has only your one sketch, so the calculation counts three real figures from the Causality publication, recorded on a stated date. Swap in your own figures when you have them.
Put a figure beside the observation
Choose a sketch or photo that helps explain your observation, and save it beside the article. For this example, use your own PNG and name it context-sketch.png, giving you content/keep-the-context/context-sketch.png. If you choose a JPEG, keep its real extension and use that filename in the Markdown below and in the notebook calculation later in this guide.
To give images a URL, add static_assets to the source:field-notes entry in gazette.toml. For the original starter, the authored array becomes:
authored = [{ source = 'source:field-notes', target = 'content', static_assets = { route_prefix = '/media/field-notes/' } }]

Edit the existing array and keep any other source entries and settings, including markdown_profile if you enabled math.
Add the image to content/keep-the-context/index.md using a path relative to that article:
![Sketch showing the observation point and the direction of the light](context-sketch.png)

Field sketch: the position and lighting that help explain the observation.

Describe what the image shows in its alt text. The following paragraph supplies context and credit; it remains ordinary explanatory text. To bind that text to the image as a caption, use a theme with the figure components described below. Restart the preview after changing gazette.toml, following Start the publication. Open the article and check the image and explanation. If the build stops, check the filename and the static_assets entry.
Warning
Check the whole selected source. This setting can publish supported files anywhere under that source, even if you never link to them. Move private exports out of the source. Gazette copies the images with their dimensions and metadata intact. Prepare them before publishing and check them at the widths readers will use.
For crops or thumbnails, see image transformations. To publish vector artwork, see static SVG images. Both use resource recipes in the workspace.
Use a diagram when the relationship is the point
Export a diagram as PNG or JPEG and include it as above. Put the relationship it explains in the surrounding text too. To render a .dot file as PNG during the build, configure and allow a local Graphviz renderer.
Field Notes uses static figures. If your theme offers an interactive figure, use its documented options and keep the explanation readable without the interaction. See Choose a reading form for using what a theme already provides.
Add a short note where it matters
A footnote keeps a brief explanation close to the sentence it qualifies. Add this to the same article:
Keep the instrument's resolution with the reading.[^resolution]

[^resolution]: Record both the unit and the smallest increment the instrument can distinguish.

Save and refresh after the rebuild. Follow the numbered link to the footnote, then use the return link. Gazette numbers the footnotes you reference. Keep any condition the reader needs to understand the claim in the sentence itself.
Give a longer tangent its own space
For a longer derivation or worked example, create content/keep-the-context/notes.md. Write ordinary Markdown without frontmatter:
# Comparing two observations

Before interpreting a difference, compare the conditions under which each note was made.

## What to keep fixed

Record the instrument, units and observation window alongside the comparison.

Save, then open Notes beneath the article. You should see Comparing two observations. Gazette keeps these headings and anchors within the article's Notes. There is no new page or collection entry. If you build themes, see how article Notes reach the template.
Typeset a calculation when the publication is ready for math
Follow Typeset mathematics to turn on the renderer, then add an equation to this note. Give the symbols and units in the surrounding text. Keep using that guide's preview request after adding a figure or notebook.
Bring saved notebook results into the article
Three figures can be individually modest and still add up. The calculation below records their byte counts, combined size and each figure’s share. The notebook at the end of this guide uses actual image files from Gazette's local draft publication output of 16 November 2026; their hashes identify the versions counted. It uses only Python's standard library.
Reproduce a saved calculation
Create a Python 3 notebook in an editor that saves nbformat 4.5. Copy the four cells shown at the end of this guide in order: the context, the file records, the calculation and the interpretation. Use Markdown cells for prose and code cells for the two programs. Copy the code, not its printed results. Run all cells from the beginning and check the results, then save as content/keep-the-context/analysis.ipynb. Gazette publishes those saved results; it never runs the notebook. The second program should print:
Total: 347,269 bytes (339.13 KiB)
admissible-paths.png: 33.92%
query-tree.png: 34.45%
retrodiction-horizon.png: 31.63%

The observations are included in the notebook, so reproducing this arithmetic needs no download. If your editor exports an older notebook or omits cell IDs, use an editor or export option that writes nbformat 4.5; renaming the file does not convert it. This calculation needs neither image configuration nor a math renderer.
For your own figures, collect the same fields before running the total. For example, with the notebook editor's working folder set to content/keep-the-context/, this code reads the context-sketch.png you added earlier:
from pathlib import Path
from hashlib import sha256

figure = Path("context-sketch.png")
data = figure.read_bytes()
record = {
    "name": figure.name,
    "bytes": len(data),
    "sha256": sha256(data).hexdigest(),
}
print(record)

Replace the example's resources list with records for the figures you actually want to compare, then rerun and save. Use the exported file if you resized or transformed the original: that is the version the reader receives. Record the observation date in the notebook’s opening cell. Rerun and save whenever you change the code or input records.
Attach the saved result
With analysis.ipynb saved beside the article, attach it to the page. At the top of the article's existing frontmatter, before [content], add:
notebooks = ['keep-the-context/analysis.ipynb']

Start the path from content/, your source root. analysis.ipynb alone would look directly in that root, while content/keep-the-context/analysis.ipynb would repeat the root directory. Keep the rest of the frontmatter. Save and refresh after the rebuild. Gazette shows the notebook after the article today. As the article's evidence it belongs in the article's Notes, read on request, and that move is in front. Check that all four cells and both saved outputs appear, in the order you saved them. If you list several notebooks, they appear in the order you list them. They stay with the article without creating separate pages or downloads.
Gazette can show Markdown and code cells, saved streams and errors, and supported text, JSON, inert HTML, PNG and JPEG results. Remove widgets, raw cells, SVG and other unsupported outputs before attaching the notebook, even if a cell also has a supported result. Check for saved errors you did not mean to show.
If notebook Markdown links to plot.png, put that image beside the notebook and include it through the same static_assets setting. The notebook reference covers attachments inside a cell and limits on saved results. For crediting the material, see Authorship, citation and reuse.
Decide whether readers need controls
The saved notebook lets readers inspect the calculation you checked. A table may be enough to show its result. Add browser controls if trying different inputs would help them answer another question; for these figures, that means seeing how much of the total remains when one is left out.
A component is a named reading form that a theme supplies, such as the reading-comparison and process-path of Base, Gazette's shared theme. An island is a component that also loads a small browser module so it can respond to the reader.
Form	Choose it when	Example	
Static component	A recurring reading form needs consistent presentation, with no browser interaction.	Base's reading-comparison presents an ordinary Markdown table.	
Component island	A reusable component needs its own interaction while keeping a readable starting form.	Base's process-path turns an ordered account into selectable steps.	
Page module	The behavior belongs to one article's particular question or data.	This guide's image-size checkboxes sum selected files.	
Saved notebook	Readers need to inspect the calculation and the results you checked.	This guide's notebook records the files, hashes, total and shares.	
Compare image sizes
The table gives each figure’s size and its share of the combined total.
Figure	Bytes	Share	
Admissible paths	117,797	33.92%	
Query tree	119,621	34.45%	
Retrodiction horizon	109,851	31.63%	
All three	347,269	100%	
The largest accounts for roughly a third of the combined bytes. File size is one publishing consideration alongside the detail a reader needs to see.
Add the readable comparison first
Copy this section into content/keep-the-context/index.md. Keep the explicit heading anchor: the script uses it to place the controls. You can change the visible heading without changing that anchor.
## Compare image sizes {#compare-image-sizes}

Three image files from Gazette's local draft publication output of 16 November 2026:

| Figure               |       Bytes |    Share |
| -------------------- | ----------: | -------: |
| Admissible paths     |     117,797 |   33.92% |
| Query tree           |     119,621 |   34.45% |
| Retrodiction horizon |     109,851 |   31.63% |
| **All three**        | **347,269** | **100%** |

The saved notebook below records the file names and hashes. One KiB is 1,024 bytes; all three total 339.13 KiB.

Give this page its own script
Create content/keep-the-context/compare-resources.mjs with this complete program. Its values are local to the module; it needs no library, server request or variable supplied by another script. Checking a box changes the sum shown to the reader. It does not remove an image from the publication.
const resources = [
  { name: "Admissible paths", bytes: 117797 },
  { name: "Query tree", bytes: 119621 },
  { name: "Retrodiction horizon", bytes: 109851 },
];

const heading = document.getElementById("compare-image-sizes");
if (heading) {
  const controls = document.createElement("fieldset");
  const legend = document.createElement("legend");
  legend.textContent = "Choose which figures to include in the sum";
  controls.append(legend);
  const checks = [];
  const result = document.createElement("p");
  result.setAttribute("role", "status");
  const fullSize = resources.reduce((total, item) => total + item.bytes, 0);
  function update() {
    const selected = resources.filter((item, i) => checks[i].checked);
    const bytes = selected.reduce((total, item) => total + item.bytes, 0);
    result.textContent = `${selected.length} files: ${bytes.toLocaleString("en-US")} bytes (${(bytes / 1024).toFixed(2)} KiB), ${((100 * bytes) / fullSize).toFixed(2)}% of all three.`;
  }
  for (const item of resources) {
    const paragraph = document.createElement("p");
    const label = document.createElement("label");
    const check = document.createElement("input");
    check.type = "checkbox";
    check.checked = true;
    check.addEventListener("change", update);
    checks.push(check);
    label.append(check, ` ${item.name}`);
    paragraph.append(label);
    controls.append(paragraph);
  }
  update();
  controls.append(result);
  heading.after(controls);
}

In the article's existing frontmatter, place this resource table after notebooks and before [content]. Keep collection and project declarations before any [[resources]] table too.
[[resources]]
inputs = ['keep-the-context/compare-resources.mjs']
build = { kind = 'browser-module', entry = 'keep-the-context/compare-resources.mjs' }
output = '/assets/field-notes/compare-resources.js'

Both inputs and entry start at the configured content/ source root, just like the notebook attachment. output is the script's public address within the site. Give another page's script a different output address. This declaration compiles the module; the image static_assets setting is not needed for it.
Let Field Notes load the page's resources
The current Field Notes starter does not include page scripts automatically. Open your publication's theme/templates/page.html and add this loop immediately before </head>. If you already added it, keep one copy. Leave the existing presentation block and other template content in place.
{% for resource in presentation.resources %}
  {% if resource.kind == "stylesheet" %}
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ resource.url }}">
  {% elif resource.kind == "browser-module" %}
  <script type="module" src="{{ resource.url }}"></script>
  {% endif %}
{% endfor %}

The loop loads resources declared by the current page. Gazette supplies their resolved URLs for the local preview or configured publication address. Module scripts run after the document has been parsed, when the comparison heading is available. The page-resource reference explains the declaration and theme connection.
Restart the preview with the same request you used for Field Notes. Open the article and uncheck Query tree: the total should change from 347,269 to 227,648 bytes. Tab to a checkbox and press Space. Uncheck all three and check that the total reaches zero. Disable JavaScript and reload: the complete table and saved notebook should remain readable, without inactive controls. Re-enable JavaScript afterwards.
If the controls are missing, check the heading anchor, the two source-root paths and the template loop. A successful compilation alone does not load a script into the page. When replacing the data, update the notebook records, the article's table and the module together, then rerun and save the notebook.
The notebook holds the dated calculation; the browser controls let readers explore subsets of the same figures. They work independently, so changing a checkbox leaves the saved result intact.
Reuse a reading form across articles
When several articles need the same reading form or interaction, look for an existing theme component. If none fits, develop it with the theme and leave each article’s data and explanation beside that article. The one-page image calculation above can stay with its own page.
Note
Check your theme's components. The examples below use Gazette's Base theme. Use them only in a theme that provides those definitions and their resources. The Field Notes starter does not include Base; copying these blocks into that starter would produce an unknown-component error. Its notebook and page-module examples above work through the declarations and template loop already shown.
Keep an image and its caption together
In a theme providing figure and figure-caption, put one image and its caption inside the same figure:
::::figure

![Sketch showing the observation point and the direction of the light](context-sketch.png)

:::figure-caption

Field sketch: the position and lighting that help explain the observation.

:::

::::

The outer fence has four colons and the caption's fence has three. Alt text describes the image for someone who cannot see it; the visible caption supplies context or credit. Keep the article's continuing argument outside the figure. Gazette carries the bound caption into the image's metadata too, so the visible and machine-readable accounts use the same words. A paragraph beneath an ordinary image does not create that connection by itself.
Preview the figure at a narrow reading width and check that the caption stays with it. If you maintain a theme, the figure contract explains how to declare these components.
Present a comparison without adding behavior
In a theme providing reading-comparison, give the comparison a meaningful label and keep the table as Markdown:
:::reading-comparison {label = "What belongs beside an observation"}

| Detail              | Why keep it?                         |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Instrument and unit | Make the value interpretable.        |
| Observation window  | Establish which period it describes. |

:::

The component wraps the table in a labelled section. It has no browser module and adds no controls. The table still carries the comparison. You can see the same component comparing the guide's source files in Why an article has one home.
Let readers move through an ordered account
Base's process-path keeps a complete ordered list before JavaScript runs. Each process-step needs a heading and its explanation:
::::process-path {label = "From an observation to a checked note"}

:::process-step

### Record the conditions

Keep the instrument, unit and observation window with the reading.

:::

:::process-step

### Compare like with like

Check those conditions before interpreting a difference.

:::

:::process-step

### Keep the working

Save the calculation beside the explanation so another reader can follow it.

:::

::::

The outer fence has four colons so it can contain the three-colon step blocks. With the theme's interaction loaded, readers select step headings to open their explanations; keyboard users can activate the buttons and move among them with Up, Down, Home and End. Without JavaScript, all three explanations remain in order. Automatic progression is off by default. Use an ordinary numbered list when showing everything at once serves the reader better.
The theme declares an island's module and the function that mounts it; the article supplies the headings, explanations and component arguments. For process-path, Base declares the module and its mount function. The component contract explains that connection for theme authors.
Carry the method into a real article
The three sample figures above come from Causality's articles on endpoint-constrained paths, the cost of a query and reconstructing from a noisy record. In What did selective memory buy?, a saved notebook recomputes summaries from Reckon's retained evaluation results. The article keeps the workload, negative results and measurement costs beside those numbers. Its analysis uses the same saved-result form for a research comparison.
For an interaction that changes a model, RawFish's opinion comparison lets a reader vary a small illustrative influence model; its trajectories remain simulated possibilities. What can you distinguish with one more move? spends an observation budget and shows which distinctions remain possible. Both keep the explanation readable alongside the controls, so the interaction helps readers examine the argument.

body:
Your first publication
Start Field Notes, a small site with two articles. Edit the first in Markdown, then open the result in your browser. You can keep the site and continue writing when you finish.
Before you start
Important
You need Python 3 and a local Gazette executable. If you need to build it, follow Build Gazette from source. Keep the terminal where you set GAZETTE_SOURCE, your checkout of Gazette's own code, and GAZETTE, the executable.
Start the publication
Create your publication in a new folder:
export GAZETTE_PUBLICATION="$HOME/gazette-notes"
cd "$GAZETTE_SOURCE"
python3 examples/first-publication/create.py "$GAZETTE_PUBLICATION"
cd "$GAZETTE_PUBLICATION"
export GAZETTE_REQUEST="$GAZETTE_PUBLICATION/preview-request.json"

Choose another folder if gazette-notes already exists. The script leaves existing folders alone. Your articles are in content/, a source: a folder the workspace declares as holding writing. gazette.toml is the workspace, the configuration Gazette reads, and it connects that source to the theme. preview-request.json tells Gazette which site to open. These guides call the folder holding all three your publication folder.
Start the preview:
cat "$GAZETTE_REQUEST" - | "$GAZETTE" preview-sites \
  --local --allow-listeners --local-urls --watch \
  --listen site:field-notes=127.0.0.1:0

Keep the terminal open. When Gazette reports ready, open the url for site:field-notes. It will look like this, with a port chosen for your session:
"url":"http://127.0.0.1:3908/"

On the Field Notes home page, open Keep the observation with its context.
Make your first edit
Open the new gazette-notes folder in your editor, then open content/keep-the-context/index.md.
The block between +++ markers describes the article. Update its title and description inside [content]. Use your own note, or try this example:
title = 'After the rain'
description = 'Which garden paths stayed wet after an overnight shower.'

Replace the heading and text after the closing +++ with:
# After the rain

The path under the apple tree was still wet at noon. The open path beside the shed had already dried. I will check both again after the next shower.

[[id:content:review-a-note|Read the next note]].

Save and wait for the terminal to report a successful rebuild, then refresh. You should see After the rain and your new observation. Follow Read the next note to open the second article, then choose Field Notes in the header. The home page should show the new title and description.
Your article still lives at /keep-the-context/, its address on the site. You changed its title, leaving its slug and place in the home collection intact. The link to the second note uses that note’s identity, so Gazette can still find it if its address changes later. Articles, collections and journeys follows those changes through a larger publication.
Stop and continue later
Press Ctrl+D in the preview terminal to stop. To resume there, run the preview command again.
In a new terminal, open your Gazette checkout and repeat the variable assignments in the build setup. You can reuse the executable you built. Then set your publication paths:
export GAZETTE_PUBLICATION="$HOME/gazette-notes"
export GAZETTE_REQUEST="$GAZETTE_PUBLICATION/preview-request.json"
cd "$GAZETTE_PUBLICATION"

Use the folder and request file you last previewed. Run the preview command and open the newly reported URL.
If your edit does not appear
If the terminal reports a failed rebuild, fix the error it names, save and refresh. Gazette serves the last good build in the meantime. Restart the preview after editing gazette.toml.
Next, Write in VS Code or Articles, collections and journeys.

body:
From one site to many
After connecting Field Notes to its workbook, you have two publications with a useful path between them. The same arrangement can connect a personal site, a research publication and product documentation. Each keeps its own readers, writing and appearance.
Keep the four jobs clear
Field Notes puts a small example of each job in one folder. A larger workspace can select them from separate places:
Writing. Field Notes keeps articles and their resources in content/. In a larger workspace, the writing stays in the owning project's Content folder, with its Notes, figures and other resources. One publication can select several project sources.
Configuration. Field Notes uses gazette.toml to choose its sources, address, theme and outputs. One larger workspace makes those choices for the publications you are reading here.
Compilation. The same Gazette executable resolves the pages and their relationships, then supplies HTML, navigation and discovery outputs.
Design. Field Notes has a small theme of its own, theme:field-notes. A larger publication can use shared reading and navigation behaviour while its world supplies the visual language. These publications share Base through their world themes.
For example, Pale's product guides stay with Pale, but readers encounter them at RawThoughts' Pale entrance. A standalone Pale essay belongs to RawThoughts' Blog. The source owner, the article's place in the publication and its address answer different questions; selecting the source supplies no reason to duplicate it.
Follow an idea across publications
How Pale fits together explains why a working system needs a sufficiently stable description of the work it runs. It then leads to MONAD, which asks what a principled change of a description would need to preserve. The crossing has a reason: the second publication develops the research question raised by the first.
RawThoughts uses Carrier; Causality uses Lattice. Their shared Base theme can present the destination's visual language at the crossing, while each page keeps its own publication's composition. Gazette supplies the destination information; the theme decides how to show it. Field Notes' workbook exercise establishes the link and address behaviour, but its starter theme does not reproduce those world treatments.
The same workspace also connects getHarsh, Post-AGI Economics, Sleepwalker and DAO Studio. Their different purposes remain visible even when an idea gives readers a reason to move between them.
Expand the workspace when the writing needs it
Start by deciding who the next publication is for and which writing belongs there. Select its sources, publisher, address and theme, then add the references that help readers continue a thought. A related subject can need a collection within the existing site; it does not automatically need another domain.
Preview both sides of each crossing and follow the return path. Local addresses belong to that preview session; keep the publication references in the articles. Before delivery, review the selected pages with their publisher. Sharing a compiler or theme leaves each publisher's approval separate.
Gazette builds these publications on its own, from the sources you selected. Pale asking for a build through Gazette's own interface for a broader task, and permitted Weave records among the sources, are the two connections in front. Gazette needs no live call to Scope, Counsel or Reckon to turn those captured inputs into a publication.

body:
Search, feeds and discovery
An article reached through search should make the same claim as the page a reader opens. Gazette derives the page, search record and structured data from the same title, description and relationships, so you can correct the writing in one place. Each output still has its own selection: a feed of published articles can omit a draft that appears in your local preview.
Add a sitemap, search data and structured data to Field Notes, then check them against the article a reader sees. You can also add a feed for new articles. The starter theme has no search box. This guide builds the data a search interface would use.
Choose the outputs
In gazette.toml, find the [[brands.publications]] block for site:field-notes. Add this table before the next brand or publication. If machine already exists for that site, add the entries to that table.
[brands.publications.machine]
sitemap = true
json_ld = true
search = { language = 'lexical', fields = ['title', 'description', 'body', 'keywords'] }
markdown_alternates = { enabled = true, directory_page = 'index.md', file_page = 'append-md', media_type = 'text/markdown', discovery_rel = 'alternate' }
llms = { enabled = true, coverage = 'all-pages', description_from = 'content:field-notes', representation = 'markdown-alternate', include_human_link = true }

Output	What a reader or tool receives	
sitemap.xml	The publication's canonical page addresses	
search.json	Page records and the text fields enabled for search	
site.jsonld	Structured descriptions of the pages and their declared relationships	
Markdown counterparts	A Markdown representation beside each canonical page	
llms.txt	A reading guide linking to those Markdown counterparts and, here, their HTML pages	
description_from uses the collection's description to introduce llms.txt. all-pages lists all eligible pages from the build. Give each included article a description a reader can use.
The lexical search profile indexes the listed fields without reducing words to English stems. Use english if you want English stemming. Choose the profile yourself. Neither detects the language.
Inspect the result in your preview
Stop the preview with Ctrl+D and restart it to load gazette.toml. If your current request includes the workbook, keep --listen site:workbook=127.0.0.1:0 as well. Keep the math request if you enabled it.
cat "$GAZETTE_REQUEST" - | "$GAZETTE" preview-sites \
  --local --allow-listeners --local-urls --watch \
  --listen site:field-notes=127.0.0.1:0

Use the new Field Notes URL from the ready event.
Open /search.json and /llms.txt. Find the collection and both notes. For the first note's Markdown, open /keep-the-context/index.md or append index.md to its current journey address.
Open /sitemap.xml and follow one page address. --local-urls makes it open this preview. A regular build uses the configured public address. Replace https://field-notes.example/ before publishing your own site.
Open /site.jsonld for the site-wide data. In the first article's page source, find application/ld+json. It should describe the same article and title. The starter embeds this data when you enable json_ld.
Edit the first note's description in content/keep-the-context/index.md. Save and refresh search.json after the rebuild. The entry should show the new description. An edit to the article body also changes its search text and Markdown counterpart.
Keep one main heading for the article and make it agree with the declared title. Use second- and third-level headings to develop the argument. The title supplies the article’s name and headline in structured data; the description supplies its description. Author, publisher and dates come from their own declarations. A heading cannot supply a missing author or publication date. Inspect these fields beside the rendered page so a machine receives the same claim a person reads.
Warning
Discovery settings do not make a page private. The local files include drafts. Check what your public build includes. Hiding a page from discovery leaves it accessible by URL if you still publish it.
Add a feed when there are updates to follow
Add a JSON Feed for dated, published articles. Put these tables in the Field Notes publication block before the next brand or publication:
[brands.publications.machine.feeds]
identity_base = 'https://field-notes.example/'
selection = { kind = 'articles', residence = 'all', lifecycle = ['published'], require_published_date = true }
omit_when_empty = true

[[brands.publications.machine.feeds.channels]]
id = 'feed:notes'
channel = 'content:field-notes'
path = '/updates.json'
format = 'json'

Restart the preview. /updates.json stays absent while the starter's articles are undated drafts because omit_when_empty is on. To add an eligible article, set lifecycle to published and put its publication date inside [content]. For example, published = '2026-11-09' means November 9, 2026. Save and wait for the rebuild, then open /updates.json and check for that article. This change only affects the local build.
Use a domain you control for identity_base and keep it stable. See the feed format requirements for Atom, RSS and JSON Feed. Atom needs named authors and modification timestamps. If you know only a calendar date, leave the time unspecified rather than using midnight as a guess.
Check the reading experience as well as the files
Open an article directly and check that its title, description and opening explain what the reader found. Use keywords that describe the work. Search and answer systems decide for themselves what to index, rank and cite.
Try a missing page such as /a-note-that-does-not-exist/ in the local preview. Gazette returns a 404 recovery page with a link home when the Home page was built, and a Search link when that page was built. Field Notes has no Search page. This lets you check the local recovery experience; the eventual host needs its own missing-page handling.
A theme can compose the publication’s home-page sharing card from its landing visual and H1, using an existing image or a frame from its film. Base includes the generated image in the page’s initial sharing metadata. Follow the theme recipe and local renderer setup; capture must be explicitly enabled when building.
An existing PNG or JPEG selected through identity_assets.link_preview takes precedence over generation. Keep that resource selected for the site. The generated recipe covers the publication’s home, not every article. The Field Notes starter has no sharing-card recipe; use a theme that supplies one, or configure an existing preview image with a theme that presents it.
Before publishing, set the publisher’s crawler policy and inspect the generated robots.txt alongside the public sitemap and included pages. The deployment guide explains workspace defaults and per-site overrides. Crawler rules request how bots use the site; they do not make a page private. Follow Review and export a publication to check what the build actually contains before handing it to the publisher.
If you are adding a search interface, see the search record format. For a theme integration, see discovery files and embed page JSON-LD.

body:
Articles, collections and journeys
A publication's reading structure decides where each piece lives and how a reader moves between pieces. You declare it on the pages themselves, and Gazette derives the listings, reading order and next links from those declarations.
Use a collection when several pieces develop a shared question. Use a journey when reading them in a particular order helps the argument unfold: a later explanation may depend on an earlier observation, or several pieces may tell one continuing story. Shared keywords alone do not establish either relationship. A self-contained article can stand on its own, with links from the discussions it helps.
In Field Notes, the two starter articles can be read on their own. Add a third, then put the original two in an order that takes the reader from observing something to interpreting it. You can stop after either task.
Add an article to the collection
Create content/a-new-note/index.md in your publication with this complete page:
+++
collections = ['content:field-notes']

[content]
id = 'content:a-new-note'
title = 'A question worth returning to'
description = 'Keep a useful question beside the observations that prompted it.'
keywords = ['field notes', 'questions', 'observation']
schema_type = 'Article'
lifecycle = 'draft'
language = 'en'
slug = 'a-new-note'
attributions = [{ principal = 'owner:field-notes', role = 'author' }]
structure = { kind = 'page', family = { kind = 'article' } }
+++

# A question worth returning to

An observation can leave a better question than the one you started with. Write that question while the details are still close enough to examine.

Save and refresh after the preview rebuilds. The new title should appear in the collection and open /a-new-note/. Gazette builds that list from collections. The starter selects Field Notes as its home at /; the article’s slug supplies a-new-note beneath it. If the article should stand on its own, leave that field out and link to it where it helps. A file move alone does not change its collection.
Use a journey when the order matters
A journey belongs in a collection because the sequence develops part of that collection's question. Field Notes can keep growing through independent observations while this journey provides a particular sequence from recording an observation to interpreting it. Other articles need not join that sequence to contribute to the collection.
Stop the preview while changing the reading order. Create content/first-reading/index.md with the original two notes as its steps:
+++
[content]
id = 'journey:field-notes-first-reading'
title = 'From observation to interpretation'
description = 'Record the context, then examine what the observation supports.'
lifecycle = 'draft'
language = 'en'
slug = 'first-reading'
structure = { kind = 'journey', collection = 'content:field-notes', members = [{ content = 'content:keep-the-context', primary = true }, { content = 'content:review-a-note', primary = true }] }
+++

# From observation to interpretation

Begin with the circumstances of the observation. Then ask which explanation it supports and what you would need to distinguish another explanation.

Remove collections from both notes. They now belong to the journey. Leave the new question in Field Notes as an article someone can read on its own.
Keep both notes’ identities and slugs. Their membership now gives them addresses beneath the journey: /first-reading/keep-the-context/ and /first-reading/review-a-note/. You do not need to write those paths into the notes. Their existing identity links, such as [[id:content:review-a-note|separate the observation from the claim]], follow the new addresses. In the current Field Notes starter, open the new journey in VS Code to get Gazette feedback; it is discovered from the configured content source. For an older setup with explicit file lists, follow Write in VS Code.
Restart the preview with your current request and listeners. Open the journey from Field Notes and follow both steps. Check the new addresses and follow a link between the notes. Old addresses do not become redirects automatically; the later section explains how to preserve an address readers already use. Your theme controls how the steps look. Gazette uses the order in members.
Give a developing branch its own subcollection
If Field Notes grows beyond observation, give that subject its own branch. Create content/observation-practice/index.md:
+++
[content]
id = 'content:observation-practice'
title = 'Practising observation'
description = 'Keep the circumstances of an observation separate from the explanation it invites.'
lifecycle = 'draft'
language = 'en'
slug = 'observation-practice'
attributions = [{ principal = 'owner:field-notes', role = 'author' }]
structure = { kind = 'collection', parent = 'content:field-notes' }
+++

# Practising observation

Begin with the circumstances you can describe. Return to the question when a new observation changes what you think the first one supports.

The parent makes this a subcollection of Field Notes. In the question article, change its collections entry to content:observation-practice. Set the journey's structure.collection to the same value. Its notes still belong to the journey, so leave collections off those notes.
Keep the contributions’ existing slugs. Their new placement derives these addresses:
Independent question:
  /observation-practice/a-new-note/
Reading journey:
  /observation-practice/first-reading/
First journey note:
  /observation-practice/first-reading/keep-the-context/
Second journey note:
  /observation-practice/first-reading/review-a-note/

Keep each identity and leave its existing identity links in place. Open the new collection in the Gazette-enabled VS Code window to get feedback through the starter’s source discovery.
Restart the preview. From Field Notes, open Practising observation. It should offer the question and the journey. Follow the two notes and check their addresses against the paths above.
Preserve an address readers already use
The starter’s notes have only been previewed locally. If you are reorganizing published writing, keep its released addresses working. Gazette does not report a released address that a move or slug change leaves without an alias: gazette check passes and the address stops working without a message, so keep a list of the addresses you have released and give each moved page an alias. Inside the note’s [content] block, the route field sets its address and can redirect earlier ones. Without it, Gazette derives the address from the article's collection and slug:
# In review-a-note/index.md, after the branch change above:
route = { path = '/observation-practice/first-reading/review-a-note/', aliases = ['/review-a-note/', '/first-reading/review-a-note/'] }

This is an address exception: the explicit path takes precedence over the derived address. Keep aliases for addresses you actually released, including any earlier aliases. If you later change this note’s placement, update its explicit path too. Its identity links still name the same note.
Check each retained old address in the preview. It should redirect directly to the current one. Apply the same care to the journey and collection if readers already used their earlier addresses; the routing reference explains the full declaration.
Keep product documentation separate from editorial writing
If you are organizing product help, give its root collection a documentation purpose:
[content.structure]
kind = 'collection'
purpose = 'documentation'

Keep the collection’s identity, title, slug and placement. If it has an explicit address exception, retain that declaration too. Its children still join a collection or journey as usual. They can appear in search and stay out of Blog and ordinary collection listings. Order them by what a reader needs to understand or do. For architecture and code reference, publish developer documentation separately.
Keep a useful reference without claiming membership
When a piece already has a home, link to it in context. Useful compute leads to the serving article through the cost of waiting. Runtime portability leads to the same piece through memory and scheduling. See Why an article has one home for that editorial example. If you are writing a theme or integration, see membership rules and journey navigation.
Taxonomies let you classify writing across those homes. An observation term could connect a Field Notes article with a piece in another collection without moving either or putting them in a reading order. Declare the taxonomy and its terms in the workspace, then assign the relevant pairs in each page's [content].taxonomies. A collection's classifications do not automatically apply to its articles. The workspace can also configure term listings for readers to browse. Follow the taxonomy declarations when you need that additional way into the work.

body:
Publish developer documentation
Open a repository guide in Mintlify, then follow a link from Field Notes to that guide and back. Keep editing product help in your publication and developer guides in the code repository.
Configure the documentation site
Start with your Field Notes publication. Follow Add a manual to Field Notes. Return here when your publication has the Notes tooling guide and the settings check passes.
The sample guide links back to https://field-notes.example/keep-the-context/. If you moved the note into a journey, update that link in the guide before you assemble it.
Build and open the preview
This walkthrough uses port 3908 for Field Notes and 3909 for Mintlify. You will restart Field Notes on 3908 in the next section. If either port is in use, choose another and change the corresponding map and listener below.
Leave your Field Notes terminal open. In a second terminal, restore the Gazette and publication paths, then run this in the Field Notes directory. Replace /absolute/path/to/your/publication with its full path:
mkdir -p "$HOME/gazette-doc-builds"
"$GAZETTE" assemble-docs --local --workspace-json --site site:field-notes \
  --output-parent "$HOME/gazette-doc-builds" \
  --preview-link-bases-json '{"https://field-notes.example/":"http://127.0.0.1:3908/"}' <<'JSON'
{"kind":"local","root":"/absolute/path/to/your/publication","workspace":"gazette.toml"}
JSON

Open the directory printed in the result and start Mintlify’s CLI:
cd /directory/printed/in/the/result
npx mint dev --classic --port 3909 --no-open --telemetry=false

Open the address Mintlify prints. In the sidebar, choose Build an integration → Notes tooling. If you edit the original guide, assemble again and start Mintlify from the new output folder.
Follow links between the two previews
In the first Field Notes article, add [Developer guide](https://docs.field-notes.example/notes-tool/overview). If you chose a different address for the guide, use it in this link.
Keep the Mintlify terminal running. In the Field Notes terminal, press Ctrl+D to stop the earlier preview, then restart it on the port you put in the Mintlify build's map. In this command, use the address Mintlify reported. The example uses IPv6 (http://[::1]:3909/). If it listens on IPv4, use http://127.0.0.1:3909/.
cat "$GAZETTE_REQUEST" - | "$GAZETTE" preview-sites --local --allow-listeners --local-urls --watch \
  --listen site:field-notes=127.0.0.1:3908 \
  --preview-link-bases-json '{"https://docs.field-notes.example/":"http://[::1]:3909/"}'

If your current request also includes the workbook, add --listen site:workbook=127.0.0.1:0. Keep both previews running. Open the note in Field Notes, follow Developer guide, then follow Return to the note in Mintlify. If either link opens an .example host, check the map on the build that produced that link.
Use your own public domains for another project. Leave the public links in the sources. Omit the two preview maps when you build for public addresses. To include API reference from your code, see Run a documentation generator.
