body:
Review a publication before release
Open the generated publication and follow the argument as a reader would. Are the words, figures and qualifications there? Can you reach the next part? Does the page reveal anything that should have stayed private? A successful build gives you something to review. The publisher decides whether that result is ready to release.
This guide covers review and the checks after delivery. Gazette prepares the output for the publisher’s review and explicit confirmation before delivery to the configured Git destination. Set up hosting before the first public release so the host can serve the approved files. The developer release guide supplies the commands. You can keep writing and previewing locally while preparing for release.
Read the result with its sources
Start with the exact output you intend to release. Read each changed page beside its source and inspect the presentation. An editor may have approved the words before a template change hid a qualification, cropped a figure or exposed private metadata. Check the words and what the reader actually sees together.
For example, the serving article compares burst and spaced requests. Both schedules have equal throughput, but their response times differ. If the chart survives while the arrival conditions disappear, the page keeps the numbers and loses the explanation. Follow the same comparison through its machine-readable output: the conditions still matter there.
When a source or theme changes after review, inspect the affected output again. Approval should identify the result the publisher saw.
Follow the complete reading path
Compare the output's page addresses with those of your last release. Gazette does not list a released address that the new output no longer serves, so a moved page without an alias leaves readers' bookmarks broken with no diagnostic. Open collections and journeys from their entrances and follow their links. A journey promises an argument in a particular order. Leaving out an unapproved member can remove the premise its next step needs. Supply the approved members or deliberately revise the reading path before releasing it.
An external citation can remain external. The question is which pages your publication promises as its own reading path and which it cites elsewhere. Why an article has one home explains how membership and useful references serve different purposes.
Check privacy across the whole result, including metadata, downloadable files and attached resources. A private source may help you write a public explanation without belonging in the published output itself. The current preparation flow checks the selected content and assets, runs the configured disclosure and output checks, and retains the result for inspection. Its preparation instructions describe the inputs that flow requires.
Agree what each publisher will release
Keep the selected sites, reviewed output and destinations clear. Each publisher approves their own scope. One person may act for several publishers, but approval for one destination does not extend to another by association.
The confirmation applies to the reviewed output, sites and destinations, and is used once for that release. Changed output or scope needs another review. Follow Reviewing and confirming with the person responsible for each site. Signed authorisation is optional; a local preview supplies no permission to publish.
Check the destination, then the served page
A successful push tells you that Git accepted a change. GitHub Pages or Mintlify may still need to build and serve it. Read back the destination, then open the public page and follow the changed reading path. Check every selected site; one working destination tells you nothing about whether another still serves an older result.
Keep those observations separate. If the remote holds the expected commit but the page is old, investigate the hosting build and delivery. If the push response was lost, first establish what the remote received. Repeating the push on the assumption that nothing happened would make the uncertainty harder to resolve.
The developer guide describes reading back and settling a release, including the separate observations of the host build and served output. If those observations cannot settle what happened, stop and reconcile the recorded attempt before trying again.
Continue from a known result
If the released page needs a correction, identify the result to replace and prepare the change for review. If an earlier publication needs restoring, inspect what is available to restore and obtain the publisher’s approval for that result. Rebuilding old source may produce something different when its dependencies have changed; inspect it before treating it as the old publication.
Your local preview remains a place to experiment. At release, the practical question is more specific: did readers receive the connected work the publisher approved? The reviewed output, the destination’s state and the served pages let you answer it.

body:
Review and export a publication
Read your Field Notes publication as a visitor, then export the HTML and assets to a fresh folder. You can do both locally. The starter contains drafts and is set up for local use only.
Read the publication as someone arriving for the first time
Open the URL Gazette reported for this preview.
From the home page, open each note and follow its links. Then open a note directly in a new tab. Check that its opening makes sense without the home page.
Read the page in a narrow window. Open its figures, equations and Notes. If your theme offers light, dark or reduced-motion settings, try the ones your readers will use.
If you changed a title, look for it in the article, the collection and your discovery files. If you connected another publication, follow both directions.
Decide which edition you are reviewing
Each page declares its own lifecycle in [content]:
State	What it means for your review	
draft	Work still being prepared. You can read it in the local preview; a release candidate cannot include it.	
published	Work marked for publication. It still needs to be selected for the release and approved by its publisher.	
archived	Earlier work retained as an archive. It can remain available when deliberately included in a release.	
These values do not upload or delete files. A local export can contain all three states, so do not treat everything in its output folder as approved for public delivery. Search and feed selections separately determine which pages appear in those reading paths; omitting a page from a feed does not make its address private.
Review a collection or journey together
Read the collection's introduction alongside the articles you intend to release. Changing the introduction's state does not change the states of its articles. Check their links, Notes and required resources as part of the same selection.
For the Field Notes journey, both the observation and interpretation steps need to be ready. A release candidate cannot silently omit one step or change their order. If the second step is still a draft, finish it or hold the journey; a successful preview of the first step does not establish a complete reading sequence. The release guide explains how Gazette checks the selected pages and their dependencies.
Export the site files
Choose an existing output parent outside the publication's source folders. For example, create a new directory in your home folder:
mkdir "$HOME/gazette-output"

You can reuse that parent directory. From your publication folder, export the site with the workspace on standard input:
cd "$GAZETTE_PUBLICATION"
"$GAZETTE" render-site --local --site site:field-notes \
  --output-parent "$HOME/gazette-output" < gazette.toml

Gazette prints a result naming the directory it created, a fresh folder beneath the output parent that holds the HTML and resources. If you added the workbook, run the command again with --site site:workbook. The command reads gazette.toml alone, so it cannot follow the extra file that math adds with includes. If you enabled math, or prefer to work in conversation, use Work with an agent and ask for an export:
Keep a generated copy of my saved Field Notes publication in a fresh folder beneath this output parent. Keep its current settings and enabled math, use public addresses, and leave my sources, saved request and existing results unchanged. Tell me where the files were written or why the export failed.
Give the agent the saved request path and the full path to the output parent. The stage_rendered_site tool exports one publication per call, so ask for the workbook separately. For client integration, see the tool inputs.
Note
The export and preview use different addresses. Gazette reports the new folder holding the HTML and resources. Keep using the browser preview for review. The export uses the configured public addresses, including the starter's .example host, so opening index.html from disk cannot reproduce the preview's links. For using the files in another tool, see the developer rendering guide.
Prepare a real publication with its publisher
For a public release, set up the destination and agree who can approve the publication. The publication’s host serves the files from that destination. The deployable flag selects output for delivery. Set up hosting with its provider. Review a publication before release follows the checks from the selected output to what readers receive. The developer release guide supplies the current release and recovery procedure. Once the site is public, repeat the reader checks there, including links between product help and developer docs.

body:
Select content sources
Move the second Field Notes article into a research/ folder. Readers can still find it in the same collection and at the same address. The same setup lets you publish a note from a separate project without copying it into this one; Why an article has one home explains how its reading paths can change while the article stays together.
Give the second note its own source
Stop the preview. From your publication directory:
cd "$GAZETTE_PUBLICATION"
mkdir research
mv content/review-a-note research/
pwd -P

Use the directory printed by pwd -P plus /research as the new source path.
In gazette.toml, add the research binding to the existing publication's authored array. For an unchanged starter, the result is:
authored = [
  { source = 'source:field-notes', target = 'content' },
  { source = 'source:research-notes', target = 'research' }
]

Keep the options on your existing source records. If the moved note uses figures or math, give its new source the same static_assets or markdown_profile settings it needs.
Add the new source declaration, substituting the actual absolute path:
[[sources]]
id = 'source:research-notes'
location = { kind = 'filesystem', root = '/absolute/path/to/gazette-notes/research' }

Write the full path in TOML. Gazette does not expand $HOME. target names the folder within the build input. Keep the note’s identity, slug and membership as they are. Its new source is bound to the same publication, so the address stays the same. The first note’s [[id:content:review-a-note|Read the next note]] link still reaches it, including if you already placed it in a journey.
Read the result
Restart with your current command and GAZETTE_REQUEST. Keep preview-math-request.json if you enabled math. In the preview, follow the first note into Review a note before drawing a conclusion. It should open at the same address, now built from research/review-a-note/index.md.
In the current Field Notes starter, open research/review-a-note/index.md in the Gazette-enabled VS Code window. The editor discovers it from the source you added to gazette.toml; there is no per-page list to update. If feedback is missing, follow the editor recovery steps. An older workspace using explicit file lists still needs its old entry replaced with the new path; follow the same guide before changing that discovery mode.
Choose a source deliberately
Important
Point each source at material you mean to include. Use filesystem exclusions for unrelated files. To build from a fixed revision, see the Git source options. Before delivery, check the pages and resources the build will expose.
With the sources in place, Articles, collections and journeys shows how to choose how the pieces read together.

body:
Typeset mathematics
Add an inline equation and a displayed fraction to Field Notes.
Important
You need Python 3, Node 20 or later, and GAZETTE and GAZETTE_SOURCE from the starter setup. Gazette includes KaTeX in adapters/math/. It runs locally without an npm install or a typesetting service.
Choose the Node executable
Stop the preview. In your gazette-notes directory, check which Node executable your shell uses:
node --version
export GAZETTE_MATH_NODE="$(node -p 'process.execPath')"

Run the setup with the source checkout you built and the request you last used. It creates two files and leaves existing files alone:
python3 "$GAZETTE_SOURCE/examples/first-publication/configure_math.py" \
  --gazette-source "$GAZETTE_SOURCE" \
  --request "$GAZETTE_REQUEST" \
  --node "$GAZETTE_MATH_NODE"

math-runtime.toml records the executable and renderer. preview-math-request.json keeps your current sites and enables math, with limits of 32 expressions, 64 KiB input, ten seconds and 1 MiB output.
Enable math for this content source
In gazette.toml, add this at the very beginning, before [composition]:
includes = ['math-runtime.toml']

If includes already exists, add math-runtime.toml to the existing array. Keep the settings file beside gazette.toml.
In the Field Notes publication's existing authored array, find the record whose source is source:field-notes and whose target is content. Set markdown_profile = 'publication-math' inside that record. For the original, single-source starter, the complete array then reads:
authored = [{ source = 'source:field-notes', target = 'content', markdown_profile = 'publication-math' }]

Keep the other settings and source entries. This profile applies to Markdown in this source, including Markdown in attached notebooks. It leaves other sources alone and does not run notebook code.
Write and preview the calculation
Use the equation to support the note's explanation; readers still need to know what was counted and under which conditions. Add this section to content/keep-the-context/index.md, after its existing text:
## A count over a fixed interval

For a fixed observation window, the mean rate is $r = n/t$.

```math
r = \frac{n}{t}
```

Here, n is the count and t is the duration. State the duration's unit beside the calculation.

Save the article. Start a preview using the new single-line request:
export GAZETTE_REQUEST="$GAZETTE_PUBLICATION/preview-math-request.json"
cat "$GAZETTE_REQUEST" - | "$GAZETTE" preview-sites \
  --local --allow-listeners --local-urls --watch \
  --listen site:field-notes=127.0.0.1:0

If your request also includes the workbook, add --listen site:workbook=127.0.0.1:0. When Gazette reports ready, open the URL for site:field-notes, then open your first note. Look for the inline equation and a displayed fraction with n above t. Gazette writes MathML into the article, so this theme needs no extra component or browser script for the example.
Keep using the math request as you edit. Save, wait for the rebuild and refresh the tab. Press Ctrl+D to stop the preview. Restart it after changing the workspace, Node or the renderer.
Correct the particular failure
What happens	What to check	
Dollar expressions remain ordinary text	Check that the article's source uses publication-math, then restart the preview	
Preview refuses the request before rendering	Keep preview-math-request.json as the single compact JSON line generated above; preview reads its initial request from one line	
Gazette reports a different Node executable	Update the math renderer to use the intended Node version	
Typesetting fails	Check the TeX expression and the renderer files. Gazette stops if the renderer rejects a command	
Gazette reports a formula, time or size limit	Check the files in that source before raising the limit	
Use backticks to show dollar expressions as text. See supported math notation or configure a renderer for another setup. You can also add a figure or notebook to the same article.

body:
Update the math renderer
If Gazette stops typesetting after you replace Node or update the math adapter, rebuild its settings and reuse your math-enabled Field Notes request.
Keep the old settings and request
Stop the preview with Ctrl+D. Set GAZETTE_REQUEST to the request you last used. The helper requires fresh paths for both files. These commands back up the old files and copy the current request before generating replacements:
(
  set -e
  cd "$GAZETTE_PUBLICATION"
  gazette_math_recovery_dir=$(mktemp -d "$GAZETTE_PUBLICATION/math-recovery.XXXXXX")
  printf 'Backup directory: %s\n' "$gazette_math_recovery_dir"
  cp "$GAZETTE_REQUEST" "$gazette_math_recovery_dir/current-request.json"
  mv math-runtime.toml "$gazette_math_recovery_dir/math-runtime.toml"
  mv preview-math-request.json "$gazette_math_recovery_dir/preview-math-request.json"
  gazette_math_node=$(node -p 'process.execPath')
  python3 "$GAZETTE_SOURCE/examples/first-publication/configure_math.py" \
    --gazette-source "$GAZETTE_SOURCE" \
    --request "$gazette_math_recovery_dir/current-request.json" \
    --node "$gazette_math_node"
)

Warning
If a command fails, read the error and look in the printed backup directory before trying again.
The new math-runtime.toml records your current Node executable. The new request keeps your workspace and sites, and resets math_generation to the default limits. If you changed those limits, copy the values you still need from the backup. Keep the include and Markdown profile in gazette.toml.
Restart with the new settings
Start the preview with the new request. If it includes the workbook, keep --listen site:workbook=127.0.0.1:0 as well:
export GAZETTE_REQUEST="$GAZETTE_PUBLICATION/preview-math-request.json"
cat "$GAZETTE_REQUEST" - | "$GAZETTE" preview-sites \
  --local --allow-listeners --local-urls --watch \
  --listen site:field-notes=127.0.0.1:0

Open the new preview URL and check the inline equation and displayed fraction. Keep this request for later edits.

body:
Why an article has one home
An article can answer more than one reader's question without becoming several copies. The challenge is to represent its different contexts without making each context another authority over its words. Take an article about the cost of a completed inference request. A reader comparing infrastructure suppliers might encounter it in a collection about procurement. A reader learning how serving works might reach the same article after pieces on batching and latency. Its argument is unchanged, but the route through it is different.
One placement, more than one way to arrive
In Gazette's editorial model, an article has one structural placement. It can stand alone, belong directly to a collection or subcollection, or occupy a step in a journey within one of those collections. That choice says where its argument is developed, not every place where its argument might be useful.
A collection gathers work around a shared question. Subcollections give a deeper inquiry room to develop without losing its relationship to the larger one. A journey within that inquiry makes an authored reading order explicit. Membership and order have different jobs: grouping related arguments does not, by itself, tell a reader which premise comes first.
The procurement journey might begin with the workload, move to the capacity promise and end with accepted output. If our cost article belongs to that journey, a serving discussion can still refer readers to it after explaining batching and latency. The reference creates another way to arrive, not a second membership. The serving discussion can explain why the detour matters and where to resume.
That is why a journey is not just a collection sorted by date. The order carries an editorial argument. A later article can supply a premise that the reader needs first; an older article can become the final comparison. When order is meaningful, it deserves an authored decision rather than a filename convention.
An independent blog article also remains legitimate. Not every useful thought needs a series, and a collection should not exist merely to surround one short page with navigation. The structure should express the work's actual depth.
There is an example in this publication. Serving tokens is a service problem stands alone. Useful compute refers to it because request arrivals and accepted outputs affect a compute purchase. The article about runtime portability reaches it through a different question: what happens to live memory and scheduling when the backend changes? Neither reference turns the serving article into a chapter of another container. Its argument stays at one address, while the surrounding questions give the arrival different meaning.
A page has one home
Copying the article into every collection would make navigation easy at first. Later, a correction might reach one copy but not the others. Citations, discussion and publication dates could diverge. Readers would no longer know whether they were seeing the same argument. One source, one publication home and one structural placement prevent that drift. An index can list the page, another article can cite it and another journey can offer it as a detour. A correction then reaches the same argument wherever a reader arrives from, while the surrounding discussion explains why it matters in that context.
The source bundle and the published address are separate decisions too. This guide occupies blog/one-article-several-reading-paths/index.md in Gazette's selected content source. Its declaration names the identity content:gazette-reading-paths, membership in Gazette’s help and the slug why-an-article-has-one-home. Gazette combines that placement and slug with RawThoughts’ routing rules to derive /gazette/why-an-article-has-one-home/. Membership gives the page its reading context; the slug supplies its own part of the address. Both can change while the source folder stays in place. One file is enough for its argument. Figures, notes and notebooks shows a fuller bundle in the same publication: its source folder, rich-documents/, keeps the guide beside the notebook it displays and the small browser program that lets a reader compare image sizes:
rich-documents/
  index.md
  analysis.ipynb
  compare-resources.mjs

Part of the guide	Meaning	
index.md	The explanation, content:gazette-rich-documents identity and membership in Gazette's introduction	
analysis.ipynb	The saved file-size calculation, attached to that article	
compare-resources.mjs	The article's optional browser comparison, compiled as a page resource	
Workspace selection	Gazette's content source is composed into the RawThoughts publication	
/gazette/figures-notes-and-math/	The guide's reader-facing address, independent of its source-folder name	
Gazette brings the saved notebook and declared resource into the same article. A reader can study the complete calculation or change the selected subset without arriving at a competing version of the guide. The controls leave the saved result intact, and the table remains readable without them. A notes.md companion can similarly extend an article with a longer derivation under the same identity. These files have different jobs within one authored work; their presence does not create additional articles or collection memberships.
The pattern also works across publications. A personal essay can lead into a formal treatment of a question; a technical account can lead into its economic consequences. Each publication can frame the connection in its own voice, while the destination gives the other argument room to develop. A useful crossing tells the reader what they will find there, not merely that the two pages mention similar things.
The structure must reach every reader
If the human page shows a journey but the machine-readable representation only sees isolated text, the publication tells two different stories. If search invents a relationship that the page does not declare, it creates a third. Gazette’s compiler resolves the publication once, giving navigation, search, feeds and structured data the same articles, relationships and canonical destinations to express. A theme can then give each publication a different experience without reconstructing where the argument belongs. A reader following the collection and a machine inspecting the page should encounter the same explanation of where the argument belongs.
To apply this to your own writing, choose the home in which each argument develops, put dependent explanations in a deliberate order and link to useful detours where the reader needs them. Articles, collections and journeys takes you through those declarations in Field Notes. Gazette can detect a missing journey member; you decide why that member belongs in the sequence.

body:
Work with an agent
An agent arrives at Gazette over a local MCP server, and one call gives it the same account of your publication that the command line and the editor use: its pages, their addresses, how they belong to collections or journeys and where each one is edited. The VS Code extension gives you that account as you type.
Ask your agent why a note appears where it does, then have it rename the note and check the result. Use the publication folder from Your first publication.
Connect the local server
If your agent already shows Gazette in its MCP server list, skip this step. Otherwise open a terminal in your publication directory:
cd "$GAZETTE_PUBLICATION"

For Codex:
codex mcp add gazette -- "$GAZETTE" mcp

For Claude Code:
claude mcp add --transport stdio gazette -- "$GAZETTE" mcp

Use /mcp in the terminal client to check that Gazette is connected. If you replace the Gazette executable, reconnect to use the new build. For another setup, see the Codex connection guide or Claude Code connection guide. A manual configuration needs the absolute executable path and the argument mcp over standard input and output. Your client starts and stops the local server. This setup works without a publishing account. If you are writing your own client, connect it to Gazette and run a first check.
Ask about the publication you made
Give the agent the absolute path to your gazette-notes directory and ask:
Use Gazette to review gazette.toml in this directory for site:field-notes. Read its local sources. Show the pages, their current addresses, how they belong to collections or journeys, and where I edit each one. Do not change files or start a release.
If the agent needs a tool name, ask for review_publication. Check that the answer finds both notes and any reading paths you added. Ask it to show the first note's title and address in the source. If you moved the note into a journey, look for its current address and the old ones you kept as aliases.
Make a change
Rename the first note to “Record the context” in its declaration and heading. Keep its identity, current address, body and reading relationships. Save the change in the existing source, then inspect the publication again.
If you already chose that title in Write in VS Code, ask for another and use it below.
A title change is safe because the identity and address stay put; a change to an identity, slug or route is not, and Gazette's check does not say what else points at the old one. Ask the agent to list the references to it with authoring_references before it edits. The agent edits the file and asks Gazette to check it. Review the edit, then refresh after the preview rebuilds. The new title should appear in the article and its collection or journey at the same address.
Use the current editor context when it matters
If the question concerns an unsaved passage, use Gazette: Inspect Current Editor with MCP in the connected editor. It shares the current editor text, including unsaved changes.
Caution
To take that context to a separate client, use Export Current Editor Context. The export can include your sources and unsaved writing. Share it only with the client you want to read it. Save first if you want the preview to use the same text.
Ask the agent to preview, then close it
Give the agent the current saved request path named by GAZETTE_REQUEST, then ask:
Start a local preview of this saved publication, keeping its current sites and enabled math. Read its local sources, use local addresses and free loopback ports, and show me the ready address. Stop that preview when I finish and tell me if it fails to close.
Open the reported address and ask the agent to stop its preview when you finish. Your files stay where you edited them. For a client integration, see how a preview starts and stops. To share a build, see Review and export a publication.

body:
Write in VS Code
You reach Gazette from the editor through its language server, which gives you the same account of the publication that the command line and a connected agent use: a diagnostic on the page you are typing, and a way to jump to the source behind a result. Your agent has the same account through its own connection, Work with an agent.
Use VS Code to catch a mistake before it reaches your preview. Keep the Field Notes preview open so you can compare the saved page with what you are typing.
Open your publication with the extension
You need VS Code 1.96 or later. If you have not set up Gazette in VS Code, follow Open the local extension from a source checkout. Return here with the Field Notes folder open in that window.
Change a title and repair a broken link
Open content/keep-the-context/index.md. If VS Code opens a preview, choose Reopen Editor With → Text Editor. Whatever its title is now, change it to this one:
title = 'Record the context'

Change the heading to match:
# Record the context

Check that the new heading appears in Outline. Then find the link to the second note. Its label is separate the observation from the claim in the starter, or Read the next note if you followed the garden example. Change only its identity from id:content:review-a-note to id:content:missing-note, keeping the label. Open Problems to inspect the unresolved destination.
Open the second note, content/review-a-note/index.md, and find its [content].id: content:review-a-note. Restore the first note’s destination to id:content:review-a-note. Once the error clears, use Open Link or Go to Definition on the repaired link to open the second note's source.
If you already moved that note by following Select content sources, look in research/review-a-note/index.md. Its identity remains the same when you move it into a journey or change its slug, so the repaired link can still find it.
Save the first note, wait for the preview to rebuild and refresh. The article and its collection or journey entry should now read Record the context at its current address. Follow the repaired link to the second note.
Inspect the page you are writing
Gazette: Page Details shows where this page comes from and where it sits in the publication. Before you change a page's identity or slug, use Find All References on it to see what links to it; Problems reports a broken link only after the change.
In gazette.toml, Go to Definition on 'owner:field-notes' opens the author's declaration.
Gazette: Inspect Current Editor with MCP reads unsaved text from the active editor. The ordinary preview reads your saved files. See Work with an agent for the next task.
If feedback is missing
The current Field Notes starter finds its pages through gazette.toml. Adding or moving a page beneath content/ requires no per-page editor list: open the page to get feedback. A file outside that folder must belong to another configured content source; opening an unrelated folder does not add its files.
Open Output → Gazette. Check that you trust the publication folder, Gazette: Server Path in User settings points to your executable, and gazette.workspace.configuration selects its gazette.toml. Check any reported configuration error and that the page belongs to a configured content source, then open the page again. For an older workspace using explicit file lists, check that its selection includes the page. After correcting the setup, use Gazette: Restart Server if feedback is still missing.
An older workspace may still use explicit file lists. Those keep it in that mode even when gazette.workspace.discovery is true. If you want automatic discovery, follow the migration instructions to preserve selected content and manual support. Removing only one list can leave other explicit selections active.
If the extension never loads, return to the local extension setup. To integrate a different editor, see the language server guide.
Reopen this editor
Reopen the same Gazette-enabled window or profile and the publication in GAZETTE_PUBLICATION. If you deleted the profile, repeat the extension setup and point it at the same files.

body:
Pale
Open a repository you already use. Pale shows which review instructions apply and what will change before you install them. Define who is involved, what belongs to whom and what each person or agent may do in one workspace. Pale compiles that description on your own machine for tools such as Claude Code and Codex.
A harness over the tools you already use
Work can span your projects, household, company and clients, and each coding tool you use would otherwise need the same instructions repeated in every session. Pale is a meta harness, a harness over the tools people already use, so each of them draws its permissions and context from one description of your world. It shows where an assignment stands while each person and application keeps its own records and permissions, and it brings you back into the conversation when someone needs a decision.
Among the products, Pale is the part through which the others act, and each of them can also be used without it; Scope then works with Weave. You can configure a workspace and add repository guidance locally today. The live connection to your coding tools is the part being built.
From your description to work you can return to
Take an account review. The customer system holds the account and a reporting tool produces the comparison. A report for the wrong period still needs correction, and the next person should be able to see that and find the original work. Pale gets from your description of the world to that work in four steps; the first two run locally today.
Describe your world
Say who is involved, which projects, households, organisations and clients you act within, and what each person, agent and application may do. The description is yours, and Pale compiles it without inventing anything. Your agent can help you write it.
Let Pale compile it
Pale checks the description and fixes it as one version. That version is the boundary your agents work inside: their permissions and their context come from the same source. Before a change takes over, you can see what it would affect.
Let your tools ask at every step
Before Claude Code or Codex acts, it asks Pale what is allowed and which context the task needs. The customer record stays in the customer system, and the reporting tool keeps the comparison it produces. Routine progress can stay quiet. A request for consent, a conflict or a result that needs review brings you back into the conversation.
Return to the result
Open the original work and see which decisions are still due. PaleUniverse, the view of your world as Pale compiled it, shows how the work fits into your workspace and where its settings came from. Pale keeps genealogy, the history of context, so a result links back to what it relied on and what followed while each record stays in the system that owns it. When something was wrong, change the description and the next step follows it.
Questions about Pale
How do my coding tools use Pale?
Through a live connection at every step: before Claude Code or Codex acts, it asks Pale what is allowed and what context the task needs, and Pale answers from your compiled description, so every tool works from the same account of your world. A refusal protects anything only where the host enforces it. That connection is the part being built. Today the local tools in the guide add shared coding instructions to a repository and inspect your workspace.
How does my agent help me write the description?
The description is the one thing everything else depends on, so Pale helps you write it. Its editor support and its agent connection use the same compiler. What the editor shows about an edit to your workspace, your agent can review in conversation and get the same answer. Today you can inspect a workspace and compare a proposed edit with the local tools in the guide.
Does Pale replace the systems I already use?
Pale connects the systems you already use rather than taking their place. Each keeps its own records and permissions. When you need the source, Pale takes you back to it.
Can I bring my own setting and systems?
Pale is for your world, not a default one, so you describe your own people, projects and systems in a workspace. A machine binding tells Pale where to find their files and programs. Each application needs its own working integration.
What does PaleUniverse let me explore?
PaleUniverse is for seeing your world as Pale compiled it and following any result back to the description behind it; it is planned for a coming release. Its first views show your World, open the Source behind it and compare a proposed Change. Later views follow work in progress (Now), system health (Doctor) and a result's genealogy: what it relied on, what changed and what followed (Trace).
Where should I start?
Start with a repository you already use. Pale installs shared coding instructions for Claude Code or Codex beside the ones the repository keeps, and shows what a proposed workspace change would affect before you apply it. The Pale guide takes you through choosing a task and using your workspace.

body:
Inspect your workspace
You want a repository to use a security-review role, and need to know what else depends on that choice. Before installing the new guidance, check what Pale would use for the project on this computer and compare the proposed edit with the current workspace.
Important
Use your existing workspace. The repository guidance starter is enough to try the role comparison. The runtime checks also need a Package distribution and machine paths set up.
Choose the configuration you mean
Use the terminal where you set PALE in the source-build instructions. Find the root pale-workspace.toml, the project's ID, the ID of the setting it runs in and the machine ID. Use the IDs in your workspace files. The machine binding supplies the paths and executables on this computer.
Point CURRENT_WORKSPACE at the workspace you use now. For the repository guidance starter, set the three IDs to repository, local-guidance and local, respectively. For a runtime workspace, replace the example IDs with its own project, execution workspace and machine IDs. Keep the same shell open so you can reuse pale_here below.
CURRENT_WORKSPACE='/absolute/current/pale-workspace.toml'
PALE_PROJECT='demo'
PALE_EXECUTION_WORKSPACE='default'
PALE_MACHINE='local'

pale_here() {
  "$PALE" --workspace "$CURRENT_WORKSPACE" --project "$PALE_PROJECT" \
    --execution-workspace "$PALE_EXECUTION_WORKSPACE" --machine "$PALE_MACHINE" "$@"
}

If you are using the repository guidance starter, continue to compare the role change. For a runtime workspace, check the current configuration first.
Check a runtime workspace
pale_here validate

If validation reports a missing declaration, machine path or Package file, fix that input and run it again. This check leaves repository files alone. Check whether an application is running through the application itself.
Then read the compiled profile:
pale_here summary

Check project_id and execution_workspace_id, then look at each entry in repositories:
Field	What it tells you	
repository_id	Which repository this entry describes	
surfaces	The guidance and settings Pale would generate	
execution_paths	The ways this repository is configured to run work	
activation_selected_execution_path_ids	Which paths are configured for activation in this repository	
If a repository or agent path is missing, check how it is linked to the project and which Packages it uses. A listed path tells you how the workspace is set up. Use pale_here compile if you also need the generated file counts and checksums from the compilation.
Compare a candidate without applying it
Keep the proposed workspace in a separate folder. Use the same project, execution workspace, machine and Package distribution. Keep the project's starting Package list the same. To change the distribution or that list, validate each copy against its own Package inputs and inspect the results separately.
If you set up the repository guidance starter, copy its whole folder, including the locks, to a new folder. Leave the copy pointed at the same repository and Pale checkout. In its pale-workspace.toml, change the repository role's resource_id from change to security. Keep CURRENT_WORKSPACE pointed at the original starter. Set CANDIDATE_WORKSPACE to the edited copy.
CANDIDATE_WORKSPACE='/absolute/candidate/pale-workspace.toml'

pale_review() {
  pale_here review-configuration --candidate-workspace "$CANDIDATE_WORKSPACE" "$@"
}

pale_review preview > review.json

In review.json, check project_id and execution_workspace_id. Look at profile_change.state. If you changed the starter's role, it should read changed. Then read the first page of up to ten entries:
pale_review impacts --limit 10 < review.json

If nextOffset is a number, run the command again with --offset NUMBER, using that number and the original review.json. A null value means you have reached the end.
A state of affected means the item depends on something you changed. Its own value can still be the same. In the starter example, inspect the affected entries, including workspace-manifest and responsibility_closure, to see which parts of the workspace depend on the role. For a runtime workspace, run summary for both copies with the same IDs to compare their resulting settings. To inspect individual values from an integration, see how configuration review works.
Each request checks the saved preview against a fresh comparison. If you edited either workspace since the preview, run pale_review preview again and review the new results. Leave the old JSON alone.
Important
Accepting a review does not apply it. To accept the review, run pale_review accept < review.json. Use reject or cancel for those decisions. Pale returns your decision and leaves both workspaces and repository files as they were.
To install guidance from the edited starter, set CURRENT_WORKSPACE to the candidate manifest and GUIDANCE_WORKSPACE to its directory. Reuse pale_here from this page and start at Review the changes to make a new guidance plan. For a runtime workspace, follow the file-plan instructions using the candidate.
Editor support
Use the VS Code setup guide to connect the extension to its language server. The small example there demonstrates the editor connection. Open your configured workspace for the full profile.
Use Pale: Select Profile Context, then open Pale Profile in the Explorer. The language server can point to problems and take you to the declaration behind a result. Configuration review uses the files as they appear in the editor, including unsaved edits.
Return to Introduction to Pale for the broader product, or continue with repository guidance.

body:
Add coding instructions to a repository
Pale supports two coding hosts today, Claude Code and Codex. Give either a shared way to review changes and check its work. Pale adds links to that guidance in the repository’s AGENTS.md and keeps the project instructions you already wrote there, including your build commands and conventions. Both hosts use this one entry file, with separate skills and references for each.
This setup installs guidance for your coding host. It does not start Pale’s resident service; your host reads and uses the installed instructions in its own session.
Set up a starter workspace
Use a Git repository you can write to and a local build of Pale. In the same terminal, replace the three example paths below. Use a new folder name for GUIDANCE_WORKSPACE so the starter copies into that folder directly.
export PALE_SOURCE='/absolute/path/to/pale'
export PALE="$PALE_SOURCE/target/debug/pale"
export GUIDANCE_WORKSPACE='/absolute/path/to/new-guidance-workspace'
export REPOSITORY="$(cd '/absolute/path/to/your/repository' && pwd -P)"
cp -R "$PALE_SOURCE/docs/examples/guidance-workspace" "$GUIDANCE_WORKSPACE"

If you built the executable elsewhere, set PALE to its actual path. In $GUIDANCE_WORKSPACE/machines/local.toml, set distribution_root to your Pale checkout and checkout_root to the path from printf '%s\n' "$REPOSITORY". Leave the other settings as they are.
Use this helper for the remaining commands. It keeps them pointed at the same starter and repository settings.
pale_here() {
  "$PALE" --workspace "$GUIDANCE_WORKSPACE/pale-workspace.toml" \
    --project repository --execution-workspace local-guidance --machine local "$@"
}

pale_here distribution-info --lockfile > "$GUIDANCE_WORKSPACE/distribution.lock.toml"

Keep distribution.lock.toml with the starter. If you update the Pale checkout, regenerate the lock and review a new plan before applying it.
Choose your coding host
Set PALE_HOST for the host you want to use. The remaining commands use that choice throughout planning, installation, checking and removal.
Host	Run this assignment	Generated guidance and skills	
Codex	PALE_HOST=codex	.pale/guidance/codex/index.md and .codex/skills/	
Claude Code	PALE_HOST=claude-code	.pale/guidance/claude-code/index.md and .claude/skills/	
Choose one row and run its assignment in the same terminal. Read AGENTS.md before planning if it exists. If your repository points to shared rules elsewhere, keep that link and the rules it supplies. Existing client or upstream instructions keep their own conventions.
For Claude Code, use version 2.1.285 or later with its built-in AGENTS.md support enabled. Open /config and set Project instructions to claude-md-and-agents-md so Claude Code loads the shared file even when there are also CLAUDE.md instructions in the project or its parent directories. This is a host setting; putting it in the repository’s project or local settings will not enable it. See Claude’s instruction-file settings for user, managed or invocation configuration. Pale leaves your host settings and existing CLAUDE.md alone.
If an earlier Pale installation added its guidance to CLAUDE.md, first follow Remove generated guidance below with PALE_HOST=claude-code and that installation’s original workspace, project and repository selections. A newly copied starter cannot take over another installation. Review that removal, apply it, then return here for a fresh installation plan. Your own text stays in CLAUDE.md; the new contribution goes into AGENTS.md. Resolve any interrupted write before either operation, using the recovery link below.
Review the changes
pale_here guidance plan --repository source --host "$PALE_HOST"

The plan lists files to add, update, keep or remove, followed by their text differences. Lines starting with + are additions; lines starting with - are removals. The surrounding text helps you see where each change belongs.
Find the proposed change to AGENTS.md. Check that your own instructions and any other host’s contribution are still there. Match each new link to a file in the plan.
Read the role and policies. The starter covers how to investigate a change, respect project rules and safety, and verify and review the work. Pale includes the instructions those policies depend on. For other roles or policies, see choose Package guidance.
Review the .gitignore change. Pale adds a block for its local lock, recovery record and remembered plans, preserving your existing rules. This works in ordinary repositories and linked worktrees.
Check every proposed path, especially removals. If Pale reports a conflict with an existing file, open it and agree on the change with the repository maintainer. Keep the existing instructions while you resolve it.
The plan leaves your instructions unchanged and remembers the proposal for this host. Each new plan replaces the previous one for that host. You can review the output in your terminal or save it by adding > "$GUIDANCE_WORKSPACE/guidance-plan.txt" to the command and opening that file. Keep saved output with the project: it can contain your project’s instructions.
Apply the plan
When the changes look right, apply the plan with the same host and workspace settings:
pale_here guidance apply --repository source --host "$PALE_HOST"

Pale checks the files and settings again before it writes. If the plan has changed, generate and review a fresh one. When the command succeeds, it reports Published source guidance and the number of changed files.
Open AGENTS.md and follow the new role and index links. Check the guidance and skills at the paths in the host table. Start a fresh session of that host in this repository. In Claude Code, use /memory to confirm that AGENTS.md appears among the loaded files.
Then ask the agent running in that host to use the instructions for a small task, such as checking the links in a README. Follow its findings back to the actual links and destinations. Check which instructions it used and whether the result helps you fix the page. Seeing a file in the loaded list confirms that it reached the host; the task shows how the agent used it.
Check for drift
Run the planning command again. If the files and settings still match, every file is marked keep. Applying that fresh plan reports 0 changed files. The plan from before installation is now out of date, so run a new one even when you expect no changes.
Review any proposed update before applying it. Pale can refuse to overwrite a file someone edited by hand, including its block in .gitignore. Compare that file with the proposed version and resolve the difference before you retry.
Warning
Keep the interrupted-write record. If a write was interrupted, keep .pale-source-guidance-recovery.json and review the recovery choices before running another apply. The CLI can help you restore the earlier files or finish cleanup after a completed write.
Remove generated guidance
Plan the removal, review its output, then apply it:
pale_here guidance plan --repository source --host "$PALE_HOST" --intent remove
pale_here guidance apply --repository source --host "$PALE_HOST" --intent remove

Pale removes the selected host’s generated files and its contribution to AGENTS.md. Your own project text and the other host’s contribution stay. For an earlier installation recorded in CLAUDE.md, removal uses that recorded location. The local lock, remembered plan and their .gitignore rules also stay, ready for the next installation.
Add the other host
Change PALE_HOST to the other value in the table. If you are adding Claude Code, first set its Project instructions as described in Choose your coding host. Then start again at Review the changes: read that host’s proposed files, apply its plan and try a small task in that host. Pale remembers a separate plan for each host; removing one host’s guidance leaves the other’s in place. The developer contract covers automation and recovery.

body:
Introduction to Pale
A new coding session begins with a familiar job: explain the project, point the agent to its instructions and make sure it knows how to check a change. When several repositories share a way of working, those explanations can drift apart. Changing the review method in one place leaves you wondering where else it applies.
Pale lets you write your world once, and compiles it into the permissions and context the coding tools you already use ask for at every step. You describe that arrangement once, select the methods a responsibility needs and inspect what a change would affect, whichever host and model an agent runs on. Its local configuration tools let you begin with the repositories you already use.
Start with a repository
Start with either task using a local source build:
Add coding instructions to a repository. Review what Pale proposes for Codex or Claude Code, then install it alongside the instructions you already keep there.
Inspect your workspace. Find what applies to a project and compare a proposed edit before changing files.
Note
Today you can try the two local tools above. Connecting your everyday chat tools and handing work to agents needs a deployed Pale service and its integrations, which are the part being built.
Put the responsibility in its setting
Suppose the job is reviewing code. Your workspace says which project the repository serves, who carries the responsibility and which applications are involved. The same description can distinguish your own project from client work, or a repository from the service that runs its code.
When review is a continuing duty, a role names that duty separately from whoever performs it. The reviewer can change while the responsibility remains. The structure a responsibility needs explains when to introduce a role and what a handover should preserve.
A project can run in several settings, each an execution workspace. A machine binding supplies the paths to files and executables on one computer. If Pale cannot find the checkout, fix its machine binding. If the review belongs to the wrong project, fix that relationship in the workspace. Connecting an application still requires the access that application grants.
Choose how the review should work
A Package supplies reusable roles, procedures and policies. Select a code-review procedure for this responsibility, and Pale can turn it into instructions and skills for your coding host. The repository keeps its own build commands and conventions alongside them. After installation, ask the agent to use the guidance on a small task and follow its findings back to the code. The useful question is whether those instructions helped it do the work.
See what a changed method affects
Now suppose you choose a different review procedure from a Package you already use. Which responsibilities depend on that choice? Compare the current and proposed workspaces to find them. A responsibility can depend on the change even when its final settings stay the same; the review shows that connection too.
The comparison returns your decision without saving it to either workspace. If you also want to install different instructions, read the file plan before applying it. Seeing how a choice affects the workspace and agreeing to change repository files are separate steps.
When the work crosses applications
A code review is one responsibility. An account review might involve several: the customer system holds the account, a reporting tool produces a comparison, and the receiving team decides whether it is useful. A report for the wrong period still needs correction after the tool finishes. Pale carries that work between applications and brings you back into the conversation when a decision is needed.
That requires more than calling tools. The design distinguishes asking contributors for advice, handing work to another system, checking progress and requesting a stop. If the reporting tool's reply goes missing, it may already have acted. Pale checks the application's records before trying again.
The coding host must enforce Pale's permission decisions: a refusal has to prevent the action. How Pale fits together explains how permission, context and recovery connect the host to Pale's service.
Use connected applications for their own strengths
Weave keeps the organisation's account and work records. Scope supplies permitted context for a task, while Counsel provides judgment and memory assistance. Reckon runs the evaluation lab, and its design adds the services for investigating whether a changed method helped. What Reckon learns comes from Pale's genealogy, the history of context: an append-only map of references showing where work came from, what it relied on and what followed, with each record staying in the system that owns it.
Integrated requests for Scope's context, Counsel's judgment and Reckon's evaluations pass through Pale. Each receiving application checks the caller's permission and keeps responsibility for its own result. Each product can also be used without the others under its own access rules, except Scope, which works with Pale, Weave or both; adopting one does not require adopting the whole set.
For example, Gazette builds a publication directly from selected sources, which can include permitted Weave records. It needs no live context, judgment or evaluation call to compile them. Pale can arrange the publication work through Gazette's own interface.
Explore the whole picture with PaleUniverse
PaleUniverse connects the picture of your world to the source that describes it, and is planned for a coming release. Its first views show your World, open the Source behind it and compare a proposed Change, so you can follow a responsibility back to its declaration. Later views follow work in progress (Now), system health (Doctor) and a result's genealogy: what it relied on, what changed and what followed (Trace).
The question behind the system
Building a place to think explains the motivation: returning to work without having to reconstruct its context each time. Structure takes effort to prepare and maintain, so the cost of understanding asks whether it repays that effort. Improving the system between runs follows how results could inform a change to the method.
MONAD studies what descriptions preserve and when they need to change. MUON and HENA explore adaptive units and their collective organisation. These research questions connect to Pale's ambition while the current tools work with an explicit workspace.
Harsh Joshi is Pale's author, and RTEPL owns the project. Pale comes in two profiles of the same community code, with the same rights: Bare selects the smallest working set of parts, and Curated assembles a reference selection of connected products.
Build an integration
To embed or extend Pale, read the developer architecture or choose an SDK. For the first repository task, return to adding coding instructions with a repository you control.

body:
Privacy notice
RawThoughts Enterprises Private Limited (RTEPL) is responsible for deciding how personal data is used on rawthoughts.in, causality.in, sleepwalker.in and post-agi-economics.org, and on their subdomains, including the documentation at docs.rawthoughts.in and docs.causality.in. RTEPL publishes and operates these websites. This notice explains the information handled when you read these websites or use their contact and reading tools.
Visiting the website
GitHub Pages hosts these publications. Serving a page involves connection information, including your IP address and the page requested. GitHub logs visitors’ IP addresses for security, including when a visitor is not signed in. GitHub handles that information under its privacy statement and may process it outside India.
Mintlify hosts the documentation at docs.rawthoughts.in and docs.causality.in. Serving those pages involves the same connection information, which Mintlify handles under its privacy policy and may process outside India. Mintlify's own visitor telemetry is turned off for these sites. Mintlify also provides those two sites' search, page tools and display settings, under the same privacy policy; the in-browser search, assistant tools, display settings and passage links described below belong to the other websites.
On the other websites, search runs in your browser against each website's own index, so what you type is not sent to a search service. Your search is kept in the search page's address, so like any address it can reach GitHub with a page request, appear in your browser history and go with the address if you share it.
If your browser has an assistant that supports it, each page offers that assistant two read-only tools: the text of the page you are reading and the same in-browser search. They work on what the page already shows and send nothing to us; what the assistant does with what it reads follows its provider's terms.
Contacting us
A contact link opens a new message in your own email application. The website does not receive or store the message as a form submission. If you choose to send it, your email service and the recipient's mail service handle the correspondence. Any professional work that follows has its own correspondence and agreement.
For privacy questions, a grievance or a request concerning your personal data, write to info@rtepl.co.in. Include enough information to identify the request, but do not send passwords or unnecessary identity documents. We respond within 30 days and may ask for proportionate verification before disclosing or changing personal data.
Reading preferences
The display settings remember your colour and motion choices in your browser on this device. You can change them in Settings or clear the website's stored data through your browser. These preferences are used to display the page; they stay in your browser and are not sent to us.
After a page loads, your browser may request a few linked pages from the same site and keep copies on this device. These are ordinary page requests to the site's host. The browser can discard the copies, and clearing the site's stored data removes them.
Asking about a passage
When you select text and choose a reading assistant, the link opens that provider with the selected passage, nearby context, the section and article titles, the publication's name, and the article and publication addresses. The passage is limited to 4,096 characters and the nearby context to 1,024. Selecting text alone prepares the link in your browser; choosing the provider sends it there.
The assistant is an external service. The request is included in its link, so it can also appear in your browser history. The provider's own terms, privacy policy and your account settings govern what it does with the request and any conversation that follows. Reading the article does not require using an assistant.
How long information is kept
We keep no record of visits on our own systems; GitHub and Mintlify keep their connection logs for the periods their policies set. Correspondence you send is kept for as long as the matter it concerns needs it and as the law requires.
Security and incidents
These websites hold no accounts and receive no form submissions. If a personal-data breach affects you, we inform you and the authorities as applicable law requires.
Your choices
Following another external link takes you to that service under its own data practices.
You may ask us about your data, request correction or deletion, withdraw consent or raise a concern using the contact above. Requests are handled under applicable law; information needed to comply with a legal obligation or resolve a dispute may need to be kept. Withdrawing consent does not undo processing that has already occurred lawfully.
Changes to the website's data practices will be reflected in this notice. A new optional use that requires consent will ask for that consent rather than treating continued reading as agreement.

arguments.label: Products

questions.question: How can I try the products?
questions.answer_html: Start with a task: give coding agents shared repository instructions, build a publication or work through a RawFish rehearsal. The first two run from a local source build, and each guide says what you need before you begin. RawFish's guide reads without installing anything, because the retained prototype covers only part of the rehearsal it describes.

questions.question: What question do these products answer?
questions.answer_html: How does a person or an organisation form a working picture of its work, act through it, learn from what follows and stay accountable as agents do more of the work? Each product answers a part of it, and each can be used alone except Scope, which brings its context from Pale, Weave or both. Weave keeps the records, Scope brings the context a task needs, Counsel judges where rules leave a choice, RawFish rehearses a direction before anyone commits to it, Gazette publishes a body of thought, and Pale is the meta harness through which they act, a harness over the tools people already use.

questions.question: How do these products fit together?
questions.answer_html:
Together the products form one system a person runs, with people deciding: the records hold the world, something is observed, a person decides what to do about it, a direction can be tried before anyone commits to it, the act goes out, and its outcome returns as a record that shapes what is learned next. What joins them is one problem: agents decide far more often than people, so by the time an agent writes, what it read has usually changed. A read says what else to read, and a write is tried for what it affects before it goes in; the Systems collection follows that through the parts. Pale's local tools, Gazette and Reckon’s laboratory run today and the other parts join one at a time; each product's page says what runs and the problem in front of it.

In the integrated system, requests for Scope’s context, Counsel’s judgment and Reckon’s evaluation pass through Pale. Scope always works with Pale, Weave or both: Weave keeps the records and points to the files around them, Pale keeps the history of what each piece of work relied on and what followed, and Scope combines the two into one account an agent can ask for what it needs. Without Pale, Scope is how an agent reads Weave. Harsh describes three sides that keep the system improving safely: the recursive self-improvement side, where Microsoft's SkillOpt, Reckon and Counsel are joined by Pale's genealogy, its history of what each piece of work relied on and what followed, and improve the methods between runs; the continual-learning side, where a person's workspace and Pale's SDKs, language server, VS Code extension and MCP let a person and their agent keep rewriting the description of their world; and the context engineering and alignment side, where Scope, that genealogy and Weave give each act the context it needs and keep it within bounds. Gazette builds publications from the sources you select and does not call Scope, Counsel or Reckon; supplying it an organisation's permitted Weave records is the connection in front. RawFish rehearses a decision through a simulated world. Reckon, under Causality, supplies the separate evaluation instrument. Pale’s introduction explains how those contributions fit without moving their records or decisions into one application.

Weave alone is a headless Jira and Salesforce, a database with a capable interface, and that is an intended way to use it. Pale alone is a hook runtime and context declaration engine that asks you to tune your files and knowledge closely, an orchestrator of agent sandboxes and a permission system for agents. Together they give something more: people and agents working inside one organisation and across several, each instance kept separate, reads and writes delegated across instances, and a structured memory for people and agents, serving the same headless Jira and Salesforce to both.

questions.answer_html: Open a product’s guides to understand it or try a supported workflow. Use the developer docs at docs.rawthoughts.in to build the product, integrate with its code or extend it.

arguments.label: From a decision to an inspectable rehearsal

questions.question: Which decisions can I rehearse?
questions.answer_html: Creator scenarios explore how posts and announcements might reach loyal followers, new viewers, critics and quiet audiences. Internal policy looks at how managers communicate workplace changes and where a rollout could stall. Public policy looks at capacity, unequal effects and incentives. RawFish uses representative group types and excludes simulations of identifiable people and sensitive workplace sources. The rehearsal guide explains which scenarios and sources fit.

questions.question: What do I receive from a rehearsal?
questions.answer_html: The scenario, settings, risks and questions for field investigation. Read, Ask and Analysis help you tell what came from source material, what agents did during the run and what the report inferred. A generated persona cannot speak for a real person or population. The findings guide explains how to distinguish a report’s claims from their supporting evidence.

questions.question: Can I use a local model?
questions.answer_html: Choose a local model or explicitly select an external provider. Before running, read Preflight’s model-readiness result, scale, latency and available cost estimate. Choose graph memory separately; a local report model alone does not tell you where memory sends data.

questions.question: How can I compare runs?
questions.answer_html: Keep the conditions aligned, change the proposal or random seed, and compare the separate runs. A saved run retains its own settings and report. The findings guide explains how to compare the evidence behind a difference.

questions.question: What could follow if a decision were taken?
questions.answer_html: A rehearsal tries a direction before it is taken, so that you can see what could follow if the decision were taken: a reaction you did not expect, a constraint the plan neglected, a question for the people affected. These are questions to investigate, not predictions, and a generated persona cannot speak for a real person. Comparing a direction taken with one not taken is what RawFish is designed around: it varies one thing you declare in the same simulated world and compares what follows. Today a second version of a proposal gets its own scenario and report beside the first, and the comparison is the next piece to build. The findings go back to the people deciding. Weave can link a rehearsal to the proposal it tested as evidence while the run and its report stay with RawFish, and the reviewer still decides.

questions.question: Where can I explore the underlying questions?
questions.answer_html: Rehearsal and evidence develops the interaction mechanisms, quiet audiences and kinds of variation a simulation needs to make understandable.

questions.question: Where should I start?
questions.answer_html: Start with the rehearsal guide. It follows a workplace decision from proposal to findings and needs nothing installed, because the rehearsal it describes is the rebuild's design and the retained prototype covers only part of it. The prototype guides also read without its code. Only running the reference prototype needs a source checkout, and its developer walkthrough covers that.

questions.answer_html: Its six-step cockpit takes a scenario through saved settings to a generated report. Understand the reference prototype follows a creator announcement and explains what its results can support. Developers can use the local walkthrough for startup and configuration.

body:
Models, memory and the work between them
Before a creator sends an announcement through RawFish, they need to know which services will read it and whether those services can do the work. The report model and graph memory have separate connections. Either can fail while the other works, and choosing a local report model leaves the memory clients to be configured separately.
This guide explains those choices in the reference prototype. For the source setup and service settings, follow the configuration procedure.
Check the model before starting
The prototype can use native Ollama, another local server with an OpenAI-compatible API, or an external provider. Choose a model that the selected server actually provides and check that it can return the structured responses report generation needs.
Preflight shows the provider, model and address alongside readiness, proposed run size, estimated tokens, latency and available external cost. Use those results to decide whether to proceed or reduce the run. If the price is missing, the cost is unknown. A scale guard can stop an oversized run before launch.
For the creator considering daily clips, the model can help parse the pasted announcement and later write a report. Creator's Simulate step records completion without running agents. Changing the model can change the proposed reactions in the report; it does not test a different simulated conversation.
Caution
An external provider can receive the announcement during parsing or report generation. Check where each call goes before supplying material.
Choose how the graph is kept
Source development can use a deterministic in-process memory mock without Neo4j. Graphiti mode uses Neo4j and its own model, embedding and reranking clients to work with the graph. Those clients have separate settings from the report model. Check each one's recipient and the material it processes and retains.
Match the embedding dimension to its model, and choose the reranking model separately. The prototype's locked Neo4j dependency falls outside Graphiti's declared supported range, so this arrangement remains experimental. The local Docker recipe selects Graphiti; choosing mock memory in a host-side setting does not change that recipe.
A successful report call tells you the report model answered. To check memory, follow its own storage and retrieval path. That is also how you find which part needs attention when the application can write a report but cannot retrieve the records behind it.
Reach the model from the host and from containers
The local recipe runs Ollama on the host and the application and Neo4j in containers. A probe running on the host can reach Ollama through localhost. From a container, that address points back to the container itself.
The recipe therefore keeps separate addresses for the host probes, the Docker application and Graphiti's client. When changing provider or model, update every caller that should use the new service. Otherwise, a request can continue reaching the old local model while another uses the replacement. Check the connection from the application as well as from the host.
When a report fails, follow the error to that call. A model timeout needs a different remedy from an unavailable graph store. Report validation can also reject the text returned by a working model. Identify the failed step before retrying the rehearsal, so that the retry does not merely repeat work that already succeeded.
Check who can use the application
Authentication can reject an application request before either service is called. In a source build using the prototype's browser key, matching the frontend and backend keys satisfies that key check. The key is delivered in the frontend, however, so it cannot authenticate separate people or isolate their data. The local recipe binds ports to loopback; a shared deployment would need its own access and data boundaries.
Once the services are ready, you can examine the report. Keep the scenario, model and configuration with it, then use Read the findings to distinguish a statement drawn from the announcement from a proposed reaction to it. Readiness tells you that the chosen services can be reached; the audience's response still needs investigation.

body:
Read the findings
A creator announces that daily clips will replace weekly long-form explainers. A RawFish report suggests that regular viewers may read the change as abandonment. The announcement tells you what will stop; finding out how viewers interpret it requires another kind of evidence. Reading the report means following that difference through its claims.
Start with the run that produced the report
In Findings, Read opens the report, Ask lets you question it and Analysis shows settings, lineage and comparisons. Keep the scenario, model and configuration alongside the claims you examine.
The current Creator prototype asks a model to write this report after recording a completion marker. It runs no agent conversation, and its report prompt uses neither the cohort statistical settings nor the evidence catalog. Treat its proposed audience reactions as questions to investigate, including any labelled “simulated observation.” The reference-prototype explanation follows the complete announcement through that path.
Ask what supports each claim
The report model uses five labels. In the planned rebuild, each claim would also connect to the appropriate source or simulated event. An illustrative parking-policy rehearsal shows the different kinds of support:
Label	Example	What would support it	
Grounded in source	The policy assigns enforcement to a contractor	The passage in the supplied policy	
Simulated observation	A traders' cohort objects to losing customer parking	An action or interview recorded in the simulated run	
Inference	The objections appear to be coordinated opposition	The observations and reasoning behind that interpretation	
Assumption	The traders' association will not endorse the policy	The stated premise, who supplied it and what changes if it is wrong	
Needs validation	A free pilot might change real traders' response	Investigation with the people affected	
A label tells you what to look for; it cannot supply missing evidence. Even with recorded simulated events, claims about equity or workplace adoption, morale and dissent still need real-world validation. Generated personas are not a sample of real people.
Use Ask to test the explanation
Return to the creator announcement and ask:
Which concern comes directly from the announcement, and what recorded action supports the claimed audience reaction?
Check the answer against the report and available data. You can verify that new explainers would stop by reading the announcement. There is no recorded Creator conversation to support the proposed feeling of abandonment, so that question goes to actual viewers.
Caution
Keep quotations with their source. A generated quotation must not be presented as testimony.
Compare the change you actually made
Suppose the creator revises the announcement to keep one long-form episode each month. Comparing that proposal with the original requires two separate runs, their other inputs aligned and both valid reports retained. Read them side by side to see whether they raise different questions about the archive, the clips or the remaining episode. Model wording can vary even when the premise stays the same; neither agreement nor disagreement tells you how many real people share a concern.
The prototype's settings comparison does a different job: it contrasts saved configuration with its parent snapshot. It helps you check what changed in the settings, but does not compare audience reactions or show an effect from changing the seed.
Decide what to investigate next
Turn a concern into a concrete action: clarify the announcement, check an operational constraint, interview affected people or try a reversible pilot. Keep the unanswered question with it. “Would a monthly long-form episode address the concern?” gives the creator something to investigate. The report cannot settle that by declaring that the audience rejects daily clips.
The rehearsal inquiry develops the broader questions behind imagined audiences and changed premises. Rehearse a decision explains the workflow linking claims to their evidence.
