body:
Rehearse a decision
A team is preparing a return-to-office policy. Asking whether staff will like it tells them little about what to change. Asking where the proposed phasing conflicts with team responsibilities gives them something to work on: a timetable, an exception or a responsibility that needs clarifying.
RawFish helps you rehearse a decision this way. You describe the proposal and the people it affects, then examine how it could go wrong in a small simulated world. The useful result is a better question or a proposal worth revising before it meets the real setting. The retained prototype covers only part of this, so the steps below follow the rebuild's design.
Note
Using the reference prototype? Its Creator walkthrough generates a report without running an agent conversation. Treat that report as a model's response to your material, not a record of simulated exchanges.
Give the rehearsal something to question
Start with the proposal people would actually encounter. For the workplace team, that means the policy text and its rollout dates, rather than a summary saying that people must return to the office. Add the question about phasing, the groups affected, what success would look like and the failures you want to examine.
Then make the assumptions visible. Do managers have time to explain the change? Are teams working to the same schedule? What would change each group's view? Include the strongest case for the proposal as well as the objections. A rehearsal built entirely from reasons to reject the policy is unlikely to tell you much about why it might work.
Begin with pasted text. Review any scenario details or groups RawFish suggests before using them. Uploads and live feeds need their own source controls before they can become part of a run.
Choose the decision context
RawFish calls each kind of rehearsal a lane. The choice changes the groups, language and questions in the report:
Lane	Bring a decision about	Look for	
Creator	A post, announcement, newsletter or episode	Lost context, audience confusion and tensions between groups of readers	
Internal policy	A workplace change or rollout	Conflicting responsibilities, manager bottlenecks and unclear exceptions	
Public policy	A regulation, consultation or civic decision	Implementation constraints, unequal effects and unintended incentives	
The workplace proposal belongs in Internal policy. It needs groups such as employees and managers, with their different responsibilities. A public consultation needs a different account of who is affected and how they can respond. Neither calls for inventing the thoughts of a named person. The design uses aggregate groups and archetypes; it excludes impersonation, decisions about named employees, workplace-emotion inference, election influence and fabricated constituent voices.
Important
Use only material you have authority to use. Sensitive workplace material is excluded. Internal-policy rehearsals take no public social feeds, and public-policy rehearsals take no workplace material.
Decide who hears what
The Build step turns the scenario into a graph of groups, institutions and channels. This is where the workplace team can examine an assumption that might otherwise pass unnoticed: does everyone read the complete policy, or do managers explain it to their teams? Those are different situations, even with identical policy text.
In Cohorts, describe how the groups take part: their activity, response delay, active hours, sentiment and influence. Policy lanes also account for how strongly people hold their initial views, how others influence them, when they compromise and how trust decays. Creator uses the smaller set its own model needs.
Read each control's value, where it came from and its uncertainty. A default is a starting assumption, not a measurement of the people affected. Lock a value while changing another, or follow the source behind it. This matters when interpreting a reaction: did it emerge from an exchange, or did the setup largely decide it?
Follow the exchange into the report
Before a run, Preflight checks the chosen model and shows the proposed scale, token estimate, latency and any available external cost. Choose Ollama or another compatible local server, or explicitly configure an external provider. An unknown price remains unknown. Graph memory can call other services even when the report model runs locally. The model and memory explanation follows where those different calls can send data.
Simulate freezes the configuration and runs the exchange round by round. In the workplace case, follow a manager's explanation and the responses to it. A creator conversation or a public comment uses its own lane's language. Follow a report's claim back to the actual events in the run; a plausible exchange in the report is not enough.
Findings has three ways into that result: Read for the report, Ask for questions about its support, and Analysis for settings, comparisons and underlying data. The scenario, settings, seeds and model stay with the run. They let you inspect its conditions, although a later model call may produce different wording. Read the findings explains how the five claim labels distinguish a source passage, an assumption and a simulated reaction.
Change one thing you can account for
Suppose the workplace team revises the rollout dates. To compare that proposal with the first one, they need to keep both versions and know what else changed. Save keeps a configuration revision before execution; Save and re-seed makes a separate variant with different random draws, leaving the base run available.
A variant changes the configuration. An ensemble repeats one configuration with different random draws. The first lets you examine a changed premise; the second helps reveal how much results vary under the same premises. Keep a change to the rollout dates separate from a change in random draw. Compare the settings first, then the reports and what supports them. A missing report cannot count as agreement, and changing a slider does not by itself show how sensitive the outcome is to that factor. Full sensitivity analysis, outside priors and individual-trait editing are later work. Comparing a direction taken with one not taken is what RawFish is designed around: it varies one thing you declare in the same simulated world and compares what follows. Today a second version of a proposal gets its own scenario and report beside the first, and that comparison is the next piece to build.
Take the question back to the real setting
The rehearsal might expose an exception the policy never addressed or a responsibility that two groups understood differently. The team can revise the proposal, ask affected people about the problem or try a reversible operational change. Generated personas are not a sample of employees; their reactions help identify what to investigate. That is also how a lane earns weight over time: observed outcomes, compared with what its rehearsals proposed, calibrate it.
RawFish works on its own, inside another application that owns the work, or as a service another tool calls. In the rebuild's design its engine is organised in three layers other tools can call, the swarm, the comparison of a direction taken with one not taken, and the lanes, and its parts, such as a run, a cohort, a claim or a comparison, are components any host can show, so a chat or another application can render one as a card beside its own work. The retained prototype is neither layered nor built from components that way. It is a peer of the tools it is used with: a rehearsal of how people might react to a change can sit beside a calculation of what that change costs, composed in a notebook, with either one going first. Pale can compose the two without a notebook and coordinate a rehearsal with its follow-up investigation, and a method in Pale's library, for a search-optimisation or policy question, can run a rehearsal as one of its steps; Weave links it to the decision and discussion, while the rehearsal itself stays with RawFish. The team still decides what to change after examining the findings.
The same distinction applies to other decisions. A library considering mandatory appointments might uncover tension between predictable staffing and unplanned access. Service records, conversations and a trial can show whether that tension occurs in practice. A rehearsal about a publication might suggest that an unfamiliar reader misses a qualification; actual reader feedback can test it, while the publisher still decides what to release.

body:
Understand the reference prototype
A creator wants to replace a weekly long-form explainer with daily clips. Before announcing the change, they want to know what regular viewers might misunderstand and what a newcomer would need to find. RawFish's reference prototype explores how to carry that question from a scenario into a report, keeping the inputs and settings available for inspection.
The prototype is an earlier implementation, separate from the planned rebuild. It is not available as a public application or hosted service. Developers with its source checkout have a local walkthrough and configuration guide. The account below explains the work it can represent without requiring that checkout.
Continue through the six cockpit steps
Consider this fictional announcement:
Our channel is replacing its weekly long-form explainer with short daily clips next month. The full archive stays available, but new explainers stop. We have a fixed production budget and want newcomers to understand the work without losing the depth regular viewers value.
Stress question: where does this announcement leave viewers unsure what they will receive?
Assumptions: regular viewers value the explanations; newcomers need a shorter entrance; the team cannot produce both formats daily.
Success: viewers can distinguish the new clips from the archive and find the explanation behind a clip.
Failure modes: regular viewers read the change as abandonment; a newcomer sees an excerpt without its qualification.
What could change a view: a clear route to the longer explanation and an honest account of what production will stop.
The question is more useful than asking whether “the audience” likes short videos. It identifies a change the creator can explain or revise. Keeping the assumptions beside the announcement also makes them available to challenge: perhaps regular viewers value the weekly rhythm more than the format itself.
The cockpit gives that work six places:
Step	What belongs there	What the Creator prototype does	
Scenario	The announcement, stress question and source material	Accepts pasted text and proposes a title, question and cohorts	
Build	The setting in which the question will be examined	Saves the run and shows its configured stakeholder cohorts connected to it by TESTS_AGAINST relationships	
Cohorts	The groups and assumptions about their behaviour	Keeps settings and their origins available to inspect and change before launch	
Preflight	The resources and conditions of the proposed run	Checks the provider, model, address, readiness, scale, token estimate, latency and available external cost	
Simulate	Execution of the configured rehearsal	Records a deterministic completion marker for Creator; it does not run an agent conversation	
Findings	The report, questions about it and supporting records	Makes a separate model call to generate a report, with Read, Ask and Analysis views	
Build's graph describes the run and its configured groups. It is not a world or influence network inferred from the announcement. The initial Creator cohorts, Long-time fans, Gen-Z skeptics and Casual viewers, are authored archetypes rather than measured audience groups. Their names invite different questions about the clips, archive and future explainers; they do not establish how actual viewers divide into groups.
The prototype also has Internal policy and Public policy lanes, with different scenario fields, report questions and a different runner. Creator's completion behaviour does not describe those runners. The planned workflow explains the distinct decisions each lane is intended to serve.
Keep the scenario with its settings
Suppose the creator changes the Long-time fans' Sentiment bias from 0 to -0.2. The prototype can save that change, refresh the settings hash and prepare the run again. The workbench also carries activity, influence and active hours; policy lanes add opinion-drift controls. Origin labels distinguish a supplied value, a lane default, a prior and a random draw. They identify where a value came from, not whether it measures a population.
Note
A saved setting is not an executed experiment. Creator saves the changed setting in configuration and completion metadata, but its report prompt does not use that setting. Changing the sentiment value is therefore not a test of audience sentiment.
Reseeding records the old and new settings in lineage and prepares the same run. It does not create a second executable run or report. Separate variant runs belong to the rebuild design. That difference matters when comparing results: an account of what changed in configuration cannot substitute for two executions under those conditions.
The scenario itself needs equal care. The prototype accepts pasted text; its other source markers do not connect an upload, cache, feed or graph import. An unsaved draft stays in page memory, whereas a saved run has an identifier and backend state. Keeping an address is not the same as preserving an unsaved draft or giving another person access to a saved one.
Read what the run actually supports
The announcement says that new explainers will stop. A report may propose that long-time viewers would read this as abandonment. The first statement can be checked against the text. The second needs evidence about viewers.
Caution
Creator's report has no executed conversation behind it. A reaction labelled “simulated observation” is still a proposal from the report model on this path. A generated quotation is not testimony.
Read the findings explains the five claim labels and how to question their support. A model call can also fail report validation: text returned by a provider is not necessarily a valid report. Keep the scenario, model choice and any error with the result being examined.
Compare settings before comparing reactions
The prototype's Analysis view compares the latest settings with their parent snapshot. Its present, missing and corrupted categories describe settings subjects. They can expose a lost or changed input; they do not establish that two valid reports were compared.
A different announcement asks a different question. Replace “new explainers stop” with “one new long-form explainer will remain each month; daily clips replace the other weekly editions.” In the prototype, this requires a separate scenario and report, with the provider, cohorts and other settings kept aligned. The original draft, stress question and both run identifiers give the comparison a basis.
Read the reports side by side. Does the monthly explanation change the proposed concern about abandonment? Does ambiguity about the archive remain? This is a manual comparison of separate scenarios, not an automatic paired experiment. Wording can vary between model calls, and a missing or invalid report leaves the comparison incomplete. Neither result estimates how many real viewers share a concern.
The useful next step is a question the creator can take to viewers, or a clearer announcement they can try. RawFish's planned rebuild would connect simulated events to findings and preserve separate variants. The reference prototype helps expose why those connections matter before a polished report makes them easy to overlook.

arguments.label: From a task to useful context

questions.question: Does Scope grant access to a source?
questions.answer_html: Scope gives a task its context at every step, bounded by what that task may see. Access stays with the source's owner: owners supply copies with secrets removed, and Scope checks what the caller may use for the task before it searches anything, so it widens no boundary of its own. On the integrated path, Pale carries the request and response.

questions.question: Does it need a model?
questions.answer_html: Scope can bring a task its context with or without a model; the choice decides what material may go into the account. Strict mode excludes all model-made material, including cached summaries and embeddings, so every line comes from a source owner's copy. Full mode can use Counsel's memory host through Pale, or through a direct library connection when Scope works with Weave alone. Scope and the host each check permission. The mode guide explains that route and permitted fallback.

questions.question: Where should I start?
questions.answer_html: Follow the equipment-order walkthrough to see what a useful answer must preserve, how a changed source affects it and what missing information leaves unresolved.

questions.question: How does Scope learn whether its context helped?
questions.answer_html: Opening or quoting a source does not establish that it improved the work. Scope's learning design compares what was offered, what the agent used and how the task ended. When context helps develops that comparison and its connection to Reckon.

body:
Scope
Scope gives an agent the smallest fresh account it needs to continue a task. It brings the question back together with the decisions, sources, people and open questions that give it meaning. When the world changes, the context needs to change with it, so Scope works as a cache does in any development stack: it is optional, keeps derived context over what Pale and Weave hold and is never the source of truth. The repository holds an empty Rust library today, and the service that answers an agent is the work in front of it.
Remember the world around the task
A new session should not mean explaining the project again. Among the products, Scope brings the context a task needs. It works with Pale, Weave or both: Weave keeps the records and points to the files around them, Pale keeps the history of what work relied on and what followed, and Scope combines them into one account an agent can ask for what it needs. Without Pale, Scope is how an agent reads Weave. With Pale, Scope reranks as the history of what work relied on and what followed updates, and writes back a pointer to the context it gave each agent, so the chain from what an agent was given to what it did stays whole. It helps an agent find the owning account, understand why a choice was made and see what remains open. Scope selects from snapshots supplied by their owners. The original knowledge stays with those owners, so rebuilding an index must not lose the thought. Its first use is to help Claude and Codex resume work across Harsh Joshi's connected writing and projects.
People and circumstances belong in that account too. How a colleague prefers a decision explained can improve a draft; it cannot give an agent permission to send it.
Pick up the work with its context intact
Consider returning to an essay in a fresh agent session. Its title is not enough: the agent needs the original argument, the current draft, the publication's purpose and the decisions that explain the revision. A worked publication slice shows those sources together.
Start with the task
Say which essay is being revised, who it is for and what needs to change. Developing the argument and approving its publication are separate tasks.
Use the sources the task can see
Source owners provide permitted snapshots. Scope checks their use and freshness before searching them, keeping the original argument and current decisions ahead of optional background.
Receive a useful account
Read the original, the working draft and the relevant decisions together. A useful slice explains what changed and what remains unresolved, with links back to the sources. A short summary that loses the argument has not done the job.
Continue as the world changes
If a decision changes, refresh the context that depended on it. The previous answer should still explain what the agent knew then, subject to the source owner's retention rules. Unrelated work can continue.
Questions about Scope
Does Scope grant access to a source?
Scope gives a task its context at every step, bounded by what that task may see. Access stays with the source's owner: owners supply copies with secrets removed, and Scope checks what the caller may use for the task before it searches anything, so it widens no boundary of its own. On the integrated path, Pale carries the request and response.
Does it need a model?
Scope can bring a task its context with or without a model; the choice decides what material may go into the account. Strict mode excludes all model-made material, including cached summaries and embeddings, so every line comes from a source owner's copy. Full mode can use Counsel's memory host through Pale, or through a direct library connection when Scope works with Weave alone. Scope and the host each check permission. The mode guide explains that route and permitted fallback.
Where should I start?
Follow the equipment-order walkthrough to see what a useful answer must preserve, how a changed source affects it and what missing information leaves unresolved.
How does Scope learn whether its context helped?
Opening or quoting a source does not establish that it improved the work. Scope's learning design compares what was offered, what the agent used and how the task ended. When context helps develops that comparison and its connection to Reckon.

body:
Context for a task
You return to an equipment order after a few days away. Which version was approved? Has anything arrived? What still needs an answer? Finding the folder is only the beginning: the agent needs enough of the history to tell those things apart.
Scope supplies that account from records their owners permit it to use. Follow one equipment order to see which records belong in the answer, what they support and when they need to change. Scope's repository holds an empty Rust library today; the service that answers an agent is the work in front of it.
Work out what the update needs
Suppose you want to send a colleague an internal delivery update. The request could be:
Prepare an internal delivery update for order 42. Use approved revision 3 and the latest permitted supplier report. Include the approval reference and report date, and identify any missing arrival estimate. Do not use another client's records.
The approval and the supplier report answer different questions. Keeping both matters more than collecting every mention of the order.
Question	What supports the answer	What you can conclude	
Which order may proceed?	Approval naming revision 3	Revision 3 was approved; an earlier quotation is not the current instruction	
What has arrived?	The supplier's dated partial-delivery report, revision 7	The supplier reported a partial delivery at that time	
When will the rest arrive?	No current estimate	You still need an answer from the supplier	
Open the approval and the report. If they support the answer, the update could read:
Revision 3 of order 42 is approved. In report revision 7, the supplier says part of the order has arrived. We still need an arrival date for the rest.
Include the report date and approval link when drafting from real records.
The colleague's needs also shape the message: a formal summary and a short decision update may use the same evidence differently. Scope's private mental model keeps that context about people, roles and priorities, with sources and dates that say when it applies. A person's role can change, and a project's long-term importance can differ from its priority this week. A communication preference helps with the draft; it does not authorise sending it or making a commitment.
Use the records this task permits
For this update, the order's owner supplies copies of the approval and supplier report. Each copy identifies its original, revision and date, how long it remains usable and what the task may do with it. Scope answers from that dated material. The owner keeps access to the supplier's mailbox and supplies a new report when it is available; Scope does not open the mailbox itself.
Keep the quotation, approval and delivery report identifiable as different records. The source-import explanation describes how those copies reach Scope without credentials or unrelated conversations.
The request's wording cannot enforce access. Scope checks what its caller may use before looking for relevant material. Each instance has an expressly defined data owner and permitted uses; a shared company name, folder or machine does not establish that arrangement.
Caution
Check the audience before using the report. Permission to read it internally may exclude sending it to a model or quoting it in a public update. Access to two clients' records does not make both sets appropriate for either client's task. Finding the right context for the work develops that distinction.
A source owner can also select a Gazette site export. Pale arranges its import into Scope, so later tasks can use the captured publication within the same source and permission checks.
See what the answer leaves open
The answer should let you trace each part of the update: which approval it used, which report supports the delivery sentence and why no arrival date is given. Scope calls that response a context bundle. It keeps the source references, revisions, age and gaps with the answer, so you can check the account rather than trust a fluent summary.
The missing arrival estimate calls for new evidence from the supplier. A useful passage left out for space calls for a narrower question or a larger response. An unavailable search method may call for a different way to find the record. Those are different problems, and the answer should say which occurred without exposing records the caller cannot access.
Important
Keep the approval and its limits in the answer. If the size allowance cannot hold required context, Scope should report that problem rather than silently omit it. The bundle helps prepare the update; approving the order, sending the message and accepting delivery remain separate actions.
An order reference may be enough to find the approval. A question about “maintenance” may need help finding a report that calls it “servicing.” The retrieval-mode guide explains strict lookup and model assistance from Counsel, including what happens when that assistance is unavailable. Neither can supply the absent arrival estimate.
Return to the task without losing its history
A new session should be able to reopen the same bundle and source references. A later supplier report should produce a new answer, leaving the earlier account intact. Keep a task current follows that change and explains corrections and withdrawal.
Source removal must also reach dependent summaries, embeddings and learned links. If deletion makes an old answer impossible to reconstruct, its history needs to say so. It must not preserve a disguised copy merely to make replay possible.
Parallel work raises another question: if one agent changes a premise, which parts of another agent's reasoning need attention? When an agent's context changes underneath it explores Scope's proposed semantic transactions. Ordinary retrieval does not depend on that research being complete.
Find out whether the context helped
An agent reporting that it used the supplier report tells us something about the draft, but not whether the update was useful or correct. Scope's learning programme would compare what it offered, what the agent reported using and how the work ended.
Through Pale, Reckon would compare retrieval and memory choices on the same work; each comparison is an intervention contrast, not proof of what caused the outcome. That evidence could support a proposed change to Scope's retrieval policy, followed by review and a separate release. When context helps explains the comparison.
To build the Scope library and set up for development, follow Building the library.

body:
Keep a task current
A supplier has sent a new delivery report. Before rewriting the whole update, find the sentence that depends on the old one. Scope keeps the earlier answer and prepares a fresh account on request. The approval may be unchanged even though the delivery has moved on. The service that answers an agent is the work in front of Scope; the example follows what its design asks of a refresh.
Refresh the part that changed
In the equipment-order example, approval revision 3 says which order can go ahead, and supplier report revision 7 says only part of it arrived. If revision 8 confirms the rest has arrived, change the delivery sentence and its source. The approval sentence still uses revision 3.
When returning to the task, reopen the source references and check whether they still answer today's question. The old bundle explains what the agent knew then; it cannot keep itself current as the order progresses.
Decide what an old report can still support
Yesterday's report can support “the supplier reported a partial delivery yesterday,” if historical use is still permitted. It cannot establish that delivery remains partial today. Importing it again changes neither its observation date nor how long it is valid.
Important
Wait for the evidence the task requires. If the update needs today's delivery position and no permitted source supplies it, pause the work that depends on that position, including drafting. You could instead prepare an explicitly historical account. Calling an unsupported current account a draft does not resolve the missing evidence.
Optional context is different: the owner's policy may allow work to continue with the gap made clear. More room in the answer can help with omitted detail, but cannot make an old observation current.
Keep unaffected work when a premise changes
One agent may be drafting while another updates a source. Ask which revision the draft used, what changed and which conclusion depends on it. In this example, the approval and the rest of the draft may remain useful while the delivery claim needs revision.
Scope's semantic-transaction research asks how to identify that affected reasoning without restarting unrelated work. When an agent's context changes underneath it develops the proposed approach.
Correct or withdraw a source
Suppose the supplier corrects the report: the equipment was dispatched, not delivered. Obtain the correction as a new revision, refresh the context and change the delivery claim. Editing only the agent's summary would leave the incorrect report available for the next request.
To withdraw the report, its owner must explicitly identify it for removal. Simply leaving it out of an export is not enough: an interrupted export should not erase valid records.
Revoking access stops later use. Deletion also removes source-derived material under the applicable policy, including summaries, embeddings and learned links. Earlier lawful use does not permit keeping those copies indefinitely.
Caution
Deletion can make an old answer impossible to reconstruct. Its history should explain which evidence is no longer available, rather than promise a replay without that evidence.
The implementation guide explains how imports distinguish omission from removal and how a request handles invalidation. The order example shows what the corrected update must preserve.

body:
Understand the retrieval modes
An order number gives you something exact to look up. A question such as “what maintenance does this equipment need?” may require finding instructions that use different words. Scope combines exact searches with optional model assistance. The service that answers an agent is the work in front of Scope; this page follows what its two modes do in that design.
When each mode helps
Strict mode can find the approved order revision by reference, or a report through its words and links. Full mode can also connect “maintenance” in the question to “servicing” in the instructions.
Mode	How it finds context	Model-generated material	
Strict	Reference and keyword lookup, links between permitted records, and fixed rules	Excludes summaries, embeddings and inferred links made by a model	
Full	The same methods, with model-assisted search or reranking from Counsel	Keeps source and model references with embeddings, candidate links and summaries so they can be refreshed or removed	
Both modes check which records the task may use before searching. Finding a related passage cannot make a restricted record available, and neither mode can invent the missing arrival estimate in the equipment-order example.
If the model service is unavailable
A request can allow a fallback to strict retrieval. Scope identifies that change in the answer, and you can still find the order by reference or search the permitted records by keyword. If the request requires full mode, it must fail rather than silently supply a different kind of answer.
Tip
Try a narrower question if related ideas are not being found. An exact phrase or reference may be enough. You can also ask the source owner where to look; increasing the answer's size cannot replace the unavailable search method.
Connect model assistance with permission
In the integrated setup, Pale checks the request and permission to send the selected records, then connects to Counsel's memory service. When Scope works with Weave alone, it runs without a Pale daemon and uses its own grants for retrieval. For full mode it calls the local or remote memory host named in Scope’s configuration through Pale's Counsel port, used as a library.
Permission to retrieve a report and permission to send it to a model are separate. The memory host checks the caller, the selected model profile and whether these records may be processed for this owner, relationship and purpose. It also checks the budget and any withdrawal of permission. Scope checks the returned material before adding it to a retrieval snapshot and again before use.
Counsel's memory and judgment services have separate profiles, models, caches and permissions. Connecting the memory service does not enable the judgment service.
Check what a cached summary describes
Suppose full mode summarised supplier report revision 7 as a partial delivery. Revision 8 then confirms the rest has arrived. The summary's bytes have not changed, but it can no longer answer today's delivery question.
Permission can change even when the report does not. If the owner withdraws permission for model processing, Scope cannot keep supplying the old summary under that withdrawn permission. Retiring the model profile that produced it also stops new use. Restoring an old index or backup cannot undo either change.
To make those checks, Scope keeps the summary connected to its source revision, the model service and profile, and the particular processing request that produced it. The earlier answer may remain evidence of what was known then, subject to its retention and deletion rules.
Warning
A cached summary still needs permission for model-generated material. If the host becomes unavailable, an allowed strict fallback would use the source reports directly. It would exclude summaries, embeddings and model-inferred links before selecting candidates; their age does not make them model-free.
The developer mode explanation describes that separation. Either mode still needs to preserve the approved revision, the reported delivery and the unanswered question, as the order example shows.

conditions.title: Fix one workflow
conditions.explanation: Follow a costly workflow from request to accepted result, make handovers and exceptions clear, and measure the improvement. Begin with a paid audit; build and ongoing support follow where they earn their place.

conditions.title: Pale for one team
conditions.explanation: Set up Pale to coordinate one team's agent work, shaped around the people, tools and permissions that team already has. We agree the scope with you, starting from the work that matters most to that team.

arguments.label: Engagement stages

questions.question: Is this right for our business?
questions.answer_html: It fits recurring work whose delays, rework or failures cost the business. Bring a sponsor who can approve change and an operating owner who knows the daily work. We start with one workflow and a result worth improving.

questions.question: What should we send you to get started?
questions.answer_html: Send a recent example: what should happen, what happens instead and what it costs your team or customers. Include who owns the workflow and the result you want to improve. No technical specification needed.

questions.question: Does the audit commit us to a build?
questions.answer_html: No. You receive a diagnosis and recommendation as a separate paid engagement. If a sprint is worthwhile, we agree its scope and acceptance conditions before building.

questions.question: When is a retainer useful?
questions.answer_html: When changing requirements, growing use or recurring problems need continuing product and architecture work. It is optional, with a scope agreed around that work.

questions.question: Do we need AI or new software?
questions.answer_html: Often the useful change is a better process, configuration or connection between existing tools. We build software or use AI where it closes a real gap and improves the result.

questions.question: How will we know it worked?
questions.answer_html: Agree the baseline and measures before building: perhaps fewer repeat visits, less rework or a shorter gap between completed work and billing. Test those measures across routine work and failure cases.

questions.question: Can we ask about one of your products?
questions.answer_html: Yes. Tell us which product interests you and what you need it to do, and we shape the engagement around your work. A Pale pilot starts with one team. DAO Studio's products are also available through RawThoughts consulting, with scope, integration, deployment and licensing agreed for each engagement. DAO Studio retains its product ownership.

questions.question: When is this a poor fit?
questions.answer_html: When nobody can own the workflow, provide access to the people doing it or approve change. “Add AI” also needs a problem behind it. We need one useful result we can agree and test together.

questions.question: Who will we work with?
questions.answer_html: Harsh Joshi, Principal Consultant at RawThoughts, leads the product, architecture and hands-on engineering work alongside your operating and technical owners.

body:
Make work flow across teams and systems
Your AI pilot gives good answers, and nobody on the team can say what it actually did or what happens when it's wrong. Most of the time that's not the model being stupid. It's the process around it.
We take on one expensive workflow at a time, through a paid audit, then a build sprint, then a retainer if it earns one. Pale can also be set up for one team in your organisation, shaped around that team's people, tools and permissions.
Discuss your workflow
Start with the workflow whose delays or failures matter most. Improve it, measure the result and use what you learn to decide what comes next.
Email RawThoughts
Paid audit
Find where one workflow loses time, effort or money. We work through it with your team and leave you with a baseline and a recommendation: change the process, configure or connect existing tools, or build what is missing.
Implementation sprint
Build and integrate the agreed change around your existing systems. Your team tests the whole workflow with us, including handovers, approvals and failures, against the business result agreed in the audit.
Architecture retainer
Keep the workflow working as your business changes. We review results with your team, resolve recurring problems and adapt the system where needed. Continue only when that ongoing work earns its place.

Where the work gets stuck
See where one real workflow loses time, effort or money, with a starting point against which your team can measure an improvement.
Acceptance and handovers
Know what a completed handover should contain and what result your team would accept before agreeing to a build.
What to change first

Often the useful change is a better process, configuration or connection between existing tools. We build software or use AI where it closes a real gap and improves the result.
How will we know it worked?
Agree the baseline and measures before building: perhaps fewer repeat visits, less rework or a shorter gap between completed work and billing. Test those measures across routine work and failure cases.
Can we ask about one of your products?
Yes. Tell us which product interests you and what you need it to do, and we shape the engagement around your work. A Pale pilot starts with one team. DAO Studio's products are also available through RawThoughts consulting, with scope, integration, deployment and licensing agreed for each engagement. DAO Studio retains its product ownership.
When is this a poor fit?
When nobody can own the workflow, provide access to the people doing it or approve change. “Add AI” also needs a problem behind it. We need one useful result we can agree and test together.
Who will we work with?
Harsh Joshi, Principal Consultant at RawThoughts, leads the product, architecture and hands-on engineering work alongside your operating and technical owners.
Discuss your workflow
Email RawThoughts

body:
Weave
In Weave’s design, a customer’s failed export stays linked to its investigation, review and the check that it works again. Customer relationships and work tracking share the same records, so people and agents can follow the work from the chat rooms, assistants and browser clients they already use.
One world for relationships and work
Those records are the reason Weave exists. Whoever comes next, whether a person, an agent or both, picks up the story from what was kept rather than from a long conversation. That matters most for agents, which decide far more often than people: by the time one writes, what it read has usually changed, so the story it picks up has to be the current one. A customer relationship can include several agreements and many jobs, and Weave lets people and agents return to the original request, the work they agreed to do and the decisions made along the way. Each organisation keeps its own records. Something new enters through Radar, the part of Weave that brings in an observation or a proposed direction for review; it becomes work only when someone takes responsibility for it.
Weave is the part of the products that keeps the records, and it also stands on its own: alone it is a headless Jira and Salesforce, a database of the organisation's records behind a capable interface. No Weave service runs yet; the design is written and the first build, one account taken through to accepted work, is the work in front.
As in Radio became Spotify, the need persists while the way of meeting it changes: agreeing work and seeing it through can now happen in a conversation, while Weave keeps the responsibility, result and acceptance clear for whoever returns to it next.
Let the commitment outlast the conversation
A customer’s export fails. A colleague can investigate the timeout while another improves the error message. Weave keeps both jobs linked to the customer's request, with a clear record of who took each one on and who can accept the result.
Agree the work
Link the investigation to the customer’s request and the relevant service agreement. Record what result the team agrees to deliver. A possible next step stays a proposal until someone turns it into a commitment.
Accept responsibility
Record who agreed to supply the trace and explanation. A person or an agent can take on the investigation, with their own identity and role. An agent joins the team follows that responsibility.
Supply the result
Connect the delivered result to the assignment so it can be reviewed. Handovers preserve earlier contributions, and recurring duties keep a separate occurrence each time, giving a returning colleague the right history.
Review and accept
The person named to review the investigation decides whether the trace and explanation answer the question. Record what they accept, what needs a correction and who still owes a result.
Questions about Weave
Can an acceptance message close the work?
Yes. Weave keeps acceptance with the person allowed to give it, so the message needs to identify the work and come from that person. If the result meets the agreed conditions, the reviewer only needs to confirm once.
Does Weave depend on Pale?
Weave keeps the records and stands on its own. When both are present, Weave holds the organisational records while Pale coordinates execution and its evidence, and together they let people and agents work inside one organisation and across several, each instance kept separate.
Can separate organisations work together?
Yes. Weave is built for work across organisations, and each keeps its own instance, records and decisions. A client can offer work and a provider can take it on, with each side deciding what to accept and what the other may see. Weave also serves teams that work without agents.
Is there an app?
Weave has no app of its own; it meets people where they already work: it describes each card and view, and the surface a team already uses renders it: a chat room, an assistant or a browser client built on the public interfaces. A card shows the current record, says when it is stale and leaves out what the reader may not see, wherever it appears.
Where should I start?
Start with the Weave guide, since Weave is for keeping a commitment clear from request to acceptance. It follows one failed export from the customer's message into two jobs, and shows who takes each one on and who accepts the result.

body:
An agent joins the team
An editor asks an agent to check the links in a collection of articles. The agent should have a name, an assigned job and a place to report its findings. The editor should be able to ask it about a broken link without wondering which of several agents answered through one shared bot.
In Weave's design the agent joins like any member. Consider a publication team that connects Weave to Pale: Weave keeps its relationships and work, and Pale configures the agents' roles and coordinates their permitted actions. The service is not built yet, so this example follows the design.
Give the agent a place in the organisation
The team authorises an agent to act as its publication checker. Its role covers reading the selected draft articles, checking their destinations and preparing a report. The editor keeps responsibility for accepting the report and deciding whether the publication is ready.
On this connected path, adding the agent and granting its role is an authorised change in Pale's configuration, and Weave records the resulting membership and role. Creating a task for an unfamiliar name or mentioning that name in chat adds no member and grants no permission.
The role and the actor answer different questions. The publication checker is a responsibility that might later pass to another agent. The particular agent keeps its own identity and history, including the checks it actually performed. An organisation can then change who holds a role without changing who did the earlier work. Which software runs the agent and which model it uses are recorded with each act but do not change who the agent is: the same agent, run tomorrow on different tooling, reads and writes the same records under the same name.
Agree one result the editor can review
The editor creates a specific assignment: check the selected collection's links and supply the destination, result and any unresolved problem for each one. The work names the collection revision and the editor who will review it. A colleague's suggestion that someone should “check the site” can remain a proposal until the responsibility is made definite.
The agent takes the assignment under its publication-checker role. That assignment supplies neither access to unrelated drafts nor permission to send messages to authors outside the team. If a destination is unavailable, the report should distinguish an unavailable page from a confirmed broken link. A missing result remains visible rather than turning into a successful check.
This gives the human reviewer something concrete to assess. The agreed job is a link report, with enough evidence to understand its findings. It is not an instruction to rewrite an author's position or to publish the collection.
Let the agent speak as itself
In the team's permitted chat, the agent appears under its own identity. It can explain that a destination moved, ask about an ambiguous reference or point the editor to its completed report. Another agent checking figures appears separately, with its own assignment and contributions.
The work card opens the current Weave record. It shows who is responsible and what happens next, rather than creating a second task in the conversation, and it looks the same in whichever chat room or assistant the team uses. The room sees only the material it is allowed to receive; being mentioned in the report does not make an outside author a room member.
Important
A message saying “done” is a report, not acceptance. The agent submits its result for review. The editor decides whether that result meets the assignment.
If the editor replies that the link report is accepted, that message carries the decision when the system can identify the editor, the exact work and the permission to accept it. An ambiguous “approved” needs clarification. If acceptance was recorded but the reply was lost, recovering the result does not require the editor to approve the same report again.
Keep acceptance attached to what was checked
Accepting the link report finishes that assignment. The figure check could still be open, and the publisher would still decide whether the collection should go out. Gazette builds the publication from the supplied writing and configuration; a successful link report does not supply an author's acceptance or a publisher's permission.
If the articles change after the check, the earlier report remains a report about their earlier revision. The team can assign a further check for the changed material without pretending the first agent reviewed it already.
Hand the role over without rewriting its history
Suppose another agent takes over publication checking. Unstarted work moves to the verified successor. An active check pauses further effort until an explicit handover accounts for the results already obtained, the links still unresolved and any outside request whose outcome is unknown.
The successor's work carries its own identity. Earlier findings keep their original contributor. Revoking the first agent's role stops further action under that role and leaves the completed history intelligible.
The point is ordinary teamwork: a person can see who joined, what they may do, which job they accepted and who reviewed their result. From a request to accepted work develops the same responsibilities across a customer's investigation and delivery. Weave's design lets organisations use it with people alone, and agents, Pale and chat are optional connections to that shared work model.

body:
From a request to accepted work
A customer writes in: the export timed out, and the error told them nothing. Two things need doing. Someone has to find where the timeout happens, and someone has to write an error message that actually helps. They are different jobs that may finish on different days, and both still answer to the same complaint. Weave keeps each piece of work tied to the request it came from, with its own person responsible and its own reviewer. Weave is not built yet; the steps below follow its design.
Continue an export investigation
Agree what each job should produce before assigning it. For the investigation, that means a trace and an explanation of where the timeout occurs. For the message change, it means proposed wording, evidence of its behaviour and review by the receiving team. Each work item refers to the customer’s original report.
Role	Responsibility in the investigation	
Creator	Makes the investigation a definite commitment	
Assignee	Supplies the agreed trace and explanation	
Reviewer	Decides whether that result meets the agreed conditions	
Customer	Reported the problem and needs the export to work	
The customer raised the problem; the creator made the work exist. Those can be different people. An agent could investigate and a human review the result. One person could hold several roles where the rules allow it, but each action still records the role they used.
An agent joins the team follows the membership and role behind an assignment, including how the agent appears in conversation under its own identity.
Let a conversation become definite work
The customer’s message starts the conversation. The person allowed to commit the team records what it will deliver, where the request came from and who will decide whether the result meets the agreement. The investigator takes responsibility for supplying the trace and explanation.
Important
That assignment does not give the investigator access to customer data or permission to send messages. Those permissions must already cover the action. An existing work item can carry the request if it uniquely matches the responsibility; a similar title is not enough.
When the investigator supplies the trace and writes “done”, the comment keeps their report. Submitting the investigation for review is a separate action. The reviewer then decides whether the trace and explanation answer the agreed question.
The reasoning behind this distinction is in Turning a conversation into work.
Keep the result and the remaining responsibility visible
Accepting the investigation leaves the message change open. Accepting the message change still leaves a further question: can the customer complete the export? That outcome needs its own check against the goal agreed before the work began.
A provider may accept its own delivery while the receiving team asks for a correction. Weave keeps both decisions and the evidence behind them. A missing trace leaves a clear request for evidence; a disputed explanation leaves the review and correction visible.
If the review cannot go through, the next step depends on what happened. A missing trace calls for the trace. A changed work item calls for reading its current version. Agents decide far more often than people, so by the time one writes, what it read has usually changed: a read says what else to read, and a write is checked for what it affects before it is committed alone, made together with others or proposed to the owners. If a reply gets lost, check whether the first request took effect before sending it again. Developers can see how the system reports each case in command outcomes.
Hand over the investigation
Unstarted work can pass to a verified successor. An active attempt needs an explicit handover: pause new effort, account for the work already done and resolve who may continue. The successor needs the existing results, remaining responsibility and any outside action whose outcome is still uncertain.
The first investigator keeps credit for the trace they produced and the role they held. The successor takes responsibility for the work that remains. If someone loses permission to act, their unfinished work comes back for a decision about who may continue.
Suppose you review the exports every month. Each review is its own piece of work with its own acceptance: this month's stays separate from next month's. A missed review follows the schedule's stated policy, so it cannot disappear as the calendar advances.
Review in chat
Chat is an optional way to reach the same work. The person named to review the investigation could reply, “Accepted: this trace answers the timeout investigation.” The message can carry the decision once Weave can identify the sender, the work they mean and the decision they are allowed to make. The reviewer should only need to approve once.
If “approved” could mean either the investigation or the message change, the system asks which one. A card opens the current record and shows when its information is stale or unavailable. It does not create another task to maintain. The same card, with the same fields and the same checks, appears in whichever chat room, assistant or browser client the team uses; Weave describes it and the surface renders it. Being mentioned grants neither access to the record nor membership of the room.
Run the relationship as well as the task
The investigation can sit within a mandate, a particular commercial commitment to the customer. The account relationship continues across mandates. An account manager keeps that continuity; an account executive carries a particular opportunity or promise. Delivery still has its own assignee and reviewer.
Run a relationship across several mandates follows an ongoing reporting service alongside a proposed integration. It shows how a changed assessment can affect one opportunity without changing the service already owed.
Carry an observation through review
Repeated export failures may begin as a Radar observation, something noticed that is worth investigating. The traces, possible explanations and counter-evidence belong together until the reviewer can decide what they establish. Accepting a finding does not assign its follow-up automatically; the finding becomes work only when someone takes responsibility for it, with an owner and an agreed result.
Review an observation before it becomes work follows that decision, including rejection, deferral and a review that finds no material change.
Client and provider keep separate records
A client and a provider each keep their own records and acceptance. The client offers an investigation; the provider decides whether to take it on. Delivering a trace on the provider's side does not accept it for the client.
An outside contact can stay in the relationship history without becoming an internal member or software user. Linking records for the same person across organisations preserves each side's history and access rules. The developer guide to Instances explains this exchange; the relationship example follows its commercial consequences.
Define the records and actions your organisation needs
A domain defines the kinds of records, relationships and actions an organisation needs. The first domain, commercial work, covers accounts, people, evidence, Radar observations, goals, work, comments, files and schedules. The SDK lets other organisations describe their own domains.
The developer guide Extending Weave explains how those rules are defined and versioned. For the people doing the work, an important consequence is that a new definition cannot silently change what an earlier investigation meant or how it was accepted.
Work independently or with Pale
Weave's design serves an organisation of people alone. Chat, agents and Pale are optional. With Pale connected, Weave keeps the business records and work; Pale checks permission and coordinates permitted work. Their histories link where they concern the same work.
The path to Scope for context, Counsel for judgment and Reckon for evaluation goes through Pale. Without Pale, Scope still reads Weave directly and is how an agent reads Weave; Weave itself never calls Scope. Gazette may read Weave facts directly for publication. These connections are the work in front of Weave once its first vertical runs.
Availability
No Weave service runs yet. The first version is a headless service, accessed through APIs, SDKs, a command line and agent interfaces. It ships no browser application of its own: the cards and views it describes are rendered by the surfaces a team already uses, and a browser client is one more of those. It has no built-in models. The developer overview explains the architecture for anyone considering an integration or extension.

body:
Run a relationship across several mandates
Consider the team that prepares regular reports for the customer whose export failed. The customer now wants a data integration as well. It sounds promising, until access to the data falls through. What should the team do next? It still owes the reports. It needs to resolve the access problem before it can take on the integration. And someone needs to explain both to the customer.
Weave keeps that whole relationship in view: what has been promised, what is still being considered and who is carrying each part forward. The service is not built yet; this example follows how its commercial records help a team work through those decisions.
What have we already promised?
The reports belong to an agreed service commitment, which Weave calls a mandate. The integration is an opportunity: work the team is considering, with no delivery promise yet. Both belong to the customer's account. Each report also needs its own work item, so the person preparing it and the person reviewing it can follow that report through to acceptance.
The account manager looks after the continuing relationship. An account executive carries a particular opportunity or mandate. In a small team, the same person might do both; a larger account might have several executives and delivery teams. Weave records each person's participation and when it applies. A person working on several accounts keeps one record, with their roles connected to each account. When a new contact takes over, the history should still show who made an earlier assessment or promise.
Those roles help the team find the person to talk to. Permission to commit delivery or accept a result still comes from the authority given to that person for the work. The account executive may be pursuing the integration while someone else decides whether the delivery team can take it on.
The access falls through
At discovery, the sponsor describes delays and the operating owner offers access to the records. That gives the team a problem to investigate and a way to investigate it. When access becomes unavailable, the opportunity is blocked. The reports continue under their existing mandate.
At the next review, the team needs to explain why its assessment changed. Weave keeps the original assessment and its supporting evidence alongside the later one: what was known, what pointed the other way, when the information was gathered and how much confidence it supported. The criteria used, the assessor and the reviewer's decision belong with each assessment. Calls, emails, meetings and research can supply that evidence, with their sources and access rules preserved.
Suppose the customer later offers a smaller dataset. That may make a narrower integration worth considering. The team can assess it afresh, and the new assessment can supersede the old one. The earlier reasoning remains available to anyone asking why the work did not proceed sooner.
Important
Check whether the team may take the work at all before you score it. A high score never overrides a forbidden use or any other disqualifying condition.
The decision should tell the team what to do next. A blocked opportunity has an obstacle to resolve, such as the missing access. A deferred one waits for a stated condition or review date. A rejected one keeps the reason for declining. A superseded assessment points to the newer judgment while preserving the grounds for the earlier one. These distinctions matter when an interested customer returns: the team can see whether to investigate, wait or explain why it declined.
For an account review, a read-only export brings together the outstanding reviews, missing or old evidence and changes since the last review. Updates are still made in the records themselves. The relationship inside the account develops why that history is more useful than a contact list and a score.
Agreeing the next piece of work
The smaller dataset may be enough for a workshop. The sponsor suggests one; someone authorised to commit the delivery team then needs to agree what it will produce, who will do it and who can accept the result. Once agreed, the workshop gets its own work item and evidence. From a request to accepted work follows the assignment, review and handover.
If another provider will run the workshop, the client offers the work and the provider decides whether to accept it. Each keeps its own records. The provider reviews what it delivers, and the client separately decides whether that result meets its request. Recording a contact in the account gives that person no internal access or approval role; the developer guide to instance exchange explains how the two organisations exchange work.
The account manager can now return to the customer with a useful answer: the reports are continuing, the smaller dataset gives the integration another chance, and the workshop needs an agreed commitment before anyone owes its delivery. In the relationship itself, the useful question stays the same: who owes the next result, under which commitment, and who may accept it?

body:
Review an observation before it becomes work
Several customer exports fail after a change of data source. The timing gives the team a reason to look, and the cause is still open. Weave’s Radar feature keeps the observations, possible causes and the reviewer’s decision together, so that noticing something, proposing an explanation and deciding what it changes stay three separate steps. Radar is not built yet; this page follows its design.
Start with what was observed
“The new source caused the failures” is an explanation to test. Keep the failed-export references, traces, source change and observation times together so the reviewer can compare what happened before and after the change.
Consider alternatives alongside it. Perhaps export size increased at the same time, or the old source has the same timeout. Missing traces leave a question unanswered. An agent can gather material it is allowed to see and suggest an explanation. The person named to review it decides what the material supports.
Source material keeps its own access rules and age. Copying last month's trace into a new Radar observation does not make it evidence of today's behaviour.
Where a proposed direction can be tried before anyone decides, say by pricing its effect or rehearsing how customers might react with another tool, the proposal keeps a reference to each run as evidence. The run stays with the tool that made it, and trying a direction decides nothing; the reviewer still does that.
Decide what the finding changes
The reviewer compares the explanation with its evidence and alternatives, then records a decision and the reason for it.
Decision	What to keep	
Accept	The finding the evidence supports, including its limits	
Reject	Why the explanation does not follow, alongside the original observation	
Defer	The missing evidence or condition for reviewing again	
No material change	What was checked, the strongest alternative and the next question	
A trace might show that the timeout happens while reading from the data source. The reviewer could accept that location and wait for a comparison before deciding what caused it.
Note
A run that could not obtain a required trace cannot claim to have found no material change.
Later evidence may support a different conclusion. A new review preserves what the earlier decision relied on, as far as the source's retention and erasure rules permit. If evidence is missing or erased, the gap stays visible.
Create follow-up deliberately
An accepted finding might justify a comparison run, a source correction or a change proposal. It becomes work only when someone takes responsibility for it: a person allowed to assign the work names who will do it, what result they owe and who will review it.
Link the later result to the observation and question it addresses. In the export investigation, a trace can answer the investigation while the error-message change and the customer's outcome remain open. That guide follows how the resulting work is reviewed and handed over.
For developers, the observation and review domain design explains how the records and rules preserve these separate decisions.

body:
Gazette architecture
Gazette publishes a body of thought from the whole to its parts, and makes that structure what readers, search, feeds, JSON-LD and llms.txt index. It builds a publication from its writing, workspace and Theme: the compiler resolves a page's identity, relationships and address once, and HTML, search, feeds and structured data use that same result. Among the products RawThoughts builds, Gazette carries approved work outward, and it works as a product of its own. To make a publication, start with Your first publication.
The inputs to a publication
The workspace configuration names the sites to build, their content sources and their themes. Writing can stay in several repositories or directories: the workspace selects the sources that contribute to each site. A theme supplies templates, styles and other resources for its presentation.
Publication names, domains, source selections and publisher choices belong in the writing and workspace. The engine resolves those declarations; a theme presents the resulting values. Keeping site values out of shared engine and theme code lets another publisher use the same behavior without inheriting someone else’s identities or destinations.
Gazette reads those files into memory before compiling them. That lets a build use the same captured article throughout, even if someone saves another edit while it is rendering. The workspace guide explains how to select local directories and Git repositories.
Follow an article through the build
flowchart LR
    A[Saved files] --> B[Capture and parse]
    C[Workspace and site addresses] --> D[Resolve pages and relationships]
    B --> D
    D --> E[Shared page model]
    E --> F[Theme and HTML]
    E --> G[Search, feeds and structured data]

An article's identity, title and address serve different purposes. For example, these metadata fields identify one article:
[content]
id = "content:arrival-note"
title = "Early arrivals"
route = { path = "/early-arrivals/" }

The ID identifies the article in collection membership and other declared relationships. The title is what readers see. The route determines its address. If its title changes to Before the crowd while its ID and route stay the same, it remains the same article at /early-arrivals/, in the same collection. The following stages carry that change into the site.
Parse the writing
Gazette reads the article's metadata and parses its Markdown body. The Markdown adapter returns headings, links and other document structure together with their locations in the source. Gazette uses those locations to report a broken reference beside the text that caused it.
The compiler then interprets that structure as a publication: an article can belong to a collection, credit an author and link to another page. The content model describes those declarations.
Resolve the relationships
The Field Notes collection identifies its member by content:arrival-note, so it still contains the renamed article. The article also links to Station map, a page on a second site called Travel Guide. The workspace gives Travel Guide the public base https://travel.example/; Station map declares the route /station-map/. Gazette resolves the link to https://travel.example/station-map/. In a local preview that address can use the destination's local listener; a public build uses its public base URL.
This is also where Gazette detects missing destinations, conflicting identities and invalid relationships. Every consumer receives the resolved destination rather than calculating an address independently. See links and crossings and routing.
Render the result
The theme receives the article's body, title, navigation and resolved links as page context. It decides how to present them. The Field Notes listing and search index now receive Before the crowd as its title and /early-arrivals/ as its route. The article's Station map link receives the address resolved above. Those values come from the same resolved publication.
Feeds, sitemaps and JSON-LD also use that model. They can describe the same article at the same canonical address without each output reparsing the original Markdown. The theme contract defines the values a template receives; the Tera guide shows how to use them.
Trusted code and saved results
Theme templates and external generators are trusted code. Capturing their inputs and bounding accepted output do not make their execution a sandbox. A generator runs with its process permissions; its staging directory determines where Gazette puts files, not what the generator can access. Review the selected programs and their build scripts before running them.
Browser-module compilation removes supported TypeScript type syntax but does not type-check the program. Stylesheets and notebook output have their own supported profiles; Gazette displays saved notebook results without running cells. The theme contract, resource guide and generator guide explain those limits.
Compilation and host operations
The compiler resolves relationships in memory. The application asks the host to read a directory, start a preview server or write output only when the operation needs it. This lets an editor use the same compiler to check an unsaved document.
The compiler works with captured inputs and shared data types. When an operation needs filesystem, rendering or storage access, it uses a port: a Rust interface describing that capability. An adapter implements it, such as the filesystem adapter for local reads or the Tera adapter for templates. The application coordinates these operations, and the SDK assembles the capabilities a program needs.
The SDK's architecture test reads Cargo's actual dependency graph and checks the permitted production dependencies between Gazette crates: core depends on no other Gazette crate, ports depend on core, compiler on core and ports, and application on those three. Host adapters remain outside that chain. The test checks crate dependencies; the port and adapter design determines where host operations belong.
For example, an editor can analyse a document while you type using its in-memory text. A publication preview additionally needs the configured files, theme rendering and local listeners. Its application operation acquires those capabilities before serving the result. The preview guide explains the session lifecycle; local rendering covers build results and failures.
Share behavior across interfaces
The CLI, agent tools and editor integrations use the same compiler through Gazette's SDK. They adapt its operations to different callers:
Interface	When to use it	
CLI	Check, build, preview or release a publication from a shell	
MCP	Let an agent call Gazette operations with structured requests and results	
LSP	Add diagnostics, navigation and supported edits to an editor	
Node SDK	Embed Gazette in a Node application through Node-API	
One operation registry supplies the shared operation names and CLI families used by grouped help, MCP discovery and the editor's command routes. The interface coverage test compares the actual CLI commands, initialized MCP catalogue and VS Code routes, including every declared mode, so adding an operation must preserve its reachability through those interfaces.
An editor supplies its current document buffers for analysis. A filesystem build reads saved files from the configured sources, so save an edit before expecting it in that preview. These operations reuse Gazette's parsers and heading/reference analysis. A new interface translates its protocol into the existing SDK operations instead of implementing another parser or route resolver.
For integration examples, use the JavaScript SDK, MCP quickstart or language-server guide.
Build and deliver independently
Gazette can build and preview a publication from its configured writing, sources and theme without Pale or Weave. Optional fact providers and publisher-specific policy checks extend that input and review process; they do not replace the workspace’s publication choices or turn themes into live query clients. The supported fact-provider behavior and proposed evidence records are distinguished below.
A valid publication model does not establish that its writing is public or approved. Candidate policy checks inspect declarations and their uses; output disclosure checks inspect rendered files. Neither grants publication permission. Writing output to a local directory, preparing an authorized release and delivering it are separate operations; follow output materialization, policy checks and release preparation for their contracts.
The delivery path uses Git for objects and refs and the GitHub integration for Pages build observations. A successful push does not establish what readers receive: served-output observations compare selected routes with the expected bytes. Cloudflare and Vercel delivery adapters remain future integration work. After a lost delivery response, inspect the recorded outcome before retrying; a missing response does not establish that the write or push failed.
Where to extend Gazette
Choose the part that owns the behavior you want to change:
Change	Start with	Checks to extend	
Add a content relationship or change how it resolves	crates/gazette-compiler/src/authored/ and the content model	Content graph tests check membership, ordering, missing targets and cycles.	
Change a page's appearance or add a theme component	The theme contract and Tera templates	Tera adapter tests exercise captured templates, inheritance, escaping and limits; inspect the changed theme in the browser too.	
Connect a new storage mechanism	The storage port and store API	Application placement tests protect source/output separation; the existing SQLite connection and writer tests demonstrate read permissions and transaction checks.	
Add an editor or agent integration	The shared SDK, LSP or MCP contract	LSP protocol tests exercise framed messages and editor state; interface coverage checks CLI, MCP and editor operation reachability.	
A build produces output to inspect. Use the release workflow to prepare, approve and deliver it, and the source-build guide to check an implementation change.
Proposed optional fact evidence
A future integration could attach evidence to a selected fact for a publisher's checker. The proposed record would identify the fact and its owner, source revision and digest, validity or replacement, permitted public fields, relationship evidence and applicable consent. This is an optional design proposal, not an implemented schema or a required record for every person, organisation, brand or publishing fact.
The current compiler validates declarations and references. External-fact providers can supply the supported display-name field through the existing fact port, and configured policy checks can evaluate a publisher's own rules. Neither mechanism authenticates all of the proposed evidence or grants publication permission. A future record must preserve those distinctions and leave the source owner's meaning and permitted use with that owner.

Add analytics and browser tools
Add analytics or browser WebMCP to a Theme by declaring the client, its settings and its browser files in the workspace. Gazette checks those inputs before rendering and passes their URLs and settings to the Theme. Analytics starts only after consent.
