Releasing covers how approved output reaches its destinations, which is what you check here afterwards. Preparing deployment files covers the hosting files a publication emits.

Preparing deployment files
Gazette prepares deployment files inside the same bounded output tree as pages, resources and discovery documents. Rendering does not deploy a site, change a domain, contact an account or approve publication. The existing local and candidate content selections still decide which pages enter that tree.
Hosting files
Select hosting in the publication's processing configuration:
[defaults.publication.processing]
hosting = { provider = 'github-pages' }

The native SDK supplies the GitHub hosting file provider. Each selected publication emits an empty .nojekyll. A custom DNS host in its configured public_base_url also emits CNAME with that host and a final newline. A default *.github.io address needs no CNAME. Paths do not enter CNAME, and a loopback address cannot substitute for the production domain. Preview may replace links with listener addresses, but hosting files use the original configured production address.
Application callers can supply the pure gazette_ports::hosting::HostFiles service through the *_with_host_files rendering methods. Existing methods use no provider and reject a publication that selects hosting. Development preview selects this service through watch::Adapters.host_files. Provider files pass through ordinary path collision checks and output limits before a complete tree can be returned.
Crawler policy
Crawler rules belong to the workspace or publisher, with site overrides using ordinary publication inheritance. Gazette does not infer which crawlers search, answer questions or train models.
[defaults.publication.machine]
sitemap = true
robots = { enabled = true, rules = [
  { user_agent = '*', allow = ['/'] },
  { user_agent = 'ExampleTrainingBot', disallow = ['/'] },
] }

The example bot name illustrates a publisher-selected rule; it does not identify a real service. robots.txt preserves group order and emits each group's allowed paths before its disallowed paths. Gazette appends an absolute Sitemap line only when that assembly actually emits a sitemap. A site's rules array replaces inherited rules as a whole; enabled = false suppresses the file while preserving the inherited configuration. Omission emits no policy. Duplicate user-agent groups, directive injection and unbounded rule sets fail validation.
These directives request crawler behavior. They do not make content private or prevent access to files.
Terms of use
[defaults.publication.machine]
terms = { path = '/terms/', tdm_reservation = true }

path is the site-relative route of the publication's terms page, beginning with /. Gazette joins it to the production public_base_url, so preview output still names the published terms. It inherits like robots, and a site can override either field. Any declared terms adds the address to JSON-LD as usageInfo. With tdm_reservation = true, Gazette also writes .well-known/tdmrep.json with one rule, [{"location":"/*","tdm-reservation":1,"tdm-policy":"<terms URL>"}], and adds a presentation.discovery entry where kind is tdm-policy and url is the terms address, so a Theme can emit the matching <meta> elements. Omission emits none of these.
A publication's Mintlify documentation applies the same reservation and crawler rules to its own host. A TDM reservation states the publisher's terms for text and data mining. Like crawler rules, it requests behaviour and does not restrict access to files.
Browser manifest
[defaults.publication.machine]
web_manifest = { enabled = true, short_name = 'Example' }

manifest.webmanifest takes its name from the publication brand, its start address from the selected home or publication base, and its scope from that base. It uses browser display mode and includes the selected compiled site icon when present. short_name is optional. The output declares application/manifest+json; a Theme discovers its address through presentation.discovery where kind is web-manifest, and can emit a <link rel="manifest"> element. This metadata does not add offline support or promise browser installation eligibility.
Theme-owned missing page
A Theme can declare render.not_found = 'not-found.html'. This recipe inherits through explicit Theme dependencies and produces 404.html. It receives the ordinary presentation context, including publication metadata, chrome, selected resources and discovery links, with presentation.surface.kind = 'not-found'. The top-level site field carries the publication site key. Its page-specific fields are not_found.url, not_found.home_url and nullable not_found.search_url. These are absolute addresses, so navigation still works when a host serves the page for a deeply nested unknown URL.
The missing page has no invented authored content identity. Its private render evidence records the template, model digest and exact output digest separately from authored pages. Native preview serves those same retained bytes with status 404 for an unknown page address. A Theme without this recipe keeps the preview's plain fallback and emits no 404.html.
Related contracts: workspace presentation, Theme reference and preview.

Run a documentation generator
When a library changes, its API reference needs to change with it. Gazette can run the library's documentation tool and place the result beside its handwritten guides. TypeDoc reads TypeScript declarations; Rustdoc reads Rust code and comments. Gazette supplies their selected files, runs the configured command and assembles its output into the documentation site.
This guide is for the developer setting up that build. If you already have generated reference on disk, start with Choose an input format and assemble it directly. To add a handwritten guide first, follow Add a manual to Field Notes.
Follow the source into the reference
Suppose your library adds an optional argument to a function. You update its declaration and explain the new argument in its code comment. The generator reads those changes and produces the signature and explanation; you keep the longer example in the handwritten guide. Both need to describe the same version of the library, so select one prepared source tree for them, or compare their selected bytes before assembly.
The TypeDoc example below has three results you can inspect: the captured source files, the generator's reference.json, and a Mintlify directory containing that reference and docs.json. Gazette keeps the generator's files even if the later assembly fails. You can correct the assembly and reuse those files without running TypeDoc again.
You have	Start here	
API output already on disk	Choose an input format. You can assemble these files without running the generator again.	
A Rust library	Prepare and run Rustdoc.	
A TypeScript project	Configure and run a TypeDoc job.	
TypeScript declarations that need to preserve qualifiers	Use the Markdown formatter.	
A changed generator or adapter	Compare the generated reference with its source.	
Install the generator and its dependencies before running the job.
Caution

Review the selected tools and build scripts. They run with the process’s permissions. The staging directory limits where Gazette puts files, not what a generator can do.
Configure a TypeDoc job
This example assembles one library's TypeDoc JSON. You need a built Gazette, an installed TypeDoc toolchain and a source directory containing typedoc.json plus its complete selected project files. A minimal options file is:
{
  "entryPoints": ["src/model.ts", "src/api.ts"],
  "tsconfig": "tsconfig.json",
  "disableGit": true,
  "disableSources": true,
  "treatWarningsAsErrors": true
}

Use your library's actual entrypoints, TypeScript configuration and required local imports. Include every file the generator needs in the selected source. The paths in typedoc.json are relative to that captured input; they must not depend on files elsewhere in your checkout.
The supported TypeDoc profile uses TypeDoc 0.28.20 and TypeScript 5.9.3. Install the complete tool and its dependencies outside the source directory. When selecting another version, compare the generated declarations and build the resulting documentation before using it.
Save the following as reference-workspace.toml. The source names your library's files; the navigation entry places its generated reference under library/reference. The recipe gives Gazette the command to run. Replace the absolute paths and fill in the executable observations described just after the example:
[[principals]]
id = "owner:library"
kind = "person"

[[sites]]
id = "site:library"
publisher = "owner:library"
deployable = false

[[projects]]
id = "project:library"
lifecycle = "active"
visibility = "public"
availability = "available"

[[sources]]
id = "source:library"
location = { kind = "filesystem", root = "/absolute/library-input" }

[[brands]]
id = "brand:library"
name = "Library"

[[brands.publications]]
site = "site:library"

[brands.publications.documentation_repository]
name = "library-docs"
path = "/absolute/intended-docs-repository"

[brands.publications.documentation_repository.build]
target = { kind = "mintlify", theme = "mint", primary_color = "#315c4a" }

[[brands.publications.documentation_repository.build.modules]]
project = "project:library"
slug = "library"
title = "Library"

[[brands.publications.documentation_repository.build.modules.navigation]]
kind = "reference"
slug = "reference"
title = "API reference"

[brands.publications.documentation_repository.build.modules.navigation.input]
kind = "generated"
source = "source:library"

[brands.publications.documentation_repository.build.modules.navigation.input.recipe]
program = "/absolute/node"
executable = { bytes = 123456, sha256 = "<node-sha256>" }
arguments = [
  { kind = "literal", value = "/absolute/tool/node_modules/typedoc/bin/typedoc" },
  { kind = "literal", value = "--options" },
  { kind = "input", path = "typedoc.json" },
  { kind = "literal", value = "--json" },
  { kind = "output" },
]
environment = {}
version_arguments = ["/absolute/tool/node_modules/typedoc/bin/typedoc", "--version"]
expected_version_sha256 = "<complete-version-stdout-sha256>"
output = { kind = "file", path = "reference.json" }
format = "typedoc-json"

input selects typedoc.json in the captured source, and output names a new file in the job's output directory. Gazette passes the literal arguments directly, without a shell or PATH lookup. This example captures the files currently on disk. To require a particular commit, choose a repository source; a local capture alone does not establish a Git revision.
Record the tool you intend to run
The recipe records Node's byte count and SHA-256, plus the SHA-256 of TypeDoc's version output. Before filling those fields, select the exact Node executable, TypeDoc script and installed dependency tree. Run the script's --version with the recipe's explicit environment and retain all its stdout bytes, including newlines. Hash those bytes for expected_version_sha256.
These observations let Gazette stop if the executable or version output changes between setup and generation. They do not approve the installed packages: review those separately, including plugins and build scripts. Recipe fields explains machine-bound paths, environments and validation commands when your integration needs them.
Run and interpret the result
Create separate existing private parents for generator jobs and target stages, outside every source directory selected for this documentation build. Gazette refuses overlapping sources and output locations, including an ignored target/ directory inside a selected repository. Then invoke the selected Gazette:
gazette assemble-docs --local --site site:library --allow-execute \
  --generator-parent /absolute/private/generator-jobs \
  --output-parent /absolute/private/documentation-stages \
  --generator-timeout-ms 30000 --max-generator-jobs 1 \
  < reference-workspace.toml > documentation-result.json

A successful report has status: "documentation-assembled-local":
jobs[0] identifies the retained generator input/output stages, version observation, generation invocation, complete tree and selected artifact.
directory is the new Mintlify target stage. For this example it contains docs.json and the original TypeDoc JSON at artifacts/library/reference.json.
repository.path is the configured intended destination. Assembly does not create or replace that repository.
Open the target with your local documentation provider and inspect symbols, examples and links. For a real library, compare the complete public declarations, not just a few rendered signatures. Target formats describe what the adapter accepts; Mintlify integration explains assembling manual sections alongside this reference.
Reuse a generator result
To assemble the same result again without running TypeDoc, bind a source to the original job's retained output root and replace the navigation input with:
input = { kind = "artifact", source = "source:retained-reference", selection = { kind = "file", path = "reference.json" }, format = "typedoc-json" }

Retain and check the original artifact/tree identity when selecting that root. Use selection = { kind = "directory", path = "reference" } for a directory format; omitting path explicitly selects the entire capture root. A file or directory declaration must match the retained entry. Neither target assembly nor repeated adaptation runs the generator again.
Configure a Rustdoc job
Use the Rustdoc provider through the same configured generator runner. It builds the selected library with Cargo, uses Cargo’s resolved package identities and actual compiler artifacts to locate each dependency version, and gives the resulting HTML to the existing Rustdoc converter. Renamed dependencies and multiple versions of one crate keep their own links.
Important

Select a complete installed nightly toolchain. This provider uses Rustdoc’s unstable external-root options. Configure absolute paths to Cargo, rustc and rustdoc from that toolchain, and to Python 3.12 or newer. Provision Cargo’s locked dependencies beforehand; generation runs with --offline --locked and fails if a dependency is unavailable.
Put rustdoc.json in the selected source tree. For a library whose package manifest is at the root:
{
  "manifest": "Cargo.toml"
}

manifest must select one package with a library target. Include its workspace manifests, lockfile, local dependencies and source files in the capture. A workspace-only manifest is ambiguous and is refused. For Gazette’s Rust SDK, use "manifest": "sdk/rust/Cargo.toml" and "features": ["native-local"] over the complete selected repository. no_default_features defaults to false; set it explicitly when that is the intended API.
Crates from crates.io receive version-specific https://docs.rs/<package>/<version>/ roots. For another registry, a Git dependency or a local package with published reference, supply dependency_roots in the same JSON object:
{
  "dependency_roots": {
    "example-dependency@1.2.3": "https://docs.example.org/example-dependency/1.2.3/"
  }
}

A name@version key must identify exactly one resolved package. When two sources use that same name and version, use Cargo’s complete package ID. Roots must be absolute HTTPS directory URLs. Gazette does not infer a documentation address for unpublished local or Git dependencies. Unresolved local links fail the subsequent target assembly; a URL declaration does not prove that an external host serves it.
In the workspace example above, keep the source, module and reference selection and replace the recipe with:
program = "/absolute/python3"
executable = { bytes = 123456, sha256 = "<python-executable-sha256>" }
arguments = [
  { kind = "literal", value = "-B" },
  { kind = "path", path = "machine:reference-tools/rustdoc.py" },
  { kind = "literal", value = "--cargo" },
  { kind = "path", path = "machine:nightly/bin/cargo" },
  { kind = "literal", value = "--rustc" },
  { kind = "path", path = "machine:nightly/bin/rustc" },
  { kind = "literal", value = "--rustdoc" },
  { kind = "path", path = "machine:nightly/bin/rustdoc" },
  { kind = "literal", value = "--input" },
  { kind = "input-root" },
  { kind = "literal", value = "--output" },
  { kind = "output-root" },
  { kind = "literal", value = "--config" },
  { kind = "input", path = "rustdoc.json" },
]
environment = { PATH = "/absolute/nightly/bin:/usr/bin:/bin", CARGO_HOME = "/absolute/provisioned-cargo-home" }
version_arguments = ["-B", { path = "machine:reference-tools/rustdoc.py" }, "--version"]
expected_version_sha256 = "<complete-provider-version-stdout-sha256>"
output = { kind = "directory", path = "reference/example_library" }
format = "rustdoc-html"

Bind reference-tools to the installed provider directory and nightly to the selected toolchain through the workspace’s machine file. The explicit --cargo, --rustc and --rustdoc arguments keep those machine locations out of captured source options. Existing JSON options may still name these tools; if a tool is selected in both places, every declaration must name the same path. Conflicting JSON or repeated command-line selections fail before preparation. Missing selections fail rather than consulting PATH.
Replace example_library with the library’s Rust crate name, such as gazette_sdk. Resolve the Python executable to its actual file before recording its byte count and SHA-256; the runner refuses an executable symlink. Observe /absolute/python3 -B /absolute/tools/rustdoc.py --version for the version digest. Select any linker and native build prerequisites through the recipe’s explicit environment as well. The provider records the selected Cargo, rustc and rustdoc versions and executable digests, and refuses replacement during the job.
A recipe with machine coordinates must load its owning workspace and machine binding. Put machine_binding = "machine.local.toml" at the root of reference-workspace.toml, with the tool roots in that machine file. Supply the local workspace selector through --workspace-json; a detached TOML buffer has no machine roots:
printf '%s\n' '{"kind":"local","root":"/absolute/workspace","workspace":"reference-workspace.toml"}' |
  gazette assemble-docs --workspace-json --local --site site:library --allow-execute \
    --generator-parent /absolute/private/generator-jobs \
    --output-parent /absolute/private/documentation-stages \
    --generator-timeout-ms 300000 --max-entries 40000 > documentation-result.json

This example allows a five-minute invocation (the runner's maximum) and up to 40,000 entries in the generated output set and assembled tree. Generator inputs have independent CLI limits:
Flag	Default	Counts	
--max-generator-input-entries	10,000	Entries across all generator input copies, including directories and hidden files.	
--max-generator-input-total-bytes	536,870,912 (512 MiB)	Combined file bytes across all input copies.	
--max-generator-input-file-bytes	67,108,864 (64 MiB)	Bytes in one input file.	
--max-generator-input-depth	64	Descendant levels within each input tree; immediate children have depth one.	
A source used by two jobs counts twice against the entry and total-byte allowances. For example, add --max-generator-input-entries 20000 when repeated copies need that allowance. Zero does not restore the default.
Increasing --max-entries changes output limits only; --max-source-bytes bounds the workspace input on stdin. Source acquisition keeps its separate native defaults, including 10,000 entries; larger acquisition limits remain available through MCP assemble_docs and the SDK. These bounds limit a run; they cannot guarantee that it completes.
Inspect the original, prepared and generated files
The job’s input stage keeps the original captured source. Its output stage contains:
prepared/: the same selected files, with private, hidden cfg(doc) dependency imports appended only to the chosen library root. Original declaration and example bytes remain intact. Source-derived aliases avoid existing names; a detected collision fails preparation.
reference/: native Rustdoc HTML, runtime companions and source views. The configured crate directory is the reference selected for assembly.
preparation.json: original and prepared source identities, exact dependency package/version/artifact identities and link roots, provider identity, tool observations and each native invocation’s result.
Cargo and tool output files for diagnosing a failure. Cargo’s disposable compilation products are removed after successful reference capture; failures keep their residue in the same job output.
The existing native runner checks the original input before and after the invocation. The provider also checks that preparation changed only the library root and that neither source copy changed during generation. Warnings, including broken comment links, fail Rustdoc. The shared converter then checks the complete selected reference’s local pages and fragments. Keep these checks distinct from comparing the public API and reading the assembled reference.
Reuse a completed reference/ tree through the artifact-input path; preparation does not run again during that assembly. Keep prepared/, logs and preparation.json with the private job result. They are not manual pages or publication inputs.
What the runner reads and keeps
Field	What it tells the runner	
program, executable, version_arguments, expected_version_sha256	Which executable bytes and version output to require. A mismatch stops before generation. Pin imported packages and plugins separately.	
arguments	literal passes a value; path resolves an explicit tool path through the workspace and machine binding; input names a file; input-root names the full working directory; output names the result; output-root names the output stage. No shell expands these values, and the runner does not guess from the language.	
environment	The child's complete environment. Strings stay literal; an explicit { path = "machine:tools/packages" } value resolves through the captured machine binding. The runner inherits no environment and does not search PATH.	
output, format	Which file or directory to use and which adapter format should consume it.	
validation_arguments	Optionally run the same executable over the output with output or output-root. A nonzero result, changed files or extra files fail the job. The validator cannot replace generated bytes.	
The recipe's program accepts an absolute executable path, a workspace-relative coordinate or machine:name/path, using the same machine binding as source roots. For example, select program = "machine:python/bin/python3" and environment = { PYTHONPATH = { path = "machine:packages" } } when an interpreter and its package directory live outside the captured project. Each typed environment value names one path; strings such as "machine:packages" stay literal, with no interpolation or path-list expansion. The selected executable must still pass the native file and digest checks; a symlink is not a replacement for the real executable selection.
All selected generator coordinates bind before the first job stage is created. The binding comes from the loaded workspace's captured machine file, never from the process directory or a later file read. Supplied TOML buffers have no native workspace or machine roots, so they require absolute executable coordinates and absolute typed environment paths. Generator input and input-root arguments still name the retained source stage; they are not machine paths. Version arguments accept literal strings and explicit { path = "machine:tools/cli.js" } values. Generation and validation arguments use { kind = "path", path = "machine:tools/plugin.mjs" } for the same resolver. Unknown roots, missing workspace context, malformed coordinates and expanded commands above the native limits fail before any job stage is created. Strings that merely contain machine: remain literal; no field interpolates paths. The exact executable and version-output checks remain required.
Gazette checks job count, permissions and the target's names, presentation and formats before staging. Every job starts with the captured inputs and an empty output directory. Gazette checks the inputs and version, runs the generator once, then captures its complete result. Repeated input stages and all generated outputs count against the shared limits.
Diagnose a failed job
Failure	What to do	
Executable or version mismatch	Check the selected tool and all its installed dependencies before recording a replacement in the recipe.	
Generator exit or timeout	Inspect its exact invocation, retained stages and native cause. A successful prefix remains evidence.	
Missing selected result or file/directory mismatch	Compare the recipe with the actual captured tree; preserve the residue.	
Validator failure or changed output	Keep generation and validation results separately. Correct the source/tool selection for a new deliberate job.	
Target adaptation or staging failure	Inspect the retained artifact first. A completed generator need not run again merely because the later target failed.	
Staging refusal before any job starts	Check that both parent directories exist outside all selected source roots. An ignored build directory inside a source repository still overlaps it.	
Result delivery lost or too large	Keep the original request and stage paths. Inspect those directories before trying again: the generator may have run even though you received no result.	
When the full report will not fit, Gazette returns a smaller failure report with the original stage paths, completed or active commands and their identities. It may omit version text while keeping its digest and byte count. If the target returns Invalid, read failure.target_diagnostic: context locates the problem in the build, reason describes it, and omission flags say whether details were left out to fit the response. This diagnostic contains no artifact body and opens no additional file. If the CLI cannot write stdout, it reports failure and attempts to preserve the smaller report on stderr.
Before distributing generated files, inspect them for private source paths and other information you did not intend to publish. Time, byte and entry limits help control a run's size; tools and plugins still need the review described at the start of this guide.
Local TypeDoc Markdown formatter
Use this formatter when direct TypeDoc JSON conversion loses detail your API needs, such as readonly in an anonymous declaration or index signature. It uses TypeDoc's local-plugin and theme mechanism to produce Markdown. Page titles remain escaped plain text with generic constraints and defaults intact; TypeDoc supplies the model, routes, comments and body links. The two adapted type-formatting partials keep their upstream MIT notice, and the package lock records the installed tool dependencies.
Copy the complete tools/documentation-reference source directory to a private tool directory outside the manual's captured source. Retain package.json, package-lock.json, plugin.mjs, provider.mjs, both partials/*.mjs, upstream.json, UPSTREAM-LICENSE and test/. The plugin imports the provider helper and derived partials; copying just the manifests is incomplete. Exclude any existing node_modules, then provision the copy explicitly:
cd /absolute/private/reference-formatter
/absolute/node /absolute/npm-cli.js ci --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund
/absolute/node --test test/*.test.mjs

Use a Node version within the tool's supported range, then record the exact executable and version output in the recipe as above. Install dependencies before generation; Gazette does not run npm for you. Run the formatter's own tests after changing it.
For retained TypeDoc JSON, select the exact original model and any source-file companions it names. The merge loader may require those captured declarations even when source links are disabled. For Mintlify, hide the producer's repeated banner and breadcrumbs while retaining its H1 for the target's title and original anchor. An options file can select:
{
  "entryPointStrategy": "merge",
  "entryPoints": ["reference.json"],
  "theme": "contract-markdown",
  "hidePageHeader": true,
  "hideBreadcrumbs": true,
  "hidePageTitle": false,
  "readme": "none",
  "disableSources": true,
  "disableGit": true,
  "treatWarningsAsErrors": true,
  "fileExtension": ".md",
  "entryFileName": "index",
  "router": "member",
  "expandObjects": true,
  "expandParameters": true,
  "useCodeBlocks": true
}

useCodeBlocks: true puts declaration signatures in fenced code blocks. Setting it to false uses inline code and blockquotes; the local plugin preserves qualifiers in either form but does not override that presentation choice.
Pass that options file as an Input argument to the pinned TypeDoc script, and its output directory as Output, through the ordinary configured native runner. Bind formatter to the complete installed tool directory and pass both plugins through TypeDoc's repeated --plugin option:
arguments = [
  { kind = "path", path = "machine:formatter/node_modules/typedoc/bin/typedoc" },
  { kind = "literal", value = "--options" },
  { kind = "input", path = "typedoc.json" },
  { kind = "literal", value = "--plugin" },
  { kind = "path", path = "machine:formatter/node_modules/typedoc-plugin-markdown/dist/index.js" },
  { kind = "literal", value = "--plugin" },
  { kind = "path", path = "machine:formatter/plugin.mjs" },
  { kind = "literal", value = "--out" },
  { kind = "output" },
]
version_arguments = [{ path = "machine:formatter/node_modules/typedoc/bin/typedoc" }, "--version"]

Keep plugin locations out of the captured options. TypeDoc includes its TypeScript installation path in version output, so relocating the tool requires a new version observation and digest even when its files are identical. Import the resulting directory as format = "markdown". Keep the original JSON and each formatter run's report and output. To change presentation, change the formatter and run a new job; leave the earlier output available for comparison. Reassembling an unchanged Markdown directory needs no generator run.
Compare the complete public API with its original declarations, including readonly and optional modifiers, generic constraints and defaults, overloads, and nested mapped and conditional types. Build the documentation, follow its links and navigation, and read the signatures as they appear on the page. A successful build can still show an inaccurate signature. Directory Markdown navigation defaults to lexical order. Use the format's pages and directory selections to name chapters and derive their symbol groups from generated directories. Gazette checks that the expanded navigation includes every page exactly once.
Check the generated reference
        
Before adopting a generator or changing its version:
Compare every public symbol with the source declarations. Check signatures, readonly and optional modifiers, overloads and generic constraints.
Follow links between generated pages and from the manual into reference. Check the original fragment targets too.
Build the complete documentation target with its intended provider. Open representative long signatures, code samples and nested navigation in the browser.
Keep the generator request and original output so a later formatting change can be checked without guessing what the tool produced.
Use the format reference for each supported input profile and its limits. Compare the result with the API it describes before giving it to readers.

Discover editor sources
Open the folder containing gazette.toml to get editor feedback for its configured publication. Gazette reads the root, its exact includes and the separate machine binding, then selects authoring files from the resolved workspace. Sources can live outside the open folder. The configuration supplies their owners and logical paths; opening a neighbouring repository does not add it to the publication.
The VS Code extension uses discovery by default when no explicit source lists are supplied. A folder without the selected configuration stays inactive. The first-publication starter enables this mode, so adding a page beneath its configured content source requires no editor-list update. Existing explicit selections keep their named-file contract.
What enters the editor session
Configured role	Selection	
Workspace	The root and its exact non-recursive includes. The saved machine binding supplies native roots separately.	
Publication content	Files under each selected content source, with its literal includes, exclusions, subtree and logical placement. Markdown, structured landings and notebooks supply text. Other files supply path and observed size only.	
Retained-only content	Metadata only, including files whose suffix would otherwise select a text parser.	
Legal text	Each exact configured legal entry. Siblings are not selected.	
Authored manuals	Exact files named by manual navigation, plus explicitly retained support files. Generated references are separate.	
Themes and plugins	Each exact declared package manifest. Discovery does not walk the package's template or dependency directories.	
The shared compiler owns the filename rules and logical placements. Package manifests have package-qualified editor paths, so equal filenames in different packages remain distinct; their native URIs and configured manifest paths stay intact. The filesystem adapter owns confined reads and refuses links below selected roots. Equal repeated bindings collapse only when their native file, logical path and role agree. Conflicting meanings are refused. Discovery describes working files; it neither verifies repository pins nor produces captured build evidence. Asset size is an observation, not a digest or retained payload.
For manual support outside navigation, set gazette.workspace.manualSupport to { "source": "source:manual", "path": "docs/support.md" } entries. Each path is relative to that configured source. When migrating an older explicit selection, verify that every retained manual still identifies the same native file before removing its old locator. Nonempty legacy source lists continue to select the explicit mode.
Initialize another client
Choose one absolute native workspace directory through rootUri or a single workspaceFolders entry. If both are present, they must agree. Send these initialization options:
{
  "native_selection": {
    "allow_read": true,
    "discover": true,
    "workspace": "gazette.toml",
    "manuals": [
      {"source": "source:manual", "path": "docs/support.md"}
    ]
  }
}

Omit manuals when configured navigation supplies all manual inputs. allow_read permits the native reads for this session; it grants no build or publication effect. The server advertises experimental.gazette.sourceDiscovery.selectSource = "gazette/selectSource".
Before forwarding a newly opened file's text, call gazette/selectSource with { "uri": "file:///work/content/new.md" }. It returns selected, the current generation, and exact configuration watchFiles, including the separate machine binding and declared configuration files that are currently missing. An unrelated path causes no source scan. A new path under a configured content source refreshes membership before admission. The server also handles first-open discovery directly through didOpen.
Use gazette/editorSnapshot for the current selected roles and opaque asset observations. Forward text only for admitted sources. workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles refreshes native membership; clients should watch the current selected files and configuration paths. Neither these requests nor the editor writes source files.
Repair without losing unsaved work
An unreadable root refuses startup. A readable root with a configuration error remains editable. Current root and included-document overlays drive discovery, so an unsaved correction can restore the selection. The machine binding uses its saved contents and remains outside workspace compiler documents.
Refresh preserves open text and versions for files that remain selected and advances the same session's generation. Invalid configuration retains the existing buffers for repair. A native discovery failure makes successful semantic analysis unavailable and reports the reason on the root document; it does not reuse an older success. Correcting the configuration or refreshing restored sources rebuilds the selection. A valid change that removes a file also clears its diagnostics. The client retains unsaved text for files outside the new selection and sends it again if they become selected later.
Closing a configuration overlay restores its native baseline and refreshes membership. Saving acknowledges the exact current text before refreshing. Content edits use the current selected session without walking native sources on every keystroke. All retained text, identifiers, overlays, metadata and diagnostic responses remain bounded by the SDK and transport limits.
The VS Code client waits for native admission and current open text before querying. Configuration overlays are reconciled before content overlays, and a changed native context renews the symbol provider through the pinned client's public feature registration. This refreshes an article's outline after configuration repair even when the article's editor version has not changed.
For the implementation, start with the native SDK session, LSP dispatch and VS Code lifecycle. The explicit session contract continues to govern full-text versions, source-bound queries and reviewed edits.
The native editor host check runs in a real local macOS VS Code with isolated user-data and extension directories. Set GAZETTE_VSCODE_ISOLATED=1 and GAZETTE_TEST_EXECUTABLE to the exact candidate executable. Open the generated first-publication example in a disposable folder named native-editor-starter; the check creates a page there and exercises its first-open diagnostic and completion, configuration repair and preservation of an unsaved page in the same server process. For an existing workspace, set GAZETTE_VSCODE_READ_ONLY_WORKSPACE to its absolute path and GAZETTE_VSCODE_NATIVE_PAGE to one selected authored page; that mode changes only isolated editor buffers and checks that saved source bytes remain unchanged. The workspace must already use discovery without legacy source lists. These checks establish the local development host behavior; VSIX installation and other hosts need their own qualification.

Feeds
Generate Atom 1.0, RSS 2.0 or JSON Feed 1.1 from the same resolved pages that supply the Theme, search and JSON-LD. You configure which pages belong in the feed, and Gazette writes the feed files and gives the Theme their URLs.
Set a channel, format and article rules below, then expose the result through Theme discovery. Add a lifecycle filter for public feeds so that drafts or archived pages stay out. For a publication walkthrough, see Help readers find the work.
Explicit publication configuration
Configure feeds inside an existing brand publication's machine table:
[brands.publications.machine.feeds]
identity_base = "https://identity.example/publication/"

[[brands.publications.machine.feeds.channels]]
id = "feed:updates"
channel = "collection:home"
path = "/updates.atom"
format = "atom"
scope = { kind = "collection", recursive = true }

The referenced channel is an existing same-site content object. Its title, description, language, dates and attributions remain authored facts; the feed configuration does not declare them again. Names come from the shared principal catalog. path uses the existing file-route codec and the publication's serving base, including its mount prefix. Omission disables feeds; an explicitly empty channel list is invalid. Duplicate feed keys or output paths fail configuration, as do directory paths and conflicting identities across publications. All outputs share the site's collision and byte/count limits, including page, redirect, resource, graph and model files.
A publication can explicitly select dated published articles across all editorial residences. Channels may then omit scope, selecting that same-site candidate set:
[brands.publications.machine.feeds]
identity_base = "https://identity.example/publication/"
selection = { kind = "articles", residence = "all", lifecycle = ["published"], require_published_date = true }
omit_when_empty = true

[[brands.publications.machine.feeds.channels]]
id = "feed:updates"
channel = "collection:home"
path = "/updates.json"
format = "json"

The selector admits article-family pages, not collection or journey landings or documentation pages. It also excludes article-family pages inside a documentation collection. An explicit structural scope without this article selector retains its own selection rules. lifecycle must be nonempty and contain distinct native states. require_published_date tests the authored date's presence, retaining its calendar or timestamp precision. No date comes from file metadata. An explicit channel scope can narrow these candidates while retaining its traversal semantics; without a publication selector, every channel must declare its scope.
omit_when_empty = true omits the complete filtered empty feed in every format. No zero-byte placeholder appears in the output inventory or stage. The configured output path remains reserved against other feeds, files and directory prefixes. The default false emits an empty feed and requires that format's channel facts. Omission does not bypass channel or original candidate binding validation.
Choose feed IDs and entries
Set identity_base to a stable HTTP(S) namespace you can keep if the publication moves. Gazette appends #feed= and the percent-encoded feed key for a feed ID, or #content= and the percent-encoded content key for an item ID. Changing a title, format, route, serving address or feed key leaves an item's ID intact. Changing its namespace or content key creates a new ID. An ID need not open in a browser. Declaring a namespace does not verify ownership. See Atom's identity rules.
Scope	Complete entry selection	
{ kind = "site" }	All other same-site content, in canonical URL order.	
{ kind = "collection", recursive = false }	Direct collection members and structural children, in canonical URL order.	
{ kind = "collection", recursive = true }	Those children plus descendant collections, journeys and their editorial members, deduplicated and in canonical URL order.	
{ kind = "journey" }	The channel journey's exact authored member sequence.	
Gazette uses the channel for metadata and excludes it from entries. A missing, foreign or wrong-kind member fails the whole feed. An empty journey stays empty. Gazette resolves every candidate before applying publication filters. It never adds a date cutoff, limits the entry count, inherits the publisher as author or invents a missing date.
Site feeds also use the discovery rules. A configured channel that cannot be discovered fails. A valid member that cannot be discovered stays out, without making the feed fail. Eligible entries keep their original order. Private compiler inspection applies structural and publication filters without hiding entries based on discovery.
What each feed format emits
The private inspection result uses complete PageData for the channel and entries. Emitted feeds omit ineligible endpoints and raw container-member details. JSON uses _gazette; XML carries JSON text in gazette:metadata under urn:gazette:syndication. That technical namespace does not verify a subject or define a registered ontology. The serializer leaves out private source coordinates and keeps the existing lifecycle, relationship, attribution and source values. JSON exposes the feed ID in _gazette_feed.id, RSS in gazette:id and Atom in its standard id.
Atom requires an explicit timestamp-valued modified on channel and entries. Each entry requires its own named authors; channel authors cannot fill a gap. An empty feed also requires named channel authors. Body HTML is escaped text with type="html"; explicit summary text remains separate.
RSS requires the channel's explicit description. Entry descriptions contain full body HTML. Named authors use dc:creator, not a fabricated email in author. Standard dates are emitted only for whole-second timestamps; calendar dates and fractional timestamps remain exact in metadata rather than being promoted or rounded. RSS field meanings.
JSON Feed emits full body HTML and text, optional explicit summary and exact timestamp fields. Standard root authors/language are omitted to prevent inheritance; item values are its own declarations. Unnamed author records remain in metadata, not invented names. No deprecated singular author alias is emitted. JSON Feed fields.
Calendar-only dates never become midnight. No format consults a clock. XML character, namespace and syntax checks cover the complete output before success; carriage returns use character references to survive XML newline normalization. Byte limits bound wire output and temporary metadata encoding, not a process-wide allocation or CPU sandbox.
Theme discovery
Site assembly exposes presentation.feeds only for successfully serialized outputs. Each entry carries id, channel, the authored channel title, resolved serving url, format (atom, rss or json) and media_type. The address comes from the same feed projection as its wire output, including a selected local preview base or publication mount. Themes need not reconstruct a feed route.
The list is shared by the site's page, alias, continuation, graph, taxonomy and mirror render contexts. Omitted empty feeds never appear; retained empty feeds appear only if their format validates and emits successfully. When no feed is emitted, or when rendering a standalone page without site assembly, the field is absent. Themes should guard it with is defined. This discovery contract does not alter selection, publication eligibility or the reserved output paths.

Install Gazette from source
Build the gazette executable on Linux or macOS. The same binary can check configuration, render a publication and run the local editor or agent server.
For agent use, build the executable below, put its directory on your shell's PATH, then open your publication folder and install the Gazette plugin. One plugin directory supplies the Claude Code and Codex skill and MCP configuration; Claude also receives explicit language-server discovery settings. The integration is under qualification and currently requires a source build.
What a build needs
Start with a local Gazette source checkout and the usual C build tools. Install the toolchain in rust-toolchain.toml: Rust 1.94.0, including rustfmt and clippy. Rustup installs this version when you run Cargo from the checkout. If you manage Rust another way, install that version yourself.
Build the executable
From the Gazette repository root, run:
cargo build --locked --release --bin gazette

Cargo writes target/release/gazette unless your Cargo configuration chooses another target directory or target triple.
Check that it runs
Set these two variables so the publication tutorial can find your checkout and executable:
export GAZETTE_SOURCE="$(pwd -P)"
export GAZETTE="$GAZETTE_SOURCE/target/release/gazette"
"$GAZETTE" --help

You should see Gazette's command help. If you use a custom Cargo target directory, set GAZETTE to the executable path printed by Cargo with --message-format=json.
Use the build
To start a publication, follow Your first publication. Its setup script needs Python 3. To embed Gazette in an application, see Gazette architecture.
For other commands, use gazette --help or gazette <command> --help.
Contributor checks
If you are changing Gazette, install Git with git-http-backend, OpenSSL, Python 3, curl and Node 22.18 or newer. Run these checks from the repository root, passing the tool paths to the test suite:
cargo fmt --all --check
cargo check --workspace --all-targets --locked
cargo test --workspace --all-targets --locked --no-run
GAZETTE_TEST_NODE="$(node --print 'process.execPath')" \
GAZETTE_TEST_CURL="$(command -v curl)" \
GAZETTE_TEST_GIT="$(command -v git)" \
GAZETTE_TEST_OPENSSL="$(command -v openssl)" \
GAZETTE_TEST_PYTHON="$(command -v python3)" \
cargo test --workspace --locked --no-fail-fast -- --test-threads=4
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings
cargo doc --workspace --locked --no-deps
python3 tools/generate_distribution_evidence.py --check

The last command validates the locked inputs and builds the dependency inventory in memory. Release and editor packaging generate notices beside their artifacts; see distribution generation for local output and verification commands.
Math tests require the Node version above. Tests for generators, Graphviz, Chrome and the native addon run separately with the executable inputs described in their guides. The source build does not install those optional tools.
Generate distribution notices
The offline generator reads the distribution configuration, exact Cargo, npm, Python and Go locks, checksum-verified assets and bundled libgit2/SQLite licence records. It generates NOTICE, THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md and SBOM.spdx.json for the release or editor package. Vendor licences remain with their source.
Validate the inputs and generated model without writing files:
cargo fetch --locked
python3 tools/generate_distribution_evidence.py --check
python3 -m unittest discover -s tools/tests -p 'test_distribution_evidence.py'

To inspect or package the output, choose a temporary or release directory:
python3 tools/generate_distribution_evidence.py --output-root target/distribution
python3 tools/generate_distribution_evidence.py --check --output-root target/distribution

Important

Generate from the release source. Packaging generates fresh notices from the locked inputs; no copy is committed. --check without a destination validates inputs in memory; with a destination it also requires every generated file to match. A lock, asset or licence checksum mismatch still fails either check.
Local Cargo packages use their repository-relative manifest path, name and version for inventory identity. External packages retain their full Cargo source identifier, name and version, including Git revisions and distinct registries. Cargo's absolute local package IDs remain internal graph keys only. Moving the same checkout therefore preserves the inventory without merging packages from different homes or sources. Cargo metadata documents these fields. Exact upstream licence spellings remain in the notices and comments; only known legacy slash spellings are normalized in SPDX expressions.
The portable workflow generates into the runner's temporary directory and checks that output. The tagged-release job packages freshly generated source notices and inventory alongside the executable, then attaches a separate binary SBOM and checksums.
Prepare a release binary
The tagged-release workflow builds with cargo auditable on Linux and macOS. It remaps source paths beneath the build user's home to /build-home, then the checkout to gazette, so the more specific checkout mapping takes precedence. It also strips debug information, including linker entries that source-path remapping does not cover. Before assembling the archive, it rejects a binary containing either original path. This check covers those two literal prefixes; it does not establish that every embedded string is suitable for publication.
A local source build above does not apply these release settings. Run the workflow and check its actual release artifact before distributing it.

Gazette for agents
Gazette meets each actor where it works, with the same publication model behind every mode: a person writing in an editor arrives through the language server, an agent helping in Claude Code or Codex through the MCP server and its skill, and a build or integration through the command line and SDKs.
Open a publication folder containing gazette.toml, then connect Gazette to Claude Code or Codex. This plugin supplies one Gazette skill and one local MCP server to both hosts. Claude Code also receives language-server settings for configured Markdown, TOML and notebook files. Gazette reads the sources declared by the publication; no generated file list is needed.
This is a source-checkout integration under qualification. The package does not install the Gazette executable. Installation and removal have been checked in isolated Claude Code and Codex homes. Claude connected to the installed MCP server; Codex discovered the installed skill and invoked a Gazette tool. Real-model use, Claude language-server feedback and matching page diagnostics across the interfaces still need qualification.
Prepare the executable
Build Gazette, then make that build available as gazette on the PATH of the shell that starts your agent. From the Gazette checkout, a source-build example is:
cargo build --locked --release --bin gazette
export PATH="$(pwd -P)/target/release:$PATH"
gazette --help

Keep this shell open and change into the publication folder before starting the agent. If Cargo uses a different target directory, use that build's directory instead. No release installer or public marketplace listing is implied by these instructions.
Claude Code
For a session-only trial, start Claude from the publication folder with the plugin directory in your Gazette checkout:
claude --plugin-dir /path/to/gazette/integrations/agents

For an installed project plugin, add the checkout's local marketplace and select the plugin:
claude plugin marketplace add /path/to/gazette --scope project
claude plugin install gazette@gazette-local --scope project

Start a new Claude session in the publication folder. Check /mcp for the Gazette connection and /plugin for loading errors. The plugin passes explicit discovery and read settings to gazette lsp; an empty initialization request remains unsupported. The directory must contain gazette.toml. Use a separate project scope for unrelated repositories, and resolve any other plugin claiming the same file extensions before relying on feedback.
Ask Claude to check the publication and explain a diagnostic. To exercise language-server feedback, edit a disposable page to reference a missing identity, confirm the reported location and repair it. MCP and LSP currently use separate sessions, so a saved-file check cannot establish what is in an unsaved editor buffer.
Remove an installed project plugin from that publication folder with:
claude plugin uninstall gazette@gazette-local --scope project

Codex
Codex supports the same skill and MCP configuration through its manifest. The checkout's .claude-plugin/marketplace.json uses Codex's supported compatibility layout. With a Codex CLI that provides plugin marketplace and plugin add:
codex plugin marketplace add /path/to/gazette
codex plugin add gazette@gazette-local

Start a new session in the publication folder and confirm that Gazette's skill and MCP tools are available. Ask it to check that publication, then inspect the workspace and diagnostics in the actual result. Codex's manifest does not register Claude's language-server entry; use the MCP tools for Gazette feedback in Codex.
Remove the installed plugin with:
codex plugin remove gazette@gazette-local

These installation and removal commands were checked with Codex CLI 0.169.0-alpha.11.1 and Claude Code 2.1.325. The Codex host check invoked check_workspace on supplied configuration without a model turn; it does not establish automatic skill selection or a complete publication workflow. Installing alongside a manually registered Gazette server can expose two separate sessions; resolve that duplication deliberately when migrating an existing setup.
Integration details
The MCP reference describes tool discovery and operation inputs. Editor discovery covers the language server's source selection, read permission and behavior during configuration repair. The LSP contract describes synchronization and query results. No plugin setting grants build, network or publication permission to those operations.
The host formats are described in Claude's plugin reference and OpenAI's plugin packaging guide. The skill and server settings stay in this directory; the repository-root marketplace only makes that package discoverable.

body:
Write with Gazette in VS Code
Gazette checks the pages and configuration of a publication while you write. It supplies diagnostics, completion, outlines and navigation using the same native program that checks and builds your site.
Connect your publication
Install the VSIX for your host's operating system and architecture through Extensions → Install from VSIX…. For a remote workspace, use the package for the remote host.
Open the folder containing your publication's gazette.toml and trust the folder if you know its contents.
Open gazette.toml or one of its configured pages. Gazette selects the publication's files from its configuration, including sources outside the open folder. The package includes the native program; no separate executable setting is needed.
This extension works with an existing Gazette publication. It does not create a publication, content folder or theme for you.
Write and check
Open Problems to see Gazette's findings and select a finding to reach its source. In a page's frontmatter, invoke Trigger Suggest to see supported fields and publication references. Hover over a supported field or reference for its meaning. Use Outline for page headings and Go to Definition on supported publication references.
A new page beneath a configured content source receives feedback when you open it. Gazette checks unsaved edits too: you can correct a configuration error without restarting the server or losing unsaved article text.
Run commands from the Command Palette. Gazette: Check Saved Site checks saved inputs; save your edits first when you want that check to include them. Gazette: Run Command… lists the native application operations. Review the selected operation's inputs and any confirmation before running it. Editor feedback does not publish your work.
Recover a connection
If startup fails, the notification offers Choose Gazette Program, Open Settings and Show Output. The output explains which program Gazette tried to start and why the connection failed. After correcting the program or settings, run Gazette: Restart Server.
To use another Gazette executable, set Gazette: Server Path to its absolute path in User Settings on the computer or remote host running the extension. It must support native editor discovery. Clear that setting to return to the bundled program.
Folders without the selected configuration stay inactive. For a configuration named differently from gazette.toml, set Gazette: Workspace Configuration to its path relative to the open folder. Leave the fixed file-list settings empty to use automatic discovery. If two open Gazette folders include the same pages, turn off Gazette: Authoring Enabled for the folder that should not supply their editor feedback.
Licence
Gazette is licensed under AGPL-3.0-or-later. The package includes its licence, native program notices and notices for the bundled editor dependencies.

body:
Gazette editor integration
Extend Gazette's VS Code client without duplicating compiler behavior. The extension connects a workspace to the language server, starts application operations through MCP and presents diagnostics, navigation and reviewed edits.
Use the integration guide to load the extension or debug its connection. To edit your publication, follow Write in VS Code.
Build and check
From the repository root:
npm --prefix integrations/vscode ci --ignore-scripts
npm --prefix integrations/vscode run check

check typechecks, compiles and runs the Node tests. npm run build inside this directory compiles the test modules into ignored dist/ and bundles the installed extension into ignored bundle/ with esbuild. The package contains the client bundle, its dependency notices and the language client's process-shutdown helper; test modules and node_modules stay out of the VSIX. Edit src/, never the generated JavaScript. Building does not install Gazette or change editor settings. The source-checkout launch procedure owns the executable selection, separate development window and connection check.
To prepare a local VSIX, first build the Gazette executable for this host, then run the following from this directory after the checks pass. Installed-extension help becomes its details page; this README remains the source contributor's guide. The package includes that executable and the bundled client. Packaging does not publish or install the extension.
npm run package -- --server /absolute/path/to/gazette --out /absolute/path/to/gazette.vsix

The packaging tool checks the program's reported target, builds the client and assembles a temporary package beneath ignored dist/, with the native program in server/. It generates and checks fresh distribution notices in that same directory from the locked source inputs, rather than copying the held source-root inventory. It copies the installed help to that package's README.md, creates a platform-specific VSIX with pinned VSCE, then removes the temporary package. Run it on macOS or Linux, on arm64 or x64, with the matching native build; other targets are not supported by this tool. The offline generator needs the locked Cargo dependencies in the local cache; run cargo fetch --locked from the repository root when preparing a new build environment. The installed extension uses its bundled program when the User setting is empty. A source-checkout development host still needs an explicit User executable setting because no program is retained in the checkout.
Where to change the client
Responsibility	Source	
Activation, selected folders and language-server lifecycle	extension.ts	
Application operation selection and dispatch	applicationCommands.ts	
Folder-bound native MCP transport	applicationSession.ts	
Named application command routes	applicationCommandCatalog.json	
Extension contributions and configuration declarations	package.json	
The route catalog names operations; live native discovery supplies their schemas, effects and lifecycle relationships. Change the native owner when an operation's meaning changes. The client must preserve exact argument/result text and current source/version checks rather than adding its own parser or policy model.
Application operations
The application operation contract owns the picker, guided/advanced requests, confirmation, receipts, canonical follow-up preparation and session retirement. It also explains how an uncertain post-dispatch outcome differs from a refusal before dispatch. Do not recreate those rules in command-specific handlers.
Current editor context
Visible authoring context and sessions and overlays describe source selection, unsaved buffers, recapture and stale-result rejection. Editor context and export owns the read-only MCP handoff and private export. A source-setting change refreshes its authoring composition; it does not retire a separate application session.
Use the native editor features
The editor feature map connects Open Link, definitions/references, symbols, hover, reviewed fixes and page companions to their shared native contracts. The LSP reference defines source precision and protocol results.

Test a client change
Run npm --prefix integrations/vscode run check after changing the client. It type-checks, compiles and runs the Node tests. Test the affected command in an actual VS Code development window too; a simulated client cannot show whether the editor presents the right diagnostic, source or action.
When updating the language client, check diagnostic versions and handler registration order. The native LSP contract defines the source and version checks the extension must preserve.
The installed help and changelog travel with the package. The screenshot below shows the native missing-reference diagnostic and collection completion in the generated Field Notes starter. Its PNG is included in media/, but VS Code's installed Details view does not render relative image links. Adding this image to the installed help therefore awaits an approved public image address. Before public distribution, set the approved repository address and extension icon, check the public help and image links, and qualify each platform package. The changelog marks the current candidate as unreleased until that work and publication are complete.
Gazette checks a new Field Notes page and offers a collection reference in VS Code.
