Private compiler inspection remains available without altering the canonical graph. Selected Atom, RSS and JSON feeds borrow the original typed page projections retained by this same render pass. They do not decode the site JSON to reconstruct dates, links or relationships. The complete site inventory owns their paths, byte limits and collision checks; feed failure cannot yield a successful partial site or authorize publication. Private evidence stays outside the generated tree. It records input origins, configuration and Theme identities, chosen template entries, page-model and HTML digests, static-asset origins keyed by output path and capability compilation receipts keyed by capability. The output inventory covers every emitted byte, including assets, compiled browser modules/stylesheets, aliases and the JSON artifact. No timestamp, stage directory or mutable remote observation is inserted into the output. Public disclosure still requires separate validation. Home share cards A Theme can declare a render.social_card recipe for the publication's selected Home. The card uses that Home's rendered body, its first H1 text (or the existing page title when no H1 is present), and the one media element selected by the recipe. An explicitly configured identity_assets.link_preview takes precedence. A declared recipe still has to resolve its template and resource requirements when capture is skipped. The recipe's resource_requirements names ordinary, independently enabled resources. Select card-only modules and styles with use = "dependency"; they are supplied to the card context without adding them to the normal page's scripts, styles or preload roots. The normal world resources and the same module import map remain available. See Theme recipes and workspace renderer bindings for those declarations. Browser execution requires explicit invocation permission and pinned Node and browser executables. The engine supplies the capture helper; the workspace cannot replace its script, arguments or environment. The helper loads retained resources, keeps the source body inert, inserts only the selected media, waits for the Theme's completion event, and returns a PNG. A video recipe supplies its media kind and optional seek time explicitly. Treatment declared on the selected media or its nearest source ancestor is preserved; no replacement artwork is generated. Pure Rust render APIs do not start a browser. Use render_publications_with_generations or check_and_render_publications_with_generations with explicit SocialCardGenerationOptions when native capture is intended. The checked path runs candidate checks once before compiling the Theme and capturing the card; capture failure never repeats those checks. Local render and preview requests accept social_card_generation for bounded overrides, while --allow-execute grants the generation permission separately from workspace renderer selection. Preview capture uses the URLs of its already held listeners. { "social_card_generation": { "allow_execute": true, "timeout_ms": 30000, "cards": 6 } } This is a local-render request fragment. Preparation and qualification requests retain their complete-object decoding rules. Capture limits separately bound each request, aggregate requests and assets, complete responses, and decoded PNG pixels. The output joins the ordinary site inventory and its collision and disclosure checks; a browser result alone does not establish publication readiness. Native process and capture evidence stays in private render inspection, outside the generated site. Back to local rendering.

Prepare templates and browser resources Choose the Theme templates, resources, capabilities and heading data that the renderer uses. Declare providers and browser resources Capabilities describe typed publication meaning. Providers supply that meaning. Plugins are captured packages that may export providers and independently declare resources. Resource recipes therefore belong to package resource declarations, not to provider declarations or capability selections: package = "search-plugin" [providers.search] implements = ["publication.search/v1"] [resources."module:search"] inputs = ["dep.ts", "main.ts"] build = { kind = "browser-module", entry = "main.ts" } Workspace composition binds the two axes independently: [composition.plugins] "search-plugin" = { state = "enabled" } [composition.capabilities] "publication.search/v1" = { state = "enabled", provider = { kind = "plugin", package = "search-plugin", provider = "search" }, requirement = "optional", allow_absence = "no-native-acquisition" } [composition.resources] "module:search" = { state = "enabled", resource = { owner = { kind = "plugin", package = "search-plugin" }, resource = "module:search" }, output = "/assets/search.js", use = "site" } Plugin activation, capability binding and resource selection are three separate atoms. A provider/resource reference does not activate its package; a package selection does not select any export; and neither capability nor resource proves the other. All three inherit through their own workspace/site maps and retain independent selection origins. Gazette acquires provider results before deterministic compilation, while Tera receives only frozen capability outcomes and compiled logical resources; it never invokes a provider. An output names a file route beneath the configured publication base. Resource inputs are an unordered complete retained set. The recipe entry must belong to that set, and every relative source import must resolve within it. Filenames never select a compiler or establish a capability. The JavaScript adapter uses SWC to parse, erase TypeScript syntax and bundle one ESM entry from captured .js, .mjs and .ts files. Constant propagation and dead-code elimination run before compact emission. The emitter removes formatting whitespace while preserving runtime semantics and selected legal notices (/*!, @license and @preserve); those notices count toward the complete output limit. It does not rename public exports or remove features merely because a first page load does not use them. Oxc checks input and output grammar and lexical/module early errors without retaining another semantic model. This is not type checking, browser execution or a security sandbox. Imports must name exact relative files (./dep.ts, or confined ../dep.ts); there is no extension search, filesystem fallback, package installation or network lookup. Unbound aliases (including @theme, @workspace, @site and @capabilities), npm resolution, asset imports, JSX/TSX, CommonJS and import.meta are unsupported and fail. Import a library from another source Shared libraries are dependency resources, not automatically loaded capabilities: [composition.plugins] "shared-resources" = { state = "enabled" } [composition.resources] "module:shared" = { state = "enabled", resource = { owner = { kind = "plugin", package = "shared-resources" }, resource = "module:shared" }, output = "/assets/modules/shared.js", use = "dependency" } The selected package resource owns its local inputs and browser-module recipe. Its package has an exact source binding. Site declarations replace the complete atom, and { state = "disabled" } blocks inherited imports. Theme and plugin packages remain parallel sources; selection does not imply a directory-based permission hierarchy. An importing site or page resource names only the logical dependency: build = { kind = "browser-module", entry = "main.ts", imports = { "@shared" = "module:shared" } } Source import { value } from '@shared' is linked through the native JavaScript AST to the selected canonical URL. Each reachable shared module is emitted once; local relative dependencies remain bundled, while cross-source ESM identity is preserved instead of inlining a separate stateful copy into every consumer. Unreachable dependency resources are not emitted or given script tags. A literal import('@shared') may use the same declared alias to load a shared module on demand. Computed specifiers, relative or absolute dynamic imports, and import options are rejected. Deferred edges remain in the complete output and verification graph but are excluded from the initial preload closure; a module also reached by a static import remains eager. Missing/disabled bindings, unselected package resources and output collisions fail explicitly. The private render evidence binds module sources, manifests, recipes, dependencies and output bytes. The application also derives one sorted browser-module graph from those exact emitted references. Site JSON receives the complete graph; each page's Theme context receives the standard import map and only that page's eagerly reachable modulepreload closure. Literal aliases appear only when they survived compilation, and one site cannot bind the same alias to two module identities. Theme may inline the map and render preload links, but Gazette never turns either into a module execution script, and emits no standalone preload manifest, guessed priorities or wall-clock timestamps. This is not browser or deployment approval. Compile stylesheets from declared files The styles adapter uses Grass for an explicit .scss, .sass or .css entry and emits its compressed output. Sass loud comments (/*! … */) remain in that output; ordinary source comments do not. Compression preserves significant whitespace in strings and calculations, and the same output-byte and reference checks apply. Variables, mixins, nesting, @use, @forward and supported Sass imports resolve only against captured files. Extensionless and partial-name resolution follows Grass; decoded import literals are first checked with Grass's own AST, not a second Sass grammar. URL syntax, query/fragment/percent-bearing paths, absolute or escaping paths and unsupported explicit suffixes fail instead of being reinterpreted. There are no native load paths, filesystem fallback or network reads. Consumed sources must be valid UTF-8 and valid for the selected grammar. The initial profile rejects dynamic imports and sass:meta, including dynamic load-css; supported deterministic built-in modules include color, list, map, math, selector and string. Declaration-only imported fragments such as color: red; are unsupported by the selected Grass parser. Nested imports of complete rules remain supported; Gazette does not manufacture wrapper rules. Lightning CSS validates emitted CSS without error recovery; it is not another transform or minifier. Parsed URL values, including every quoted or url(...) candidate in image-set and -webkit-image-set, enter the existing resource reference set. The application resolves them against the stylesheet's public output address and requires every target in the final site inventory. External, data, fragment and escaping URLs cannot bypass that same-site closure. Gazette does not select a browser-specific subset or fetch anything while compiling. Native gradients, finite nonnegative resolutions and optional type(...) hints are preserved; hints do not certify an image format or waive a candidate's existence. Nested sets and unresolved resource functions, including image sets in opaque custom-property values, remain unsupported. Unresolved CSS @import, unsupported resource-loading functions, @namespace, @-moz-document and opaque/unknown at-rules fail. @font-face admits the closed retained-WOFF2 and local-only fallback profiles described in page resources; other font-face shapes fail. Random/unique-ID functions cannot produce successful nondeterministic output. Ordinary supported CSS, custom properties and gradients remain available. This bounded profile is not complete CSS compatibility, browser execution or security certification. Resource assembly and Theme context The application checks the compiler's input identity, dependency membership and output bounds before assembly. It compiles once per exact selected package resource. Distinct resources cannot claim one output, even when their bytes happen to match. Generated resources enter the same checked inventory as pages, static assets, aliases and the model artifact; they cannot overwrite any of them. Every page's presentation.capabilities and the site model's capabilities map carry the same typed provider outcomes. They contain no resource URL, recipe or compiled-byte identity. The site model's resources map preserves every selected compiled resource. Each page's ordered presentation.theme_resources contains only the logical resources declared by the effective Theme, joined to the same public facts: logical id, kind, url, literal output, compiled-byte sha256, byte count, checked references and image geometry when applicable. Interfaces add no compiler. Theme can consume its declared resources without deriving URLs or kinds: {% for resource in presentation.theme_resources %} {% if resource.kind == "browser-module" %} {% elif resource.kind == "stylesheet" %} {% endif %} {% endfor %} The Theme requirement does not select a resource, activate a plugin, select a provider or establish ownership. The independently resolved composition must bind and enable every required logical resource before compilation. Private capability evidence retains the owner-qualified provider, selection origin, failure policy and exact provider outcome. Separate resource evidence retains the package/source identity, selection origin, use, manifest/input identities, recipe, reachable dependency hashes, compiler profile and output hash. These facts do not establish authorship, runtime behavior or publication permission. All declared inputs affect private input identity; an unused prerequisite need not alter the compiled program or public output. Resource compilation limits Resource compilation has independent retained-input and emitted-program ceilings. PublicationOutputLimits.resource_metadata_bytes defaults to 4 MiB and charges capability evidence, site resources and page-local resources together, before per-selection receipt/model fanout. The convenience render operation receives it through PublicationRenderLimits.output. Complete-site output limits and template-context limits still apply separately. These are logical budgets, not a bound on SWC's internal AST allocation or CPU time. For styles, Grass returns a complete CSS string before the emitted-byte limit can be checked. Grass's admission/compiler parses and Lightning CSS's validation also allocate intermediate state. Neither that limit nor the captured-source boundary promises bounded intermediate memory, execution time or complete hostile-input panic isolation. Optional capability absence An optional capability may permit exactly the observed allow_absence = "no-native-acquisition" outcome when no admitted provider runtime produced a value. A required capability cannot carry that permission. The shared public outcome is typed unavailable and contains no resource URL. Resource selection and compilation remain independent: missing recipes, inputs, outputs, compiler tools, invalid bytes, compiler failures and exceeded budgets fail the resource path and are never relabeled as capability absence. Page-local script/style selection follows the bounded page-package profile, including its unambiguous top-level entry selection or explicit resource declarations. Arbitrary discovery outside an owned package, richer notebook capabilities and platform-specific browser scheduling remain unsupported. The separate static notebook profile consumes configured attachments. Shared heading model Every Markdown HTML render uses the retained body's single heading allocation. The page's headings array exposes those same source-ordered records: level, text, id, URL-ready fragment, original body-byte span, location precision and parent (the nearest preceding lower-level heading's array index, or null). Skipped heading levels do not manufacture hierarchy nodes. Theme may choose a table-of-contents presentation without reparsing text, allocating IDs or encoding fragments again:
{% for heading in headings %} {{ heading.text }} {% endfor %}
All parser-recognized explicit IDs and emitted footnote/reference IDs reserve names before automatic allocation. Automatic headings use the pinned slug library's ASCII transliteration, then source-ordered -1, -2 collision suffixes; an empty slug uses section. Gazette promises no other implementation's slug algorithm. Explicit IDs remain exact and case-sensitive; fragment encodes them for URL use (café → #caf%C3%A9). Heading text includes text, inline code and image alt text, with spaces for breaks; markup and footnote-reference labels are excluded. Duplicate parser-recognized explicit IDs, whitespace/control-bearing IDs and unsupported heading attributes fail. The native heading-attribute grammar supports #id and .class; arbitrary attributes do not acquire raw-HTML permission. Gazette checks the exact source extent of an attribute block already recognized by the native Markdown adapter and rejects a second ID token at that token's exact byte span; it does not introduce a parallel Markdown or heading-attribute grammar. Footnote labels use injective ASCII aliases, with upstream fn- and fnref- structural prefixes. Percent and Unicode labels are not rejected merely to retain an old adapter workaround. Gazette derives the emitted footnote closure from retained source structure: root references admit reachable definitions recursively, references in image labels and unreachable definitions remain source evidence without creating backlinks, and emitted occurrences receive deterministic source-order ordinals. Raw HTML remains unsupported. These IDs are unique within one Markdown body, not across arbitrary Theme markup. Explicit embedded namespaces are checked against the final emitted IDs before reference callbacks; callers still own distinct namespaces across bodies. This is local structural navigation, not certified public navigation or publication permission. Anchor allocation is lazy, cached and bounded independently from HTML and inspection output; a failure returns no partial heading index or page. The retained presentation manifest names a template directory and package namespace. For example, a root package with namespace root can expose page.html as the qualified virtual entry root/page.html:
{{ body_html | safe }}
body_html already includes the authored heading. See the page-template example for that layout. A root Theme resolves browser chrome colors either directly for its unpaletted selection or on each named palette. Both values are parsed as complete CSS color values during manifest admission; template literals, site/world names, currentcolor and unresolved custom properties are not substitutes: browser_theme_colors = { light = "#ffffff", dark = "oklch(20% 0.02 250)" } palettes = [ { id = "palette:night", browser_theme_colors = { light = "#f8fafc", dark = "#0f172a" } }, ] Choose a template for one page Framed authored input can select an exact entry in the retained virtual Theme namespace, independently of its content family: +++ template = 'root/guides/article.html' [content] # The complete ordinary content declaration follows. +++ Here root is the selected Theme package's declared namespace. Place template at the metadata root, not inside [content]. The effective page entry is selected in this order: The composing site's effective page_templates binding for that exact content identity. The retained source's template value, when present. The selected root Theme's render.page entry. The site inherits the workspace template map when its own map is omitted. An explicit site map replaces the complete workspace map; an empty map clears it. Use per-content presentation selection to configure these bindings without changing the source body. Plain native Markdown has no source template value, but a composition binding for its exact derived content identity still takes precedence over render.page. Gazette does not infer templates from families, filenames or collections. Generated listing continuations reuse their owning index's effective entry. Configured entries are checked against the retained namespace before template compilation. Escaping source selectors fail structural parsing; a missing effective source entry fails rendering without a partial site tree or stage. The Theme's optional render.alias recipe remains separate: an alias requested without that entry fails instead of using the page recipe. The compiler retains the selector and its source coordinates; private render evidence records the actual entry. It is presentation selection, not another content identity or JSON-LD fact. Candidate exclusion removes its selector along with the excluded page. This selection grants no Theme or publication approval. Here body_html comes from Gazette's bounded Markdown renderer, not arbitrary raw input. Theme remains responsible for context-appropriate presentation. The Theme-owned alias entry receives the same model, including the canonical target. Alias and mirror contexts expose the existing target as presentation.redirect_destination, with native identity, site, destination presentation and link kind relative to the actual serving site. The existing route.canonical_url remains the URL; themes need no URL parsing to classify the ordinary anchor. Gazette does not invent redirect markup or claim a template implements an HTTP redirect. Alias-output validity beyond structural/UTF-8 checks still needs Theme and certification evidence. Back to local rendering. The native CLI exposes the per-file resource input ceiling as --max-resource-file-bytes on render-sites, its preview commands and materialize-sites. The equivalent MCP publication input is max_resource_file_bytes, including operations that embed that input. Both default to 256 KiB. Increasing this field leaves the resource aggregate input ceiling, decoder pixel and encoded-byte limits, and emitted-output ceilings unchanged. Set it to the largest input the selected publication needs; an explicit 4 MiB ceiling admits images within the default raster encoded-byte profile.

Public routes
A page’s readable content.slug combines with its publication’s routing rules and editorial placement to give it a public address. The content ID stays stable when the address changes. An explicit route.path handles an address exception; its aliases redirect released old addresses, while the output path tells Gazette where to write the file.
Set the base URL in the brand's publication binding:
[[brands]]
id = "brand:example"
name = "Example"

[[brands.publications]]
site = "site:example" # Must also exist in the workspace's sites table.
public_base_url = "https://example.test/publication/"

Gazette reads the public base here. A brand name, site key, repository remote, source folder or documentation_repository path cannot supply it. The developer documentation output has its own destination.
The resolved route keeps three address roles: url is the record’s serving address; canonical_url is its original’s serving address and may be local in an explicit preview; public_url is the original’s canonical public address from the immutable publication configuration. Public linked-data identities use public_url, while navigation can remain within the selected preview.
Routes from editorial placement
Opt in on the publication binding and name its home by exact content ID:
home = "content:home"
routing = { articles = "/blog/", collections = "/collections/", projects = "/", pages = "/" }

Each prefix must be a directory route. articles serves standalone article pages; collections serves root editorial collections; projects serves project pages and root documentation collections; pages serves other standalone pages. Configure the categories the publication uses. A missing rule fails when a root needs it. The configured home derives / without a slug; its page family remains as authored.
In a page or container’s existing [content] table, declare its own readable component:
slug = "first-step"

A slug is one URL component with the same Unicode, escaping and confinement rules as a full route. It is independent of the content ID, display title, source folder and project name. Gazette does not invent a slug. Once routing is enabled, an unrouted non-home node must provide one.
Every contained node appends its slug to its immediate editorial parent’s resolved directory route. A collection follows its parent collection; a journey follows its containing collection; a leaf follows its sole collection or journey. Thus a root systems, nested collection practice, journey walking and leaf first-step produce /collections/systems/practice/walking/first-step/. Changing the root slug changes all derived descendant addresses while retaining their own slugs and stable IDs. Exact identity links follow the new addresses without rewriting their visible labels.
Containment can cross configured sources bound to the same site: a publication collection can contain a product journey while each body and its media stay in their original bundle. Source paths, About/Mentions/Context edges and browsing links do not determine routes. Invalid or cross-site containment fails before derivation. A file route cannot serve as a derived child’s parent.
A root documentation collection with slug gadget serves its introduction at /gadget/, with a child getting-started at /gadget/getting-started/. Project facts join after these routes exist. Developer documentation keeps its separate configured destination.
Existing explicit routes take precedence and retain their canonical, alias and mirror declarations. A derived node adds no automatic aliases. All explicit and derived routes pass the same canonical, collision, base URL and output checks; generated paths also consume bounded text allowances. Derived values have no fabricated frontmatter span. Without publication routing, a missing route remains unrouted for structural inspection.
Explicit address exceptions
Inside the existing [content] table, add the route:
route = { path = "/guide/", aliases = ["/old-guide.html"], mirrors = [{ site = "site:other", path = "/guide-copy/" }] }

Declaration	Where the reader goes	File within that site's output	
Primary route	https://example.test/publication/guide/	guide/index.html	
Alias	https://example.test/publication/old-guide.html	old-guide.html	
Mirror	The other site's configured base plus /guide-copy/	guide-copy/index.html in the other site's output	
A deployment prefix remains in URLs and does not appear again beneath the output root. / maps to index.html. Use a trailing slash for a directory index. A path without it names a file, even without an extension. Gazette never falls back to a slug from a title or filename.
Use aliases for old addresses on the same site and mirrors for a redirect on another configured site. Both point directly at the canonical URL. A mirror does not move the content, copy the body or grant republishing rights. Missing sites or base URLs, duplicates and collisions fail. A mirror may point at a page whose repository and project placements have separate declarations.
Rendering a mirror needs a configured alias template. Its MirrorModel has content, canonical_site, serving site and url, and route.canonical_url. The mirror also gets the serving site's presentation: Theme, palette, capability outcomes, compiled resources/modules and interaction/search bindings. Gazette uses their configuration rather than deriving those choices from the Theme's identity. Same-site aliases get the full page model. model.json stores mirror values under mirrors, keyed by output path.
A site can render only mirrors. Search, feeds, sitemap, JSON-LD and llms.txt do not list those redirects as pages. Excluding the canonical object also excludes its mirrors. Check the deployed redirect separately from the local render.
Syndicated bodies
If you author a copy on another publication, declare the original by content ID:
route = { path = "/republished-guide/", canonical = "content:original-guide" }

The original must be in the resolved content set, have its own route and name no other canonical target. Missing originals, self-reference and chains (including cycles) fail. A build cannot include a copy and exclude its original. The declaration records the relationship without copying the body, comparing the text or deciding rights.
Value	Where Gazette gets it	
url, output path, relative body links and source	The copy	
canonical_url and the canonical object reference	The original	
Publisher, author, rights holder and lifecycle	The copy's own declarations	
Page metadata and graph records keep the canonical object reference. Article JSON-LD names the original without assigning the copy's breadcrumbs or publisher to it. Search keys and feed links use serving addresses. Sitemaps include originals and omit copies and redirects. A mirror declared on a copy still leads to the original.
Address validation
Gazette encodes safe percent escapes and Unicode consistently in URLs and uses decoded UTF-8 for output names. Case and Unicode normalization stay as written. The schema rejects traversal, repeated or encoded separators, nested escapes, controls, queries and fragments. An HTTP(S) base needs a directory prefix and cannot contain credentials, a query or fragment. The url library normalizes hosts, schemes and default ports, and gives a host without a path /. Gazette does not test whether a provider serves the address.
Gazette checks all declared routes together, including draft and archived objects and container landings. Self-aliases, duplicate aliases, overlapping primary and alias routes, /guide/ versus /guide/index.html, file/directory conflicts and shared public addresses fail. Two sites can use the same relative path when the addresses differ. The output writer separately checks for collisions with emitted files and filesystem case or Unicode aliases.
ResolvedContent::route owns the compiled value. PageProjection::route borrows it, and CompiledTheme::render_page passes it through the shared model. Consume that value instead of reconstructing the canonical URL. Gazette normalizes alias order and keeps source spans and digests. Expanded URLs have their own text limit using the content limit, so repeating a long base across many objects still uses that allowance.
A preview map supplies session-only bases through ResolvedContent::base_url. The route compiler uses them for local addresses without changing the workspace or stable IDs. Templates, assets, resources and feeds use the same bases. Sites outside the preview set keep their original locations. The renderer does not replace URLs independently.
An explicit or derived route needs a configured base. HTML, JSON-LD, graph, navigation, search, feed, sitemap and llms.txt use these compiled routes. Rendering the redirect, writing files and approving release are separate operations. Use the dedicated contracts for external canonical overrides, relocations and symbolic cross-site lookup aliases.
Next
Links and crossings shows how these routes become links within a publication and across publications. Read the generated site files lists the files a build writes at each route.

content.title: Bind machine-bound programs to the machine you build on

body:
Bind machine-bound programs to the machine you build on
A Gazette build can run native programs bound to one machine: math typesetting and policy checks select their command in the workspace. Use the existing machine_binding file to locate each program's executable, working directory and any path arguments on each machine. Gazette resolves these together from the captured configuration before comparing command digests or executing anything.
Declare the command once
The root workspace selects its usual local binding:
machine_binding = 'tools/studio.local.toml'

A checker declaration can then use named roots:
[policy_check]
program = 'machine:python/bin/python3'
directory = 'machine:checker'
arguments = [
  '-B',
  { path = 'machine:checker/check.py' },
  'policy',
  '--project',
  { path = 'machine:documents/Projects/Example' },
]
environment = {}

The selected tools/studio.local.toml supplies those roots alongside its other machine settings:
[roots]
python = '/opt/example/python'
checker = '/srv/workspaces/checker'
documents = '/srv/documents'

A root value can be absolute or relative to the binding file's parent directory. The command never discovers another binding file, searches PATH, expands environment variables or uses the process's current directory. Root names and confined suffixes use the existing source-coordinate rules.
Program, directory and typed argument paths accept three forms: an absolute native path; machine:name with an optional confined suffix; or a workspace-relative path, with . selecting the workspace root. Workspace-relative paths are relative to the selected root workspace, including when the declaration appears in an included module. They are not relative to the command's working directory. Absolute paths retain their existing spelling, including / as a working directory; Gazette does not canonicalize paths or follow links while binding configuration.
String arguments remain literal. For example, 'machine:checker/check.py' is passed exactly as written; { path = 'machine:checker/check.py' } resolves to the native path. Environment values also remain literal. Use typed path arguments only where the program expects a filesystem path.
Use the same binding for math
Math keeps its existing retained resource source and entrypoint. Only its program coordinates need machine bindings:
[math_typesetter]
source = 'source:math-typesetter'
entrypoint = 'render.mjs'
program = 'machine:node/bin/node'
directory = '.'
arguments = []
environment = {}
executable = { bytes = 12345, sha256 = '0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef' }

Add node under the existing binding file's [roots] and replace the illustrative executable length and digest with the selected executable's actual values. The typesetter still requires a pin and receives its entrypoint from captured resources. A checker pin is optional for ordinary local execution and required for independently bound candidate/output checks; see configured policy checks.
Capture, compare and execute
Pure workspace compilation validates declarations without resolving native roots or reading files. Native workspace loading captures the selected binding with the other configuration files. configuration::ResolvedWorkspace::math_command() and policy_command() expose the native commands resolved from those retained bytes. Single-site and multi-site acquired inputs expose that same configuration through configuration().
An absent command returns None. A selected command with an unknown root, no required workspace context, a non-UTF-8 native path or excessive expanded text returns runtime_command_binding when requested. It cannot become an unconfigured checker or a successful check. An unused command's binding error does not prevent inspecting the workspace or using another independently configured command. Detached TOML can still use absolute native commands, but has no machine or workspace-relative context.
Both declarations and expanded native commands enforce the existing limits: at most 256 arguments, 64 environment entries and 64 KiB across program, directory, argument and environment text. Native execution additionally requires absolute program and directory paths and explicit execution permission. Binding does not establish that a file exists, that a program is trusted or that its effects are confined.
The independent policy command_sha256 is the SHA-256 of compact JSON for the bound gazette_core::process::Command, including the absolute program, directory, resolved path arguments, literal arguments, environment and executable pin. Do not hash the portable declaration. Relocating a program may preserve the logical workspace declaration while changing this native command digest; independent expectations must select the new command deliberately. The captured machine file remains configuration evidence. An already acquired build never reopens a changed binding file to replace its command.
Executable pins still cover only the executable file. Scripts, imports, retained policy sources and other inputs keep their own checks. A bound command and successful invocation do not supply publication approval.

body:
Gazette Node API reference
Use this reference when embedding Gazette in a Node application. Start with the complete configuration example to load the addon and interpret a result. The examples below illustrate individual calls; publication recipes, retained trees and journals are inputs supplied by your application, not objects this SDK creates implicitly.
The TypeScript declarations describe the JavaScript types; the Rust SDK defines the JSON request and response shapes. To build the addon, use the package setup.
Find a method
You need to	Methods or contract	
Check configuration and locate its fields	Configuration example: checkWorkspace, fieldOrigin, compositionOrigin	
Use the package from TypeScript	Package contract	
Inspect a page and its supplied companions	inspectPagePackage	
Inspect supplied text	inspectMarkdown, inspectDocument	
Inspect a file from a pinned source tree	inspectMarkdownTree, inspectDocumentTree	
Render publications and obtain their files	renderSites, renderSiteFiles	
Assemble developer documentation	assembleDocumentation	
Review content before rendering	reviewPublication	
Run the configured qualification checks	qualifySites	
Prepare local release output	prepareSites	
Compare served pages with retained output	observeDelivery	
Read recorded release history	inspectReleaseHistory	
Shared input and result conventions
All calls are synchronous. Supply text as Uint8Array bytes (including Node buffers), and queries use the Rust SDK FieldQuery/CompositionOriginQuery JSON contracts. Source spans are half-open UTF-8 byte ranges, not JavaScript UTF-16 string offsets. Configuration calls resolve the complete supplied workspace; no default or inferred field receives an invented origin. Text-inspection calls parse only the supplied Markdown or explicitly framed document.
Inspection results are exact native JSON strings; renderSiteFiles and assembleDocumentation additionally return owned binary payloads as described below. The addon does not turn native integers into JavaScript numbers. Use a lossless JSON reader when needed; ordinary JSON.parse is the caller's numeric-conversion decision. The included TypeScript declarations describe this string boundary, not an independently generated complete workspace schema.
TypeScript package contract
The package exposes native ESM through its import export and explicit declarations through types. It is not a CommonJS-only package: the internal createRequire loads Node's native addon, while consumers use ordinary ESM. There is no separate TypeScript compiler or configuration implementation.
Pass complete workspace TOML to this function. The configuration example shows a minimal valid workspace and how to interpret its result.
import { loadGazette, type NativeJson, type ProjectionLimits } from '@rtepl/gazette';

const gazette = loadGazette('/absolute/local/gazette.node');
export function checkConfiguration(sourceToml: string): NativeJson {
  const source: Uint8Array = new TextEncoder().encode(sourceToml);
  const limits = { sourceBytes: source.byteLength } satisfies ProjectionLimits;
  return gazette.checkWorkspace(source, limits);
}

Gazette declares the frozen function properties as readonly. NativeJson is a string alias, not proof that an arbitrary caller-created string passed native validation. Query strings still use the Rust query grammar; declarations do not pretend to validate their embedded JSON or expose a second typed workspace model. Safe-integer, UTF-8 and semantic checks remain native runtime responsibilities. No ambient Node types are required to consume these declarations: the public boundary uses standard strings, numbers and Uint8Array. Consumers choose their own host declarations for APIs such as TextEncoder or Node buffers.
Supplied page-package inspection
inspectPagePackage(request, options?) projects the Rust SDK authoring session's existing PagePackageOwnership result from caller-supplied workspace, document and companion bytes. It performs no filesystem discovery or source acquisition and does not independently resolve resources.
const pagePackage: NativeJson = gazette.inspectPagePackage({
  workspace: new TextEncoder().encode(workspaceToml),
  documents: [{ path: 'guide/index.md', bytes: framedDocument }],
  companions: [{ path: 'guide/image.png', bytes: imageBytes }],
  query: 'guide/index.md',
});

The result is the exact native optional ownership JSON: a matched authored page contains the application-owned source, content, resolved resources and package digest fields, while a standalone document serializes as null. Paths and bytes are explicit inputs; the JavaScript layer neither probes the live filesystem nor adds a compatibility resolver. Duplicate or invalid supplied paths and native authoring failures throw bounded {code} errors.
selectionEntries, identifierBytes, sourceBytes and resultBytes are independent safe-integer ceilings. The defaults are 4,096 entries, 16 KiB per identifier, 16 MiB across workspace/document/companion bytes and 1 MiB for the serialized result. The operation is synchronous and retains no session handle.
Workspace failures throw an Error whose message is the serialized shared Rust SDK workspace::Failure (code, explanation and available diagnostics/span). Treat these as private: they can contain supplied identifiers. Host failures use node_limits, node_source_utf8, node_query, node_query_limit, node_input_limit, node_result_limit or node_encoding. Host type-conversion failures are ordinary Node-API errors and need not have JSON messages.
Optional ProjectionLimits preserve native TOML defaults when omitted. Query JSON defaults to 16 KiB and serialized results/failures to 1 MiB. Numeric options must be nonnegative safe integers. Source bytes are bounded before copying and parsing; query bytes before JSON decoding; the shared Rust writer bounds each serialized write before buffering. These are logical per-call limits, not an OS memory/CPU sandbox. Calls are synchronous and introduce no unbounded worker queue.
Supplied Markdown and framed documents
inspectMarkdown(bytes, options?) returns the shared Rust SDK's {inspection, html?} JSON. inspectDocument(bytes, options?) returns {document, html?} and requires explicit +++ TOML delimiter lines. These are separate entrypoints: neither filenames nor source contents select a different parser implicitly. The SDK parses once and returns the complete requested report.
const markdown: NativeJson = gazette.inspectMarkdown(source, {
  html: true,
  limits: { sourceBytes: source.byteLength, factBytes: 1_048_576 },
  resultBytes: 1_048_576,
});
const framed: NativeJson = gazette.inspectDocument(framedSource, {
  html: true,
  sourceBytes: framedSource.byteLength,
  metadata: { sourceBytes: 65_536 },
  markdown: { outputBytes: 1_048_576 },
});

MarkdownLimits exposes the native sourceBytes, nodes, depth, factBytes and outputBytes ceilings. Document options separately expose the complete sourceBytes, TOML metadata byte/node/depth ceilings and markdown body limits. Every omitted field uses its native SDK default. resultBytes independently bounds complete serialized results and defaults to 1 MiB; logical projection bounds are not interchangeable with serialized JSON length.
Exact UTF-8 bytes are checked before copying and parsed without newline or BOM normalization. Markdown ranges are body-relative; a document also reports the body's full-source span. The addon does not turn these into UTF-16 coordinates. Optional HTML uses the SDK's existing safety rules. Raw HTML, unsafe URLs, framing or any other requested-projection failure throws without a partial inspection. No themes, source acquisition, publication rendering or release are implied.
These two operations expose native failures as redacted JSON {code} messages; they do not echo private source, metadata or provider diagnostics. Pre-copy source ceilings retain markdown_limit or document_limit. Invalid UTF-8 and invalid numeric/result bounds use the existing host classes. Successful inspection itself deliberately contains supplied source-derived text and must still be treated as private data.
Explicit pinned-tree inspection
inspectMarkdownTree(treeJson, permission, options?) and inspectDocumentTree(treeJson, permission, options?) expose the same native complete-tree acquisition as CLI/MCP inspection. They do not replace the supplied-byte operations or infer framing from a filename.
treeJson is the exact Rust markdown::input::Tree selection: absolute root, independent complete-tree identity, confined regular-file document, and optional native limits. No pin is inferred from the selected page. All entries, including hidden/companion assets, participate in acquisition and pin verification before parsing the retained document. No fallback, directory scan outside the selected root, or second file read occurs.
const inspected = gazette.inspectMarkdownTree(exactTreeJson, {
  allowRead: true,
  queryBytes: 16_384,
}, { html: true, resultBytes: 1_048_576 });

TreeOptions.allowRead is mandatory; false refuses native access. queryBytes defaults to 16 KiB and bounds selection JSON before decoding. Duplicate fields, positional/null native maps, unknown fields, relative roots and escaping document paths are rejected. Capture ceilings in treeJson.limits, parser/HTML ceilings in the existing MarkdownOptions or DocumentOptions, and complete serialized resultBytes remain independent. Tree identity and native integer lexemes cross as exact JSON, not a second JavaScript schema.
Success adds the shared input: {identity, document} evidence to the existing inspection/document report. Omitted HTML stays omitted. Errors expose bounded native {code} classifications; permission refusal is markdown_read_permission. Read access and matching bytes are not publication approval. Calls are synchronous and return no retained handle; previously returned JSON remains original evidence, while another call must acquire and validate its inputs again.
Private local publication rendering
renderSites(recipeBytes, options) consumes the Rust SDK's exact LocalPublicationRecipe JSON (gazette-local-publication-set/1), including the complete workspace TOML and explicitly selected site render choices. This is the same recipe as CLI local rendering and MCP render_sites, not another workspace schema. Both local: true and allowRead: true are required before acquisition.
Optional recipe math_generation and diagram_generation each separately permit and bound their configured native generator using allow_execute. Omitting either performs no corresponding acquisition. Native commands are not sandboxed; their effects are not covered by source-read permission and a failed or interrupted invocation must not be blindly retried. Rendering consumes the retained results without invoking the command.
const report: NativeJson = gazette.renderSites(recipeBytes, {
  local: true,
  allowRead: true,
  inputBytes: recipeBytes.byteLength,
  resultBytes: 8 * 1024 * 1024,
  limitsJson: '{"acquisition":{"sites":2},"output":{"total_bytes":1048576},"max_total_output_bytes":2097152}',
});

inputBytes defaults to the native TOML source-byte ceiling; limitsBytes defaults to 16 KiB; resultBytes defaults to 1 MiB. These safe-integer host ceilings are independent. Recipe bytes are checked before native decoding. limitsJson is a bounded, duplicate-safe named JSON object. Its optional fields compose existing Rust types without coercing their integers through JavaScript:
Field	Native owner	
syntax	toml::Limits	
acquisition	build::PublicationSetAcquisitionLimits	
output	source::Limits, applied per site	
max_total_output_bytes	build::PublicationSetRenderLimits::bytes	
max_total_output_entries	build::PublicationSetRenderLimits::entries	
Omitted fields retain native defaults. Unknown fields, positional objects, null objects, duplicate keys and invalid native integers are rejected before source reads. Nested acquisition.sources, when supplied, requires the native PreparationLimits fields; it is not a partial patch or an override language.
The Rust SDK captures the exact pinned sources once and renders the whole set through its shared model, resource compilers and Theme. Success returns the full PublicationSetInspection. A failed sibling throws that same complete inspection as Error.message, preserving every success and failure; it never becomes a smaller successful set. Earlier native failures expose only {code}. Complete reports are private and can contain source paths, authored text and diagnostics. Result exhaustion throws node_result_limit, never a truncated JSON report.
This operation returns evidence, not generated file bytes or a persistent handle. Its retained inputs and outputs are released after serialization. It performs no staging, policy subprocess, preview listening, database access, signing, network publication or certification. Synchronous native limits bound logical work, not wall-clock execution; callers must not mistake this for a cancellable worker.
Deliver generated files to JavaScript
renderSiteFiles(recipeBytes, options) uses the same permissions, recipe, acquisition, compiler and complete-set checks as renderSites. It returns { report, sites: [{ site, files: [{ path, bytes }] }] }. report is the same exact native inspection JSON string. Each bytes value is an owned Uint8Array, including for binary assets; no text decoding or Base64 transport is imposed. Site identities and paths follow native deterministic order. Directory entries remain in the report inventory and do not receive fabricated file payloads.
Native max_total_output_bytes and max_total_output_entries bound the complete generated set before delivery; resultBytes independently bounds report JSON. An incomplete site set throws its full inspection before any file delivery, never returns only the healthy sites. Changed returned buffers cannot alter source trees or later calls. The result itself is not deep-frozen, a filesystem stage, a persistent native handle, a certified release, or permission to publish. Both methods share one native render invocation per call; neither reruns the compiler to fetch files or uses CLI/MCP as an internal bridge.
Documentation repository assembly
assembleDocumentation(workspaceBytes, site, options) returns Mintlify build files assembled from the selected site's repository manuals and imported or generated API reference. Supply complete workspace TOML as bytes and its declared site key.
The workspace selects each project's manual pages, companions, reference inputs and navigation. Gazette captures the selected source trees; only the selected pages and artifacts enter the output. Ordinary publication and Theme sources are not required by this operation. See Mintlify integration for the build flow and input formats for compatibility and selection rules.
const documentation = gazette.assembleDocumentation(workspaceBytes, 'site:example', {
  local: true,
  allowRead: true,
  limitsJson: '{"output":{"total_bytes":1048576}}',
});
const report: NativeJson = documentation.report;
const files = documentation.files; // PublicationFile[] with owned Uint8Array bytes

Both permission fields are required. inputBytes bounds workspace bytes before UTF-8 decoding (native TOML source-byte default); limitsBytes bounds the exact limits JSON, optional generationJson and optional previewLinkBasesJson individually (16 KiB default); resultBytes independently bounds the complete report (1 MiB default). Host ceilings must be nonnegative safe integers. Native limitsJson composes syntax: toml::Limits, acquisition: source::PreparationLimits and output: source::Limits. Omitted sections use existing SDK defaults; acquisition uses the documentation pipeline's publication-acquisition source defaults. A supplied acquisition object uses its native required fields, not a partial patch. Duplicate keys, positional/null maps and unknown fields are rejected before acquisition. Native integer values remain exact JSON, not JavaScript numbers.
For private preview links to product help, previewLinkBasesJson supplies the shared public-base to literal-loopback-base map as a JSON object. Malformed or non-object JSON refuses with node_query; the native routing contract validates the selected bases. The local preview-link contract owns its path-preservation rules and private-output limits. Omit the map when assembling ordinary public destinations.
The result is {report, files}. report is the existing Rust build::documentation_output::Report serialized without a competing schema: exact captured input/configuration evidence, brand-selected repository, separate manual page/companion evidence, reference artifacts and the complete target inventory. directory is null because the assembled target is not staged. jobs is empty when no generators run. File payloads reuse PublicationFile, in native path order; directories remain in the report. The target's complete output limits apply before any file delivery. Returned buffers cannot mutate native sources or later results. Binary-safe delivery does not imply the selected target accepts arbitrary binary companions.
Any failed required manual or reference input rejects the entire operation. Before effects and when no generator runs, native failures expose bounded {code} messages; permission refusal is documentation_permission, invalid site spelling is documentation_site, and transport errors retain the existing node_* classes. Configured native-generator inputs retain the SDK's documentation_generation_required classification when generation is unselected; there is no automatic execution or substitution of imported bytes.
To run the workspace's configured generators, additionally select allowStage:true and a strict named generationJson request:
const generated = gazette.assembleDocumentation(workspaceBytes, 'site:example', {
  local: true, allowRead: true, allowStage: true,
  generationJson: '{"parent":"/absolute/existing/private-jobs","max_jobs":2,"directory_bytes":256,"entry_bytes":64,"allow_execute":true}',
});

The existing absolute parent contains fresh input/output stages, rather than the documentation repository's final destination. Three required fields bound the generated jobs and their path names:
Field	What it limits	
max_jobs	Number of configured generated-reference jobs across the entire selected documentation navigation, from 0 through 128. Imported references and manual pages do not count. Zero is valid only when no generated jobs are selected. This is not a concurrency limit or a count of subprocess calls.	
directory_bytes	Maximum native byte length of each full canonical stage path, from 1 through 1,048,576. It includes the parent, separator and generated .gazette-stage- name with 32 hexadecimal digits. Unix OS bytes are measured before directory creation.	
entry_bytes	Maximum UTF-8 byte length of each selected output file or subdirectory's relative path, from 1 through 1,048,576. Selecting the capture-root directory supplies no relative path. This does not limit artifact contents or count entries.	
Source file sizes, inventory counts and other content limits remain separate. Optional input uses native source::Limits; timeout_ms defaults to 30,000 (1–300,000), and max_capture_bytes to 1 MiB (at most 64 MiB). allow_execute independently defaults false. allowStage alone never permits commands. The configured recipe owns executable pins, arguments, artifact selection and format; the JS request does not introduce a generator schema. Native commands are not sandboxed and can perform their configured effects.
The Rust SDK reserves complete custody response capacity before acquisition or stage creation, executes the selected jobs once, then assembles their retained artifacts through the same target adapter. All files are delivered together, with actual jobs in the native report. A later generator or assembly failure, or full-report overflow, rejects with the SDK's compact original custody JSON, not a bare code or successful subset. Inspect completed jobs, failure evidence and exact Unix stage-path bytes; do not automatically retry, clean up or infer rollback. If the native operation violates its reserved delivery bounds, Error.message contains JSON with code: "documentation_delivery_contract" and a custody debug string describing the jobs and stages. That string is diagnostic text, not a stable JSON schema, and this exceptional response can exceed resultBytes. A missing native file payload instead throws node_output_contract. Keep the original request and the complete error; inspect the reported stages and completed jobs before retrying or deleting anything. Host termination or allocation failure can prevent any JavaScript response, even after a generator has run or a stage has been created.
No final-target staging, database, signing, provider publication or public admission is performed. The configured destination is not created or replaced. Generator execution evidence alone does not qualify language fidelity or hosted compatibility.
Private publication review
reviewPublication(workspaceBytes, site, options) returns the Rust SDK's complete build::PublicationReview as exact JSON. It uses the shared native acquisition, corpus parsing, graph resolution and review owners without calling the CLI or MCP. Workspace bytes are TOML and site is the exact configured acquisition site; neither is an ambient path or inferred selection.
Important

This Node method does not accept retained typesetting results. If the publication contains mathematics that needs those results, use the Rust retained-math API or the CLI/MCP review path. Review does not run a typesetter; allowRead cannot enable one.
const review: NativeJson = gazette.reviewPublication(workspaceBytes, 'site:example', {
  allowRead: true,
  resultBytes: 8 * 1024 * 1024,
  limitsJson: '{"review":{"uses":100000}}',
});

allowRead is mandatory. Native sources are captured once and parsed/resolved through their existing owners. The full private review preserves source evidence, drafts, nested uses, assets, composition and uncompiled obligations. Native Markdown/notebook/raster projection runs; Theme/resource programs, policy processes, staging, databases, signing and network publication do not. Review identity is not approval, certification, permission to publish or a retained handle.
inputBytes bounds workspace bytes before UTF-8 decoding (native TOML source-byte default), limitsBytes bounds limits JSON (16 KiB default), and resultBytes independently bounds the complete JSON result (1 MiB default). Host ceilings are nonnegative safe integers. limitsJson composes existing Rust types: syntax: toml::Limits, acquisition: source::PreparationLimits, corpus: corpus::Limits, graph: publication::content::Limits, and review: build::ReviewLimits. Omitted sections use native defaults; acquisition uses the publication pipeline's source defaults. Its supplied object requires the native fields, not a partial override. Duplicate keys, unknown fields and positional/null objects at every nested limits boundary fail before acquisition. Native integer lexemes remain exact JSON rather than JavaScript numbers.
Any acquisition, corpus, graph or review failure throws a bounded native {code} message with no successful subset. Permission refusal is publication_permission; invalid site spelling is publication_site. Host failures retain existing node_* classes, including node_result_limit rather than truncated JSON. Successful review contains private source-derived values and must not be treated as a public-safe report.
Complete-set technical qualification
qualifySites(recipeBytes, { allowRead: true, allowPolicyExecution: true }) passes the exact QualificationRecipe JSON bytes to the Rust SDK operation used by CLI qualify-sites and MCP qualify_sites. The same captured candidates, selected native policy checks, rendering and output qualification produce the complete QualificationReport. Read permission is required independently of checker permission; omitted checker permission denies execution. Explicit native math/diagram generation requests retain their own permissions. Math executes its exact retained provider tree. Graphviz uses Gazette's file-free DOT profile, fixed arguments, empty environment and a verified disposable working directory; its ambient native libraries, plugins and fonts are still not a sandboxed or portable provider identity.
Only a complete technically qualified site set returns normally. Every other native outcome throws its complete JSON report, retaining all requested sites, including failed and not-run members. Neither qualification nor a certificate grants publisher approval, preparation, signing or deployment authority. This operation creates no Gazette output stage, store or Git preparation.
inputBytes and resultBytes default to 4 MiB; native acquisition, checker, rendering and evidence limits remain independent. A bounded failure envelope is reserved before execution. If the complete report cannot be delivered, the error has code qualification_response_unavailable and the SHA-256 of the exact input recipe bytes. Configured programs may already have run: retain the original request and inspect native outcomes, never infer rollback or retry permission. If even that envelope cannot fit, execution does not start. Catastrophic host failure, cancellation or lost transport cannot guarantee delivery of any report.
Complete local preparation
prepareSites(recipeBytes, options) consumes the Rust SDK's existing LocalPreparationRecipe JSON. It captures and renders the selected site set, then performs explicitly permitted fresh staging, durable preparation and local Git worktree initialization through that same native operation. It does not initialize a journal, acquire publisher authorization, sign, push or deploy. The exact existing journal must be initialized separately with its own permission.
const report: NativeJson = gazette.prepareSites(recipeBytes, {
  local: true, allowRead: true,
  createStage: true, recordPreparation: true,
  advanceWriterGeneration: true, reserveLocalCoordination: true,
  initializeWorktree: true,
  limitsJson: '{"read":{"allow_coordination_files":true}}',
  resultBytes: 8 * 1024 * 1024,
});

local and allowRead are required. Every optional effect flag defaults denied: createStage, recordPreparation, advanceWriterGeneration, reserveLocalCoordination, writeCoordinatorAnchor, initializeWorktree and allowPolicyExecution. They map to the native staging, record, writer/session, anchor, worktree and policy permissions, respectively. Coordination-file effects remain separately explicit in limitsJson.read.allow_coordination_files. The recipe's selected math execution uses its existing separate permission. Configured subprocesses are not sandboxed by this addon; native source-read or local-preparation acknowledgement does not authorize arbitrary subprocess effects.
inputBytes, limitsBytes and resultBytes retain the other publication methods' independent safe-integer defaults. limitsJson composes native syntax, acquisition, output and read types as duplicate-safe named JSON. Omitted fields retain native defaults; supplied nested acquisition values use their native required fields. output feeds both rendering and staging. Limits cannot override the top-level permission flags. Other native operation bounds retain their defaults; this is not a second recipe or configuration language.
Success returns the exact complete native report. Native failure throws that complete report in Error.message, including any completed prefix, failed stage, journal generation, checker or Git custody. The shared Rust delivery owner reserves the complete original reconciliation coordinates before execution. If the final native report cannot fit resultBytes, the error carries that reserved reconciliation-required envelope: original journal, expected header, coordinator selection and ordered site/preparation IDs. These are not current observations. A budget too small for the fallback throws node_result_limit before any native execution. No truncated report or smaller successful site set is returned, and no operation is automatically retried.
Keep the original request coordinates independently. Host termination, allocation failure or loss after return cannot establish rollback. Inspect native history before deciding further work. Preparation evidence remains private and is not publication approval, certification or a release receipt.
Observe served output
observeDelivery(requestBytes, { inputBytes, resultBytes }) consumes the exact Rust delivery::Request JSON used by CLI observe-delivery and MCP observe_delivery. The optional JavaScript options contain transport bounds only; both default to 1 MiB. The native request selects the existing retained output root and independent tree identity, exact routes/base URL, pinned curl, native limits and each options.http permission (allow_read, allow_execute, allow_network). No permission is implied by addon loading, a loopback address or a transport bound.
Every selected route is observed once. A complete match returns the native delivery::Report JSON string; differences, HTTP failures and unavailable responses throw that same complete report with no dropped routes. Whole-request refusals retain native stable error codes. Response body contents are not returned. These observations neither rebuild output nor establish publisher approval, unselected-route correctness, provider readiness or release settlement.
A request-bound delivery_response_unavailable envelope is reserved before effects. If the complete result exceeds its bound, HTTP requests may already have occurred; preserve the original request and do not infer rollback or retry safety. An envelope that cannot fit prevents native observation. No transport envelope guarantees delivery through catastrophic host failure or cancellation.
Immutable release-history inspection
inspectReleaseHistory(requestBytes, {allowRead:true}) exposes the Rust SDK's five existing history readers through one closed selector: authorization, leases, consumption, attempts or reconciliations in kind. The exact JSON request also contains absolute database, record_id, optional expected_header (the native store::JournalHeader, or null), and optional read (native store::ReadOptions). Native defaults apply; coordination-file permission must be explicitly enabled with read.allow_coordination_files. No request automatically selects the latest record, opens a writer or repairs a database.
HistoryOptions.inputBytes defaults to 16 KiB; resultBytes defaults to 1 MiB. Duplicate keys, unknown fields and positional maps are refused. Decode original request bytes without rounding native journal coordinates through JavaScript numbers. Results remain complete native JSON strings, including absent-record evidence; expected-header mismatch and native storage failures throw {code}.
Before reading, the operation reserves a bounded history_response_unavailable envelope with the exact request digest. If the complete report cannot be delivered, that envelope reports possible read/coordination-file effects, not partial history or success. Too little room even for the envelope prevents the read. Observation does not renew expired approval, consume authorization, resample a destination, retry delivery, settle a release or prove anti-rollback.

Gazette JavaScript and TypeScript SDK
Call Gazette directly from a Node application. Your code supplies configuration or publication inputs; the native addon uses the same Rust engine as the CLI, agent server and editor. It returns native JSON and, for generated files, binary buffers.
The browser entrypoints provide search, analytics and public reader tools without loading the addon. If you want to use Gazette rather than embed it, start with your first publication.
Build and load the local addon
The package is currently private source, not a published npm package with a prebuilt binary. You need Node 22 or later and the Gazette source-build prerequisites.
Build the addon
From the Gazette repository root:
cargo build --locked -p gazette-node

Package it for Node
Cargo produces target/debug/libgazette_node.dylib on macOS or target/debug/libgazette_node.so on Linux when using its default target directory. If you selected a different Cargo target directory or target triple, use that build's actual library path. The JavaScript loader requires a .node file at an absolute path. Copy the library to a new .node file using the repository helper:
node sdk/js/tools/package-addon.mjs /absolute/build/libgazette_node.dylib /absolute/local/gazette.node

node sdk/js/tools/package-addon.mjs /absolute/build/libgazette_node.so /absolute/local/gazette.node

Use the absolute paths to your build and a new destination file.
The helper copies without rewriting the library and checks the input/output SHA-256. It refuses an existing destination. If it fails after creating a file, inspect that file before choosing another destination; it never removes your files automatically. The SDK does not install an addon or select a Node runtime.
Check a configuration and locate a field
Suppose your application lets an author edit publication configuration. It needs to reject an unknown publisher and point to the exact declaration being inspected. This example supplies a complete small workspace, validates it, locates a field in the original bytes, then demonstrates a semantic error. These calls inspect only the supplied text; they do not open source directories, render a page or publish.
Save the following as sdk-example.mjs in the Gazette repository root. The relative import uses this checkout's loader; it does not install a package.
import { loadGazette } from './sdk/js/index.mjs';

const gazette = loadGazette(process.argv[2]);
const sourceToml = `[[principals]]
id = 'owner:example'
kind = 'person'

[[sites]]
id = 'site:example'
publisher = 'owner:example'
deployable = false
`;
const bytes = new TextEncoder().encode(sourceToml);
const compilationJson = gazette.checkWorkspace(bytes);
console.log('Workspace valid');

const origin = JSON.parse(gazette.fieldOrigin(bytes, JSON.stringify({
  kind: 'site', identity: 'site:example', field: ['deployable'],
})));
console.log('Deployable literal:', new TextDecoder().decode(
  bytes.subarray(origin.span.start, origin.span.end),
));

try {
  gazette.checkWorkspace(new TextEncoder().encode(
    sourceToml.replace("publisher = 'owner:example'", "publisher = 'owner:missing'"),
  ));
  throw new Error('Expected invalid publisher to fail');
} catch (error) {
  const failure = JSON.parse(error.message);
  console.log('Invalid publisher:', failure.code);
}

Run it with your packaged addon:
node sdk-example.mjs /absolute/local/gazette.node

The output is:
Workspace valid
Deployable literal: false
Invalid publisher: workspace_invalid

compilationJson is the complete resolved workspace as a JSON string, including its source digest. A failed compilation throws a native failure instead of returning a partially resolved workspace. The field query identifies a site and an explicit field; its half-open span addresses UTF-8 bytes in the supplied text. Decode those bytes as shown rather than using those offsets to slice a JavaScript string, whose positions use UTF-16.
The example parses the small origin/failure records, whose offsets fit safely within its supplied input. Native responses can contain integers beyond JavaScript precision. Preserve the original JSON and use a lossless reader where those values matter. Configuration diagnostics can contain your supplied identifiers; keep private inputs and their diagnostics out of public logs.
If loading fails, check that the argument is an absolute .node path, that the library was built for your operating system and architecture, and that the loader and addon come from the same checkout. An older addon can lack an operation required by the current loader. Invalid TOML reports toml_invalid; an unresolved publisher reports workspace_invalid. Correct the input and call the pure checker again. For effectful rendering/preparation calls, follow their own failure and recovery contracts rather than applying that retry pattern.
Continue with the operation you need
Integration task	Reference	
Inspect configuration, field origins, Markdown or page packages	Node API reference	
Render a selected publication and receive HTML/assets as buffers	Rendering and file delivery	
Assemble developer manuals and generated references	Documentation assembly	
Review, qualify or prepare publication output	Node operation contracts	
Compare served output or inspect immutable release history	Delivery, history	
Integrate browser search, analytics or WebMCP	Browser SDK integration	
The TypeScript declarations describe the ESM exports, readonly methods, options and return types. NativeJson is a string boundary, not a second workspace schema. The detailed reference explains synchronous calls, independent input/result limits, permissions and native failures. The SDK currently has no standalone store administration, release dispatch, persistent parsed handles, Wasm interface or distributed native-binary installation.
Run the SDK tests
The native-addon tests compare what the addon returns with an independent Rust SDK read of the same input, so a passing run describes the addon and Rust bytes it was built from; rebuild before running them after any change. The addon crate denies handwritten unsafe code; napi-rs's generated registration can emit its own local allowance, and the rest of the workspace keeps its unsafe-code prohibition.
Build the addon and the Rust reference examples, then package the addon as described above:
cargo build --locked -p gazette-node --lib --examples
node sdk/js/tools/package-addon.mjs target/debug/libgazette_node.dylib /absolute/local/gazette.node

Each test takes the packaged addon's absolute path. publication.mjs, inspection_tree.mjs, history.mjs, documentation.mjs and preparation.mjs also take the matching Rust example from target/debug/examples/ (publication_reference, inspection_reference, history_reference, documentation_reference and preparation_reference):
node sdk/js/tests/history.mjs /absolute/local/gazette.node target/debug/examples/history_reference

native.mjs and typescript.mjs read the workspace_reference example's JSON on standard input. typescript.mjs also takes the absolute path of a TypeScript compiler script. It copies only the declared package payload into a fresh isolated consumer and compiles it with strict NodeNext resolution, skipLibCheck: false, no ambient types and noEmitOnError; the consumer then runs the supplied-source operations and compares complete values with the Rust reference, and compile-time negative cases check wrong types, unsupported methods and readonly methods. Withholding the declarations must make compilation fail.
target/debug/examples/workspace_reference > /absolute/local/workspace-reference.json

cargo test --locked -p gazette-launcher --test publication_render js_qualification:: -- --ignored --test-threads=1

The browser modules need no addon: node --test sdk/js/tests/search.mjs sdk/js/tests/search-browse.mjs sdk/js/tests/analytics.mjs sdk/js/tests/webmcp.mjs, with GAZETTE_TEST_TYPESCRIPT naming a typescript.js for the declaration checks. The portable workflow, .github/workflows/portable.yml, runs all of these.

Store
Gazette uses a SQLite journal for the workspace registry and release history. The registry lists sites, projects, pages, routes and relationships and can be rebuilt from the workspace. Release history is append-only. Keep its preparations, approvals, attempts, observations and settlements. The site cache sits beside the journal and can be deleted. It is keyed by the inputs that can change the rendered bytes.
Creating a journal
gazette initialize-store --help

Run initialize-store against an empty private directory. It refuses to overwrite, import or upgrade an existing database. Inspection, backup, verification and restore also refuse an unsupported version, altered schema or foreign tables.
The current schema is version 6. A new journal applies 0001-journal.sql, 0002-collection-purpose.sql, 0003-collection-navigation.sql, 0004-project-lifecycle.sql, 0005-collection-order.sql and 0006-project-subject.sql. The registry stores a collection's optional purpose, authored navigation and member order separately from its page families and containment, and accepts the five project states: planned, active, paused, done and closed. Project kind and public entity identity have separate optional columns. This executable refuses journals from versions 1 through 5. There is no in-place upgrade or automatic reclassification of old project records. Keep the old journal and its backups when you change executable versions.
For release work, run gazette enroll-local-coordinator before the first write. It keeps an anchor outside the journal with the state expected after each committed change. This detects a journal restored on its own after an accident or crash. Someone who controls both files can change both.
The writer and the journal header
A single writer holds the journal at a known generation. A write request supplies the expected header, {schema_version, journal_id, journal_epoch, writer_fence}. If it differs, Gazette refuses the write. Acquiring a writer advances the generation even if the following operation fails.
gazette acquire-writer, gazette release-session and gazette recovery-session hold a writer. gazette inspect-journal and gazette inspect-store run read-only SQL and acquire no writer generation. SQLite WAL and shared-memory coordination files can still require maintenance, which has its own permission.
The registry
gazette reconcile-registry replaces all workspace rows in one transaction and reads them back. Removing a declaration removes its rows. The chosen publication identifies which source bytes to read. The registry still includes configured foreign sites and disabled or unused declarations. Use gazette inspect-registry to check all rows without writing.
Rebuildable means the retained workspace inputs can supply the registry again; it does not promise that the whole rebuild is atomic or succeeds in one pass. Gazette prepares the complete model, acquires a writer, replaces the rows and closes the writer in separate stages. The row replacement is atomic, but a later failure does not undo an acquired writer generation or an already verified replacement. Inspect the reported stage and store state before retrying.
The registry includes each project’s repository address and declared origin (original, successor-fork or convenience-mirror with an upstream), its single primary placement and any mirror placements, plus routes, aliases and redirects served for other sites. See the content model for their meanings.
Principal websites and ordered same_as references have their own rows. A change to either changes the desired registry identity. A site website keeps its declared site reference, while an external website keeps its explicit URL. Neither proves identity or supplies a contact address. The current schema creates these tables only for a new journal.
Backing up
gazette backup-store --help
gazette verify-backup --help

Choose a fresh backup directory
Declare the authored, staging, generated and live journal roots. Gazette checks that the new directory is outside them.
