Supported contexts and strict-versus-tolerant analysis follow the shared LSP contract. The editor applies a user-selected proposal to its buffer and sends the changed source through ordinary native reanalysis. This protects the implemented workspace identity queries, document-local heading and footnote navigation, and selected cross-document definition/reference results. Every returned selected sibling is rebound to the exact open document, version and text observed at request time before the result is admitted. General repository-wide navigation, rename and automatic source writes remain outside this contract.
Changing source settings restarts affected compositions. Folder addition and removal invalidate compositions that depend on those roots, including nested ownership changes. Shared physical-file custody prevents two compositions from claiming the same selected file. Restart requests coalesce. Each session retains custody of a client whose stop failed; no replacement is admitted for that folder while cleanup is uncertain. Startup failure attempts cleanup, and shutdown attempts every folder even if one fails. Transport errors do not trigger automatic restart loops. Generic lifecycle logs omit source text, executable paths and transport payloads; native diagnostics remain private editor data.
The authoring path requires trusted local file workspaces. It does not install tools, download binaries, save sources, execute notebooks, build, sign or publish. Selecting an executable is user trust, not release authorization.
Explicit application operations
The separate application command controller uses one native MCP process per explicitly selected folder. It uses the same bundled program or explicit User override as the language server, with the same trust and workspace-override checks. It starts the fixed mcp command with a bounded response-size option, without a shell or arbitrary argument customization. The native result limit stays below the editor's 8 MiB frame limit so complete multi-site receipts retain envelope room. It does not depend on a successful LSP source capture. No configured authoring source is read merely to start this operation path.
The command palette exposes:
Gazette: Run Command…: find any CLI command by its readable name or command spelling, then prepare its request. Choosing a command opens the request without executing it; Execute Operation Request runs the reviewed input. For a keybinding, use gazette.runCommand with the CLI command spelling as its args value, for example "check"; this entry also activates Gazette when the extension has not started yet.
One registered command identifier for every CLI application-command family. The extension-owned route catalog names the corresponding MCP operation or operations; it contains no schemas, defaults or implementation. Existing gazette.application.* keybindings and API calls also start the extension when needed. These specialist identifiers stay out of the Command Palette. Direct invocation resolves only the family's mapped live tools; all mapped names must exist in the freshly discovered catalog or the command fails before a request is opened.
Gazette: Create Operation Request: choose a folder, discover the live native tool catalog, select one live capability neighborhood, narrow it by the native operation intent, and then select one operation. Intent groups containing common operations precede advanced-only groups, and common operations precede advanced operations within a group, so the complete lifecycle is not exposed as one flat decision surface. The editor validates and retains the native capability, intent, effect, prominence, closure, typed relations and terminal-result owner; it does not reconstruct those facts from names. Then choose a bounded guided request or the explicit advanced JSON editor. The complete raw catalog is not opened implicitly; Show Application Tools remains the explicit drill-down. An optional exact tool-name command argument is also checked against that same fresh catalog. This generic picker preserves full CLI-backed MCP coverage when native tools evolve. The guided path derives required and optional fields, descriptions, fixed choices and primitive input affordances from that exact live schema. It begins with no optional choice, never applies a schema default and delegates authoritative validation to native Rust. Advanced JSON retains the complete structural projection with every scalar leaf null; there is no handwritten schema inventory, permission default, path/tool substitution, enum choice or schema-generated approval. Guided input is deliberately limited to schemas with at most eight required live-schema leaves. Those schemas use native VS Code Quick Input steps with a visible step/total, Back navigation and cancellation; the controller rechecks the folder-bound session after every step. A schema with more than eight required leaves opens Advanced JSON directly instead of presenting a long serial wizard. Cancelling a guided step creates no request buffer, and neither guided preparation nor automatic Advanced JSON opening dispatches a tool.
Gazette: Execute Operation Request: dispatch the exact associated editor buffer. The explicit command is sufficient only when the live descriptor coherently identifies a read-only, idempotent, non-destructive, closed-world operation. Every local, destructive, external/open-world, repeat-sensitive or conflicting profile requires an additional modal confirmation. The binding contains its URI/document object, original folder, original session and selected tool. Native Rust accepts or rejects the request; the extension does not duplicate operation validation or permission rules. Live annotations are presented as a plain effect profile: read-only versus state-changing, destructive, external/open-world and repeat-sensitive work are visible before dispatch. The editor never infers authority consumption from a state change. Conflicting native hints are shown as an unknown effect rather than guessed.
Gazette: Show Application Tools: show the raw private live catalog without invoking a tool.
Gazette: Show Application Result: reopen the last retained raw JSON-RPC response without invoking the operation again.
Gazette: Stop Application Session: explicitly retire the native process. Failed or uncertain cleanup retains custody and forbids replacement.
Request and result documents are unsaved private JSON text. The parsed catalog is used only for picker presentation; original schema and result bytes remain raw, including integer/string lexemes. The exact argument text is passed to the native transport, which removes only framing whitespace outside strings for LF delivery; it never serializes a parsed argument object. Native duplicate-key, integer and operation-schema checks remain authoritative. After a terminal native response, the editor first shows a concise success, reported-failure or native-RPC-error postcondition with an Open Full Receipt action. The exact raw private response is retained and opens only through that action or Show Application Result; it is never copied into the notification or rewritten into a successful result. When live metadata names another operation as the terminal-result owner, success instead says that the held lifecycle remains active and names that exact owner. After a successful native result, typed relations and the terminal-result owner may be offered through Prepare Canonical Follow-up…. Choosing one first delivers the retained receipt, then opens only an inert schema-derived request for the selected live operation. It never dispatches, retries, infers authority or treats the relation as permission. The editor offers no automatic follow-up effect. No source, request, schema or result is automatically saved. Visible editor errors preserve the transport's safe operational distinction: not-dispatched work can be corrected, native failures require inspection of retained evidence, and an unknown post-dispatch outcome explicitly forbids blind retry and points to inspection/read-back/recovery. Private native text and paths are never copied into the notification.
Before dispatch, the controller rechecks current trust, machine settings, exact folder membership, active document object, version and full text after dialogs. Cancellation before any required confirmation sends no tool call. Saved/copied request buffers cannot acquire a binding by matching content. Folder removal, executable changes and clean session retirement invalidate old bindings; no request silently moves to a replacement process. Application sessions do not restart with LSP settings.
Full native results open as read-only, named JSON documents. Reopening the same result reuses its view; it does not create a dirty untitled buffer or require a save to close. Closing the view does not discard the retained session receipt.
After dispatch, a folder/editor change cannot discard the returned receipt or claim cancellation of native effects. The raw response is retained before the postcondition is shown. Declining its receipt action or a display failure blocks another dispatch until Show Application Result delivers the evidence. There are at most 32 retained folder sessions and 32 open prepared requests. The native transport independently bounds each request frame and response; these host bounds do not replace operation-specific native limits or effect permissions. One in-flight native request is allowed per session; concurrent calls are refused, not queued or retried. A busy/uncertain process is never killed to admit another. Completed tool failures, pre-dispatch refusals and unknown outcomes remain three different editor states. An unknown or absent native dispatch disposition for tools/call is presented as outcome-unknown, retains process custody and forbids retry. Catalog discovery is effect-free: failed tools/list retires that catalog session without claiming that an application operation ran. The message names any exact canonical inspect, observe, reconcile or recover relations as inert evidence or recovery-related guidance only. Their relationship does not make them safe or authorized. A completed failure may prepare one of those requests after displaying its receipt; neither path runs a follow-up effect.
Stopping is graceful EOF plus observed process completion, not cancellation, successful native handle closure or release settlement. Explicitly finish/close native handles using their owning tools before retirement. Extension shutdown attempts both authoring and application cleanup, preserving failed custody. Selecting a tool or a trusted executable does not authorize its effects: supplied native permissions, source pins, signed authority and operation invariants still apply. This editor path introduces no tool installation or publication policy.

What to verify after changing the integration
Run the extension checks when changing the client, then exercise the affected behavior in a VS Code development window. In particular, check unsaved text, navigation and stale-result rejection after changing the language-client dependency. Tests cannot show how a diagnostic or action reads in the editor.

Workspace compilation
A workspace is the configuration that declares one publication or several connected ones: their sites, brands, content sources and Themes, in a root gazette.toml plus any files it lists under includes. Run gazette check in a publication folder to check that configuration and its pages before rendering. The command line and MCP use the same SDK check. For a configuration buffer alone, use gazette check --stdin. The commands below call the executable as "$GAZETTE", the path the install guide sets; if gazette is on your PATH, use that instead.

I need to…	Start here

Load a workspace spread across several files	Load an explicit file set

To create and preview a publication, follow Your first publication. For the roles of configuration, compilation and rendering, see Gazette architecture.
Check a complete small workspace
Save this as workspace-example.toml. Both sites name one explicitly declared publisher; they remain distinct sites even though that reference is shared. The brand supplies each publication's public base so routed content can resolve its addresses.
[[principals]]
id = 'owner:writer'
kind = 'person'

[[sites]]
id = 'site:notes'
publisher = 'owner:writer'
deployable = false

[[sites]]
id = 'site:research'
publisher = 'owner:writer'
deployable = false

[[brands]]
id = 'brand:field-notes'
name = 'Field Notes'

[[brands.publications]]
site = 'site:notes'
public_base_url = 'https://notes.example/'

[[brands.publications]]
site = 'site:research'
public_base_url = 'https://research.example/'

With a built Gazette executable, check the supplied bytes:
"$GAZETTE" check --stdin < workspace-example.toml

The JSON result contains the resolved workspace and a digest of the supplied text. The example addresses configure route resolution; no request is sent to them. This input has no content or Theme source and creates no files or served site. Change one publisher to owner:missing and the complete check fails with a native reference diagnostic instead of returning a partially resolved workspace.
An integration can also locate the explicit deployable declaration:
"$GAZETTE" check --stdin --origin '{"kind":"site","identity":"site:notes","field":["deployable"]}' < workspace-example.toml

The returned span addresses the original UTF-8 bytes. Defaults do not acquire invented source positions. The JavaScript SDK example shows the same check and source lookup embedded in an application.
Choose what the check reads
Run gazette check from the publication folder or any folder beneath it. Gazette searches upward for gazette.toml, stopping at the repository boundary. Choose a different folder with --workspace-root /path/to/publication; --workspace-file other.toml selects another root document there. An invalid selected workspace fails instead of falling back to another one.
A local check reads the declared sources, checks page structure and references, and returns workspace_location, checked_sites and diagnostics. Problems also appear one per line on standard error, with their source file and position when available. A failed check exits unsuccessfully while retaining its diagnostic report on standard output. Checking does not render a Theme, run a typesetter or publish. A workspace without content has configuration to check but no pages.
To choose a fallback for folders that have no workspace, run gazette config set workspace /path/to/publication. Gazette saves the absolute selection in $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/gazette/config.json, or $HOME/.config/gazette/config.json when XDG configuration is unset. An explicit request takes priority, followed by a client folder, the process start folder, then this saved default. The result names the source of the choice. Finding a local workspace never changes the saved default.
Standard input is read only with --stdin or a mode that explicitly requests an input, such as check build --local or --retained-math-stdin. Use gazette check --stdin < workspace.toml for a detached configuration-only check. It returns the resolved configuration and source digest, without reading page sources. Empty input is checked as supplied text; it does not select a local workspace.
Use gazette check build --local when you also want to validate the site build. It takes the same gazette-local-publication-set/1 JSON as render-sites, reads the declared files and runs the renderer without keeping a stage. See Render publications locally for the recipe.
In a build or preview request, choose a workspace.kind:
Kind	Input	
supplied	One complete TOML buffer	
local	Absolute root, document path relative to that root, and independent loader limits	
Both compile the workspace once. Build, preview, qualification and preparation use that compilation and keep its source information in the result. Gazette reads the source when the request calls for it. It does not add file reads, rendering or release to a workspace-only check.
Unsupported fields fail the check. The schema covers pinned sources, Themes, plugin activation, capability-provider bindings, resources and field origins. Before the first release, the workspace format has no compatibility promise.
For a site with its own brand, use the single site block. Shared publication settings let sites inherit declared workspace and publisher defaults while retaining their individual overrides.
Explicit modular workspace documents
Put includes in the root workspace file when you want to keep configuration in several files:
# gazette.toml
includes = ["principals.toml", "sites/notes.toml"]

List every required file relative to that root. An include cannot add another include. Gazette reads the listed files and rejects missing, duplicate, extra, linked, special, changing or case-aliased paths. It does not scan siblings or fall back to another workspace. Gazette first reads the root to learn which files to capture, then checks that those root bytes still agree when it reads the complete set.
Every file uses the same schema. List declarations combine, but a workspace-level singleton table belongs to only one file. A duplicate identity or conflicting reference fails the same way it would in a single file. An include never overrides a declaration just because it appears later.
Use the Rust SDK's configuration::load_workspace(root, workspace_path, limits) or run the CLI:
"$GAZETTE" check workspace /absolute/config-root --workspace gazette.toml --allow-read

In MCP, call load_workspace with the absolute root, root-relative EntryPath, read permission and limits. The CLI and MCP report the document inventory and compiled result. Each document gets its own path and digest. The set has a version-framed digest in path order. An origin query returns the declaring file, its digest and the span in that file.
For a standalone buffer, supply source to MCP check_workspace or use gazette check --stdin. A detached buffer cannot load includes or resolve workspace-relative source roots because it has no containing directory. To check pages as well, use the native workspace selection described above.
Name the objects and their references
Keys are opaque, case-sensitive namespace:local values with nonempty parts and no whitespace/control characters. Their declaration proves no identity.
A publisher must explicitly reference a declared person or organization. Authors, brands, contacts and controllers are not fallback publishers.
At least one site is required. Projects without placements remain in the complete desired state. Omitted declarations are not recovered from a store.
A rendered placement requires a documents source reference and logical target. Disabled placements may omit that binding; any supplied binding still resolves. Source selections are shared declarations, not inferred from project names.
Duplicate keys, conflicting identity forms, duplicate site/project placements and unresolved references fail the entire compilation. Independent semantic failures accumulate deterministically; schema errors stop dependent resolution.
All state axes, placement roles and placement flags are required. No active/public/available or deployable defaults are manufactured. Unknown fields and enum values fail.
Declaration order does not change resolved topology. Exact source identity includes comments, whitespace and order; it is not an artifact digest.
A successful pure check means internally resolved topology only. It does not certify content, verify owner facts, reconcile the registry, establish an exact source pin, bind a Theme envelope or authorize publication. Failures produce no partial workspace on stdout and exit unsuccessfully. Correct the declaration and rerun the complete check; no native recovery is needed because no state was changed.
Project lifecycle uses planned, active, paused, done or closed. It remains separate from the project's visibility and availability, and from content's draft, published or archived state. Earlier project-state spellings are rejected rather than silently translated.
Origins and introspection
Origin queries explain which declaration supplied a value. They inspect the same parsed workspace used by resolution; they do not load another source of truth.
Find where a field was declared
The shared compiler can retain the original syntax alongside the resolved workspace with workspace::ParsedWorkspace::parse. Its origin operation takes one FieldQuery: declaration kind, exact identity and typed key/index path. It returns the original UTF-8 byte range and source digest. Semantic sorting does not change the source coordinate, and source-binding keys stay distinct from similarly named principals. No textual name search or second TOML parser is involved.
For the documentation-repository declaration in repository settings:
"$GAZETTE" check --stdin --origin '{"kind":"brand","identity":"example:brand","field":["publications",0,"documentation_repository","path"]}' < workspace.toml

The whole workspace must resolve before a location is returned. Missing or defaulted fields receive no invented origin. Field arrays use original source order; string components are exact decoded TOML keys, not dotted paths. The read-only command cannot be combined with source acquisition. These coordinates are not LSP UTF-16 positions or ownership evidence. Typed composition inheritance has its own winning-source query. Imports and a complete override-history view remain outside this query. Current LSP/MCP authoring sessions project compiler-owned declarations, references, effective values and winning origins without reparsing the workspace in an interface; see the LSP contract. Cross-document edits, rename and formatting remain separate editor capabilities.
Publication origins
Publication fields have a separate PublicationOriginQuery with a site and typed field path. ParsedWorkspace::publication_origin and ParsedWorkspaceDocuments::publication_origin return the winning value, its workspace-default, publisher or site scope, and the original document coordinates. The CLI exposes the same explanation as gazette check --why contacts.rights --site site:notes; see shared publication settings.
Composition origins
Each resolved Selected<T> retains its winning SelectionOrigin. For an effective Theme's source field:
"$GAZETTE" check --stdin --composition-origin '{"site":"example:site","field":{"kind":"theme"},"path":["source"]}' < workspace.toml

Use {"kind":"plugin","package":"search-plugin"} for plugin activation, {"kind":"capability","capability":"publication.search/v1"} for a capability atom, or {"kind":"resource","resource":"module:search"} for a resource selection. A relative path such as ["provider","package"] selects one field; an empty path selects the whole atom. The Rust operation is ParsedWorkspace::composition_origin with the shared CompositionOriginQuery. It follows the resolver's winner back into the original AST, preserving quoted keys, original site order, Unicode/CRLF byte coordinates and exact source digest. Inherited values point to workspace source, never fabricated local fields. Omitted fields still have no explicit location. Origin queries cannot be combined with each other or source-acquisition options.

Local build defaults
[build] owns the default sites list and local_drafts choice. Optional corpus_bytes sets the aggregate authored-input ceiling, including opaque assets, and math selects native typesetting. Invocation overrides win; omitted settings retain Gazette's native defaults. Execution permission stays with each call, never in this configuration. See local rendering for the direct workspace command, math defaults and input-size report.
Native gazette check and MCP check_workspace use the same configured corpus ceiling without running math. An explicit SDK CorpusLimits.source_bytes takes precedence, including a lower value. Per-document parser and source-acquisition limits remain separate.
Social-card renderer
An optional root-level social_card_renderer binds the exact Node and browser executables used by Gazette's fixed capture helper. Each field is a PinnedExecutable: an absolute program path and an executable table with the file's positive byte length, at most 256 MiB, and complete SHA-256. Both pins use the existing native command validation. Neither executable is found through PATH, and selecting them grants no execution permission.
The binding has exactly two fields, node and browser. It accepts no caller arguments, environment, working directory, source binding or helper entrypoint. Helper bytes are embedded engine inputs; selecting a renderer does not add a workspace source. A split workspace may declare the binding in one included configuration document. Two declarations fail even when equal, so document order cannot select a different executable. Pins establish executable-byte identity, not the identity of shared libraries, fonts or other ambient runtime inputs.
The Theme separately declares the social-card recipe, including its template, dimensions and media selection. An explicit publication link-preview asset keeps precedence over generated output.

Configure navigation and discovery
Set which content appears in reading indexes and what the site emits for search engines and other readers.
Start with a taxonomy catalog if you want to list pages by topic. Use generated reading indexes for site navigation, machine-readable outputs for discovery files and preferred source invitations for an optional reader action.
Taxonomy catalog and language scope
Append explicit catalog declarations to the workspace example:
[[taxonomies]]
id = "taxonomy:subjects"
label = "Subjects"
language = "EN-us"
terms = [
  { id = "term:systems", label = "Systems" },
  { id = "term:publishing", label = "Publishing" },
]

Taxonomy and term records reject unknown fields. IDs are exact keys; labels must be nonblank and control-free, and never generate identities or slugs. Taxonomy IDs cannot collide with principal, site, project or brand identities. A term's identity is the pair (taxonomy, term): the same term key may occur in another taxonomy, but repeated taxonomy IDs or term IDs within one taxonomy fail. Omitted catalogs and term lists remain empty. Resolution sorts catalogs and terms by ID; Workspace::taxonomies, taxonomy and Taxonomy::term share those validated records without label or sibling-taxonomy fallback.
language uses the shared BCP 47 syntax validator and normalizes subtag casing (EN-us becomes en-US). It is a content-language constraint, not merely the label's language: content assigned to this taxonomy must explicitly resolve to the exact same normalized tag. Missing content language, en or en-GB does not match en-US. An omitted taxonomy language is neutral and accepts content with any or no language; it supplies no default. Malformed tags fail, and the application bounds each tag to 255 input bytes. This does not perform language detection, registry alias canonicalization or translation matching.
Content declares exact membership pairs as described in the content model. All content states are checked; unknown taxonomies/terms and mismatched language return errors, never dropped classifications or a successful partial graph. This does not establish taxonomy hierarchy, term routes, indexes, filters or publication admission.
The same retained workspace AST supplies taxonomy origins, for example:
gazette check --stdin --origin '{"kind":"taxonomy","identity":"taxonomy:subjects","field":["terms",0,"label"]}' < workspace.toml

That coordinate addresses the original Systems label even after ID sorting; the language origin retains the original EN-us bytes. Omitted fields have no fabricated span.
Generate reading indexes
A publication can bind listings to an existing index page with an empty Markdown body. The index keeps its authored identity, title, site, route and selected template; the listing supplies its entries from the existing content graph.
Selection considers every captured Content binding and applies the discovery rules shared by the other outputs. It does not create another collection or a second maintained catalogue.
brands.publications.search_page may select one existing, same-site, canonically routed Page independently of the shared chrome atom. Its resolved destination is available at presentation.search.page when search is configured, and at presentation.chrome.shell.search.page alongside the shared search-control copy. The legacy chrome no_script_destination remains an independent fallback; it does not opt a publication into the full-page search role. Missing, foreign-site, unrouted or republished search pages fail binding rather than inventing /search/.
For a complete browse fallback, bind that declaration-only index to select = { kind = "all-pages" }. This selects the publication's discoverable, canonically routed Page, Collection and Journey records from the same captured graph. It excludes the index itself, foreign-site records and republished copies; assets and generated continuation routes never become content records. The configured search-page identity is also omitted from the emitted search corpus, so it does not appear as its own result. The same listing ordering, shallow metadata, pagination and independent resource bounds apply. It does not invent editorial containment or add search to article browsing locations. Search ranking may use only the publication's configured fields; the empty-query browse index is a complete discovery view rather than ranked results. The Theme chooses its search layout by the resolved destination's content identity, while keeping the selected world presentation. No route or site-name convention is part of the engine contract.
[[brands.publications.listings]]
content = "content:blog"
select = { kind = "standalone-articles" }
order = { by = "published", direction = "descending", undated = "last-title-then-id" }
pagination = { page_size = 15, next_pages = "page/{number}/" }
alternate_order = { order = { by = "published", direction = "ascending", undated = "last-title-then-id" }, path = "oldest" }

[[brands.publications.listings]]
content = "content:collections"
select = { kind = "root-collections" }
order = { first = ["collection:foundations"], remaining = "title-then-id" }
pagination = { page_size = 20, next_pages = "page/{number}/" }

A product's related writing uses a separate explicit selector, not an editorial container or a copied article directory:
[[brands.publications.listings]]
content = "content:example-mentions"
select = { kind = "project-articles", project = "project:example", scope = "ecosystem", residence = "all", explore = "content:blog" }
order = { by = "published", direction = "descending", undated = "last-title-then-id" }
alternate_order = { order = { by = "published", direction = "ascending", undated = "last-title-then-id" }, path = "oldest" }
pagination = { page_size = 15, next_pages = "page/{number}/" }

The landing must be a canonical project-family page or root collection with a direct about assertion for that exact project.
scope defaults to site; ecosystem considers canonical eligible articles across the captured publications, including collection and journey articles. An article qualifies through its own direct about or mentions declaration, or an actually emitted resolved body/Notes link to the landing. Unused definitions, images, inherited container context, labels, folders and coincidental URL text do not qualify. Candidate discovery applies before reference expansion.
All references share the native complete-view edge/text bounds; exhaustion fails rather than returning a shorter list. The subject view retains each article's own canonical site and route, and does not become its global browsing ancestry.
Optional residence defaults to all, preserving existing selections; standalone keeps articles with no declared editorial parent and collected keeps articles with a collection or journey parent. It never uses directory paths.
Optional explore names an existing configured unfiltered index in the view's own publication. It resolves to a shallow native destination even when the related set is empty; foreign, missing, non-index or already project-filtered targets fail instead of becoming a guessed fallback.
standalone-articles selects article-family pages with no editorial parent; hiding a parent from discovery never makes its articles standalone. root-collections selects editorial collections with no parent collection. Article selectors, including project-articles, exclude pages classified as documentation through their collection purpose or documentation family. The content purpose contract describes inheritance and the independent search/all-page behavior. Republished copies are excluded. Priority identities must name unique same-site candidates of the selected kind, even when a candidate is not discoverable. Remaining candidates sort by literal authored title and stable identity.
Publication ordering uses only the authored published value, with explicit descending (newest first) or ascending (oldest first) direction. Each complete eligible corpus is sorted before slicing; changing direction never reverses just the current page. Neither modified, filesystem dates nor content lifecycle supplies chronology. Local inspection remains draft-inclusive; an explicitly narrowed candidate/discovery selection governs its own outputs.
A reading index can mix calendar dates and timestamps. It orders calendar days in the requested direction, using the authored day for a date-only value and the UTC day for a timestamp. Within each day, timestamps come first and compare their actual instants in that direction; entries with an unknown time follow them in both directions. This is a display convention, not a claim that an unknown time was midnight or later than the known times. Equal instants and equal date-only values use title then identity; entries without a date come last, also by title then identity. Original date precision and offsets stay intact. For example, 2026-10-06T00:30:00+14:00 belongs to the UTC day 2026-10-05, alongside the equal instant 2026-10-04T20:30:00-14:00. The optional latest item uses that same editorial-day convention: it considers only the newest day, selects the latest timestamp or uses title then identity for equal dates, and remains absent if that day mixes date-only values and timestamps. Older mixed precision cannot suppress a clear newest-day choice. This identifies an editorial-day winner without inventing times or timezones for calendar dates; it does not establish an absolute instant for them.
Pagination requires a positive page size and a confined relative directory with exactly one {number} placeholder. An index at /blog/ with page/{number}/ produces continuations such as /blog/page/2/. The public or preview base supplies their serving URLs; capture paths do not. Empty selections retain one empty index view. Collisions with content routes, aliases, mirrors, taxonomy outputs or file ancestors fail the complete build. Whole-projection page, link and text ceilings apply; Gazette never truncates a successful listing to fit.
An optional alternate_order admits only the opposite published direction over the same candidates and pagination. Its confined relative path is joined beneath the original index: oldest gives /blog/oldest/ and /blog/oldest/page/2/. The original index and continuation URLs remain unchanged. Every generated view has the same authored index identity, with a native variant discriminator; alternate page one is a generated output, not another owner or article. Both ordering roots and every continuation share the same collision and aggregate expansion checks. Article browsing locations retain the primary ordering.
The Theme receives listing with ordered items, counts and optional previous/next URLs. Native pages contains first/last/current plus at most two neighbors on each side, at most seven distinct endpoints, with current and gap_before facts. Optional sorts links each available chronology to its own page one, resetting pagination. Rendering these same facts twice supplies consistent top and bottom controls without client-side sorting or template route construction. Continuations reuse the index's template and identity, replace only the serving route and slice, and do not become additional articles or search records. The site model's output-keyed listing_pages, site graph, sitemap and JSON-LD carry the applicable generated views. See the Theme contract for the context fields.
Machine-readable publication outputs
machine selects site-root sitemap.xml, llms.txt, search.json and site.jsonld, plus canonical-page Markdown counterparts beneath the configured public or local-preview base. Omission disables each output. sitemap and json_ld are booleans; search is omitted, a concise lexical or english profile, or a strict { language, fields } selection. For example:
# Inside the existing publication's machine table.
search = { language = "english", fields = ["title", "description", "keywords", "route", "body", "notes"] }
graph = { enabled = true, path = "/graph/" }

Search language selects the token-processing profile, not the page language. fields must be a nonempty distinct list drawn from title, description, keywords, route, body, notes, summary and projects. Concise profiles select title, body, summary, projects and keywords. Each emitted search record retains its complete discovery-safe metadata alongside the selected plain ranking values in indexed; selecting notes does not create another search identity or merge commentary into the main body.
The optional graph table selects a view of the existing discovery graph through the selected Theme's declared graph entry, not a second graph or a template selector. /graph/ maps to graph/index.html using the ordinary route compiler. enabled = false emits no graph view and refuses an invocation that requests one. Enabled configuration fixes the destination; a different invocation output is refused. Omission leaves the explicit invocation-level graph selection available. Missing Theme entries, unsafe routes and output collisions fail the site rather than silently dropping its view.
markdown_alternates and llms are strict named tables with required fields, not booleans or positional arrays. Unknown fields, unsupported profile values and wrong types fail parsing. These are publication representations, not another repository/path convention or a generated-reference destination.
The alternate profile's supported values are exactly directory_page = 'index.md', file_page = 'append-md', media_type = 'text/markdown' and discovery_rel = 'alternate'. With enabled = true, /guide/ materializes guide/index.md, while /guide.html materializes guide.html.md; each URL uses the site's resolved base. This covers rendered canonical pages, generated taxonomy views and listing continuations, independently of discoverability. Aliases, mirror redirects and noncanonical syndicated copies do not receive alternates. enabled = false omits their files and the optional presentation.markdown_alternate Theme binding.
Enabled llms requires enabled alternates. Its description_from names a selected, same-site, discoverable canonical page with an explicit nonempty description, used as the guide's introduction. representation is exactly markdown-alternate; include_human_link = true pairs each Markdown link with its actual serving HTML link, while false omits that pair.
coverage = 'all-pages' selects every eligible built canonical page from this publication's actual render selection. Each entry uses the existing authored title and nonempty description. Listing continuations and alternate orderings are omitted from the guide; their HTML and Markdown files remain available through the canonical index. Newly authored pages therefore enter the guide without a second catalogue. Aliases, mirror redirects, noncanonical syndicated copies, undiscoverable content and identity-free companions do not become duplicate entries. Configured taxonomy views also enter the catalogue with their exact labels and routes; their catalogue has no authored purpose field, so no summary is invented. The complete model and emitted guide are bounded; a missing page purpose or exhausted bound fails rather than silently shrinking coverage.
The default coverage = 'curated' preserves the existing explicit reading path: sections[].contents supplies exact identities and section/item order, including intentional repetition. All-pages mode requires sections to be absent or empty; a stale curated catalogue cannot quietly override complete coverage. Omission or enabled = false produces no llms.txt. The selected Theme may provide an inherited render.llms entry to format the native model; without one the native bounded Markdown writer supplies the neutral guide. Its text encoder preserves ordinary prose punctuation and escapes characters that could become Markdown formatting, links or HTML.
The example assumes content:home exists with that declared description. Pure workspace checking validates the schema, not captured content eligibility. During publication rendering, missing, excluded, undiscoverable, foreign, mirror-only or noncanonical curated references refuse the site rather than silently shrinking its guide. A missing description refuses it too. The same resolved routed pages feed HTML, alternates and curated links; no second catalogue or live template read is involved. Selection is not public admission: current local renders include drafts and archived content. See discovery outputs for scope, format limits and explicit failure behavior. Search selects token processing and ranking fields, not a browser library, query algorithm or cross-site fetch. See search documents. identity_assets assigns semantic roles to site-used resources already enabled by the site's effective composition. A dependency-only module cannot fill an identity role. The role never selects or names a file by convention. Site icons may use admitted PNG, JPEG or inert SVG resources; link previews use PNG or JPEG. Theme receives the resolved resource records through presentation.identity_assets. JSON-LD also supplies the page's json_ld template/model field from the same resolved facts. See its projection and ownership contract.
Preferred source invitations
This optional publication setting supplies a link for a reader to choose the publication as a preferred Google source. Gazette derives https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=<canonical-host> from the publication's canonical domain or subdomain root, independently of local serving URLs. It selects a source host, not an article or a /blog/ subtree. The invitation loads no provider SDK and contacts Google only when the reader follows the link.
[brands.publications.processing.preferred_sources]
enabled = true
provider = "google"
articles = true
label = "Prefer this source on Google"
description = "Find more writing from this publication."

[brands.publications.processing.preferred_sources.pages."article:one"]
enabled = false

Omission or publication-level enabled = false emits no invitation, even if a page override enables it. articles = true includes the article family regardless of collection nesting. Exact pages overrides take precedence over that article default and optionally replace label and description. Utility and index pages need an explicit opt-in. Overrides must name real, routed content in that publication; missing or foreign references fail resolution.
Labels and descriptions are nonempty plain text without control characters, bounded to 160 and 1,024 UTF-8 bytes respectively. A publication can declare at most 1,024 page overrides. Copy and article keywords are not instructions sent to Google. The canonical source must be a public domain root without a port; IPs and local hosts are refused. A page projects preferred_source with href, label and description through the existing page and discovery views. Templates render that supplied action and its explanatory copy without another JavaScript configuration, domain list or selection rule.
The compiler integration tests exercise page selection and exclusion, invalid copy and source scope, unresolved page references, and canonical targeting during local preview. The host tests cover domain and subdomain targets and rejected preview or article addresses. A theme check should also verify placement, one accessible link with its description, external-link attributes, no provider script and omission from unselected pages.
Google handles the account flow, source eligibility, confirmation and cancellation. A local render cannot establish live eligibility, and a click cannot establish that a reader added the source. Before release, check eligibility through Google's own tool and review the exact rendered invitation. Existing structured data, discovery, analytics and consent settings retain their separate contracts; the invitation reports no preference completion or conversion.
Back to workspace.

Compose themes and site resources
Attach a Theme, choose providers and shared resources, and set presentation for a single page or the whole site.
If you want to…	Read	
Attach a Theme and declare its package sources	Theme and package composition	
Use a shared file for a Theme resource	Supply a declared Theme input	
Compile a Theme to check templates	Compile templates	
Override the template for one page	Per-page presentation	
Change navigation and utility copy	Site chrome and control copy	
Declare Themes, plugins and browser resources
Workspace-level [composition] declares reusable defaults. Each site's composition declares only its own selected changes. The compiler first resolves the workspace and site choices. After acquiring the selected Theme packages, check_metadata adds their resource defaults beneath those choices. Metadata checks and rendering use that completed composition; workspace-only editor queries show the declarations available before package acquisition.
# Root tables must precede the example's [[sites]] and other array tables.
[composition]
theme = { package = "theme:base", palette = "palette:light" }

[composition.plugins]
"search-plugin" = { state = "enabled" }

[composition.capabilities]
"publication.search/v1" = { state = "enabled", provider = { kind = "plugin", package = "search-plugin", provider = "search" }, requirement = "optional", allow_absence = "no-native-acquisition" }
"publication.analytics/v1" = { state = "disabled" }

[composition.resources]
"module:search" = { state = "enabled", resource = { owner = { kind = "plugin", package = "search-plugin" }, resource = "module:search" }, output = "/assets/search.js", use = "site" }

Theme and plugin packages have separate bindings to configured sources using explicit filesystem, exact repository or parent-gitlink coordinates. Paths and pins are not repeated in Theme, capability or resource selections. A repository source must name its actual checked-out commit before acquisition can succeed.
Inside a site declaration, for example:
[sites.composition]
theme = { package = "theme:research" }

[sites.composition.plugins]
"search-plugin" = { state = "disabled" }

[sites.composition.capabilities]
"publication.search/v1" = { state = "enabled", provider = { kind = "gazette", provider = "static-search" }, requirement = "required" }

[sites.composition.resources]
"module:search" = { state = "disabled" }

The examples show declaration shape, not a complete production configuration; all referenced source keys require explicit definitions. Resolution rules are:
Omitted Theme, plugin, capability and resource atoms inherit independently. An empty map means no local changes; it does not erase workspace selections.
A site Theme replaces the entire Theme binding. Its omitted palette means no named palette; another Theme's palette is never carried across implicitly.
Each capability entry replaces the whole selected binding, including its failure policy. Partial provider records cannot merge into a valid selection.
Each plugin entry activates or disables one package as a whole atom. Package activation is independent from its catalog/source binding and from every provider or resource it exports; neither export reference activates it.
Each resource entry independently replaces its package-qualified resource, output and site/dependency use as one atom. It does not activate or prove a capability.
Explicit state = "disabled" remains in the result and cannot fall through to workspace or Theme discovery. Extraneous fields on disabled entries fail.
ProviderRef::Gazette selects a Gazette-owned implementation. ProviderRef::Plugin selects one provider exported by one exact captured plugin package. Neither form is a contribution scope or inheritance origin.
Resource ownership is separately package-qualified as Theme or plugin. A Theme never chooses the provider or performs acquisition.
Source references in all package bindings are checked, including defaults shadowed by every site. Missing sources, owners and misspelled variants fail rather than discovering a substitute.
Required/optional expresses selected policy only. Optional does not authorize arbitrary degradation or provider substitution. Source reads require the explicit acquisition operation below. Provider execution, resource compilation and certification remain separate later phases.
Per-site expansion is bounded before cloning each retained selection. Caller TOML nodes independently caps total resolved Theme/plugin/capability/resource entries; caller source_bytes independently caps their logical site, selection, package, provider, source and palette key bytes. These are separate from input parsing budgets. Exceeding either yields workspace_limit, never a partial site set. The source digest retains exact bytes; equivalent declarations can yield identical resolved values with different source digests.
Let a Theme supply its resources
A Theme can declare each resource's default output beside its inputs and recipe:
[[resources]]
id = "stylesheet:world"
inputs = ["styles/world.scss"]
build = { kind = "stylesheet", entry = "styles/world.scss" }
output = "/assets/world.css"
use = "site"

output enables this default when the Theme is selected. use defaults to site; dependency is available for browser modules reached through another module. A declaration without output still requires an explicit workspace selection. The output must be a file route, and use cannot be supplied without an output.
Defaults follow the selected Theme's dependency graph. A dependent Theme can replace an inherited resource by declaring its own output for the same resource ID. Shared ancestors reached through two branches contribute one declaration; competing declarations from independent branches require an explicit declaration in their dependent Theme. Each resolved default retains its declaring package.
Workspace and site resource selections override these defaults as whole entries. An explicit state = "disabled" blocks the default; disabling a resource named in resource_requirements fails admission. metadata.inspect().composition shows the effective values and their theme, workspace or site origins. Emitted resources and their URLs come from that same composition.
Acquire the effective composition
gazette check --stdin --acquire-composition example:site < workspace.toml

For a native modular workspace, select the root and exact configuration file:
gazette check --workspace-root /absolute/workspace --workspace-file gazette.toml --acquire-composition example:site

The same selectors work with --publication and its review or registry projection. Native selection rejects simultaneous TOML on standard input. It uses the shared workspace loader, retaining include-file evidence and resolving relative source roots without depending on the process directory. Detached standard-input TOML keeps its original semantics.
This operation compiles the whole workspace before reading the effective Theme package graph and the explicitly enabled plugin packages. Capability-provider and resource references must point into that admitted package set; they never activate a package implicitly. It captures each exact source key once, including shared resource inputs mounted by selected Theme packages and their admitted dependency closure, preserving all consuming selections and their origins in the compiled configuration. Different keys are not merged just because paths or commits match. Disabled, shadowed and other-site sources are not opened; their configuration references still must be valid. Each selected repository or parent-pinned submodule uses the same confined, exact-pin reader as documentation acquisition.
The Rust SDK's build::acquire_composition returns an AcquiredInputs with retained bytes keyed by source identity, not invented documentation placements. Its inspect() projection matches CLI JSON and includes configuration and native verification but not file payloads. This is private operator evidence: configured paths remain present, so do not publish the report. Later native changes cannot alter the retained capture; a new acquisition performs new verification.
--max-placements bounds unique source keys for this operation before any native read. --max-acquired-entries and --max-acquired-bytes bound aggregate retained inventory, tightening each native capture to the remaining allowance. Per-source limits remain enforced, including a separate per-source Git metadata allowance. All selected sources must succeed, even if a consuming capability is optional; failure returns no successful subset, fallback or implicit degradation.
The operation cannot be combined with documentation acquisition/parsing or origin queries. It writes nothing, executes no provider, accesses no network and does not certify a build. An empty effective composition returns an empty capture, not a usable Theme. Capture alone does not verify Theme/plugin/provider identity, named palette membership or compatibility.
Check captured package declarations
Each Theme or plugin package binding explicitly names its manifest and captured source. There is no default filename, scan or lookup in another repository:
# This root table precedes array tables in the workspace document.
[design_inputs]
tokens = "example:tokens"

[[sources]]
id = "example:theme"
location = { kind = "filesystem", root = "/absolute/path/to/theme/publication" }

[[sources]]
id = "example:tokens"
location = { kind = "filesystem", root = "design/tokens" }

[[theme_packages]]
package = "theme:base"
source = "example:theme"
manifest = "theme.toml"
resource_inputs = { "shared/_tokens.scss" = { input = "tokens", entry = "dist/scss/_tokens.scss" } }

[[plugin_packages]]
package = "search-plugin"
source = "example:theme"
manifest = "search-plugin.toml"

Replace the absolute Theme root with your source directory before acquisition. Use a revision-pinned repository source when the build must bind a particular commit. Manifest paths and package-local resource paths are relative to the captured subtree. A Theme manifest owns templates, render entries, palettes, components and Theme dependencies. A plugin manifest independently exports providers and resources:
package = "search-plugin"

[providers.search]
implements = ["publication.search/v1"]

[resources."module:search"]
inputs = ["scripts/search.js"]
build = { kind = "browser-module", entry = "scripts/search.js" }

Providers and resources are separate exact-key maps. One package may export both; that does not make a provider own or produce the static resource.
Supply declared Theme inputs from a shared source
design_inputs maps workspace-local aliases to existing source keys. Names match [a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,63} exactly; they are not package identities, filesystem paths or capability selections. Every source and alias reference must resolve even when its package is unselected. An alias alone neither selects a package or resource nor permits a native read.
The example's theme_packages.resource_inputs supplies the Theme's logical shared/_tokens.scss input from the retained dist/scss/_tokens.scss entry of example:tokens. Add the mapping to the existing package record, not a second record with the same identity. Both paths are literal confined EntryPath values. The logical target must already appear in a resource's inputs within that package's own manifest, for example:
# Resource declaration inside the existing theme.toml, not workspace frontmatter.
[[resources]]
id = "style:main"
inputs = ["styles/main.scss", "shared/_tokens.scss"]
build = { kind = "stylesheet", entry = "styles/main.scss" }

Here styles/main.scss remains package-local and can import ../shared/tokens through the existing Sass input resolver. The manifest may supply its output and use as a resource default, or the workspace may select them through composition.resources. The input alias alone does not emit a stylesheet. Package-local inputs need no mapping. Mounted inputs are supported for Theme resource bindings, not plugin bindings, page companions or Tera templates.
Acquisition captures each selected source key once under the existing source-count, entry, byte and revision budgets. Shared aliases to one key do not duplicate that capture. Only selected Theme packages and their admitted dependencies bring their mounted sources into acquisition; unused aliases and unrelated packages do not trigger a directory scan. Native reads still require the caller's explicit permission and the configured source's normal confinement and pin checks.
Metadata rejects undeclared logical targets, absent or nonregular retained entries, and any target that exists both in the Theme capture and in a mount. Compilation assembles an exact virtual resource-input tree from those retained bytes and uses the existing resource adapters; it does not copy inputs into the Theme repository or grant the compiler live source access. Retained replay uses the same captured bytes, even if native files subsequently change.
Private resource evidence records the original alias, source key, entry, source-binding digest, retained tree identity and file digest. Public resource URLs and Theme resource records retain their existing shape without these coordinates. See resource compilation for the page-resource boundary.
Mounted dot-image resources use the same explicit diagram acquisition as package-local DOT: exactly one declared input, the configured pinned dot_renderer executable and separate execution permission. Acquisition resolves the mount to its original retained source and entry, invokes the provider and retains the checked PNG bound to those exact bytes. Later rendering verifies that retained binding and projects the PNG into the resource's virtual input/dependency namespace without rerunning the provider or reading native files. Original source provenance and virtual resource paths remain distinct. An executable pin does not attest Graphviz's shared libraries, plugins, fonts or ambient dependencies.
Check the package manifests
gazette check --stdin --acquire-composition example:site --check-composition < workspace.toml

The Rust equivalent is acquired.check_metadata(toml::Limits::default()). It borrows retained source bytes and parses each selected manifest once using the shared TOML parser. metadata.inspect() returns the acquisition evidence and Theme/plugin package maps keyed by their canonical package identities, with exact source bindings, manifest paths, digests and parsed declarations. Theme entries also expose retained resource-input origins. This is private operator output, not suitable for public publication; it is not a public manifest-AST or byte-coordinate accessor.
Complete manifests reject unknown fields, duplicate set entries, empty provider capability lists and invalid resource recipes, even in unselected declarations. Effective selection then requires:
The exact selected Theme and its optional declared palette name.
A nonempty retained template directory.
Each selected provider to be exported by its exact Gazette or plugin owner and declare the exact requested capability.
Each selected resource to be exported by its exact Theme or plugin package.
Every selected resource input to exist as a retained regular file, either package-local or explicitly mounted through its Theme binding.
Palette/provider/capability/resource/input lists express sets, not execution order. The typed declaration sorts them for deterministic projection and bounded lookup; the retained AST preserves their original order and exact source coordinates. Several selected capabilities may share one provider. Resources are admitted and compiled independently, so this never implies a shared output.
Independent providers do not need to be Theme-owned. Disabled selections are not checked as active providers or resources. Optional capability policy cannot silently skip broken package metadata or resource inputs. An absent Theme fails this check; an empty acquisition is not sufficient. Failures return no successful metadata subset or fallback.
CLI --max-source-bytes and --max-nodes independently bound configuration parsing and the aggregate selected manifest set; --max-depth applies per file. The SDK accepts those metadata limits separately from acquisition. The operation performs no new native reads, writes, provider execution, rendering or publication. Metadata checking validates declared package members and their selected inputs. Resource compilation, provider execution and Theme rendering check their behavior in subsequent operations.
Compile the configured templates
gazette check --stdin --acquire-composition example:site --compile-templates < workspace.toml

This performs the same complete metadata check, then compiles only the effective Theme's explicitly declared templates subtree. It is mutually exclusive with --check-composition, document parsing and origin queries. No native source is reopened after acquisition and no files are generated. CLI compilation uses the shared default rendering ceilings; SDK callers can supply explicit render::Limits to build::compile_templates(&metadata, limits).
Every regular file inside each admitted package's selected template subtree is parsed, including nonstandard suffixes; invalid unused templates fail compilation. Gazette strips that package's template-directory prefix and mounts the retained name beneath its declared virtual namespace. Includes, inheritance and root entry selection therefore use <namespace>/<subtree-relative-name>, never an unqualified subtree-relative name. Metadata, capability inputs and sibling directories outside the declared template roots are not templates. The SDK returns an owned compiled Theme that can render supplied presentation context after the retained acquisition is dropped or native files change.
The CLI returns the same private compilation evidence as the SDK: configuration digest, site/Theme/palette selection, source coordinates and full-tree identity, manifest path/digest, selected directory and template-tree identity. Native paths make this operator evidence, not public output. It proves neither palette behavior, capability execution nor admitted content-to-page projection. See the rendering contract for escaping, bounded-output and trusted-template limits.
Choose a template for one page
The Theme manifest supplies defaults for the existing content structures and page families:
[render]
page = "page.html"
home = "home.html"
collection_directory = "collection-directory.html"
kinds = { article = "reading.html", collection = "index.html", journey = "sequence.html", project = "product.html", utility = "utility.html" }
modes = { "mode:home" = "home.html" }

kinds accepts article, documentation, project, index, utility, extension, collection and journey, directly matching the compiler's existing content model. documentation means a page explicitly declared with that family; it does not turn product help into a separate family. Help retains its authored article or collection structure and documentation purpose. modes uses the exact mode already declared by an extension page's presentation, without deriving it from a title, path or site. The engine does not prescribe a Theme's mode names.
home selects the exact content named by the publication's home. collection_directory selects an index whose listing declares root-collections. These roles come from declared relationships, independently of page titles and routes. An authored project catalogue without a distinct declared role keeps its explicit page template.
Kind, mode, home and collection-directory entries inherit through declared Theme dependencies and are qualified with the namespace of the package that supplied them. A dependent package can override an entry; competing independent providers require an explicit choice. All selected entries must exist in the captured template namespace. An explicit page template wins, followed by its workspace binding, its declared mode, its home or collection-directory role, its kind, and finally render.page. Listing continuations follow the same choice as their index.
Select a retained page template without putting a world-specific path into authored Content:
[sites.composition.page_templates]
"content:product-introduction" = "example/product.html"
"content:publication-about" = "example/about.html"

The table belongs to that exact site's composition. Omission inherits the complete workspace map; page_templates = {} explicitly clears it, and a nonempty site map replaces the default map atomically. Every key must resolve to content owned by that site. Each entry must name a regular file in the admitted virtual Theme namespace. There is no filename, route, title, wildcard or folder-based selection.
The selection does not change content identity, editorial membership, route, author, or source provenance. Its original configuration document is available through composition-origin inspection with field = {kind = "page-templates"} and the content key in the remaining field path.
Site chrome and control copy
composition.chrome supplies skip-link, navigation, footer, search and settings labels. Each label inherits independently: an explicit site value wins over the workspace value, which wins over the selected Theme’s declared default. The same rule applies to each namespaced regions key. Empty strings are rejected rather than treated as omission.
A Theme declares its defaults under [chrome] in its manifest, using the same copy fields as the workspace. Dependencies supply omitted labels; a dependent package may override individual labels. Conflicting declarations on separate dependency branches require an explicit override. Gazette keeps each winning package or workspace/site origin. It supplies no built-in English copy.
For example, a site can change one label while inheriting the other controls:
[sites.composition.chrome.shell.settings]
title = "Reading preferences"

Workspace compilation resolves workspace and site declarations. Captured Theme admission completes their defaults; inspection, review, component rendering and page rendering use that completed composition. Rendering requires complete labels for the visible controls. Workspace origin queries resolve each explicit workspace or site label’s retained source span; a table assembled from several origins has no single source span. Admitted Theme labels retain their declaring package in the composition’s origin map.
The ordered destinations are separate: composition.navigation and composition.footer each inherit when omitted, while an explicit empty site list clears only that list. Changing the menu therefore does not replace shared chrome copy. These fields control presentation; they do not activate a capability or release a publication.
An entry may supply an optional namespaced key alongside label and destination. Keys are unique within each navigation or footer list and survive resolution unchanged. They let a Theme address one configured destination by meaning without matching visible wording or a content/site identifier. Gazette assigns a key no layout or product meaning; omission preserves an ordinary ordered entry.
The optional regions map carries bounded presentation copy under owner-namespaced keys. Gazette validates and transports at most 256 effective regions in stable order; the Theme assigns their layout, component and visual priority.
Before Theme rendering, every navigation destination is resolved through the selected content graph and canonical route table. Cross-site destinations retain their actual home site and optional Theme/palette presentation. Search copy may also name one no_script_destination; it must resolve to an existing routed page, so Gazette never fabricates fallback HTML or derives a destination from a label. The no-script destination inherits only from an explicit workspace or site declaration. Themes supply labels, not content destinations, reading handoff endpoints or control selections. Set shell.search.enabled = false in a workspace or site chrome declaration to suppress inherited search copy; a higher-layer explicit true can restore it. Copy alone never selects the search index or its provider.
[composition]
navigation = [
  { label = "Home", destination = "content:home" },
  { label = "Notes", destination = "content:notes" },
]
footer = [
  { label = "Privacy", destination = "content:privacy" },
]

[composition.chrome]
skip_to_content_label = "Skip to content"
navigation_label = "Primary navigation"
footer_label = "Site footer"

[composition.chrome.regions]
'region:preface' = "A deliberate opening note"

[composition.chrome.shell]
close_label = "Close"

[composition.chrome.shell.search]
trigger_label = "Search"
title = "Search this site"
field_label = "Query"
loading_message = "Loading results"
empty_message = "No results"
unavailable_message = "Search is unavailable"
no_script_destination = "content:search"

[composition.chrome.shell.settings]
trigger_label = "Settings"
title = "Display settings"
color_mode_label = "Color mode"
color_mode_system_label = "System"
color_mode_light_label = "Light"
color_mode_dark_label = "Dark"
motion_label = "Motion"
motion_system_label = "System"
motion_reduce_label = "Reduce"
motion_allow_label = "Allow"

Optional composition.chrome.reading_assistance declares user-invoked external reading handoffs as typed data, separately from search/settings and generic region copy. The Theme receives the same object at presentation.chrome.reading_assistance; omission remains absent. For example, appended to the chrome declaration above:
[composition.chrome.reading_assistance]
label = "Ask about this passage"
prompt_template = "Explain {selection} from {article_title} ({article_url}) on {site_name} ({site_url}). Section: {section_title}. Context: {context}"
selection_limit = 4096
context_limit = 1024

[[composition.chrome.reading_assistance.providers]]
id = "assistant:chosen"
label = "Ask a chosen assistant"
endpoint = "https://assistant.example/new"
query_parameter = "prompt"

This example endpoint demonstrates shape, not a working service. The composing workspace chooses the actual providers and their supported prefill endpoints; Gazette embeds no provider registry or endpoint fallback. Providers retain declared order and unique namespaced IDs. Endpoints must be explicit HTTPS addresses without credentials or fragments. They cannot already contain the selected prompt query key, including its percent-encoded spelling. query_parameter matches [A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_-]*, with at most 64 ASCII characters.
Prompt templates accept only the single-brace slots selection, article_title, article_url, site_name, site_url, section_title and context; selection, article_url, site_name and site_url are required. Unknown or unbalanced braces fail validation. Templates allow newlines and tabs, but no other control characters. The template and selection limit each cap at 4096 Unicode characters; selection must be positive. Context caps at 1024 Unicode characters, with zero explicitly excluding it. Labels cap at 256 Unicode characters; endpoints cap at 2048. One to eight providers are permitted. Reading assistance keeps its existing whole-object selection: a site with no chrome declaration inherits the workspace’s assistance, while a site with its own chrome declaration must explicitly supply the complete assistance object to retain handoffs. Omitting it from that local declaration suppresses the inherited handoffs. This selection does not merge endpoints or prompts label by label. Origin inspection retains nested source spans, and provider occurrences and text bytes are charged before site expansion clones the object.
The Theme may offer a reader action that inserts the supplied page/site values, bounds the selected text and nearby context, and URL-encodes the prompt. It opens the configured destination only after the reader chooses that action. Gazette validates the settings without filling prompts or making requests; the configured endpoint still needs to support the intended prefill behavior. These settings are presentation data, not content metadata or a JSON-LD relationship.
Select page invitations
composition.invitations selects where a Theme may offer a link below a page. Each namespaced key inherits independently from the workspace; a site's entry replaces the complete policy. Footer entries and template names do not select an invitation.
[sites.composition.invitations."theme:services"]
state = "enabled"
destination = "content:services"
articles = true
pages = { "content:about" = true, "content:personal-essay" = false }

articles includes article-family pages, including those within collections. Exact pages entries override that default: true selects the page and false excludes it. To select only named pages, set articles = false. An explicit state = "disabled" suppresses the inherited invitation on the whole site. Omission inherits; an empty map makes no changes. Selection does not change a page's lifecycle, authorship or publication approval.
The destination must resolve to existing routed content. Each page override must name routed content in the selecting publication, including collection and project landing pages and excluded entries; missing and foreign references fail rather than disappearing silently. Selected pages expose invitations["theme:services"].destination, using the same resolved content and route fields as navigation. Preview URLs follow the destination site's preview route. Unselected pages omit the map, and generated views have no authored-page invitation. presentation.chrome.invitation_destinations exposes the configured targets by semantic key independently of those visible selections, so a destination can receive handoff context without inviting itself or requiring a footer link. The Theme supplies appearance and copy and can suppress a repeated invitation already present in the body.
Project resource destinations
Optional project resources declare independent navigation roles. The existing repository remains repository metadata; resources.github instead declares a GitHub navigation endpoint when no repository is established. Both together are refused, so there is one configured source of the GitHub action. These fields select no acquisition, deployment, public availability or implementation state.
[[projects]]
id = "project:example"
name = "Example"
lifecycle = "planned"
visibility = "public"
availability = "unavailable"
repository = "https://code.example.test/team/example"
resources = { landing = "content:example", code_documentation = "https://docs.example.test/example/", learn = "content:example-guide", mentions = "content:example-mentions" }

landing names the project's canonical introduction by exact content identity. It must be a routed, canonical project-family page or root collection with a direct About declaration for that project. A root collection's About describes the collection itself, not its children.
Pages receive optional projects[].landing with id, title, serving url and source-relative destination values. Learn, Mentions and repository addresses do not fill a missing landing. Selecting this link adds no About/Mentions assertion or project-ownership relationship.
A project-articles listing may omit its legacy landing field when the project owns this resource. When both are declared they must agree; without either, listing resolution fails. This gives every article view the same exact landing without copying it into each selector or inferring it from another page.
Each resource field is optional and has a specific destination contract:
Field	Destination	
code_documentation	An explicit public HTTPS address for separate developer manuals/reference.	
learn	An existing documentation-family page or this project's explicitly selected root-collection landing. Another collection is not an implicit fallback.	
mentions	A project-articles index selecting the same project. residence = "all" combines standalone and collected articles.	
blogs, thoughts	Independently configured article views using that same selection, ordering and pagination mechanism.	
The compiler resolves serving URLs and destination classification once. URL validation rejects credentials and malformed addresses without contacting a host. The action order is code-documentation, Learn, GitHub, Mentions, then separately configured article views. A missing resource stays absent; the Theme can show its unavailable state without substituting a broad site or organisation index.
A project-family host with exactly one directly declared about project receives the same shallow resource projection in its page model and hosted-component context. A root collection receives that projection only when it is the selected landing for its single About project and satisfies the same canonical-route checks. Ambiguous or inherited relations do not choose a project. The Theme supplies visible labels and action hierarchy from composing chrome. Native Markdown alternates lower the same component formatter, preserving these anchors; SQLite retains each optional declaration independently. JSON-LD keeps codeRepository confined to the actual repository field and represents learning/article/collected-article/manual resources as subjectOf references, not hosted-state claims.
Back to workspace.

Configure publication identity and delivery
Set who publishes, what the site includes, and where its site or developer docs can be delivered.
If you want to…	Read	
Display the name, website or contact of a person or organisation	Principal display names, principal websites and contact links	
Choose who publishes or operates a site	Independent site responsibilities	
Bind content, legal copy or a documentation mount	Brand publication settings	
Point a developer docs build or release at its own destination	Documentation repository settings and publication destination	
Principal display names
A principal may supply name beside its id and kind. This is an explicit display value, not an identity join or evidence of legal identity, consent or publication approval. Present names must contain a non-whitespace character and no control characters; accepted spelling and spacing are preserved. Different principal keys may have the same name. Omission stays absent, with no key, email, brand or publisher fallback.
Content attribution borrows the selected principal from this catalog. It does not maintain a separate author-name schema; see direct attribution.
Principal websites and identity references
The principal can explicitly select its website, independently from any site it publishes or any contact interface:
[[principals]]
