id = "person:writer"
kind = "person"
name = "A writer"
website = { kind = "site", site = "site:personal" }
same_as = ["https://writer.example/"]

A site website names a declared publication with a public base URL. Its resolved website.url follows the selected public or validated local-preview address; website.canonical_url retains the configured public address for identity data. An outside website uses website = { kind = "external", url = "https://writer.example/" }; both resolved addresses then retain that explicit HTTP(S) value. Native website.destination carries the same link-destination shape as body links: kind, optional exact target site, relationships and destination presentation. Typed site websites classify relative to the owning rendered page or listing; explicit outside websites remain external without hostname inference.
same_as is an ordered list of explicit public HTTP(S) identity references. Declared owned accounts add their resolved URLs to the owning principal after those entries, without duplicates. Duplicate entries, credentials, whitespace and unsafe URL schemes are rejected. These declarations express the owner's selected identity links; Gazette performs no remote identity verification. Without an explicit identity reference or owned account, identity links stay absent. A publisher role, display name, email or displayed social profile establishes no ownership. Page attributions and generated listing items expose the same resolved website and principal data. A Theme can link an author's name with rel="author" without rejoining the catalog or embedding a publication-specific address.
Configure a contact link
Gazette has no generic principal contact field. In particular, contact_email and arbitrary contact maps are rejected as unknown fields rather than being accepted as identity, copied into public output or hidden in an extension bag.
Publication contact interfaces are a separate, supported contract: the brand publication may declare contacts.correspondence, contacts.rights and contacts.discovery. These explicit addresses are available through the shared publication metadata, without joining them to a principal or verifying a mailbox. They neither establish identity nor imply legal responsibility. Publication profiles select workspace accounts through accounts, or retain inline social values. Displaying a profile supplies no principal identity claim; only an explicit account owner adds its URL to that principal’s same_as links.
Principal-owned contacts are not part of the current schema. Use publication contacts for those interfaces rather than adding an unrecognized principal field.
Declare accounts once and select them for display
Keep each public account in the workspace registry, then select its ID wherever a publication should display it:
[[accounts]]
id = "account:writer-github"
platform = "github"
handle = "writer"
owner = "person:writer"

[[accounts]]
id = "account:shared-video"
platform = "youtube"
handle = "@SharedChannel"

[[accounts]]
id = "account:writer-linkedin"
platform = "linkedin"
url = "https://www.linkedin.com/in/writer/"
owner = "person:writer"

The owning principal must already be declared. Omit owner while ownership is unresolved; a publisher, operator or administrator is not an inferred owner. The account can still be displayed. An owned account contributes its URL to that principal’s identity links even when none of the publications displays it. Gazette does not verify account control remotely.
Inside an existing site with its own name, or an existing [[brands.publications]] table, select the accounts:
accounts = ["account:writer-github", "account:shared-video"]

The same IDs may be selected by several sites. Workspace and publisher defaults may also select accounts; a nearer list replaces the entire inherited list, and accounts = [] clears it. Each publication can select one account per platform. Duplicate IDs, duplicate platform-and-URL pairs, unknown owners or selections, repeated selections and collisions with an inline social platform are errors.
An explicit public HTTP(S) url wins. When it is absent, github, x and youtube derive their standard profile URL from handle, accepting one optional leading @. Other platforms, including LinkedIn, require an explicit URL. Handles and optional channel_id retain platform metadata; neither grants access nor enables an integration. Derivation rejects path separators, query or fragment syntax and empty handles.
Selected accounts supply the existing site.metadata.social profiles, so Themes and discovery use the same resolved metadata as inline profiles. gazette check --why social.youtube.url --site site:notes reports the registry declaration that supplied the value, pointing to the handle when the URL was derived. Query accounts to inspect where the publication’s selection came from. Editor navigation follows account selections and their declared owners across included configuration documents.
Independent site responsibilities
Sites may also select rights_holder and default_author principal keys:
# Inside an existing [[sites]] table; all keys must name declared principals.
rights_holder = "example:rights-holder"
default_author = "example:writer"

The rights holder may be a person or organisation; default_author must name a person. A published content object with no attributions credits that configured default author. Any explicit attribution, including a rights-holder-only declaration, keeps its own meaning and prevents this fallback. Draft and archived objects receive no default author. The resolved graph supplies the same credit to the byline, JSON-LD and other consumers. Selecting a default author is a publication policy choice; it does not turn an agent's draft into that person's published work.
rights_holder remains independent site context and supplies no missing content rights claim or licence. Neither field inherits from a publisher or sibling site.
Each site may declare roles alongside its separate publisher reference:
# Inside an existing [[sites]] table; these principal keys must be declared.
roles = [
  { principal = "example:canon-authority", role = "canon-authority" },
  { principal = "example:controller", role = "data-controller" },
  { principal = "example:operator", role = "site-operator" },
  { principal = "example:processor", role = "data-processor" },
]

The core PublicationRoleBinding supplies one exact principal/role pair. The compiler validates every principal and rejects duplicate pairs; it normalizes the set without choosing a primary holder. Multiple principals may have the same role, and one principal may explicitly have several roles. Omission means no declaration, not inheritance from a publisher, another site or workspace defaults. Original TOML positions remain available for editor navigation after normalization.
Page and search data carry the same borrowed principals under site.roles. Site/discovery graphs retain the bindings and only their referenced principals; role edges consume the graph budget. JSON-LD uses the existing technical gazette:siteRoles vocabulary with an explicit site reference, not invented Schema.org properties or author/affiliation aliases. Standard feed authors remain content authors. The complete private registry receives these same bindings.
Role bindings describe the declared responsibilities. They do not create page authorship or establish the authority, consent or publication approval behind a role.
Brand publication settings
A site with its own brand
This complete configuration keeps the publication beside its site identity:
[[principals]]
id = "person:writer"
kind = "person"
name = "A writer"

[[sites]]
id = "site:notes"
name = "Field notes"
publisher = "person:writer"
deployable = false
domain = "notes.example"
port = 8080
language = "en"
contacts = { correspondence = "mail@notes.example" }

domain is a hostname and selects its HTTPS root. Use public_base_url instead when the publication has a deployment prefix or another explicit address. port is the short form of local_port; neither spelling starts a listener. Declaring both spellings of one setting is an error. theme = "theme:example" selects an already configured Theme package; a table may also select its palette. Use either that short form or composition.theme.
The name makes this site its own brand, with the stable generated brand key brand:<site-id>. Publication fields such as authored, machine, processing, legal and documentation_repository belong directly in this site block. Their contracts are the same as in the full brand-publication form below. A second publication binding for the same site is an error.
To keep an existing brand key or declare a parent, add its identity beside the site's name:
# Inside the [[sites]] table above.
brand = { id = "brand:notes", parent = "brand:journal" }

Here brand:journal must be declared elsewhere, using either form. Omit parent for an independent brand. The inline table declares the brand; it does not refer to or merge with another declaration of the same ID. It requires the site's name, and duplicate brands, missing parents and parent cycles remain errors. Brand parentage supplies no publisher, rights holder or author defaults.
Without brand, site:notes still creates brand:site:notes with no parent. Keep the full form for several publications under one brand. Editor navigation follows inline IDs and parent references to their original source; brand field origins find id and parent in the inline table and name beside it. Use publication-origin queries for the effective publication fields and their defaults.
Shared publication settings
Declare shared values once and override only the fields that differ:
[defaults.publication]
language = "en"
machine = { sitemap = true, json_ld = true }

[[publishers]]
id = "person:writer"
publication = { contacts = { rights = "rights@notes.example" } }

The publisher ID must name an existing principal. A publication receives workspace defaults, then the settings of its site's declared publisher, then its own fields. This works with both site forms and with explicit included configuration files. Supported shared fields are language, contacts, accounts, social, machine and processing. Identity, sources, routes, legal selections and chapter order remain explicit.
Tables merge field by field; scalars and lists replace the inherited value. An explicit false or empty list therefore remains an override. An empty table contributes no fields. Defaults are checked even when unused, and the resulting publication must satisfy the complete schema. Publisher settings do not reach another publisher's sites through a common brand, source or Theme.
From a workspace directory, inspect the winning value and its original document and field:
gazette check --why contacts.rights --site site:notes

Use --workspace-root /absolute/workspace for an explicit local workspace, or supply a complete single-document configuration on stdin. The result identifies the site, publisher or workspace default that supplied the field, its source span and its effective value. Query a scalar or list; a merged table can have several origins. This reads configuration without building or publishing a site.
A brand with several publications
The publication's Theme-rendered authored sources are selected here independently of the developer-manual/code-reference documentation destination:
[[brands]]
id = "example:brand"
name = "Example Public Brand"
[[brands.publications]]
site = "example:site"
public_base_url = "https://example.test/"
home = "content:home"
language = "en"
contacts = { correspondence = "hello@example.test", rights = "rights@example.test" }
social = { github = { url = "https://github.com/example", handle = "example" } }
authored = [{ source = "example:authored", target = "publications/example" }]
documentation_repository = { name = "chosen-domain-doc", path = "/absolute/generated/domain-doc", destination = { kind = "git", remote = "https://example.invalid/chosen-domain-doc.git", branch = "published" } }
machine = { sitemap = true, search = 'lexical', json_ld = true, markdown_alternates = { enabled = true, directory_page = 'index.md', file_page = 'append-md', media_type = 'text/markdown', discovery_rel = 'alternate' }, llms = { enabled = true, description_from = 'content:home', representation = 'markdown-alternate', include_human_link = true, sections = [{ title = 'Start here', contents = ['content:home'] }] } }
identity_assets = { site_icon = "image:site-icon", link_preview = "image:link-preview" }

authored is an array of bindings; each source references an existing explicit [[sources]] declaration. Declaration order is retained. Select owner-held roots explicitly rather than copying their pages into one central source. The singular table form is not accepted. target is a logical corpus prefix, not a URL, output folder or inferred project identity. The same ContentBinding shape serves project-documentation placements; the owning field supplies its role. Equal or nested prefixes across authored sources and enabled project-document placements fail complete configuration resolution before any native reads. Disabled placements do not reserve a corpus prefix.
An existing authored or project-document ContentBinding may also name retained_only, an exact set of source-relative opaque files kept solely as input evidence:
# Replace the existing binding, not the publication or source declaration.
authored = [{ source = "example:authored", target = "publications/example", retained_only = ["metadata.bin", "guide/metadata.bin"] }]

Every listed entry must be a captured regular opaque file. Its bytes, inventory entry and provenance remain unchanged, but it has no content, page-companion, asset or output obligation. The disposition stays visible in private inspection. Absent paths, directories, Markdown, notebooks, duplicate paths and conflicting dispositions for the same source are refused. This is not a basename, dotfile, glob or directory-ignore rule; unlisted unknown inputs still fail publication. Relative links, declared resources and program/notebook dependencies cannot use retained-only bytes. Mounted Theme resource inputs and native tools whose exact selected source is a full-tree dependency cannot consume them either.
An optional brand parent names another declared brand. Missing parents and cycles fail resolution; parentage supplies no publisher, controller, contact, language or author inheritance. A publication's optional home names a routed same-site content object in its selected graph. Building one site does not require acquiring another site's home. Excluding the selected home refuses the affected publication rather than silently choosing another page.
Publication language is a normalized BCP 47 tag and supplies the language of content that omits its own. An explicit content language wins. Contact roles remain independent; after shared settings are resolved, omitted values stay absent. Named social profiles require an explicit public HTTP(S) URL; optional handle and channel_id retain supplied platform metadata without enabling an integration. Pages, discovery views and Theme contexts borrow one resolved site.metadata view. It exposes the serving home URL, including an explicit preview prefix, but no native source paths or private deployment coordinates.
The optional static_assets = { route_prefix = "/media/example/" } inside that same binding selects a directory destination for supported local byte transport. It applies equally to authored sources and project-document placements. There is no independent asset-path setting in Theme or an adapter. See the static-asset contract for supported suffixes, source-relative references, shared model fields, bounds and the distinction between copied bytes and public/capability admission.
Compose owner-held legal copy without duplicating it
A brand publication may select exact owner-held legal entries through legal. Each binding names the retained source identity separately from the composed page's identity and route. Add the following fields inside an existing [[brands.publications]] table whose site is already declared:
legal = [
  { source = "example:legal", entry = "terms.md", source_content = "content:owner-terms", id = "content:site-terms", route = "/terms/", family = "utility" },
]

example:legal must have its own ordinary [[sources]] declaration. Its selected terms.md uses a reduced TOML-frontmatter profile, not a site-assigned authored page declaration:
+++
[content]
id = "content:owner-terms"
title = "Terms"
description = "The owner's reusable terms."
lifecycle = "draft"
language = "en"
+++
# Terms

The owner's retained legal prose.

Only id, title, lifecycle and optional description and language belong to that source profile. Site, route, structure, authorship and other page fields are refused. source_content must match the exact source declaration. Gazette retains its body and original coordinates while producing the explicitly named Utility page; it does not rewrite the owner source or create a corporate site. Several publications may reuse one source with distinct output IDs and routes. Source and output identity collisions fail rather than silently choosing a copy.
A binding may also list aliases, released old addresses on the same site that redirect to the composed page. They have the same meaning and checks as an authored route's aliases: each is a site-relative route path, "/tnc-policy/" writes tnc-policy/index.html, and self-aliases, duplicates and collisions with any other route fail.
legal = [
  { source = "example:legal", entry = "terms.md", source_content = "content:owner-terms", id = "content:site-terms", route = "/terms/", aliases = ["/tnc-policy/"], family = "utility" },
]

The composed page receives the publication's shared publisher, roles and public contacts. Its source declaration, entry and digest remain separate from the output identity in private evidence. The publisher must still establish the notice's authorship, legal authority and approval; composing it supplies none of those decisions.
Processing choices describe intent, not running services
The same publication may declare processing independently of its legal source bindings and site roles:
# Inside the existing [[brands.publications]] table.
processing = { hosting = { provider = "github-pages" }, analytics = { enabled = false, provider = "google-analytics" }, subscription = { enabled = false, provider = "google-apps-script" }, discussion = { enabled = false, provider = "giscus" }, webmcp = { enabled = false } }

Hosting names the intended provider; it does not prove deployment. Explicit disabled choices remain visible in private inspection and never activate a service, acquire its credentials or invent a public endpoint. Composed legal pages receive legal_processing with the selected hosting and explicit feature switches. Disabled provider details stay out of that public context; publisher, roles and contacts remain in the one shared site view.
Enabled analytics requires an explicit measurement_id and independently selected publication.analytics/v1 capability. Enabled browser WebMCP requires explicit tools and the independently selected publication.webmcp/v1 capability; its search tool also requires the publication's existing machine search selection. These public client bindings freeze before rendering, without contacting Google or a browser. They load or register nothing automatically. See browser capabilities for exact configuration and Theme composition. Absent or disabled processing conflicts with an enabled corresponding capability instead of silently hiding it. Enabled subscriptions remain unsupported and refuse with workspace_processing_unsupported before source acquisition. WebMCP's browser tools are separate from Gazette's local MCP interface. Enabled Giscus requires the existing selected native discussion capability and its site or rendered-project repository binding; an optional repository must match that binding exactly. Disabled discussion conflicts with an active native discussion selection rather than merely hiding it from the legal page. Unknown provider fields and identities are refused. These declarations do not establish service activity, privacy compliance, consent or publication approval.
Set defaults for project Markdown
An optional field on the existing project placement selects plain Markdown lowering:
[[placements]]
role = 'primary'
site = "site:notes"
project = "example:project"
render = true
discoverable = false
documents = { source = "example:docs", target = "native/example" }
native_markdown = { route_prefix = "/docs/example/", lifecycle = "published", language = "en-US" }

This replaces the corresponding example placement; do not append a duplicate site/project pair. The profile requires the document binding, an explicit directory route ending in /, and a content lifecycle. It applies only to unframed project Markdown, never to publication-authored input or explicit TOML frontmatter. Disabled placement sources remain excluded. The compiler uses the same shared source binding, corpus, graph and route resolver, not a separate native-doc publication model.
The optional language uses the same validated, case-normalized tag type as authored content. It supplies a default only to these unframed native documents; framed content does not inherit it, even when its own language is omitted. When the native profile omits language, the publication's configured language can supply it. If both omit it, language remains absent. Neither filenames nor programming languages select one. This profile supplies no taxonomy memberships or classification inheritance.
The native Markdown contract describes derived coordinate identities, H1/filename title evidence and README/index route selection. Source-relative Markdown links resolve against retained targets; missing/escaping targets and unsupported fragments fail. No collection, authorship, about/mentions or public approval is inferred. Selecting published is an explicit default state, not certification or release permission.
Mount project manuals on an existing site
documentation.mounts selects Theme-rendered native documentation without inventing a project record or a Mintlify destination. It belongs to the workspace root, independently of brands.publications.documentation_repository:
[[documentation.mounts]]
site = "example:site"
landing = "content:home"
name = "Product documentation"
source = "example:docs"
route_prefix = "/manual/"
render = true
discoverable = false
lowering = { lifecycle = "published", language = "en-US" }

The site and source must already be declared. A rendered mount requires explicit lowering.lifecycle; optional language applies only to unframed Markdown, using the same native-document lowering and retained source-relative link resolver as project documentation. Its landing must resolve to an existing same-site routed content object in the selected graph. Theme receives documentation_mount.name and the shared resolved documentation_mount.landing, not private source paths. That association creates no editorial residence, project identity or semantic mention.
render = false validates and reports the declaration without acquiring its source, rendering pages or adding discovery output; lowering may then be omitted. discoverable = true requires rendering. Neither switch approves publication. This renders documentation through a publication Theme. For a separate developer site, use the Mintlify documentation target.
Developer-manual and generated-reference repository settings
The developer-manual and generated code/API-reference target is selected in the brand's publication binding. Its name/path are not inferred from a domain and are not duplicated in the Mintlify adapter, project records or a second site-level setting. Each configured project module may select authored manual sections, generated reference sections or both in one ordered navigation model.
[[brands]]
id = "example:brand"
name = "Example Public Brand"

[[brands.publications]]
site = "example:site"
documentation_repository = { name = "chosen-domain-doc", path = "/absolute/generated/domain-doc" }

Set documentation_repository on the existing selected publication; the enclosing tables above show its placement, not additional brand or publication declarations. workspace::compile resolves the site link; Workspace::documentation_repository borrows that sole configured target. The repository name may differ from the local directory name. One brand may configure several publications, each with a separate target; conflicting site bindings or reused exact destination paths fail resolution. Missing settings mean no configured target, never an invented domain_doc directory.
The local path uses the same native root grammar as source and publication output roots: . selects the explicitly loaded workspace, a confined relative path selects its descendant, and an absolute path selects an external directory. Relative coordinates require retained native workspace acquisition and never use the process current directory. Detached supplied TOML can describe such a path, but cannot materialize it without that native coordinate. The destination must already exist; assembly and declaration alone never create it or grant writes.
An optional delivery selection can use the table form below. Replace an existing inline documentation_repository value rather than declaring both forms:
[brands.publications.documentation_repository]
name = "chosen-domain-doc"
path = "/absolute/generated/domain-doc"
destination = { kind = "git", remote = "https://example.invalid/chosen-domain-doc.git", branch = "published" }

This destination belongs to the complete documentation repository and never inherits the authored publication's destination. Omission is local-only. Exact duplicate remote/branch selections across authored and generated repositories, including two targets on one site, fail complete workspace resolution. Different branches remain different selected targets; Gazette does not infer whether a remote spelling aliases another native repository.
This declaration selects a destination and documentation inputs. Assembly checks target compatibility; native output operations separately check paths and require write permission. Configuration does not create a directory, Git repository or hosted site.
Select repository developer manuals and generated reference here. Product-user guides remain owner-held Content rendered as Gazette collections; commands and filenames do not determine that audience. A brand's publication binding does not establish publisher, rights or legal ownership.
Publication destination
Delivery selection belongs alongside the brand's other publication settings:
[[brands.publications]]
site = "example:site"
destination = { kind = "git", remote = "https://example.invalid/publication.git", branch = "published" }

Add destination to the existing publication table rather than declaring that site twice. Workspace::destination borrows this sole selection. Omission means local-only operation; no remote, branch or provider is inferred. A Git delivery target is not a GitHub account or deployment-platform integration.
The compiler validates the exact remote text and literal branch grammar using the same rule as release authorization verification. It rejects unknown target kinds, malformed tables and duplicate exact remote/branch selections across sites. It does not normalize or resolve remote aliases, probe reachability or infer that differently spelled remotes are distinct native repositories.
Local preparation stores the authored selection in its immutable intent and includes it in the private output-policy input, not in public output. A declaration does not create a branch, configure Git, establish the remote pre-state, select credentials or grant permission to publish. Developer-manual/generated-reference repository settings remain a separate path and do not inherit this publication destination implicitly.
Back to workspace.

Choose and read workspace sources
Bind a project to source files, check which files Gazette will read, and inspect the parsed documents before you build.
Add a project's documentation
Extend workspace-example.toml from the first example with the declarations below. They place one project's documentation on the existing site:notes; the principal, sites and brand already declared there stay unchanged.
[[projects]]
id = "example:project"
name = "Field Notes tooling"
lifecycle = "done"
visibility = "public"
availability = "gated"

[[sources]]
id = "example:docs"
location = { kind = "filesystem", root = "/absolute/path/to/field-notes-tool/docs" }

[[placements]]
role = 'primary'
site = "site:notes"
project = "example:project"
render = true
discoverable = false
documents = { source = "example:docs", target = "docs/project" }

Replace the absolute source root with your documentation directory, then check the complete file:
gazette check --stdin < workspace-example.toml

This checks the declarations without reading the source. Continue with source acquisition to read it. The filesystem source observes current local files. For a revision-pinned repository source, select kind = "repository", its repository root, the full lowercase commit ID and a confined subdirectory; use the repository's actual checked-out commit.
role is required. Every project that has any publication placement has exactly one primary placement and may have zero or more mirror placements. The primary is the project's canonical documentation home; a mirror is another publication placement for that same project. This edge neither creates a syndicated content copy nor a route alias/redirect, and it is unrelated to projects.origin (original, successor-fork or convenience-mirror). Missing, unknown, all-mirror and multiple-primary declarations fail complete workspace resolution.
A source root is a typed portable selection: . means the selected workspace root, a confined relative path means a descendant of that root, and an absolute path deliberately selects an external native root. Relative roots are resolved once by the application after the workspace itself has been selected; they never consult the process current directory during compilation. The logical spelling, not the observed absolute location, participates in configuration identity.
A local authored tree that is not a Git repository uses the distinct filesystem source kind. subdirectory is optional and, when present, is a confined literal selection beneath its resolved source root:
[[sources]]
id = "example:authored"
location = { kind = "filesystem", root = "sources/authored", subdirectory = "content" }

Acquisition retains one bounded complete tree and its exact bytes. The resulting tree identity is observation evidence only: it is not an atomic external snapshot, repository revision, admission, rights, permission or release approval. Repository and parent-gitlink sources continue to require their exact pins; failure never falls back between source kinds.
The example deliberately combines a completed project, public visibility and gated availability. These axes are independent. Placement controls are also explicit independent selections, not evidence that materialization or discovery is permitted. deployable belongs to the whole site, not a project placement, and does not authorize release. No source, database, output directory or remote is opened by this command.
projects.name is an optional explicit display value, preserved exactly. Blank or control-containing names fail; omission emits no name and never substitutes the identity key, repository folder or a page title. Equal names do not join distinct project identities. The same catalog value reaches Theme/page data, search, graph, JSON-LD and the private registry, including name changes/removal through complete-set replacement. This is local declaration/projection, not owner identity or public-field approval, and it does not delegate the field to an external fact provider.
projects.repository is an optional, explicitly published repository address, independent of acquisition roots, Git remotes and source pins. Workspace resolution requires an absolute HTTP(S) URL with a host and no credentials, whitespace, control characters or backslashes. Accepted spelling is retained exactly rather than normalized into another identity. Omission stays absent; compilation never contacts the address or substitutes an observed origin remote. The same project record supplies Theme, page/search/graph and private registry data; JSON-LD projects it as codeRepository. It is not a deploy destination, software licence, fork classification, reachability result or public-field approval.
projects.license is an optional owner-evidenced SPDX expression for the project's software at the selected source revision. Gazette validates strict SPDX syntax and retains the exact admitted expression; it does not canonicalize lax aliases, derive a licence URL, inspect repository files or infer a value from the repository address, source capture, package manifest or content. Omission stays absent/held. The same typed project value reaches Theme/page data, search, graph, JSON-LD and the private registry. It is never a content licence, chain-of- title decision, public admission or permission to publish.
projects.origin declares project lineage independently from names, addresses, state, ownership and client relationships. It is optional: omission means unspecified, not original work. The closed forms are:
# In the relevant [[projects]] declaration, select exactly one form:
origin = { kind = "original" }
# origin = { kind = "successor-fork", upstream = "project:upstream" }
# origin = { kind = "convenience-mirror", upstream = "project:upstream" }

An upstream must resolve to a distinct project in the same catalog. Cycles and unknown/wrong-kind endpoints fail complete workspace resolution; names and remote URLs cannot repair them. The upstream scalar participates in existing editor definition/reference navigation and source-origin inspection. A lineage edge does not create a placement, content membership, publisher role, rights grant, or a client engagement. The same declaration supplies page/search/graph data, JSON-LD and private registry projection; public discovery cannot expose a private or unlisted upstream through this edge. Public upstream identity references do not automatically export that project's full record or require hosted docs.
Syndication selections also belong to the brand publication, not to a renderer; see feed configuration and identity. Developer-manual and generated code/API-reference selection also belongs to the brand's existing documentation_repository.build: exact project modules, explicit manual page/asset selections, reference inputs, source bindings and target options are resolved there once. Its separate local acquisition/assembly path does not turn manuals into authored-document placements or publication ContentNodes. See configured documentation assembly.
Bind named roots on each machine
Use a named root when the same workspace reads content or writes output in different locations on different machines. Select the machine-binding file in the root Gazette document, before its tables:
machine_binding = "tools/studio.local.toml"

[[sources]]
id = "example:manual"
location = { kind = "included-filesystem", root = "machine:documents/Project", include = ["docs"] }

The selected binding supplies its roots table. It can also contain settings for other tools; Gazette reads only this table:
[roots]
documents = "/absolute/content"
repositories = "/absolute/repositories"
builds = "../generated"

Absolute values keep their native meaning. Relative values start at the binding file's parent directory, so ../generated above selects the workspace's generated directory. Gazette does not expand environment variables or home-directory markers, search for another binding, or fall back to the process current directory. Root names start with an ASCII letter, contain letters, digits, _ or -, and have at most 64 bytes. A machine:name coordinate selects the bound root itself; its optional /path uses the same confined-path rules as other relative selections.
The same coordinates work in publication output.directory and documentation_repository.path, such as machine:builds/notes and machine:builds/notes-doc. The binding selects paths; it grants no read, write, execution or publication permission. Keep machine-specific values in the existing private binding file, outside committed publication configuration.
Native workspace loading captures the selected binding alongside the root and included documents, then resolves paths from those retained bytes. The binding is not an included configuration module and cannot be selected as one; only the root document may choose it. Its exact bytes remain in acquisition evidence, while the portable declarations determine logical configuration identity. A missing or invalid binding stops workspace loading; using an unbound root stops the operation that needs it. Supplied TOML bytes alone cannot resolve named roots: load the workspace from an explicit native root to use them.
The native LoadedWorkspace result includes its selected native_root and source_roots, a map from configured source keys to resolved native roots before each source's subdirectory selection. CLI, MCP and SDK consumers use this projection instead of interpreting root spellings themselves. Unbound roots are absent, so an unused source does not prevent loading the workspace. This private projection is neither source acquisition nor proof of existence, branch or revision. Derived contexts must match the native workspace root and check the complete configuration inventory, including the binding, before reusing these paths. Moving identical configuration files requires a new native load; the logical configuration digest alone does not identify machine-specific inputs.
Select filesystem inputs
For a manual source, name the files and directories it may read:
[[sources]]
id = "source:manual"
location = { kind = "included-filesystem", root = "tool", include = ["docs", "README.md"] }

include takes one to 128 unique literal paths relative to the source root. Each path must exist with that exact spelling, including letter case. A file includes only itself; a directory includes its complete tree, including hidden files. Gazette retains necessary parent directories and keeps paths relative to the root, so these inputs arrive as docs/… and README.md. Adding a sibling folder does not expand the capture. Missing selections, symlinks, unsupported files and exceeded size or depth limits stop acquisition. The declared includes remain in generated-source provenance.
Includes select current local bytes, including held edits. Add expected_branch = "main" to the location when the read must happen on a particular local branch. Gazette checks the branch at the exact repository worktree root before and after capture. A different branch, detached or unborn HEAD, invalid branch name or missing repository stops acquisition; Gazette never checks out a branch or changes Git state. Omitting the field keeps ordinary filesystem capture, with no Git requirement.
The branch check does not pin a commit or establish that working bytes match committed content. Use a repository source when the request requires revision verification. The direct SDK placement format uses kind = "included_filesystem" with the same root, include and optional expected_branch fields. Generated-source provenance retains the includes and the checked branch requirement.
Exclude named paths
filesystem continues to capture the complete selected root. For a worktree that intentionally omits administrative or replaced files, use a distinct contract:
[[sources]]
id = "source:theme"
location = { kind = "filtered-filesystem", root = "/absolute/theme", exclude = [".git", "tokens/world.css"] }

exclude contains one to 128 unique, validated relative entry paths. An excluded directory excludes its descendants. Exclusions apply before inspecting or opening that entry; all other files, including dotfiles, retain ordinary capture semantics. The selection and exact exclusion list remain in source provenance. Repository and submodule capture are unchanged. When a theme resource is mounted from a design input, its package-local counterpart must be absent from that selected capture; Gazette still rejects ambiguous local-plus-mounted origins.
Acquire pinned documentation for a site
Run gazette check --stdin --acquire-site site:notes < workspace-example.toml to read the sources for that site's rendered project placements. Gazette first resolves the declarations and checks for overlapping targets. It then checks source confinement, the pinned Git objects and aggregate limits before returning the captured inventory. A failure leaves no successful subset. The command skips disabled placements and placements on other sites. It does not fetch, check out, write, stage, open a database or approve publication.
Keep the report private. It names the configured roots, site and verification for each target. In Rust, build::acquire_site also keeps the immutable document bytes so later compiler phases can use that same capture. --max-placements, --max-acquired-entries and --max-acquired-bytes limit all acquisitions for the site. Per-source limits still apply.
Use kind = "submodule" with root, parent_commit, submodule_path and subdirectory instead of a repository commit when the parent pins the child. Gazette reads the revision from the parent's gitlink. It fails if the child is missing and never switches to a sibling clone. A workspace-relative root uses forward slashes and has no traversal, repeated separators, controls or platform prefix. An external root must be absolute and cannot contain dot components or repeated separators. Gazette does not expand home-directory markers.
Require every enabled source
Gazette represents two source-selection states only:
render = false deliberately disables that project-document placement and does not acquire it; and
render = true requires an explicit documents binding, and every selected source must be captured and verified as part of the complete set.
discoverable remains independent and cannot weaken acquisition. There is no generic required/optional field on ContentBinding; an attempted obligation field is rejected instead of being silently ignored. Consequently a missing selected source is a hard acquisition failure and never reuses stale output. Project state, visibility, availability and discoverability do not make a selected source optional.
Parse the captured project documents
Run this after choosing the workspace and site:
gazette check --stdin --acquire-site site:notes --parse-documents < workspace-example.toml

In Rust, call acquired.parse_documents(corpus::Limits::default()). The returned ParsedSite borrows the acquisition and keeps the parsed trees for later resolution. It reuses those bytes rather than reading changed files.
Gazette accounts for every regular file under its placement target and relative source path. Empty directories remain in the inventory.
Input	How Gazette parses it	
.md or .markdown (case-insensitive)	Markdown. A first line of +++ starts strict TOML frontmatter. Malformed framing or TOML fails the parse. This inspection adds no title, author, publisher or lifecycle to plain Markdown. A later build can apply a configured placements.native_markdown profile.	
.landing.yaml or .landing.yml	Structured landing. Other YAML is opaque and does not provide Markdown frontmatter.	
.ipynb	The notebook syntax profile. Gazette rejects invalid notebooks without fixing IDs, guessing roles or treating them as downloads.	
Other files	Opaque assets. The inventory records byte identities even for files that are not valid text.	
The report lists parsed and opaque inputs in path order. It can include private source information. It is not public search or a rendered site. Raw HTML can appear in parsed syntax and still fail the HTML-fragment renderer. Links do not imply collection, journey, ownership or other relationships.
--max-corpus-files, --max-corpus-bytes, --max-corpus-nodes and --max-corpus-metadata-nodes limit the entire corpus. Per-document and aggregate path limits also apply. Duplicate input and whole-set limit failures stop before parsing. A document error stops at the first failing logical path, without a partial success. For semantic checks and templates, continue to local rendering.
Resolution rules
Publication content resolves against the declared sites, projects, principals and taxonomies. Publication bindings select which source bytes enter that resolution; source paths do not supply editorial relationships.
Bind content to the workspace
The Rust API's Compilation::resolve_content consumes the existing typed content declaration and returns a ResolvedContent only after both structural relationships and every content home-site reference resolve. It borrows this exact compilation, including the source digest, instead of copying a site catalog into each renderer or database projection. site_for resolves an exact content identity to its declared home site; a matching principal or project key is not a substitute site.
Draft and archived objects are checked too. Cross-site relationships keep their explicit homes; a site's deployable=false does not make its structure invalid. There is no permission inference or lifecycle filtering. This is an internal structural phase, not a new frontmatter format, a CLI build or publication admission. See the content model for the current API and remaining seams.
Publication acquisition
build::acquire_publication captures the consumer's presentation sources, including mounted resource sources in its selected Theme/dependency closure, and all configured authored and enabled project-document sources once per exact source key under one aggregate budget. Workspace::content_bindings() is the shared role-aware view used by acquisition and mapping; content_source() resolves a logical entry back to that same declaration without guessing from public URLs. Other publications participate in graph resolution, not in the selected site's primary output. Presentation metadata checks only presentation-role sources. parse_publication borrows captured bytes; no source scan or hidden reread occurs. The local rendering path additionally verifies that each object's declared home matches the publication that owns its source binding. The source's project identity is provenance, separate from the document's explicit about/mentions, collections and journeys. Binding data does not imply authorship, rights, or public admission. Native coordinates remain private acquisition evidence.
Back to workspace.

Pale architecture
Every coding tool asks for permissions and context at each step, and the same rules end up repeated in every session. Pale is the meta harness through which Weave, Scope, Counsel, RawFish and Gazette act, a harness over the tools people already use; RawFish and Gazette run alone, and Pale may coordinate them. It starts from a description of a person's world: the people, projects, applications and permissions their work depends on. The compiler turns that description into a checked version the tools can use. Today the local tools answer what applies to a repository, what a proposed change would affect and which guidance files it would generate. The path from a Claude Code or Codex hook to the resident, where the hook asks what may happen and what context the agent needs, is the problem in front; references to each owner's records carry changes between people and agents. The same coordination model supports people working without agents. For that experience, start with Introduction to Pale.
The compiler and repository-guidance path work locally. The ordinary hook path supports an explicit hook-only connection that currently refuses native work. Successful admission through an authenticated resident and enforcement by the actual host remain unproved. An editor can already explain why a project receives particular guidance; carrying a live operation to its application also needs the route, permissions and provider checks described below.
Important

Use matching builds. The local tools compile and inspect workspaces, review changes and install repository guidance. A complete resident deployment and PaleUniverse are still in development. Use the API and contracts from the same build while a stable release is pending.
A shared engine, a personal workspace, a running deployment
Object	What it supplies	
Distribution	Reusable engine, contracts, SDKs, interfaces and Packages	
Workspace	A person's declarations about their projects, relationships and tools	
Deployment	The environment, machine bindings and running state	
A workspace may describe a household, company and client engagement together. Each has its own people, records and permissions. A connected application controls access to its records and decides what changes it accepts. Pale's ability to read or call a path gives it no authority over that path: native applications, a person's private workspace and a Pack's distribution each keep their own owner. A request that crosses them is split into separate effects, and each effect Pale has no authority for goes to its owner. Workspace declarations and machine bindings let people share the same engine while keeping their own paths and policies. Another person can describe a different world with the same engine.
Compile the description before using it
The compiler checks the source documents and resolves their relationships. The right call depends on the answer the caller needs.
Compilation	Input	What the caller can inspect	
Portable workspace	Logical labels and complete document bytes	PortableWorkspaceCompilation for authoring, inspection and comparison. The caller supplies bytes, so the compiler needs no filesystem access.	
Effective profile	A compiled workspace, a project and execution workspace, and the required Package and private inputs	The guidance and configuration that apply to that responsibility	
One-shot	The complete runtime configuration and machine bindings	A handle for the rendered repository output in memory. Plan repository changes in a separate call.	
A repository ID identifies a repository in the workspace. Machine bindings tell Pale which checkout or executable to use on this machine. For a missing document, check the compilation inputs. When the configuration compiles but an operation cannot run, check the executable and the provider.
The portable example contains one project and one execution workspace. The SDK guides show how to compile those documents in an embedded application.
Compose guidance without turning prose into permission
Packages supply reusable roles, procedures and policies. The workspace names what a responsibility needs, and the compiler resolves the prerequisites. Repositories can use the same method from one maintained source.
For example, change a repository's role from code work to security review. Its generated role and policy references can change while its own instructions continue to supply build commands and project facts. Inspect the proposed guidance first, then compare it with the repository's files in a file plan. The guidance starter runs this workflow without a runtime provider.
An agent uses the Markdown to make judgments. An operation gets permission from Pale's checks of the route, contract, capability bindings and caller authorization. The provider must satisfy that operation's contract. A provider name in a configuration file only identifies what to bind.
Package authoring explains how workspaces choose and combine resources. Package source bundles explains how to distribute them.
Compare configuration before applying a file plan
A review compares the current compilation with the proposed one. It identifies what changed and which subjects depend on that input. A dependent subject may still have the same resulting value. Keep the compilation and comparison handles for follow-up queries. A display summary or hash cannot reconstruct either handle.
To write guidance after a review, create a file plan against the repository's current files. The CLI shows the differences and remembers that proposal for guidance apply; SDK callers can also pass its digest explicitly. Pale checks the inputs and files again, preserves project instructions and refuses conflicting files or changes to files it manages. If a write is interrupted, use recovery to determine what happened before trying again.
Runtime materialization makes its own file plan and checks write permissions separately. To take over a file Pale does not manage, request adoption explicitly. Removing an adopted whole file later deletes it without restoring an earlier backup. See workspace planning for both kinds of plan, or Add coding instructions to a repository for the installation walkthrough.
Carry operations across interruptions
Delegated work can outlive its caller. If the caller loses a response, another application may still be acting. The resident gives the operation a durable handle so the caller can find it again.
Operation	What it does	
Start	Return an operation handle before dispatch	
Advance	Perform one limited resident turn	
Observe	Read the current signed records	
Cancel	Request a stop. Observe the operation afterward to learn whether it stopped.	
If a send succeeds and the response is lost, a second send may duplicate the action. Pale must check the application that sent it before deciding what to do next. Pale's journal tracks its own state transitions. The connected application keeps the record of what actually happened there. Beside the journal Pale keeps genealogy, the history of context: append-only edge records that show where a piece of work came from, what it relied on and what followed, while each record stays with its owner. The resident components keep these edges as tested records. Scope's write-back of a pointer to the context it gave each agent is the work in front; once it completes the chain, that chain is what Reckon, Causality's evaluation laboratory, learns from.
The embedding application supplies ResidentAttachment. Its carrier authenticates the resident. Its response checks verify signatures, changes to who may act and the proofs needed to reject a rollback. Use the Rust SDK or the A2A interface to attach explicitly. The ordinary CLI can load an explicit hook-only connection, which still blocks native work and exposes no operation records. Ordinary CLI and MCP startup install no resident service and provide no resident operation attachment.
Keep one implementation behind the interfaces
pale-application owns compilation, comparison, planning and operation behavior. pale-sdk exposes it to clients. The language bindings wrap that API. The CLI calls it directly; MCP reuses the CLI's dispatcher. LSP, ACP and A2A use the SDK for their editor, coding-session and delegation tasks.
Adapters implement I/O behind ports. Integrations translate between the host and Pale's API and keep using the application that owns each record.
Rust wire records define the shared contracts. The schema and language types are generated from them. Runtime calls also check the relationships in a request and whether the caller may act. Read a failure's diagnostic fields directly. If the compiler can propose a source correction, verify that its source precondition still matches before writing it.
Find the responsible layer when something goes wrong
Symptom	Where to look	
A document or reference is rejected	The diagnostic's source location and the workspace's declared documents	
A project receives unexpected guidance	Its effective profile, Package choices and comparison explanation	
A saved plan no longer matches	Changed inputs or repository file baselines	
Configuration compiles but an operation cannot run	The host capability, machine binding and provider readiness	
A resident response is uncertain	Use the operation handle and check the record in the application that owns the result.	
Scene geometry works but live intake cannot start	Check whether Pale issued the organization or comparison handle for the intended recipient.	
The interface manuals and SDK manuals define inputs, results and handle lifetimes. Scene distinguishes geometry from live workspace intake.
Extend the layer that owns the behavior
Add shared behavior in pale-application and expose it through pale-sdk. Change a wire record at its Rust definition, then regenerate the schema and language types. Put host presentation in an interface, I/O in an adapter and reusable agent procedure in a Package. Keep the core's types neutral: one application's meanings belong in its adapter or integration, and adding them to a shared kernel enum to make an adapter convenient puts that application's semantics in every user of the kernel. Integrations call the supported API.
For a new procedure, follow Package authoring. For an attached delegation, use the A2A call contract. Source layout maps the implementation, and Contributing explains contribution requirements.

Diagnose a local installation
pale doctor reports what it can establish from the compiled executable, an explicitly selected workspace and the machine's declared bindings. It keeps failed checks alongside independent results, with an explanation of what to fix. It changes no workspace files, installs nothing and performs no recovery or cleanup.
Build the CLI, then run:
pale --workspace /absolute/workspace/pale-workspace.toml \
  --project demo --execution-workspace default --machine local doctor

The four selectors use the ordinary workspace compiler. Without the complete selection, doctor still checks the compiled platform and embedded contracts and reports dependent checks as unavailable. Reports can contain selected private paths and source facts; keep them within the workspace's disclosure scope. A workspace failure retains the compiler's diagnostic code, causes, notes and safe facts; it does not suppress separately requested build measurements.
Read the checks
Each check is passed, failed, unavailable or not_selected. A pass establishes only the named observation. unavailable means required declarations or an implemented inspection path are missing; not_selected means the compiled instance does not select that optional state root or any agent execution path. Neither a successful compilation nor a matching generated file establishes resident readiness or permission to work.
The current command checks the compiled platform; admission of the embedded contract registry; workspace and distribution-lock compilation; selected repository directories and authority directories or exact files; declared reading-order containment; the bound Pale executable and native harness identities; selected state roots; and installed repository files against their admitted projection. Contract admission uses the existing registry checks, including raw schema and descriptor identities and offline reference closure. It does not regenerate schemas or repair a lock. Executable checks use the existing bounded probes of the exact declared binaries.
Exact toolchain pins, an immutable executable release with component references and notices, the core/MONAD component-selection constraint, and owner-native compatibility packets have no complete declaration or inspection path in this command. They remain unavailable. The command also lacks an authenticated resident diagnosis and actual host callback qualification: a socket, process or matching hook file cannot substitute for recovery, generation, session or enforcement evidence. Gas Town continues to own its Beads and Dolt inspection. The trust and recovery design describes the remaining deployment work.
Add --result-format json before doctor for the ordinary CLI envelope. Its result contains checks_passed, checks and builds. completion: "complete" means the report finished, including unfavorable or unavailable observations. Exit status is 0 only when all selected checks pass; failed or unavailable checks produce 1. The current missing deployment paths therefore keep a full diagnosis from returning success. CLI parsing and SDK-initialization failures retain their ordinary diagnostic behavior.
Measure build directories
Select up to 32 absolute physical directories. Doctor does not discover or clean build trees:
pale --result-format json doctor \
  --build-root /absolute/repository/target \
  --build-root /absolute/other-repository/dist \
  --build-limit 10737418240

The optional ceiling is in logical regular-file bytes per tree; equality passes. Every selected root has a result, including empty, missing and incomplete trees. A result includes logical_bytes, file_count, skipped_symlinks, complete and errors. Hard links count once per directory entry and sparse files count their logical lengths. These numbers are not allocated, exclusive or reclaimable space. Do not add overlapping roots together.
Roots reached through symlinks are refused and links inside a tree are skipped. Confined traversal admits at most one million entries and 128 levels per tree. A traversal failure leaves the total absent; later file-measurement failures retain an explicitly partial total and up to 32 errors. Concurrent builds can change a tree during the scan, so the report is not a snapshot. Review errors before using a total, and obtain the owner's deletion decision separately.
The transitional vault tool uses this same native measurement. From the repository root, select the built executable explicitly:
python3 tools/vault.py --root /absolute/knowledge \
  --pale-executable /absolute/path/to/pale \
  --build-root /absolute/repository/target --json builds

Its check command accepts the same executable and build options. The Python consumer never scans build files or builds Pale itself; an absent, incompatible or timed-out executable becomes an incomplete measurement. Other unavailable doctor checks do not discard a successfully completed build result. The vault tool retains its own existing finding format for read errors and size ceilings.
Keep build reuse separate from cleanup
Keep each working copy's Cargo target directory separate, as described in the source layout. Reusing a target can let Cargo accept another copy's stale output when source timestamps are older than its fingerprints. Disabling incremental compilation limits growth but does not fix that failure.
Compiler-result caching is a different mechanism. The bounded check below exercises an explicitly selected sccache with Rust 1.94.0, separate targets and old timestamps. It requires correct output from different source copies, a real cache hit for an unchanged dependency at one shared path, and invalidation when that dependency's include_str! input changes:
python3 tools/check_compiler_cache.py \
  --sccache /absolute/path/to/sccache \
  --toolchain 1.94.0 --work-root /absolute/disposable-checks

The check uses one private local server and a 128 MiB cache beneath its own temporary directory. It stops that server and removes only its fixture when finished. It neither changes existing targets nor installs a wrapper or global setting. Copies have equal package names and versions, but distinct path-source identities; the unchanged dependency retains one source path. A passing result qualifies those tracked Rust inputs only.
The sccache Rust limitations include untracked files read by procedural macros and uncached crates that invoke the linker. Its local cache requires one server per cache directory. Keep those limits in any deployment qualification; this check does not justify sharing Cargo targets, enabling arbitrary source generators or removing existing build material.

Getting started
Build pale from the repository, then use its built-in path computation to check the executable. The command runs without a configured workspace. The same build supplies the executable for the repository guidance walkthrough.
Requirements
Use a Pale checkout and Rust 1.94 or later with Cargo. The checkout supplies the matching Pale packages through its Cargo configuration. Cargo may download other dependencies during the build. The Pale packages are currently available as source.
Build the command-line tool
Build from the repository root
Run Cargo from the checkout root so it uses the checkout's dependency and target settings.
cargo build --locked --manifest-path interfaces/cli/Cargo.toml
export PALE="$PWD/target/debug/pale"

If your Cargo configuration uses another target directory, set PALE to that build's actual executable.
Check the command
"$PALE" --help

Look for workspace, guidance, review and action commands. Keep this terminal open so the product guides can use your PALE variable.
Continue your task
To use Pale, follow Add coding instructions to a repository or Inspect your workspace. To embed the compiler, choose an SDK and start with the three-document workspace example.
Run a first computation
Print the input contract for pale.compute.path-inventory, then pass it one path on standard input.
"$PALE" action describe pale.compute.path-inventory
printf '%s\n' \
  '{"kind":"path_inventory","payload":{"style":"posix_relative","paths":["src/./lib.rs"]}}' \
  | "$PALE" action pale.compute.path-inventory

In the JSON response, result.output.payload.entries[0].normalized_path should be src/lib.rs. Pale computes that value from the string you supplied, with no file access.
If something goes wrong
If the command is missing, check whether the build finished and where Cargo wrote the executable. Set PALE to that path. If Pale rejects the JSON, read the diagnostic and compare the input with the schema from action describe before retrying.
Use the CLI reference for structured results and errors. See the architecture for the layers that handle those requests.

Gazette integration
Convert Gazette's native render result into the receipt used by Pale's publication checks. The adapter checks that the report belongs to the request you made and keeps the original report bytes with the receipt. It does not render a site, reopen the output tree or install a Pale provider.
To create a publication, use Gazette's first-publication guide. This guide is for an application that already invokes Gazette and needs to verify its result.
Choose the report shape
Gazette result	Adapter	What you receive	
CLI render-sites --local or MCP render_sites	inspectLocalRenderReport	The complete site-set report, original JSON and digest	
An inventory-only set containing exactly one site	localRenderReceipt	A receipt with retained_files: false; pass requireRetainedFiles: false explicitly	
MCP stage_rendered_site	retainedRenderReceipt	A single-site receipt and its fresh output directory	
Single-site supplied-TOML CLI result with retained files	verifyLocalRenderReceipt from the shared verifier	Verification of the existing neutral receipt, without another projection	
The Gazette render contract defines each request and its output. Inventory-only reports describe in-memory output, not files you can open. The singleton projection refuses a multi-site report rather than dropping the other sites.
Verify a staged result
Record the request before invoking Gazette
Choose the site and canonical output parent. Use Gazette's workspace load to obtain the compiled-workspace digest, and hash the exact request you will send.
Keep these values independently of the response. Taking the expected site or digest from the response would allow a different successful render to pass as the requested one.
Check the native call's outcome
Invoke stage_rendered_site with its required local permissions and limits. Check the RPC and tool outcomes before passing the original UTF-8 report bytes to this adapter. A JSON success field cannot stand in for a successful transport.
Project the original report
The following helper can sit in your caller next to receipt.mjs. Each input comes from the request or the actual invocation, rather than an invented successful report:
import { retainedRenderReceipt } from './receipt.mjs';

export function verifyStagedPublication({
  reportBytes,
  rpcSucceeded,
  exitCode,
  toolIsError,
  expectedSite,
  expectedWorkspaceSha256,
  expectedOutputParent,
  requestSha256,
  maximumBytes,
}) {
  if (!rpcSucceeded) throw new Error('Gazette RPC did not succeed');
  return retainedRenderReceipt(reportBytes, {
    expectedSite,
    expectedWorkspaceSha256,
    expectedOutputParent,
    requestSha256,
    exitCode,
    toolIsError,
    maximumBytes,
  });
}

reportBytes must contain complete JSON. expectedOutputParent is the absolute normalized parent you requested; maximumBytes is a positive integer report limit. The adapter requires exitCode: 0 and toolIsError: false, and verifies the requested site, compiled workspace, inventory and direct-child directory.
Inspect the output before using it
The receipt keeps the inventory, directory, request digest and original JSON with its SHA-256. Its build_selection is the single requested site. Open or inspect the staged tree and compare its complete membership and bytes with the original inventory.
The adapter verifies the report, not the current files on disk. A successful check here cannot establish that an output file was not changed later.
Work with inventory-only results
For inspectLocalRenderReport, supply expectedSelection, expectedConfiguration, requestSha256, the actual exitCode and maximumBytes. The adapter compares the complete site set and configuration, then checks source failures and every site's output evidence.
Use localRenderReceipt only when that set contains one site and your caller explicitly accepts the absence of retained files. If your application needs the actual trees in memory, use Gazette's SDK set-rendering API instead of reconstructing them from an inventory.
Keep native bytes and limits distinct
The original JSON text is preserved even after parsing. A neutral receipt projection refuses integers JavaScript cannot represent safely; a parsed number must not silently replace exact native evidence. The set inspector can still preserve the original report for another consumer.
The report-size limit is separate from Gazette's rendering limits. For example, directory_bytes limits the returned path, while output budgets limit rendered data. The native request also decides source reads, staging and math or diagram execution.
The Publication manifest declares Pale's build operation, and its local-render recipe defines the receipt requirement. Using these report functions does not admit or activate that provider.
Diagnose a refused report
A selection mismatch needs the correct request or a source correction. Do not change the expectation to fit the response. Other failures include incomplete source capture, missing or extra sites, a different output parent, invalid UTF-8 and unsuccessful native outcomes.
Diagnostics omit private source and site locators. Keep the original response privately when investigating a refusal. If the report passes but a file is absent or changed, inspect the staged directory. A new render is a new result, not a repair of the old report.
Extend the adapter
Keep Gazette report interpretation in receipt.mjs and shared receipt rules in tools/publication-verification/receipt.mjs. When a native shape changes, update the interpretation and its success and refusal cases. From the Pale root:
node --test integrations/gazette/receipt.test.mjs

These tests check parsing and projection. A change to native rendering also needs its actual Gazette invocation and output checks.

Pale for Visual Studio Code
Use this extension to edit Pale Workspace configuration, inspect the resulting profile, and review a proposed change in Visual Studio Code. It starts or connects to pale-lsp and presents standard language features plus the Pale Profile Explorer. The language server and compiler remain the owners of configuration meaning and diagnostics.
Run the extension locally
Use a matching Pale source checkout, Rust 1.94 or later, Node.js 22 or later, and VS Code 1.96 or later. This is a source-development setup, not a published extension install. It lets you edit the small portable workspace below; a full machine-bound profile needs its own configuration.
From the repository root, build the language server:
cargo build --locked --manifest-path interfaces/lsp/Cargo.toml

With the checkout's default Cargo target directory, the executable is target/debug/pale-lsp. If you chose a different target directory, use that build's actual absolute path in the settings below.
The extension also needs the matching local TypeScript contracts. From sdk/js/contracts, with its pinned build dependencies available, build and pack it into an existing artifact directory:
npm run build
npm pack --ignore-scripts --pack-destination /absolute/path/editor-artifacts

Then run from integrations/vscode:
npm install --ignore-scripts --no-save /absolute/path/editor-artifacts/rtepl-pale-contracts-0.0.1.tgz
npm run build

The local archive supplies the private contracts package; npm can fetch the extension's other dependencies. --no-save leaves the owning package and lock unchanged. The contracts manual describes that package's separate build and validation behavior.
Configure an editor workspace
Create a new folder and copy the three files from the portable workspace example into it: pale-workspace.toml, resolution.lock.toml and universe.lock.toml. Keep their names and contents together. Work on this copy rather than editing the repository's example in place.
Create .vscode/settings.json in that folder:
{
  "pale.server.path": "/absolute/path/to/pale/target/debug/pale-lsp",
  "pale.workspace.rootManifest": "pale-workspace.toml",
  "pale.workspace.machineId": "",
  "pale.workspace.sources": [
    {
      "path": "pale-workspace.toml",
      "languageId": "pale-toml",
      "role": "workspace-manifest"
    },
    {
      "path": "resolution.lock.toml",
      "languageId": "pale-toml",
      "role": "workspace-resolution-lock"
    },
    {
      "path": "universe.lock.toml",
      "languageId": "pale-toml",
      "role": "workspace-universe-lock"
    }
  ]
}

Replace the server path with your actual build. Source paths are relative to the folder you open. The extension sends exactly this source list; it does not infer roles or discover the other inputs a larger workspace might need. The empty machine ID is deliberate for this portable example.
For compact Packages, register each instruction page with "languageId": "pale-page" and "role": "package-page". Register typed data with "languageId": "pale-toml" and "role": "package-data". The language server helps with the page’s +++ TOML header and leaves its Markdown body alone. An incomplete header can receive completion while the compiler reports that the page is unfinished. Keep the Package manifest and the rest of its declared inputs in the same captured source set; see Package authoring.
Open the development host
With VS Code's code command available in your terminal, launch a separate Extension Development Host. Replace the paths with your checkout, example and new editor-profile locations:
code --new-window \
  --user-data-dir /absolute/path/pale-editor-profile \
  --extensions-dir /absolute/path/pale-editor-extensions \
  --extensionDevelopmentPath /absolute/path/to/pale/integrations/vscode \
  /absolute/path/pale-editor-example

Keep Workspace Trust enabled. If asked, verify that this is the example folder you created and trust it. The extension cannot run in Restricted Mode or a virtual workspace. These separate profile directories keep the development session apart from your normal editor extensions and settings.
Open pale-workspace.toml. Its language mode should become Pale TOML after the extension starts. The three unchanged source files should compile without Pale errors in Problems. As a visible connection check, change schema_version = 1 to schema_version = "one", wait for the diagnostic, then restore 1. Open-buffer changes take precedence over the saved file. You can then change the project title from Shared notes to Team notes and keep working on the same source set.
If startup fails, check the configured executable, the three source paths and the Pale Language Server output channel. A server built from an incompatible checkout is rejected rather than silently using a different private protocol.
Select a profile context
Run Pale: Select Profile Context from the Command Palette, then choose notes and local. Open Pale Profile in the Explorer and expand Intended use case. The portable example exposes that project/setting pair, but its profile sections report No usable profile: effective-profile inspection has no selected machine identity. That is expected: these three files describe a world without supplying a machine, Package distribution or capability bindings. It is not evidence that a running provider or repository-generation setup exists.
For an already configured workspace, set its real machine ID and list its private and Package inputs with their actual roles as well. The language-server contract defines those roles and the supplied-source boundary. Once that profile is usable, the review commands below operate on its retained editor state.
From a selected Profile Explorer context:
Run Pale: Begin Configuration Review.
Edit the configured sources for that folder.
Run Pale: Evaluate Configuration Candidate.
Run Pale: Inspect Configuration Preview to read the bounded change roots, affected subjects, causal steps, and source occurrences.
Run Pale: Finish Configuration Review and choose a disposition.
Each workspace folder owns its own temporary review. The extension checks the editor, profile, instance, topology, candidate, derivation, and preview coordinates supplied by the LSP. It does not reconstruct compiler meaning. Accepting a preview records review state for a separate write gate; it does not change source. Each command is available only during its matching review phase.
Folder ownership and synchronization
Each workspace folder owns one resource-scoped pale-lsp process and one ephemeral Profile Explorer context. Multi-root windows therefore preserve folder identity rather than routing every document through the first root. The extension runs in the workspace extension host (including the corresponding remote host), restarts only the folder whose relevant configuration changed, and refreshes the tree after the server publishes a canonical analysis result. It installs one exact, glob-quoted watcher per configured source in that folder; closed-file create, change, delete, and atomic-replacement events use the standard LSP watched-files route, while open editor buffers keep precedence.
The extension is disabled for untrusted and virtual workspaces because it launches a configured executable and captures explicitly selected source files. This prevents an untrusted workspace from supplying pale.server.path. The desktop extension host loads neither a Node nor a WebAssembly Pale compiler.
Build and test the extension locally
npm test

These commands compile the extension and run its native-client boundary tests; they do not demonstrate an actual editor session or install or publish a VSIX.
The language server generates the private response types and structural checks that this extension consumes. The selected artifact covers profile contexts, profile pages and explanations, configuration review, analysis notices, and the protocol advertisement. It does not include request validators or unused response types.
