The local build checks the generated inventory and exact bytes before it compiles, then copies the runtime checks and declarations into dist. It does not reach into the language-server repository or regenerate the artifact. Client decoders still enforce request-relative coordinates, bounds, state relationships, and independent copies. Structural validation does not admit configuration, authorize a write, or prove that a provider is running.
For command-line work on an existing configuration, return to Inspect your workspace: Editor support.

Interfaces
Use the connection that fits your application. The CLI works from a shell, standalone MCP gives agents tools to inspect and review workspace configuration, and LSP gives editors feedback on Pale declarations. ACP conducts a coding-agent turn. A2A can hand work to a resident through an authenticated connection. Shared operations use the same Rust SDK.
To embed Pale in your process, choose an SDK. For workspace inspection or installing repository guidance, follow the product guides.
Choose a connection
When you need to	Use	What the caller supplies	
Inspect configuration, plan repository guidance or apply a reviewed file update from a shell	pale. Build the CLI, then see the command reference.	A command and its inputs. Read results from standard output and diagnostics from standard error.	
Let an agent inspect captured sources or review a proposed change	pale-mcp. See MCP framing and discovery.	A stdio client that supports the documented protocol revision, and the sources to review. Check the handshake before relying on a launch entry.	
Diagnose and navigate Pale configuration while editing	pale-lsp. See LSP source capture and synchronization and the VS Code integration.	Pale configuration documents. VS Code starts one server per workspace folder and exposes the Profile Explorer.	
Send one prompt through a connected coding agent	pale-acp. See ACP deadlines, updates and cancellation.	Connected input and output streams. The caller starts the agent. Pale negotiates ACP v1, creates a session and conducts one prompt turn per call.	
Inspect a Delegate handle or manage delegated work	pale-a2a. See the A2A integration.	A handle for inspection, or an authenticated resident attachment to start, advance, observe or cancel work. The caller arranges the connection.	
MCP calls the CLI's dispatcher in the same process and works from the sources supplied to the call. It has no automatic access to an editor's unsaved buffers. LSP supplies diagnostics, completion, hover, navigation and configuration review for Pale declarations. Use a language server for the project's own language to inspect its code.
The ACP conductor ends after one turn. For a later prompt, arrange another call. A2A needs a caller-supplied connection for resident operations. Discovery and installation are the caller's responsibility.
Connect a resident explicitly
A trusted embedding application can supply ResidentAttachment to an interface that accepts it. Its carrier authenticates the resident. Its response policy checks signatures, changes to who can act and the proofs that prevent replay of an older state. The Rust SDK describes those types.
Ordinary CLI and MCP sessions start without a resident. If a resident call loses its response, the operation may still be running. Observe or reconcile it before retrying.

Pale A2A interface
Use this interface when Pale hands one task it has checked and authorised to an agent system someone else operates. Each call starts, advances, observes or cancels that outward Delegate through an authenticated Pale resident attachment, reusing the Rust SDK's request and result types. The interface keeps no operation state machine or A2A wire types of its own.
Choose the operation
Build this crate against the matching local pale-sdk with Rust 1.94 or later. The public functions take the SDK's typed requests and return its results and ApiError diagnostics:
Function	Use it to	
inspect_delegate_handle	Check a supplied Delegate handle's structure without contacting a resident	
start_delegate	Create an authorized child operation and receive its durable handle before dispatch	
advance_delegate	Perform at most one resident-owned turn on that child	
observe_operation	Read the operation's current signed records	
cancel_operation	Request cancellation, then observe its outcome	
The last four require both &PaleApi and &ResidentAttachment. See the Rust SDK for the attachment's lifetime and trust requirements.
Important

Supply a working authenticated resident attachment before using the operation functions. This crate does not discover or start the service; constructing a request is not a connection.
Construct a call in your application
The start function has this signature:
pub fn start_delegate(
    api: &PaleApi,
    attachment: &ResidentAttachment,
    request: ResidentDelegateStartRequest,
) -> Result<ResidentOperationObservation, ApiError>

Construct it with ResidentDelegateStartRequest::new(parent, signed_request), where parent is the retained OperationHandleLocator and signed_request contains the exact signed common-request bytes. The request identifies an already admitted Delegate route. The caller's deployment supplies the signing and resident connection; this interface does not construct either from a task description. To inspect the exact constructor, signed-record inputs and carrier traits, run from this crate's directory:
cargo doc --no-deps --open

This opens the interface's local Rustdoc. For the request and attachment types, build the Rust SDK method reference and open ResidentDelegateStartRequest, ResidentAttachment, AuthenticatedResidentCarrierSource and ResidentResponseAdmission. The first defines the input; the latter three define how the host connects and checks returned records. These local references are generated from the matching checkout, not a separate hosted API version.
Keep remote and local outcomes separate
The effect-free inspection operation remains available for a supplied Delegate handle. It proves only canonical structure and a syntax-checked record reference. Resident custody, signatures, current authority, and disclosure still require the live attachment.
The application owns admission, durable Delegate start and dispatch, first-response and remote-task custody, observation, cancellation, and pre-Task recovery. The native A2A transport adapter owns JSON-RPC encoding, bounded response decoding, and verified HTTPS. This interface imports neither the adapter nor its private wire types.
The caller must provide an attachment whose carrier authenticates the resident and whose response-admission owner verifies signatures, authority rotation, and anti-rollback evidence. Deployment-qualified HTTPS remains an adapter concern.
The selected route is A2A v1 JSON-RPC over verified HTTPS. Streaming requires the exact admitted Agent Card's advertised support. An unidentified task remains unknown after a lost response; it must not trigger a repeated send. A cancellation response requires native read-back and does not prove Pale settlement.
This crate does not discover or start a resident. It provides no server, Agent Card publication, task listing, push delivery, alternate binding, compatibility reader, installation, or activation.

Pale ACP conductor
Use pale-acp when a coding session runs through Pale: each call conducts one turn with an established coding agent over stable ACP v1, and the caller supplies the already-connected stdio byte streams. It is a Rust conductor, not an executable launcher, an agent server or a Pale-owned language-model loop.
Conduct a turn
Construct the request
Create AcpConductor::new(), then an AcpTurnRequest with the absolute working directory and prompt text. The directory coordinate is sent to the agent. Construction reads no local files and starts no action.
Conduct one turn
Pass the connected input/output streams, AcpCancellation, a finite deadline future and an update observer to conduct_turn. Your application supplies the clock and executor. The observer runs inline and must not block; the deadline cannot preempt it.
Read the outcome
Each call negotiates ACP v1, creates a fresh native session and submits one prompt. Read the typed outcome or error. The conductor does not keep a session for another prompt or resumption.
The session tests exercise this sequence against a synthetic agent, including cancellation, silent-peer deadlines, permission rejection and transport loss. They are local protocol tests, not qualification of a deployed agent. See conduct_turn for the exact async stream bounds and error contract rather than introducing a second executor or launch wrapper.
No filesystem, terminal, or MCP capability is advertised to the agent. Permission requests select a supplied reject-once option or return cancellation; they never grant permission. These limits govern this connection, not any authority the independently operated agent already holds elsewhere.
Cancellation and incomplete outcomes
Before a prompt starts, cancellation drops the connection without inventing a native session-cancellation acknowledgement. During a prompt, it forwards one cancellation request and awaits the native terminal reason, still bounded by the caller's deadline. A cancellation request is not proof of terminal cancellation. Deadline expiry or transport loss preserves the known native session coordinate, if one was obtained; neither proves that the agent stopped or that an external effect settled.
Incoming newline-delimited JSON-RPC frames, aggregate inbound bytes and messages, prompt bytes, projected text chunks, and ordered update count have independent bounds. Aggregate limits include negotiation, permission, control, update, and terminal traffic. Text-bearing updates with non-text content fail closed instead of silently losing their payload. Stable-v1 tool calls, tool-call updates, and plans retain the exact structured values decoded by the pinned ACP SDK. They remain native agent data, not Pale operations or effect evidence. The interface creates no second update queue or transcript store.
Review Pale configuration
Use PaleApi directly for local, effect-free configuration review. Do not route SDK calls through AcpConductor. A host can give an agent admitted context, receive a proposed change, and then pass that proposal to the SDK's review workflow. The ACP session coordinate and Pale review handles remain separate. A verified person's explicit acceptance can authorize the exact proposed write when the actor, target, current source, and proposed change still match. The write remains a separate admitted effect. Acceptance does not apply the change or prove its native read-back.
The SDK can compile and compare portable workspaces, inspect source, compile an effective profile, explain findings, and review a candidate through preview and an explicit accept, reject, cancel, or stale disposition. It receives no local source capture, effect admission, action, resident observation, installation, activation, or effect authority through this ACP interface.
The review tests compose the two independent surfaces. Agent output does not automatically enter or approve a review. An ACP session ID and stop reason never substitute for a Pale profile, operation result, acceptance, or native settlement.

Pale CLI
Use the pale command to check workspace configuration, inspect generated plans, or run a selected built-in computation. The commands below describe the interface directly and assume its declared Rust dependencies are available. For a task walkthrough instead, start with Inspect your workspace or Add coding instructions to a repository. The architecture explains why compilation, review and application are separate operations.
With Rust 1.94 or later and the dependencies available, run these commands from this directory to build the CLI and discover its commands and action inputs:
cargo build --locked
cargo run --quiet --locked -- --help
cargo run --quiet --locked -- action --help
cargo run --quiet --locked -- action list
cargo run --quiet --locked -- action describe pale.compute.path-inventory

action list reads the compiled catalog and shows each effect-free built-in computation in stable identity order. action describe <id> shows the exact registry contract and payload schema; it does not maintain a second CLI-specific action definition. Add the global --result-format json option before action for machine-readable output. The existing action <id> form runs the selected computation from standard input or a confined input file.
Workspace commands require the workspace manifest, project, execution workspace, and machine selections shown in help. These identities are not interchangeable. action can run without a workspace. plan saves one plan file per repository in stable compiled order, but does not apply those plans. Its --out path must be an absolute directory without ..; Pale creates the directory when it is absent. apply and remove are separate operations that require saved plans to match freshly rebuilt plans before changing targets.
Diagnose a local installation
pale doctor checks the selected workspace, its lock and bindings, installed repository files and explicitly selected build directories. It reports missing declarations and unavailable runtime observations separately from failed checks, without repair or cleanup. See Diagnose a local installation for selectors, build-size units, limits and exit status. A complete report does not establish resident readiness.
Check and read Package sources
Use the compiler's Package reader without selecting a workspace:
cargo run --quiet --locked -- packages check --root ../..
cargo run --quiet --locked -- packages show pale.design:animate --root ../..
cargo run --quiet --locked -- packages check --write --root ../..

--root names the distribution folder containing packages/. check reads every family, checks declarations and reading links, and reports stale indexes. show presents a body's declared required and optional reading before its authored method. Omit the resource to inspect the complete catalog as JSON. Add the global --result-format json option for a machine-readable body or check result.
Add --caller-root /absolute/notes --caller-root /absolute/repositories to check incoming Markdown links and qualified resource IDs from those trees. --exclude-caller Records skips that directory name at any depth; longer exclusions name a subtree relative to each root. A broken caller prevents index writes. The authoring guide explains capture limits, default exclusions and which references are checked.
check --write regenerates only family INDEX.md files. It checks sources and all index preconditions before writing, replaces each file atomically and reads the result again. It preserves authored method bodies. The update is not a transaction across files: if a write fails, inspect the reported outcome before retrying. A successful source check neither selects the guidance for a project nor activates runtime permissions.
Review and install Package guidance before activation
guidance inspect projects selected Package judgment through the source-only API, before a runtime execution path exists:
cargo run --quiet --locked -- --workspace /absolute/workspace/pale-workspace.toml \
  --project repository --execution-workspace local-guidance --machine local \
  guidance inspect --repository source --host codex

Select --host claude-code for Claude's layout. The human result lists proposed files and a separate contribution to the project instruction file. Add the global --result-format json option to inspect the complete SDK-owned file bodies, paths and hashes. Inspection reads inputs and writes nothing; it does not replace local project facts, observe installed-host readiness or grant tool invocation. Operations, recipes, modes and lifecycle delivery/gates require the runtime route and are refused here.
Both hosts contribute to one AGENTS.md; their native skills and references retain separate paths. Each owns only its marked entry contribution, so removal preserves the other host and surrounding project text. Pale leaves independent CLAUDE.md instructions alone. For Claude's native loading setting and migration from an earlier Pale-owned CLAUDE.md contribution, follow the guidance starter.
With the same workspace selections, guidance context --repository source prints private repository scope and the session's declared source reading order. Each entry shows its configured machine authority root and relative reference separately; each reading root needs an explicit read-only authority-access declaration. Use permitted native tools to distinguish a directory root from an exact-file root. Relative references resolve beneath a directory, or from a bound file's parent while remaining confined to that exact file. The command writes no files and does not read the referenced documents. Keep its output within the project's disclosure scope: it contains private paths and is separate from the portable Package files and AGENTS.md contribution. No host option is needed. Without a reading order for this repository's session entry, the output says so; paths alone establish neither ownership nor acceptance of a duty. JSON output contains the same text as a string in the ordinary result envelope.
guidance plan --repository source --host codex compares the selected methods with the checkout. It lists files to add, update, keep or remove and shows a text diff with surrounding context. --intent apply is the default; use --intent remove to review removal of that host's owned files and exact entry contribution. The plan binds source selection, native root, file/parent identities, prior bytes, modes and write order. Conflicting unowned or edited targets are refused. JSON includes the observed UTF-8 text, exact proposed bytes, hashes and modes, including preserved local instructions; keep it within the project's disclosure scope.
After displaying the complete proposal, the CLI saves only its identity in .pale-source-guidance-review-codex.json at the target root, with mode 0600. Claude Code uses .pale-source-guidance-review-claude-code.json. Each host's latest successful plan replaces its earlier review, including a change of intent. Instruction files remain untouched. This file remembers what was shown; it does not establish that a person approved it. After reviewing the output, apply with the same workspace selections, repository and host:
cargo run --quiet --locked -- --workspace /absolute/workspace/pale-workspace.toml \
  --project repository --execution-workspace local-guidance --machine local \
  guidance apply --repository source --host codex

For Claude Code, use --host claude-code in both commands. For removal, use --intent remove in both. Each apply rebuilds the source profile and observes the target again; changed inputs are refused before target writes. After a successful install, run another plan before applying again: it should show keep, and applying that unchanged proposal writes no guidance files. If the remembered review is missing, run plan first. Automation may still pass --expect-plan DIGEST explicitly; it uses the same checks. Neither saved JSON nor a retained SDK plan bypasses them. Successful publication confirms file read-back, commit and journal cleanup. It does not establish that a coding host used the guidance, or activate runtime tool admission.
A pending interruption journal blocks normal writes. Review recovery using guidance recovery plan --repository source --host codex --intent restore-before and execute that exact decision using guidance recovery apply with the same selectors, intent and --expect-recovery REVIEWED_SHA256. Both commands also accept --intent finalize-published: that choice retains a complete observed after-state and finishes cleanup; it does not fill missing writes. A restore keeps independent edits and conditionally removes only recorded empty directories. Conflicting state is refused for owner adjudication. A matching uncheckpointed after-image establishes data, not who wrote it. JSON recovery review includes full proposed bytes and evidence; null means no pending journal was observed, not that the repository or host is ready.
The plan includes a managed block in the root .gitignore, excluding .pale-source-guidance.lock, .pale-source-guidance-recovery.json and both review files. The block is applied with the guidance and shown in its diff; existing rules and file permissions are preserved. This works in ordinary repositories and linked worktrees without modifying Git's administrative directories. An edited or malformed managed block stops planning so user additions cannot be silently overwritten. The exclusions remain after guidance removal because the cooperating lock and latest review remain. Planning before the first apply can leave a review file visible to Git; it contains only a format identifier and digest, not instruction text.
The temporary recovery journal contains private before-images and stays when recovery is needed; retain it until reconciled. Diagnostics distinguish writes that never started, confirmed restoration and uncertain outcomes, with coordination effects reported separately. An uncertain outcome requires native inspection before another decision, rather than a blind retry.
The repository-guidance starter supplies the source declarations and setup steps. distribution-info --lockfile prints the native inspector's exact TOML lock to stdout, without consuming an existing lock. Review that proposed lock before replacing a workspace pin. With --result-format json, the result is the same TOML document as a JSON string in the ordinary envelope. No lock-writing authority is implied.
Runtime plan and apply retain their separate admission requirements; a source-guidance result is not their input.
Review a configuration change
Keep the current and candidate manifests in separate local source roots. Use the same project, execution workspace and machine selection for both:
cargo run --quiet --locked -- --workspace /absolute/current/pale-workspace.toml \
  --project demo --execution-workspace default --machine local \
  review-configuration --candidate-workspace /absolute/candidate/pale-workspace.toml \
  preview > review.json

The result is an indented JSON summary. Pale reads Package sources from the baseline only; the candidate uses that same Package meaning. These disk reads do not include unsaved editor buffers.
Inspect a bounded page of affected and unaffected facts using that same summary:
cargo run --quiet --locked -- --workspace /absolute/current/pale-workspace.toml \
  --project demo --execution-workspace default --machine local \
  review-configuration --candidate-workspace /absolute/candidate/pale-workspace.toml \
  impacts --limit 10 < review.json

Use the returned nextOffset as --offset for the next page; null means the end. Every invocation reconstructs the review and checks the complete original summary before returning a page. Changed compiled review coordinates are rejected, including private-instance changes. Zero or omitted --limit uses the SDK default, and the SDK caps larger limits. These checks do not establish unchanged source bytes, an editor revision, or native readiness. Affected describes dependency reachability, not necessarily a changed target output.
After inspecting the preview, repeat the command with accept < review.json instead of preview > review.json. Pale recaptures and evaluates the inputs, then compares the complete summary before returning the selected decision. reject, cancel and stale use the same input. Use stale only when you have separately established that the relevant source or conversation changed.
None of these review decisions writes configuration. A changed summary is rejected: inspect a new preview before deciding again. A separately authorized write must still check its source bytes immediately before applying the change.
Use an attached resident
The ordinary pale executable exposes no resident operation commands. Its hook command can connect using an explicitly selected protected configuration, described below; it discovers no endpoint. A trusted embedder can provision a ResidentAttachment with its authenticated carrier source and response-admission policy, then call run_with_resident_attachment. The Rust SDK reference instructions lead to ResidentAttachment, AuthenticatedResidentCarrierSource and ResidentResponseAdmission, the types the embedder must implement or supply. An observation attachment enables only resident observe; an operation attachment enables the complete command tree below. The ordinary executable neither advertises nor accepts these commands:
pale resident observe ...
pale resident invoke start|advance ...
pale resident consult start|advance ...
pale resident delegate start|advance ...
pale resident cancel ...

Each command reads one already signed common request from --signed-request. It never creates a signature or opens resident storage. Start results return a durable handle before dispatch. Pending and uncertain results are not terminal; observe or reconcile them before another attempt. When command output contains signed records, it exposes them as exact canonical JSON strings, with their immutable storage references reported separately.
An embedder can supply either a hook-only or operation attachment for pale hook. An observation attachment cannot deliver hooks. The ordinary executable reads one native event from standard input and accepts an explicit connection configuration:
pale hook session-start --workspace WORKSPACE --repository REPOSITORY \
  --provider-binding BINDING --provider-binding-identity DIGEST \
  --resident-hook-config /absolute/private/hook.json < native-event.json

The closed JSON document requires schema_version: 1, absolute paths in endpoint_configuration and caller_credential, trusted caller_public_key and resident_public_key pins as arrays of 32 bytes, and timeout_ms between 1 and 30000. The endpoint configuration names the socket. The credential file contains a separately provisioned raw 32-byte Ed25519 seed matching the caller pin. Configuration and credential files must be regular, single-link, mode 0600, with owner-private immediate parent directories and no symlink traversal. Loading creates no keys or directories and changes no permissions. These filesystem checks do not protect against other processes with the same user ID, inspect ACLs or protect backups; file custody must be selected and qualified for the deployment. Never put a private key in repository hook configuration.
The connection authenticates the pinned resident before sending the native event, preserves its exact bytes and static route, and sends at most once within the selected deadline. The config option is a local connection choice; it is not added to the ten routing arguments sent to the resident. Missing or unsafe configuration and failed authentication block delivery. A refusal preserves the resident's reason. A lost or malformed reply leaves the outcome uncertain and requires reconciliation.
Important

The file configuration supplies a connection, not permission to run a tool. It has no independent response authority, so the ordinary executable continues to block native work with exit status 2. It supplies no resident operation commands, signed-record access or protection against a host skipping its hook.
An embedder can instead supply the SDK's provision_admitted_hooks attachment with independent response admission. After the resident saves preparation and dispatch and rechecks current authority, and the caller admits the exact response, the embedded hook command writes its native standard error and standard output and returns its selected exit status. It adds no result envelope. Production authority, deployment integration for interrupted-response recovery and proof through actual agent hooks remain unfinished.
Results and failures
pale compiled-identity reports the SDK version, interface protocol, and build target without reading a workspace or verifying installed bytes. It is an executable-handshake response, not a resident health check.
Add --result-format json to a supported command to receive exactly one JSON object on standard output:
{
  "completion": "complete",
  "result": {}
}

result is either the exact structured SDK or dispatcher value, or a typed CLI transport projection when the command combines several owner results. completion is complete, partial, or non_terminal. It describes whether that result is complete, not whether its facts are favorable. A conclusive failed-no-effect materialization result is complete; a bounded page with a continuation is partial; a configuration preview awaiting a decision is non-terminal.
This format is available for doctor diagnosis, compiled identity, control-store inspection, Package distribution, source-guidance inspection/planning/publication/recovery, configuration review, built-in action discovery and execution, compilation summary/validation, materialization results, resident operations supplied by an embedder, saving plan files, and surface-status reporting. An independently admitted repository-hook response keeps the native host's output format and exit status instead of using this envelope.
The plan result describes the selected plan kind (apply, adopt, or remove) and the plan files saved in stable repository order. The publications field lists those completed saves with their paths and operation counts. If saving stops, stopped_repository_id names that repository and diagnostic explains the failure. Every listed file was durably saved before the result was returned.
A conclusive stop produces partial. An unknown write outcome produces non_terminal: the stopped repository's plan file may already exist, even though its save was not confirmed. Inspect and reconcile that exact file in the output directory before trying to save it again. In both cases, standard output keeps the result envelope while standard error reports the failure through the selected error format.
Read the command's result, not just its exit status. For example, a completed control-store inspection can report a missing store; it does not create one or prove that a resident is running. A successful computation likewise does not prove provider availability, installation, or permission to apply a plan.
Post-parse failures go to standard error. Use --error-format json for an indented object containing diagnostic, diagnosticIdentity, authoringCorrections, and authoringLocation. The nested diagnostic keeps its original canonical contract; its identity is supplied by the SDK. Corrections preserve the compiler's exact source precondition, replacement, field/index path and proof subject. Missing evidence is an empty correction array and a null location, not permission to guess an edit. Human output shows the same available source evidence with escaped values.
This evidence is returned to the caller within the request's workspace and disclosure limits. Match the current source and review the change before writing; reporting a suggested edit neither applies it nor proves current editor contents. If the SDK cannot initialize, JSON output contains only severity, code and summary. SDK diagnostic and source-correction fields are unavailable. Command syntax errors and help retain Clap's own output. The exit-status contract distinguishes invalid input, blocked work, operational failure, and uncertain effects. Correct rejected input before retrying; reconcile an uncertain effect before attempting it again.
Shared command implementation
The CLI calls pale-sdk for application behavior and owns only command-line parsing, presentation, and process exit status. Its only internal Pale dependency is pale-sdk; it does not implement another compiler or diagnostic policy.
The reusable command dispatcher is also consumed by the separate pale-mcp interface. MCP disables the default native-local feature and therefore receives neither local adapter composition nor the pale executable. MCP protocol behavior never becomes a hidden CLI subcommand.
Building or using the CLI does not activate or install a Pale resident.

Pale language server
Connect pale-lsp to an editor that needs diagnostics, completion, hover, navigation and configuration review for Pale Workspace files. The server uses Pale's compiler for both the explanation and any proposed source correction.
A host editor integration supplies configured sources, maintains one server per workspace folder, and presents profile inspection and configuration-review commands. The language server does not discover editor workspaces by itself.
Connect an editor
The pale-lsp binary communicates over standard LSP stdio. The initializing client must capture the selected sources. Pointing the server at a folder does not make it discover or scan configuration files. After initialization, a standard workspace/didChangeWatchedFiles notification may refresh only an exact source URI already registered in that captured set.
The initialize request requires rootUri and initializationOptions with:
Field	Caller responsibility	
rootManifest	Supply the root manifest's logical label relative to rootUri.	
documents	Supply the complete captured source set for the compiler request. Each document has uri, languageId, role, and complete text.	
machineId	Optional at initialization, required for private effective-profile inspection. Selects a declared machine; it does not establish native readiness.	
Document URIs must remain lexically within the root and have distinct logical labels. Use pale-toml for configuration TOML and typed Package data (package-data), pale-page for a Package page with a +++ TOML header (package-page), and pale for plain Package text, with the matching compiler source role. The closed role inventory is owned by DocumentRole, not inferred from filenames or prose. The initialization tests show the exact wire shape; decoding that shape is not evidence that the supplied configuration compiles.
Package page completion, hover and navigation use only the header and keep the original source positions, including CRLF and Unicode text. Markdown and the delimiters receive no TOML assistance. An unfinished header can receive structural help within the compiler’s header-size limit; compilation still requires a closed header and a nonempty body. The complete source remains part of the Package release identity.
After initialization, send normal open/change/save/close notifications and watched-file events for the exact configured source set. A changed closed file replaces its saved bytes; a missing, unreadable, invalid, or over-limit source is removed from the effective snapshot and reported through the existing editor error channel. An open buffer remains authoritative until close. Text changes use UTF-16 positions and incremental synchronization. One analysis worker compiles the current snapshot. Incomplete syntax can still receive structural assistance, but cannot manufacture an admitted profile. Profile inspection keeps the selected project and execution workspace distinct from configuration authority and labels retained older results as stale. Query cancellation suppresses delivery; it does not interrupt an API operation already running. Capacity failures return their unit, the known ceiling, the minimum observed demand, and a safe recovery instruction in the LSP response-error data. A field is omitted when its exact value belongs to the SDK rather than this transport.
Review configuration
The server calls the editor-safe pale-sdk façade. It is not a second TOML compiler or a language server for arbitrary programming languages in the repositories on which an agent works.
The private pale/workspace/configuration-improvement method carries one human-governed review over the compilation already retained for the exact editor generation and selected profile context. It advances through explained baseline, evaluated and diagnosed candidate, preview, and an explicit accepted, rejected, cancelled, or stale disposition. Invalid current buffers cannot be evaluated through last-known-good evidence, and accepting a preview records no source mutation or native effect; any write remains a separate authority gate.
While a preview is current, the same private method can return a bounded page of change roots and impact records. It can also explain one affected subject and return its exact candidate source occurrences. Every detail request repeats the editor, profile, private instance, and preview coordinates. A stale or cross-workspace request is rejected instead of being answered from another retained compilation.

Pale resident native host
Use this Rust component to connect a Unix-domain socket listener to an assembled Pale resident service. ResidentLocalHost borrows ResidentFrameService; ResidentWorkTurnCoordinator schedules frame, retained-phase and recovery turns. Admission, custody and execution remain in pale-application; framing and kernel credentials remain in the Unix-socket adapter.
The composition root supplies the service, an exact endpoint, frame limits, absolute connection deadlines, a positive retained-connection limit and ResidentConnectionAuthentication. The authentication input borrows a selected connection signer, operating-system random source and a bounded lookup of allowed caller keys. The listener challenges the caller, verifies the signed request and signs the response for that exact request. Connection keys establish neither a Pale principal nor application permission; the existing signed application request still passes its own authority, session and recovery checks. ResidentLocalHost::bind never discovers a principal, opens authority stores or chooses a signer. It refuses an occupied endpoint without removing it. Directory confinement, permissions and final endpoint removal belong to that deployment's lifecycle owner.
Call run_one when the native event loop offers a turn. An optional deadline pair permits one new connection. Accept and readiness observation do not wait; reading a ready partial frame remains bounded by its original deadline. The bounded connection queue is retained across turns. A later offer does not renew existing deadlines. Each authentication turn reads at most one ready frame, so a caller that stops after the resident proof does not block another ready client. Application recovery can advance while a handshake waits or is rejected. The caller-key lookup runs again before application dispatch, including after a ready request was deferred behind other work. After one frame or a frame failure, the connection closes without replay. Transport expiry does not cancel an operation or discard application recovery.
Native hook frames carry the exact repository command arguments and the original event as a UTF-8 string. The application retains the verified caller key with the event decoded from that same frame. The complete canonical frame is limited to 262,144 bytes; malformed, unauthenticated or mixed-family requests reach no session lookup. The application checks current caller and session authority, the original native occurrence and its protected operation state. A refusal returns its bounded failure class. With explicit response inputs, the application can retain preparation and dispatch with their checkpoints, recheck permission and disclosure, and return the exact prepared output. Without a selected handler it returns handler_unavailable; the listener supplies no response authority itself. The caller must independently admit the response before release to a native host. The SDK preserves the distinction between rejected input, denied admission, missing configuration and unresolved recovery; recovery and replay conflicts require reconciliation before another attempt.
An explicitly configured deployment can load LocalEndpointConfiguration from the Unix-socket adapter, then call ResidentLocalHost::bind_configured. Its local JSON file contains only a version and an absolute endpoint:
{ "schema_version": 1, "endpoint": "/absolute/private/runtime/resident.sock" }

The loader selects no default or fallback and creates nothing. It bounds the read, refuses symlink traversal and hard links, requires effective-UID ownership, a 0600 regular file and owner-private parent directories, and retains the endpoint parent's identity for the next bind or connect. It captures configuration; it does not establish a live lease.
Those checks cover POSIX ownership and mode bits. They do not inspect ACLs, exclude another process with the same UID or authenticate the server. Mutual connection authentication supplies the peer proof independently. The deployment still qualifies its ACL and administration boundary, selects the actual connection credentials and supplies signed application request admission. This native endpoint file contains no principal, grant or credential and does not replace a Pale workspace or machine binding.
Important

This is a native listener library, not an installed resident service.
Its Rust composition entrypoint is available; a standalone configured process still needs the selected writer/trust, connection credentials, record signer and independent anchor implementations. Ordinary CLI/hook wiring to the explicit configuration loader, native-tool-to-operation registration and provider admission remain separate unfinished integrations. No production credentials, test authority or default endpoint is built into this component.
Build and check this independent component from the repository root:
cargo test --manifest-path interfaces/resident/Cargo.toml --locked --offline

Its socket tests use actual kernel credentials, transport signatures made with isolated fixture keys and the application-owned in-memory conformance service. They exercise the authenticated listener and protected request boundary; application authority signatures, custody and anchors are synthetic. They do not qualify a production deployment.

Pale MCP server
Use pale-mcp when an agent in a coding session needs to know what a workspace configuration means before anyone edits it: what applies to this repository, what a proposed change would affect and why, and which files Pale would generate. Each call answers from the documents and observations the agent supplies, and whether the change goes ahead stays with the workspace's owner. It also provides smaller tools, such as path normalization and schema validation. Calls use the shared command implementation exported by pale-cli, not parsed terminal output or a second compiler.
Connect and discover
With Rust 1.94 or later and the dependencies available, build from this directory in the local checkout:
cargo build --locked

For local development, configure an MCP client to launch cargo with run --quiet --locked from this directory. This avoids assuming which target directory the enclosing checkout selected. A packaged client instead launches the built pale-mcp executable with no arguments. This is a stdio process, not an HTTP server or an interactive shell. The client sends one JSON-RPC request per line and reads protocol responses from standard output; process failures go to standard error.
Pale accepts the initialize exchange used by Claude and Codex and self-contained MCP 2026-07-28 requests. Initialization supports 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28. The server echoes a supported requested revision; for another revision it proposes 2026-07-28, which the client must support before continuing.
Clients that initialize a connection
Send initialize, read its response, then send notifications/initialized. Subsequent requests use the negotiated revision and can omit protocol metadata. Send each message below as a separate line, waiting for the preceding request's response:
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-11-25","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"example-client","version":"1"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list","params":{}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"compute_path_inventory","arguments":{"style":"posix_relative","paths":["src/./lib.rs"]}}}

The first response identifies pale-mcp, its negotiated revision and capabilities. The notification receives no response. The tool list supplies names and input schemas. The final call returns the normalized path src/lib.rs; the path is input data, not a file opened by the server. Match replies by id. Initialization lasts for this process connection and keeps no compilation or review session. A second initialize on the same connection is rejected.
Clients that send self-contained requests
For MCP 2026-07-28 without initialization, every request carries these two metadata fields:
{
  "_meta": {
    "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28",
    "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {}
  }
}

Send these three requests as separate lines, keeping the metadata in each:
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"server/discover","params":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/list","params":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}},"name":"compute_path_inventory","arguments":{"style":"posix_relative","paths":["src/./lib.rs"]}}}

Discovery identifies the server and supported revisions; the tool call produces the same result as the initialized example. A self-contained request does not initialize later requests. An initialized client may also send complete 2026-07-28 metadata for an individual request; malformed or unsupported explicit metadata is rejected in either mode. resources/list and resources/templates/list discover the available contract resources.
Results and limits
Review workspace configuration
For a real workspace, use compile_portable_workspace with the complete workspace example or your application's captured sources. The discovered schema specifies the root label and each labelled document's text content. The result summarizes the compilation; it does not keep an MCP compilation session. Send the sources again when a later tool needs to reconstruct that compilation.
For configuration review, call review_configuration with action: "preview", a complete captured baseline, and a candidate containing workspace and private sources only. The candidate uses the baseline's Package; it cannot supply another Package tree. The discovered input schema defines these roles. The result contains the SDK-owned summary object and the first bounded impact page. Return that complete summary object when you finish the review. Use the profile, explanation, and impact tools for further detail. To inspect one review subject, send action: "inspect" with the same sources and summary, the subject from an impact entry, and the three advertised bounds. Pale checks the summary before returning the compiler's causal explanation and bounded candidate-source evidence. An incomplete source scan is reported as incomplete. sourcePageState is complete only after both evidence sections are exhausted. retained_review_required means that more evidence exists, but MCP keeps no review handle and cannot accept the SDK's owner-bound cursor. Use a retained SDK or editor review to continue the exact scan.
For a profile entry's specific reason, pass its explanationHandle and the same captured compilation sources to explain_effective_profile_entry. The result's explanation is the SDK-owned evidence, or null when the handle does not belong to the freshly compiled coordinates, including the private instance. This is distinct from portable workspace change/impact explanations and does not establish current editor contents or native readiness.
To finish, send action: "finish" with the complete sources again, the complete preview summary, and an explicit accepted, rejected, cancelled, or stale disposition. Pale reconstructs the review and checks the complete summary before returning a terminal result; it retains no MCP review session. Malformed or mismatched summaries fail with the SDK's diagnostic. Matching summaries prove the compiled review facts, not unchanged raw source, an editor generation, or human authorization. Acceptance does not write files; cancelled is a review disposition, not interruption of an in-flight computation.
Discover result schemas
tools/list supplies output schemas for compilation, comparison, review, effective profiles, plans and the registered native actions. Keep these schemas with the tool you call rather than reconstructing response shapes from prose. Today tools/list returns 23 tools in about 824,000 characters of definitions, about 767,000 of them output schemas, and the input schemas describe 55 of their 390 properties; an agent that reads the whole list spends that much context before its first call. Contract validation is the exception: its schemaId selects the successful document shape, so the descriptor does not advertise one generic-object output schema. The SDK's generated contracts own the actual shapes.
Handle a rejected call
An API-rejected tool call returns a short code: summary text block and a structured tool error containing diagnostic, diagnosticIdentity, authoringCorrections, and authoringLocation. The nested diagnostic keeps its canonical contract. The short text helps a caller route the failure without repeating the complete diagnostic. Structured content remains the exact detailed source. Corrections preserve the SDK's exact source precondition, replacement, typed path and proof subject; missing evidence is an empty array and a null location.
Source evidence is returned only to the requesting caller, within that request's workspace and disclosure limits. It does not authorize a write, establish current editor contents or broadcast configuration to other agents. Match the current source and review the proposed change before writing. Invalid protocol metadata or tool arguments can instead produce a JSON-RPC error. Inspect that distinction rather than treating every response as a successful tool result. If the server rejects the protocol revision, use a client that supports the selected revision; retrying the same incompatible request will not help.
Malformed tool-argument errors include a bounded decoder class and field path. They do not echo rejected values. An unknown field name is omitted while its containing object remains visible, and path_truncated reports when the path cannot fit the transport ceiling.
Embed a resident connection
The standalone pale-mcp process uses the request-local, effect-free command set. Embedders can instead provision a resident attachment with their own authenticated carrier source and response-admission policy, then start the server with run_with_resident_attachment. An observation attachment adds only Observe; an operation attachment adds the other resident operation tools. Pale's resident owns their durable state; MCP does not add another task store, replay requests, or treat a client disconnect as cancellation. Observe an uncertain operation before you decide whether another action is safe. When a resident result contains signed records, it exposes them as exact canonical JSON strings, with their immutable storage references reported separately.
The standalone interface offers no durable task, progress, cancellation, resumption, or agent-session control. Input framing and concurrent requests are bounded in both modes; an overloaded process rejects a request rather than queueing work indefinitely.
Only journeys selected for conversational agent use are exposed. MCP transport availability never widens Pale authority, proves resident readiness, or proves a native effect.
For a command-line walkthrough of the same configuration question, see Inspect your workspace. For an embedded client that must retain handles and continue source scans, use the SDK manuals.

Pale
Every coding tool asks for permissions and context at each step, and the same rules end up repeated in every session. Pale is the meta harness through which Weave, Scope, Counsel, RawFish and Gazette act, a harness over the tools people already use; RawFish and Gazette run alone, and Pale may coordinate them. It lets an integration answer which configuration applies to a responsibility and what a proposed edit would change. Supply the workspace documents and Pale resolves how people, projects, repositories and systems relate. Packages add reusable roles and procedures. The SDK, command line, editor and agent interfaces share one Rust implementation. These answers come from the local tools today; the path from a Claude Code or Codex hook to Pale's resident, where the hook asks what may happen and what context the agent needs, is the problem in front.
Start with your integration
Build the command-line tool
Build from source and run a computation on supplied data.
Embed the compiler
Choose a language binding and compile a workspace from your own application.
Connect an editor or agent
Find the protocol that fits your host and check what the caller supplies.
To inspect a workspace or install coding instructions in a repository, start with the product guides.
What can run locally
The local tools compile and inspect configuration, compare proposed changes and write shared coding instructions to repositories. See Working with a workspace for the inputs and comparisons, and Package authoring for how to compose guidance from a single source.
A complete resident deployment needs an authenticated connection, configured trust and a managed lifecycle. The compiled configuration describes the connections. The applications themselves control access and must be started separately. Pale architecture follows a change from compilation to a repository update.

Select and author Package resources
Write a Package when several projects need the same role, procedure or policy. The Package owns that method; a workspace chooses where it applies. Start with an exported resource, follow its prerequisites and change its source rather than the generated host files. For ordinary repository generation, use Add coding instructions to a repository.
Shape a family around the work
Give each topic an entry that says when to use it, what decision it helps make, where it sits among the families and which kind of duty selects it, so the page knows its place. An index shows each entry's kind: a doctrine is a guide read before deciding, an operation a task with declared outputs, a role the instructions for one kind of actor, a stack the syntax of a library or tool and a policy_family a set of rules a project can apply. tool_recipe, capability_policy and governing_order are typed data, described under Put declarations beside the method. A short table can point to the references needed for different tasks. Give each reference one job, with a snippet, before-and-after comparison or filled table when that makes the method usable. Split where a reader can use a part independently; merge explanations that always need to be read together. Keep the features, cases and reasons while removing repetition. Length alone decides neither.
Use Write an instruction an agent can follow when drafting the method. Each step that checks or keeps something says where its result belongs and when the step is finished. A result usually goes into the changed artifact, a maintained test or the reply. When recording a decision is the task, name its home, such as the repository’s decisions page. Keep records that a product or later step actually consumes; avoid creating a report just to show the instruction was followed.
Close an instruction path once with three or four questions about the result. Reference leaves do not need another checklist, and the questions should not replay the steps. For header-authored pages, the renderer chooses the page’s closing questions or the single set supplied by required reading; optional reading supplies none. Preserve unique instructions from a former leaf checklist in the shared method before removing the repeated checklist.
Put library and tool syntax in a page with a [stack] use. A stack can share its body with a guide. Show commands or APIs for the supported version, how to read their output and a worked example. A Langfuse overlay, for instance, can find observations for a known trace ID and distinguish an empty result from fields the query never requested.
Declare required reading with uses, adding task-specific reading under [task]; use see_also for optional reading. Across Packages, use scope = "external", declare the dependency and refer to an exported ID. A same-Package guide may be internal. Update references and consumers together when changing an exported name. Do not keep a second page merely to repeat the new page under an old name; any required compatibility belongs in the tool.
The current corpus declares methods and their relationships in page headers while listing sources and resources explicitly in each manifest. A page is the one home for its guidance: each manifest lists it once, and no second copy of it stays under an earlier name or declaration file. The compiler also accepts the compact inventory below; keep the manifest and source declarations in agreement. Let the renderer print prerequisites instead of copying its generated text into the body. For direct source reading, the family INDEX.md lists entries and prerequisites, and each entry links its task guides. Use pale packages show pale.design:animate --root /absolute/distribution to preview a body with its reading links. Run pale packages check --root /absolute/distribution to check declarations, body links, heading fragments and index freshness. Add --write to regenerate family indexes after those source checks pass. The compiler supplies the catalog, body preview and indexes through the same reader; these commands need no workspace selection.
To check documents that refer to the library, repeat --caller-root for each directory: pale packages check --root /absolute/distribution --caller-root /absolute/notes --caller-root /absolute/repositories. The check reads Markdown links into this distribution’s packages/ directory and qualified resource IDs in inline code, such as pale.design:animate. It rejects missing files, missing heading or anchor targets, and unknown IDs; fenced examples and unqualified code words are not resource declarations. An invalid caller prevents --write from updating any index. Links into generated indexes are checked against their proposed replacement, so regeneration cannot silently remove a caller’s heading target. Diagnostics identify the caller and line without copying the linked URL or query.
Caller capture reads .md and .mdx files without following symlinks. It skips .git, target, node_modules and the distribution’s own Package tree, whose links are already checked. Use --exclude-caller Records to exclude that name at any depth, or --exclude-caller archive/old for a subtree relative to each caller root. Choose exclusions for the actual records and generated output; excluding a live caller removes it from the check. A capture error is a failed check. The command accepts at most 16 caller roots and 256 exclusions; each tree is limited to 250,000 traversed entries, 64 directory levels, 4 MiB per file and 128 MiB of retained text, with 64,000 documents and 256 MiB across the request. This explicit authoring scope does not configure a workspace or install a recurring check.
Write for the person doing the work: who acts, on what, with which result. When a technical word hides the action, explain the action. Keep a technical term when the reader needs its precise meaning. Dates and versions belong where they change the method; run logs, hashes and an account of writing the guide belong elsewhere. Use a full stop in place of an em dash.
Keep each prose paragraph on one source line. pale packages check reports wrapped paragraphs in live resource bodies and refuses index writes until they are formatted. It leaves code, maths, tables, front matter and deliberate Markdown hard breaks alone; documentation-only files are outside this check. The repository check, python3 tools/package_navigation.py, also runs Prettier with the repository configuration and proseWrap: never on the compiler's live-body list before checking or regenerating indexes. It needs Prettier on PATH; use --formatter /absolute/path/to/prettier to select another installed executable. A missing or failing formatter fails the check, including with --write. Both commands leave authored text unchanged. Run the formatter's --write only on the reported files you are editing; documentation files and generated indexes are outside the formatter check.
Before	After	
Verify the selected native projection.	Open the generated page and check where the button takes you.	
Retain evidence of the interruption boundary.	Close the drawer while it is opening; say in the review whether it stopped where intended.	
Check the exact dependency closure.	Install in an empty checkout and list the failed imports in your reply.	
A resource description names the job in the words someone would use to ask for it. Its outputs say what the person gets back and where.
For optional wording prompts, run python3 tools/package_text.py --word-list /path/to/words.txt from the repository root. The caller supplies a UTF-8 file with one word per line; a final * also matches its continuations, and blank lines are ignored. Keep that list with the workspace's writing choices. The tool has no built-in vocabulary. Without a list it reports page sizes only. Add --baseline /path/to/earlier/checkout to compare both versions with the same list. The report identifies whether a list was supplied and gives counts and sentences to reread; wording and size warnings never fail the command. Keep a word when its precise or ordinary meaning helps, and rewrite the action when the word obscures it. Reading the method decides whether it works.
Review the method from its sources
Start with who will use the method, the decision or action it should improve and the sources behind it. Read those sources before changing the structure. Distinguish original reasoning, conventional advice, quotations and passages too close to a source. Changing synonyms or shuffling sentences leaves borrowed expression intact. Explain the idea in a structure and examples suited to this reader, and retain the attribution and licence notices the source needs. If its origin or permission is unresolved, identify that passage in the review and hold its publication until the question is settled.
Look for the judgment that makes the page useful: the conditions under which a rule applies, why it exists, the trade-off, observable criteria, failure cases and an example that exercises the reasoning. A heading followed by slogans needs that missing substance. Decide whether the existing page needs deeper explanation, a separate reusable part, a merge with its duplicate or a different home. Keep needed history when replacing a method; another owner's decision goes to that owner. Put findings and unresolved choices in the requested review, with enough detail to make the change, rather than creating a second catalogue of the corpus. End the review of a page with one decision about it: keep it, deepen it, split it, merge it with its duplicate, move it to its owner, rederive it from the principle in place of the source, add the attribution it needs, hold it back until its origin is settled, replace it with a successor, remove it, or hand its mechanics to another owner.
Watch for one rule repeated in several roles, Markdown restating a declaration field by field, tiny pages that only point at each other, or a large page mixing independently changing subjects. Keep one home for shared meaning and link its users. Explain relationships instead of duplicating their declarations. Keep machine paths, credentials, project status and a particular consumer's model choice in that consumer's configuration. Tool-specific syntax and supported versions belong in the relevant overlay. A method must leave another owner's effects and permissions with that owner.
After writing, check declarations, links, examples and contradictions with neighbouring methods. Read for what a capable person can now decide or do. Mechanical checks answer whether the Package can be accepted and rendered; use in a project and permission to publish still need the checks and decisions for those tasks.
Put declarations beside the method
A compact Package omits both sources and resources from [package]. The compiler derives its inventory from the retained files; supplying just one inventory is invalid. Keep release metadata and dependencies in package.toml:
[package]
id = "example.review"
version = "1.0.0"
schema_version = 1
title = "Review methods"
description = "Review changes and their evidence."
compatible_compilers = ["pale-surface@1"]

Start an instruction page with a +++ TOML header, followed by its Markdown body. For example, review.md can supply both a guide and a task from one body:
+++
description = "Review a change against its intended behaviour."
[guide]
[task]
outputs = ["In the reply: actionable findings with evidence, or what was checked and what remains uncertain."]
+++

# Review a change

Read the intended behaviour, trace the changed caller and check the result against that intent.

The relative path without .md supplies the ID, here review. A header with no explicit use declares a guide. Adding [task], [role], [policy] or [stack] declares those uses; include [guide] when the same page must also be selectable as a guide. Each use retains its own kind and visibility even though it shares the body. Page uses declares required reading for every use; task.uses and role.uses add their own reading. see_also stays optional. References use the same local or external forms shown below. A child such as review/security.md also reads its nearest authored parent topic, which must declare a guide. The host renders these prerequisites as Read first links.
A page may finish with ## Before handing off and three or four unchecked questions. Keep the questions in the method that owns them. Generated page uses put that set after host, tool and reference instructions. When a page has no set of its own, its required reading can supply one; optional reading cannot. If required methods supply different sets, write the questions that close this page’s task instead of relying on an arbitrary choice. Useful checks that belong inside the method stay in its prose. Check the generated instruction, including its final questions, rather than requiring a repeated checklist in every source leaf.
Keep data without an instruction body in typed .toml files. Their path without .toml supplies their ID, and kind selects tool_recipe, capability_policy or governing_order. For example, read-only.toml declares a capability ceiling:
kind = "capability_policy"
exposure = "internal"

[policy]
permitted_capabilities = ["repository.read"]
permitted_effects = ["read"]

The nested payload is respectively recipe, policy or governing_order; its existing rules still apply. Unknown kinds and fields are rejected. Plain Markdown without a header and other supporting files remain documentation. Every retained file contributes its exact bytes to the release identity, including documentation and unselected data. Nested Packages and competing declarations for one path-derived resource remain invalid.
Explicit inventories can also list header-authored pages and typed data alongside older declaration files. A typed data source must declare exactly one resource whose ID, kind and exposure match the file. Its top-level kind selects the same grammar for compilation and editor assistance. Files listed as documentation contribute to release identity without supplying resources. Use that role for material that travels with a Package, such as licence texts and attribution, and not as a second home for guidance that a declared page already carries.
The compiler, catalog and host renderers accept these pages. Editors register a page as package-page with language pale-page, and typed data as package-data with language pale-toml; the language server supplies header assistance without parsing the Markdown body as TOML. Header-authored pages declare guidance in every family; Engineering, Automation, Publication, Design and Finance also have typed data. Design's explicit inventory lists its declared pages and typed data, with its licence and attribution files as documentation. A compact Package derives membership from its sources and does not mix in a separate resource inventory.
Select a resource for the actual task
A Package's package.toml identifies its release and exact dependencies. Membership comes either from its explicit inventories or from the compact source declarations above. Each resource has an ID, kind, definition source and exposure. A workspace can select exported resources; an internal archetype can support a concrete operation without becoming a workspace entrypoint.
Making a Package available through the project's package_seeds and exact distribution lock does not select every resource in it. The project's capabilities file selects operations, doctrine, roles, stacks and run modes by their appropriate semantic fields. Repository declarations separately select roles, stacks and policy families. A dependency on another Package makes its declared release available; it does not load all that Package's instructions.
For a project that already selects the exact Engineering release, this capabilities-file fragment selects its exported verification operation:
[semantic]
operations = [
  { selection = "exact", resource = { package_id = "pale.engineering", resource_id = "testing/repository" } },
]

The Engineering manifest exports that ID. Its task page declares the operation and its dependencies. Read first links reach the testing method and execution method. It also requires the project-test capability through the repository verifier recipe. Selecting it does not supply the project's command or a working provider.
Operation exposure is a separate consumer choice. For example, append this binding to the same capabilities file to offer the selected operation only through explicit user selection:
[[operation_bindings]]
operation = { package_id = "pale.engineering", resource_id = "testing/repository" }
[operation_bindings.binding.selection]
kind = "user_only"
aliases = []

Without an operation binding, the selected operation remains unbound. This exposure choice still supplies no project-test provider, command authorization or execution evidence. Private bindings can narrow Package ceilings; they cannot rewrite the operation's requirements, fallbacks or evidence contract.
Choose by the requested decision. Engineering's review reviews an exact change and its evidence; testing/repository requires a native check. A task that only needs a judgment resource can select doctrine instead of an operation. For example, this alternative fragment selects Design's rendered interface judgment:
[semantic]
doctrine = [
  { selection = "exact", resource = { package_id = "pale.design", resource_id = "inspect" } },
]

These fragments belong in a complete workspace with its selected sources and run policy. Repository guidance can render selected methods, roles and policies without a runtime provider or execution path. It refuses selected runtime operations rather than turning them into plain guidance silently. Runtime rendering separately needs the selected terminal path, provider-binding record and local machine binding. Detecting an installed host does not create that provider record. See the workspace contract for configuration and repository planning.
Select more resources when the task needs them, rather than because descriptions share a word. An explicit all_from_package selector is broader: it selects every exported resource of that semantic field's kind from the named Package.
Read composition as part of the contract
Typed references tell the compiler what belongs together. They also tell a human reading the sources which guidance must be read before applying a method.
Header field	Meaning	
Page uses	Make required guides available through Read first links for every use of the page	
[task], [role] or [stack] uses	Add required reading for that use	
extends under a use	Include the declared parent of the same kind	
see_also	Name optional reading without selecting or installing it	
The older separate declarations remain supported: operation doctrine_refs and guide requires compose their required bodies, while see_also keeps reading optional. Header-authored uses keeps those methods in their own linked pages.
Design’s rendered inspection method requires browser access, which itself requires accessible tasks. Each required method is available once through a Read first link even when several selected resources reach it. Motion, responsive recomposition and independent design review remain optional references from that entry. Their availability does not require performing all those tasks for every rendered inspection.
A local reference uses { scope = "local", resource_id = "..." }. A cross-Package reference names the owner explicitly:
uses = [
  { scope = "external", resource = { package_id = "pale.engineering", resource_id = "execution" } },
]

The importing Package must declare the exact dependency and reference an exported resource of the expected kind. Renaming a folder, adding a prose link or placing a file beside another Package does not create that relationship.
Keep governing relations attached to the selected use
Governing scopes and endpoints can name different kinds of resources. Add kind when a page declares several uses; omitting it is valid only for a target with one declared use. Admission preserves that kind in the resolved relation, including scope, ordering, narrowing and obligations. A capability ceiling's policy field already requires a capability-policy resource.
For example, a compact Package with a change role and two policy pages can declare this reasoning order in order.toml:
kind = "governing_order"

[governing_order]
schema_version = 1

[[governing_order.order]]
scope = { scope = "local", resource_id = "change", kind = "role" }
purpose = "reasoning"
before = { scope = "local", resource_id = "change/impact", kind = "policy_family" }
after = { scope = "local", resource_id = "review", kind = "policy_family" }

Selecting the change role activates this relation and its dependencies. Selecting only that page's guide leaves the role's order inactive. An external endpoint adds kind beside resource, and the chosen use must be exported by the declared dependency. Order and narrowing endpoints must have matching kinds. The compiler rejects an omitted kind on a shared page rather than choosing a use from the other endpoint.
Author the source that owns the behavior
Extend an existing resource when the change belongs to its task. Add a resource when it has a distinct selection or ownership boundary. Keep project commands, service addresses, credentials, accepted visual references and local acceptance criteria with the consumer; they are inputs to a reusable method.
For a new operation in an existing Package:
Write the method in Markdown, keeping the reasoning and failure cases needed for the task. Compose an existing base through a typed reference instead of copying its body.
Declare the page’s task use, description, required reading and expected outputs in its header. Its path supplies the ID. Add a capability requirement only when it needs one. Its capability policy sets the permitted scope; the consumer supplies providers and may narrow it.
Let a compact manifest derive membership from the pages and typed data, or list them in an explicit inventory. An explicit inventory must agree with every declared use and exposure; supporting documentation supplies no resources.
Check the changed Package, then review each consumer's updated pin. Leave an existing pinned release unchanged. The compiler's release-content identity identifies the actual source; a version label or checkout revision alone does not.
Engineering’s review page declares a task, role and policy over one method, with the guide kept internal. Its task needs no native capability:
[task]
roles = [{ scope = "local", resource_id = "review" }]
outputs = ["In the reply: findings ordered by consequence, with the supporting code or check and any uncertainty.", "Checks run, what was unavailable, and the conclusion supported by this review."]

This is the task section inside that page’s header, not a standalone declaration file. The full header requires the change method through uses. The body owns the review method for all its uses, and generated host skills remain projections to inspect. Older families can still declare internal archetypes and exported concrete operations in separate tables; migrating them must preserve their composition and capability requirements.
Doctrine additionally declares its allowed placement. standalone_judgment can appear as an on-demand skill, operation_procedure belongs inside a selected operation, and startup_policy belongs in sealed startup context. Keep that distinction when adding references: a composed procedure does not thereby gain a standalone skill destination.
Keep body links aligned with typed references
A local Markdown link in a resource body must reach a manifest-owned standalone doctrine body in the same Package, with an explicit typed relationship from the referring resource. Use an inline link such as [method](method.md), optionally with a heading fragment. An operation uses doctrine_refs for supporting doctrine; a doctrine entry uses requires for prerequisites and see_also for optional references. A prose link alone never adds selection.
When the target is selected, the renderer rewrites the link destination to its host skill path, retaining the label, optional title and anchor. When the target is unchosen, it prints the target's title, Package and source path, including any anchor, instead of installing the page or emitting a broken link. The authored source and its digest stay unchanged. External URLs and code examples retain their authored text. Reference-style local links, paths outside the Package and targets that have no standalone skill are refused. Cross-Package composition uses typed references rather than a guessed relative checkout path. When supporting doctrine is composed only inside an operation, follow its typed declaration and body source; do not invent a projected standalone link for it.
Check the changed boundary
From the source repository, the maintained checks are:
python3 tools/package_navigation.py
cargo test --locked --offline -p pale-application --test packages
cargo test --locked --offline -p pale-application --test compile current_corpus

The repository runner checks formatting, declarations, reading links and index freshness. The first Rust suite checks that each Package lists its own files and that the compiler accepts them. The second exercises current Package journeys on both hosts, including required composition, optional reading, link destinations and missing-provider errors.
