PaleGo
PaleGo is the Go SDK for Pale. Use it to compile workspace configuration, inspect validated results, or call the available local operations. It calls the canonical Rust SDK through cgo and returns Go values and errors. Each client retains its Rust-side handles; the Pale application implements the behavior.
Build the native library
Use Go 1.26, Rust 1.94 or later, and a C compiler for cgo. The current linker configuration supports macOS and Linux. From sdk/go in this checkout, run:
CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target cargo build --release --locked

The target directory must stay at target/release, where cgo expects the library on macOS and Linux. This checkout's Cargo configuration resolves its local pale-sdk = 0.0.1 dependency. If you build elsewhere, provide those matching dependencies explicitly. The build may download dependencies; it does not start a resident.
Compile a workspace from memory
Pass an application's complete source batch to CompilePortableWorkspace. RootManifest is the logical relative label of the root; Documents contains that root and its selected module and lock documents as labelled byte slices. The SDK does not open those labels as host paths.
After building the native library, save this as examples/workspace/main.go under sdk/go, creating those directories if needed. Run go run ./examples/workspace from sdk/go. It loads the complete workspace example:
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "os"
    "path/filepath"
    pale "github.com/getHarshOnline/pale/sdk/go"
)

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
}

func run() error {
    client, err := pale.NewClient()
    if err != nil { return err }
    defer client.Close()

    var documents []pale.Document
    for _, label := range []string{"pale-workspace.toml", "resolution.lock.toml", "universe.lock.toml"} {
        bytes, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join("../../docs/examples/workspace", label))
        if err != nil { return err }
        documents = append(documents, pale.Document{Label: label, Bytes: bytes})
    }
    workspace, summary, err := client.CompilePortableWorkspace(
        pale.PortableWorkspaceRequest{RootManifest: "pale-workspace.toml", Documents: documents},
    )
    if err != nil { return err }
    defer workspace.Close()
    fmt.Println(string(summary.Bytes))
    return nil
}

In the printed summary, expect workspace_id to be notes-workspace and source_document_count to be 3. Keep workspace for inspection or comparison; close it when finished, then close its client. A rejected input returns an error; there is no partly compiled workspace to use.
The workspace contract explains configuration selection. For command-line use instead of embedding, follow Inspect your workspace.
Inspect a contract
This program creates one Pale client, checks the capabilities available to Go, reads the generated diagnostic schema, and handles an unavailable schema as a typed diagnostic. Save it as examples/contract/main.go under sdk/go, creating those directories if needed:
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"

	pale "github.com/getHarshOnline/pale/sdk/go"
)

func main() {
	if err := run(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}

func run() error {
	client, err := pale.NewClient()
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	defer client.Close()

	capabilities, err := client.Capabilities()
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	fmt.Printf("Go can call %d Pale capabilities\n", len(capabilities))

	schema, err := client.ContractSchema("diagnostic.v1")
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	fmt.Printf("%s\n%s\n", schema.RegistryID, schema.SchemaSHA256)

	_, err = client.ContractSchema("not-a-selected-schema")
	if err == nil {
		return errors.New("unavailable schema unexpectedly succeeded")
	}
	var diagnostic *pale.DiagnosticError
	if !errors.As(err, &diagnostic) {
		return err
	}
	fmt.Printf("%s: %s\n", diagnostic.Code, diagnostic.Summary)
	return nil
}

Run it from sdk/go:
go run ./examples/contract

Find a method or result type
From sdk/go, use Go's local reference for the matching source:
go doc Client
go doc Client.ComparePortableWorkspaces
go doc WorkspaceComparison

go doc reads declarations without invoking the native operations. The native library is still required when compiling or running a consumer. This is a local reference, not a promise that this private version is on pkg.go.dev.
Manage client and handle lifetimes
NewClient() verifies the embedded contract bundle and native-action registry. The returned client owns every opaque Rust handle created through it. Always close the client; Close() drops the API instance and all of its handles. It does not cancel a call or execute a Pale operation.
Share the returned *Client; do not copy the Client value, which contains its synchronization state. Opaque handles may be copied: copies refer to the same Rust-held state. PortableWorkspace, WorkspaceComparison, and EffectiveProfile have an idempotent Close() that invalidates their copies and releases that view. Independent derived comparisons, profiles, observations and review stages stay available; copied result documents remain readable. Close views when finished so a long-lived client need not retain each of these views until shutdown.
Observation snapshots, page cursors and subjects also have an idempotent Close() so a long-lived client need not retain them indefinitely. Closing a snapshot leaves its independent selectors available. ObservationPageResult.Close() closes all subjects and the continuation originally returned by that page, including copied handles; the copied fact data stays readable. Keep the page open while any selector is needed, or close unwanted children individually. During pagination, obtain the next page before closing the previous one to retain at most two page batches. These calls release local memory only.
Authoring navigation returns typed source locations and reusable resolved or completion identities. Close the navigation result when those identities are no longer needed; it releases the originally issued identities even if its public fields were reassigned. Individual identities can also be closed. Copied identity descriptions remain readable data. They cannot alter or recreate the native identities and relationships held by those handles.
Read results and diagnose errors
Capabilities() lists the operations exposed by this Go binding. It does not check whether configured machines, providers or a resident are available. ContractSchema() returns Go-owned metadata and a copy of the exact generated schema bytes from the Rust contract bundle.
API failures use DiagnosticError. Read its typed fields or preserve Canonical; do not parse the error message as a protocol. A BridgeError reports client or handle misuse, or a bridge failure. It contains Code and Message, without SDK diagnostic or source-correction fields.
DiagnosticError.Identity comes directly from the SDK. AuthoringCorrections and nullable AuthoringLocation retain exact compiler-proved source evidence. Match a correction's expected source at its labelled path before applying it; these copied values do not authorize a write and remain readable after client closure. The Go source and private native library must be rebuilt together; missing diagnostic metadata is rejected, not silently treated as absent evidence.
Compilation and configuration review
CompilePortableWorkspace() compiles an explicit set of labelled source bytes. It does not scan the current directory.
InspectStandaloneAuthoring() reads grammar facts for a selected document role. InspectAuthoring() on a workspace or profile reads those facts from its retained compilation. These methods return typed AuthoringInspection values; Go does not reconstruct the grammar.
Effective-profile operations keep declared intent, portable effective state, and private machine realization separate.
InspectLocalControlStore() observes one selected store without creating or repairing it. Physical Ready is not writer or resident admission.
Configuration improvement uses consuming review stages. Copies of a stage share the same consumption state. Failed preparation leaves its explanation available for retry; commit requires the same explanation handle that prepared the candidate, not another explanation with equal contents.
PreviewLocalConfigurationImprovement(LocalConfigurationImprovementRequest{...}) captures BaselineManifest and CandidateManifest with common ProjectID, ExecutionWorkspaceID, and MachineID selectors. It returns the same preview handle. Only the baseline supplies Package content; no candidate Package installation is required.
Observation delta and visual-lens requests expose only the API's cooperative preflight cancellation result. Other calls do not claim in-flight cancellation.
Calls are synchronous. A client serializes its native calls, response decoding, and closure. Do not treat a method call as background work merely because its input or result is small.
An accepted, rejected, cancelled, or caller-proved stale configuration preview is an effect-free review result. It does not change source or grant authority. Local publication and materialization methods are different: they cross bounded native I/O and require their exact admission, receipt, read-back, and reconciliation rules.
Client.CompiledInterfaceIdentity() reports compiled SDK version, interface and target claims. LocalCompilation.VerifyCurrentExecutableBinding() checks the current host executable against the captured workspace binding, not the loaded native library's bytes. Neither call observes a resident or establishes process health. Local settlement checks this same binding before making changes. A workspace bound to a separate Pale CLI executable cannot be settled directly from a Go host.
Verify the package
After building the native library, run the Go tests from sdk/go:
go test ./...

The public Go API contains no C types. Requests are copied into bounded Rust-owned memory, and responses are copied back into Go-owned values. Tests under tests/ load the real native library and replay the canonical cross-leaf contract, diagnostic, workspace, improvement, and native-action cases. The runtime capability assertion detects missing or extra Go operations. Effectful local publication and settlement tests use only a temporary workspace and require exact receipt and owner read-back convergence.
Generated native contracts
The contracts package and its per-family contracts/types subpackages are a checked-in, deterministic Go projection of every canonical initial-v1 contract family. Generation runs in models-only mode. Go records and closed scalar enums improve authoring, while structural validation and semantic admission remain in pale-sdk. A constructed Go record is not proof that a contract is valid.
The generator verifies an explicit bundle directory and every registry digest. It records the exact bundle, pinned generator, dependency lock, behavior options, and output set in a pretty-printed source coordinate:
go -C tools/contract-codegen run . \
  --bundle /absolute/path/to/agent-surface.v1
go -C tools/contract-codegen run . \
  --check --bundle /absolute/path/to/agent-surface.v1

PyPale
PyPale (pypale) is the Python SDK. Use it to compile workspace configuration, inspect a profile, or review a proposed change. It calls the canonical Rust SDK and returns Python values, typed errors, and handles to validated state. The Pale application implements the behavior; Python supplies the language interface.
The public import is pypale; the compiled module remains private as pypale._native.
Build a local wheel
Use Python 3.9 or later and Rust 1.94 or later. Activate an isolated Python environment, then work from sdk/python.
Build the wheel
python -m pip wheel --no-deps . --wheel-dir dist --config-settings="maturin.build-args=--profile release --locked"

Install that wheel
Use the exact filename printed by the build:
python -m pip install "/absolute/path/to/pypale-0.0.1-<wheel-tags>.whl"

Important

Use the normal Python backend above. Direct maturin build produces an intermediate wheel without the final constructor typing. Packaging details explains the difference for SDK maintainers.
The build and installation may fetch dependencies. Keep the same Python environment for the examples below.
Compile a workspace from memory
An editor or build tool can supply the documents it already holds. Pass the logical root label, such as pale-workspace.toml, and every selected document as (label, bytes). Include the root itself and its selected modules and locks. Pale resolves those supplied documents without opening their labels as files.
After installing the local wheel, save this as compile_example.py in sdk/python and run python compile_example.py. It loads the complete workspace example:
from pathlib import Path
from pypale import Pale

folder = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "docs/examples/workspace"
labels = ("pale-workspace.toml", "resolution.lock.toml", "universe.lock.toml")
documents = [(label, (folder / label).read_bytes()) for label in labels]

api = Pale()
workspace = api.compile_portable_workspace("pale-workspace.toml", documents)
print(f"{workspace.workspace_id}: {workspace.source_document_count} documents")

Expect notes-workspace: 3 documents. The returned workspace is the compilation to inspect or compare with a separately compiled candidate. In an editor, use its buffers in place of this file loader. A missing source or invalid relationship raises PaleDiagnosticError instead of returning a partly compiled workspace. The handle keeps its validated state available while you query it.
Portable compilation checks the workspace description. It does not load Package implementations or generate repository guidance. The workspace contract explains the complete configuration selection; Inspect your workspace shows the corresponding command-line task.
Inspect a contract
This example checks which API capabilities the installed wheel exposes, reads the exact embedded contract-bundle identity, retrieves one generated schema, and handles a rejected lookup.
from pypale import Pale, PaleDiagnosticError

api = Pale()

print(f"Python can call {len(api.capability_ids)} Pale capabilities")

bundle = api.contract_bundle_identity()
print(f"contract members: {bundle.member_count}")
print(f"schema set: {bundle.schema_set_sha256}")

diagnostic_schema = api.contract_schema("diagnostic.v1")
print(diagnostic_schema.schema_uri)
print(f"schema bytes: {len(diagnostic_schema.bytes)}")

try:
    api.contract_schema("not-a-selected-schema")
except PaleDiagnosticError as error:
    print(error.diagnostic.code)
    print(error)

Pale() verifies the embedded contract bundle when it constructs the facade. It does not start a daemon, activate a generation, or perform a native effect. capability_ids lists the operations exposed by this Python binding. It does not check whether configured machines, providers or a resident are available.
contract_schema() returns metadata and the exact generated schema bytes from the Rust contract bundle. An API-reported failure raises PaleDiagnosticError. Use error.diagnostic for the typed view and error.diagnostic_bytes when you need the exact canonical diagnostic bytes. Python argument errors can raise TypeError; reuse of a consumed review stage raises ValueError.
Compilation and configuration review
For the exact available methods and signatures in your installed wheel, use Python's generated help:
python -c 'from pypale import Pale; help(Pale)'

The wheel also ships pypale/_native.pyi and py.typed for editor navigation. These describe this build; there is no separately published complete Python method reference on this documentation site.
Choose a compilation or review operation
compile_portable_workspace() compiles an explicit batch of labelled source bytes. It does not scan the current directory.
Effective-profile methods keep declared intent, the portable effective profile, and machine realization separate.
inspect_local_control_store() classifies one principal or deployment store without creating, repairing, or admitting it. Ready is a physical state, not writer or resident authority.
Configuration improvement uses phase-typed handles for inspect, explain, propose, evaluate, diagnose, and preview. The prepared route reuses an admitted candidate. A failed preparation is retryable, while commit requires the same explanation handle that prepared the candidate, not another explanation with equal contents.
preview_local_configuration_improvement(LocalConfigurationImprovementRequest(...)) captures a baseline and candidate workspace and returns the same preview handle. The request selects baseline_manifest, candidate_manifest, project_id, execution_workspace_id, and machine_id. Only the baseline supplies Package content; the candidate needs no Package installation.
Configuration-improvement stages are linear. A consuming transition makes the prior stage unavailable. A preview can end as accepted, rejected, cancelled, or stale. Acceptance performs no source mutation and grants no authority. mark_stale() records only drift that the Python caller has independently proved.
Keep handles alive
Other journeys also return handles to Rust-owned admitted state. Python cannot fabricate the state behind a handle. A handle retains the state it needs even after the originating Pale object is released. Do not reuse a handle after a consuming transition.
Page subjects and dependencies
WorkspaceComparison.subjects(limit, continuation=None) discovers full subject identities from either retained input, including predecessor-only subjects. PortableWorkspaceCompilation.direct_dependencies(subject, limit, continuation=None) returns the selected root and its direct proof inputs, including typed facts, rules and provenance. Cursors bind the exact owners and raw limit; dependency cursors also bind the full subject. Zero selects 64 rows and values above 256 cap at 256, within Python's unsigned-16-bit argument range. These bounds do not limit total bytes or retained memory, and neither query grants recipient access.
The package also provides a strict frozen Pydantic workspace-module builder. The builder improves Python ergonomics only. Rust owns typed sealing, generated schema validation, the module digest, and canonical JSON.
Run native operations from the bound host
compiled_interface_identity() reports compiled SDK version, interface and target claims. verify_current_executable_binding(compilation) checks the current Python executable against the captured workspace binding, not the loaded extension's bytes. Neither call observes a resident or establishes process health. Local settlement checks this same binding before making changes. A workspace bound to a separate Pale CLI executable cannot be settled directly from Python.
ABI and typing maintenance
The following sections are for changing and testing PyPale itself. Applications using a built wheel can return to the workspace contract or choose an interface.
ABI and typing
pyproject.toml owns the Python build and dependency requirements. uv.lock freezes the conformance environment without narrowing the public Pydantic compatibility range.
The wheel includes py.typed and native type stubs generated from collected PyO3 declarations. Factory-only classes get a required positional-only NoReturn constructor argument before rendering. This prevents ordinary typed direct construction while preserving real constructors, named factories and enum members. Runtime rejection remains PyO3-owned; Any, casts and ignored errors are not security boundaries. Unqualified inherited construction fails the build instead of being guessed. Unknown module exports remain unknown, including the external diagnostic exception. The small public stub adds only that exception's typed attributes and explicit builder reexports. PyO3's create_exception! does not emit that class stub. Replacing the exception with a Python subclass would raise the selected ABI's Python floor.
Cargo tests verify translation laws. The native acceptance gate must also build and install the mixed CPython wheel in an isolated environment, then run tests/native_abi.py against the shared conformance fixtures. Importing a renamed Cargo library file is not equivalent ABI evidence.
From sdk/python, with the installed wheel's environment active, run:
python tests/native_abi.py tests/fixtures/cross-leaf.v1

After installing the wheel, run the strict public-consumer check with the pinned checker:
python tests/typecheck.py --pyright <Pyright-1.1.408-executable>
python tests/factory_constructors.py --pyright <Pyright-1.1.408-executable>

That check must accept the valid consumer and reject incorrect field types, unknown attributes, and wrong improvement phases. A syntax-only stub check is not a substitute.
Packaging details
The backend delegates compilation and metadata to pinned Maturin 1.15.0. A build-only tool reads the exact extension's PyO3 metadata with pinned pyo3-introspection 0.29.0, adds unavailable constructors to the collected class model, and uses its existing stub renderer. Pinned wheel 0.45.1 owns final unpacking, checksum verification and repacking. All other wheel member bytes, including the extension, metadata and licences, must remain unchanged. Direct maturin build output is an intermediate package: it bypasses this constructor-typing correction and is not the final SDK wheel.
PEP 660 editable installation (python -m pip install -e .) uses the same backend. It generates python/pypale/_native.pyi from the extension Maturin installs there. Those are generated files, not authored stubs. As with Maturin, an editable build updates the source extension before all later checks finish; a failed build returns no wheel but does not restore an older extension/stub pair. Use a disposable checkout when testing this route. A PEP 517 source build (for example python -m build --sdist, with the build frontend installed) includes the backend and locked stub tool. This checkout resolves unpublished Rust 0.0.1 dependencies through the root .cargo/config.toml. Building the unmodified source archive currently requires those same explicit Cargo patches to an available dependency checkout; the archive does not bundle that checkout and is not a standalone public distribution. Once dependencies resolve, it uses the same final-wheel route. Neither path uses a stale generated stub as fallback.

Pale Scene
@rtepl/pale-scene compiles Pale inspection results into renderer-neutral geometry for Node.js. It owns layout only: Pale keeps semantic identity, relationships, authority, and evidence; a client owns rendering, transient attention, live observation joins, and instrumentation. This package provides no editor, renderer, desktop host, or browser build.
The output contains nodes, ports, routes, declared gates, and optional route-contact annotations. Stable structure stays visible across generations. Activity, consultation, handoffs, evidence movement, and reconciliation remain temporary client-side emphasis over that structure; Scene does not turn every causal fact into a permanent edge or infer live activity from geometry.
Choose the entry point that matches the question:
@rtepl/pale-scene validates geometry, runs ELK off the main thread, and can estimate contacts between accepted routes.
@rtepl/pale-scene/organization reads recipient-qualified organization results, selects a topology, and compiles a scene.
@rtepl/pale-scene/change reads one recipient-qualified comparison for Source and Change presentations.
Geometry-only use does not load @rtepl/pale. The package requires Node.js 24.16 or later. You can build and run the geometry example below without a resident.
Build the local package
From sdk/scene, with Node.js 24.16 or later and its pinned build dependencies available, run:
npm run build

The build produces dist/. Package that output and the two runtime dependencies from this checkout into an existing artifact directory:
npm pack --ignore-scripts --pack-destination /absolute/path/scene-artifacts .
npm pack --ignore-scripts --pack-destination /absolute/path/scene-artifacts ./node_modules/elkjs ./node_modules/paper

This creates the local Scene archive, elkjs-0.12.0.tgz and paper-0.12.18.tgz. Keep those exact dependency versions: the workers load their pinned files. Nothing is published to a registry.
Create a new empty consumer directory. In it, save package.json containing {"private":true,"type":"module"}, then install all three local archives:
npm install --offline --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund \
  /absolute/path/scene-artifacts/rtepl-pale-scene-0.0.1.tgz \
  /absolute/path/scene-artifacts/elkjs-0.12.0.tgz \
  /absolute/path/scene-artifacts/paper-0.12.18.tgz

The geometry entry needs no @rtepl/pale peer. In this consumer, save the example below as layout-example.mjs and run node layout-example.mjs. It uses the installed package's worker and requires no resident handle.
Lay out two connected nodes
This example runs ELK in a worker and prints the accepted node and route counts. The coordinates use scene layout units, not device pixels.
import { ElkExecutor, GeometryPlan } from "@rtepl/pale-scene";

async function main() {
  const plan = new GeometryPlan({
    nodes: [
      { id: "source", width: 40, height: 30, ports: [{ id: "source-out", side: "EAST" }] },
      { id: "target", width: 40, height: 30, ports: [{ id: "target-in", side: "WEST" }] },
    ],
    relations: [{ id: "flow", sourcePort: "source-out", targetPort: "target-in" }],
  }, { nodes: 2, ports: 2, relations: 1, points: 32, depth: 1, coordinateMagnitude: 10_000 });
  const executor = new ElkExecutor({
    requestBytes: 100_000, resultBytes: 100_000, deadlineMs: 10_000,
    totalRequestBytes: 100_000, totalResultBytes: 100_000, totalActiveMs: 10_000,
    oldHeapMb: 128, youngHeapMb: 32,
  });

  try {
    const result = await executor.run(plan);
    if (result.kind !== "completed") {
      throw new Error(`Layout ${result.kind}: ${result.reason}`);
    }
    console.log(JSON.stringify({ nodes: result.geometry.nodes.length,
      routes: result.geometry.routes.length }));
  } finally {
    await executor.close();
  }
}

void main();

Expected output:
{"nodes":2,"routes":1}

The non-completed result includes a closed kind and reason. The finally block releases the worker after success or failure.
Integrate organization and change views
Important

Organization and change intake require opaque recipient-qualified handles issued by Pale's application authority. PaleJS can consume these handles but does not yet acquire them from a resident, so live intake is unavailable. Scene cannot create the handles from source documents, portable compilations or public coordinates. Use the same native SDK installation for the handle and Scene; use the geometry entry point for runnable integrations today.
The JavaScript SDK describes these inspection types. The Rust SDK explains the resident attachment.
Start a recipient-qualified organization intake
Pass a RecipientQualifiedWorkspaceInspection to OrganizationIntake, along with the per-query and aggregate limits. This function shows that typed boundary:
import type { RecipientQualifiedWorkspaceInspection } from "@rtepl/pale";
import { OrganizationIntake } from "@rtepl/pale-scene/organization";

function openSceneIntake(inspection: RecipientQualifiedWorkspaceInspection): OrganizationIntake {
  return new OrganizationIntake(
    inspection,
    { inspected: 64, returned: 64, copiedStringBytes: 1_048_576 },
    {
      queries: 256,
      recordVisits: 16_384,
      sourceVisits: 16_384,
      records: 4_096,
      occurrences: 8_192,
      sourceOccurrences: 8_192,
      copiedStringBytes: 16_777_216,
    },
  );
}

Every page and continuation returns to that object's current authority and disclosure check. Closing the intake releases Scene's retained references.
Inspect a workspace change
WorkspaceChangeIntake retains one recipient-qualified SDK comparison. Subject, change-root, and current-impact pages advance independently. Point comparison, contributing-root, direct-dependency, and full source/proof reads accept only occurrences issued by that intake. A full read selects the exact prior or current side and preserves the native SDK page. Continue through the opaque value returned beside that page; it binds the exact intake, occurrence, and side before another native read can start. The comparison owner rechecks authority and disclosure for every call, including each continuation. Appearance IDs are local to the intake and establish neither semantic identity nor authority.
Compile an organization scene
OrganizationSceneCompiler binds one topology selection to its exact admitted inspection. It can produce a full scene, reuse an accepted layout, or complete one bounded region. A completed OrganizationScene keeps the semantic coordinates, actual plan options, route witnesses, qualified inspection owner, and prior correspondence used to produce it.
Reuse and regional layout first require the comparison to retain the same qualified predecessor and current inspection owners. Matching public digests are insufficient. Scene then reads the admitted pair summaries and checks that their coordinates still match the two scene sources.
Each topology captures its enumeration and selection coverage when it is created. Coverage says whether enumeration was incomplete, stopped by an exact resource limit, or exhausted, and whether the topology selected exactly the enumerated occurrences. Endpoint queries and repeated appearances do not expand enumeration coverage. Full, reused, and regional scenes retain the current topology's coverage; layout cannot improve it or inherit it from a prior scene.
The structural lens states what spatial proximity means: layout constraints, not semantic similarity or authority. Nearby objects are not necessarily related. A coordinate does not establish causality, disclosure, freshness, or native readiness.
Route witnesses distinguish explicit relations, derived relations, and directional services. Service routes join the selected provider and consumer scopes. Their contract identity and requirements remain in the retained SDK entry. Explicit relations retain the locality reported by the SDK.
scene.canonicalRouteOrder() derives a stable back-to-front order from the retained route-binding order. Use scene.orderRoutes(ids) only when a client needs an explicit presentation override. Each item keeps its zero-based depth and semantic route witness beside its placed route. Retained and encoded output is charged to the scene's shared budget.
Depth controls occlusion and composition only. It establishes no causal order, priority, authority, execution order, evidence strength, or boundary crossing. Contact analysis consumes the same scene-bound order instead of reconstructing it from route IDs.
scene.declaredGates associates a routed native endpoint with its relation witness, appearance, port, and route. A declaration in an unknown state remains unknown. An unrouted declaration has no placement. These associations belong to one scene generation; they are not cross-generation gate identities and do not prove that a native provider exists.
scene.boundaries also retains routed service boundaries and the five independent service requirements already present in the SDK witness. These associations do not create a gate, authorize a crossing, or prove completion. scene.generation is the opaque handle for the accepted source, structural lens, coverage, constraints, correspondence, and encoded publication.
Use the intake endpoint() and incidentRelations() queries when you need a selected neighborhood instead of full workspace enumeration. These queries share intake budgets but retain their own SDK pages and source occurrences. They do not consume the enumeration cursor. Incident queries include explicit and already-derived relations only; they do not imply a complete neighborhood. Each bounded intake read accepts an optional AbortSignal. A cancelled signal stops the next read before it starts; it does not interrupt a native call already in progress.
Replacing a selection rejects an older completion. Reuse performs no layout. Regional completion keeps its local input and result. The existing executor owns worker cancellation and release. The compiler rechecks cancellation and selection before it publishes a result. A source descriptor is not recipient or resident authority. The retained inspection owner remains the authority for later semantic and observation queries.
Run layout and contact analysis
Supply bounded geometry to GeometryPlan, then call ElkExecutor.run. A successful result contains accepted geometry. A failed run leaves its semantic input usable. Await close() to finish worker termination.
For optional crossing and depth annotations, call plan.contactInput(geometry, routeOrder, limits) with accepted geometry and a complete route order. Then call ContactExecutor.run. Later routes are drawn above earlier routes. OrganizationSceneCompiler.contacts also retains the selected scene and rejects stale publication.
Contact analysis runs Paper 0.12.18 core in a fresh confined worker. Its results are floating-point estimates in the root coordinate frame. Empty output does not prove that no contact exists. Extreme scales, cusps, retraced curves, and constant curves can produce incomplete results. A contact does not create a semantic relationship or change route geometry. Accepted annotation output is charged to the same aggregate Scene budget before it is returned.
The worker loads only pinned core files and used built-ins. It rejects an ambient DOM module before loading it. This confinement does not make the Node worker API browser-compatible.
Each stage has its own resource limits
Pass one SceneBudget to the organization intake when a complete scene compilation needs a shared ceiling. The budget follows that intake through topology, layout, and accepted output. It charges work, Scene-owned retained bytes, encoded output, and a deadline. Completed work is not refunded after a later failure. Retention counts remain separate because a count and a byte charge answer different questions. The deadline stops between bounded operations; it cannot interrupt a synchronous native call already in progress.
Scene-owned byte charges cover copied strings, local projection values, and accepted renderer-neutral output. They do not estimate native SDK graphs, worker heaps, caller copies, or process RSS. If the caller omits a budget, Scene uses its conservative default aggregate work, retention, output, and deadline ceilings. Supplying a budget narrows or replaces those defaults explicitly.
Each executor limits request bytes, response bytes, active time, and lifetime totals. Only one worker runs at a time. Active-time charges end after worker termination because replacement work remains blocked until then. They do not include retained caller results, native buffers, idle time, or total process memory. Query counts, copied strings, geometry cells, encoded messages, and worker heap settings measure different resources.
Scene occurrences and coordinates are presentation-local. They do not prove semantic identity, permission, execution activity, or a relationship at a route crossing. Raw portable compilations and comparisons are not Scene input.
Build and test
Build the package:
npm run build

Choose a check by the behavior you need to verify:
Command	Runnable checks	Blocked checks	
npm test	Geometry, workers, contacts, public errors, build boundaries and performance-report checks.	Does not include the separate recipient suite.	
npm run test:recipient	None until the recipient-handle requirement above is met.	Organization and change execution; no test-only authority substitutes for the required handles.	
npm run test:package -- /path/to/pale-sdk.tgz /path/to/organization-fixture	Installed geometry, packaged workers and compilation of the recipient-qualified type boundary.	Organization execution is reported as blocked.	
npm run qualify:performance -- --output /path/to/scene-qualification.json	Structural geometry performance, with optional contact measurements.	The recipient-qualified organization profile is reported as blocked.	
The recipient suite runs separately from npm test.
The package test installs the built Scene package and the native SDK archive into a disposable offline consumer. The SDK archive establishes dependency identity. The organization fixture is retained and hashed, not converted into an inspection handle. The archive and fixture must come from the same SDK qualification. The test does not build Rust at runtime or read another source checkout.
Run the separate geometry performance qualification when you need representative machine evidence:
npm run qualify:performance -- \
  --output /path/to/scene-qualification.json

The structural profile covers 8, 256, and 2,048 nodes. It enforces input, retained-output, wire-byte, worker-time, and caller-delay ceilings. It also requires byte-identical full, reused, and regional output with the pinned ELK algorithm. Warmups are checked but excluded from per-run summaries.
The caller-delay ceiling qualifies observed scheduling for that representative run. It is not a portable scheduling guarantee or a runtime interrupt bound.
The report records wall time and whole-process RSS. RSS includes setup, warmups, workers, and backend allocations, so it remains measured evidence, not a portable memory limit.
Contact analysis is optional because it has no certified completeness or numeric-error bound. Add --include-contacts to measure it separately. That measurement does not qualify contacts as part of the structural profile.

Compile and compare a workspace
Start with the three-document example, then follow the guide for your binding above. It describes a project called notes and its local execution workspace.

Match the operation to the host
Use portable methods when your application already has the source bytes, such as in an editor. Filesystem and process calls require a binding that exposes the operation and the permissions that call checks. Resident calls also require an authenticated connection. WebAssembly provides the portable subset and preserves 64-bit values without rounding them to JavaScript numbers.
Check the binding's capability list for the method. To check whether a provider can serve the request, use its own status. The build guides produce packages for local use. Publishing them is a separate step.
Lay out a visual view
Pale Scene uses ELK to lay out geometry for your renderer. To build Scene from source, make the @rtepl/pale TypeScript declarations from sdk/js available to the compiler. A project that uses only Scene’s geometry entry point can run without installing @rtepl/pale.
Live organization and change views need handles Pale issues for the intended recipient. PaleJS can consume those handles, but it cannot yet acquire them from the resident. Use the geometry entry point for an integration you can run today.

Source layout
Change compiler behavior in the engine, host behavior in an integration and shared procedures in a Package. These components have their own source folders and manifests in one Git repository, with no Git submodules.
Folder	What it holds

adapters/	Filesystem and process I/O, the SQLite control store, local sockets, A2A exchange, etcd anchor storage and the macOS signing helper	
sdk/	pale-sdk and the Python, JavaScript, Go and WebAssembly SDKs, plus the scene compiler	
interfaces/	The command line, MCP, language server, ACP, A2A and the resident's local listener host	
integrations/	One thin integration per product Pale works with	
packages/	Reusable working methods and guidance for agents

Dependencies run one way
Arrows point from the caller toward the layer that serves it.
flowchart TD
    MCP["pale-mcp"] --> CLI["pale-cli"]
    CLI --> SDK["pale-sdk"]
    Protocols["LSP, ACP and A2A"] --> SDK
    Bindings["Language SDKs"] --> SDK

pale-cli depends on pale-sdk alone within Pale. pale-mcp calls the CLI dispatcher directly, without parsing terminal output. The other client interfaces call the SDK. Each product integration uses the interface or SDK its host supports. Integrations never import engine internals or another integration.
The resident listener host builds the server from the application service, Unix-socket adapter and work-turn coordinator. It depends directly on the application, adapter and ports. Its Rust library runs on an event loop the caller manages. To install a resident, supply authentication and trust inputs the service accepts, connect a signer and anchor, and verify that startup works with those settings. The macOS signer and etcd anchor supply mechanisms for those bindings. The filesystem adapter uses the same protected reader for endpoint and signer-policy data.
The maintainer trust and recovery design keeps proposed storage, signing and recovery contracts together. It distinguishes implemented components from the later offline procedures and deployment work; it is not a guide to commands available in the ordinary executable.
The maintainer agent-surface specification explains generated repository files, host configuration and the identities needed to join native tool events to Pale operations. It identifies the current components and the unfinished admission and enforcement path.
The workspace-language contracts describe the full module language, cross-owner apply and staged activation. The implementation compiles local workspace and agent-guidance inputs; adopted modules, cross-owner apply and resident activation are not built. The workspace manual keeps the supported commands and examples separate from that implementation design.
The component method explains the reusable dependency-direction check: keep application rules independent of infrastructure. Pale's interface dependency tests supply the repository-specific check for the standalone interfaces and language SDKs, the resident composition and the A2A adapter. They inspect the declared Cargo dependency scopes, aliases, versions and sources against those components' allowed dependencies. They do not inspect every Rust import or establish that every business rule has the right owner.
Run this check from the repository root:
cargo test --manifest-path tools/repository-quality/Cargo.toml --locked --test interface_dependencies

Split modules by responsibility
Use the same splitting convention across all Rust crates so a reader can carry what they learned from one crate into another. Each submodule owns one cohesive responsibility and opens with a //! comment explaining it. Names follow the particular module's responsibilities; a renderer and a filesystem adapter need not have the same child names.
When a module acquires a second responsibility, separate the concerns during that work. Keep the root thin: its module documentation, declarations and re-exports preserve the public API while the child modules own the implementation. Keep helpers private or visible only to the smallest scope that needs them. Splitting a file must not expose new production API merely to make the split compile.
Keep Rust test files under the crate's tests/ directory. Integration tests exercise the public API. Internal unit tests can remain in the owning module's Rust scope through a #[cfg(test)] module declaration with #[path] pointing into tests/; their physical location does not require public helpers. Put repeated setup in shared test fixtures rather than copying it between cases, and keep those fixtures out of production builds. These are the same rules for new modules and for earlier splits touched by a change.
Contracts are generated from Rust
Edit the Rust wire record when a contract changes. Regenerate the JSON Schemas under contracts/ and run the conformance vectors in every language. Never edit the generated schemas by hand. Unreleased contracts stay at v1, with no aliases or compatibility readers.
From the repository root, use the checked-in descriptor manifest to generate schemas in a separate directory. Verify those files with the same inputs.
cargo run --locked -p pale-contract-codegen -- generate \
  contracts/bundle/agent-surface.v1/agent-surface-schemas.v1.json \
  /absolute/path/generated-contracts
cargo run --locked -p pale-contract-codegen -- verify \
  contracts/bundle/agent-surface.v1/agent-surface-schemas.v1.json \
  /absolute/path/generated-contracts

The descriptor registers the contracts. The Rust records define their structure. Generation fails when they disagree, and verification checks the resulting files against the generated bundle. Review that bundle before replacing the checked-in one, then use each SDK's maintainer instructions to regenerate its language types. Regenerate stale output from the owning source.
Give each working copy its own Cargo target directory. A reused target has emitted schemas from a disposable prototype instead of the live source. If bundle verification reports a mismatch from a reused target, repeat it in a fresh target before changing the checked-in schemas. Sharing targets across working copies needs that stale-generator failure reproduced and fixed first.
Building and testing
Run the engine and adapter tests from the repository root.

Prepare guides and API reference together
tools/prepare_reference.py captures one selected working copy, including uncommitted source and the complete manual, and rebuilds the public JavaScript and WebAssembly declarations. It runs the SDK build, declaration, ABI and packed-consumer checks in a disposable working copy with its own Cargo target, incremental compilation off and compiler wrappers disabled. Rust dependencies must already be available offline; Node.js 22 or later, npm, Cargo, rustc and wasm-pack must be on PATH. npm installs the locked development dependencies needed for these checks.
Supply the publishing workspace's three source-option files explicitly. TypeDoc options must omit installed plugins, and Rustdoc options must omit tool paths: the consuming workspace selects those tools separately. The preparer preserves the option files' exact bytes.
python3 tools/prepare_reference.py \
  --source /absolute/path/pale \
  --output /absolute/path/fresh-prepared-source \
  --typedoc-options /absolute/path/typedoc-options.json \
  --typescript-config /absolute/path/tsconfig.json \
  --rustdoc-options /absolute/path/rustdoc-options.json

The output parent must exist and the output directory must be new. Keep it outside the selected source or in an ignored build directory. Do not edit the selected source during preparation: a changed file, mode or file inventory rejects the capture. The working copy must match that source before commands run and afterward, except for explicitly rebuilt SDK outputs. Symlinked source members are rejected. Generated declarations, their WebAssembly companions, Node type declarations and the actual packed contracts dependency accompany the captured Rust source and manual. preparation.json records source identity, tools, attempted commands, results, declarations and the complete prepared tree; .reference-preparation/ retains command logs and the contracts archive. A command that cannot start or is interrupted retains its error and available log, with no claimed exit code. A failed run records its failure and cannot be used as a completed source.
Preparation does not run TypeDoc or Rustdoc. Select the completed tree for both the manual and reference generators so they describe the same code. The native checks establish the selected platform's behavior; they do not establish a cross-platform release or publication approval.

Working with a workspace
To compile a Pale workspace, give the SDK the root pale-workspace.toml and the documents it names. An editor can pass the documents it already has. A local client that reads from disk can use the filesystem adapter. The resulting compilation describes people, projects, responsibilities and the systems they use.
Start with the portable example below to compile documents and compare an edit. For command-line work, follow Inspect your workspace or Add coding instructions to a repository. To extend the declarations, see local module authoring and project owners and repository duties.
Try a complete portable workspace
The portable example describes a notes project with one local execution workspace:
Logical label	Source

resolution.lock.toml	Release choices, empty in this example	
universe.lock.toml	The workspace's release lock	
Pass all three documents to an SDK's portable compilation call, using the labels in the table. The Rust example prints notes-workspace: 3 documents followed by notes / local.
Keep the returned compilation handle. Next, change the project title from Shared notes to Team notes in a second copy and compile it with the same IDs and lock documents. Compare the two handles to inspect what the edit affects. This example has no Package releases, repositories or execution paths, so it stops at inspection and comparison.
Review a proposed change
An embedded application keeps both compilation handles and their comparison handle for further queries. The Rust example shows how to read pages of impacts, compare values and explain a subject.
The title edit produces one source change. Some impact rows read Affected: Equal: the subject depends on the changed document, but its compiled value stayed the same. Read the before and after values to distinguish a changed input from a changed result. Both compilations remain available, and comparison leaves the source files unchanged.
Compare local configuration with the CLI
For configuration review, compare current and candidate workspaces with the same project, execution workspace and machine. Pale uses the baseline's captured Package definitions for both. It rejects a different distribution lock digest or a change to the project's starting set of Packages. For either change, validate each workspace against its own Package inputs and compare those results separately.
review-configuration impacts lists affected and unaffected subjects a page at a time. A subject is affected if it depends on a changed input, even when its value stays the same. accept, reject, cancel and stale return a decision without writing files.
Pass the complete preview summary to the CLI on standard input. It reconstructs the comparison before returning a page or a decision. If the summary no longer matches, generate a new preview. The product review task shows the commands.
The MCP interface rebuilds each review from the supplied sources. If a source scan needs a continuation tied to its original handle, keep that handle in the SDK or editor. A copied cursor or digest cannot restore it.

CLI option	Meaning

Check, plan and apply
Use the planning command for the files you want to update. Keep the plan with the command and configuration that produced it.
Shared source guidance
Use guidance inspect to see the role, policies and proposed files for a coding host. To compare that output with a checkout, run guidance plan --repository source --host codex (or --host claude-code). The plan lists files to add, update, keep or remove and shows their text differences. It leaves instructions unchanged and remembers only the proposal's identity in an owner-readable file at the repository root. Use --result-format json for exact before/after text, hashes and modes.
After reviewing the plan, run guidance apply --repository source --host codex with the same workspace selections and host. Pale retrieves that host's remembered proposal and recomputes it from current inputs before writing. Changed sources, files or permissions require another plan. It preserves project instructions and refuses conflicting unowned or edited managed files. The plan also includes a .gitignore block for Pale's lock, recovery and review files; other ignore rules remain unchanged. These commands write guidance before runtime tool activation.
The product task follows that path. The CLI contract describes ownership, private coordination files and recovery.
Runtime materialization
Runtime plan saves one plan per repository. apply and remove both rebuild the plan and require it to match the saved plan before changing files. An apply plan can remove obsolete generated content. To remove all Pale-managed content, generate and use a removal plan.
Adopting a file Pale does not own requires --adopt-unowned at both planning and application. Whole files must match the state recorded in the plan. For managed blocks, Pale requires valid markers and preserves the surrounding text. Removing an adopted whole file deletes it without restoring a pre-adoption backup.
Use surface-status to compare current files with the runtime plan. If a file differs, check the cause and create a matching plan before writing. The CLI reference defines results and failures.
Runtime apply requires a runtime plan. Use the result of guidance plan with guidance apply.
What Pale writes into a repository
Pale writes host instructions, roles, skills, references and bindings into repositories named by the workspace. Both coding hosts use one AGENTS.md. Source guidance adds a separately owned block for each host and leaves the rest of that file under the project's control; runtime rendering produces one shared entry for the selected paths. Runtime output can include hook settings and activation data for that machine. Pale writes to the named repositories and leaves global agent settings alone. The guidance starter explains how to load the shared entry alongside existing Claude instructions and migrate earlier Pale installations.
The repository owner decides what to commit. Keep private machine bindings, coordination files and the copies saved for interrupted-write recovery out of public output.
Author local modules before publication
A workspace can name unpublished module sources with module_sources = ["modules/studio.toml"] inside [workspace]. Keep module_manifests and the release/adoption selections empty for this source-only path. The root still selects the component files in source_components; each module names their logical IDs instead of supplying component digests.
# modules/studio.toml
schema = "pale/workspace-module-source.v1"
schema_version = 1
module_id = "studio"
source_components = []
imports = []
exports = []
extensions = []

[[resources]]
kind = "organization"
resource_id = "company"
authority_resolver = "company-authority"

Run pale --workspace /absolute/path/pale-workspace.toml check-source, adding --result-format json for the complete report. No project, execution-workspace or machine selector is needed. The Rust SDK exposes the same operation as PaleApi::inspect_local_workspace_source(LocalWorkspaceLocator), with the native-local feature.
This check validates module structure, computes selected component digests, resolves project owners and repository duty references, and uses the existing responsibility and organisational translation lowerers. Its report identifies the phase as source_only. A content digest identifies the lowered meaning; separate source evidence records the exact input bytes, so changing a comment changes the evidence without changing that meaning. Machine bindings, Package distributions and credentials are not read.
Source-only inspection currently accepts local modules without release imports or experience-composition files. It does not link arbitrary declaration namespaces or normalize runtime policy. Duties retain attributable omissions for publisher and adopter coordinates until those releases exist. Publication fields are rejected in a local module source. Preparing a published module later requires explicit publication identities and the normal release, signature and admission checks; this report cannot be used as an admitted workspace handle. Ordinary workspace compilation rejects a root that still selects local module sources.

Name a project's owner and repository duties
A project may declare owner as a reference to a selected module resource. For example, owner = { kind = "organization", module_id = "studio", resource_id = "company" } names the organisation selected as company by the selected studio module. Use kind = "principal" for a person who owns a project in their own capacity. The module and resource must exist in the selected set (adopted releases for ordinary compilation, local sources for check-source), and the resource's kind must match. Leaving owner absent leaves ownership unspecified; a directory, author or repository user does not fill it in.
A project-to-repository membership may name existing duties with responsibility_derivation_ids = ["verify-source"]. The list is sorted, unique and limited to 1,024 IDs; each must resolve to a responsibility derivation selected by the root manifest. The referenced record retains the duty's inputs, provider, consumer, acceptance and other answers. A repository shared by two projects can therefore have different duties in each project without being declared twice.
In ordinary workspace compilation, these references participate in source navigation and the selected topology's identity. Source-only inspection retains them in its report and content digest; it does not produce that compilation's navigation index. They declare relationships; they do not supply signed module admission, appoint a provider, accept a result or widen repository access. The private guidance context output currently shows the selected repository and source reading order; it does not yet render these owner and duty records.

Architecture
Follow a request through the prototype to see where to make a change. The Flask API manages the shared lifecycle and calls a lane adapter to validate the scenario, prepare run files, start the runner and generate the report. The Vue cockpit reads each lane's catalog and manifests. Some payload builders still name the three existing lanes, so a new lane needs frontend changes too.
Using RawFish leads to cockpit tasks. The rebuild contract describes the planned replacement.

A lane supplies its meaning through an adapter
A lane registers an adapter implementing the use-case interface, a lane manifest, a statistical manifest and a cohort pack. The catalog route returns the lane's personas together with its required lane_manifest, and the cockpit renders many scenario, cohort, report, timeline and control surfaces from those declarations. A field that does not apply to a lane is omitted from its manifest rather than shown disabled.
All lanes use / and /run/:runId? in the browser and /api/sim/use-cases/<lane_id>/... on the backend; there is no separate policy application or browser route. Keep the stable ids creator, internal_policy and public_policy when tracing a request. Each policy lane owns its adapter and manifest, and policy_core supplies identity helpers, though the current policy implementation still shares a policy-scope mapping internally. Run and report calls use RawFish's provider router; Graphiti has separate model, embedding and reranking clients.
The SimulationUseCase protocol leaves scenario and report types to the lane. Each adapter supplies the validation models and an artifact_names mapping from logical names to files inside a run directory. The generic layer can find a report without assuming every lane writes the same filename. Its report_schema enables schema validation on stored reads. The report_draft_schema can limit model output to fields the model supplies, while the application adds the run ID and records which input produced the report.
Adapters opt into shared report checks through guardrail_capabilities. An adapter that already performs those checks internally declares that fact, so dispatch does not apply demotions and other side effects twice. An unsupported optional capability raises NotImplementedError, which dispatch exposes as 501 CAPABILITY_UNSUPPORTED. This is different from a provider failure during a supported operation. The registry checks required member presence rather than call signatures; conformance tests still have to exercise behavior. Its process-wide singleton makes built-in registration simple, but tests must restore registry state when they add temporary adapters.
The cockpit also needs lane-specific frontend integration. Launch hard-codes seed presets and parser identity by lane. The run store repeats the parser-identity mapping, chooses separate creator and policy scenario payload builders, and chooses a public-policy or internal-policy stakeholder fallback from the lane id. A fourth genuinely distinct lane therefore needs changes and tests at those cockpit seams in addition to its manifests, cohort pack and adapter. Follow extending RawFish for the adapter and frontend changes. The rebuild aims to remove those lane-id branches.
A run's lifecycle
In the run store, Build the world first creates the run, then prepares it and reads the graph. Creation stores the lane, scenario, provider and statistical settings. Preparation delegates ontology, persona and artifact work to the adapter. The cockpit then navigates to the saved run identifier. This separates an editable in-memory draft from backend state; reopening the draft address cannot recover its text.
Consider changing the creator cohort's sentiment before launch. The workbench first changes local settings. Save patch constructs JSON Patch operations and sends the last saved settings hash. The backend takes the run lock, rejects starting, running, completed and reported phases, checks an expected hash when supplied, validates paths and values, then writes the configuration files and state. A stale hash returns 409. A path the backend does not allow returns 422. The cockpit always sends a hash, but the API accepts a request without one.
If the run was prepared, the edit marks it for preparation again. The cockpit calls prepare with the changed hash before proceeding. This matters because accepting a settings change alone does not regenerate the personas and artifacts consumed by execution. Preflight then checks the selected provider and scale, and Launch swarm starts the prepared run through the runner adapter. Status polling supplies progress; completion permits report generation.
The runner implementation differs by lane. The creator adapter does not start an agent subprocess: it writes creator_deterministic_mock_v1 completion metadata containing the statistical settings and returns control to dispatch. Its later report calls a model with the scenario, stress question, persona and segment identities/types. It discards the evidence catalog and does not read cohort statistical settings, so it cannot explain observed interactions or the effect of changing those settings. The policy adapters use the OASIS runner bridge and need their own execution tests.
The current reseed route also mutates that same run's configuration. It appends a lineage event containing parent and changed settings, and the cockpit prepares the same run again. The event is a settings variant, not another executed run. The Compare panel compares its settings with the parent snapshot. The backend fills its findings buckets from settings-subject presence without loading both reports, so those buckets cannot establish report validity or an observed effect of reseeding. Reseed uses the same refused-phase set as patch. Neither route includes failed in that set, so the backend phase check leaves a failed-run mutation gap. The cockpit additionally freezes failed runs and offers duplicate as draft; its frozen controls do not close that API gap. Separate variant runs are a rebuild target.
Mutating routes wrapped in the idempotency helper accept Idempotency-Key: the same key and body reuse a response, while a changed body under that key is refused. The cockpit derives keys from the operation, run and selected payload. This prevents some accidental retries; it is not a transaction over the whole run. Individual files use atomic replacement, but a later failure can leave the sequence partly written. Report publication has the same boundary.
Models and memory
Run and report model calls use the provider router, whose current factory builds RawFishLiteLLMClient on LiteLLM. The provider mode is local_ollama, local_openai_compatible or external, chosen for each run and kept with it; local modes need no external key. This client requests a JSON object unless JSON mode is off, strips enclosing code fences and parses the response as an object. The separate structured wrapper delegates to it because it advertises no strict JSON-schema capability. The audited client records model, mode, tokens, latency and phase into run metadata. Graphiti has its own model and embedding configuration; router selection alone does not configure that separate client.
Memory is chosen separately with ZEP_MODE. The prototype memory interface finds entities of declared types, lists one type, sets the ontology, adds episodes, searches, and reads all nodes or all edges.
mock, the default, needs no service. It keys entities from the scenario hash and cohort names, extracts by matching the ontology against seed text, and returns seeded search results. Unsupported operations fail explicitly.
graphiti is an experimental local Neo4j profile. The dependency lock pins Neo4j 5.23.0 for the simulation engine, below Graphiti’s declared minimum. A lock that installs does not establish supported dependencies.
Hosted Zep is a deprecated experiment pinned at zep-cloud 3.13.0. It warns on use and implements neither writes nor search. Removing it remains a release proposal, not completed behavior.
The Graphiti adapter creates its model, embedder and reranker independently, each with its own endpoint and model. Selecting a local run provider does not configure them. The intended local profile uses local OpenAI-compatible endpoints for all three and Neo4j Community bound to loopback with a mandatory password. Entity types must be typed models generated from the ontology; each episode needs a reference time; errors must remove credentials from connection strings.
The prototype rejects OpenAI’s cloud host wherever it constructs the store. Blocking that host does not prove endpoint confinement. The selected release profile still needs tests for unexpected network access, telemetry with the switch off, unset and on, stored telemetry identifiers and concurrent group isolation. Direct synchronous add_episode calls must expose failures and read each write back; a queued provider’s acknowledgment is not proof of ingestion.
Structured-output handling
The active RawFishLiteLLMClient advertises supports_json_schema=False. Its _parse_json strips enclosing Markdown fences, calls json.loads and rejects a non-object response. Both loose and strict JSON modes send response_format={"type": "json_object"}; off omits that request. The client does not use the legacy prose extraction, malformed-JSON repair or schema-validation retry loop. LiteLLM receives the configured generation timeout and transport retry count: the code defaults are 60 seconds and one retry, while the environment template selects 120 seconds and one retry. A run using the template therefore differs from the code default.
The retained PolicyLLMClient has a different parsing path: strip fences, try strict JSON, decode an object or array embedded in prose, extract balanced braces, then remove control characters and trailing commas. Final failure raises LLMJSONParseError with an excerpt capped at 500 characters, rather than logging the full response. Its strict mode rethrows a failed JSON-object request; loose can fall back to a second request without response_format; off starts with that second path. Its own defaults are LLM_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=60, LLM_MAX_RETRIES=2, 8,192 tokens for ontology and 16,384 for reports. Those settings do not describe the active router's implementation.
The structured wrapper checks the wrapped client's capabilities. With a schema, declared support and an exposed OpenAI client, it requests strict JSON-schema output and retries validation failures up to its configured limit (two by default), feeding the validation error back to the model. Provider or JSON-decode failures fall back to the wrapped client's chat_json. PolicyLLMClient can advertise that capability through LLM_SUPPORTS_JSON_SCHEMA; the current router does not. The wrapper sums usage across its strict-schema validation attempts, and the audited client writes one entry per logical call with the reported tokens, model, mode, latency, phase and timestamp. That aggregation does not establish accounting for unreported retries inside another provider client. The Rust rebuild still needs its own implementation and checks.
Scale and configured defaults
The prototype's pure scale guard multiplies ensemble size, stakeholder-segment count and rounds, treating each factor as at least one. Its caps are 500 normally and 5,000 when the expensive tier is explicitly enabled. This raises the ceiling rather than removing it. The API's preflight and reseed snapshot in use_cases.py and the policy runner each evaluate the guard from their own resolved inputs. They do not reuse one durable decision across the whole run. The API's rough token estimate defaults to the scale product multiplied by 150; it is not a measured model rate.
The rebuild must record one scale decision and reuse it at preflight, start, metadata, replay and receipt, as required by the target verification cases. Its token estimate must use a measured basis or say “No estimate yet”. The prototype's configured agent-and-round defaults below are separate from the stakeholder-segment count supplied to the guard; these settings alone do not establish which runner executes or whether the controls affect its behavior:
Lane	Configured default	Mock-profile default	
creator	30 agents by 2 rounds	12 by 2	
internal policy	50 by 4	24 by 3	
public policy	80 by 5	32 by 3	
Reports
Report generation finds a completed run before calling the lane generator. For policy reports, the model supplies claims and sections. RawFish adds the run ID and input details, checks the claim labels and runs the language guard. The draft schema keeps those application-owned fields out of the model's response. It cannot make a generated claim true.
JSON, rendered Markdown, report metadata and lifecycle state are written in sequence. The stored JSON route validates the adapter's schema but does not repeat the language guard or verify the recorded digest and embedded run identity. It can return JSON written before a later publication step failed. Keep generation errors and the run/report context when reading results. HTTP 200 or file presence alone does not mean report publication completed. The product contract sets the rebuild requirements, and guardrails describes the checks.
The findings task shows how these limits affect a reader using the creator announcement example.
