Detailed verification cases
The cases below belong with the implementation they check. Record the source revision and digest, the built artifact where relevant, how the check ran, its result and location, observation date, limits and any required owner or signature. Keep source inspection, generated output, a running instance and a release distinct so the result says exactly what was established.
Names: check identifier mappings, what each parser accepts, serialized output, the migration state and removal of retired names.
Browser surface: the two routes and six steps, with data as a Findings mode only. Refuse unknown and repeated query keys, a mode outside Findings, draft payloads on Launch and Run, and lane or source overrides on saved runs before loading run data. Exercise valid draft and saved-run links and the cockpit sharing contract. Retired routes stay absent.
Manifest and catalogue: exercise the one nested schema and its validation, with no second way to read a competing manifest.
Policy lanes: check the separate internal-policy and public-policy fields over their common mechanics, without a generic policy scope replacing either.
Accepted sources: check paste and refuse every other source kind at preflight and creation. At prepare and start, refuse a restored run without the server's record of valid paste input, before an adapter does anything. Separately try an omitted source, a caller-declared parser and a connector label. Each must fail to replace the actual accepted bytes and their origin. Inspect the saved run, graph and receipts as well as the reply; the prototype observations show why the reply alone is insufficient.
Workbench changes: require the expected settings hash and request identity. Repeating an unchanged request returns its original receipt and variant; reusing its key for changed input conflicts. Exercise recovery after a crash.
Comparison: use the generic endpoint with the base and variant IDs only. Refuse extra fields before reading either run, keep the run-scoped route absent and prove the cockpit sends the same two-field request. A valid settings pair with absent or malformed reports still has a statistical diff, while the findings buckets reflect the report loader's actual results.
Report read-back: qualify the shared report loader through data, Markdown, chat, compare and export. Substitute changed bytes, a foreign or superseded generation with internally consistent metadata, and an unhedged overclaim. Verify refusal before disclosure, prompt construction or export. Include the exact committed artifact as a control, and confirm that absent and corrupt reports remain distinct.
Report publication: interrupt after staging JSON, after staging Markdown and after the commit but before its reply. Before commitment, no reader exposes the staged report. After commitment, an authorised read verifies both digests against the same receipt. Recover the exact attempt and verify that a retry after commit adds no second publication.
Stored identity: one canonical settings projection; metadata, timestamps, storage identifiers and provenance notes never change the hash of equal settings.
Scale: test below, at and above the cap, and confirm that every consumer uses the same recorded decision.
What a result supports: seed heuristics, calibration, provenance, validity, uncertainty and claim class kept separate.
Capability honesty: no route, control, event, agent, connector or evaluation appears from a flag or label alone.
Logs and security: use recognisable test values to check that forbidden content reaches neither routine nor error logs. Check source roles and permitted scopes separately.
Access and permitted changes: a request under one data controller cannot read or change another's runs, and the cockpit changes only the fields the workbench allows.
Build inputs: record the source state, dependencies and their inventory and origins against the exact built artifact. Check its digest, handling of secrets and rollback.
Rights and publication: review the exact changes being released, their notices, contributors, authority to supply the source, conditions, required signature and source offer.
Distribution: a fresh install, build and run from the candidate artifact, and offline and recovery limits where claimed.
Matching behaviour across modes: standalone, embedded and remote use the same simulation rules, with work and storage owned as described in Run ownership and transitions. Removing a connection preserves each owner’s records and independent operation.
Run-state recovery. Exercise every transition, cancellation race, duplicate, crash, restart and replay against the current run generation and revision. Keep the simulation result separate from acceptance, outside effects and settlement. Use the known prototype failure cases as regression inputs for these checks. Status, synchronous generation, queue admission, the queued worker and the watcher must use the committed terminal record for the exact lane, run and generation. Withhold the expected terminal evidence and offer a foreign-lane or superseded result. Re-prepare the same run with its old completion present, then repeat with a valid new completion. The old job must refuse before generation or terminal state writes in both cases. Queue the new completed attempt under its own job and prove that only an exact retry returns its original receipt.
Event outbox, if chosen: commit the run change and event together. Check duplicate suppression, recorded delivery progress, gaps, replay, outages and deletion. Events must contain no secrets, and removing delivery must preserve standalone run state.
Cockpit consistency: manifests, run states, evidence labels and unavailable states render the same in every mode. Give an independent reviewer the selected build, its source revision, reference screens and observations from each mode. Compare both rendered screens and actual interactions against the state and capability requirements in this contract. Keep each mode’s native observations with that build and report any original the reviewer could not open.
Cockpit route and workbench contracts
These are rebuild requirements. The retained prototype differs as described in architecture; the API and durable receipts below are not a claim that those requirements are implemented.
Two browser routes
Path	Shell	Query it accepts	What it is	
/	Launch	lane?, source?	the lane catalogue, the paste-only console and admitted seed suggestions	
/run/:runId?	Cockpit	step?, mode?, lane?, source?	one cockpit shell for a draft or a saved run; lane and source only before a run exists	
Report, chat, compare, sensitivity, history, priors, personas, provenance and the statistical controls are Findings modes, docks or overlays inside the cockpit, never routes. The query values are exact:
step   = scenario | build | cohorts | preflight | simulate | findings
mode   = read | ask | data          only with step=findings; data renders as "Analysis"
source = paste                      the only admitted source in the first version

step=analysis is neither accepted nor emitted. source=live, cached, graph, upload values and connector names are rejected until both a registry capability and a route contract admit them. Unknown values and unknown keys fail closed rather than snapping to something nearby. No other route is accepted or redirected, and there are no route stubs or route-building discovery hooks.
The cockpit follows these rules:
With a runId, the saved run owns the lane and lifecycle, and a lane or source in the query is rejected rather than allowed to override it.
Without a runId, the shell reads the local draft store; with no draft it returns to Launch. There is no draft query parameter.
Without a step, a draft opens Scenario and a saved run opens its furthest admitted step.
Findings links are /run/:runId?step=findings&mode=read, ...&mode=ask and ...&mode=data. Each claim, evidence, graph-node or act view has a typed identifier. In the web host every overlay level creates a history entry that Back undoes; embedded hosts use the same identifiers in their own navigation. The shared design specifies the identifiers rather than requiring fragments in every host.
A run's lane is fixed when the run is created; changing lane means going back to Launch or to the still-unsaved draft. Before a run is saved the draft owns its lane, and after that the run does; the cockpit resolves the matching admitted lane manifest and rejects any query or request-body value that disagrees with the run. All three lanes use the same routes, and no lane has a browser path of its own.
What a link may never carry
RawFish keeps manifests, scenario text and reversible encodings, source bytes and authority evidence, credentials and keys, cohort and persona payloads, runtime state, and mutation bodies and receipts out of every URL component. Scope, actor, controller, rights holder, classification and custody resolve through their native owners. Test each forbidden value with recognisable synthetic content. Inspect the complete URL, browser history, referrers, logs and analytics through navigation, sharing, refresh and opening a new tab; none may carry the value.
Before a run is saved, the draft lives in a local ephemeral store kept out of browser history, referrers, logs and analytics. Moving a draft to another device is not supported; any future design must still keep scenario text out of the link.
Run identity and sharing
One run has four surface spellings, and they are typed mappings, not aliases: runId in the browser, sim_id in the lane API, base_run_id for the source of a lineage and variant_run_id for its fork. Each parser accepts only its own spelling; adapters map through a typed run-identity object, never by copying field names.
Sharing is a command, not a route or a mode of the environment chip, which only shows status. It is unavailable for a draft. For a saved run it copies the canonical /run/:runId link with the current step, and in Findings its mode, and nothing else: no lane, source, draft state, overlays, credentials, mutation state or authority evidence. A copied link grants no access; the recipient still passes the run's own admission.
The workbench makes the consequential choices visible
The statistical workbench sits in Cohorts, between the cohort map and preflight. It resolves the lane declarations, operator edits and locks, admitted priors, salts and seeds into one configuration. Preflight, preparation, execution, reports and comparison all consume that configuration, so none can silently make a different choice.
The operator sees the proposed agents and cohorts in relation to the graph. Each admitted control has a slider and an exact numeric input, alongside its provenance, default basis, validity scope, uncertainty and lock. An admitted prior also shows its weight and source.
Save explains which fields change. Save and re-seed explains what is recomputed and creates a variant; comparison keeps that changed configuration apart from ensemble members, which repeat one configuration under different seeds. An impact estimate appears only when compatible evidence exists.
It renders only fields its lane's validated statistical manifest enumerates, never a control synthesised from a backend field, a non-canonical name or a screenshot, and it omits unsupported fields rather than showing them disabled. A field without a proven preparation or runtime consumer is read-only or absent, and a successful save is not proof the engine used it. The workbench uses the same panels, cards, chips, buttons, label-and-value rows, meters and state variants as the rest of the cockpit. Colour, type, focus, spacing and disabled behavior come from the shared component system.
Editing renderers compose the per-cohort numeric controls, active-hours policy, admitted drift fields, admitted priors, salts, seeds, locks and the command footer inside Cohorts. State renderers keep overrides, provenance and validity visible on cards, rows and the preflight summary without merging them.
Lineage and impact renderers keep the base run, the variant run and the lineage record apart and show only compatible evidence that is qualified by its method, with absence shown as absence. Readiness rendering consumes one typed decision about scale, provider, cost and latency and never assembles a second one. Manifest identity is shown (the admitted manifest reference, digest and schema version, the settings hash and the seed) without becoming something the operator can edit.
Two surfaces depend on the workbench without being its slots: the comparison in Findings data mode renders the route's compare result and the exact pair of settings hashes, and the system dashboard renders sampling and reseed events only from admitted event records, never by relabelling a prose warning as an event.
The editor has four compact sections: activity and sentiment (activity, rate, sentiment, influence, response delay, active hours); drift, with the Conservative, Default and Volatile preset, only for lanes that have drift fields; priors, only when a working priors connector and attachment record are admitted, so the paste-only first version shows none; and salt and seed (run seed, per-cohort salts, provenance, locks and the admitted reseed scopes). Every continuous control has both a slider and an exact numeric input, and neither silently clamps, rounds or reinterprets the other. The preflight meter is read-only and shows one typed decision about scale, provider, cost and latency rather than assembling its own; a local provider never asks for an outside key, and external cost appears only when an external provider is chosen.
The salt and seed section shows the resolved run seed, each cohort's salt, how it was derived and whether it is locked, reading the stored values rather than recomputing the formula. An explicit salt is shown as distinct from a derived one, and the interface never claims a salt changes behaviour unless a preparation or runtime consumer is proven.
Each value shows its provenance as a chip, beside its validity, and the two never merge:
Provenance	Meaning	How it renders	
user-set	the operator chose it	filled chip, editable if unlocked	
manifest-default	it came from the lane manifest	outlined chip; editing makes it user-set	
inferred-from-prior	derived from an admitted prior	chip links the prior and its digest	
sampled	drawn from a declared distribution	dashed chip links the seed and distribution	
inferred-from-parseScenario	suggested by parsing the scenario	chip links the parse receipt; a suggestion is not acceptance	
The workbench value flags sit beside it (separate from flags qualifying the report’s evidence and claims): prior weights that do not sum as declared, a value in a narrow region of prior support, a value outside a registered evidence range (unavailable without a calibration record), a value beyond the attached prior, and a cohort locked against reseeding. A preset creates no sixth provenance value.
The footer has two separate commands. Save stores a revision before the start without reseeding. Save and re-seed forks a statistical variant run, with two scopes: re-seed all unlocked cohorts, or use a new run seed. Before either, the editor shows a one-line, field-level diff, and before re-seeding it also names the unchanged cohorts, the seed and lock effects and the fact that a new variant will be created; the server returns the authoritative receipt, lineage identity and forked run. The accepted single-cohort derivation takes entropy from the canonical hash of the variant’s ordinal, bound to the exact base configuration and target cohort. Replaying the same ordinal must reproduce that cohort-only variant while every other cohort stays bit-identical. Its canonical bytes, journal fields and fixtures still need to be fixed and proved; until then the command and control remain unavailable.
For Save and Save and re-seed, test the control’s readiness, submit the request and independently read back its exact durable result. The editor keeps HTTP acceptance separate from a saved change.
A pending command stays visibly pending until a terminal durable receipt arrives.
An exact replay shows the original receipt and variant, not a fresh success.
A stale configuration keeps the operator's draft, loads the current configuration and asks for an explicit review.
An invalid path, lock, range, prior, schema, key or capability points at the affected control and applies nothing.
Reconciliation in progress blocks further changes and tells the operator the server must finish recovering.
A reused key with a different body shows as a safety conflict and is never retried under a hidden new key.
The variant strip may look like the ensemble chips, but the meaning differs: ensemble members replay one configuration under different member seeds, while variants are different configurations. Each chip shows the base run, the forked run and the lineage record apart, with a settings-hash prefix, the seed and the reseed scope; selecting one makes it the subject of comparison without altering it, and the strip's plus command opens the editor for a new prospective variant. Findings in data mode compares base and variant settings separately from report evidence, keeps present, missing and corrupted evidence in separate buckets, and never takes an absent row to mean two runs are equal. Sharing uses the canonical run link; focusing a variant is a bounded identifier inside the shell, never uploaded configuration.
An impact preview renders only from a compatible, typed, lane-scoped sensitivity result bound to its source run, settings hash, varied field, method, perturbation, metric, scope and digest. Otherwise it says "No compatible impact estimate available." and never estimates from a slider position, cached prose or a field name. Every preview is after the run only; co-occurrence rather than cause unless a separately admitted method proves more; qualified by its method, kernel, perturbation and scope; one-at-a-time when the analysis is; and passed through the language guard, with a receipt over the exact rendered text. That receipt proves only that the guard's versioned lexical rules ran, not that the preview is true, correct, causal or free of prediction.
The workbench will not: rerun sensitivity while a slider moves, use unsupported causal or predictive wording, offer any way round scale admission, tag acts live without an admitted capability, show policy-only drift in the creator lane, edit the fixed interquartile-mean aggregator, store an active-hours preset name in place of resolved hours, time zone and daylight-saving policy, show any upload, live, cached, browser, sensitive or graph control in the paste-only first version, or push scenario counterfactuals or trait edits through statistical reseed.
The workbench API
These are the only operations on statistical configuration, all under the lane API:
Method	Path	Request	What it does	
GET	/api/sim/use-cases/{lane_id}/statistical-manifest	optional exact version	returns the lane's statistical manifest, with no wrapper or shadow defaults	
GET	/api/sim/use-cases/{lane_id}/simulation/{sim_id}/statistical-config		returns the configuration the simulation's current-config pointer selects	
PATCH	.../simulation/{sim_id}/statistical-config	{ops: RFC6902[], expected_hash} and Idempotency-Key	Save: appends a revision before the start and returns one receipt; never creates a variant	
POST	.../simulation/{sim_id}/statistical-config/reseed	{expected_hash, scope, reason?, ops?, seed?} and Idempotency-Key	Save and re-seed: forks one variant run with its lineage record and configuration and returns one receipt; never changes the base run	
GET	.../simulation/{sim_id}/statistical-lineage		the base settings hash and lineage records	
GET	.../simulation/{sim_id}/variants	optional axis=statistical	statistical variants only; scenario or counterfactual axes are rejected	
POST	/api/sim/use-cases/{lane_id}/simulation/compare	{base_run_id, variant_run_id}	the three-bucket comparison, the statistical diff and the exact settings-hash pair	
There is no second compare endpoint, and optional compare fields are rejected until their behaviour and result contract are admitted. The catalog is published at GET /api/sim/use-cases/{lane_id}/catalog. Lane discovery, cohort packs, connectors, evaluations, scenario, prepare, start, status, report and sensitivity are operation families that stay uncallable until each has an exact method, path, envelope, admission rule and error behaviour; a manifest flag, a rendered control, a frontend function name or a handler name cannot make a route exist.
Save and re-seed may touch only fields the lane's statistical manifest declares, inside these paths; one bad operation rejects the whole request with 422 path_not_in_allowlist:
/cohorts/*/statistical/*    /cohorts/*/drift/*    /cohorts/*/priors/*
/run/persona_salts/*        /run/run_seed         /run/ensemble_n
/run/ensemble_seeds         /run/t_structure      /run/t_narrative
/run/drift_horizon_rounds   /run/assumption_confirmation_ratio

The reseed scopes behave exactly:
scope=all_cohorts keeps the run seed, samples a fresh salt for every unlocked cohort once inside the journal transaction, and stores the salt map and its sampling provenance before replying; a supplied seed is rejected.
scope=new_run_seed takes the supplied seed or samples one inside the transaction, then derives every unlocked cohort's salt from it. This is the only scope that accepts a seed.
scope=this_cohort is rejected until its ratified derivation is frozen and proven.
Every change carries an expected hash and a derived key
Every Save and re-seed carries expected_hash, the exact settings hash the client read. A missing value fails validation; a mismatch returns 409 stale_config with the current configuration and writes nothing. The server compares inside the same durable transaction as the change and its receipt.
The request identity is derived, and for Save and re-seed the Idempotency-Key header is mandatory and must equal it; a missing or mismatched key is rejected before anything changes:
PATCH   sha256(canonical_json({operation: "patch-statistical-config-v1",   lane_id, sim_id, body}))
RESEED  sha256(canonical_json({operation: "reseed-statistical-config-v1",  lane_id, sim_id, body}))
COMPARE sha256(canonical_json({operation: "compare-statistical-runs-v1",   lane_id, body}))

Compare may derive its key on the server after validating its two-field body. It reads the exact settings and uses the report loader to distinguish compared, missing and corrupted findings. It has no expected hash for a mutation.
For Save and re-seed, admission checks the key against the canonical request and then looks it up in the durable journal. An exact finished match returns the original receipt before checking the expected hash. An exact unfinished match enters recovery. A match with a different body returns 409 idempotency_key_reuse. Only an unseen key goes on to compare the expected hash and change state. An exact duplicate therefore gets the same receipt and, for re-seed, the same seed, salts, lineage identity and forked run. A shared seed or settings hash never makes two different requests the same.
The mutation receipt
StatisticalConfigMutationReceiptV1
  schema_id, receipt_id, operation_id
  operation                         patch | reseed
  lane_id, sim_id, idempotency_key, canonical_request_sha256
  expected_statistical_settings_hash
  prior_config_ref, prior_config_sha256, prior_statistical_settings_hash
  result_config_ref?, result_config_sha256?, result_statistical_settings_hash?
  variant_id?, variant_run_id?, lineage_ref?
  disposition                       applied | exact_replay | rejected_stale |
                                    rejected_invalid | rejected_key_reuse |
                                    reconciliation_required
  received_at, committed_at?
  journal_id, journal_epoch, writer_fence
  error_code?, error_evidence_sha256?
  canonical_receipt_sha256

The configuration digests identify exact artifact bytes, and the settings hashes identify the canonical settings. Request, receipt, artifact, settings and writer identities are all distinct, and none stands in for another.
One durable journal per simulation records, in a single transaction, the admitted request, the hash compare-and-swap, the immutable result bytes, the lineage or variant record, the new current-config pointer and the terminal receipt. On retry, look up the canonical request identity and return the original committed result; an unfinished record enters recovery before any new write. An unfinished operation without a durable disposition is reconciliation-required. Rebuild materialised JSON only from the authoritative committed journal record, checking its journal epoch, configuration revision and settings format. An incompatible journal version must stop recovery without rewriting the authoritative record. Receipts and the bytes they reference stay for the run and every descendant variant, and leave only through the retention protocol with a durable tombstone.
Exercise request replay and rebuilding the derived JSON for both Save and re-seed, including a duplicate while the first request is pending and a restart after commit before response. Exercise an incompatible journal version and verify the exact settings bytes, lineage and variant identity after repair. These checks qualify configuration mutations only.
Names and storage cutover
These are requirements for the rebuild and its selected release candidate. Existing prototype names and stores require an explicit migration; this contract does not report that cutover as completed.
The canonical names
The product is RawFish for display and rawfish for packages, modules, loggers, configuration, containers, services and images; the source directory is RawFish/. The target vocabulary combines the lane catalogue with the route and workbench contracts above: the two browser routes, the six steps, the three Findings modes, the short lane identifiers, the five value provenances, the five claim labels and the typed run identities.
Parsers reject these spellings wherever they appear; each has a negative fixture and a canonical round trip:
Rejected	Canonical	
steps setup, personas, run, report, analysis	scenario, cohorts, simulate, findings; Analysis is only the label of Findings data mode	
a generic policy lane, a scope selector, long-form lane identifiers	internal_policy and public_policy	
a free hex accent for data identity	a named shared data-colour role; the manifest schema defines its serialized form and version transition	
a flat, bare, optional or second-accessor catalog manifest	the required nested lane_manifest	
knobs, lane_extensions, suppressed catalogues	the one fields list	
analysis_dock_panels	analysis_panels	
capability_states, live_act_tagging members	nothing: live act tagging is absent in this schema version	
connector role prior, singular transport or placement declarations, setup, report or analysis placements, generic owner-decision fields	role priors, transports and placements arrays, placement launch, the admission-decision pair	
the validity flag outside-real-world-range	outside-declared-evidence-range	
surrogate sensitivity names	generic_sensitivity_result, only when a real capability is admitted	
an in-place reseed, or a reseed that emits a counterfactual or trait edit	Save and re-seed forking a statistical_reseed variant	
a scope label, account, process, repository or company standing in for a role	separate principal, controller and relationship scopes; separately evidenced acquisition actor, legal entity, data controller, rights holders, source authorities, artifact issuer and custodian	
A selected transport on a source bundle is singular by design: it is one admitted member of its connector's transports, not an alias for the array.
No alias survives, and one would have to be earned
There are no aliases in the first RawFish contract. If a migration ever needs one, define and test its bounded parser support before any code accepts it. RawFish records the canonical term, non-canonical value, rendered label, exact parser surface, expiry, serializer output, migration state and owner, and removal proof against stored data and actual callers. An undocumented parser fallback is a defect, not an alias.
Where the name MiroFish may appear
MiroFish's name may appear only where the text is genuinely about the upstream work: the inherited licence text, upstream attribution and source-offer notices, citation metadata, clearly bounded provenance sections, and code comments whose only purpose is recording upstream origin. A whole file is not exempt because of its name; mixed files fence their provenance so the rest is still scanned, and tests, snapshots, fixtures and generated artifacts are all scanned. The name never appears in the interface, package names, logger names, container names, graph identifiers or asset names.
Names are proven mechanically
Brand: enumerate the exact release inventory from the candidate artifact, reject the upstream brand or its addresses outside provenance, require the RawFish brand on every product surface, and check the upstream licence and citation text is intact.
Routes and lanes: parse the actual route table and require only the two routes; exercise every canonical query value and reject every non-canonical one; scan instructions, examples and snapshots for non-canonical routes; admit the three lanes and reject a generic policy lane.
Manifests and registries: validate canonical fixtures, parse, serialise and parse again every enum and field, reject every non-canonical envelope and spelling, and prove a source bundle's transport is one admitted member of its connector's transports.
Absent surfaces: enumerate the retired upstream pages and direct report, graph and simulation endpoints; generic policy scope; preset listing/fetch and scenario preview/validation handlers; counterfactual and surrogate-explanation handlers; duplicate compare handlers; and model-driven persona or ontology generators on the product path. Prove their absence from source, generated code, imports, routes, tests, documents, packages and the release artifact. A replacement requires its own typed operation and capability contract rather than reviving a retired handler; the intervention and counterfactual comparison layer, which the first version leaves out, is such a replacement and not a revival.
Test volume is not a gate: keep the smallest set that proves rejection, the round trip, state migration and behaviour.
Storage starts fresh, but nothing is abandoned
RawFish's storage starts fresh under its own names, with no path for reading any other storage, but a fresh start never licenses dropping data. Before any new volume identity is used, every existing volume on the machine that RawFish's storage could replace gets a terminal fate, approved by whoever owns that storage and proven one of three ways: read back in place, exported and restored into isolation and replayed, or deleted with its absence read back. Exporting or hashing a volume is not terminal, and RawFish refuses to start while any such volume's fate is unresolved.
Stored records follow the same rule: any record RawFish meets needs an explicit decision to migrate, quarantine or retain it, never a silent reinterpretation. A mechanism moved under a new RawFish owner lands only when that owner accepts its behaviour and the previous import or route is gone, and the split into two policy lanes is done only when both lanes are admitted and no generic policy surface remains.
Any destructive cutover of a volume, service, container, image or remote follows seven steps, planned before acting:
bind the exact source storage, runtime artifact, source and target service and container identities, storage inventory, data digest, schema version and rollback plan;
stop writers and prove the fence;
copy or transform into a separately named target without deleting the source;
verify the target's bytes, application-level consistency, permissions and ownership;
start the exact candidate against the target and run bounded health and meaning checks;
write a durable completion receipt;
keep the source volume until the agreed rollback and retention window closes.
An interrupted or ambiguous step goes to reconciliation. A search, an existing backup or a container that starts is not proof.

RawFish's layers
RawFish's design lets another product ask for the part of a simulation its question needs. The rebuild's design has three layers, each defined once: a swarm simulation, an intervention and counterfactual comparison, and the lanes. The rebuild contract does not define the layers yet, and the prototype in this repository is not layered this way, so read this page as the design and architecture for what the prototype does.
The swarm simulation runs a world
In the design it takes a prepared world, built from the source material a request names with the scenario, cohorts and limits chosen for the run, and a seed schedule. It returns a run: its state, artifacts, findings and the record of what the simulated agents did. The agents are generated personas, so what they do generates hypotheses to investigate and says nothing about a real population. Today the Creator lane runs no swarm: its runner writes a deterministic completion marker.
The intervention and counterfactual layer compares arms
In the design it takes one declared thing to vary in the same simulated world, a baseline arm and one or more varied arms, and runs the arms on a shared seed schedule so that what differs between them is the declared change and not the draw of the dice. It returns a contrast between the arms with its spread. A contrast between arms is an intervention contrast and not an identified causal effect. Today the prototype declares baseline, counterfactual and sensitivity variants, where a counterfactual variant names the base variant it differs from, and it has endpoints that compare saved statistical settings; the catalogue's analysis settings keep counterfactual analysis disabled. The comparison layer is not built and gets its own contract; the rebuild contract's list of retired surfaces bars the prototype's retired counterfactual handlers from returning, and the layer is a separate operation.
The lanes supply a domain's questions
A lane supplies a domain's questions, cohorts, scenario fields, report sections and caveats; the domains are such as a creator announcement, an internal policy or a public policy. In the design a lane never reimplements the comparison, and the comparison never reimplements the swarm, so each mechanism has one home and one set of checks. Today three lanes register through manifests and adapters, and a fourth needs cockpit changes as well; Extending RawFish shows how.
What a caller supplies and receives
In the design a caller asks at the layer its question needs, through an SDK or API, the command line or an agent protocol, and none of these exists yet. The caller supplies a request that names its inputs and its limits: what the evidence is allowed to support, the budget and what happens if an input or provider becomes unavailable. A change to an existing run names the revision it expects, so an old request cannot overwrite newer work. The caller receives references to the run, its state, artifacts, findings, evaluations and the record of a cancellation. A run, an arm, a claim and a finding are each addressable, so a caller can refer to one on its own, for example a planning tool that tries a direction beside another, or a work record that links a rehearsal to the proposal it tested. Today the cockpit supplies an expected hash for saving a settings patch, but the backend accepts patches without it.
Components a host renders
In the design RawFish serves components with the descriptors that say how to render them, and the host surface renders them: a run, a cohort, a claim with its evidence or a comparison of two arms can appear as a card in a chat or another host, with the same fields, staleness and access filtering. The standalone cockpit is a composition of those components. Today the cockpit is one Vue application.

RawFish runbook
Use this reference when changing the prototype's services, authentication or API integration. For an ordinary local session, follow the startup and cockpit walkthrough; service configuration covers the model and graph-memory choices.
Browser and API contracts
Surface	Behavior	
/ on the frontend	Launch and lane selection	
/run	Draft cockpit, with text held in page memory	
/run/<run_id>	Saved cockpit; step selects a step and mode=read, ask or data selects Findings	
/api/sim/use-cases/<lane_id>/catalog	Lane catalog, including its required lane_manifest	
/api/sim/use-cases/<lane_id>/evals/preflight_meter	Scale and provider-readiness result	
Lane ids are creator, internal_policy and public_policy. The local recipe exposes frontend port 3000 and backend port 5001 on loopback. It does not provide separate authenticated users. The architecture explains current behavior; the rebuild contract defines the intended replacement.
Configuration sources and caller boundaries
.env.local.template defines host settings for the Docker-backed stack. docker-compose.local.yml supplies container addresses and loopback ports. process/local_stack.sh starts and stops services, acquires models and runs probes. Some readiness failures only warn, so inspect the individual health results rather than relying on the final banner.
The recipe runs native Ollama on the host and fixes Graphiti with Neo4j for memory. Containers reach the host through a gateway. Changing a host URL or ZEP_MODE alone does not change the corresponding container configuration. Use RAWFISH_CONTAINER_LLM_BASE_URL for RawFish's container model address and RAWFISH_CONTAINER_OPENAI_BASE_URL for Graphiti's.
RawFish's RAWFISH_LLM_* fields and Graphiti's OPENAI_* fields configure separate clients. An adapter must preserve that separation. An unknown external model price is cost_unavailable, not zero.
Authentication changes are a developer deployment concern
The local Docker recipe fixes AUTH_ENABLED=false and exposes ports only on loopback. An auth-enabled source build requires:
A random SECRET_KEY of at least 32 characters.
AUTH_ENABLED=true.
Matching API_KEY and VITE_API_KEY values. With FLASK_DEBUG=false, the backend rejects the example placeholders.
For source development, put the backend values in the root .env and the browser's VITE_API_KEY in frontend/.env.local. Keep VITE_API_KEY in the root file too because backend startup validates it. Restart Vite after changing its environment, or rebuild built frontend assets. A stale browser key can return 401 while the health endpoint succeeds.
Warning

The browser key is public to its readers. VITE_API_KEY is embedded in JavaScript. It enables prototype requests but does not identify a user or separate their data. Shared operation needs sign-in, per-user data access and network protection that this prototype does not supply.
Return to choosing a lane for cockpit use.
Deployment boundaries
Run the production backend with one worker. The existing npm run backend:prod command selects gunicorn -w 1 --threads 8; a different launcher must also keep -w 1. The simulation runner holds process handles, monitor threads and run state in process-local maps. Multiple workers can send status or stop requests to a process that does not own the run. Extra threads do not remove that single-worker requirement.
The browser uses same-origin /api requests by default. If you set VITE_API_BASE_URL for a different API host, add that exact origin to connect-src in frontend/index.html before building the frontend. Its current Content-Security-Policy permits 'self' and http://localhost:5001; an unlisted origin is blocked by the browser even when the API is reachable. Set the backend's ALLOWED_ORIGINS to the actual frontend origins. Browser connection policy and the backend's origin allowlist are separate checks.
Keep the OASIS runner's execution limits explicit. The settings template selects these defaults:
OASIS_DEFAULT_MAX_ROUNDS=150 supplies the round limit when the caller gives no positive max_rounds.
OASIS_MAX_ROUNDS_CAP=200 remains the hard ceiling even when the caller requests more rounds.
OASIS_MAX_AGENTS_CAP=1000 rejects a run whose configured agent count exceeds the cap.
OASIS_ROUND_TIMEOUT_SEC=600 sets the simulation scripts’ per-round timeout in seconds.
OASIS_RUN_TIMEOUT_SEC=7200 sets their total-run timeout in seconds.
The runner clamps calculated rounds to the selected limit and rejects excess agents. These controls apply to the OASIS execution path; Creator's deterministic completion marker does not run an OASIS swarm. They also remain separate from RawFish's ensemble × stakeholder-segment × rounds scale guard. Raising a limit increases permitted work and potential provider cost.
Check a change
Run make ci from the repository root for the full local check. Install and start local Ollama with the configured model first: the provider probe and required report smoke make real requests.
Command	Use it to check	
make hygiene-gates	Source hygiene, type checks and encoded UI and product rules	
make closure-gates	Drift from the prototype's route, manifest and workbench rules	
make smoke	Generic dispatch with mock dependencies	
make probe-llm	The local model's structured JSON response pattern	
make smoke-local-report-required	Creator report generation, read-back and chat with a local model	
make test-backend	Backend pytest suites	
make test-frontend	Frontend Vitest suites	
make build-frontend	Frontend production build	
make test-browser	Desktop and mobile Playwright smoke	
make smoke checks the generic dispatch path with mock dependencies. make smoke-local-report-required checks that a real local model can generate a Creator report and respond in chat after the runner writes its completion marker. For a change to policy execution or reports, run that lane's tests separately.
Diagnose a changed integration
Follow the failing caller. A host model probe can pass while a container uses an unreachable address. A RawFish model call can pass while Graphiti's Neo4j, embedding or reranking client fails.
The scale guard counts ensemble size, stakeholders and rounds. Changing its cap or override changes which runs the application admits. Source markers remain metadata; saved ids remain record identifiers.
make down stops the local containers and preserves data. The purge path removes named graph and runner-state volumes. Save needed reports and settings before a deliberate reset; use the shutdown task for an ordinary session.

Using RawFish
This walkthrough is for developers with the actual RawFish reference-prototype checkout. It covers local startup, model and memory configuration, one complete Creator session and shutdown. For editable source, use the repository setup; the runbook holds authentication and integration checks, and architecture explains the implementation. The rebuild contract describes the planned replacement.
Work through a fictional creator announcement: enter the scenario, save a cohort setting, check the model and read a generated report. Keep the run so you can compare it with a revised announcement.
In this prototype, Creator's Simulate step records completion without running agents. Generate report makes a separate model call to write the report. Policy lanes use a different runner. The fresh rebuild is planned and there is no hosted service.
Caution

Your input can reach the model provider. Use nonconfidential material suitable for that provider. Preview and simulation can send it there.
Start the local stack
Important

Start from the RawFish checkout. You need that checkout, Make, Python 3, Docker with Compose v2 and a running Docker daemon, plus native Ollama.
If you need to work on the source first, see the developer setup.
From the checkout's root:
make init

This creates .env.local and refuses to overwrite an existing file. Open it and replace NEO4J_PASSWORD and SECRET_KEY; use at least 32 characters for the secret. Check the model names and embedding dimension against the models you intend to run. Configure the prototype's services explains those choices and the different host and container addresses.
Start the stack, then inspect it:
make up
make status

The first start can download models and images and build the application. The recipe runs Ollama on the host and RawFish and Neo4j in Docker. It probes the model's structured JSON responses, which report generation needs. If the probe fails, resolve the named model, endpoint or response-format error before continuing.
Open http://localhost:3000/ in your browser to reach Launch. The backend health endpoint is http://localhost:5001/health; use make logs to investigate a service that is not ready. Check the individual health results even if startup prints its final banner.
This recipe disables authentication and binds ports to loopback. For changes to authentication or network exposure, use the developer runbook.
Configure the services
Configure the model that reads your scenario and writes its report, then choose how the prototype stores the world graph. In Creator, choosing a model changes report generation. The Simulate step still records completion without running agents. Create the settings file in local startup before applying these examples.
Choose the model that receives the input
For native Ollama on the host:
RAWFISH_LLM_PROVIDER_MODE=local_ollama
RAWFISH_LLM_MODEL=qwen3-coder:30b
RAWFISH_LLM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1

For another local server with an OpenAI-compatible API:
RAWFISH_LLM_PROVIDER_MODE=local_openai_compatible
RAWFISH_LLM_MODEL=qwen2.5:7b
RAWFISH_LLM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8000/v1

Neither local mode needs an external provider key. Replace the model name with one your server provides and your machine can run. The examples do not install models. Preflight checks availability and the structured responses report generation needs.
To use an external provider instead:
RAWFISH_LLM_PROVIDER_MODE=external
RAWFISH_LLM_PROVIDER=openai
RAWFISH_LLM_MODEL=gpt-4o-mini
RAWFISH_LLM_API_KEY=<provider-key>
RAWFISH_LLM_BASE_URL=https://api.openai.com/v1
RAWFISH_CONTAINER_LLM_BASE_URL=https://api.openai.com/v1

Caution

External processing. Your input can leave the machine when you use an external provider. Use only suitable, nonconfidential material.
Preflight shows an estimated cost when the price is known, or cost_unavailable when it is not.
The make up recipe still starts native Ollama and Neo4j and pulls its configured local models. Changing the router mode does not remove those dependencies or convert the recipe into another deployment.
Distinguish the host address from the container address
On the host, localhost:11434 reaches native Ollama. Inside a container, localhost points back to that container. The local recipe therefore uses the host gateway:
Caller	Default model address	Override in .env.local	
Host-side RawFish probes	http://localhost:11434/v1	RAWFISH_LLM_BASE_URL	
RawFish in Docker	http://host.docker.internal:11434/v1	RAWFISH_CONTAINER_LLM_BASE_URL	
Graphiti in Docker	http://host.docker.internal:11434/v1	RAWFISH_CONTAINER_OPENAI_BASE_URL	
If you use another local server, set the address for each caller that needs it. A successful host probe does not mean the container reaches the same service.
Important

Replace both local addresses. The host probes and Docker application have separate endpoint settings. Changing only the provider and model leaves the local Ollama addresses in place. Use the chosen provider’s address for both callers. In a native source run that should use the provider’s default address, clear the stale RAWFISH_LLM_BASE_URL and any LLM_BASE_URL fallback instead. The Docker recipe still needs its explicit container override because an empty value selects its local default.
Choose the graph-memory arrangement
For source development, ZEP_MODE=mock uses a deterministic in-process store without Neo4j. Graphiti mode uses Neo4j and its own model, embedding and reranking clients. These are separate from the RawFish provider router.
A host-side Graphiti configuration is:
ZEP_MODE=graphiti
NEO4J_URI=bolt://localhost:7687
NEO4J_USER=neo4j
NEO4J_PASSWORD=<local-password>
OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1
OPENAI_API_KEY=local-graphiti-key
OPENAI_MODEL=qwen3-coder:30b
OPENAI_EMBEDDING_MODEL=nomic-embed-text
OPENAI_EMBEDDING_DIM=768
OPENAI_RERANKING_MODEL=qwen3-coder:30b

The OPENAI_* names belong to Graphiti's client; the shown address is local. Match the embedding dimension to the model you use. The prototype's locked Neo4j dependency falls outside Graphiti's declared supported range, so Graphiti mode remains experimental.
The Docker recipe fixes ZEP_MODE=graphiti and uses bolt://neo4j:7687 inside its network. Setting ZEP_MODE=mock in the host file does not switch that recipe to mock memory. Developers changing this setup can follow the configuration reference.
Follow the failure to the dependency
Symptom	Check	
missing_external_key	Supply the key for the chosen external provider, or choose a local mode.	
Local model request times out	Confirm the server is running, the model is installed and this caller uses the right address.	
Graphiti unavailable	Check Neo4j and Graphiti's model, embedding and reranking settings. A working RawFish model call tests a different client.	
API requests return 401	In an auth-enabled source build, match the frontend and backend keys. See the authentication reference.	
Scale guard blocks launch	Review ensemble size, stakeholders and rounds before increasing the cap.	
Caution

The browser key does not protect a shared service. In a source build, the frontend's VITE_API_KEY is included in the JavaScript delivered to the browser. Matching it to the backend key makes prototype requests work; it does not authenticate separate people. The local recipe exposes its ports only on loopback. It does not supply sign-in or separate users' data for a shared service.
When the services are ready, continue with choosing the lane.
Choose the lane and keep the draft in view
Launch offers Creator, Internal policy and Public policy. Each supplies different scenario fields, groups and report questions. Use Internal policy for workplace changes and Public policy for civic decisions. Choose Creator and Paste for this walkthrough.
The other source markers, cached, live and graph, do not connect an upload, cache, feed or graph import. Start with pasted text. Drafts stay in page memory until a run is created: reloading or opening the draft address elsewhere loses the text and returns to Launch. Changing lanes after saving requires a new run.
The cockpit keeps draft text out of URLs and refuses links that carry it, but it cannot remove text you have already copied into an address or browser history.
Continue through the six cockpit steps
Paste this fictional announcement on Launch:
Our channel is replacing its weekly long-form explainer with short daily clips next month. The full archive stays available, but new explainers stop. We have a fixed production budget and want newcomers to understand the work without losing the depth regular viewers value.

Stress question: where does this announcement leave viewers unsure what they will receive?
Assumptions: regular viewers value the explanations; newcomers need a shorter entrance; the team cannot produce both formats daily.
Success: viewers can distinguish the new clips from the archive and find the explanation behind a clip.
Failure modes: regular viewers read the change as abandonment; a newcomer sees an excerpt without its qualification.
What could change a view: a clear route to the longer explanation and an honest account of what production will stop.

Choose preview parse to inspect the suggested title, question and cohorts, then Draft scenario. parse seed in Scenario parses the current text again. This prototype provides one text area and a cohort plan, so keep the full scenario text alongside your run.
Scenario: check Stress question, choose paste under Source posture, then Build the world to open Build.
Build: choose Build the world again to create and prepare the saved run. A run identifier and world panel should appear. Here the graph shows the run and its configured stakeholder cohorts joined by TESTS_AGAINST relationships; it is not a world or influence network inferred from the source. Inspect those settings, then choose Tune cohorts.
Cohorts: inspect the groups and save a configuration change using the next section before launch.
Preflight: check provider mode, model and address, then refresh preflight. Review readiness, scale, token estimate, latency and available external cost. Choose Launch swarm when ready.
Simulate: follow status and the console. Creator completes through its deterministic marker. If the run halts, inspect the error; duplicate as draft makes an editable copy. There is no Stop control.
Findings: after completion, open Read and choose Generate report if none is loaded. Wait for the background job, then inspect the tagged claims. Simulation completion and report generation are separate steps.
The initial cohorts are Long-time fans, Gen-Z skeptics and Casual viewers. These are authored archetypes rather than measured audience groups. For this example, look for ambiguity about what happens to the clips, archive and future explainers.
Save a configuration or create a variant
Before launch, select Long-time fans. Change Sentiment bias from 0 to -0.2, then choose Save patch. Wait for the settings hash to refresh without an error. The cockpit prepares the run again after a saved edit; refresh preflight before launching.
The workbench also shows activity, influence and active hours, plus opinion-drift controls in policy lanes. Values carry origin text, such as your input, a lane default, a prior or a random draw. An origin tells you where a value came from, not whether it measures a real population. The cockpit has no per-field lock control.
Note

A saved setting is not an executed experiment. For Creator, this saves the changed setting in configuration and completion metadata. The report prompt does not use that setting, so it is not a sentiment experiment.
Reseed variant increments the seed and records the old and new settings in lineage. It changes and prepares the same run; it does not create a second executable run or report. Save any field edits first because the seed-only request does not include them. Both controls freeze after launch. Separate variant runs are part of the rebuild design.
Read what the run actually supports
Findings offers Read, Ask and Analysis; the last uses mode=data in saved-run addresses. Read the findings explains the claim labels.
Creator’s report proposes reactions without an executed conversation behind them, even when a claim is labelled “simulated observation”. Check those proposals against the announcement, then take unresolved questions to actual viewers. A generated quotation is not testimony.
If report generation fails validation, keep the error and model choice together when diagnosing it. A successful model call does not necessarily produce a valid report.
Compare settings before comparing reactions
Open Analysis, then Compare and refresh compare. After reseeding, it compares the latest settings with their parent snapshot. stat diffs counts changes. The present, missing and corrupted buckets reflect settings subjects; they do not establish that two valid reports were compared.
To compare announcement text, start a second run from Launch. Keep the first draft and question, but replace “new explainers stop” with “one new long-form explainer will remain each month; daily clips replace the other weekly editions.” Align the provider, cohorts and other settings. Keep both run identifiers and valid reports.
Read the reports side by side. Does the monthly explanation change the proposed concern about abandonment? Does ambiguity about the archive remain? This is a manual comparison of separate scenarios, not an automatic paired experiment. Wording can vary between model calls, and a missing or invalid report leaves the comparison incomplete. Neither result estimates how many real viewers share a concern.
Return to a saved run and finish locally
Launch's Past runs list remembers saved run identifiers in this browser. Opening one loads its lane and phase from the backend. There is no dedicated Share control. A saved address carries run identity and cockpit state; it grants no access by itself. An unsaved draft address does not preserve or transfer the draft text.
Stop the stack when finished:
make down

This preserves container data and leaves native Ollama running.
Caution

Purging removes saved data. make purge removes named volumes, including graph and runner-state data. Use it only for a deliberate reset after saving anything you need.
The prototype does not provide full sensitivity analysis, a counterfactual editor, live action labels or hosted multi-user use. Continue with interpreting the findings or the planned workflow.

content.title: How a request gets its context

body:
How a request gets its context
Scope's design lets a caller ask about a task without opening the original sources. Owners read their records and send Scope copies. Scope checks what the caller may use before it searches those copies. The service and contracts are still planned. The development guide builds the current library.
In the equipment-order example, the owner supplies approval revision 3 and report revision 7, which says part of the order arrived. While the caller prepares the update, report revision 8 arrives. The request needs a consistent view while Scope prepares a newer one for later requests.
flowchart TB
    accTitle: From an owner-supplied source to a context bundle
    accDescr: Scope verifies an owner's snapshot and stores the records in Dolt. A compiler prepares a fixed retrieval snapshot in advance. Scope holds the snapshot steady for a request, checks what the caller may use, and signs the answer.
    Owner["Owner reads its source"] --> Import["Scope verifies the supplied snapshot"]
    Import --> Store["Store verified records in Dolt"]
    Store --> Compiler["Prepare retrieval ahead of requests"]
    Compiler --> Snapshot["Fixed retrieval snapshot"]
    Snapshot --> Retrieve["Check access and find context"]
    Caller["Permitted task request"] --> Retrieve
    Retrieve --> Bundle["Sign the answer with its sources and gaps"]

Dolt is the planned durable store for accepted records and Scope's receipts. Retrieval indexes are rebuildable views of those records, access rules and a released retrieval policy. Changing an index can change which passage appears first; it cannot change the order approval or make a restricted report accessible. The retrieval backend still needs to be chosen by benchmark.
Owners hand Scope snapshots; Scope never reads a source
An adapter runs in the source owner's own environment. It reads the repository, mailbox or application and produces a secret-free snapshot with a size limit. Its manifest identifies the records, revisions, observation times, validity, classification and origin. Content hashes bind the submitted bytes. Scope checks the owner's signature or an explicitly delegated adapter's signature before accepting them.
A familiar path, account or local process does not establish ownership. Keep credentials and provider commands outside Scope's schemas, errors and logs. If the adapter cannot supply a source, Scope must report the gap rather than crawl the original itself.
The adapter stages a complete candidate privately. Scope checks it before making one new generation visible, so readers continue to see the previous supplier report while its replacement is checked. Producing an export and accepting it are separate events. A caller needs the accepted generation to know whether its update has arrived.
Leaving an item out of an export does not delete it. Removal needs a tombstone from someone with permission to withdraw the record. A policy may generate that tombstone from absence only for a verified complete export. The design specifies that exception for website exports. Other sources need their own policy, schema, adapter and tests. The supplier report therefore requires an explicit removal record.
A context bundle explains itself
Scope signs one context bundle for each answer. The bundle names the items, source revisions, observation times, validity periods and important gaps. It also points to the record of how Scope chose the items. To obtain a larger or fresher answer, make a new request. Leave the earlier signed bundle intact.
For the order update, keep approval revision 3, what report revision 7 says and the missing arrival estimate. Ask the supplier for the estimate. If a useful passage was left out for space, try a narrower question or allow a larger response. Explain the difference without revealing sources the caller cannot see.
Extra quotations can bury the current approval. Put required and explicitly pinned items first, within the caller's permissions. If the response limit is too small to keep them, say what requirement could not be met. Return a partial result only when the request permits it. A task that needs no context can say so.
Each search method proposes candidates, and fusion combines their rankings. The separate A-MAC-lite item scorer uses content type, how recently someone accessed an item, novelty and verified reports of use. A high score cannot establish whether a supplier's report is true. Keeping these mechanisms separate from source records lets developers compare retrieval changes without rewriting those records.
Eligibility comes before ranking
Check what the request may use before searching or ranking. Eligibility includes the caller, controller scope, relationship, purpose, classification, source validity, age, revocation, deletion and permission for model processing. Apply those checks during graph walks and model-assisted retrieval too. Filtering only the final answer is too late if excluded material has already influenced it.
An order for one client cannot become eligible for another client's update because the wording is similar. A record permitted for internal drafting may still be forbidden for model processing or publication. None of these permissions authorises an external action.
Each instance serves one controller scope, which identifies who controls the data, what the instance may hold and how it may use it. Integrators must show why the caller and sources belong there. A company name, website, folder or shared machine cannot establish that.
Freshness follows source revisions and validity
Use the source's revision, observation time and validity policy to decide whether it is current enough. A recent import cannot make an old delivery report fresh. Before answering, compare the snapshot's revisions with accepted revisions, check the request's age limit, and recheck access, revocation and deletion.
If a task requires today's delivery position and no permitted source supplies it, stop the drafting or analysis that needs it. If the context was optional, the owner's signed policy may let the work continue. Record what was missing and acknowledge the limited result. Calling the work a draft cannot grant permission. A task that needs no context can proceed without a bundle.
The product freshness guide explains what an old report can still support.
Every request reads one frozen snapshot
A compiler prepares a retrieval snapshot before the request arrives. It uses the records Scope has committed, the released retrieval policy and the access rules for those records. Each request pins one snapshot, keeping it fixed while it reads. This keeps approvals, reports and permissions from drifting out of step during the request.
Accepting report revision 8 does not rewrite a request already using revision 7's snapshot. The next request can use the newer snapshot once it is ready. Whether the first request may finish depends on its freshness requirement and any access changes. A routine index replacement can let existing readers finish. If access has been revoked or a record deleted, Scope must withhold the affected result.
Compiling in advance keeps index building off the request path and lets you reproduce a result from the same inputs. Measure how long it takes for a verified update to appear in a ready snapshot. A watcher, webhook or timer can prompt a check. Only a verified update can change what Scope has stored.
Rollback must check an older snapshot against current access and invalidation rules, then activate it with a new increasing activation marker. It cannot restore an old grant or deleted material.
Scope works with no model at all
Strict mode
Strict mode finds candidates by reference, keyword and links between permitted records, using fixed rules. It excludes model-generated summaries, embeddings and inferred links, even from the cache. It must start, recover and answer without a model service.
Full mode
A memory host with separate processing permission would supply embeddings, candidate links, summaries or reranking. This can find passages whose wording differs from the question. Keep the source and model identity for each result so it can be removed when an input changes.
Both modes check what the task may use before they search. In the integrated design, Pale carries the request and connects to Counsel's Memory and Embedding Host. Permission to use that host does not extend to Counsel's separate judgment service.
Standalone Scope uses its own grants and revocations. In full mode, it links Pale's Counsel port library and calls the memory host selected in its own configuration, without a Pale daemon. The host separately checks permission to process the supplied material; a Scope retrieval grant does not grant that permission. This connection is part of the planned design. The kernel crate has no memory-host connection.
When the memory host is unavailable, fall back to strict mode only if the request's policy permits it. Identify that change in the result. A request requiring full mode must fail, not return an empty success or reuse cached model material as “strict” context. The product mode guide explains how the distinction affects a task.
Use is reported, and outcomes are separate facts
After receiving a bundle, the caller reports which items it used. Scope checks and signs an acknowledgement. The report might show that a draft used the delivery report. It cannot establish that the delivery claim was correct or that anyone approved the draft. Keep issuing the bundle, delivering it, showing it to a model and using it as separate events.
A later read returns the same signed bundle the caller used if access still permits it. A refresh creates a new bundle. Connecting use to an execution episode still needs its own published identifier. A caller must never substitute its local run ID.
Nothing improves itself
Scope records what it considered, what it returned, what it left out and what the caller reported using. These records help compare retrieval policies. Frequent use alone cannot show that an item helped. An agent might quote an outdated report or succeed without the extra context.
Use the comparison to propose a change. A person reviews it before release, and making a release active is a separate step. The optimiser cannot edit its own evaluation or widen access. A better retrieval policy changes rankings and indexes. The earlier source records stay intact.
What Scope is not
Scope supplies context and keeps its own records of who could use it and who reported using it. Source access, credentials, scheduling and external actions stay with their owners. A signature tells the caller who issued the bundle. Check the source for truth and obtain separate permission to act.
Correction or withdrawal must reach dependent snapshots, bundles, embeddings, summaries, learned links and caches. Deletion removes source-derived material and keeps only the history and receipts policy permits. An old decision may then become impossible to reconstruct. Restoring a backup cannot revive revoked access or deleted context.
The product correction guide explains the source owner's part in that consequence.

body:
Development
Build the standalone Rust library before you make a change. The current build has no context service. Use the architecture to see where to add a source adapter, a storage change or a retrieval rule.
Building the library
You need Rust and Cargo. Run the commands from the repository root. The crate has no external dependencies.
Build the library
cargo build --locked --offline --manifest-path kernel/Cargo.toml

Cargo should finish building scope-kernel. Keep --locked so that the command uses the repository's lockfile.
Check the current test target
cargo test --locked --offline --manifest-path kernel/Cargo.toml

Cargo currently reports zero unit tests and zero doc tests. This command checks that the test targets compile.
Where a change belongs
Start in kernel/ for library work. It holds the crate alone today. Admission of each source owner's snapshot arrives as one module per owner, as Source imports lists the owners, each with its first admission check and test. Keep repository, mailbox and database access with the source owners.
A folder is created with its first operation and test, and each lives in the place below.
Folder	What goes there	
cli/ and daemon/	The command line (scope resolve, read, report-use, migrate, seed, optimize and permissions) and the daemon, the single writer of accepted records, with its local transport, restricted loopback bridge and the diagnostic stream.	
schema/	Storage migrations V001 to V005, run by the journaled runner on Durability and recovery.	
protos/	Client transport and language definitions, generated with buf generate after contract validation.	
bindings/python/ and bindings/typescript/	The Python binding, a maturin build of the kernel published as scope-kernel, and the TypeScript client @rtepl/scope-client, whose hooks and components are for React. A Hugging Face or PyTorch integration is a possibility only if a learned scorer needs a training path.	
dashboard/	Contract tests for the diagnostic client, which a separately owned viewer renders; the stream's design is on Diagnostics.	
plugins/	Client plugins, such as the admitted browser plugin the daemon's loopback bridge serves.	
The paper in paper/ is separate from the service design.
Publish schemas, a generated manifest, canonicalisation examples and contract tests in the planned contracts/ directory. Clients will pin that manifest by hash. Wait for it before writing an integration.
Rules every change keeps
If you change	Keep this rule	
Source adapters	The source owner reads the original and keeps credentials. Scope accepts only the supplied snapshot.	
Stored data	Keep credentials, provider-session material and executable credential bindings out of schemas, data, bundles, acknowledgements, logs and diagnostics. Check that even a non-secret source or grant reference is allowed.	
Retrieval	Check access and validity before searching or ranking. A high score cannot make a source eligible or remove context the task requires.	
Persistence	Commit the complete change before readers can see it. Rebuild indexes from committed records.	
Signed records	Canonicalise with RFC 8785, hash with SHA-256 and sign over the contract's domain prefix. A record's digest does not cover itself.	
Learning	Propose, review and release changes separately. Production retrieval cannot rewrite its own policy.

Scope engineering
Scope's architecture separates acquiring source material, selecting context and recording its use. Source owners supply secret-free snapshots; Scope keeps the accepted projections in its own Dolt store and answers permitted requests with bounded bundles it signs itself. Scope's design uses a Rust daemon. The developer introduction explains how this context lets a new session continue the work with its history and purpose intact.
What exists in code today
The scope repository contains the Rust kernel crate, an empty library that the design's modules build into. It builds without sibling checkouts. The repository's development guide owns the build commands and layout, including the separate research paper. Contracts identifies what must be published before consumers can integrate.

An owner's helper reads its source with its own credentials and hands over a secret-free snapshot. Scope admits it and swaps the namespace to one new generation. An admitted request pins that snapshot, passes eligibility and runs the permitted routes. Scope fuses and trims the results to budget, records its decision and signs the bundle.
Means performs calculations from owner-held facts; the owner's workspace selects permitted inputs and retains the run records. The core negative paths
A caller claiming another role, controller scope or relationship scope without a valid grant is denied before any source byte is read.
A stale or revoked required source makes context-critical work fail closed. Where policy permits a limited retrieval result, the exact signed bytes and visible limitations travel together. A revoked or unauthorised item remains excluded.
Two writers racing on the same revision leave one winner and one conflict; there is never a last-write-wins update.
A crash before or after a semantic change, an inbox acknowledgement, a use-receipt commit or an outbox publication replays to exactly one durable result.
A redelivered event, import or use receipt creates no duplicate state, thanks to compound identity and idempotency.
A superseded or deleted source invalidates dependent bundles and views, leaves a tombstone preserving lineage, and leaves unrelated canon intact.
Compaction that drops a material caveat or source digest is rejected, and deleting the derived view leaves the source evidence rebuildable.
A model proposing a Skill or configuration change leaves the canonical source unchanged until its owner accepts and releases it.
Diagnostic queries scoped by role or controller cannot infer hidden nodes through counts, maxima, timing, errors, telemetry, receipts or replay cursors.
With Pale removed, Scope still resolves strict-mode requests under its own signed grants. A Pale binding alone cannot admit a standalone request. Restore a snapshot and cache with valid artifacts from an earlier integrated run. Supply a declared memory-host profile and a valid Scope retrieval grant. With the configured standalone memory-host route present but no separate host-invocation and disclosure permission, a new full-only request is refused. A request permitting strict mode can receive a model-free bundle. Verify that neither request invokes the host or uses the retained model artifacts. As the positive control, supply the exact permitted host, profile, input and separate grants and verify full mode without a Pale daemon; revoke either grant before delivery and verify refusal.
A research export with missing or expired authority, widened use, mixed real and synthetic provenance, a raw prompt, private payload or hidden reasoning, an invented outcome, leakage across splits or an undeclared omission is denied.
Evidence from a direct Claude Code or Codex path, or from Gas Town with no organising owner, enters only by exact owner references; any attempt to synthesise an organisation or an episode is denied, and export invalidation records uncertainty and downstream custody instead of claiming remote bytes were recalled.
A semantic-inferred edge with missing evidence, profile or confidence, a forged occurrence or frontier reference, or a claim that an acknowledgement proves an effect, response or outcome is rejected, and nothing changes in the owner's or Pale's genealogy.
Reject a source helper that leaks credentials or returns an unbounded or mutable projection. A helper result or wake cannot stand in for a committed owner publication. Scope’s outbox certifies only its own committed revision.
A case lacking exact source, controller, purpose, rights or model-use evidence, containing secrets or presented as already minted is not proposed to Reckon; a rejected, deferred or tombstoned case, a stale version or missing use authorisation cannot enter a bundle or experiment; minting, use, evaluation, ruling, release and activation are tested as independent transitions.
Equal sealed inputs producing a different snapshot digest, a partially visible build, or one request seeing mixed semantic, policy or snapshot identities quarantines the candidate and keeps or forward-reactivates the previous snapshot.
Affinity changing an admitted edge, provenance, tombstone, source fact or genealogy, or a planner considering an ineligible item before the controller, relationship, purpose and model-use wall, fails conformance.
Strict mode needing an embedding, model summary, learned link or live provider, a memory-host loss silently weakening policy, or an unavailable route reported as a success fails the mode and degradation proof.
A vector candidate relying only on filtering afterwards, lacking an exact-scan comparison, or leaking excluded populations through results, traversal, timing, cardinality, cache or error shape beyond the profile is disabled and certification is rejected.
A decision record that lacks the complete eligible, action and policy evidence while claiming replay, or a lawful deletion that leaves payload in an embedding, affinity or cache or calls a hash reconstructible content, is rejected.
An evaluation, Reckon custody, owner release, genealogy occurrence or Pale activation that activates Scope's retrieval policy by itself, or a Scope activation that changes Pale's state, is rejected as a collapsed lifecycle.
A repository alias, remote URL or checkout path presented as identity, a Git location bound to the wrong repository projection, or a checkout or worktree path stored outside resource_locations is rejected before the V005 generation can replace the active one.
