body:
Resources and locations
One logical resource, a spreadsheet or a report or a codebase, routinely lives in several places at once: a local folder, its owner's Drive, a client's Drive where it was shared, a shared drive, a Git commit and a folder that Drive for Desktop keeps in sync. If agents treat each of those as a separate thing they upload duplicates, edit stale copies, lose track of which version counts, and never realise that the file shared with an accountant is the same one exported locally. Scope therefore keeps one resource with many locations, lets the owner say which location is canonical, and reports drift between copies without ever repairing anything itself. Every row is Scope's derived context; the file, the Drive object, the repository and the rights to them stay with their owners.
A resource is one thing; its locations are many
CREATE TABLE resources (
    resource_id        VARCHAR(128) PRIMARY KEY,   -- opaque, immutable, allocated in the owner's namespace
    source_owner       VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    source_namespace   VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    `key`              VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,      -- human alias; may change
    resource_type      VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL,       -- spreadsheet, document, codebase, image, pdf, presentation, data, config, folder
    project_key        VARCHAR(64),
    brand_key          VARCHAR(64),
    description        VARCHAR(512),
    created_at         DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    semantic_owner     VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    source_record_ref  VARCHAR(1024) NOT NULL,
    source_version     VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    authority_class    VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    lifecycle_state    VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    controller_scope   VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    relationship_scope VARCHAR(128),
    classification     VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    provenance_refs    JSON NOT NULL,
    observed_at        DATETIME NOT NULL,
    valid_through      DATETIME,
    revision           BIGINT NOT NULL,
    supersedes_ref     VARCHAR(1024),
    deleted_at         DATETIME,
    tombstone_ref      VARCHAR(1024),
    visibility         VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'private',   -- private, internal, client, public
    FOREIGN KEY (project_key) REFERENCES projects(`key`),
    FOREIGN KEY (brand_key) REFERENCES brands(`key`),
    UNIQUE (source_owner, source_namespace, `key`)
);

CREATE TABLE resource_relationship_grants (   -- who may see a 'client' resource
    resource_id        VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    controller_scope   VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    relationship_scope VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    purpose_ceiling    VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    source_record_ref  VARCHAR(1024) NOT NULL,
    source_version     VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    revision           BIGINT NOT NULL,
    authorized_at      DATETIME NOT NULL,
    revoked_at         DATETIME,
    PRIMARY KEY (resource_id, controller_scope, relationship_scope, revision),
    FOREIGN KEY (resource_id) REFERENCES resources(resource_id)
);

CREATE TABLE git_repos (   -- one-to-one repository subtype of a codebase resource
    resource_id             VARCHAR(128) PRIMARY KEY,
    source_owner_ref        VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    source_record_ref       VARCHAR(512) NOT NULL,
    source_record_sha256    CHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    source_revision         VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    source_route_ref        VARCHAR(512),               -- opaque, non-secret owner route
    admission_ref           VARCHAR(512) NOT NULL,
    admission_sha256        CHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    origin_url              VARCHAR(512),               -- owner-reported remote fact, never identity
    upstream_url            VARCHAR(512),               -- for forks
    is_fork                 BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
    default_branch          VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'main',
    working_branch          VARCHAR(128),
    parent_repo_resource_id VARCHAR(128),               -- when a submodule
    submodule_path          VARCHAR(512),               -- path inside the parent repository, not a checkout path
    FOREIGN KEY (resource_id) REFERENCES resources(resource_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (parent_repo_resource_id) REFERENCES git_repos(resource_id)
);

CREATE TABLE resource_locations (
    location_id        VARCHAR(128) PRIMARY KEY,   -- opaque, immutable
    resource_id        VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    location_type      VARCHAR(24) NOT NULL,       -- local, drive, drive_sync, git_checkout, git_worktree, git_snapshot
    link_type          VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'original',
    local_path         VARCHAR(1024),
    drive_workspace_key   VARCHAR(64),
    drive_file_id         VARCHAR(128),            -- this location's own file id
    drive_target_id       VARCHAR(128),            -- for a shortcut: the file it points to
    drive_path            VARCHAR(512),
    drive_shared_drive_id VARCHAR(128),
    drive_mime_type       VARCHAR(128),
    git_repo_resource_id VARCHAR(128),             -- typed repository identity, never a slug or path
    git_path           VARCHAR(512),
    git_branch         VARCHAR(128),
    git_commit         VARCHAR(40),
    shared_with        VARCHAR(255),
    last_verified      DATETIME,
    last_modified      DATETIME,
    content_hash       VARCHAR(64),                -- owner-produced, for drift
    source_version     VARCHAR(255),               -- native version, etag or commit
    observed_at        DATETIME NOT NULL,
    valid_through      DATETIME,
    lifecycle_state    VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active',
    deleted_at         DATETIME,
    UNIQUE (location_id, resource_id),
    UNIQUE (location_id, git_repo_resource_id, location_type),
    FOREIGN KEY (resource_id) REFERENCES resources(resource_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (drive_workspace_key) REFERENCES workspaces(`key`),
    FOREIGN KEY (git_repo_resource_id) REFERENCES git_repos(resource_id),
    CHECK (location_type IN ('local', 'drive', 'drive_sync', 'git_checkout', 'git_worktree', 'git_snapshot')),
    CHECK (
        (location_type IN ('git_checkout', 'git_worktree', 'git_snapshot') AND git_repo_resource_id IS NOT NULL)
        OR
        (location_type NOT IN ('git_checkout', 'git_worktree', 'git_snapshot')
         AND git_repo_resource_id IS NULL AND git_path IS NULL AND git_branch IS NULL AND git_commit IS NULL)
    ),
    CHECK (
        location_type NOT IN ('git_checkout', 'git_worktree')
        OR (resource_id = git_repo_resource_id AND local_path IS NOT NULL)
    ),
    CHECK (location_type <> 'git_snapshot' OR (git_commit IS NOT NULL AND link_type = 'git_snapshot'))
);

CREATE TABLE resource_canonical_location_heads (   -- exactly one fenced head per resource
    resource_id                VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    revision                   BIGINT NOT NULL,
    expected_previous_revision BIGINT,
    previous_head_sha256       VARCHAR(64),
    canonical_location_id      VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    authority_ref              VARCHAR(1024) NOT NULL,
    authority_sha256           VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    source_record_ref          VARCHAR(1024) NOT NULL,
    source_version             VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    canonical_head_sha256      VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    committed_at               DATETIME NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (resource_id, revision),
    FOREIGN KEY (resource_id) REFERENCES resources(resource_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (canonical_location_id, resource_id)
        REFERENCES resource_locations(location_id, resource_id)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_drive_file_id   ON resource_locations(drive_file_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_drive_target_id ON resource_locations(drive_target_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_local_path      ON resource_locations(local_path);

A resource identifier is allocated inside the owner's source namespace and is never derived from a title, a path, a Drive filename, a repository slug or the human alias; the alias can change, and can collide across owners, without changing identity. Folders are resources too, with their own locations. A codebase becomes a repository projection only through the one-to-one git_repos.resource_id primary- and foreign-key join. Its project and brand associations are therefore read from the resource row and are not repeated on git_repos. A Git location names that same repository through git_repo_resource_id; checkout and worktree locations must locate the repository resource itself, while a git_snapshot may locate a contained resource and uses git_path to say where it appeared. The composite canonical-head foreign key prevents one resource from selecting another resource's location.
Only the owner says which copy is canonical
A location never declares itself canonical. Canonicality changes only by a new, predecessor-fenced head in resource_canonical_location_heads whose authority and source revision can be independently resolved: revision one has no predecessor, and every successor increments by exactly one and binds the prior head's hash. Scope projects the owner's choice. It never infers canonicality from freshness, edit time, file identifier, sync state or reachability.
The kind of link decides what a copy means
Link type	What it is	Own file id?	Do edits reach the original?	Can it drift?	
original	The file itself, where edits happen	Yes	It is the source	No	
shortcut	A Drive pointer that opens the original	Yes, its own	Opens the original	No	
copy	An independent duplicate	Yes, a new one	No	Yes	
shared_view	The same file seen from another user or workspace	Same as the original	Yes	No	
sync_mirror	Drive for Desktop keeping a local folder and Drive in step	Same content on two surfaces	Asynchronously, not guaranteed	Yes	
git_snapshot	The file frozen at a commit	Not applicable	No	Yes, behind the working tree	
symlink	A local path pointing at another path	Pointer	Yes	Only if broken	
Within one provider namespace and one owner-issued identity map, the same Drive file identifier is evidence of one underlying file; it is never enough across providers, owners or unbound exports. A different identifier is evidence of a distinct provider object, not by itself proof that the content was copied. A shortcut carries its own identifier and an owner-reported target. A sync_mirror label never guarantees propagation and never authorises an edit; lag, conflict and failed propagation stay possible. Symlinks are resolved by the owner's filesystem exporter, which never follows a link outside its admitted root and reports loops and broken targets; Scope imports that projection and never crawls the filesystem or repairs a link.
Three synthetic situations show what the model must distinguish:
A quarterly compliance sheet in its owner's Drive, shared with a client's workspace, has one original and one shared_view with the same file identifier. The owner decides whether either view is writable.
An architecture document with a shortcut elsewhere and a stray copy in an old folder has one original, one shortcut with its own identifier and target, and one copy whose hash may diverge.
A README held locally, in a Drive-synced folder and in Git has an original, a sync_mirror and a git_snapshot. The bundle reports which location the authority-backed head selects, the owner's declared mirror relation, the Git snapshot, and the applicable lag and freshness limits.
A finance workbook export requires the owning export contract's completed run and output evidence, exact workbook hash and owner's canonical head before it can be labelled original. For Means, one completed run record identifies the exact verified workbook bytes and the accompanying release; no second artifact-release receipt is required. Scope neither creates the export nor promotes a local file without that evidence.
Drift is evidence, and repair belongs to the owner
When comparable owner-produced hashes disagree, Scope records drift. It never diagnoses a sync conflict, picks a winning replica or repairs anything. The repair flow always leaves Scope and comes back:
Scope freshness or drift evidence
  -> a separately admitted effect by the resource owner
  -> the owner's effect receipt
  -> a new owner-issued projection or event
  -> Scope admission and an atomic generation replacement

A Weave schedule through Pale, or a standalone operator, may invoke Scope's read-only drift check; the owner's own process performs the drift read under its own identity and credentials, emits bounded versions and hashes as an admitted projection, and Scope compares them with the pinned canonical version and records an observation or proposal. Any repair or work item is requested separately from its owner.
Location type	The evidence the owner's exporter supplies	
Local	SHA-256 over the admitted bytes, plus the source revision	
Drive	The provider object identifier and version, plus the provider checksum where one exists	
Git	The commit and object identity, optionally a SHA-256 over normalised bytes	
Drive sync	Separate evidence for each copy, plus the owner's mirror relation and observation time	
A provider's modified time is a freshness observation. For native Google formats, the source owner selects any normalised export profile. For a workbook, that comparison identifies each source revision, exporter, options, exact output and receipt, intended reader and calculation engine. Agree the interpretation before computing a normalised digest, including date basis, locale, time zone, precision and calculation behaviour. A filename, timestamp or provider checksum supplies neither the source revision nor an equivalence mapping.
Check file identity separately from the workbook model, saved results and recalculated output. Compare the complete file digest with its receipt; compare required sheets, order, visibility, typed cells, formulas, formats, resolved names and relationships, chart inputs and validation; read saved caches, errors, blanks and zero separately; and recalculate a disposable copy in the intended engine when the claim needs its values or display. Repacking can preserve the model while changing bytes. Test an equivalent repack, a changed formula with a plausible cached result, changed input with stale or missing output, and a date serial interpreted under a different date basis. If a required source revision, feature or reader check is missing, leave that comparison unavailable rather than claiming equivalence.
For receipt-bound append intervals, inventory every package part by path, type and digest and compare adjacent retained exports. Check intended cell, table-range and filter-range changes; if an intermediate export is missing, bound the change to the verified interval without attributing it to one append. Resolve relationship IDs with their referring attributes, owning part, type, target mode and target before accepting renumbering. Compare changed style or conditional-format rules, ranges, priorities, formulas and referenced styles separately from their observed display. Give every changed part a disposition; test harmless renumbering, the same ID with a different target and a formatting change beside a valid append. Scope records the owner's reported comparison, coverage and unresolved checks; neither equal bytes nor equivalent output changes the canonical location chosen by the owner's head.
Every change to the resource map is one expected-revision Scope transaction carrying source, provenance, supersession and tombstone state. Dolt commits or tags are made only at declared, reviewed snapshot, release, audit or rollback boundaries; ordinary mutations are not individual commits.
Visibility is a ceiling on what a bundle may contain
The visibility field decides what may enter a caller's bundle. It is not permission to share anything outside Scope, which stays a decision for the resource owner and Pale.
Visibility	Scope may return it to	Scope withholds it from	
private	Exactly the permitted controller scope, relationship scope and purpose	Every other scope	
internal	Admitted scopes inside the owning controller	Client and foreign scopes	
client	Exactly the relationships the owner granted, within the grant's purpose ceiling	Every relationship not granted	
public	Public retrieval, within purpose, size and freshness limits	Deleted, revoked or otherwise restricted items	
Widening visibility needs a new owner-authorised source revision; no agent, model, score or transport event can widen it. Protective narrowing takes effect immediately, fails closed, and becomes an explicit owner update or proposal rather than a silent rewrite of the owner's policy. Visibility is enforced while the graph is being walked, not filtered afterwards, because an agent cannot un-see context once it is in its prompt; filtered nodes never enter items, diagnostics, counts, timing classes or aggregate scores.
def visible_to_context(resource_id, request_scope) -> bool:
    resource = load_resource(resource_id)
    if resource.visibility == "private":
        return request_scope.matches_private_owner(resource)
    if resource.visibility == "internal":
        return request_scope.controller_scope == resource.controller_scope
    if resource.visibility == "client":
        grant = latest_grant(resource_id, request_scope.controller_scope,
                             request_scope.relationship_scope)
        return (grant is not None and grant.revoked_at is None
                and purpose_ceiling_allows(grant.purpose_ceiling, request_scope.purpose))
    if resource.visibility == "public":
        return not resource.deleted_at and request_scope.within_purpose_ceiling()
    return False

Content from Gazette's site exports is never physically deleted by ranking; a bundle may omit it only with an explicit omission, while an owner's deletion or revocation still propagates as a tombstone.
Repositories are first-class resources
CREATE TABLE git_branches (
    id                 INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    repo_resource_id   VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    branch_name        VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    branch_type        VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'feature',   -- default, working, feature, upstream, release, protected
    tracks_remote      VARCHAR(255),
    last_commit        VARCHAR(40),
    last_commit_date   DATETIME,
    ahead_of_default   INT,
    behind_default     INT,
    pr_number          INT,
    pr_state           VARCHAR(16),                  -- open, merged, closed
    pr_url             VARCHAR(512),
    FOREIGN KEY (repo_resource_id) REFERENCES git_repos(resource_id),
    UNIQUE (repo_resource_id, branch_name)
);

CREATE TABLE git_worktrees (
    id                   INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    repo_resource_id     VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    location_id          VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    location_type        VARCHAR(24) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'git_worktree',
    branch_name          VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    reported_creator_ref VARCHAR(255),               -- owner-issued actor reference, optional
    owner_event_ref      VARCHAR(512) NOT NULL,
    owner_event_sha256   CHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    created_at           DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    is_active            BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
    FOREIGN KEY (repo_resource_id) REFERENCES git_repos(resource_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (location_id, repo_resource_id, location_type)
        REFERENCES resource_locations(location_id, git_repo_resource_id, location_type),
    CHECK (location_type = 'git_worktree')
);

The fixed git_worktrees.location_type value is only a foreign-key discriminator: its check and composite reference prove that location_id names a git_worktree location for the same repository. It is not a second location record and carries no path, lifecycle or canonicality.
Repository identity comes only from a fresh owner-issued snapshot carrying its observation time, source version, immutable resource identity, declared remotes, branch roles and any owner-reported checkouts and worktrees. A local path, remote URL, branch label, repository name or planned rename never becomes an identity or an alias; Scope never runs git or gh, never checks gh auth status, never fetches and never infers a rename. A repository rename changes the mutable human alias on resources, not resource_id. Every clone or checkout is its own git_checkout location row; every worktree is a git_worktree location row referenced by git_worktrees; and the only physical path is resource_locations.local_path. Moving a checkout retires or supersedes the old location and admits a new location under the same repository resource. Neither the move nor an additional clone changes the canonical head: only a fresh owner-authorised successor head may select the new location. The remote URLs and submodule_path remain owner-reported repository facts, not local locations or canonicality.
Scope can answer only what the fresh snapshot supports: the repository's identity and declared fork relationship, branch roles and ahead-behind counts at observation time, owner-reported checkout and worktree activity, and which owner route produced the projection. A stale snapshot cannot rename a resource, add or retire a location, move the canonical head or replace a newer generation. Scope cannot answer which account or credential to use, and it has no universal staleness threshold for worktrees; freshness is judged against the owner's published policy.
Part of Scope engineering.

Retrieval
Scope's retrieval design selects a small, useful and fresh context bundle from the material a request may use. Each request pins one frozen snapshot prepared away from live traffic, checks eligibility before ranking, and records what it considered and why. Retrieval settings may change candidate selection and order, but cannot change source facts or access permission.
Go-live requires the compiler, frozen snapshot and full adaptive rehearsal. The initial active policy uses deterministic rules; the learned machinery is rehearsed offline and stays switched off until a separate approved release and activation. The planner, evidence window, learning permissions and strict mode below form that accepted design. The local comparisons below decide whether a retrieval mechanism earns its place; research supplies candidates, not proof on Scope's workload. Scoring defines how eligible items are ranked.
Retrieval may touch ranking, never truth
Retrieval state may affect which candidates are considered, their order, recall, latency and cost. It may not create or change a source's facts, revisions, deletions or effects; Scope's admission, provenance, freshness, contradictions or tombstones; Pale's events or Pale's genealogy, its append-only history of what work relied on, what changed and what followed; a caller's identity, eligibility or authority; any authorisation of work, owner ruling, release or activation; or the contents of Pale's packages or compiled generations. Scope keeps its state in four classes so that this line can be tested:
State	How it is kept	Examples	
Accepted truth	Durable Scope transactions; recovery is authoritative	Admitted revisions, provenance, freshness, tombstones, bundles, use receipts, decision evidence	
Released retrieval policy	Immutable releases with ruling, compatibility and rollback evidence	The deterministic planner, route, fusion and budget settings	
Rebuildable projections	Content-addressed, disposable, rebuilt from sealed inputs	Affinity, keyword, vector and graph indexes, the frozen snapshot itself	
Caches	In the running process only	Decoded blocks, query caches, transient scores	
Deleting the last two classes may cost quality or speed and must change nothing in the first class, in any source or in Pale's genealogy. The compiler must be able to delete and rebuild every projection without touching accepted records. If deleting a projection changes truth, the implementation has built a competing truth store and fails.
One request binds many coordinates, and none is an alias for another
Coordinate	Owner	What it establishes	
Source revision or frontier	The source owner	How current the source is	
Scope's semantic head	Scope	Which admitted derived context is current	
Scope's writer fence	Scope	That no stale writer can commit	
Retrieval-policy release	Scope's responsible owner	The exact approved retrieval behaviour	
Snapshot identity	Scope	The exact compiled projection bytes and logical digest	
Permission and authority policy	The named authority, Pale or the standalone owner	The eligibility inputs	
Pale's contract set and compiled generation	Pale	The integrated consumer binding	
Pale's deployment activation fence	Pale	The order of Pale's local adoption	
Genealogy frontier	Pale	How far causal accounting has progressed	
A counter inside one domain is never a content identity or proof of order across domains; the snapshot's manifest binds each exact coordinate reference and hash instead of inventing one global generation.
Checks run in a hard order
authenticated request
  -> controller, relationship, purpose, classification and model-use admission
  -> source validity, tombstones, revocation and freshness
  -> required context and explicit owner or user pins
  -> planning of the optional retrieval routes
  -> candidates from each route, inside the eligible set only
  -> deterministic fusion, diversity and budget
  -> durable decision evidence
  -> signed context bundle
  -> later: the bundle read, the use report and receipt, the outcome evidence

Nothing later can undo an earlier step. Affinity and planner scores stay below deterministic structural relevance, current responsibility and frontier, freshness and explicit pins; they can neither suppress mandatory context nor bring back an item the wall excluded. The exact task identity is the task reference; a derived task feature may exist only when its procedure, version, inputs, uncertainty, rights and expiry are recorded, and a label such as "code review" is never a global task ontology.
Four routes search inside the eligible set
Route	What it does	
Exact	Looks up a stable Scope item, resource or reference, and any explicit owner pin	
Keyword	Searches a pinned, model-independent index with deterministic tie-breaking	
Graph	Walks Scope's admitted context relations only, within a bounded depth	
Vector	Searches labelled model-made representations, only where the profile permits and isolation is proved	
An unavailable optional route reports itself as missing. It never returns an empty success and never changes eligibility.
The first planner is deterministic
The first deployed planner finishes exact and pinned lookups and required-context work before choosing optional routes. Its rules depend on the request: exact lookup for IDs, keyword search for names or phrases, graph search for connected context and vectors for semantic wording where model use is permitted. Per-route and total budgets limit latency, candidates, bytes and tokens. Results are merged by rank with stable tie-breaking, then diversified and trimmed to the response budget; required context and pins survive those steps.
An approved learned policy is compiled into the snapshot. It makes its permitted choices locally and repeatably; Scope does not call the memory host on every request to choose search methods.
Missing routes, timeouts and truncated candidate sets remain explicit. If more context would exceed policy or budget, the planner returns the permitted no-context, degraded or fail-closed answer. Reciprocal rank fusion is a comparison baseline, not a selected algorithm; its constants are benchmark work. A-MAC-lite scores eligible items and fills the response budget, without owning route planning, fusion or the snapshot.
A compiler freezes one snapshot, off the live path
The compiler reads only Scope's accepted state, the exact released policy, the compiled permission and eligibility slice, the controller, purpose and model-use ceilings, the source and revocation frontiers, and pinned toolchain and dependency identities. It creates no semantic head, source revision, permission or genealogy edge; it pins those inputs and emits a rebuildable artifact with a manifest, validation evidence and a rollback anchor.
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> NO_CANDIDATE
  NO_CANDIDATE --> INPUTS_SEALED
  INPUTS_SEALED --> BUILDING_OFF_PATH
  BUILDING_OFF_PATH --> BUILT_UNVERIFIED
  BUILT_UNVERIFIED --> VALIDATING
  VALIDATING --> VALIDATED_CANDIDATE
  VALIDATED_CANDIDATE --> OWNER_RELEASED
  OWNER_RELEASED --> READY_COMPATIBLE
  READY_COMPATIBLE --> ACTIVATING
  ACTIVATING --> ACTIVE
  ACTIVE --> DRAINING
  DRAINING --> RETIRED

Apply the forward rollback procedure to the previous snapshot. Scope requires an authorised transition from active or degraded, a new snapshot activation fence and a recorded drain of the failed successor.
The build must resolve every input, contract pin, frontier, permission slice, policy release, toolchain and component preimage exactly. It runs apart from active readers. Validation then checks logical determinism, structural equivalence, counts, referential integrity, eligibility isolation and the declared performance margin.
A successful build or evaluation cannot release itself. The owner releases the candidate, and readiness checks compatibility with the running Scope and, for integrated use, Pale's consumer binding.
Activation changes Scope's head and fence atomically. New requests take the active snapshot; existing requests keep their pin until completion, cancellation or expiry. Retention protects those readers and every rollback target.
A build may wait for a missing frontier or permission slice, resources, an external model artifact, the owner's review, the Reckon evaluation and recorded decision required for a learned promotion, Pale's compatibility or old readers draining, and none of those waits permits partial visibility. Safe endings are a rejected input, a deterministic build mismatch, an invalid candidate, the owner's rejection, released but inactive, an incompatible successor, active, degraded, rolled back and retired. A partial build, mixed identities or an ambiguous activation is a dead path that goes to quarantine and reconciliation.
Freshness is checked at request time
Compare a result’s recorded inputs before use, then rebuild, take a permitted fallback or stop the affected request.
Before using a snapshot, the request compares the semantic head, permission slice, revocation frontier and freshness the snapshot was built from with the current ones and with the request's own staleness limit. A match proceeds. A soft freshness miss on a request that only benefits from context triggers reconciliation or a rebuild, and if still allowed, an explicitly degraded answer with limitations. A miss on required context, revocation or permission fails closed. An older snapshot may be used after the head has moved only under an explicit consistency profile, and the decision records the exact gap. A snapshot touched by a tombstone or revocation on an eligible item is never reused for a new request, even though its file is immutable. Watchers, webhooks, polls, Nostr deliveries, file events and clock ticks only wake this comparison; none of them advances an authoritative head.
The snapshot pin fixes the request's inputs while it runs. Before issuing the bundle, Scope orders issuance against its effective permission, revocation and tombstone frontier. If an invalidation wins, withhold the affected result and use the request's declared refusal or separately admitted degradation path. A routine snapshot swap can let pinned readers drain under still-valid authority. Restoring a backup or rolling back the active snapshot cannot restore disclosure permission. A later exact bundle read has its own check. Only the source owner can widen an item's visibility through a new revision; narrowing takes effect immediately. Visibility limits what may enter a bundle and never grants permission to share it elsewhere.
Four record meanings are accepted
A retrieval-policy release binds the owner's ruling and release identity, the base release and rollback anchor, the atomic component set (eligibility version, deterministic planner and gate, route profiles, affinity profile, fusion, diversity and budget profile, model-use ceiling) with each component's reference, hash, version and compatibility range, the training, evaluation and evidence references and limitations, the controller, purpose and profile it applies to, and its issuer, digest and signature. Components may carry separate versions, but activation selects exactly one compatible manifest; swapping one component alone is not an activation.
A snapshot manifest binds the exact semantic head and root, the released policy, the permission slice and revocation frontier, the controller, relationship, purpose, model-use and isolation profile, the source-frontier vector and when freshness was constructed, the compiler, toolchain, dependencies, features and build parameters, the keyword analyser and index identity, the graph representation, any vector and model identities, the affinity root, the logical and component digests, counts, size and validation results, the compatible Scope and Pale contract references, and its predecessor and rollback anchors.
An activation receipt records that one released, compatible snapshot became ready, active, degraded, draining, rolled back, retired or rejected under an exact activation fence, with predecessor and successor, reason, health and compatibility evidence and drain state. It never activates Pale.
Decision evidence is kept for every request: the request, caller, task reference, purpose and criticality profile; any task feature with its inputs and uncertainty; the semantic head, policy, snapshot and permission, revocation and freshness coordinates; the eligibility and required-context outcomes; the routes considered, invoked, skipped, unavailable or failed with reasons and budgets; the complete eligible candidate set; each route's candidates, scores and features; the fused order, required pins, selected and omitted candidates with reasons; degradation, isolation and model-origin markers; the bundle's reference, hash and creation state; and, joined later, the read, the use receipt and the outcome references. Bundle creation, delivery, reading, consumption, outcome, acceptance and settlement are distinct facts, and this record is Scope's evidence, not a causal edge. The bundle carries only the decision evidence's reference and hash.
Decision evidence is kept, then lawfully forgotten
For a defined evidence window, Scope keeps the complete caller-visible eligible set, each route's candidates, features and scores, the selected and omitted results, the policy and snapshot identities and the outcome references needed for replay. The data owner's rights, purpose, privacy, model-use, expiry and deletion policy set the window. Deterministic logs without non-zero support or propensity evidence support observed replay and limited sensitivity analysis only. At lawful expiry or deletion Scope removes source-derived payload, embeddings, model summaries and links, active affinity and dependent caches. It retains only the hashes, tombstones, records of requests and results, and event references the applicable authority permits. Context use supplies no consent for evaluation, training, derivative models, reusable generalisation, disclosure or transfer outside the controller; each needs its own permission. Compaction or deletion of accepted context needs an owner-reviewed tombstone. Scope marks a decision unreconstructible when its replay inputs are gone. Deleting affinity or a snapshot changes no source fact; deleting, revoking or superseding semantic or source input invalidates every dependent snapshot, affinity feature and decision cache.
For deletion, bind the owner's decision, exact source revision, retention rules and holds, then trace every copy that can reconstruct, identify, return or influence use of the target: history, replicas, journals, indexes, features, exports, outcomes, backups and relevant keys. Check immediate access denial, derived-state invalidation, payload removal, permitted residual retention and other copy holders' confirmations separately. Inspect surviving digests and metadata for disclosure; predictable input may be recoverable from its hash. Cryptographic erasure needs every usable key copy and plaintext residue accounted for.
Use a disposable target with old snapshots and derived copies. Test stale readers, in-flight exports, queued work, retries and rebuilds while unrelated scopes continue working. Confirm denial while cleanup is pending and after restart or restoration from a pre-deletion backup, applying independently preserved current permission before exposing restored state. Reconcile uncertain effects before retry. Report which copies were checked, remaining holds, physical or provider limits and outstanding holder confirmations; logical inaccessibility alone does not establish physical deletion.
Affinity is disposable, and learned control stays inside the wall
Affinity records which context tended to help together. It is versioned, linked to its evidence and disposable. Sharing requires an explicit permission edge: a lesson stays inside its role, project or relationship unless the compiled permission graph explicitly connects the scopes for that use. A shared data owner alone does not permit reuse. Evidence may include co-use, task features, recency, source class, bundle position and separately admitted outcomes; observations, associations, predictions and causal evidence keep their labels. A learned policy may propose which optional routes to run, their effort and candidate budgets, affinity weights, the rank-merging rule and how to divide the response budget. Eligibility, source facts, required context, freshness, revocation, the evaluator and release permission remain outside its control. The relation is named across the ecosystem because the compiler and its callers need to distinguish it from source relationships, permission and Pale's genealogy, its append-only history of what work relied on, what changed and what followed; Scope owns its detailed meaning and lifecycle.
Strict mode needs no model; full mode may use Counsel
Strict mode excludes all model-derived artifacts. It allows exact references and pins, the model-independent keyword index, walks over Scope's admitted graph, and deterministic rules, rank merging, diversity and budgets. It excludes every embedding, model summary, model-inferred link, learned reranker and model-derived feature, however old, and must start, recover and answer without Counsel, Reckon or a model provider. It is a useful mode in its own right.
Full mode may use artifacts produced through Counsel's admitted memory-host route. Scope verifies the producing service, deployment and exact invocation before admitting an artifact. It also checks the selected profile, admitted input, source frontier, controller, relationship, purpose and rights. Requests resolve against the pinned snapshot, with eligibility checked again at use. Retiring a selected profile prevents new use of its artifacts, including through an old index, a cache or a restored snapshot. The same refusal applies to an artifact outside the permitted source frontier or under an expired or revoked grant. Retained audit evidence keeps the original artifact references and the reason use stopped, subject to deletion policy.
When the full path loses a required host operation, test host unavailability, a retired profile, stale retained output and revoked processing permission separately. Check fresh and retained artifacts under the same current eligibility rules; a cached success cannot hide a failed required operation. Scope refuses a full-only request. A request that permits strict fallback uses the model-free selection path above, excluding model artifacts before candidate selection. Host availability changes neither source authority nor evidence retention. The integrated full path is required for Scope's go-live rehearsal.
Vector search must prove its isolation level
Scope profiles select output safety (no ineligible result), traversal-influence isolation (ineligible records cannot change eligible candidates or ranking), or observable noninterference (hidden changes stay within specified timing, count, cache, error and resource limits). Trace every search branch, graph walk, reranker and shared budget. Partition and filter before candidate limits and ranking; filtering only the response allows hidden records to consume slots or change traversal. Bind cache keys and invalidation to scope, permissions and revision.
Fix a permitted query and population, then change only ineligible records, including a high-scoring decoy and enough hidden records to fill a limit. Compare reached candidates, final order and allowed observations separately against exact search of the eligible set. Use post-filtering as a negative control. Test cold and warm reads, revocation and a missing partition. Repeat timing and resource measurements against declared limits. The exact oracle establishes results for those inputs, not physical isolation or another route's timing; bind each conclusion to the tested implementation and identity.
Scope keeps hard controller boundaries and incompatible private relationship groups in physically separate indexes. The compiler must prove compatibility and equal visibility and model-use ceilings before admitting a shared group. Eligibility precedes search and reranking. When the selected level cannot be proved, the slice uses exact search of its eligible set if that path satisfies the level, or omits vectors.
One backend is chosen by benchmark
Scope's native benchmark fixes the workload, data, environment, build versions, warm-up, repetitions, metrics, correctness gates and target before comparison. Measure the baseline distribution and profile its bottleneck, state one causal hypothesis, change one material variable and rerun under the same conditions. Inspect noise, outliers, startup, cache state, contention, transfers, memory, slow-tail risk and work shifted to another component. Keep a change only when its useful improvement exceeds noise while preserving correctness and resource limits. Record both versions, comparable measurements, uncertainty and shifted costs; stop at the target, flattened gains or unstable measurements. An unmeasured change remains a hypothesis.
A local benchmark chooses exactly one reference backend behind stable interfaces. Launching several competing backends is ruled out. The candidate choices concern different parts of retrieval:
Part	Candidates to compare	
Graph route	petgraph Graph or Csr, a custom compressed layout, or sorted adjacency	
Keyword route	Tantivy, another embedded keyword engine, or a simple exact token index	
Snapshot storage	Direct immutable files or memory maps, embedded SQL, or another content-addressed store	
Snapshot publication	ArcSwap, a read-write lock, read-copy-update, or restart-plus-manifest	
Vector route	Exact scan, physically scoped filtered approximate search, or no vectors	
Candidate sets	Sorted vectors, dense bitsets or Roaring sets, chosen by density	
Compare correctness, deterministic rebuilds, request pinning, crash/restart/rollback, tail latency and margin, memory/disk cost, controller isolation, deletion, portability, maintenance, security and licence. A fetched successor from upstream research, repositories, models or licence sources is a proposal input. It becomes eligible for compilation, rehearsal or promotion only after its immutable inputs are pinned and admitted.
The generic libraries live in rtepl-common. Scope pins the versioned libraries for immutable graphs, model-host lifecycle and trust checks; it keeps its own compiler, snapshot, optimiser, policy, records and runtime. Shared libraries hold no private values or Scope schemas, and standalone Scope needs no running Pale daemon. The Counsel port is planned as a Pale crate, Pale's product-specific interface.
Standalone, integrated and degraded paths stay valid
Situation	What happens	
Standalone Scope, without Pale and over Weave	Its owner configures admission and retrieval without a Pale daemon, and Scope reads Weave through Weave's port. Strict mode needs no Reckon or Counsel service; full mode uses the configured memory host through the shared Counsel port, with the host's separate permission checks. An unavailable or unqualified full route refuses full-only requests; permitted strict fallback excludes model-made outputs.	
Integrated with Pale	Pale pins Scope's contracts and consumer binding; each product activates its own compatible identity	
An owner publishing directly	Bypasses Scope entirely and still reaches Pale's event domain after its own admission	
Strict degraded	Exact, keyword and permitted graph routes only, model-made artifacts excluded	
Context-enhanced degraded	Explicit limitations, age and missing-route evidence, only where the request's policy allows	
Context required but unavailable	No bundle and no effect path	
A failed build	The previous snapshot continues; the candidate is quarantined	
An ambiguous activation	New dependent requests stop, the activation journal and head are reconciled, pinned readers finish, then the prior or a validated successor is forward-activated	
Pale incompatible	The prior compatible pair continues, or the integrated path fails or degrades; standalone Scope stays available	
Reckon unavailable	Ordinary deterministic Scope continues; a new learned promotion waits	
Apply compatible-pair qualification to Scope’s policy and snapshot identity and Pale’s consumer binding. The handshake binds Scope’s contract set, the permission slice and the degradation profile. Scope and Pale release and activate in separate stores with independent counters. Each integrated request carries both identities. Event acknowledgement, genealogy, native release, Reckon custody and rehearsal evidence carry no activation authority. A committed policy or snapshot transition may enter Pale's genealogy only as a generic owner-lifecycle occurrence carrying an opaque Scope reference; genealogy never dereferences snapshot bytes or turns affinity into causal lineage.
The handshake uses three messages: Pale publishes the hash of the permission slice Scope may use; a changed hash asks Scope to rebuild in the background; Scope reports “snapshot S built for slice H,” and Pale binds that compatible pair. An unchanged slice hash needs no rebuild. The previous good pair can continue only while the request-time permission, freshness and revocation checks above still allow it. This avoids recompiling every second: unrelated changes in Pale's world leave Scope's usable snapshot alone.
Observability never leaks hidden scope
Scope's redacted metrics and receipts distinguish semantic-head age and reconciliation state; snapshot build, validation, release, readiness and activation state; compiler duration, digest stability, bytes and component counts; request pinning, cold and warm latency and per-route, fusion and budget cost; eligibility, required-context, missing-route, degradation and fail-closed reasons; candidate, selected and omitted counts, only after scope filtering; model-origin and strict-mode paths; old-reader drain, rollback and invalidation lag; evidence-window expiry and unreconstructibility; and vector isolation test results. Metrics never expose hidden-scope counts, cross-controller maxima, candidate identities, payloads, credentials or private configuration.
Source content is data, never instruction
The compiler treats all source-derived content as data: content cannot change control policy, include paths, the model provider, build instructions or where artifacts live. Inputs are bounded, canonicalised, hashed and admitted before compilation, with negative fixtures for poisoning, prompt and control injection, cache-key confusion, wrong-controller substitution and digest ambiguity. An implementation must prove exact dependency, model and data pins with a complete bill of materials; licence expressions, notices, patent and hosted-service terms; reproducible logical builds across supported machines; no secret or reference leakage in artifacts, logs or bundles; backup, restore and forward rollback without claiming atomicity across stores; deletion propagation through snapshots, embeddings, affinity and caches; deterministic fallback without optional models or vector services; and clean standalone portability with no private default values.
Eighteen falsifiers decide whether retrieval is correct
For each falsifier, identify the observable requirement, producing component, fixture state, failure result and environment needed to distinguish correct behaviour. Use the repository's real entry point and runner; check what a command does before executing it. Verify that a failed test reached the intended assertion rather than failing in setup. Where practical, a deliberate regression in a disposable copy proves the check can catch the fault; restore the exact candidate and rerun. Use controlled ports for local decisions and real adapters for transactions, retries, permissions and integration.
Confirm which assertions actually ran, keeping passed, failed, skipped and filtered cases separate. A green command with no relevant tests establishes no behaviour. Review tests for hidden order, missing refusal paths and assertions that merely mirror implementation. Report the checked artifact, environment, results and limits, distinguishing product defects, test defects, harness failures, unavailable capabilities and unrun checks. Scoring
Scope's initial scoring design uses A-MAC-lite to rank items that have already passed the eligibility checks. Its four factors are a prior by content type, recency with a half-life per type, a brief novelty boost, and support from accepted caller use reports. The formula exposes each contribution so that later comparisons can test whether the score is useful.
Scoring can reorder and trim optional context, but cannot delete, supersede or tombstone an item, authorise a retrieval method, widen eligibility or suppress required context. A-MAC-lite is a local starting formula, not evidence that these factors or defaults outperform simpler scoring on Scope’s workload. The comparisons below must establish that before a successor is selected.
Four kinds of content, each with its own prior and half-life
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub enum ContentType {
    Legislative,   // laws, regulations, compliance rules, curated reference
    Entity,        // people, organisations, projects
    Transaction,   // email threads, documents, task outcomes
    Ephemeral,     // session context, temporary notes, drafts
}

Content type	Prior	Half-life	
Legislative	1.0	Never decays	
Entity	0.8	90 days	
Transaction	0.5	30 days	
Ephemeral	0.3	7 days	
These values are the canonical defaults, and the half-lives are configurable per deployment. The scorer keeps the name A-MAC-lite; Reckon's moving-average comparison arm is a different algorithm with a different name, and golden-parity tests name exactly the algorithm they match. Before reading or emitting either profile, map its serialised identifier to the producer revision, configuration and actual algorithm. A familiar token or successful decode cannot establish the behaviour that produced an old score. Preserve that version's meaning and refuse an ambiguous mapping. Distinct algorithms need distinct canonical identities. Any temporary alias needs an owner-approved same-contract mapping, specified readers and versions, one canonical write form and a removal condition supported by usage. Test a permitted legacy read, canonical write, ambiguous identifier, retired alias and a well-formed record whose familiar token names different behaviour in another producer profile. Run a distinguishing input through the actual algorithms as well as their parsers and writers.
The formula
Source validity, revocation, classification, visibility, contradiction and the request’s freshness requirement govern eligibility before scoring. Qualify eligibility separately from the score and outcome using the controls below. An item that was accessed but has expired or been revoked stays ineligible, and access recency can only rank eligible candidates; it can never extend a valid-through time, suppress a tombstone or override an owner's revision.
recency    = exp(-ln 2 * days_since_last_access / half_life)      (1.0 when the half-life is infinite)
novelty    = max(0, 1 - retrieve_count / novelty_threshold)          novelty_threshold = 5
confidence = min(1, use_receipt_count / confidence_threshold)        confidence_threshold = 10
raw_score  = prior * recency * (1 + novelty_weight * novelty)
                   * (confidence_floor + (1 - confidence_floor) * confidence)
                                                                      novelty_weight = 0.3, confidence_floor = 0.5
raw_max    = max(content_type_priors) * (1 + novelty_weight)          = 1.3 with these values
normalized = raw_score / raw_max

After five retrievals the novelty boost is gone. With the default configuration, the confidence multiplier rises continuously from 0.5 with no accepted use receipts to 1.0 at ten receipts; one receipt gives 0.55 and nine give 0.95. Only the consumed item references in a newly accepted caller report advance use_receipt_count and last_used. Ignored items, bundle inclusion alone and exact replay add no use credit. This confidence measures support from admitted caller reports.
Scores are normalised by the maximum for the active configuration, never clamped. Interfaces and displays use the normalised value in the unit interval; storage keeps the raw score, the maximum, every component, the formula version and the configuration hash. Neither value is a probability or a calibrated confidence. Old scores are recomputed or kept under their original formula version, never silently reinterpreted.
The domain fails closed
Every numeric prior, half-life, weight, floor and runtime age must be finite, and age cannot be negative. A numeric half-life must be strictly positive; no decay is represented by None, not by a floating-point infinity. Every prior and the confidence floor lie in the unit interval. The novelty weight is not negative. Both thresholds are at least one. At least one prior is positive, so the maximum is finite and strictly positive. An unknown content type, a missing entry, an invalid configuration or input, a non-finite intermediate value or a non-positive maximum returns a typed scoring error; the scorer never panics, divides by zero, emits NaN or infinity, or clamps a bad configuration into a different one.
pub struct ScoringConfig {
    pub half_lives: HashMap<ContentType, Option<f64>>,   // None = infinite
    pub content_type_priors: HashMap<ContentType, f64>,
    pub novelty_threshold: u32,
    pub novelty_weight: f64,
    pub confidence_threshold: u32,
    pub confidence_floor: f64,
}

pub struct ScoreBreakdown {
    pub raw_score: f64, pub normalized_score: f64, pub raw_max: f64,
    pub prior: f64, pub recency: f64, pub novelty: f64, pub confidence: f64,
    pub formula_version: String, pub config_hash: String,
}

pub fn compute_score(content_type: ContentType, days_since_access: f64,
                     retrieve_count: u32, use_receipt_count: u32,
                     config: &ScoringConfig) -> Result<ScoreBreakdown, ScoringError> {
    validate_scoring_domain(&content_type, days_since_access, config)?;
    let prior = config.content_type_priors[&content_type];
    let recency = match config.half_lives[&content_type] {
        None => 1.0,
        Some(hl) => (-f64::ln(2.0) * days_since_access / hl).exp(),
    };
    let novelty = (1.0 - retrieve_count as f64 / config.novelty_threshold as f64).max(0.0);
    let confidence = (use_receipt_count as f64 / config.confidence_threshold as f64).min(1.0);
    let raw_score = prior * recency * (1.0 + config.novelty_weight * novelty)
        * (config.confidence_floor + (1.0 - config.confidence_floor) * confidence);
    let raw_max = maximum_for_config(config)?;
    ensure_finite_score(raw_score, raw_max)?;
    Ok(ScoreBreakdown { raw_score, normalized_score: raw_score / raw_max, raw_max,
        prior, recency, novelty, confidence,
        formula_version: FORMULA_VERSION.into(), config_hash: config_hash(config) })
}

Golden vectors cover zero thresholds, all-zero priors, missing entries, zero, negative and non-finite half-lives, negative and non-finite ages, NaN and infinity in every floating field, extreme counters, exact normalisation boundaries and every typed failure. Property tests require every admitted result to be finite and between zero and one.
Scores are never global
A score is keyed on the full scope: principal, controller, optional relationship, evaluation scope, the exact owner-issued role reference, and the immutable role and assignment evidence. Two roles that render with the same label in different organisations, clients, purposes or assignments never share counters or learned utility, and a path with no organising owner still presents an admitted role and purpose and never invents a placeholder.

Recording what was available as well as what was selected makes the decision inspectable. If A, B and C were returned and the work went well, that alone says nothing about whether D would have helped. Keeping A through F as candidates, with their scores and the chosen set, supports replay, candidate training and later policy comparisons within admitted uses and the governed evidence window. Off-policy estimation additionally needs the logging policy to have given relevant alternatives non-zero probability; a deterministic scorer gives unchosen items zero probability, which ordinary inverse-propensity methods cannot repair. The use receipt records the admitted caller's report. Owner-derived output mentions follow the derivation contract and remain a separate, labelled feature.
Use receipts and owner-event inbox records are committed durably before they are acknowledged. Only the rebuildable score and diagnostic projections may be batched, under a deployment-selected interval, size and memory budget and on graceful shutdown, with one Dolt commit per batch; the batching pattern is on Durability and recovery.
A comparison fixes its evidence and controls before scoring
Define the exact candidate population, counted unit, decision time, evidence available then, eligibility policy, formula version and outcome definition. Keep eligible, disqualified and unresolved cases separate, applying the owner’s rule when a condition cannot be checked. Retain each decision’s reason and the strongest relevant contrary evidence. Test a high-scoring candidate blocked by policy, stale or missing eligibility evidence and a case exactly at the valid boundary; inspect selection and the exported view. Different rules or evidence create a new comparison with its own population.
Fix candidate identities, case revisions, budget, environment, rubric, blocking criteria, scorer, threshold, uncertainty policy and aggregation before comparison. A mechanical checker must reject known-bad controls at the intended check. A judgment rubric needs examples separating adjacent grades and checks that style or verbosity does not dominate. Keep tuning cases out of the holdout. Report disagreement, unstable results, missing coverage, threshold sensitivity and regressions hidden by averages; an average never cancels a blocking failure. Keep screened, eligible, assigned, scored and outcome-observed counts separate, with their time window and missing or pending outcomes. Outcomes observed only for selected cases justify claims about that group, not every candidate. A score is no probability without separate calibration.
The initial comparison includes recency * log(1 + retrieve_count), A-MAC-lite, Reckon's moving-average utility, shaped credit, ablation attribution and a priority rule. Reckon's moving average is u_new = (1 - η) * u_old + η * credit * outcome, with η = 0.1 and a unit-interval clamp, exercised against eligible frozen vectors. Proportional and smooth-positive credit variants require published zero-total, non-finite and replay cases; existing utility feeding credit is not evidence that shaped credit beats equal credit. Ablation supports a causal claim only under a separately accepted causal-evidence profile. The priority comparator utility + (max(ablation_delta, 0) + max(counterfactual_delta, 0)) * 0.5 ranks and never deletes.
Before running, declare eligible owner outcomes, their utility mapping, controller scope, complete resolve/use/outcome evidence, datasets, splits, seeds, tolerances, hardware, non-inferiority or improvement thresholds, information-loss and leakage limits. Keep budget omissions visible. Precision and recall are diagnostics; outcomes remain a vector of separate owner facts. Set the required evidence from diversity, support and uncertainty, not a universal row count. Prefer the simpler policy when results are materially equivalent; do not invent a margin after seeing results. Evaluation records and release preserve the comparison and the separate owner decision.
A learned scorer, budget gate, learned credit model, trajectory model or reinforcement-learning memory policy remains a research candidate requiring a measured gap in simpler methods. Future-use or outcome labels cannot be features from the same event, and an incumbent score cannot serve as its own target evidence. Use time- and controller-held-out cases, calibrated uncertainty and abstention. Unselected items are not negative examples; deterministic logs give them zero propensity and cannot support inverse-propensity estimates for unseen alternatives. Randomised exploration needs its own permission and logging. A learned budget gate cannot delete, and destructive memory operations remain owner-reviewed proposals. Eligibility, required context, privacy, source binding and strict mode never become learned choices.
The response is filled greedily within its budget
Bundle selection is budgeted, and nothing about selection changes the graph or the sources:
Compute each candidate's encoded or token cost and the whole response's cost; node count alone is not a budget.
Apply visibility, freshness, classification and the task's required and optional context before any optimisation.
If eligible optional material still exceeds the budget, keep every required item and its dependencies under their explicit requirement (graph degree never creates an implicit protection floor), rank only the optional eligible items by utility per unit of cost with provenance, and omit the lowest until the response fits.
Record every omitted requirement or item and any resulting limitation in the bundle.
Optionally propose a bounded compaction under an owner-published schema; canonical and source rows stay unchanged.
This greedy selector makes no claim to be an optimal knapsack and has no authority to delete. Content from Gazette's site exports and legislative material is never physically removed by ranking; a bundle may omit it only with an explicit omission carrying the exact adapter, owner, snapshot and row provenance. Mentions derived from outputs, content hints and every other feature enter scoring only when their owner's exported schema admits them.
