Source imports
A new owner snapshot reaches Scope through a bounded import. The owner reads its source using its own credentials and supplies a secret-free, content-addressed set of chunks. Scope checks admission, verifies the bytes against the signed digests and stages the candidate privately. An accepted new import advances the namespace once. Readers see the new generation and its receipts only after the required commits and anchor advances. The same path serves repository manifests and Gazette site exports.
Admission comes before parsing
Every import is admitted before its body is parsed, and the caller's intent and the verifier's admission are separate records that never hash each other. The import body's hash is SHA-256 over its exact canonical form. Who may admit it is one of three branches:
Branch	Who signs the admission	What else must hold	
The resource owner	The owner itself	No delegation or Pale fields; in standalone mode the admission binds the owner's active trust record and the checked authority checkpoint	
A delegated adapter	The adapter the owner named	The owner-signed delegation is present, active, unexpired, non-transitive, names that adapter and role, and covers every requested owner, namespace, scope and purpose	
Pale's admission principal	Pale, after validating the caller's request	The same owner-signed delegation naming Pale's admission role, plus the exact accepted deployment binding, capability session grant and caller-signed request; a Pale process identity alone is never the owner's consent	
In a Pale deployment the caller first signs a common request whose body is exactly the import; after validating it and the owner's delegation, Pale's admission principal signs the import admission, binding the request, the deployment and session evidence, the delegation and the same body hash. Scope consumes the immutable triple of request, admission and body through its admitted port, and for a federated call the destination's federation admission as well. No record hashes a future container that hashes it.
Scope resolves every issuer, delegation, deployment binding, session grant, request and federation admission key and hash, and rejects anything unknown, retired, rolled back, revoked, expired, in the wrong role or out of scope. A durable admission journal records the issuer, key epoch and request identifier with the admission's canonical hash; exact replay may return the earlier disposition, and reuse with any different authority, delegation, binding, scope, body hash, times or signature fails closed. Only after canonicalisation, signature and expiry are verified does Scope parse those bytes, and then the body's source owner must equal the permitted owner, its namespace must be one of the permitted namespaces, and its principal, controller and relationship scope must match the admission and the delegation. A caller, path, repository, provider account, deployment or payload can never declare itself the owner or widen a namespace.
A signed profile sets each deployment's limits
The deployment's operator authority issues a signed import profile for each instance, mode, deployment binding and scope. It must choose positive values no greater than these absolute ceilings, and it must also set numeric budgets for the activation transaction and its p95 and p99 latency on its pinned hardware and content store. Lower limits for a particular owner are normal; crossing any limit rejects the import before anything becomes visible.
Limit	Ceiling	
Chunks per import	4,096	
Records per chunk	2,048	
Uncompressed bytes per chunk	8 MiB	
Manifest size	4 MiB	
Items per import	1,000,000	
Tombstones per import	1,000,000	
Total payload	8 GiB	
One inline payload	64 KiB	
Staging age	24 hours	
Validation wall time	30 minutes	
Concurrent staging sessions	8 per namespace, 32 per instance	
There is one active profile head per exact tuple of instance, mode, deployment binding and scope, and the selected profile record is itself that head: its reference, canonical hash and epoch are what every manifest, body and receipt pins. Epoch one has no predecessor; each successor increments once, binds its predecessor, and either activates a replacement or retires the head. Standalone profiles bind the exact authority checkpoint and carry no deployment fields; integrated profiles bind the exact Pale deployment. The whole active-head set is rooted in the durable-state checkpoint, so a restored lookup table cannot quietly select another profile. An unknown instance, a stale head, the wrong controller, an expired or retired profile, a checkpoint rollback, or a compiler proposal racing an operator successor fails before any chunk is read; the two compete on one compare-and-swap head.
The adapter stages content-addressed chunks
The staging manifest is signed by the exact admitted adapter: its instance, version and binding and its acquisition receipt must match the owner's delegation or the integrated admission. It binds the source, scope, mode (full or delta), requested and expected generations, the checked profile head, and the ordered list of chunks with their kind, first and last source record, record count, byte size, schema and content hash. A mutable profile, an unsigned manifest, the wrong adapter, a stale binding or an unverified acquisition receipt fails before any chunk is read.
Check required coverage and freshness for each owner scope, partition and task. Trace the source position acquisition covered through staging and activation to the exact generation Scope's readers can use; inspect that visible generation separately from the import acknowledgement. The latest source event, acquisition position, stage completion time and readable generation answer different questions. One partition's highest checkpoint cannot establish coverage for another. Keep missing, incomplete, stale and unknown data distinct from a verified empty result. A no-change result establishes freshness only for the window and scope acquisition actually checked. Test a quiet source, recent rows with incomplete coverage, a missing partition, successful processing of an old input and a reader still serving the predecessor. The adapter supplies the exact acquisition receipt. The imported records retain their source observation and validity coordinates.
Each chunk is an immutable canonical array of exactly one kind of record:
item {
  source_record_ref, source_version,
  record_schema_id, record_schema_sha256,
  content_digest,
  inline_payload? | immutable_content_ref?      # exactly one
  classification, authority_class, lifecycle_state,
  provenance_evidence[] { provenance_ref, provenance_sha256 },
  observed_at, valid_through
}

tombstone {
  source_record_ref, source_version,
  tombstone_kind                                # explicit | policy_omission
  deletion_or_absence_reason,
  authority_reference, authority_reference_sha256,
  complete_set_policy_ref?, complete_set_policy_sha256?,
  first_absent_generation?, current_absent_generation?,
  absence_evidence_ref?, grace_evidence_ref?, reconciliation_evidence_ref?  # each with its hash
  observed_at
}

Chunk indices run contiguously from zero; manifest entries sort by kind, first record and index; ranges never overlap; and the concatenated records are globally sorted and unique by source record, with no key appearing as both an item and a tombstone. Each item names its record schema and carries exactly one bounded inline payload or an admitted immutable content reference whose bytes match its digest; a mutable path or URL is not enough.
Two digests bind the whole snapshot
The manifest digest is the staging manifest's own canonical hash. The snapshot digest is SHA-256 over the canonical object {digest_profile: "scope.source-snapshot.v2", manifest_digest, ordered_chunk_content_hashes}, where the array lists each chunk's index, kind and content hash exactly as the manifest does, and each chunk's hash covers every record field and representation. Cross-language vectors cover empty, single and many chunks, full and delta imports, tombstones, inline and referenced content, and the negatives: wrong order, overlapping ranges, count or byte drift, null, self-inclusion, stale staging and changed content.
Generations advance one at a time
To activate a new import, generation one requires an empty namespace and no expected predecessor. Every successor must request exactly the previous generation plus one and name that previous generation. Skipped, reused, stale, zero or ambiguous generations conflict on that path. Staging is content-addressed and idempotent: hash validation may run in parallel outside the single writer, each chunk is installed with create-or-verify semantics, and the writer records chunks in bounded transactions under a candidate generation nobody can see. Abandoned staging is deleted only after the profile's age, with no active import lease, against an exact inventory of the manifest and chunks, with an immutable cleanup receipt; a referenced or active chunk is never swept by age alone.
Activation is short, ordered and anchored
Imports never hold one long SQL transaction. The sequence is:
Install and verify the immutable chunks under the signed profile.
Validate the complete staging manifest and the candidate semantic root while the previous generation stays visible.
Take the namespace's generation head and Scope's writer fence.
In one short transaction, compare and swap the expected generation, install the validated root and persist the signed import receipt, the sql_activated journal entry, the gated receipt outbox and the first durable-state checkpoint covering the new frontiers.
With every receipt and the new generation still hidden and admission still gated, advance the anti-rollback anchor to that checkpoint.
Create and verify the exact Dolt commit.
Sign the audit-anchor receipt over that commit and semantic root. Persist it and its successor checkpoint together, then create and verify the Dolt commit containing them. Advance the independent anchor to the successor checkpoint.
Verify the two advances in order before revealing the receipt pair or new generation and reopening admission.
The SQL commit and the Dolt commit are separate durable boundaries and are never described as one atomic operation. The append-only journal moves through prepared, chunks_staged, manifest_validated, sql_activated, dolt_anchored, anchor_receipt_committed and receipt_visible, with terminal rejected, conflict or abandoned branches only where their rules allow. Restart resumes exactly:
Last durable state	What restart does	
prepared or chunks_staged	Verify the immutable chunks and continue, or abandon under the cleanup policy; the previous generation stays visible	
manifest_validated	Recheck the generation head and run the one activation compare-and-swap; a stale head conflicts	
sql_activated	Keep admission closed. Verify the stored semantic root, receipt bytes and first checkpoint. Complete or read back that exact anchor advance before creating or verifying the first Dolt commit.	
dolt_anchored	Verify the first advance and its Dolt commit. Use the stored identifiers, times, root and commit to recover the exact audit-anchor receipt and successor checkpoint.	
anchor_receipt_committed	Verify the stored audit-anchor receipt, its successor checkpoint and their Dolt commit. Complete or read back the second anchor advance before exposing the generation and receipt pair.	
receipt_visible	Exact replay returns the original receipt pair	
Changed bytes, an impossible jump, a wrong commit or root, a competing head	Quarantine and fail closed; never synthesise success	
A lost anchor acknowledgement is reconciled against the exact checkpoint reference and hash. The expected predecessor permits the pending advance. The exact successor confirms it already happened. A conflicting pair goes to recovery under Durability and recovery. A staged import leaves the previous generation queryable until the activation swap. After that swap, admission stays closed while the journal finishes. Performance fixtures measure validation and ingestion separately from activation, at p50, p95 and p99, across contention, independent namespaces, staging ceilings and each crash boundary.
Apply the exact commit recovery procedure to each Dolt commit and its Scope checkpoint. Independent namespaces can share a physical table, and the branch can contain staged changes from other tables. The writer fence must protect the checkpoint's full change set while it is staged and through the commit. Bind that set and its expected predecessor before committing. Read back the pinned commit and verify its changes against the checkpoint before opening admission. A mismatch keeps admission closed. Exercise the import commit scope fixture.
If the commit reply is lost before the hash is recorded, identify the candidate in the branch history using the checkpoint's expected parent and change set. A unique exact match permits only the outstanding recovery step, under its own guards. If history is ambiguous or the candidate cannot be established, keep admission closed and apply the original recovery guards before any retry.
Omission never deletes
Apply the snapshot admission method to the owner's coverage and removal evidence. Scope applies exactly the manifest-bound items and authorised tombstones at the activation swap. Omitted records keep their disposition. A delta requires a source contract that defines ordered delta semantics.
Only the site export can submit policy-derived removals, through its own separately versioned, owner-signed policy and policy-head types. A new source must publish its own policy, head schema, adapter and fixtures. When a policy is present all three head fields are required. The signer must be the resource owner, the policy must cover the import, and the signed head must be the selected, non-rolled-back active head for the same scope. Recheck that head at activation, under the same guard that protects the generation swap, and retain its reference, hash and epoch in the receipt. Every policy_omission tombstone must be inside a tombstone chunk bound by the manifest and both digests. It carries the policy, absence, grace and reconciliation fields, and its authority reference resolves the deterministic tombstone contract. An explicit tombstone omits those fields.
Every disposition gets exactly one receipt pair
Apply the command replay procedure after Scope’s admission and scope checks. Scope resolves the original admission and the import’s semantic identity before checking the generation for a new activation.
An exact replay of an admission and request returns its original visible receipt and audit-anchor receipt, even after the head advances. If the disposition is still pending, recover it through the journal. The replay never creates a second pair or starts a second activation. Changed reuse of an admission identity fails closed.
For a new admission, the semantic uniqueness key is the source owner, namespace, principal, controller and relationship scope, mode, requested and expected generations, profile hash, staging manifest hash, manifest digest and snapshot digest. Reusing an import identifier or that key with a changed body conflicts. An exact semantic match to an import with a visible committed receipt pair produces a duplicate pair under the new admission, referencing both original receipts, even if the head has since advanced. A pending match remains subject to the original import's visibility gate.
A request that still needs a new activation conflicts if its expected generation is stale. Compare and swap the head under the writer fence before installing a new generation.
A committed receipt carries the profile and manifest references and hashes, both digests, the chunk and byte totals, the committed generation, the accepted counts and the commit time. A duplicate echoes those original fields. Its top-level admission fields bind the new admission, whose disposition is journaled and anchored without applying any items or tombstones or advancing the generation. Conflict and rejection receipts carry no committed generation, zero accepted counts and a bounded reason. The receipt's evidence depends on the branch: an owner admission forbids delegation and Pale hashes; a delegated admission requires the delegation's reference and hash; a Pale admission requires the delegation plus the deployment binding, session grant and caller request, and the federation admission when federated. Every terminal receipt needs its audit-anchor receipt before it is complete, and the anchor names a generation only when the import committed or duplicated one.
Each source reaches Scope through its owner
Repositories. The repository owner's process produces a pinned manifest or event projection: identity, declared remotes, branch roles, ahead-behind counts and owner-reported worktrees at an observation time. Scope never discovers credentials through gh auth status or runs git or gh. The resulting tables are on Resources and locations.
Google Workspace. Where an owner uses the gws command-line tool, its own admitted helper selects the owner-managed configuration, performs the read and produces a bounded, versioned, secret-free export or event projection: email threads and Drive documents as references with source versions, classification, provenance and freshness. Account selection and credentials stay inside that helper's process, and any account isolation it uses is applied and tested there. Scope stores the projection, provenance and any opaque route needed to read freshness; it never selects an account, switches global authentication, exports that environment or calls gws. Weave holds export-production schedules, and away-work follows Weave → Pale → execution. The owner retains source credentials, export ownership and authority for admitted manual exports; Scope has no provider polling loop. Scope commits each accepted derived revision with its own outbox entry. Owner publications qualify separately for Pale's direct route.
Means runs. Means reads owner-supplied facts under the grants declared by the owner's workspace. That workspace retains the owner's run snapshot, results and run record; Means keeps no store or service of its own. An owner may select a retained run reference or projection for Scope's snapshot contract, keeping immutable references to the original legal, corporate, banking, ledger and filing records. A Means result does not replace those original authorities. The adapter must map the selected projection into Scope's snapshot contract and preserve the run's identity and source references. Scope resolves only the admitted reference or projection and never changes the source records or saved calculation. Retained inputs stay within their owners' access and retention limits; a correction creates a later run, and a retained result needs current permission before new use.
Weave. Weave's changing organisational state reaches Scope through Pale by the changing-source path, with Weave's own helper keeping its credentials and admission. It is never a direct Weave-to-Scope integration. That holds for what Weave's own work sends: Weave itself never calls Scope. In the other direction Scope reads Weave through Weave's port, with Pale or without it; without Pale, Scope is how an agent reads Weave, as Architecture explains. The separate question of what Weave work may ask Scope to retrieve remains on Contracts.
Gas Town. Gas Town may export bounded execution-history snapshots or event references. Its owner's helper reads back native records through gt or bd as needed. Scope receives the bounded projection under its own admission contract.
Creative work. Once the creative owners publish an export contract, an adapter admits only an owner-issued classified manifest, native run and review receipts, and explicitly approved asset reference and hash pairs; raw prompts, asset bytes, provider credentials, mutable workflow state and whole-workspace crawls are rejected.
Research knowledge and history. Current accepted findings belong to the readable owner pages; necessary original research and ruling evidence stays with its owner. Weave's Radar manages research directions and findings; Scope consumes only the export the owner selects, not a registry assumed to be a live resolver. The adapter defaults to current accepted owner knowledge and includes proposals or historical records only on an explicit bounded request. It preserves source, decision, version and historical/proposal status, never sweeps across subjects, returns unresolved conflicts rather than merging them, enforces confidentiality, and never promotes a finding, applies a ruling or changes a policy or model. A market-context bundle may carry source identities, the owner's accepted policy and worldview references, references to retained Means runs, or explicitly requested candidate-review context, never holdings in an unbounded prompt and never an allocation or trade instruction. Reading an old accepted-state projection does not establish that it is today's authority.
The site export arrives through Pale, never from Gazette directly
In Scope's design the import consumes a complete, versioned, content-addressed post-build export under Gazette's artifact and signing contract. When the import is selected, Pale invokes Scope with the owner's delegation, its common request and the separate import admission bound to the body hash. Scope applies admitted records to its own website_* tables in the store at port 3309. The kernel is an empty library today, so the website module has yet to be written. Scope's input is the export, with no access to Gazette's build, SQLite store or release journal. The publisher's release policy governs approval to publish.
The complete export must validate against its exact schema before the generation swap. Staged chunks remain private while that validation runs. Every owner key, relation key, source reference and hash, generation, visibility and deletion marker is preserved. Nodes and edges come only from owner-declared records or an owner-signed deterministic transformation; unknown or ambiguous members fail admission, and Scope never repairs them by matching paths, URLs, domains, names, handles or email addresses. Author projections stay source-qualified. Build caches and rendering artifacts are excluded unless the manifest admits them, and a generated rendering such as graph.json or JSON-LD never fills a missing record. Every derived item binds the admitted adapter contract, owner, snapshot, generation and exact source record. Fixtures cover canonical and aliased content, index pages, nested content, wrong or missing keys, ambiguous relations, scope denial, stale or revoked generations and deletion propagation.
A publication agent asking about a research site gets bounded publication context from owner-declared records, with exact provenance, omissions, freshness and visibility limits. A technical agent resolving a private client project does not reach site nodes at all when no admitted edge connects them; private nodes never become reachable from public ones merely because a relationship exists outside the graph, and the publisher's rules can still forbid traversal or export. Reachability is necessary, never sufficient, for publication. Site content is never physically deleted by ranking, the hop budget, scoring, owner-published property filters and a per-source budget bound what one response carries, and content hints stay disabled until the export schema or a signed transformation defines them. Scope's website_export_generation means the last site generation Scope committed; making an export does not advance it, a failed import leaves the previous generation intact, and a task that required the rejected generation fails. Import and rebuild are benchmarked against the export fixture before promotion.
Part of Scope engineering.

Scope
Scope is the ecosystem's cache for context: it sits on Pale, Weave or both, because what an agent read has usually changed by the time it acts. It gives each agent session the context to continue earlier work without asking the person to reconstruct its history. It connects the immediate task to the project's longer purpose, selecting the relevant facts, decisions and reasons without handing the agent every record.
Like any cache it is optional and never the source of truth. With Pale it reranks as genealogy updates arrive and writes a pointer to the context it gave each agent into Pale's genealogy, and it never writes Weave's state; without Pale it runs standalone, over Weave, and is how an agent reads Weave. Today the kernel is an empty library: the design below is the work in front of it.
Source owners supply copies and retain access to the originals. Scope's answer names the records it used, their revisions and the gaps that matter to the task.

What the architecture separates
In Scope's architecture, the source adapter uses the owner's tools to read the original and sends Scope a snapshot without secrets. Scope stores verified revisions and builds a separate search index before answering requests. Each request reads one prepared snapshot so its records and access rules agree.
The separation lets developers rebuild the search index without rewriting source records. A new ranking rule may change what a caller sees first, within the same access rules.
The architecture keeps context offered, context reported used and evidence that it helped separate when comparing retrieval policies.
On the integrated path, Pale checks the request and passes along Scope's signed bundle byte for byte. Standalone Scope, without Pale and over Weave, uses its own signed caller grants. Strict retrieval must work without model-generated summaries, embeddings or links. In standalone full mode, Scope's design links Pale's Counsel port library and calls its configured memory host without a Pale daemon; on the integrated path Pale invokes the host. Either way, the host checks processing permission separately. The architecture chapter explains these connections and what can make a request fail.
To contribute now, build the library and follow the architecture for the part you plan to change. Client integrations need the published caller API and import formats; wait for those contracts before writing a consumer.

Scope
Scope is the ecosystem's cache for context, the part of RawThoughts' one system that brings the context a task needs. It sits on Pale, Weave or both, because what an agent read has usually changed by the time it acts and a task needs the smallest fresh account of what matters. It gives agent sessions the context to continue earlier work, connecting the immediate task to its project's longer purpose and decisions. Like any cache it is optional and never the source of truth. Its design has two supported modes: integrated, through Pale, and standalone, without Pale and over Weave. With Pale it reranks as genealogy updates arrive and writes a pointer to the context it gave each agent into Pale's genealogy, and it never writes Weave's state. Each source owner supplies a secret-free snapshot and keeps access to the original. Scope selects a bundle of fresh context the caller may see, kept within the request's size limit, with its sources, age and omissions. The caller retains its own authority to act. This repository holds Scope's Rust code and developer documentation.

Suites of a paragraph
A suite with its own folder carries cases long enough to need one. These are the suites whose cases fit a paragraph, kept beside the requirements they apply.
Integration
Select and qualify each optional provider independently. Removing it must preserve source records and unknown outcomes. A delivered message cannot establish command acceptance, outside effect or consumer settlement.
Causal lineage
Exercise the actor/subject and engine-appended lineage cases in operation roles, and result-to-parent matching in Pale integration. Caller parents cannot overwrite engine history.
Conformance
Compare the same operation through every enabled surface. Preserve variants, payloads, errors, revisions, actual actor and unknown outcomes. A protocol that cannot express a capability reports it unsupported rather than inventing parity.
Presentation
Exercise fresh, stale, denied and unknown views; mandatory relations; several related objects without an invented primary; nested/reverse reads, counts, search and artifacts. A renderer records submitted intent, never a native outcome by itself.
Read back
Confirm exact command, occurrence, source version and provider coordinates independently. Substitute another genuine object or digest and require refusal or unresolved state. A later revision must not overwrite the result recovered for an earlier command.
Portability
Build from a clean checkout on Linux and macOS using the declared toolchain and lockfile. Run the repository architecture and source checks on each. A platform build proves only that the crates and entry points build until cases for Weave's runtime exist.
Concurrent commands
Concurrent edits by a person and an agent. A changed task and an added relationship invalidate a stale command; the actor must reread and propose again, nothing is silently overwritten, and the refusal names the reason.
Capability resolution
Prove exact actor, capability, target, context, policy, purpose and freshness resolution. Cover denied, ambiguous, unavailable and stale bindings; selecting a provider grants no permission. Use the separately deployed deterministic local provider before any live vendor.
Atomic occurrence delivery
Exercise the HTTPS delivery cases and lost command reply. Prove each committed change and its occurrence appear together, including deletion, cancellation and acceptance; delivery failure cannot roll back the source commit.
Definition evolution
Definition evolution. Versions one and two coexist; new records take the active version two; an old record stays on version one until a guarded adoption; an incompatible GraphQL change gets its own type coordinate; removing a version blocks new use while historical evaluations still render.
Contracts
Generate language forms from the producing declaration and run positive and negative consumer cases across Rust, JavaScript, Python and Go. Preserve operation, definition, capability, outcome, lineage, presentation, store, interface, cross-instance and Pale contracts without a second handwritten model. Version and signing profiles remain implementation work.
Store
Run against each supported database, PostgreSQL first because the first vertical will prove it: atomic records/history/commit/outbox, record and relation conflicts, absent blockers and policy changes before commit, crash windows and unknown results. Rebuild derived indexes without changing authoritative outcomes. Backup and restore the complete recovery unit before storing valuable data.
Human-only commercial work
A human-only commercial journey. An account, an opportunity and a case, booking-like scheduled work, versioned evidence, service levels and checklists, changes to child records, a cancellation race, an exact outside audit or effect receipt and a distinct final outcome. Work scheduled more than a year out starts its eligibility later, not as a fake paused service level.

Commercial work
This first-party domain is the planned example of Weave's public extension model: relationships and commercial commitments alongside accountable work for people and agents. It must use only the public SDK, install into a clean instance and be removable without rebuilding the engine. The engine must also build and pass its own tests with no domain installed. These are design requirements; this package has no implemented business behaviour yet.
The initial definitions are Account, Person, RelationshipContext, Evidence, Radar, Goal, WorkItem, Comment, ArtifactRef and Schedule. They are ordinary installed definitions, not root engine classes or any adopter's private ontology. A second unrelated domain must exercise the same SDK before the product claims to serve a clean adopter. Neither domain gets private imports, SQL migrations, GraphQL resolvers or a client-name branch.
The first vertical uses only the part of this model it needs, and the standalone journey specifies it.

Generic work may be isolated, contextual, parented, related, dependent or scheduled. It requires no operational case, permanent agent, mandatory parent, permanent primary relationship or Pale operation. Definitions keep structural parentage, dependencies, comment ancestry, responsibility, permission and execution separate.
Relationships carry their period and purpose
Accounts, people, opportunities and relationship contexts are separate records. One person can participate in several contexts without duplication. No relation is permanently primary, and appearing in the record grants an outside person no internal role, software account or chat membership.
An account manager holds relationship continuity. An account executive carries a particular opportunity, mandate or commercial promise. A manager may steward several accounts; an account can have several mandates and stewards; a mandate can involve several delivery pods. Titles do not grant assignment, spending, effect or acceptance permission. Each delivery-pod occurrence binds its exact account, mandate, manager, executive, provider-acceptance point and consumer-acceptance point. Pod-type names remain adopter configuration.
Stakeholders have declared roles such as buyer, sponsor, technical owner or operating owner. Their labels alone grant no permission. Stewardship, next actions and review queues record the responsible owner, due date or freshness, and blocked, deferred, rejected or superseded state. Outreach, response, discovery, proposal and outcome are separate stages with recoverable histories.
Optional organisational structures include verticals, groups, discipline trees, pods and roles, with primary, leader or supporting coordination relations. A structural definition describes relationships and required evidence, never a mandatory title. A stable role binds its occupant separately from the software provider.
An assessment preserves its reasoning
Account and opportunity assessments retain qualification checks and their results, disqualifiers, counterevidence, triggers, working hypotheses, confidence, freshness, policy version, assessor and reviewer's decision. Eligibility comes before scoring: a disqualified record is not scored. Later assessments supersede earlier ones while retaining why the judgment changed.
Weekly review and calibration exports are read-only views. They preserve the unit of analysis, coverage, stale or unknown evidence, queue movement, outcomes and governing policy versions. They are not a second editable store. Fit criteria, weights, source hierarchies and outreach/review policies are independently versioned normative material; assessments name the version they used. Reusable reconciliation and export procedures have their own homes too.
Email, call, meeting and research content can be kept with its source, freshness and permitted surrounding relationships. Sending mail and other outside effects stay with their providers. A proposed next action remains commercial context until an explicit command creates work. Raise a chat conversation at a named point where people need to coordinate or decide, not for every event.
Work starts deliberately and ends with acceptance
A command with unambiguous permission, scope and destination turns conversation into work. Otherwise retain a proposal, backlog entry or question for its owner. One item represents one independently assignable and acceptable responsibility. Work nests to any depth: a step that can be assigned and accepted on its own is a child work item, while a condition its parent must meet before closing is a checklist requirement attested on the parent. Reuse an existing item only when the match is exact and unique; a similar title or linked thread is insufficient. A correction identifies the exact item when several are linked.
The actor who created the work is its creator. Keep the original speaker and message as source references, not as the creator or a delegation of permission. The record holds a short responsibility, acceptance conditions and exact conversation references rather than a copied transcript. A comment and a status change are separate commands. Each change records the actual actor, represented party or role, and work item or attempt.
Unstarted work can move to a verified successor or be revised. Active work must be fenced and explicitly transferred and reconciled. Completed work keeps its original actor and acceptance; neither it nor an outside committed effect is rewound. A policy permitting one active attempt requires concurrency-safe enforcement. Work reservations and usage grant no spending permission and replace no payment record.
Each recurring occurrence is a separate item linked to its Schedule, with its own assignee, outcome and history. Cross-team work stays scoped to its topic and creates no overall parent, council or transferred permission. Each party accepts its own responsibility independently.
Goals trace to a named person's decision and conditions agreed before work begins. Agents can propose and act within that authority, while the record preserves both the deciding person and acting agent. Goal satisfaction requires independent verification of those conditions; finishing its tasks is insufficient. Adding an agent to an organisation is a separate constitutional act, not a side effect of creating work or a contact.
See domain extension, effects and scheduling, Radar and the planned human-only journey. Tests must exercise the domain through the public SDK and interfaces.

Concepts
Weave's model connects typed, revisioned records through relations with their own identity and history. An installed domain defines what those records mean and which operations can change them. This chapter explains the contracts an interface, domain or adapter must preserve. Weave's runtime is not implemented yet.
Consider an investigation of a customer's failed export. Its trace, assignment, review and acceptance need to stay connected without becoming one task status. The product walkthrough follows that work from the participants' perspective.
The core knows a few kinds of thing: records with owned fields and independent state axes, relations with named slots, the definitions that govern both, operations and each act that runs one, and the four outcomes an act ends in. People, agents and organisations are records whose definitions let them act or be acted for, and relations and acts are records too, so everything Weave keeps forms one graph. Every business meaning, from an account to a work item, is a domain installed on top (Extending Weave).
In Weave's design, the primitive beneath these records is the object. A person, an agent, a piece of work, a relationship, a decision and a guard are each an object, and only the schemas and transitions authored through the SDK say what an object is and where it goes. This carries the rule that the engine has no root class one level further down: actor, record and relation are not kernel kinds either. “Record” stays the word people and this guide use for what Weave keeps; the object is what the kernel knows. An object's state is its readable value as its schema defines it, so its versions and the history of how it changed carry everything else: what a reader saw, what a decision rested on and what a pointer names.
Every object is public, private or protected, as fundamentally as it has an identity. That property belongs to the object, and enforcing it is the work of a guard, which is itself an object, defined a certain way and invoked a certain way. A guard invoked on a read is the access and sandboxing principle, and both federation and Pale's sandbox follow from it. Because every read crosses a guard, the cost of reading is real and cannot be designed away, only placed (queries). What protected is relative to is still being decided.
Actions are what happen to objects, and keeping them separate matters. Creating, reading, updating and deleting is the one primitive action, and it can act on any object, whether that object plays the part of an actor, a record or a relation. Not every action is a decision: appending a comment is a create and nothing more. A guard and a transition are each a decision followed by one of those actions, and they serve the same purpose from two sides. A guard decides in order to prevent something; a transition decides in order to optimise the order in which things execute. Every decision is an object and is always kept, read decisions included, because a read decision records what a later decision was based on, and the two together answer whether that basis has changed. Composition goes as deep as authors take the SDK and their schemas: a guard can compose a transition and a guard, and a transition can compose a guard and a transition.
A composition may cycle only when time or an event drives each turn, so a watch that re-arms itself or a retry after a delay is a new execution, never a loop inside one. That makes time a primitive of execution: guards and transitions need a clock and a watchdog while they run. Three clocks stay apart, because confusing them is the classic bug of distributed systems: wall-clock time for deadlines, schedules and expiry; monotonic time for a running budget, which must never jump when someone sets the wall clock; and logical or hybrid time for ordering across instances, which share no clock.
Records
A record carries its stable semantic identity, owning instance, exact definition and policy versions, revision, state, attributes, source and history, together with disclosure and retention limits. Its semantic identity is independent of its database row ID; no public interface exposes the row ID. People, configured agents, tools, organisations and other collections of actors, services, applications, accounts, evidence, goals, work items and schedules use this shared model. Their definitions give them different meaning, and the engine has no root class for any of them. “Entity” and “node” describe how a record is being considered, not another stored class. Each change keeps the acting record, the policy versions and the permission reference it was admitted under.
State can have several independent axes. The investigation can have an accepted result while a related message change remains open. A domain may also declare a transition that changes several axes together when their shared conditions pass.
Identify which system can change each field and where a reader gets its current value.
Kind of field	Meaning	
State held in Weave	The owner has made Weave responsible for this state	
Copy or computed view	Weave reads another source to show the field	
Organisation rules	The organisation's owner supplies structural roles, grants or bindings	
Foreign reference	Weave points to information held elsewhere	
For example, Weave could own the investigation's acceptance but hold only a reference to the customer's trace. Delegating a field to Weave identifies its allowed values, source, consent, retention, conflict handling, degraded behaviour and eventual removal from service. Before delegation, a missing field is not a gap the engine must fill.
A copy keeps its owner, source instance and record, source version, observation time, freshness, permitted access, purpose and model-use limits. It also names who resolves conflicts and what happens when access is revoked or the source is retired. The captured source position is called its source frontier. Context derived by another service remains distinguishable from a direct source copy. Legal and data owners supply the rights the engine enforces; storing a fact creates none.
Deletion follows the source owner's policy. An authorised deletion or suppression request affects only the matching copy, with a minimal non-content reference and deletion receipt kept where required. Replaying that receipt makes no further change. Old information or a record missing from a synchronisation result calls for review; neither is permission to delete it, and neither is a task, a workflow or a passing date. Weave never deletes copied content on its own initiative: stale, conflicting or withdrawn source state creates review work and blocks anything destructive.
Acting is a capability, not a kind
A record can act when the operation definition permits it. A person can be the subject of a contact update and the actor accepting an investigation. An agent can investigate or request a change concerning itself where the rules allow it. The engine does not need a separate class of actors.
Every command identifies the actual acting record. The service sending the request, the party it represents, the role it uses and the assignee can all differ. A service submitting an investigator’s result must identify itself and show that it may act for that investigator.
Keep these facts separate: what a record can do, its role and who occupies it, its assigned work, whom it acts for, its software account, whose data the act concerns, who holds the credential and who actually acted. The actual actor needs its own admitted evidence. It is never inferred from a machine, a label or a missing agent attribution.
A principal can be seen two ways, and both hold. Every record that can stand in the world, holding an identity, history, relationships and grants and answering for its own conduct, is a principal: a person, an agent, an organisation or a client organisation. Within one act, the principal is the party the act is for, whose interest it serves and who owns its acceptance. The second view is the first seen through one relation, acting for someone, and that relation's definition decides who may fill each end, and the engine enforces whatever it declares. The rules in the rest of this paragraph are the ones a domain for an organisation of people and agents declares, commercial-work among them. A person acts and can be acted for. An agent acts but is never the principal of an act. An organisation is acted for and acts only through a seat that a person or an agent fills. A tool or service carries or performs an act and is never acted for. A seat is an organisation's position, occupied by a person or an agent; it is a relation, not a kind of record.
Every chain of acting for ends at a person or an organisation. An agent that hands work to another agent is recorded as an intermediary, and the work stays for the same principal. In one act an agent may do only what both its own grants and its principal's delegation allow, and what it learns from a refusal cannot exceed what its principal could see. The agent answers for its conduct within its grant; the principal answers for the outcome and owns acceptance. Who created or configured an agent is a separate relation from whom it acts for, so making an agent gives no claim to be its principal.
A configured agent is one record with one identity and one history, whichever host runs it and whichever model it runs on. The harness host that ran an act and the model it ran on are separate bindings recorded with the act beside the acting record: they say how the act was performed, not who performed it. No host is privileged. Any configured agent, on any accepted host and model, reads and writes the same records, Radar included, under the same checks. Changing the host or the model creates no new agent, moves no history and widens no grant.
No command is anonymous to the record model. If agent attribution is absent, keep the credentialed session that issued the change. A default “human” label does not establish that a person performed it. An unobserved origin or actor stays unobserved. A tool definition is distinct from an invocation, and assigning work does not create a permanent agent.
Assignment gives responsibility, not permission. Membership does not automatically grant record access. A contact is not automatically a software user. These distinctions allow a person to hand work to an agent without giving it all their access, and to remain in relationship history after their own software access ends.
A commercial account, legal entity, data controller, organisation, workspace, community, principal, provider and deployment also remain distinct, even when their names match. An outside client does not become a child unit of its service provider or expose its internal organisation. Access belongs to a named acting record at a stated scope; a shared login cannot stand in for that actor. A trusted-context profile must state the privacy limits it has actually proved.
Bind outside identities explicitly
An identity binding names its issuer, instance, subject, scope, source and validity. Matching names, email addresses, domains or keys never joins records owned by different parties. A binding already accepted by one owner may follow its existing permitted relations, but cannot invent a missing relation.
A chat key reaches a Weave actor only through an accepted, revocable binding. A record may have no binding, several bindings or a stale binding without changing its owner. Membership, role occupancy, assignment, software access and permission remain separate relationships. See sign-in and access.
Relations are records
A relation has its own identity, definition, revisions, state, policy, source, validity and history. Named participant slots describe what it connects. A relation can involve more than two records; its definition sets allowed definitions or capabilities, cardinality, ordering, uniqueness and whether a participant may belong to another instance. It also declares attributes, independent state axes, operations and access rules.
An assignment might connect the investigation, assignee and role for a stated period. A later assignment involving those same participants is a different relation. A review relation connects the result to its authorised reviewer. A decision can involve several participants, and whether each one decides or is only informed is a property of that participant's slot on the decision, not a rule for the whole organisation. Two equal partners can each decide one matter and only be informed of another. Relations can receive comments and evidence, be superseded or revoked, become the subject of an operation and participate in another relation. Slot names such as dependent and prerequisite carry meaning that a bare arrow cannot.
Transaction time records when Weave learned a fact; effective time records when the fact applies. Weave’s recording history supplies the former, so a caller’s backdated effective date cannot rewrite when the assertion arrived. Binary edges can represent two-participant relations efficiently. A relation among three or more participants can also be stored through binary structures, provided the relation record keeps its own identity and joint meaning. Splitting a multi-participant rule into pairs, or checking each pair separately, can lose constraints that apply to the whole group.
Operations have seven roles
An operation declares which roles it needs. These are not seven mandatory fields on every request.
Role	Meaning	Example: accepting the investigation	
WHO	Acting record, or records where the definition allows several, and any admitted representation	The authorised reviewer	
WHAT	Subject of the operation	The investigation	
HOW	Capability and the provider that binding policy resolves for it, if required	No outside provider is needed	
WHERE	Scope or destination	The owning instance and permitted work	
WHY	Causal references supplied by the caller	The submitted result and prior context	
WHEN	Relevant validity, schedule, observation or execution-time constraints, distinct from a revision	The conditions for this decision	
Δ	Requested change; absent for a read	Accept the named result	
The operation definition makes a role required, optional, plural, forbidden or derived. The runtime adds the command identity, evaluated transition, resulting revisions and commit receipt after the transaction commits and independent read-back confirms it. A caller supplies permitted causal references but cannot forge that appended history. A transition is started by a command, by a schedule coming due or by a reaction the domain declares to a committed occurrence; all three pass the same guards, and none needs an agent to start it.
A comment may require WHO, WHAT, WHY, WHEN and Δ while forbidding an outside provider. An effect may need all seven roles; a query uses its declared actor, subject and scope without a change. These are separate operation definitions composed from shared machinery, not seven schemas or a universal request full of nullable fields.
Caller-supplied causal parents must identify occurrences the engine has already admitted. A later outside effect adds the provider's own result through a separate reconciliation; it cannot rewrite the original commit's history. Weave owns its commands, transitions, revisions and results. An orchestration service owns its own admission and execution history; the two link exact occurrences without copying either history. Each service owns a different fact about the same occurrence; neither keeps a competing causal graph.
Every command ends in one of four outcomes
Outcome	What happened	What the caller does next	
Rejected(Refusal)	A required condition failed and the requested change did not happen	Supply the missing material or permission, or resolve the other failed check, then send a new command	
Conflict(Conflict)	A revision or dependency changed	Read the current state and reconsider the request	
Committed(CommitReceipt)	The named transaction committed and read-back confirmed it	Use the recorded result and new revisions	
CommitUnknown(ReconciliationHandle)	The caller cannot yet establish whether the command committed	Look up the outcome using the original command identity before retrying	
Every interface preserves all four outcomes. It must not reduce them to a boolean or a generic success-or-error result: a refusal, a conflict and an unknown commit require different next actions.
Replay identity pairs a selector, made of the destination instance, acting identity, operation and a command key the caller supplies, with a digest of the command that must match. If a reply goes missing, use that identity to recover the result. Every outcome is final for its key: repeating the same request returns the original outcome, a refusal included, without deciding again or accepting twice. Trying again after a refusal, or editing a command, needs a new key. The store gives the full rule.
A fault inside Weave before anything is saved produces no outcome and leaves the key unused; the store explains why this is not a fifth outcome.
Important

A CommitReceipt proves only that the named Weave transaction committed and independent read-back confirmed it. It does not prove message delivery, an outside effect, another party's acceptance, goal satisfaction or Pale settlement. Each needs evidence from the system or person responsible for it. A client that decodes a Committed outcome from a reply holds a CommitReport: a report of the receipt that it confirms by reading back, never the receipt itself.
The implementation must keep CommitReceipt fields private and provide no public constructor, deserialisation, default value or conversion from another type. Only the module that runs the commit and its independent read-back may create one. Persisted receipt data and decoded reports cannot construct that proof type. These are requirements for the runtime still to be built.
Return to the investigation review for the practical difference between submission, acceptance and the customer's outcome.
Protect the decision through commit
Accepting work can depend on the reviewer's current authority, an evidence relation and the absence of a blocker. Checking only the work item's revision will miss a blocker added after validation.
Every outside fact the decision needs is gathered before the transaction begins and passed in as a value. The transaction handle must reach only Weave's store, and the types must enforce it: code that calls a provider, another instance or any other outside service from inside a decision must not compile. A slow or failing outside service then never holds a transaction open.
The application must protect every record and query result that affects the decision until commit. This read set includes policies, relationships and checks for absence. A read frontier identifies the captured state against which a dependency was checked. If someone adds a blocker, the command must conflict even when no previously read row changed.
The locking and isolation mechanism still needs implementation and testing. A transactional database alone does not establish that these checks work.
Within the transaction, record changes, history, commit receipt data and secret-free outbox commit together. A later read confirms the named commit. Queues and wake notifications prompt work or recovery; the database remains the source of truth.
An outside effect or a change in another instance happens separately and needs reconciliation. A larger activity is a resumable sequence of commands, each with its own outcome. Clients cannot submit arbitrary transaction scripts that bypass these checks.
Three kinds of change have separate writers
Change	Who writes it	Effect	
Ordinary data	Authorised people or software callers	Changes comments, assessments and work through guarded commands; nothing is recompiled	
Domain definitions	The domain owner	Installs a new immutable version; existing records change version only through explicit adoption	
Managed constitution	The organisation's owner	Supplies authorised roles, grants and bindings through a checked, staged change	
A record can contain fields managed by different writers, as long as their field sets do not overlap. A domain definition cannot create authority, and a work update cannot overwrite the organisation's constitution. Optional Pale admission still leaves Weave's local checks in place.
A managed change proceeds through capture, compilation, materialisation and confirmation by read-back before activation. Partial materialisation is not active configuration. Revocation stops new use under the applicable rules while earlier evidence retains its attribution. There is no second Weave workspace or desired-state database, and no shared editable blob spanning the three writers.
Continue to Extending Weave for declaring these rules, or return to Weave for the application layers.

Shared contract design
Weave defines each command, query and occurrence shape at its producing layer. This directory will hold generated schemas, manifests, language types and conformance fixtures, under Apache-2.0 with their own LICENSE and NOTICE when the first exists. Do not create a second handwritten semantic model here.
The following design notes describe what the producing implementation must establish. They are not released wire schemas, supported endpoints or proof of a working connector:
Committed occurrences and Pale: identity, causal parents, delivery and independent settlement.
Publication facts: exact permitted fields, source revisions and refusal before a publisher freezes its input.
Publish versioned shapes and positive/negative consumer cases as their native semantics are implemented and proved. A consumer pins that publication separately from enabling the live integration. Generated projections must preserve variants, payloads, errors and uncertainty; decoding a shape never grants permission to use it.
So that clients need compute nothing, every command answer carries the server-held command digest and a recovery instruction (look up, resend allowed or do not resend), and whether a route permits an exact resend is contract data per route and caller. The lookup by identity still needs three answers designed: an identity the server has never seen, how long an identity is kept, and a lookup answered after a restore.

Committed occurrences and Pale
This is Weave's design for publishing its own committed facts to Pale. The exact wire schema, signing profile and joint settlement format still require implementation and qualification by both owners. Compiling the crates or reading this description does not establish a supported connector.
One request through Pale and back
Take an investigation of a customer's failed export. Someone creates it in Weave, assigns it and links the request, and Weave commits the change together with its outgoing occurrence. The publisher delivers the reference. Pale reads the committed occurrence, checks that the work is permitted and chooses the agent, model, tool or machine. The executor's result comes back for that investigation and that attempt. A reviewer then accepts, rejects or reopens the investigation through a separate Weave command. If the investigation changed during the run, or a blocker appeared after the reviewer's check, the command conflicts and the result waits for a fresh decision. The sections below say what each product records and checks.
Each owner records its part
Weave owns semantic commands, record and relation transitions, organisational causal links and commit receipts. Pale owns admitted operations, leases, execution history, constitutional consequences and its journal. Neither copies the other's causal body or infers settlement from delivery.
For a command originating in Pale, Pale allocates its operation coordinate before invoking Weave. Weave records that immutable causal parent and returns its own occurrence coordinate. Pale links the result to its original operation. For a change originating in Weave, Pale records the Weave coordinate when reconciling the occurrence; Weave makes no circular update merely to acknowledge that Pale saw it.
An occurrence identifies the origin instance, incarnation or producer epoch, immutable occurrence ID and canonical content digest. Its committed actor, trigger and workflow references are preserved. Retries retain the coordinate; changed bytes under that coordinate conflict. A new delegated parent must be an actual Weave transaction, never a record fabricated by integration configuration.
Publication and recovery
The Weave commit writes its secret-free outbox entry atomically with history and result. The publisher sends a bounded reference through Pale's event admission and keeps its own delivery and recovery state. It selects no agent, model, tool or machine. A notification, acknowledgement or delivered occurrence grants no permission and proves no consumer action.
Consumers verify source identity, incarnation, digest, ordering and gaps under their pinned contract, then read back the exact committed occurrence through an authorised route. Missing native evidence leaves the outcome unresolved. A later record revision cannot replace the original occurrence's result.
When a Pale-originated command's reply is lost, a matching committed occurrence plus native read-back can supply its result to the original Pale operation. Exact replay must leave one command, transition and outbox occurrence, even after a later permitted edit. A genuine result for another command or causal parent cannot settle the original operation. A separately admitted Weave-originated event needs no return mutation just to acknowledge it.
What Weave checks on a Pale-controlled command
The enabled sign-in profile validates issuer, audience, world, instance, actual actor, operation and target, permission reference, expected revisions, purpose and limits, expiry and revocation, idempotency and causation. Weave then checks its domain rules and protected read set. Pale's approval cannot bypass local consistency, and Weave does not replay Pale's entire constitutional graph.
A fact read from Weave can inform another system's declared input; it cannot create that system's principal, delegation, permission, provider or machine binding. Managed fields have a separate writer and staged activation, as described in Concepts.
A child result is evidence for a parent decision
An engineering result returned through Pale binds the originating Weave publication, admitted handoff and exact execution attempt to the executor's committed outcome. Acceptance, rejection or reopening is a separate authorised command against the current Weave parent revision. A merge is not business acceptance.
If the parent changes while the child runs or between validation and commit, retain the child result and require a fresh decision. An optional terminal context-episode reference must match the same attempt and handoff. Weave can consider the exact executor result independently of that episode's closure or expiry; the parent command leaves the episode unchanged. Recover a committed parent disposition by its original command identity without adding another transition.
The Pale acceptance cases specify lost replies, mismatched references, independent closure, parent races and replay. Pale owns its own dispatch, context-admission and execution-replacement cases.

Publication facts
This design describes Weave's half of a publisher reading selected facts. It is not a released wire format or an implemented Weave provider. The types Gazette already has for acquiring facts do not by themselves establish this provider or allow external facts into deterministic compilation.
Read an exact permitted field
A response must identify subject, record and field, owning instance and owner, delegated field responsibility, permitted-use references, exact revision or source frontier, observation time and freshness. Resolve only explicitly selected fields under the caller's current access and purpose. A display name cannot create a principal or change who owns publication rights.
The acquisition boundary resolves and freezes the requested values and their source evidence before compilation. A set of successful reads is not an atomic cross-record snapshot unless the provider contract and acquisition prove one. Templates cannot perform live reads or silently fall back to an older local value. Installing Weave does not replace local input selections.
Refuse without substituting a value
Gazette's current ExternalFacts port uses these UnavailableKind outcomes:
Outcome	Meaning at the caller boundary	
Unconfigured	No provider was selected for this binding	
Unsupported	The provider cannot supply the request	
Missing	No current value is available	
Stale	The selected value fails the caller's freshness policy	
Revoked	The owner revoked the value or access	
Unauthorized	The caller may not acquire the selected value	
The error identifies the exact failed request item and returns no partial snapshot. None of these outcomes grants retry, fallback or publication permission. Weave's richer state may also distinguish conflicting or deleted source records, but those are not current Gazette enum variants. The provider mapping must preserve the explanation and choose an explicit supported outcome, or require a reviewed contract extension; it cannot silently invent a new variant or collapse conflict into success.
Gazette currently projects an existing principal's display name and preserves opaque provider source and revision references. Its configuration binding is not a Weave address or record identity. The adapter translates the complete request and response, and Gazette checks exact membership before freezing the capture. Extending the target set, verifying freshness, or claiming snapshot coherence requires the corresponding owner contract and tests.
Publication remains the publisher's act
Weave supplies facts, not permission to publish them. Gazette owns input capture, compilation and release; its workspace owns source selections, composition, placement, domains, routes, theme and overrides. Its registry and release journal are not a second editable Weave record store.
A person or Pale can run Gazette over local or Weave input. Gazette owns that four-case caller/input matrix and its conformance tests. An optional Radar workflow may lead to investigation, drafting and review before ordinary Gazette build and release steps; the approved draft, orchestration operation and publication release remain distinct records. Direct publication input does not require that workflow or a running Pale.

The crates
Weave is a Rust workspace of layers, with dependencies pointing toward the core (how a command runs through them). Six workspace members exist today and each holds a module comment that states its place; none yet holds behaviour. Every other crate arrives with its first real operation and test, and is added to the dependency graph in the architecture test in the same change. This page keeps what each planned crate is for, what it builds on and the rule it must keep, so the rule returns with the crate.
The crates that exist
Crate	What it is for	Builds on	
weave-core	Shared meaning: records, relationships, definitions, operations and transitions; identity, capabilities, permission, time, source, revisions and where things came from; and the pure decision over an installed operation with its plain results (the plan, Refusal, Conflict, the reconciliation handle). Business families and infrastructure stay out.	Nothing	
weave-authoring	The builders with which a domain defines its world as inert, digest-bound data. A domain built here reaches records, definitions and operations, never the ports or stores that run them.	weave-core	
weave-ports	The narrow contracts between decisions and infrastructure: storage, object storage, cache, wake, queue, search, clock, identity, secrets, observability, effects and event publication. Concrete providers stay outside.	weave-core	
weave-application	The use-case layer, where a command is checked, committed and read back. It owns the four command outcomes and is the only place a CommitReceipt is created.	weave-core, weave-ports	
weave-postgres	The canonical store of an instance on PostgreSQL, the store the first vertical proves. Record changes, history, command results and the secret-free outbox commit together. The business application reaches it only through the port.	weave-core, weave-ports	
weave-repository-quality	The home of the architecture test, which checks every other crate against this layering and the source rules. It holds no code of its own.	Nothing	
The core's intended decision is a non-async function with no ports: decide(operation, command, read set, decision instant) -> Result<Plan, Refusal>. The application derives the read set, loads it under protection, reads the instant through the clock port, calls the decision and commits its plan. The application's use cases cover definitions, checks, permission, commands, queries and transitions, and coordinate capabilities, managed rules, consequences, schedules, lineage, commits, outbox, reconciliation, recovery, schema evolution and presentation through ports. CommitReceipt has private fields and no public constructor, decoding, default or conversion from another type, so the facade and interfaces can read a receipt but never build one, and the store adapters have no dependency on the application.

Mechanics, facade and domain
Crate	What it is for	Builds on, and what builds on it

It arrives when graph mechanics first do.	Builds on no Weave crate; weave-application and weave-host build on it.

Adapters
Each adapter implements one port, builds on weave-core and weave-ports, and is composed by weave-server; weave-host also uses the clock, observability and secrets adapters.
Crate	What it is for, and the rule it keeps	
weave-cache	Rebuildable caches that speed up reads. A cache never owns records, permissions or history. No cache technology is selected.	
weave-clock	Clock observations for captured operation and schedule inputs. Time is explicit evidence, never a substitute for a record revision.
