weave-secrets	Resolution of a secret reference at the edge of an instance. Configuration holds references; key bytes stay out of records, outbox entries, logs and generated contracts.	
weave-wake	Notifications and bounded recovery prompts that tell a consumer to look again. A notification requests canonical read-back and never establishes that a record changed or work was accepted.	
With weave-postgres these are the twelve adapters that weave-server composes. The SQLite store adapter is still to be added.
Interfaces
Every interface builds on the weave facade, with no other Weave crate building on it, except where noted. Protocol access never bypasses the facade or adds permission.
Crate	What it is for, and the rule it keeps	
weave-rest	Semantic commands and narrow reads. It preserves acting identity, permission, revisions, all four outcomes and recovery. weave-server composes it with GraphQL.	
weave-graphql	Rich reads generated from installed definitions. A resolver owns no separate traversal, ranking, disclosure or pagination rules; all come from the shared query model. weave-server composes it.	
weave-mcp	A projection of the operations this protocol can faithfully represent.	
weave-acp	A projection for clients that speak ACP. Request cancellation cannot roll back an outside effect; unsupported capabilities remain explicit.	
weave-a2a	A projection for agents that speak A2A. Protocol tasks and artifacts become Weave records only through explicit commands under local rules.	
weave-cli	The command line, for authoring, operation, diagnostics and recovery.	
weave-server	The service of one instance: it composes the facade, the REST and GraphQL interfaces, the twelve adapters, schedules and the outbox. No other Weave crate builds on it.	
weave-host	The lifecycle host, for provisioning, upgrading, backing up, restoring and retiring instances. It builds on weave-ports, weave-kernel, weave-clock, weave-observability and weave-secrets, and may not depend on the business application, the facade, the commercial-work domain or the business storage adapters (weave-postgres, weave-search, weave-cache and both object-storage adapters).	
Integrations
Each builds on the weave facade, with no other Weave crate building on it. No mail, calendar, model or repository provider is selected.
Crate	What it is for, and the rule it keeps	
weave-pale	How Weave takes part in a Pale deployment: it publishes committed occurrences to Pale, with delivery and recovery. Pale's own reader and command caller live in Pale's repository, and neither half of the seam selects the other's permissions. See the Pale integration.	
weave-buzz	How Weave meets Buzz, the conversation surface: commands arrive from chat and permitted cards go back through the facade. Signed events resolve an exact actor and command; message delivery is a separate outcome. See the Buzz integration.	
weave-local-provider	The stand-in provider for the first complete service: a deterministic external-effect provider with an inspectable sink, so no live mail or calendar account is needed. It can produce rejection, duplicates, lost replies and unknown outcomes on demand, so recovery can be tested.	
weave-mail	The mail-provider family, as separately deployable packages. Native clients and credentials stay here once selected; the core keeps generic intents and independently verified results.	
weave-calendar	The calendar-provider family, as separately deployable packages. A provider binding selects no account or permission.	
weave-repository	The repository-provider family, for local Git or hosted repositories. A file write, a commit and a remote publication remain different effects.	
weave-model	The optional model-provider family: a Weave instance may call a model only behind explicit caller permission and limits. No model, catalogue, provider or deployment is selected.	
Tools
Neither builds on a Weave crate and no Weave crate builds on either.
Crate	What it is for, and the rule it keeps	
weave-contract-codegen	Keeps language bindings following the contracts, each of which has one producer, by generating the projections from the owning declarations. Generated schemas must not become a second handwritten command model.	
weave-release	Assembles a release and the capability evidence for what it contains. Building or checking the workspace does not approve publication, deployment or activation.	
Clients and emitted contracts
Thin remote clients for JavaScript and TypeScript (@rtepl/weave), Python (an RTEPL-namespaced distribution imported as weave) and Go (a module under RTEPL's getHarshOnline organisation) are planned in sdk/js, sdk/python and sdk/go. Each is a client over Weave's public REST and GraphQL contracts. It preserves the acting identity, revisions, all four command outcomes and recovery, and never opens PostgreSQL or embeds another server. Bindings are generated or checked against the producing contract, with shared positive and negative conformance cases, and domain builders must emit the same portable artifact as the reference Rust facade, so none carries a second semantic engine (Extending Weave).
Emitted schemas, manifests and generated language types will live in contracts/generated, and each thin client in its own source home. These are the Apache-2.0 parts of the repository: each brings its own LICENSE and NOTICE when it first exists, under the licence test. No contract has been generated or released yet; a change goes in the declaration at its producing layer, and the output is regenerated rather than maintained by hand.
What the architecture test holds
Inner layers cannot reach outer code, even through test dependencies: core, authoring, the commercial-work domain, kernel, ports and application depend only on what the graph above gives them.
Lifecycle management cannot read business records: the host's forbidden dependencies are listed with it above.
Pure crates stay free of ambient effects. Core, kernel, authoring and the domain may not reach the filesystem, network, environment, clock, randomness or an async runtime, and take no outside dependencies in any declaration (production, build or development).
The application exports no ports or adapters, publicly or through a type alias, and the facade will carry the same rule the day it exists; and protected outcomes (Refusal, CommandOutcome, CommitReceipt) acquire no implicit construction (From, Default or Deserialize as the type requires). A source check proves the refusal with a failing fixture and the permitted form with a passing control.
Production source holds no tests and no unchecked calls (unwrap, expect), and no file reaches 1,500 lines.
Domain and storage cannot gain runtime edges: authoring cannot reach ports, the domain cannot reach the facade, and the store cannot reach the application.

Effects, schedules and artifacts
A Weave transaction records an intent to change something outside the database. A separate provider performs the action, and Weave reconciles the provider's result. A database commit does not prove that mail arrived, a file was stored or another party accepted the work.
Resolve a capability before selecting a provider
ResolveCapability(actor, capability, target, context) returns a provider binding or an explicit denied, ambiguous, unavailable or stale result. The input includes the exact target, operation context, policy version, purpose and disclosure limits, and required freshness. The same mechanism supports messaging, publication, object storage, repository reads, meetings, code execution, models and agents without product-specific branches in the engine.
A provider binding grants no permission beyond what the actor and operation already have. The deployment supplies eligible providers, policy and bindings; an optional Pale workspace may compile those selections. Replacing a provider changes configuration, not the command rules.
Concrete providers live in separately deployable integration packages using the public SDK. They hold credentials and make native calls. Weave keeps secret references and limited result records, and owns capability resolution, effect intents, leases, reconciliation and references to settlement. Mail, calendar and outbound delivery outcomes remain with their providers.
A commit, an effect intent and a delivery attempt have independent states. Lost or duplicated jobs and provider outages cannot lose the original comment or create duplicate work. Fan-out, causal chains and recovery loops have explicit limits.
The first provider is a separately deployed deterministic local test provider with an inspectable sink. It must inject rejection, duplication, lost delivery, unknown outcomes and read-back cases. It demonstrates the contract without pretending to send real mail or requiring live vendor accounts. Live mail and calendars are not first-version prerequisites.
A recurrence creates a separate work item
A durable Schedule record produces a distinct WorkItem for every occurrence, with its own assignment, outcome, attempts and history. Each item links the schedule and policy revision and, where declared, the previous occurrence. One-shot scheduling and a paused service level are different cases.
When an organisation runs agents through Pale, scheduled work that comes due reaches an executor along Weave, then Pale, then execution. Weave owns the schedule, the work record and its own checks; Pale admits the operation and records how the work was carried out, as the occurrence contract describes. A chat runtime or any other executor cannot start scheduled work around that path.
The worker uses narrow store, clock and wake ports. The store retains schedules, commands and causal history. On PostgreSQL, LISTEN/NOTIFY supplies a wake hint; on either database a recovery timer and a bounded leased scan back the hint, so a missed notification cannot lose work that is due. This uses the existing database and a Weave worker rather than adding another scheduling system. Cron or BullMQ could later supply wake adapters only.
Each schedule declares a recovery window, backlog limit and missed-run policy:
Policy	Required result	
catch_up	Create each missed occurrence within the declared limit	
coalesce	Create one occurrence identifying those it covers	
skip	Record which occurrences were skipped	
pause_for_review	Hold the schedule for a decision	
Due-time and cancellation races must use captured clock inputs, command identity, expected revisions and native read-back. Admitting an occurrence is a command whose key comes from the schedule, its revision and the occurrence's nominal time, so a second wake replays the first answer. A wake from another instance uses that instance's occurrence identity in the same way. If Weave faults before the occurrence is saved, the key stays unused, and a later wake within the recovery window can admit the occurrence under the same key. A refused occurrence is recorded with its disposition; trying it again takes a new attempt number in the key and references the refusal. Work due more than a year away, such as a booking made far ahead, starts its eligibility later; it is not a service level falsely marked paused.
Watch deadlines without blocking work
Time spent in a state is a declared rule. Its policy revision supplies the due interval, warning threshold, escalation and conditions. An overrun record identifies the affected work, the applied rule, when it became due, when it was detected and how it was resolved. Repeated scans must not create duplicate overruns; leaving the state resolves the active overrun while retaining its history.
Monitoring and notification failures cannot block a valid transition. They remain visible and recoverable through the same outbox and read-back rules as other effects. Watching can reveal missed obligations or lost value; it cannot guarantee that neither occurs. Any rule that actually prevents a transition belongs among that command's declared guards and authority checks.
Tunable values use policy revisions, independently of the domain's definition version. A rule set may itself be evaluated in an experiment. History must name the rule revision and experiment arm actually used, including a fallback, so later comparisons describe what happened.
Keep each outcome with its decision-maker
A checklist attestation does not prove an audit or outside effect. Completion, disposition, native effect, provider acceptance, consumer acceptance, business acceptance and settlement by an optional orchestrator remain separately attributable. Each can be pending, rejected, deferred, failed, partly settled, conflicting, unknown or a no-op. A duplicate or cancellation is not success. A goal needs its own previously agreed success conditions and independent verification.
Files are managed content or external references
Kind	What Weave holds	
Managed artifact	Content through its selected object-store adapter; digest, media type, size, policy, provider coordinate, custody state and result in the store	
External reference	Owner, instance, object, revision, digest, locator, freshness, use limits and revocation details; the source retains its content and lifecycle	
Capturing an external object creates a new managed snapshot linked to the source. It does not take over the source's rights. Managed content is immutable per revision. The store and object storage share no transaction, so staging, provider finalisation, metadata commit, ambiguous outcomes, orphan cleanup, missing bytes, deletion and recovery need explicit states and independent checks.
Weave owns recovery and provider read-back for managed content. Historical locators must resolve the right revision, and consumption verifies its exact bytes. If revisions share a body, recovery must account for every referring revision. For an external reference, the source owner supplies recovery and evidence under its own retention policy.
The first conformance adapter is a confined local filesystem. It operates from an already-open root, rejects traversal, symlinks and special files, verifies digests, finalises durably and reads back independently. S3-compatible storage is required before claiming hosted support. Its tests cover conditional writes, checksums, multipart upload, versioning, read-back, namespace isolation and deletion. An S3 ETag is not Weave's content digest.
Storage, repositories, document services and transport are different provider families. A file write is not a Git commit, a Git commit is not GitHub publication, a Drive export is not the source document, and a local iCloud write does not prove synchronisation. A transport moves bytes between stores without owning them. Which carrier joins Weave instances, iroh among the candidates, is still being compared; a transport an organisation reaches through Pale stays Pale's.
Erasure removes recoverable content
An authorised erasure deletes or crypto-shreds reconstructable content under Weave's control: current and historical fields, relation properties, managed content, search surfaces, hot views, caches, exports, any future engine-owned embeddings, and eligible backup copies under the retention process. Retain only the minimum non-identifying tombstone, permission reference and erasure result. Historical reads report erased.
Commit records and outbox payloads must already minimise content. Inspect surviving metadata for disclosure as well as reconstruction: a digest of predictable input can still reveal that input. If removing inputs makes replay impossible, state that limit explicitly rather than claiming the result can still be reproduced. Test all copies and recovery paths against the controller’s retention and legal-hold rules so a retained diagnostic or backup cannot silently reconstruct erased data. Other owners confirm erasure of their own content separately.
See store recovery, instance isolation and the planned artifact and privacy cases.

Extending Weave
A domain defines the records, relationships and actions an organisation needs. First-party and adopter domains would use the same public SDK. The SDK is the only way to extend Weave, and a first-party domain gets no power an outside adopter lacks. This chapter explains the extension design through an investigation's acceptance rule. The SDK and Weave's runtime are not implemented, so there are no executable builders or package commands yet.
A domain is declared, compiled and installed
The designed path has three stages: DomainDefinition → ValidatedIR → InstalledDefinition.
Declare the business rules
Typed builders describe record types, fields, relations, operations, state changes and their conditions. Rust is the reference SDK. TypeScript, Python and Go builders would produce the same portable package artifact.
Validate the definition
The compiler primarily validates the surface the domain declares. It checks types, dependencies, permitted effects and whether evaluation will terminate. It rejects invalid or unsupported behaviour before installation. The validated intermediate representation stays private. Validation and ordering precede transactional application, so an invalid definition cannot partly change the store. The validator is typed, with a closed field vocabulary; declared dependencies and explicit precedence determine the order of changes. How installed definitions are cached remains open.
Install a version
The installed definition makes that version available to records and operations. The artifact has a schema version, a canonical form, a digest that identifies its contents and support for signing. A record refers to the version that governed it.
The builders form a closed expression tree; closures are never stored or run later. Authors use builders in ordinary languages, rather than a new source language. Raw artifact JSON is an interchange format, not the intended authoring experience. Later visual or textual tools must emit the same public artifact. The compiler's validated representation, permission plan, query plan, storage plan and hot representation remain private.
One mechanism covers types and subtypes, field constraints, relation cardinality, operation-role constraints, independent lifecycle and other state axes, guards, value-returning derivations, validations, deterministic reactions, effect intents, post-commit observers, evidence, checklists, waiting reasons, service levels, calendars, schedules, permissions, command and presentation descriptors, views, events and reporting dimensions. A transition may change several state axes together when their joint conditions pass.
Express an investigation's acceptance
In the export investigation, supplying a trace and accepting the investigation are separate actions. A commercial-work domain needs to express both:
Declaration	What it expresses	
Work, evidence and participant definitions	The investigation, supplied trace and acting records	
Assignment and review relations	Who owes the result and who can accept it	
Submission operation	Supplies a result without accepting it for the reviewer	
Acceptance operation and guards	Checks that the reviewer may accept the work, that the agreed material is present and that the conditions still hold	
Declared reads	Names the records, relations, policies and absences used by the decision	
Transition and result presentation	Records acceptance, or explains a refusal or conflict	
This example shows the rules a domain would need. The domain defines what acceptance requires. The application protects the decision through commit, and the interface presents its result. A successful response from an outside service cannot cause a provider adapter to insert an acceptance.
Compiled behaviour declares its reads, affected transitions, determinism, purity, permitted effects, captured dependency versions and behaviour version. Guard order is explicit where it affects meaning. These declarations let the runtime detect a new blocker or revoked reviewer authority, as explained in Protect the decision through commit.
Keep evaluation deterministic
Evaluation must be typed, finite and deterministic. It has no ambient access to the network, database, models, clock, randomness, filesystem or secrets. Outside facts enter only as authorised, captured inputs or as later results from the service that handled an effect. This includes clock inputs: the decision uses a captured value from its permitted source, not a caller-selected replacement for the decision’s clock. An action that depends on nondeterministic behaviour produces an effect intent for later execution. Evaluations are auditable, and an unsupported or invalid evaluation is an explicit result.
For example, accepting a trace cannot call a mail provider midway through the database transaction. Acceptance can commit with an outgoing intent; a later attempt records the provider's delivery result. A lost response can then be recovered without pretending that a database commit delivered a message.
Domain authors must declare more than an arbitrary callback would require. In return, the runtime has explicit dependencies and effects to check. Hiding rules in migrations, queue consumers or interface code would bypass those checks.
A domain cannot patch the engine or bring a second semantic engine. Remove a capability the runtime cannot constrain before an effect; detecting the violation afterwards is insufficient. A possible later deterministic WebAssembly boundary would require digest-bound modules, typed inputs and outputs, declared reads and writes, resource limits and the same lack of ambient access. It is not part of the implemented SDK.
Keep a finding distinct from its follow-up
Reviewing an observation needs separate records for the observation, evidence, proposed explanation and review. The writer proposing a finding cannot accept it. Review needs an authorised decision-maker, criteria, evidence and policy version, protected by the same read and revision checks as other commands.
A completed review can find no material change. A run that could not obtain a required source instead records the missing prerequisite. It cannot claim to have ruled out change. Later evidence can support a new review without rewriting the earlier decision or exceeding the source's retention rules.
Accepting a finding does not assign work or deliver a remedy. A separate work-creation command establishes authority and acceptance conditions, then links the result to the finding. Return to Create follow-up deliberately for the participant's decision.
Versions never rewrite history
Each record and relation revision names its immutable definition version and artifact digest. Activating a new version makes it the default for new records. Existing records keep their interpretation.
Suppose a later investigation definition requires another piece of evidence. It cannot retroactively invalidate an earlier acceptance. Moving existing work to that version requires an authorised adoption command checked against the record's expected revision. Mixed versions are normal; adopting many records is a resumable series of commands.
Retiring a version prevents new selection. Its artifact, interpretation and history remain while revisions or receipts refer to it. Definition adoption is separate from storage schema evolution. Neither can silently reinterpret old data.
A new definition version maps the names it changes explicitly. A migration that leaves a record or field out does not delete it: an omitted record stays intact until an authorised lifecycle command ends or deletes it.
Archiving a referenced artifact elsewhere does not remove this retention requirement. Lifecycle is one state axis among several, and constrained values are not database enums. The store keeps universal identities and revisions in normalised tables and declared fields in validated JSONB with declared indexes.
Policy revisions record what actually ran
A domain version defines the meaning and permitted shape of its rules. Tunable values, such as an interval or escalation threshold, belong to separately versioned policy records within that shape. Changing a threshold does not require inventing a new domain version, and a policy cannot change the domain's meaning or exceed its constraints. Both versions remain part of the transition's captured dependencies and history.
A rule set can be the subject of a test or experiment. Record the policy revision and, when applicable, the experiment assignment and arm actually evaluated. If loading an assigned arm fails and an allowed fallback runs, name the fallback and the failure; do not label the resulting transition as execution of the requested arm. Comparing candidate rules requires the same inputs and explicit differences in the rules, with effects confined by the evaluation's authority.
Packages are released on their own
Each domain has its own source and release cycle and depends only on public Weave contracts. The engine depends on no domain and must pass its kernel and application tests with none installed. Package dependencies use exact versions and digests. Conflicting extensions fail; load order cannot determine meaning or widen authority.
The first planned domain is commercial work: accounts, people, relationship contexts, evidence, Radar records, goals, work, comments, artifacts and schedules. It must install and be removable without rebuilding the engine. Its families, commercial cases and work rules live with that package. A second unrelated domain must demonstrate the same extension powers without private engine imports or client-specific branches.
Domain definitions, ordinary data and the organisation's managed constitution have separate writers. Defining an assignment relation does not grant its occupant data access or spending authority. Removing a package cannot discard history still tied to its definitions.
Contracts have one producer
Declare a contract where its meaning is produced. Generate its language forms or test them for conformance; do not maintain another handwritten command model in contracts/. That directory holds emitted schemas, manifests, generated types and conformance material, with design notes clearly distinguished from released wire formats. Variants, payloads, errors and uncertainty must survive every projection. Decoding and permission checks remain separate.
Capability resolution selects replaceable provider packages through the same actor, target, purpose and freshness rules. A binding grants no permission. The deterministic local provider is the first complete contract example; a live vendor is not required to prove it.
Licensing
The engine, application, adapters, interfaces, integrations, first-party domains and Rust SDK use AGPL-3.0-or-later. Emitted contracts, generated types and genuinely thin language bindings use Apache-2.0. A binding that carries Weave's semantic logic is not thin and falls under the AGPL.
An adopter's own systems, configuration and data stay theirs. Alternative terms require a separate agreement with RawThoughts Enterprises Private Limited.
Return to reviewing the investigation for the work these rules protect, or to Weave for the runtime's responsibilities.

Instances
Each organisation would run its own Weave instance, with a separate database, credentials, storage and keys. Organisations could exchange work while keeping their own decisions about what to take on and what to accept. This is the deployment design; Weave's runtime, host applications and exchange protocol are not implemented.
One instance per tenant
An instance could serve one person, a household or a company's members. The same design serves an organisation running its own instance and a shared hosted service: in both, every tenant is its own instance. Shared hosting still gives each tenant a separate server process or container, PostgreSQL database, application role, connection pool, storage and key namespaces. Definitions, recovery and the position reached in its occurrence history belong to that instance too.
A SQLite instance is its own database file, and several PostgreSQL databases may share a cluster. They do not share business tables or cross-tenant foreign keys. Operating a database per instance costs more, but lets a host back up or restore the client and provider separately. Each instance’s record points to the other with an external reference. A relation between two tenants on one cluster uses the same signed external reference and correspondence claim as two instances hosted apart.
Application	Responsibility	
weave-server	One instance's records, commands, queries, schedules and outbox	
weave-host	Provisioning, upgrades, backup, restore and retirement of one or more instances	
The host manages deployment lifecycle without reading business records. Its API has a separate listener or hostname, authentication audience, access checks, logs and rate limits. Tenant routing follows an authenticated binding; a request-body tenant field cannot select another instance.
Its records cover instance identity and incarnation, desired and observed runtime, deployment/database/storage/key/network references, health, readiness, migrations, backup, restore and decommissioning. Docker, Kubernetes, systemd, Terraform, OpenTofu or a managed platform can supply deployment adapters. The host owns the portable lifecycle and its result, not those platforms' implementations. Operating a deployment grants no permission to inspect or change its business records.
A running instance must remain available when its lifecycle manager or Pale is unavailable. Removing it from configuration leaves it in place. Only a caller allowed to retire the instance can start the retirement process, which includes recovery and decommissioning.
An optional controller may declare instances, release versions, bindings, sign-in profiles, domain packages, retention and desired lifecycle. Compiling those declarations has no effects. A separately permitted reconciliation makes the host attempt the change, read the provider back and record its own result. A standalone adopter reaches the same contracts through its controller, CLI or platform tools. Shared infrastructure never merges graphs, permissions, transactions, controllers or data ownership.
Work moves between instances by offer and acceptance
A client asks a provider to investigate a failed export. The provider may refuse, negotiate or take responsibility for it. The client's request and the provider's commitment are separate local records. Reviewing the provider's trace within the provider's own instance cannot accept the result for the client.
The exchange below uses HTTPS for now. The carrier stays provisional until the comparison under Sameness is a claim, never a merge is finished:
Commit the offer at its origin
The origin commits the change and its outgoing occurrence in its own database transaction.
Notify and read back
A signed notification carries the occurrence reference. The destination detects duplicates and retrieves only the source state it is permitted to read.
Decide locally
The destination forms a proposal and decides whether to accept it under its own rules and authority.
Record the destination's responsibility
A local command commits the resulting responsibility and issues the destination's own receipt. Any later result or acceptance follows its own command.
Neither instance writes the other's database or closes the other's work. The service contract describes the request, result, rights, evidence and settlement terms. Provider, consumer and any parent acceptance stay separate.
The directional contract connects independent responsibilities; it creates no parent relationship between the organisations and implies no reverse agreement. The work references both parties' accountability without copying their internal records. It binds an immutable directional service edge, governing instrument and schedule, independent provider and consumer work, handoff and expected revisions, budget boundary, cancellation, termination, dispute, compensation and reopening rules, separate provider/consumer/parent acceptance, and typed references to foreign effects and settlement. Live service work waits until the selected contract's replay and recovery have been proved.
TLS, caller authentication and an occurrence signature answer different questions. Occurrence identity includes the origin instance, origin incarnation or producer epoch, immutable occurrence ID and canonical content digest. A retry keeps that identity. Reusing it with changed bytes must fail, and missed occurrences must be recoverable. An HTTP retry key cannot replace it.
If a notification is lost, the destination would recover the missing occurrence at its origin before deciding whether to accept it. The wire format, proof of the sender’s identity and recovery behaviour still need design and testing. There is no endpoint or deployment recipe to follow yet. For what each participant owes, return to the relationship example.
Sameness is a claim, never a merge
The client and provider may each hold a record for the same person. Matching names, emails or keys are not enough to establish that connection or permit access. A revisioned correspondence claim records how far the connection has been agreed:
Strength	Meaning	
candidate	Someone proposed the correspondence	
locally_accepted	This instance accepted it	
mutually_attested	Both instances attested it	
Each query or operation declares the strength it needs. Even mutually attested records keep their local identity, revisions, rights and retention.
Correspondence between people is separate from identifying a duplicate message or equal file content. Each claim needs its own evidence and has different consequences for deduplication.
The carrier between instances, the exact attestation format and the trust evidence remain design work. Before choosing them, compare CRDTs, torrent content identity, rclone's synchronisation model and iroh under these constraints: local permission and revisions, three correspondence strengths, changed-content rejection, replay, revocation and independently owned retention. A mechanism that establishes equal bytes does not by itself establish the same person or permit a merge.
Weave stands on its own
Weave is designed for direct human and software access without chat or agent orchestration. OIDC or OAuth2 would authenticate people; signed credentials would authenticate workloads. Optional profiles would admit Buzz/Nostr identity bindings or Pale-signed admission.
An explicit no-auth profile would remove the authentication gate. It would still require an acting identity, access checks, guards, revisions and history.
Buzz conversation and Pale federation can carry references without gaining authority over Weave's records. Room or network membership does not admit work. Removing an integration must preserve records and leave uncertain results available for reconciliation.
HTTPS is the provisional first exchange carrier until that comparison is finished. Pale's planned federation between people uses Nostr through the owner's relay; transport between one person's machines remains to be chosen. Buzz uses Nostr for conversation under its own identity and access rules. The signed inner occurrence keeps its identity and owner even if another selected carrier transports it; standalone Weave requires neither Pale nor Buzz.
Continue to command recovery, or return to Weave.

Buzz integration
This planned integration lets Buzz conversation carry explicit Weave commands and display permitted views of work. Buzz owns identities, rooms, membership, messages and delivery evidence. Weave owns its records and commands. This package has no working connector yet.
Use stock Buzz through its published contracts. Weave never writes into Buzz's databases or object storage; it uses Buzz's own commands. What a consumer keeps is a limited reference to a Buzz event, the source position it has read up to and its own resulting state. Its Nostr transport is distinct from Weave's provisional HTTPS exchange between instances and from Pale's private federation transport. Conversation can end entirely in Buzz. Selecting communication does not select Buzz's own agent or workflow runtime to execute Weave work.
Bind the speaker before accepting a command
A Buzz actor is its canonical 32-byte Nostr public key; npub displays the same bytes. Display names and NIP-05 handles are mutable metadata and cannot join identities. The key is not a community, room, relay, device, deployment, session or membership.
An accepted, revocable and revisioned binding connects that key to one Weave record with acting capability and an explicit permission scope. It records the issuer, evidence, validity and revocation. Equal keys across independently admitted graphs establish the same Buzz actor only; they import no roles, membership, history, messages or permission. The binding can follow already permitted local relations but cannot create a missing edge. No Buzz-specific rule belongs in the core. A substitute provider can use its own stable handle and signature verifier under this contract.
A replacement key is a different actor unless the provider proves that the new key succeeds the old one. A later link between the two records the relationship without making them equal. Pairing or remote signing can move one existing identity to another device; it creates no new person and grants no authority.
A record can have no binding, several bindings or a stale one without changing its owner. Every acting person or agent appears individually through its own role presence. An outside contact or a referenced work item creates no software access, internal role or room membership. Keys stay in the provider's secret storage; plans, Git, logs and results contain public identity and references only.
An approval becomes one exact command
When a speaker types “approved,” resolve the key, its permitted scope, one exact action and the current target revision. Ask for clarification if several actions fit and a reply is permitted. Apply all ordinary guards. Record the actual actor in the commit; a refusal leaves work unchanged. The native chat path needs no Pale admission merely because Pale is installed. A deliberately selected Pale-controlled profile additionally requires its signed admission and still applies Weave's own checks.
Unbound identity, ambiguity, stale revision, missing evidence and revoked binding have explicit outcomes. Two rooms approving the same work at the same revision cannot commit twice. Before command admission, a relay outage leaves a visible gap or pending state until the exact signed event is reconciled. After admission, a lost response is recovered by the original command identity.
Retain the Buzz instance, signed event ID, command identity and mapping revision together. A redelivered event reconciles that original command even if the room now points to another work item. Current permission still governs read-back and replies. If the room can no longer receive a response, the outcome remains available to permitted Weave readers.
Chat-to-Weave commands and Weave-to-chat publication have separate contracts. Each identifies participating instances, field and effect limits, mapping version, idempotency, revocation and owner evidence. A room or thread can reference several records and a record can appear in several conversations. Every individual command or placement still resolves to one exact target.
A card is a view
A card shows compact identity, status, accountable role or steward and the next milestone. Expansion reads current Weave state using permitted credentials. A stale card is labelled and cannot authorise a mutation. Omit foreign objects the reader cannot see unless their owner permits an opaque placeholder. Cards create no membership, stewardship, acceptance or permission.
The card contract precedes implementation. It declares field limits, publisher, staleness clock, identity and idempotency, when access is checked, expansion credentials, fan-out limit, milestone presentation and deleted/unknown states. Weave supplies semantic and presentation descriptors; the client renders them.
A comment and its publication have separate results
When a group's declared duties include conversation, each genuine comment, reply, mention or question commits one secret-free placement obligation in the same transaction. It binds the comment revision, placement contract and idempotency coordinate. The obligation can remain unresolved; delivery waits for one permitted placement. An outage leaves the comment committed. Recovery before the transaction finds neither; recovery after it resumes the same obligation. Groups without that duty create none, and routine telemetry stays silent.
Once bound, the publication's audience and room remain fixed. A known room does not prove publication. A retry cannot invent another comment, target or room. Clarifications, refusals and card updates need their own publication permission and must respect current field and disclosure limits independently of the command permission.
An attachment upload is itself disclosure. Verify the room, exact reply anchor and attachment grant before sending bytes. Record upload and event outcomes separately; reconcile a partial upload or a later event failure under the provider's retention rules.
Publication, delivery and reading are different evidence
Milestone	What it establishes	What it does not establish	
Request recorded	One exact intent to publish	That Buzz accepted it	
Relay OK	The relay's disposition for the named event	Storage when the response says duplicate or superseded, fan-out, delivery, display or reading	
Exact-ID read-back	The original signed event was visible to that reader at that recorded point	Current visibility after replacement, deletion or revocation, delivery, or anyone's reading	
Delivery attempt	One recipient or device path was attempted	That it arrived	
Recipient delivery	Evidence that a specified device received it	Display, attention or reading	
Display	A client showed it	Attention or reading	
Own read frontier	One identity synchronised its own reading state	What anyone else read	
Other reader's receipt	A supported and permitted reading report from that reader	A response, work or acceptance	
Response	A reply or reaction referencing the event	Work, an effect or acceptance	
Communication settlement	The declared communication obligations reached their own typed end	Any consequence elsewhere, or acceptance	
No milestone proves work, outside effects or acceptance. A destination's consequence and the initiating owner's acceptance each have their own record. A milestone that Buzz cannot observe stays recorded as unsupported or unknown; it is never inferred from a later one. An observation record proves only that a consumer durably admitted a bounded Buzz reference under its provider, schema, generation and source position. A publication result needs both relay disposition and exact-event read-back, and the read-back is judged under the visibility policy that applies to that reader. A consequence result comes from the owner that performed the requested action. Unsupported or unobserved milestones stay unsupported or unknown.
When the reply is lost, retain publication_pending_reconciliation. Read back the original signed event without signing a fresh one. An affirmative duplicate response can describe an exact prior event or a losing replacement that was not stored. Read visibility and relay disposition therefore remain separate. Distinguish a different current event from an unknown result for the original. Record a permitted read-back of the exact event even while the relay's disposition is still unknown. When visibility or retention limits what can be reconciled, keep each missing milestone explicit. A historical read-back does not prove current visibility after replacement, deletion or revocation, delivery or anyone's reading. A function return, queue acknowledgement, WebSocket frame, reconnect or phone notification proves none of those later steps.
Repair gaps without claiming completeness
A source frontier records how far one subscription has demonstrably read from one source in one provider instance. It may need composite time/event ordering, overlapping reads, duplicate detection, per-room pagination, replacements, deletions and bounded gap repair. Neither a last timestamp nor EOSE proves a complete interval. Repair stays within declared limits, and gaps it cannot close stay visible. On a selected Pale route, connect the proved provider frontier to the matching durable journal admission.
What a reader sees combines their current permission to the room with the proved frontier. Distinguish permitted history, denial, deletion, retention-bound absence, stale synchronisation, known gaps, unsupported evidence and unknown state. Counts, previews and alerts must not leak denied content. A missing polling result does not prove deletion; retain historical observation references only as policy allows. Durable outward event delivery and the selected consumer's admission require their own proof before claiming that conversation reliably triggers another system.
Interrupt only where the duty calls for it
A critical failure follows an explicitly declared escalation relation to its named room under the current generation and publication permission. Ordinary delay queues quietly. The alert uses a protected link; it neither moves the work nor changes membership. Buzz owns publication evidence, while Weave records dereference, acknowledgement, expiry and resolution.
Meaningful progress can appear as natural updates when the group's contract says someone needs it. Raw logs and routine telemetry stay with their owners. Rich mail, call, meeting and research history stays in Weave; a room is raised at a named coordination or decision point. Mail and calendar delivery remains with those providers.
The intended experience includes adding Pale to a community so its configured agents join individually, role-based pickup in threads, /weave commands and calls that bring in the relevant agents. These require provider capability and integration work; they are not available commands. The acceptance cases preserve the approval, disclosure, gap and recovery branches the implementation must pass.

Pale integration
This planned package publishes Weave's committed, secret-free occurrences to Pale and tracks delivery and recovery under the occurrence contract. It chooses no agent, model, tool or machine. Pale's acquisition, query and command caller lives in Pale's own repository; each product uses the other's public contracts and records its own outcomes. Both products must run independently.
Weave reaches Scope, Counsel and Reckon only through Pale when that integration is selected, for the requests Weave's own work makes. Scope reads Weave through Weave's read port, still to be proposed by Scope's and Weave's builders, with Pale or without it, and without Pale it is how an agent reads Weave; Weave itself never calls Scope. Weave contains no built-in model catalogue, model or automatic outbound message. Scope, reading Weave without Pale, may use Counsel's memory host on Scope's side; Weave still calls no model. Direct, permitted reads of exact work, goal, relationship, decision and evidence records can hydrate context without Scope, with required blockers, omissions and budgets explicit.
A source helper reading for a selected Scope request retains the Weave credentials. It returns a revision-bound, secret-free result containing owner and permission reference, source instance and record, revision, observation time, freshness, purpose, model-use limit, revocation coordinates and conflict owner. It returns no credential, credential reference or runtime binding to Scope. Scope separately admits, deduplicates and checks freshness for its own projection; this never becomes a direct Weave-to-Scope connector.
Pale's input acquisition separates request/selection, Weave snapshot/read result, Pale capture, compilation, activation and use. Captured values cannot become “latest” lookups during evaluation or silent stale fallbacks. A result flowing back cannot rewrite the same generation's input; it belongs to a later capture. The caller owns these stages, while Weave owns its local read and command checks.
Each relation exported to Pale must name its one destination graph and edge class. Labels such as owns, parent, inside, reports-to, member, agent or belongs-to cannot be admitted as an unresolved hierarchy. Preserve Weave's edge identities and revisions and distinguish witnessed routes from direct edges. Pale owns the destination graph definitions and their acceptance. A relation read by Pale creates no principal, delegation or permission there.
The acceptance plan covers Weave's half of the seam. Publication of versioned schemas and Pale's consumer pin precede a claim of live interoperability. Reusing neutral source libraries creates no runtime connection or shared lifecycle.

Interfaces, sign-in and access
Weave is designed as a headless backend. People and software use the same commands through REST, GraphQL, SDKs, a command line and the supported agent protocols. There is no browser application in the first version: Weave's runtime supplies the rules, descriptors and components that independently built clients render.
Choose a surface by the job
Surface	Intended use	
REST and JSON	Semantic commands; identity and history; definition and package lifecycle; artifacts; event recovery and reconciliation	
GraphQL	Rich reads generated from installed definitions, through the shared query model	
Rust SDK	In-process access; re-exports the domain authoring builders	
TypeScript, Python and Go SDKs	Typed remote clients over REST and GraphQL, generated or checked against public contracts	
Command line	Authoring, operation, diagnostics and recovery; equivalent journeys must work with ordinary HTTP clients	
Signed webhooks	References that wake a consumer to read the committed occurrence	
MCP, ACP and A2A	The subset each protocol can represent faithfully, enabled by the deployment profile	
Remote SDKs never open the database or embed another runtime. The lifecycle manager, weave-host, has its own REST and SDK surface, separate from the instance service. A later browser, mobile or chat client uses these public contracts with no private write path and no ontology of its own.
REST, GraphQL and the official SDKs together cover the instance service. An authorised agent using REST can use its full surface, because an agent is an acting record like any other and not a lesser actor. Each route preserves actor identity, typed input, purpose, expected revisions, causal parents, all four command outcomes, uncertainty and recovery. Routes exposing the same operation produce the same canonical command and native outcome.
A protocol cannot claim capabilities it cannot express. Keep unsupported, disabled by profile, concealed, unauthorised, invalid, conflict, committed and commit-unknown distinguishable. An A2A task is not automatically a Weave work item; cancelling an ACP request cannot roll back an effect. Importing an A2A artifact requires an explicit Weave command. No interface adds or drops a domain guard. If an adapter cannot preserve a required field or outcome, exclude that operation from the adapter or define a distinct operation with its own approved contract.
Components look the same on every surface
A component is a unit of interface that Weave serves and a host surface renders: a card, a panel, a list or a review prompt. The word micro-frontend means only this. Weave supplies the typed command, query and presentation descriptors and the access-filtered record views that let a host's cards materialise correctly; the host, whether a chat room, a terminal, a web page, a note in a knowledge base or an agent's conversation, owns rendering and interaction. Components are not a separate browser application.
Each component is a window onto a record, never a copy of it. Opening it reads the current state with the reader's permitted credentials. A view distinguishes fresh, stale, denied and unknown state, keeps required relations visible, and applies the same checks to nested and reverse reads, counts, search and artifacts as any other query. A stale component says so and cannot authorise a change.
The same records and checks apply on every surface. A component in a chat room and the same component in a terminal show the same record under the same access rules, and a command sent from either produces the same canonical command and the same four outcomes. A panel can show several exact related records without inventing a primary account for convenience. Cards and layouts are views, not new record types or editable copies of truth. A renderer can attest that an authenticated actor submitted an intent; the application decides whether it commits. Buzz integration applies this contract to chat cards.
Four sign-in profiles feed one actor model
Profile	How the caller is identified	
Standalone	OIDC or OAuth2 for people; signed credentials for workloads	
Buzz identity	Weave verifies the Nostr proof and resolves an accepted, revocable key-to-actor binding	
Pale-controlled	An explicitly enabled profile accepts Pale's signed, bounded statement admitting the operation	
Authentication off	No authentication gate; the caller still supplies its durable acting identity	
Authentication off is a convenience for a selected local or trusted setup. It changes no operation typing, access rule, guard, revision check, history, commit record or effect rule. Weave records the active profile. There is no anonymous record model or separate test execution path.
Access is decided inside Weave
The typed policy evaluates principal, actor, action, resource, context, scopes and purpose against exact policy and definition versions and the captured read frontier. Scoped role occupancy is a first-class way to write, administer and explain that policy; it compiles into the same model rather than creating another permission store.
An embedded evaluator, preflight tool, simulation or policy projection may assist the check. It must bind the exact policy and definition digests and read frontier. Cedar, OpenFGA or OPA are possible evaluator styles, not selected owners of permission. No outside evaluator may use fresher facts than Weave or widen its rules. An asynchronous answer cannot allow a write when Weave cannot confirm the permission at commit.
Admitting a record into the graph decides what the graph may contain. It does not let every reader see every record. Access limits apply separately to records, fields and relations, for each acting person, agent or application.
The engine enforces controller, scope, purpose, disclosure, retention and model-use limits supplied by their owners. Domains define the vocabulary and policy. An orchestration service, data-loss-prevention system or legal owner can supply evidence or narrow those limits; none can widen them through an adapter. A domain and operation name the deciding person or quorum independently of seniority, family or organisational shape.
Membership is a relationship, not access. Access belongs to an identified actor within the permitted scope. A shared account or login never substitutes for the actual actor.
Revocation freezes uncertain work
Revocation immediately blocks new starts. Open or uncertain work is frozen for attention: an unconfirmed effect is not retried, and responsibility does not silently fall to someone else. A permitted transition must reassign, cancel or reconcile it. Completed work retains its attribution and evidence. A revoked caller can still replay an earlier command to learn its outcome, without seeing any content its access no longer covers.
See command recovery for commit checks and queries for access checks that cover filtering, traversal and information revealed by a result.

Weave
Agents decide far more often than people, so by the time one writes, what it read has usually changed. Weave's design makes a read say what else to read, and a write is tried for what it affects before it is committed alone, made together with others or proposed to the owners. Weave keeps the records an organisation's people and agents work from, so that whoever comes next, a person or an agent, picks up the story from what was kept rather than from a long conversation. It is a headless backend that does the jobs of a work tracker and a relationship manager together, standing on its own; other products, such as Pale, Scope and Gazette, return to its records. Accounts, commitments, evidence, goals and work share a record model, so a relationship can be followed through to what was promised, supplied and accepted, and parent and child work, comments and their relationships are records with their own history. Each actor uses its own identity and permission. The components Weave serves look the same on every host surface. An optional Pale integration constitutes roles and coordinates agents while Weave keeps the organisation's records.
The repository README records what is built. These chapters describe the design, rather than an installation recipe for a working service. Use them to trace a command, design a domain or work out what an integration owns. For the participants' experience, start with From a request to accepted work.
Keep submission and acceptance separate
An agent supplies a trace for a customer's failed export. The person named to review the investigation decides whether it answers the question. The design has a command for each action. A comment saying “done” cannot stand in for either one.
Every interface uses the same commands and checks. A missing trace causes a refusal. A newer revision causes a conflict. A lost response calls for recovery of the original command's outcome. The developer's responsibility is to preserve those checks when adding a caller or domain. Concepts explains the record model and four outcomes.
Follow a command through the runtime
The target is one Rust runtime with one relational transactional store per instance, SQLite or PostgreSQL; the first vertical will prove PostgreSQL. The same runtime runs as its own service or inside Pale's process as a module. The engine supplies records, relations, definitions and operations. A domain uses the public SDK to define its business world. Accounts, work items and Radar records are domain definitions rather than built-in engine classes.
Identify the action. The interface binds the acting record, operation, subject and expected revisions. It carries the request to the application without deciding the business rule.
Check the decision. The application checks permission and the installed domain's rules. It protects every record, relationship and absence used by that decision through commit.
Commit and confirm. The store writes changes, history, commit receipt data and secret-free outbox in one transaction. Independent read-back confirms the named commit before the committing module creates a CommitReceipt.
Deliver later consequences. A dispatcher carries committed occurrences to consumers. Message delivery, outside effects and another party's acceptance each need their own result.
A chat card can show an accepted investigation while its own update is still pending. Read the acceptance in Weave and check the card update with the chat provider. A handler that writes directly to business tables would bypass the application's checks.
Dependencies point towards the core: shared record meaning in the core, deterministic mechanics in the kernel, use cases in the application and infrastructure implementations behind narrow ports. Domain logic cannot hide in an adapter or interface handler. Keeping the decision apart from the database and from outside calls makes it repeatable from known inputs, and lets a database or an interface change without changing what a decision means. A store port inverts dependencies without promising arbitrary database support. Repository instructions govern changes to these layers.
Universal identities, revisions, relations, commands, history, commit receipts and outbox entries use normalised tables. Domain fields use validated JSONB and declared indexes. This takes more explicit modelling than a table and handler per feature, but gives every caller the same rules and recoverable history.

Graphs, queries and search
Weave's records and relations form a typed, directed, temporal graph. GraphQL types derive from installed definitions. All interfaces lower reads into one private query form and one permission check, so a resolver cannot invent its own traversal, filtering or redaction rules.
Relations retain their identity
Parallel edges are independent facts with their own revisions. Symmetry comes from a relation's definition, not invented inverse facts. Each definition decides whether self-relations and structural cycles are allowed. Traversal remains bounded even when cycles are valid. A witnessed route is distinguishable from a direct edge; neither supplies permission merely by existing.
The canonical store retains stable identities and full temporal meaning. A bounded hot view may use dense generation-local handles, compact adjacency ranges and column-style indexes. A handle never crosses an interface, becomes a foreign key, carries permission or is serialised. A generation fence rejects a stale handle. Graph, operation and memory-pressure benchmarks must establish the physical layout: memory density affects whether this model is practical.
One private query form serves every interface
The internal form is typed and bounded; it is not a public query language. Its central job is to answer how records A and B are related under stated constraints. GraphQL provides rich reads, traversal, filtering, ordering, pagination and definition introspection. REST supplies narrow identity and history reads. SDK builders, domain clients, the CLI and agent protocols expose the queries they can represent faithfully. All use the same access, temporal, redaction and pagination rules and one execution plan, so no resolver owns any of that meaning itself.
A request chooses one route, a shortest qualifying route, several bounded routes or an explanatory subgraph. It declares permitted relation types and directions, deterministic relevance policy, validity time, snapshot, and depth, node, edge, cost and result limits. Limits also cover selected fields, fan-out, filter size, page and response sizes, history range and execution cost.
The result identifies exact revisions and applied constraints, whether it is complete or truncated, and unavailable, stale or denied portions where disclosure permits. Ordering is total and deterministic. A supported continuation binds the query, resolved definitions, snapshot, access frontier and last position; it supplies no permission. An expired snapshot requires a new query.
Compatible additive definition versions share a stable logical GraphQL type and member identities, with version-availability metadata. Incompatible changes get a new major type coordinate. Every result preserves its exact definition version. Missing for that version, absent, redacted, concealed, unknown, not requested and not applicable are distinct results, never one undifferentiated null.
Five times answer different questions
Keep effective validity, observation time, record revision, read snapshot and query execution time separate. A collection of revisions does not by itself prove one atomic snapshot. Claim “no path” only after exhaustively searching the declared view; a limit, filter or unavailable history is not absence. Current disclosure rules also apply to history. The store retains the history its supported queries require rather than promising a universal bitemporal database.
The operation-algebra cases include responsibility changing from a direct stewardship relation to a role, work serving a goal, blockers and evidence supporting a decision. A relation required by the question cannot be ranked or budgeted out of the answer.
Every read crosses a guard
In Weave's design the cost of read guards is real and cannot be bypassed. Because every object is public, private or protected (concepts), every read crosses a guard, and reads are where most of a burst lands, a burst being the sudden run of reads and writes a swarm of agents produces. So the dependency walk, the traversal of the graph for everything a read or write depends on, is the heart of the engineering, and the design, the stack and the implementation must solve it rather than route around it. Pale meets the same cost with its compiler: its runtime expects the declared world not to change while it is live, so the compiler walks the graph once and precomputes the decision indexes its runtime only looks up, moving the cost from run time to compile time. Weave's objects change constantly, and delegated access adds to the difficulty, so Weave has to place the cost deliberately.
Permission covers what a query reveals
Check permission before fetching or using a fact. The check covers selection, predicates, ordering, ranking, traversal, existence, counts, aggregation, export, disclosure and model use. A concealed fact must not change visible matches, ranking, page boundaries, path existence, counts or timing. The access model supplies the decision; checking only returned fields is insufficient.
Exploration, dependencies, notifications, reporting, context hydration for Pale use the same identities and graph mechanics with different traversal policies. Each organisation authors its room layout. Notification coverage is a bounded computation over the graph, with explicit fan-out, duplicate and cycle limits. A consequence cannot quietly change the inputs that produced it, and a publication-safe view cannot replace the full record a permitted reader needs.
The store supplies first-version search
Discovery uses exact identity and revision lookup, typed filters, bounded permitted traversal and lexical full-text search over fields declared searchable. Results have stable pagination and revision evidence. Each definition declares searchability, indexes and ranking inputs. A combined search vector must not cross fields with different use permissions.
Contextual or vector retrieval belongs to a separately selected Scope integration through Pale. Scope reads Weave through Weave's read port, still to be proposed by Scope's and Weave's builders, with Pale or without it, and without Pale it is how an agent reads Weave; Weave itself never calls Scope. Scope owns eligibility, freshness, exact, lexical and graph retrieval, permitted embeddings, fusion and use evidence for its own accepted projections. It is not a Weave search adapter. Weave owns no first-version embedding index. A future external search engine could only accelerate a rebuildable view and must recheck permission and read Weave back before consequential use.

A binding implementing compiler, permission, graph, runtime, reconciliation or effect logic is not thin and falls under the AGPL.
The test is that a thin binding computes no Weave fact. Everything it shows its caller is a field the server returned, a fact about the client's own input and output (these bytes were sent, no reply arrived) or a fixed instruction the published contract declares, so two conforming clients given the same server bytes and the same input and output history show the same outcome and next step. Saving a request and its key before sending, reporting a lost reply as the client's own value, calling the lookup by identity and following the server's recovery instruction are thin. Computing the replay digest, deciding from record fields that a command committed, treating a missing lookup as safe to resend, choosing per route whether a resend is allowed, working out which commands to offer, or embedding the engine are not.
An adopter's own systems, private configuration and data remain theirs. Alternative terms require a separate agreement with RawThoughts Enterprises Private Limited. NOTICE records the scope and shared-check origin.

Radar records
Radar is the family of records through which an observation becomes a reviewed finding or a proposed direction, and through which the organisation keeps what followed. A Radar run starts by command, by a schedule coming due or by a declared reaction to a committed occurrence, the same three ways as any transition. A Radar run proposes a direction or a finding; the record connects that proposal with its observation, evidence, candidate interpretation, review, disposition, follow-up and outcome. These are revisioned domain records with their own sources and relationships. A Radar record is neither a task nor a sales opportunity. The family uses fresh native data; it selects no historical import, research schedule or successor writer. The family hard-codes no research area, department or review topology; an organisation's areas of interest, owners and thresholds are its own configuration.
A finding cannot accept itself
The writer proposing a finding or a direction cannot move it into accepted state. Review requires the permitted decision-maker, criteria, evidence and policy version, protected by ordinary read and revision checks. A ruling identifies exactly which findings it accepts, rejects, splits, defers or leaves alone. A scheduled result, review reply or planning note is not a ruling. Corrections supersede an earlier ruling rather than rewriting what happened, subject to retention and erasure rules.
A completed run that finds no material change is still a result. Completed means every required check closed and the evidence stayed below the policy's materiality threshold. It records what was checked, the strongest counter-case and what to examine next, so later research can build on it. Missing required evidence instead produces a blocked result: it cannot be presented as a completed search that found nothing. An owner's decision to leave things unchanged is a third, separate event.
An optional Pale integration may coordinate investigation and obtain context, judgment or evaluation from separately selected services. Pale keeps no second Radar store. Context is not an accepted finding; coordinating an operation is not an outside effect, verified outcome or accepted publication. An approved draft, an orchestration operation and a publication release retain separate identities and owners.
A disposition does not perform the follow-up
A disposition requesting action names the owner permitted to act. That owner independently accepts and commits its work; the Radar record keeps the reference and the later verified outcome. A finding becomes work only when someone takes responsibility for acting on it, with an owner and an acceptance condition; whether that happens depends on the journey that brought the finding in and on the rules the organisation's configuration or the domain sets. No observation, finding or ruling automatically creates work or publication. Direct work creation without a Radar record remains valid.
A possible authorisation-intake operation remains a proposal. It would bind one exact authorisation reference and apply normal work-creation checks: scope, parent, kind of work, assignment permission, budget and expected revision. It would need duplicate detection, commit and read-back, replay, partial-failure and recovery cases. Disabling it must create no duplicate or synthetic work. A Radar record marked applied or assigned would still not be a work item.
A direction can be tried before anyone decides
A proposal can be a direction as well as a finding: a change the organisation might make, not only an observation about the world. Before the permitted decision-maker rules on it, a proposed direction can be tried by a simulation, such as a projection of what it does to an owner's accounts or a rehearsal of how an audience might react. Weave never runs a simulation. The tool that owns such runs keeps them; the proposal references each run as evidence, with the run's identity, owner, observation date and limits, exactly as borrowed evidence keeps its original reference. A referenced run informs the ruling and is not the ruling, and the decision it informs, whether to spend, publish or change something, belongs to the owner the disposition names.
Once the direction has been acted on and its result is known, the outcome is recorded beside what the proposal expected. Keeping the two together is what makes the record material for later evaluation: a later reader, or an evaluation service reached through Pale, can compare expectation with outcome without reconstructing either. Weave keeps that comparison available, draws no conclusion from it and changes no rule on its own.
Failure preserves what was actually established
Evidence already gathered can survive a blocked run. When a required source revision or selector is unavailable, or changes during the run without being reconciled, preserve the evidence and label staged inference provisional. Record the missing prerequisite and next safe step; emit no current candidate or handoff from an unresolved run. A change outside the declared dependencies need not invalidate a verified snapshot.
A ruling, its application by the owner and a derived reader view have separate outcomes. Failed validation leaves the prior owner state in place and records the failed attempt. If a view fails after the owner commits, the commit stands and the view reports stale or unavailable state. Read each outcome back separately, and record which of the owner's commit and each view succeeded and which needs repair.
Compensation is a separately permitted transaction with its own result. A state-changing retry needs current permission and preconditions and references the earlier attempt. Exact replay returns the original result without another change. Downstream effects still require the destination's own commit and read-back.
Borrowed evidence does not transfer a conclusion
An exchange can offer a research dimension without supplying the recipient's decision. The recipient can reject it or find no material change without changing the source owner's conclusion. Any implemented exchange needs its own contract and independently owned acceptance.
When a review uses evaluation results, retain each original reference and its limits. A comparison across evaluator versions is a separate object. A ruling can rely on its conclusion only once the comparison matches the review question and has been accepted for current use. A repeated score label cannot establish comparability after rubric or case coverage changes.
A future import or writer replacement needs its own proof
Ordinary record imports must not quietly introduce research inboxes, ruling logs, run registers, candidate ledgers or ruling receipts as a new governance system. A separately authorised historical import or writer replacement must preserve meanings and dispositions, identify the replaced writer, exclude parallel writers, handle duplicates and the final delta, and prove independent read-back, recovery and rollback. This does not require reproducing old identifiers or operating machinery. An interface, plugin or generated view cannot silently become a writer or redirect historical results.
The planned Radar tests exercise blocked runs, no-change results, failed application, compensation, retry and downstream effects through this domain.

Commands, storage and recovery
One relational database, SQLite or PostgreSQL, owns an instance's records, history, command results and outbox. Every change uses the same guarded command path. If a caller loses the reply, it asks what happened to that exact command before attempting another change. Concepts defines the four outcomes every interface must preserve.
One store owns the durable state
The adopter chooses SQLite or PostgreSQL and supplies the connection; the first vertical will prove PostgreSQL. A store port keeps the application independent of database details; it is not a promise that arbitrary databases can preserve Weave's rules, and each supported database must pass the store's cases below. There is no separate canonical graph, event, history or business store. The kernel answers graph questions over the relational store, and a graph database such as Memgraph enters only if engineering strictly requires it, as a rebuildable view rather than a second home for records. If Twenty is selected as a client or host, it supplies neither Weave's runtime nor the store, and no decision reads a value people can edit there.
Stable identities, definition bindings, record and relation revisions, commands, occurrences, commit receipts and outbox entries use normalised tables. Definition-declared fields use validated JSON, JSONB on PostgreSQL, with declared generated or expression indexes where qualified. This is neither an entity-attribute-value model nor one table per domain.
Object storage, cache, wake notifications, queues, search, clocks, identity, secrets and observability have narrow ports. A cache, queue, index or bounded snapshot can be rebuilt from its owner; it never owns records, history, receipts, permission or causal truth. Such a component may make Weave faster; it may not make Weave's answers depend on it. Redis and BullMQ remain unselected. If introduced, they may supply cache, wake or queue functions, never a second scheduler, command store or causal ledger. Repairing a derived view leaves the authoritative revisions, command result and occurrence intact.
Every caller uses one write path

    B --> C[Domain guards and protected read set]
